Summary of Proceedings:
In March 1919, Bartholomeo Massulo petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Massulo was a subject of Italy and was initially arrested in 1917 by an Immigration Inspector charging Massulo with being an illegal alien and having advocated or taught anarchy and the overthrow of the government. Massulo was released upon depositing bail in the sum of $2,500 but was arrested later in 1919 by respondent Henry M. White, and the secretary of labor issued an order of deportation. 
The petition alleged there was no evidence to sustain said charges, and stated Massulo demanded a copy of said evidence but was denied by the respondent. Judge Neterer denied the writ, and in a stipulation, both the petitioner and government agreed the record of proceedings before the Immigration authorities and the testimony adduced would be withdrawn from the records and files of the court. 
One month later in April, 1919, the peititioner and his attorney filed an assignment of error stating the warrant of deportation was void, there was no evidence to sustain such charges, and the court erred in denying the writ of habeas corpus. The judge allowed the appeal to the Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, however the outcome and the fate of Massulo is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 23rd 1919, Taka Shibata, the petitioner, arrived in Washington as a Japanese immigrant where she met her new husband (traveling from Nebraska), Kunikichi Shibata, who the petitioner had married whilst in Japan through the "picture-bride" system. On January 5th, 1920, the petitioner was duly allowed to enter the United States and was found not likely to become a public charge due to the support of her husband. Shortly after entering the United States, it is reported that there was marital problems which prompted the petitioner to leave her new husband and live with her brother who also resided in Washington. Afterwards, a report is made, presumably by the former husband, which leads to the arrest of the petitioner charging her with being likely to become a public charge upon entry and admission to the country under false pretenses. The false pretense charge is then later dropped. On July 12th, 1920, a writ of Habeas Corpus is filed alleging that the government could not rule the marriage invalid. On July 17th, 1920, the Assistant U.S. Secretary of Labor, Louis F. Post, formally issued the order for deportation. A memorandum of points and authorities was then submitted by the attorneys for the petitioner stating among other things that the board which authorized her deportation did not properly consider the petitioner's witnesses or testimony, there was no proof that the petitioner did not marry in good faith, and that regardless of the other points that the charge of being likely to become a public charge is without evidence. The government alleged that there is no proof that the marriage is valid and thus cannot be recognized by presumption by the court. The attorneys for the petitioner saw the marriage passport and admittance into the country under the assumption of marriage as enough to constitute the validity of the marriage in the eyes of the governments of Japan and the United States. On July 14th, 1920, Judge Redkin granted the petitioner leave on bail. In August of 1920, Judge Redkin ordered the deportation stopped and the petitioner discharged. The judge made interesting citations to non-specific principles about the universal laws of marriage.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 21, 1912, Nick Mordevich filed for habeas against U.S. Marshal Joseph Jacoby. Mordevich was arrested following an incident where he was found fishing along Hales' Passage near the Lummi Reservation between April 1 and April 16, 1912. In his petition, Mordevich claims that Hales' passage does not fall within the Lummi Reservation, but under the state of Washington, thus not violating boundaries. The writ was denied on April 30, 1912, and Mordevich was ordered to remain in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Redden Jones, the petitioner, was accused of the crime of larceny in Iowa for the theft of ten dollars during his employment under Maloney & O'Brien who employed him as a clerk and servant. Judge George W. Doane of Douglas County ruled that Jones had been illegally detained as a fugitive from justice and he was discharged on the 10th of May 1890. Whether Jones was extradited to Iowa for his alleged crime is unknown, but presumably, he was not.

Summary of Proceedings: Andrew Anderson was arrested by Hudson, a policeman of Spokane, Washington, from the order of the sheriff of Spokane, charging Anderson with being a fugitive from justice of the state of Washington. He was imprisoned without any complaint for said offense or warrant being issued from Omaha. He made a petition that alleged he was unlawfully deprived for vagrancy charges and it was found that the vagrancy charges were not issued in good faith but were made to subterfuge to aid the requisition from Washington. He was released and then arrested again in the corridor of the court house upon a complaint ordered by the judge of the omaha police court with having opposed and resisted a police officer in May. The judge, Scott, decided that Anderson was unlawfully deprived of his liberty.

Summary of Proceedings: On the morning of June 18, 1898, a Douglas County District Court judge discharged three Chinese teenagers from the custody of Lem You, an employee of a corporation responsible for developing a Chinese Village for that year's Trans-Mississippi and International Exhibition. The same day, a team consisting of U.S. district attorney, Andrew Sawyer, and lawyers representing the Mee Lee Wah Village Company petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court with the aim of re-establishing Company custody over the teenagers. The girls' names were disputed: state habeas proceedings referred to them as Lun Teu, Lun Kim, and Lun Yuk, whereas federal habeas proceedings, which established that these were the same individuals, referred to them as Chin Tu Ling, Lee Shun, and Look Fung. State Judge Cunningham Scott had ordered the three girls to be placed in county jail while Dr. Lydia J. Wyckoff, a missionary advocating their return to China, raised funds for their deportation. Sawyer and the Mee Lee Wah Village Company argued that the trio owed a contractual obligation to the corporation under federal law and that they could not be returned to China until after the the close of the Trans-Mississippi and International Exhibition. The girls were released from jail and placed in the temporary custody of the U.S. marshals while the court considered their case. After hearing the evidence, Federal Judge William Munger turned the girls over to the Mee Lee Wah Village Company so that they could complete their contracts.

Summary of Proceedings: Rudolph H. Gerber petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his daughter, Anael. Gerber claimed that Anael was illegally taken from San Francisco, CA to King County, WA by her mother, Dorothy Alden Gerber, despite Rudolph Gerber being the legally appointed guardian of Anael. Dorothy Gerber responded that Anael was not being held against her will and is, in fact, a resident of King County. She stipulated that Rudolph Gerber is unfit to care for Anael and that she is now in school under the care of Dorothy Gerber. Rudolph Gerber denied these claims. The writ was dismissed, and a subsequent petition for writ of habeas corpus reveals that Dorothy Gerber gained custody of Anael.

Summary of Proceedings: Bertha Faust moved from Ashland to Omaha because her family went into debt. Because she was the oldest, her parents let her move to Omaha ten months before her arrest happened. She got a job as a domestic worker at the Grand Hotel in Council Bluffs and then got sick and went to Omaha. She rented a room at the Co-operative Hotel and obtained employment in a restaurant near 16th and Webster Streets. Three police officers came to her room at 3 AM and arrested her without a warrant; where they then incarcerated her and charged her with being a prostitute. She showed that she was not a prostitute or an unvirtuous girl, but she was charged with being an inmate of a disorderly house and of a house of assignation and assessed a fine, which she couldn’t pay. Therefore, she petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, granted, but the judge ruled that she was not illegally restrained and had to remain in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 14, 1898, David McFoy filed for a freedom suit to avoid being enslaved by William Brown. Within the suit it was specified he was to be held by the sheriff of St. Louis county until the case was decided. William Brown claimed that he was the rightful owner of David McFoy, granted to him by his father, Thomas Brown’s, last will and testament, and so William filed for a writ of habeas to see David released from the county jail and entrusted to him. David denied being William’s property, claiming that he was instead a free man, born to a free family. Both William and David brought forward numerous witnesses that supported their version of events, saying either that David was a free man born to free parents in Pennsylvania, or that he was born a slave to the Brown family in Virginia. On December 20, 1849, Judge Johnstone ruled that there was sufficient evidence to conclude that David belonged to William, but that was evidently not the last word in the case as documentation of the arguments and witnesses continued through May of 1851. The final set of documents come from David McFoy’s attorney’s moving to suppress the depositions taken by William Brown, but the final result of William’s petition and McFoy’s freedom is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Nishikawa Mamoru arrived to the U.S. by a steamer on October 9, 1918. He was committed to the Providence Hospital a day later. Nishikawa left the hospital and did not return to ship knowing that he didn't have a passport to allow him to enter or remain in the United States. He had remained in the United States since and was taken into custody on November 3, 1921, where Acting Immigration Commissioner Lynch ordered him deported. 
Nishikawa petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and claimed his imprisonment was unlawful. The writ was denied and Nishikawa was returned to the custody of Lynch to be deported.

Summary of Proceedings: In November 1923, James E. Washington filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully imprisoned and deprived of his liberty by Michael L. Endres, the Sheriff of Douglas County. Washington was imprisoned on the charge of vagrancy and sentenced to 60 days in County Jail. The petition alleged the prosecuting attorney "shifted the pretend charge of theft and prosecuted this petitioner for vagrancy." The petition further alleged the trial was without legal procedure as upon the word of a single officer who testified against Washington, the Judge found him guilty. Judge Charles A. Goss authorized the petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus. At trial, the application was denied, and Washington remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
The petition filed on 16 December 1898 states that the petitioners, Scott and McGregor, were unlawfully restrained by Sheriff McDonald. It had been alleged that the petitioners committed an assault with intent to wound (stabbing) two individuals (referenced as Jordon and Miller). The case file indicates that the two were granted a preliminary hearing and were bound to appear before the District Court. But, as the petition details, there are no actual records of this trial happening. There is no documentation of the two appearing in court, entering pleas, or being sentenced by a trial court. 

The two were originally brought to court on this charge and a charge for assault with intent to rob in June 1898. When those charges were brought to court, the Jury found the defendants not guilty. They had been confined in the county jail since that arrest despite the jury's conclusion. This petition asserts that the charge at hand (assault with intent to wound) was included in the questions assigned to the Jury in June. The Jury also found the petitioners not guilty on a general question of assault and battery. 

On 26 November 1898, Police Judge Gordon issued two separate orders to Sheriff McDonald to secure McGregor and Scott into the County Jail and keep them until they are “discharged by due course of law.” He notes that they were being held for trial in the District Court for the crime of stabbing with intent to wound on 25 June 1898. Each of their bail was set for $700.00; they were to remain in jail unless bail was posted. The petition submitted on behalf of Scott and McGregor states that the petitioners were last “arrested” around a month ago, which lines up with the date that Police Judge Gordon ordered that McDonald and Scott be held in jail until their trial before the District Court. 

On 16 December 1898, Judge Scott (District Court) ordered that the writ be allowed. Sheriff McDonald and Deputy Sheriff Stryker responded that the parties were being held for trial before the District Court, as ordered by Police Judge Gordon. Judge Scott heard the case on 19 December 1898 and decided that the parties would be remanded to custody, at the cost of the petitioners.

Summary of Proceedings: John Burke petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid. Burke alleged that he was being held illegally at Spokane County Jail under the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. He claimed he was denied a hearing for six months and denied his right to counsel. The court’s judgement stated that it appeared Burke had been discharged for unknown reasons, and thus his writ was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: On the 6th of January Jim Stevens was charged by the Police Magestrate with drunkenness and possession of liquor. He was given an $100 fine. Jim Stevens filed a habeas corpus petition on Janurary 21st 1919, in which he argued that there was not physical evidence against him nor a complaint. The petition was approved, but after the hearing the writ was denied. On Februray 27th, 1919 Jim Stevens was ordered to pay his fine and remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Adolph Guldahl, a Norwegian immigrant, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid. Guldahl alleged that he was being held illegally at Spokane County Jail under the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. He claimed he was denied a hearing and denied his right to counsel, and alleged that Richardson and Reid had no evidence proving Guldahl was guilty of such charges laid against him. Judge Frank H. Rudkin ruled that a valid warrant of arrest was issued against Guldahl under the Immigration Act of 1918. Thus, Rudkin dismissed the writ and ordered Guldahl continue to be held for deportation. Guldahl would file a second petition for habeas corpus soon after the dismissal of this one.

Summary of Proceedings: John Duffy was taken into custody by Sullivan, the chief of detectives for the Northern Pacific Railroad Company, and J.H. O'Brien, the conductor of a freight and passenger train for Northern Pacific. He had apparently attempted to break into a sealed railroad car in Montana. On October 16, 1886, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he was being unlawfully detained without being charged with a crime. He said that the men holding him didn't let him contact his friends and wanted to send him back to Montana. The writ was allowed, but the fate of John Duffy remains unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 19, 1899, Howell Morgan, who claimed to have been appointed acting U.S. Indian Agent for the Omaha and Winnebago Reservations that same day, jailed a Winnebago man named Henry Holt for assaulting him. Holt soon complained to the sheriff of Thurston County, Nebraska, that Morgan had jailed him without legal authority. Consequently, Morgan was charged in state court with falsely imprisoning Holt and jailed after his refusal or inability to pay a $500 bond. Morgan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus through U.S. attorney for the district of Nebraska, W. S. Summers, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Morgan was released from custody. However, Nebraska officials appealed this decision, and it seems that Morgan was then ordered to pay a $1,000 recognizance. His ultimate fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 9th, 1921, John Tenozar was indicted on charges of breaking and entering with the intent to steal goods and chattels. A capias warrant was issued and John was arrested. He plead guilty before Judge L. B. Day and was sentenced to two years parole. Then on January 27th, 1923, the County Attorney of Douglas County filed an information in said cause, and charged John with violating the terms of his parole. On February 6th, a hearing was held regarding this charge and Judge L. B. Day revoked parole and sentenced John to no less than 8 but no more than 10 years in the state penitentiary. On August 19th, 1923, John filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on the claims that his parole was wrongfully granted because the crime he was charged under was not a parolable offense and that the judge did not attach any provisions that he could have violated. Petition was granted. On August 29th, Sheriff Michael Endres responded to the petition. He denied all of the claims of John and affirmed that he was operating under the instruction of Judge L. B. Day. On September 4th, 1923, John and his lawyer motioned for a new trial for the following reasons: 1) the sentence was not in compliance with the law 2) the revocation of parole was not in compliance with the law 3) the court had no authority to grant parole and 4) the time for passing sentence had elapsed. On January 21st, 1924, the writ was dismissed for want of prosecution. The fate of John Tenozar is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: George Taylor said that Raymond Taylor, his five year old son, was taken from his house in April by his ex-wife and Raymond’s mother, Gertie Taylor. Gertie had sued him for divorce in September of 1903, accusing him of "cruel and inhuman treatment," such as when he threatened to shoot her. George alleged that Gertie took him while he was away at work and that she refused to let him talk to or see their child. However, George had already kidnapped the child once, according to the Omaha Daily Bee. He also alleged that Gertie told several people that this was her plan and that she even told George the afternoon when it happened that she was going to leave immediately with their child for Colorado. While the case was in session, Raymond Taylor was given to Mrs. Grace Ingram to care for. On May 29, 1903, there was an order issued, giving the custody of Raymond to Gertie Taylor and George was allowed to visit. Then on June 1, there was a motion for a new trial where the fate of Raymond Taylor is unknown. However, on July 11, 1903, George was accused with kidnapping his son, as he claimed that Gertie was not properly taking care of the boy.

Summary of Proceedings:
Cornelius O'Keefe alleged that on August 18, 1895, John McKinnon stole four meat cattle from him. O'Keefe filed a complaint against McKinnon on August 24 in the County of Yale, British Columbia. McKinnon was arrested that same day, after being found with hides that bore a brand that belonged to Mr. O'Keefe. 
On December 22, 1896, E.C. Simmons filed another complaint against McKinnon alleging that he committed the aforementioned crime. Arthur H. Kenyon, commissioner of the circuit court of the United States for the District of Washington, issued a warrant for McKinnon's extradition and arrest to face charges for larceny. McKinnon appeared before Kenyon on December 23, and his attorneys alleged that the warrant did not state sufficient facts to constitute a crime, and that Kenyon had no right to authorize McKinnon's extradition, nor to issue a warrant for his arrest due to a treaty between the United States and Great Britain. 
McKinnon's claims were overruled, and he filed a writ of habeas corpus on January 4, 1897. The petition alleged that he was restrained of his liberty in the county jail of Spokane, Washington. The writ was dismissed on December 7, 1911, because McKinnon failed to proceed in the prosecution of the case for more than one year.

In the petition, Baldwin argued that Wilson was being held on a complaint made in Idaho under an offense which he was not in Idaho during, was arrested without warrant, and has been a resident of Nebraska for more than two years. A writ was issued, but the case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924; the fate of Wilson is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 3, 1891, Fong Ling filed for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that she was unlawfully detained by the Steamship Mongkut Captain George Anderson. Anderson claimed that he detained Fong Ling because the Collector of the Port of Portland R.P. Earhart ordered her detention. Anderson believed that Fong Ling was not a native born citizen of the United States and that she was prevented from entering the United States because he argued that she was actually a subject of the Emperor of China. Judge Matthew Deady disagreed with Collector Earhart and granted Fong Ling her writ and ordered her to be released.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 18, 1920 Vito Cheala was arrested in Omaha on charges of suspicious character, with no complaint filed against him and no trial or hearing to follow. As a result, Frank Palo filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on Cheala's behalf. The respondents alleged that on October 30, 1919, the grand jury found Joe Klieeg, also known as Vito Cheala and Willie Kali, guilty on the felony charge of stealing an automobile and receiving a stolen automobile and a warrant was issued for his arrest on June 4, 1920. The respondents alleged that they arrested Cheala on June 18 with the intent to deliver him to the Douglas County sheriff due to this warrant. The court found that Cheala was not unlawfully detained and ordered him to be recommitted to the custody of the respondents.

Summary of Proceedings: In May 1869, defendant Eugene Crowne was accused by Frank Vetter of committing adultery and fornication with his wife, Lina Vetter. The defendant was committed to jail by Sheriff James McAuliff, and bail was held in the sum of $1000 to secure his appearance at the October term of the district court. In August, Crowne and his attorney Frank P. Dugan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. They claimed that Crowne had violated no law of the Territory of Washington and the cause of his restraint was illegal. An undated document stated Crowne was ordered to be discharged and his bond released. Frank Vetter, in the same month, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus for custody of his child whom he had with Lena, Susannah Vetter, after it was discovered that Lena and Eugene were headed to Oregon with Susannah and their other child Minnie (See "In the Matter of the Application of F. Vetter for a Writ of Habeas Corups).

Summary of Proceedings: William Lemke petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his nine-year-old son, Paul Lemke, from the custody of Anna Guthmann, which was granted. The 1920 U.S. federal census indicates that William was a widower and that Paul was Anna's great-nephew (presumably, Anna was the aunt of William's late wife and Paul's late mother). After hearing the evidence, the district court awarded custody of Paul to his father. Anna successfully appealed the case to the state supreme court, which overturned the ruling of the district court and returned Paul to the custody of his great-aunt.

Summary of Proceedings:
M. L. Coovert petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus after being arrested and found guilty of violating a local Washington statute prohibiting the sale of cigarettes. The petition alleged the statue was invalid as it abridged the privileges and immunities of citizens and prohibited and regulated commerce. Circuit judge C. H. Hanford found the facts and circumstances of Coovert's conduct were not sufficient to justify imprisonment and found the Washington statute prohibiting the sale of cigarettes to be in contravention of Article I, Section 8 of the United States Constitution. Coovert was released from custody and the statute was declared null and void, reversing the Washington Superior Court decision. The State of Washington appealed the decision to the United States Supreme Court, which reversed the circuit decision and remanded the case back to circuit court with direction to discharge the writ and dismiss Coovert's petition. M. L. Coovert's fate is unknown. 

As a note, the case file is very long (~400 pages), but this is primarily because they charged Coovert separately for each individual cigarette, so there are a lot of nearly identical filings.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 4th, 1923, Hattie Barnica filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her 11 year old daughter Katherine Hauser. Hattie named Katherine's grand-parents, Ira and Katie Hauser, as respondents. Katherine's biological father, Page Hauser, died in 1918. Hattie explained in the petition that she had sent Katherine to live with Ira and Katie for the duration of the school year (Sept. 1922 - May 1923). At the time of filing the petition, the agreed-upon period of temporary custody had lapsed but Ira and Katie refused to return Katherine. In a return to the petition, Ira and Katie alleged that they were entitled to custody of Katherine. They alleged that Hattie sent Katherine to live with them because she could not provide for Katherine. They also accused Hattie's husband, Albert Barnica, of being abusive and addicted to alcohol. They claimed that Katherine's treatment was so bad that when she came to live with them she was suffering from nervousness and was very sickly. Upon examination by a doctor, they found that she was emaciated, malnourished, anemic, and her teeth were decaying. They alleged that Katherine had faced this neglect and abuse ever since Hattie and Albert had a child of their own. They also alleged that Albert had been found guilty of crimes in Nebraska. Additionally, they stated that when older men would come over, Katherine would be forced to sleep in the same bed as them in a room separate from her parents. Ira and Katie asserted that Katherine did not want to and was afraid to return home to her parents, but that they had the ability and desire to care for Katherine. On June 21st, Hattie replied and denied all allegations against herself and her husband, and assured the court that Albert was of good character. Hattie claimed that Katherine had always been well cared for and that she cared for her family, and that if she was saying or feeling differently it was because of the influence of Ira and Katie. On July 5th, the judge of the County Court allowed the writ and ordered that Katherine be released to Hattie. They found Hattie to be a suitable parent and that the allegations against Albert were false. On the same day as the order, Ira and Katie filed an application for an order fixing a bond of $1000 and signaled their intent to appeal. The judge granted custody of Katherine to Ira and Katie until the expiration for the time of appeal. On December 22nd, the District Court judge agreed with the findings of the lower court and demanded the release of Katherine into Hattie's custody. Ira and Katie filed a motion for a new trial but it was overruled.

Summary of Proceedings: In early 1912, Frank Foster and Edwin Jurgens were convicted of assault and robbery with a dangerous weapon in Douglas County, Oregon, and committed to the Oregon State Penitentiary in Salem. Homer Rutherford, whose relationship to Foster is unclear, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on Foster's behalf, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Foster was remanded to the custody of the penitentiary superintendent. After this decision, Foster appealed to the Oregon Supreme Court, but not before motioning the Marion County Circuit Court to remove Rutherford as a petitioner on the case retroactively. This appears to have been done so that Foster, as the sole petitioner, could claim poverty as a reason for not paying some of his court fees. The circuit court granted the motion. While the state supreme court records are not included in the circuit court case file, published reports indicate that the upper court upheld the decision of the lower court.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 1, 1906, Lorimer Ells petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his nine-month-old daughter, Theo Virginia Ells. In the petition, Lorimer stated that his unnamed wife had died at some (unspecified) time after giving birth to Theo. The cause of her death is not stated in the case file. Theo was being held by her grandparents, Martin and Thena Prescott, who Lorimer claimed did not have legal custody over Theo. Judge Morris ruled in favor of Lorimer, and Theo was returned to her father. Martin and Thena were given the right to visit her whenever they wanted, and Lorimer was ordered to pay them twenty dollars for the care they had given her.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 13, 1898 John McCheyn was informed by the prosecuting attorney of King County that he was being charged with the first-degree murder of Edward R. Reese on April 16, 1898 in Wellington, Washington. McCheyn’s lawyer argues that McCheyn was never granted a preliminary hearing and “That upon a reading of said evidence appertaining to said homicide it conclusively appearts that your petitioner was not guilty of any crime whatsoever but was wholly and entirely justified for his actions in the premises and that no crime has been committed.” Newspaper coverage of the murder notes that Edward Reese was in a “drunken rage” when John McCheyn shot him. Upon receiving McCheyn’s writ of habeas corpus, Judge Orange Jacobs approved the writ and ordered his release from custody. Jacobs argues that the evidence of the case shows that McCheyn acted in self-defense and agreed that no crime had been committed. Newspaper coverage of the trial notes that this case is without precedent and questioned if Judge Jacobs had the authority to consider the evidence of the case. After Jacobs ordered McCheyn to be removed from custody, the prosecuting attorney for King County, James F. McElroy dropped the charge of murder against McCheyn.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 15, a complaint was made against Mary Doe alias Sloan for obtaining money under false pretenses. Oddly enough, her husband, John Sloan was the one brought into police court the next day. The proceedings against him are mysterious, as Sloan couldn't explain them to his attorney, J. Gerald MacVeigh. Nevertheless, Joseph was committed to the Douglas county jail on December 29, 1923. Shortly after, on New Year's Eve, 1923, MacVeigh filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus demanding that the Douglas county sheriff, M.L. Endres, produce Joseph in court before judge Charles A. Goss. The case was dismissed on the motion of the applicant on the same day.

Summary of Proceedings: Federal Prohibition Agent Homer D. Banner went to the Evers family residence on multiple occasions and purchased alcohol. On June 4, 1924, Richard L. Farrand, Deputy U.S. Marshal, searched the Evers residence after receiving a warrant from U.S. Commissioner Edwin Boehler and found alcohol at the residence. The petitioner, Emma Evers, was convicted by Nebraska’s U.S. District Court for unlawful sale and possession of intoxicating liquor under violation of the National Prohibition Law. Judge John F. McGee sentenced her to six months in Douglas County Jail and ordered her to pay a $500 fine. On Dec. 13, 1924, she filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that she was entitled to a shortened sentence for good conduct, as outlined under the Eighth Federal Statute, and that her sentence had expired at noon the previous day. She also argued that the fine was void because it exceeded the maximum penalty prescribed by the statute for both counts. Her petition and writ were allowed, and she was discharged from police custody on December 16, 1924.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 14, 1919, Elizabeth Kreishutz petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus for her husband, Frank Kreishutz. She contended that the superintendent of the State Hospital for the Insane, J. D. Case, unlawfully deprived her husband of his liberty. She did not know the superintendent’s real name when writing this petition. She argued that the superintendent claimed to be holding Frank Kreishutz because of a commitment. However, Elizabeth Kreishutz could not find a copy of such commitment or any process to mandate the superintendent to hold and keep Frank, so he was being held unlawfully. The judge accepted the petition and filed a writ of habeas corpus, which the superintendent responded to. However, the outcome of this proceeding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Willam Fay Ealy filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 22, 1919, claiming he was held without a warrant or charge. 

According to newspaper coverage, William Fay Ealy, a twenty-two year-old painter, allegedly murdered Elizabeth Bryan on October 21, 1919. Formal charges were filed against both Ealy and his mother, Anna B. Nemitz, for first-degree murder in the same week that they each applied for habeas corpus. The case was widely reported on in contemporary newspapers.

This case file contains documents from the habeas corpus petition of Ealy’s mother, Anna B. Nemitz.

Summary of Proceedings: In September 1916, Frances Murphy accused Chase Snyder of bastardy in an Omaha justice court. Snyder could not or would not pay a $900 bond and was placed in the Douglas County jail to await trial. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing among other things that he had informed on Murphy to the U.S. Department of Justice and that the bastardy accusation was her making good on a promise to seek revenge. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and Snyder remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 9th, 1913, C. J. Vollmer and I. Groskins, along with their attorney, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. In the petition, they alleged that they were being held without a proper warrant or charge. They also claimed that J. Z. Benson, sheriff of Grand Forks, North Dakota, and O. B. Burtness, prosecuting attorney of Grand Forks, North Dakota, had intimidated Vollmer and Groskins into giving them diamonds. Benson had apparently tracked them down to Washington in order to bring them back to North Dakota. Vollmer and Groskins stated the whole situation was a ploy by Benson and Burtness to get money and merchandise from them. Another man, D. I. McKee, had allegedly been arrested on the same charge and released based on a finding that his imprisonment was unlawful. The outcome of this case and the fate of Vollmer and Groskins are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Carston Hans Sieck, a German-born resident of Nebraska, was arrested in Millard, Nebraska on April 16, 1918, after making threats, using abusive language, and carrying and shooting off multiple revolvers outside a Soda Shop. Sieck was evaluated for insanity on April 17th and ordered to be detained in the Nebraska State Hospital for the Insane on April 18th. Sieck’s wife, Anna C. Sieck filed for Habeas on behalf of her husband May 7th. A writ of Habeas was allowed, and after several continuances and witness testimony, Carston Sieck was found to be sane by a jury and ordered to be discharged on June 15th, 1918.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 7th, 1871, a writ of habeas corpus was filed by Charles and Martha J. Gahres on behalf of Martha's daughter, Etty Dora Cravens. At the time, Etty was in the custody of Isabella Barrett and W. H. Barrett. The Barretts claimed that they had had custody of Etty for the past three years, had spent a significant amount of money taking care of her because she had been sickly, and that Martha had no home and could not provide for Etty. On June 27th, 1871, Judge Kennedy awarded custody of Etty to the Barretts. On August 30th, 1873, the Gahres brought the same writ of habeas corpus to court again. On September 2nd, 1873, Judge Lewis dismissed the writ and awarded custody of Etty to the Barretts.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 20, 1914, Herbert Wolff and his lawyers Robert Welch and Dore filed for a writ of habeas corpus. They claimed Sheriff Edward Cudihee and his agent John W. Roberts arrested Wolff without a warrant or process of law. Judge A. W. Frater allowed the petition.  Roberts claimed Wolff, along with Harry Brewer, robbed August Reets, stealing $235 from him. Brewer also filed a petition of habeas corpus (see “Habeas Corpus of Harry Brewer against Edward Cudihee (Sheriff)”). Newspapers indicated that Wolff and Brewer drugged and beat Reets before robbing him. Roberts produced a warrant for Brewer's arrest that was dated May 21, 1914, the day after the petition was filed. The outcome of the petition and Brewer’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Raleigh M. Faulkner was sentenced to three years in prison for possessing a "Confederate" banknote with the intent to defraud, he began serving his term on June 11th, 1912. Faulkner filed a writ of habeas corpus on October 21st, 1914, claiming he was being restrained of his liberty by the warden of McNeil Island Penitentiary, O. P. Halligan. Faulkner cited an Act of Congress and argued that he should have been earning sentence deduction through good behavior. On November 9th, 1914, Judge Cushman dismissed the writ and ordered Faulkner to remain in the custody of Halligan at McNeil Island Penitentiary.

Summary of Proceedings: Juan Rey Abeita, who self identified as a US Citizen and Pueblo Indian, petitioned on behalf of his three sons against Albuquerque Indian School Superintendent William B. Creager, whom Abeita claimed had refused to allow his sons to return home. The writ was granted but there is no record of the hearing and Abeita withdrew the petition a month later. Additional references in the Office of Indian Affairs and local newspapers indicate that the Office of Indian Affairs pressured Creager to release the children to avoid an unfavorable legal ruling.

Summary of Proceedings: Coong Shueng petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Louie Chung, who was being detained aboard the Steamship Danube. The Collector of Customs believed him to be a Chinese laborer rather than a merchant and therefore not allowed into the United States by the Chinese Exclusion Act. The case file includes the trial transcript, which presented several witnesses, including his business partner and two white individuals who work in or around “Chinatown” to testify that the individual was a merchant and partner in the tailoring show Wah Hing and previously lived in Portland, Oregon, for over 6 years. The Judge C. B. Bellinger granted the writ of habeas corpus, and Louis Chung was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Harry Thompson was being detained by L. T. Hall and R. Miller for unspecified reasons. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Thompson was remanded to the custody of the respondents and ordered to pay their court costs. Thompson motioned for a new trial, but this was denied. Newspaper coverage indicates Thompson had been convicted of the murder of Day Chambers and that Hall and Miller acted as Iowa police officials to return Thompson to custody for charges in Iowa.

Summary of Proceedings: On the 18th of February, 1891, Harry Brooks was arrested and charged for assault and battery. He was jailed by George C. Monroe in the Seattle City Jail. On the 26th, his writ for Habeas Corpus was allowed and he was to be brought to the courthouse of T.J. Humes, as granted by a Judge Osborn. Brooks’ lawyers argued that Claudius M. Rivers, the judge that convicted him of the crime, was not a legally appointed or qualified police judge, and that therefore his conviction was invalid. The outcome of the case in the courtroom of T.J. Humes is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Unlawfully and fraudulently cheated and defrauded the United States National Bank of Omaha, First National Bank of Omaha, Union National Bank of Omaha, and Omaha Savings Bank. They pretended to be an organization called the Omaha and Council Bluffs railway Employees Association and that they had arranged a charity ball in Omaha to raise funds to establish a free hospital ward for railroad men and their families dependent on public charity. Summary of Proceedings:
Anthony Harn was originally accused of manslaughter, later changed to first degree murder, for the killing of his employee and farmhand, Peter Nelson Eggan aka Peter Larson Agen aka Nels Peterson aka John Olson. The act of fatal violence took place on October 3, 1894. After being incarcerated for six months, Harn filed for a writ of habeas corpus on April 27, 1895. New testimony resulted in the court finding reasonable doubt of guilt. Judge Humes set bail.

Roughly half of the pages in the case file are unreadable.

Summary of Proceedings: Ethel Martin, Mrs. L. H. Hopkins, Mrs. F. Roberts, L. H. Hopkins, and C. H. Martin jointly petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham. The petitioners alleged that they were being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail without charge or permission to see their attorney. Due to the brevity of the case file, the outcome of the case and the fates of the petitioners are unknown. Newspaper coverage indicates Seattle is engaged in a public hygiene, anti-vice campaign with an intent to overcome habeas corpus challenges.

Summary of Proceedings:
Wah Ni, a resident and business owner in Portland, traveled to Hong Kong in 1892 on business and to visit relatives. Prior to departure, Ni appeared before a notary and received a signed certificate as proof of residence and his business to allow for re-entry. Nearly a year later, upon return, Ni was denied entry by a deputy collector. The deputy collector confiscated the certificate and refused to return it. Ni was informed that he had to board a steamship along with 200 other Chinese passengers to return to Hong Kong. 
Ni's application for a writ of habeas corpus was granted by the Superior Court of Pierce County and he was ordered deported by the U.S. Commissioner. An appeal was taken questioning the jurisdiction of the U.S. Commissioner. External research shows the witnesses refuted Wah Ni's claim that he was in merchant business. In the Circuit Court for the Western District of Washington, Ni's petition was denied and Ni was placed in the custody of U.S. Marshall, J. C. Drake. Ni's attorney gathered multiple affidavits from business partners and those personally acquainted with Ni to establish proof of his residence. The Circuit Court issued a writ of habeas corpus to stop the deportation, yet the results of the proceedings are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In October 1917, Edwin T. Wentz was arrested and charged with defrauding an innkeeper and was released on bail. Upon release, Wentz was re-arrested by Federal Authorities and charged with using U.S. mail to defraud and was released on bail. Immediately after release, Wentz was arrested for a third time and charged with being a fugitive of justice. At the request of the Governor of Oregon, James Withycombe, the Governor of Nebraska, Keith Neville, granted extradition to Oregon. Wentz filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds that he was unlawfully being deprived of his liberty and claimed he was not a fugitive of justice and the charges against him were a "ruse and trick" to injure him. Judge Arthur C. Wakeley granted the petition. In the Answer and Return to the Writ, it was claimed that the petitioner obtained money by false pretenses and fled the state of Oregon. In court, Judge Willis G. Sears ruled that Edwin was not unlawfully restrained of his liberty and the petitioner was remanded back to custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Stanley Fox was charged with statutory rape and default of bail on September 15th, 1919. He filed a petition for habeas corpus on September 18, 1919, in which he argued that there was insufficient evidence to hold him. The writ was denied on September 26th, 1919. Stanley Fox motioned for a new trial the next day again arguing that there was insufficient evidence to deny his writ. The motion for a new trial was denied, so he appealed to the Supreme Court of Nebraska. The Supreme Court of Nebraska heard his case in the January term of 1920. The court agreed with the original decision and decided in favor of the defendant. Stanley Fox remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Lola Williamson filed a writ claiming that she was unlawfully arrested by Charles S. Reed, the Chief of Police for the city of Seattle. She further claims that she was arrested solely on the grounds of racial prejudice, and that on December 25, 1899, Reed ordered the police to “make arrests of colored women residents in the city,” though the official charge she was arrested under was “unlawfully being a common prostitute.” She also claimed her bail was excessive at $250, which was far in excess of what a white woman would have had to pay for said crime. Reed denied this, but Judge Jacobs still granted the writ and initiated proceedings. The outcome of said proceedings is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
James Sanford was arrested on May 15, 1890 on a warrant issued by Justice John F. Miller and held in the King County Jail by Sheriff John McGraw. Sanford was held without a hearing and charged for the crime of conducting a swindling gambling game of bunco on May 12th and his first hearing was set for May 19th. James Sanford submitted a writ of habeas corpus for being restricted of his liberty. Sanford’s writ was heard by Judge Thomas J. Hume on May 17. No outcome of the writ is stated in the record. 

John W. Hall also filed for habeas corpus after being charged with the same crime. Both men filed on the same day. (See: hc.case.wa.0822)

Summary of Proceedings: Hugo Peters submitted this petition stating that he was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by John J. Ryder, Henry W. Dunn, and Michael Dempsey. His petition stated that on 26 August 1913, Peters was “forcibly brought” before Samuel L. O’Brien. The petition claimed that O’Brien was pretending to hold Police Court and was claiming to be the Magistrate of said Court. Petitioner was then forcibly subjected to a “pretended trial in said pretended Police Court.” Peters stated that Fred W. Anheuser, the City Prosecutor, appeared and conducted a “pretended prosecution” for the pretended charges of carrying concealed weapons and using profane language over a phone. O’Brien then sentenced Peters to 30 days in City Jail for each of the two charges. The petition stated that no complaint was ever filed in either of the “pretended” prosecutions charging Peters with any crimes or misdemeanors under Nebraska State Laws or Omaha City Ordinances. The word “pretended” is used because no complaint was ever filed for either charge. Because of this, the aforementioned parties had no authority to charge Peters with either crime or detain him to City Jail. The Appearance Docket stated that the writ was dismissed on 24 December 1913.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 11, 1919, Crystal Gilson was found guilty in an Omaha court of the charge of unlawful sale of intoxicating liquor, and sentenced to be imprisoned in the County jail for 60 days, and ordered to pay the costs of the prosecution or stay imprisoned until the costs were paid. On that day, Charles E. Foster, the police magistrate of the city of Omaha, sent a letter to Omaha Sheriff Michael L. Clark and ordered him to detain her. Three days later, on February 14, Gilson filed for a writ of habeas corpus. Her writ was allowed, then on January 26, 1920, the petition was dismissed for want of prosecution of cost of release. Gilson's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: G. A. Applegate was arrested and jailed for violating a Lincoln, Nebraska city ordinance against "getting and become [sic] drunk." He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the judge ruled that while the city ordinance allowed a person to be jailed if they did not pay their fine, the "part of said Ordinance imposing a sentence for said charge under said Ordinance is illegal and void." Applegate was remanded to the custody of his jailer and the police judge was ordered to set his bail at $200.

Summary of Proceedings: Joe Martin, the bound party, entered the country in 1907 from Russia and joined the IWW, a union organization, in 1914. On January 14th, 1918, the bound party was arrested on a warrant issued by the Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson (unnamed in the petition). The bound party was charged with being an alien, advocating or teaching the destruction of property, and being likely to become a public charge. On March 26th, 1918, W. P. Callahan, immigration inspector, interrogated the bound party on these issues and found the charges to be substantiated. The attorney for the petitioner does not agree that the questions were relevant. On January 8th, 1919, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed. The fate of the petition and the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 25, 1920, John H. Rogers and H.S. Scott, also known as Sherry Scott, were arrested outside the Castle Hotel Omaha, Nebraska on suspicion of their being involved in two Des Moines robberies. Immediately after the arrest, Scott and Rogers tried to bribe the officers arresting them to let them go. They were accused of not only having robbed the Des Moines State bank, but having stolen over $800 and a diamond ring from Ralph Erickson, a theater manager in Des Moines. According to the Omaha Daily Bee, $1,272.68 in small change was found wrapped in Des Moines State coin rolls in a candy box hidden in the men's suitcases. Both were farmers from Tulsa, Oklahoma. The 29-year-old Scott claimed that Rogers, who was only 19, had had nothing to do with the robbery, and confessed to having escaped from the Oklahoma state penitentiary four months ago. He claimed that he had stolen the money from a bank in Oklahoma, not Iowa. Their attorney, C.W. Britt, filed a writ of habeas corpus for their release on June 1, 1920 against chief of police Marshall Eberstein. Not only had the men been arrested without a warrant, having committed no crime in the state of Nebraska, he said, they weren't even in Des Moines on the day the robbery was committed. Apparently, there was also an attempt to extradite the men—perhaps the writ of habeas corpus was a way to combat the possibility of being sent back to Iowa. A writ and return was filed on June 10, 1920, but we know no else about the results of the case. Perhaps the men were, in fact, extradited to Iowa and the legal proceedings continued there.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 8, 1888 in Slaughter County, Washington, C.H. Smith was detained and imprisoned by Justice of the Peace of Slaughter County, James Hart, for the crime of larceny. Smith was sentenced to one year in county jail by Hart, which Smith and his attorney, Richard Osborn, challenged through petitioning for a writ of Habeas Corpus on February 8, 1889. Smith and Osborn stated that the imprisonment of Smith was illegal and unjust as a justice of the peace may only imprison someone if they fail to furnish bonds or as payment of fine or costs. The next day, Judge Thomas Burke ordered the release of Smith.

Summary of Proceedings: John W. McMenemy filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus for his son, John W. McMenemy Jr., minor, on the 26th of February of 1890 to free him from the custody of Henry P. Haze. Haze answered stating that he does not have custody, power, control, or possession of John W. McMenemy Jr. also known as "Dot" at this time. Haze did admit that he had custody of Dot on the 23rd of February, 1890 between the hours of 12 and 1 o'clock with the authority of Judge W. H. Hunter and Sherrif James P. Mallory. The petition then becomes focused on freeing Dot from the Sherrif of Douglas County. Judge Joseph R. Clarkson, in February of 1890, allows the writ and rules that Dot is being detained unlawfully. The next year, by May of 1891, John W. McMenemy is deceased. Judge George W. Doane ruled on the nature of the execution of the will on the 23rd of May, 1891. John C. Cowin and William W. Wallace were put in charge of executing the Will of John W. McMenemy. It is also ordered that Dot, his son, be put in the custody of Carrie Williamson, Dot's sister, who is paid the fifteen hundred dollars left to Dot.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 30th, 1920, Carl Gunther was arrested in Omaha under the order of the Omaha Chief of Detectives for being a fugitive from the state of Missouri. Gunther argued in his petition for freedom that he had no complaint filed against him and no bond set for his release. The judge agreed to his plea and had Detective Dunn bring him to court. Though the petition outcome is not contained in the case file, the appearance docket shows that the writ was denied; Gunther remained in custody as the Omaha police processed his extradition to Missouri.

Summary of Proceedings: E. I. Chamberlin petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of William Baskin against Seattle Chief of Police J. F. Warren. Chamberlin alleged that Baskin committed no crime and that Warren had no authority to imprison Baskin. Warren responded that he had a warrant charging Baskin with being a disorderly person and that Baskin was being held for defaulting on his bail, set at $200. Newspaper records indicate Baskin was a member of the I.W.W. and that his writ was denied. The fate of Baskin is unknown. This is one of several petitions for habeas corpus that involve Baskin.

Summary of Proceedings: John Crawley was arrested and jailed on suspicion of being a fugitive from slavery. William Logan, whose relationship to Crawley is unclear, asserted that Crawley was a free man and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, which was granted. Others asserted that Crawley was enslaved by a man named Stephen Gardier. After hearing the evidence, Crawley was released.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 15, 1918, Omaha's Health Commissioner authorized the isolation and quarantine of Maud Shaw under city Ordinance No. 9852, alleging that Shaw had been found with a venereal infection. On October 17, 1918, Jud Brown filed for habeas on behalf of Shaw against Manning and the superintendent of the detention home, Alva Burger. In the petition, Brown argued that Shaw had been confined for 4 weeks without any complaint and is free of any alleged disease. A writ was issued, but the case was later dismissed for want of prosecution on January 26, 1920; the fate of Shaw is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 29, 1920, Anna Citta crafted a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her infant daughter, Francis Citta. According to Anna, Louis Citta, her husband, was unlawfully holding and keeping Francis Citta after having kidnapped her on July 29. In a separate 1920 lawsuit, Anna had also accused Frank of being an alcoholic. Louis Citta was ordered by the court to present Francis Citta in front of Judge Aruthur Wakely at the Douglas County District Court. The case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 26, 1922 after Louis gave Anna their daughter back, said that he was "only joking," and promised to never be cruel to her again. However, the 1930 census shows Louis, Anna, and Frances living together again with two new children.

Summary of Proceedings: On 3 January 1916, Ernest R. Powell filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. On 4 January 1916, Douglas County Sheriff Felix J. McShane served the writ to Omaha Police Chief Henry W. Dunn. On the same day, both parties along with their attorneys, Julius S. Cooley (Petitioner) and George A. Magney (Respondent) appeared in Court before James P. English. All parties agreed that the cause should be dismissed without prejudice. As such, Judge English dismissed the petition without prejudice. The details of Powell’s detention are not included.

Summary of Proceedings:
Swedish citizen and "alien" Charles W. Nordstrom applied for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff Edward Cudihee. His application stated that he was being held and would be executed by hanging for the alleged crime of murder, in violation of the Constitution and U.S. law. Nordstrom claimed that a change in the Washington State statutes regulating the death penalty procedure made his execution illegitimate because it would rely on an ex post facto law and would violate his right to due process. Judge Cornelius H. Hanford sent an acerbic letter to Nordstrom's attorney, denying the application and refusing to hold a hearing, claiming that he aimed to end the series of appeals and applications that Nordstrom had previously made. Hanford stated that he had twice refused to grant a writ, and that his refusals had been sustained by the Supreme Court. Nordstrom appealed the denial. Nordstrom remained in custody, and a newspaper source reveals that he was later executed. 
For subsequent petitions by Charles W. Nordstrom before his execution, see related petitions.

Summary of Proceedings: James Herbert Van Closter and Andrew W. McLaughlin filed a writ of Habeas Corpus claiming they were detained by Sheriff E. T. Werden on a pretend warrant for the alleged fraudulent selling and disposing of mortgaged property during a lease - a complaint that was filed by John L. Miles. Closter and McLaughlin were then taken by Werden from Omaha, where they lived, to the county of Nuckolls, Nebraska. Closter and McLaughlin were released from custody on bail and made to return on the 5th of June. Upon return, Closter and McLaughlin were ordered to be released into the custody of Nuckolls County by Judge Lee S. Estelle.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 19th, 1921, Otto F. Lindner petitioned for and was given an order allowing a writ of Habeas Corpus having been taken and held in custody by Micheal F. Dempsey and Charlse Van Deusen in October of that year. Van Deusen and Dempsey presented in response that their holding of Lindner was by virtue of a warrant issued by the governor of Nebraska that was originally from the governor of Illinois that charged Lindner with non-support of wife and child and being a fugitive from justice. In replying to the response, Linder argued that he was not a fugitive from justice and was in Nebraska for his job as a traveling salesman and that his wife and child were well supported and aware of his travels. It was the 21st of the same month that the judge ordered the writ denied and Lindner be remanded to custody. Linder filed for a new trial the day after. The fate of Lindner is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 14th, 1916, a prisoner being held by the United States Army in California, escaped under Colonel David Livingstone's watch. Then, William M. Inglis made "profane, insulting and obscene remarks" about Livingstone being on watch when this occurred. This led to Livingstone sending Inglis a letter, asking for an apology. Three charges were then brought up against Livingstone, as he violated Articles of War by 'behaving with disrespect toward his commanding officer', participating in 'conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman', and disobeying orders. He then filed a writ of habeas corpus on September 13th, 1916, claiming to be unlawfully imprisoned, retained, confined and restrained of his liberty by Inglis. Livingstone was duly and legally discharged from arrest on September 15th, 1916, leading to Judge Neterer dismissing the writ on September 19th.

Summary of Proceedings: Mrs. James T. Dickey, the mother of 17-year-old Edna and 13-year-old Geraldine Sullivan, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to gain custody of the girls on August 10, 1920.The writ was directed at Mother Saint Lawrence, the Mother Superior of the House of the Good Shepherd, a convent and home for "delinquent girls" in Omaha. The girls' deceased father had placed the girls there before his death, and the Mother Superior refused to relinquish the sisters to their mother's custody. According to the Omaha Daily Bee, shortly after Mr. Dickey's death, his wife remarried and moved to Washington, D.C. The writ was successful, and when the girls appeared in court on August 11, judge Willis G. Sears granted Mrs. Dickey custody, although they had originally scheduled to appear before judge A.C. Troup. Allegedly, when the verdict was announced, the girls cried, hugging the representative sent with them from the convent and said that they didn't want to go.

Summary of Proceedings: Edna Woods petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham and the Commissioner of Health John S. McBride. Woods alleged that she was arrested on the charge of being a disorderly person and placed in the Seattle City Jail, where she was compelled to submit to a blood test for infectious venereal diseases. She claimed that those tests were found to be positive, but denied that she was infected with any such diseases. She claimed her charge of being a disorderly person was a “sham” intended to force her into medical treatment, and as such, her imprisonment was illegal. Judge Kenneth Mackintosh denied Woods’s petition for a writ of habeas corpus. She appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed with Mackintosh and also denied the petition. Summary of Proceedings: In June 1918, George Harrison was indicted for assault with a deadly weapon in the Multnomah County Circuit Court and committed to the Oregon State Penitentiary in Salem. The following spring, Harrison's attorney, Thomas Garland, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his client, which was granted. Garland claimed that the indictment against Harrison had been dismissed, rendering his detention illegitimate. After hearing the evidence, however, the writ was dismissed and Harrison was remanded into the custody of the warden.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1919, Charles Hoban filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was unlawfully imprisoned and restrained of his liberty. Hoban was charged with stealing an automobile and receiving a stolen automobile, and Police Judge, Charles E. Foster, set bail at $10,000, which the petition alleged was excessive. Respondent M. L. Clark, stated he had authority for holding Hoban on account of three arrest warrants issued by Charles E. Foster prior. Judge William A. Redick authorized the writ of Habeas Corpus, and required the magistrate to set bail at $2,500 for each of the three complaints against Hoban. The petitioner was remanded to custody subject to bail.

Summary of Proceedings: Ann was a free Black woman that was illegally confined and restrained of her liberty from John M. Jamison the jailor of St. Louis County jail. The confinement was unconstitutional because it did not consist of a warrant, or order of due process. Ann was living in Peoria, Illinois for six years as an indentured servant for Charles Ballance then she worked under William Willson. Wilson brought her from Peoria to St. Louis, and kept her there until June 17,1844 when a disagreement between Wilson’s family and Ann arose. After this Ann was placed into the hands of Constable John W. Paulding who placed her in jail under the charge of Jamison. She hoped that her writ of Habeas would help her be released, she was eventually discharged from custody of William Wilson and nothing else is known.

Summary of Proceedings: Elmer T. Prather petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren and Captain of Detectives Charles Tennant. Prather claimed he was arrested with no warrant and was being held in the Seattle City Jail with no due process under suspicion of being a fugitive from justice. Warren and Tennant responded with a warrant from the Justice of the Peace of Walla Walla County ordering Prather’s arrest on a charge of assault in the third degree. The outcome of the case and the fate of Prather are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 2nd, 1917, John F. Kinney filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his three children, John F. Kinney Jr., Cathrine Kinney, and Margaret Kinney, against his ex-wife, Mary E. Kinney. On January 15th, 1917, Judge Crawford ruled in favor of John Kinney and Mary Kinney was ordered to turn over custody of her three minor children to her ex-husband. The trial was apparently held up because of a previous restraining order issued by Mary against John that forbade him from seeing her. On that same day, Mary Kinney filed for a new trial, but was overruled by the court. She claimed that John acquired their Minnesota divorce fraudulently and he had in fact deserted her and the three children. On January 30th, 1917, Mary Kinney filed a writ of error, claiming that the court erred in finding that John was entitled to custody of the kids and erred in excluding evidence offered by Mary that proved John was unfit to have custody. The outcome of the writ of error is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Junichi Yamamoto was ordered for deportation by U.S. Commissioner of Immigration, Luther Weedin, upon a warrant which claimed that Yamamoto was in violation of Rule 11 of the Immigration Rules for not possessing a Japanese passport when entering the U.S., and also being likely to become a public charge.
Yamamoto petitioned for habeas corpus claiming himself to be an able-bodied member of the work force, and that deportation violated his right to remain silent in accordance with the fifth Amendment of the Constitution. He also alleged that there was no due process of law. The petitioner attorneys claimed Yamamoto was entitled to a three-year statue of limitation.
The writ was denied and Yamamoto was deported.
As an interesting note, several other cases in this database are cited by the judge as setting precedence for this case.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 27, 1894, Lung Duck filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Chin Kwong, Chin Hen Bow, Chin Hen Sing and Chin Lay Sam. Lung Duck claimed that Chin Kwong, Chin Hen Bow, Chin Hen Sing and Chin Lay Sam were being illegally detained on the Steamship Islander by Captain John Irving. Lung Duck further claimed that Chin Kwong, Chin Hen Bow, Chin Hen Sing and Chin Lay Sam were Chinese merchants who were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Act. Judge Bellinger denied the writ and ordered them all to remain in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Salvatore Giampapa was arrested on December 19th, 1923, after fleeing the scene of the murder of a man named Gibilterra. Following a preliminary hearing for the trial of Gibilterra's murder, Giampapa filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus for being unlawfully detained by the Douglas County Sheriff, Michael Endres. DeGeorge claimed that he was wrongly being charged with First-degree murder on the basis of insufficient evidence and that the court had failed to follow proper procedure by not setting the price of his bail. Despite the Habeas Corpus petition being granted, his writ was denied as the judge deemed that the warrant for his arrest was valid and he should be held until the outcome of the murder trial. Giampapa remained in the custody of the Douglas Country Sheriff.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 28th, 1912, R. L. Blewett petitioned for Stella Hoffman’s freedom from Mary D. Martin. Blewett acted as both the petitioner and attorney for Hoffman. Hoffman was apparently taken and held against her will by Dr. Mary D. Martin, acting as an official of the Young Women’s Christian Association of the City of Seattle. Hoffman also argued that Martin had no legal authority to do so. Judge J. T. Ronald approved the writ, and Sheriff Robert Hodge delivered the writ to Martin. The court date was set for March 29th, however the outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Emma Rupert petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that her son Clarence Rupert was being deprived of his liberty by her ex-husband Henry Rupert. She claimed that Henry had abducted Clarence while she was living in Oklahoma. Judge Holmes granted the petition. The next day, Holmes allowed the writ and ordered that Clarence be released into the custody of the petitioner. However, the couple apparently made up over time, as they were living together with Clarence and 3 new younger siblings in Lincoln at the 1910 census.

Summary of Proceedings: Emery Sarrazin petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigrant inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid. Sarrazin was a Canadian immigrant being held at the Spokane County Jail on the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property and was awaiting deportation. Sarrazin alleged his imprisonment was unlawful as he was denied his right to due process. Richardson and Reid presented both the warrant for Sarrazin’s arrest and the warrant for deportation. Judge Rudkin claimed Sarrazin’s case was similar to In re Holm, in which Rudkin ruled that affiliation with the I.W.W. did not conclusively indicate the defendant was guilty of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. Thus, the writ was allowed, and Sarrazin’s release was scheduled for a later date to give government authorities time to appeal. There is no evidence any government authorities did so. This case is related to several other petitions for writs of habeas corpus from immigrants facing deportation on the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property whose hearings fall on the same day as Sarrazin’s.

Summary of Proceedings: Elizabeth Franklin petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police J. F. Warren and Commissioner of Health J. S. McBride. Franklin claimed she was arrested with no criminal charge placed against her and was being held at the Seattle City Jail or Municipal Hospital without trial or fixed bail. McBride responded that Warren had arrested Franklin for being a disorderly person and that, upon mandatory testing, she had been found to have syphilis. McBride alleged that her detainment was a means of quarantine for the health of the public. This case may be related to vice raids occurring in Seattle at the time. The outcome of the case and the fate of Franklin are unknown.

Consequently, the writ was denied and McCartney remanded to the custody of the hospital superintendent.

Summary of Proceedings:
On April 1, 1891, Kate Burns placed her daughter, Maggie McGee, aged eight years old, in the House of the Good Shepherd with the expectation of a one-month stay. Kate failed to recover her daughter despite multiple attempts. Sister Superior Mary repeatedly refused to release Maggie back into Kate’s custody. 

On September 1, 1891, Kate Burns filed her first writ of habeas corpus for her daughter, Maggie McGee, aged eight, for her release from the House of the Good Shepherd. Witnesses were called to provide testimony about the case. Mother Superior Mary, from the House of the Good Shepherd filed a motion to quash the writ. Maggie remained in the custody of House of the Good Shepherd.

Summary of Proceedings:
Domenico Lazzaro, often referred to as Frank Rossi, and his wife, Bambino, were arrested faced deportation over alleged violations of the Immigration Act of February 5, 1917. Domenico and Bambino were accused of managing a house of prostitution and were ordered to be deported to Italy. In his writ of habeas corpus, Domenico stated that there was not enough evidence to justify deportation, and that he should be deported to Canada and not Italy since he entered the United States from Canada. Domenico initially migrated to the United States in 1904 but shortly after his initial arrival he moved to Niagara, Ontario in Canada where he lived for three years before moving back to the United States. In his petition, Domenico states that since he had lived in Canada more recently than Italy he should be deported there instead. 

Judge Jeremiah Neterer denied Domenico’s writ for habeas corpus and ordered that he remain in the custody of the Seattle Immigration Inspector and is subject to deportation. Following this ruling, Domenico immediately appealed the decision. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals later affirmed Judge Neterer’s initial ruling. Domenico again appealed to the United States Supreme Court. However, shortly after his second appeal, Judge Neterer ordered that Domenico’s appeal bond is forfeit after he failed to appear in court and failed to answer a writ of scire facias.

Summary of Proceedings: Christ Evers of West Butte, Oregon filed a writ of habeas corpus to gain custody of his son, Fred Evers from Fred Zeek. Zeek said that he has a family and that for more than a year, Fred Evers has made his home with and resided with Zeek and his family. Fred Zeek's wife was Fred Evers's deceased mother's sister. Christ was deaf, and according to the Omaha Daily Bee, "has lost to a considerable extent the use of his language." Zeek alleged that Christ Evers is not a fit or suitable person to have the care and custody of Fred Evers, that he was without means, had no home, and was a man of dissolute habits. The application of Christ Evers was denied and the petition was dismissed. The judge stated that Fred should stay in the Zeek home as his aunt was the closest thing to a mother he had after Menine Evers's death, but that Fred Zeek should work the boy less and allow him to go to school more.

Summary of Proceedings: Daniel Buckovis, the petitioner, filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus, claiming unlawful detainment by Chief of Police Martin White. Buckovis was detained due to a charge of assault with the intent to inflict great bodily injury. On January 16th, 1899, Buckovis petitioned for release by writ of Habeas Corpus, and Judge Willard W. Slabaugh allowed the writ of habeas corpus to be returnable on January 7th of, 1899. On the day of release, Buckovis was arrested again by a deputy of Chief White for the same offense that he was released for by writ of Habeas Corpus. Judge Scott R. Cunningham finds Buckovis unlawfully detained and he is released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On, November 12, 1917, C. R. Anderson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus for Minnie Smith. Smith was arrested on the night of November 8, 1917. The petition argues that there was no charge made against Minnie but that she was arrested on the suspicion of being a “disorderly person.” Anderson further states that Minnie Smith had been denied the opportunity to post bail and asked the court to allow her to post bail under the date of the hearing. Judge Mackintosh agreed to hear the writ but the hearing for the petition was delayed because the Chief of Police, Charles Beckingham, did not bring Minnie Smith to the court as ordered for the hearing date. Mackintosh issued a warrant for Beckingham’s arrest for contempt of court. The Chief of Police was arrested but the Seattle Star newspaper noted that the issue was due to a mistake at the court house. Minnie Smith and another unnamed person cases were handled by the King County Justice Court earlier in the day and were no longer in the custody of Charles Beckingham. Neither the newspaper nor the case file state the outcome of the petition or if Minnie Smith was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Jackson filed a writ of habeas corpus because he was being held against his will by the Commissioner of Labor in Washington, Henry White. Jackson allegedly entered the United States in June 1917 and was arrested in January 1918 under the authority of White. White had suspicion that he was an illegal alien from Denmark who changed his name from Peterson to Jackson so that he could get a job in the mines. It was also alleged he was suffering from gonorrhea and was part of the I.W.W.. The petitioner argued that there was no evidence supporting his arrest, but Henry White produced evidence that showed cause for his arrest. The writ was denied and Charles Jackson stayed in detention.

Summary of Proceedings:
Canadian G. Weaver Loper filed for a writ of habeas corpus on September 25, 1918. Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid held Loper on a charge of fraudulent issuing of corporate stock. Newspaper coverage stated that G. Weaver Loper was involved in a wider scandal related to the Lucky Jim Zinc Mine. 

Loper’s lawyer, Harry L. Cohen, argued that the United States Constitution and treaty law had the power to regulate Canadian corporations operating in the United States, and the State of Washington did not. Judge Frank H. Rudkin overruled this argument and denied the writ on October 2, 1918. The fate of Loper is unknown.

“Suit Against Lucky Jim,” The Spokesman-Review, May 5, 1917, Page 17.

Summary of Proceedings:
On December 19, 1918, George Howe, George Homer, and William Smith were taken into custody by the Chief of Police, Joel F. Warren. The arrest came at the request of Robert C. Saunders, the U.S. District Attorney, and Robert T. McClelland, the U.S. Commissioner. They had charged the petitioners with violating the Selective Services Act of 1917 by transporting and with an intent to sell intoxicating liquors within the “dry zones” established within five miles of U.S. military bases. Newspaper coverage of the arrest note that the petitioners were found to have 410 quarts of bonded whisky in their car and records of transactions which stated that the men had already sold 89 cases of whiskey for $6,402. 

On December 20, Joel Warren and the prosecuting attorneys moved to have the writ of habeas corpus stating that the writ violated Rule 16 of the General Rules of the Superior Courts of the State of Washington. Warren claimed that he was never served a copy of the petition as required by court rules and argued that the writ should be quashed for that reason. The outcome of the motion to quash and the writ of habeas corpus are not included in the case file. Newspaper coverage does note that a few days after the petition was filed George Homer and William Smith were released on $1,500 bail while they awaited trial. Summary of Proceedings: George Schriner was jailed in Lancaster County, Nebraska and facing extradition to Morgan County, Colorado to respond to an accusation that he had violated a state ordinance making it "unlawful to sell mortgaged personal property, contrary to the provisions of the mortgage." He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. Schriner contended that the extradition request did not allege that he had committed a crime, only that he had "sold mortgaged property." After hearing the evidence, Schriner was released.
