Summary of Proceedings: Lee Wiug petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Lee She Cheong and Lee See Won who are held on the Steamship Danube by Master William Meyers. They were not allowed to enter the port by T. J. Black the Collector of Customs who believed they would violate the Chinese Exclusion Act. However, a witness and both bound parties testified that they were merchants at En Gee Goon a cigar and a tobacco company located at No. 65 Second Street. The Judge accepted the testimony and granted the writ, releasing Lee She Cheong and Lee See Won from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Toy Chung, Toy Fon, Chan Hing, Ng Gun, Seek Sing, Fook Lung, Seek See Ling, Fook Yee Bow, Wong See Dong, Ho Ming, Chan Ngun Sun, Yip See How, On Chow, Yee Yik See, Gin Mow, Law Yick, How Him, Jung Ah Wing, Yee Bow, Duck Ah Man, Sin Bing Ming, Wing Sing, Yung Bow, Chan Wong and Chan Khut were all confined in Steamship Danube by William Meyer for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Lee Sing petitioned for writ of habeas corpus claiming that they are Chinese merchants, not laborers. Writ of habeas corpus was granted to most of them: Toy Chung, Toy Fon, Chan Hing, Seek Sing, Fook Lung, Seek See Ling, Fook Yee Bow, Wong See Dong, Ho Ming, Chan Ngun Sun, Yip See How, On Chow, Law Yick, How Him, Jung Ah Wing, Yee Bow, Duck Ah Man, Sin Bing Ming, Wing Sing, Yung Bow, Chan Wong and Chan Khut. They were ordered to be released from custody. The outcome is unknown for Ng Gun, Yee Yik See, and Gin Mow. The case file is either incomplete, or there was a court error.

Summary of Proceedings:
Margaret Roy, a subject of Scotland, and her attorney, Ralph S. Pierce, filed the petition to challenge her detainment for the purpose of deportation by the United States immigration office for "being an alien and believed to advocate the overthrow of government, [and who] disbelieved in and who opposed organized government". 
The primary claim for her release was that her detainment was due to a failure to provide her due process. She claimed that her fifth amendment rights were violated. Her claim referred to the answers she provided to an immigration hearing after her arrest in July 1918 (warrant issued June 24) where she admitted that she was a member of the IWW and believed “in mass action and organization,” but denied taking any actual actions. Further, her petition claimed that the evidence against her was based solely on IWW literature that was not actually in her possession at her arrest. Further still, she claimed that the government refused to even turn over the transcript of the hearing or the evidence they attached to it to enable her defence.
The judge approved her writ and demanded that the US government appear to demonstrate its cause for holding her.
In February 1919, the government did appear and provided the transcript of the hearing and the evidence against Roy. The judge ruled that her detainment was lawful and could continue. Presumably, she was deported afterward, but there is no evidence to be certain.
In March 1919, the government of the United States requested that the previously introduced evidence of Roy's hearing and IWW literature be removed from the case file and letters signed by Roy's lawyer agree to that removal.
See her sister's petition in the same vein, "Janet MacKay".

Summary of Proceedings:
On November 28, 1877, Joseph Wells filed to retrieve custody of his 14-year-old wife, Matty, from her mother and step-father, Martha and William Church. Joseph alleged that on June 26 Martha and William had forcibly kidnapped Matty and that William did so in order to "violate her chastity." William and Martha claimed that Matty came to their home willingly and was staying out of her own desire. In response, Joseph denied their claims and stated that William and Martha had threatened to kill him if he attempted to speak to Matty. 

While the judge's decision in the case is missing from the file, it appears as though Matty returned to live with Joseph, based on census records from 1880.

Summary of Proceedings: In August 1923, Thomas Vann petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Michael Endres, Sheriff of Douglas County, Nebraska. Vann was charged, found guilty, and sentenced to sixty days in jail for vagrancy. At trial, on appeal from police court, Vann was sentenced by Judge L.B. Day to serve an additional nine months in jail for said offense. The petition alleged Judge Day exceeded his jurisdiction in passing said sentence. Judge Day ruled that the sentence of two hundred and seventy days in jail was excessive and illegal, as the maximum limit of the municipal court of the City of Omaha for matters of said kind is ninety days, and ruled Vann be released and discharged from custody.

Chamberlin alleged that Extell committed no crime and that Warren had no authority to imprison Extell. Warren responded that he had a warrant charging Extell with being a disorderly person and that Extell was being held for defaulting on his bail, set at $200. Newspaper records indicate Extell was a member of the I.W.W. and that his writ was denied. The fate of Extell is unknown. This is one of several petitions in which Extell is a bound party.

Summary of Proceedings: Arthur alleged that Richard, the child, had been in his custody from January 1, 1901 until August 15, 1903. At that time, Richard was left with the Child Saving Institute, by May Moraine, wife of Arthur, for two weeks and at the end of the two weeks, she would determine whether she would permit the child to be adopted. On August 21, 1905, Arthur and May went to the Institute to reclaim their child where they were informed that the child had been sent out for a six month trial by some parents who desired to adopt the child. The petition was granted and was directed to the respondents, Anderson W. Clark, John Doe, and Nellie Reed. Richard Moraine was not found in their custody or in the state of Nebraska.

Summary of Proceedings: Walter Scott, an employee of the Tabitha Home, and Jennie Adams, a long-term resident there, eloped in early October 1910. Scott petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in order to establish custody of Adams, which was granted. At the same time, a case to annul their marriage on the grounds that Adams was developmentally disabled and unable to give her consent was also before the court. While the annulment and habeas corpus proceedings were pending, Adams was placed into the temporary custody of one A. A. H. Mayer. Ultimately, the court annulled the marriage between Scott and Adams but also allowed Scott's writ. The result was that although Adams was released from the custody of the Tabitha Home, Scott had no legal authority to assert custody over her.

Summary of Proceedings: Nineteen-year-old Chester Deles Dernier, a student at the University of Nebraska - Lincoln, enlisted in the U.S. Navy in the fall of 1902 while traveling in Washington State with some friends. He eventually made is way back to Nebraska, where he was arrested in Cass County for desertion. His parents, William and Gertrude Deles Dernier, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, arguing that they had not given Chester, who was a minor, permission to enlist. After hearing the evidence, Chester was remanded to the custody of his jailer. William and Gertrude appealed this decision to the the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. Chester's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 14, Leslie S. LeWald and his attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, just ten days after they first petitioned (See: In the Matter of the Application of L. S. LeWald for Writ of Habeas Corpus). In this petition, Leslie admitted that Washington Governor Albert E. Mead had a warrant for his arrest, which stated that Leslie was a fugitive from justice from Illinois, on the original charge of embezzlement. Leslie denied, however, that he was in Illinois at the time of the crime, and stated that no proof was presented of his presence in Illinois at that time. He additionally claimed that the governor did not have jurisdiction to issue a warrant in this case. LeWald also filed an affidavit stating he was unable to pay for court fees. The return from Sheriff Smith and his attorney stated that the facts in the petition were not sufficient to justify an issued writ. The outcome of this case is unknown, but it is mentioned that Judge Hatch ruled that Maurice LeWald would be allowed to visit Leslie in jail. Leslie S. LeWald’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: George Vallas was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Vallas was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Vallas and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Vallas argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. On June 27, the writ of habeas was sustained and Vallas was released.

Summary of Proceedings:
On February 25, 1893 T.E. Chase filed a petition on behalf of Thomas Gibbons for a writ of Habeas Corpus. T.E. Chase indicated that on February 22, 1893 Gibbons was unlawfully detained and held without his liberty in the King County jail of Seattle, Washington for the charge of burglary of a ship and no warrant was issued for his arrest, limiting the credibility of due process. Gibbons was detained by the Chief of Police, Andrew Jackson.

The Clerk of the Superior Court filed and processed the petition on February 25, 1893 and immediately released Gibbons from Custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Leonard Collins, the petitioner, commit an act of larceny against William Hemmings. He allegedly stole one shotgun, shovel, wagon cover, and two blankets. Summary of Proceedings: In March 1916, the Lane County Juvenile Court ordered the commitment of Constance Cheshire to the State Industrial School for Girls in Salem without ever alerting her parents about the proceedings. In December 1919, with Cheshire nearing her eighteenth birthday, her mother, Sadie Millett, and grandfather, Harry Ryan, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on her behalf, which was granted. The school superintendent, Margaret Mann, claimed that she had released Cheshire on parole to one Mrs. Charles Cleveland, whose relationship to Cheshire is unclear. After hearing the evidence, Mann was ordered to retrieve Cheshire from Cleveland and return her to the custody of her mother.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 6, 1893, Robert Dewar (incorrectly referred to as “Richard”), was charged for burglary under the oath of J.M. Shaffer, and through the warrant by William Caldwell, Justice of the Peace for the Seattle Precinct police court. Dewar was placed in jail, posted with a bail of $750 which he did not pay. According to Dewar’s attorney, Frank B. Ingersoll, Dewar had his rights violated when Caldwell did not file a transcript of court procedures, when the prosecuting attorney, John F. Miller, filed unverified information, when said attorney failed to have Dewar arraigned before the court, and when Dewar had remained in jail for over thirty days without said attorney filing information within the time period. These procedures violated Hill’s code sections 1269 and 1368. J. H Woolery, Sheriff of King County, returned Dewar to Judge Thomas J. Humes for a Writ of Habeas Corpus on August 8, 1893.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 9, 1924, Mary Pierce was sentenced by Judge John McGee to 6 months in the Dodge County Jail for violating the National Prohibition Act after selling alcohol at a restaurant (the address was 1004 South 13th Street, Omaha, Nebraska). On November 19, 1924, she filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that she should be discharged after serving three months because the cumulative sentences imposed upon her did not specify the order in which she needed to serve them. On November 24, 1924, the writ was allowed, and the judge ordered her release from police custody on November 28, 1924. On April 9, 1925, the respondent’s application to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit was approved. On January 30, 1926, the decision of the lower court was reversed, and Chief Justice William Taft remanded Mary to the custody of the respondents. The higher court also referred to the Cronin vs. William J. Fox decision.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles W. Nordstrom petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff William H. Moyer. Nordstrom was sentenced to death by hanging for first degree murder in 1892 by judge T. J. Humes. Upon Humes’s retirement, judge Orange Jacobs took the role of Judge of the Superior court of the State of Washington of the County of King. Nordstrom argued that since Humes sentenced him, Jacobs could not resentence him, and, thus, he was being held illegally. The case file does not reveal the case outcome or Nordstrom’s fate, but newspaper records indicate the writ was allowed and Nordstrom was removed from death row, but not released from jail. Nordstrom filed several habeas corpus petitions related to his sentence.

Summary of Proceedings: On January, 22, 1916, E. E. Corey was arrested by the King County Sheriff, Hodge T. Roberts. Following the arrest, Corey claimed that he was arrested and being detained without a warrant. In his reply to the petition, Roberts stated that arrested Corey based on a warrant sent to him by Adams County Sheriff, A. C. Jensen. Jensen’s warrant was issued by Judge Bert Linn and was based on a complaint issued by W. O. Miller charging Corey with the crime of seduction. The outcome of the petition is unknown and not included in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 6th, 1920, Clara Heaston submitted a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her minor daughter, Nellie Heaston. Ralph Heaston, Nellie's father, and John Clopper were named as respondents. In October 1919, Clara and Ralph divorced and Clara was awarded custody of their two children. Clara allowed the children to visit Ralph's sister in March of 1920 on the condition that she would pick them up the next morning. Clara claimed that during the night, Ralph took Nellie out of Colorado and to Nebraska and had since refused to return her. Ralph eventually placed Nellie into the custody of John Clopper. Originally, the case was to be continued to September 13th with Nellie remaining in the custody of Clopper during that time. On August 20th, a stipulation was filed dismissing the writ with prejudice and the record waived. It is unknown whether or not Nellie was returned to her mother.

Summary of Proceedings: William Butt was called into the office to give a deposition for a case he was involved in, Bensinger Self-Adding Cash Company vs. Chris Crotmak & John Hman. He did not appear when he was supposed to, so Paul Stein forcibly took Butt to the room. Butt also refused to speak and then was committed to the county jail until he consented to give evidence. Butt said that the notary public had no right to take said deposition in said room nor had Butt been notified according to law to appear in said place. The writ was allowed but ultimately the judge ruled that Butt was legally imprisoned.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 30, 1918, Lizzie Latchford filed a writ of habeas corpus to have her daughter, Ruth M. Hill, released from the custody of the Girls Parental School in Seattle, Washington. Hill had been ordered a dependent of the state by the King County Juvenile Court on March 6, 1918, and ordered to be placed in the care of Girls Parental School for a little over a year until she turned sixteen years old. In her petition, Latchford argues that she has the means to care for Ruth and has been offered by the Red Cross organization a position for her to work and assist the war effort until the school semester resumes. The outcome of the petition is not stated in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 25, 1916, the police took Maurice Greenwalt into custody. In his petition, he claimed that since then, they kept him imprisoned, detained, confined, and restrained on suspicion of committing robbery with Elmer Johnson in Douglas County. On June 27, 1916, there was a preliminary hearing and an examination of the witnesses, and it was conclusively shown that there was no probable cause for holding Greenwalt for robbery. So, the same day, Greenwalt petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he should have been discharged and the complaint should have been dismissed as a result of the ruling. He further claimed that the complaint was made without probable cause, and the evidence failed to show probable cause to hold Greenwalt. Greenwalt claimed that Felix J. McShane, Henry Schroeder, Henry W. Dunn, Steven Maloney, Michael F. Dempsey, and John Byrnes unlawfully imprisoned, detained, confined, and restrained him of his liberty. On June 27, 1916, the judge accepted the petition but removed all the named respondents in the original petition except for Sheriff McShane and County Jailer Schroeder. On June 28, 1916, the judge issued a writ of habeas corpus; however, the outcome of this proceeding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: William Denny petitioned that his 6 year old daughter was held unlawfully by the St. James Orphanage and that he was not allowed to visit or see his daughter without any just or lawful reason. May Denny, her mother, placed her there. On April 4th, the court decided to not make a decision about if the parents are fit enough to keep her at that time and instead decided that Ruby should remain in the custody of the asylum and that the parents could visit. The court also ordered that the parents had to each pay half of what it costed to keep their child in the asylum, including board, keep and clothing. Additionally, it was decided that temporary custody of Ruby be given to the orphanage until removed by the mutual consent of the parents or action of the court.

Summary of Proceedings:
On March 29th, 1876, Mary Ann and Adaline O'Neill were both convicted of being "a habitual drunkard and disorderly person" and ordered to the County Jail of Walla Walla. On April 5th, 1876, Mary O'Neill filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of herself, claiming that she had never confessed to the crime and that no testimonies were ever given at her trial. Adeline was charged but does not appear to have also filed for habeas corpus. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party is unknown. 

It appears that Mary was a frequenter of the courts for charges of drunkenness and disorderly conduct. The scans of these case files aren't very clear, so it is hard to tell whether the files represent just one habeas petition and court case, or if they represent multiple instances of Mary's many exploits.

Summary of Proceedings: Dora Foster filed a writ claiming that she was unlawfully arrested by Charles S. Reed, the Chief of Police for the city of Seattle. She further claims that she was arrested solely on the grounds of racial prejudice, and that on December 25, 1899, Reed ordered the police to “make arrests of colored women residents in the city,” though the official charge she was arrested under was “unlawfully being a common prostitute.” She also claimed her bail was excessive at $250, which was far in excess of what a white woman would have had to pay for said crime. Reed denied this, but Judge Jacobs initiated proceedings and allowed the writ to stand.

Summary of Proceedings: R. J. Alton filed for a writ of Habeas alleging that he was unlawfully held and legal hearings had been held in court concerning his case without the consent of himself or his legal counsel. Judge J. E. Bush agreed to hear Alton’s petition, ordering J. A. Callison to show up with relevant legal documentation to Alton’s case, and for Sheriff Robert Kyd to appear with Alton on August 25. Kyd acknowledged this order, and Callison showed documentation that showed Alton was being accused of illegally selling alcohol to James W. Pace without a proper license. The outcome of the case from there is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Nicolas Brown filed for a writ of habes corpus on behalf of his sons, Alexander, aged 4, and George, aged 2. He alleged that his wife, Olive, took their sons Alexander and George and left the city of Seattle “without his consent and without any provocation or cause whatsoever”. Nicolas claimed that he should have custody over the children as he is better able to educate and support the said infants than their mother. Though a writ was issued, the petitioner’s attorney motioned for the cause to be dismissed, and the case's outcome remains unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Leroy Smith was arrested for possession of cocaine leaves and morphine in Arizona and fined $100. He was then sent from Santa Fe, New Mexico, to a penitentiary at McNeil Island, Washington, under the custody of warden O. P. Halligan. Smith petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which stated that his imprisonment and restraint by O. P. Halligan was unconstitutional. The writ was approved, and Judge Cushman ordered Smith's release.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 28, 1918, John Murray filed for habeas against Julia A. McCaustland over the custody of his 10-year-old son, Harry. Murray charged that McCaustland had taken the child after the death of his wife, the mother of the child, and that McCaustland does not provide proper care for the child, even alleging that she abuses the child. McCausland accused John being an alcoholic and having threatened to kill her if she didn't surrender the boy. She also said that Murray had no home of his own and would give the boy to his sister to raise. A writ was issued and on return McCaustland provided support that she and her husband had raised the child since 5 weeks old and had adopted at 10 months, and that John Murray had abandoned the child after the death of his wife. On August 29, Judge Estelle ruled for the writ to be dismissed and the care of Harry remain with Mrs. McCausland.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis Mische was a 34 year old citizen of the Republic of Switzerland arrested on a warrant issued by the acting Secretary of Labor, J.B. Densmore. The warrant issued on January 2, 1918, accused Mische of advocating and teaching the unlawful destruction of property. On January 12, 1918, Mische was granted a hearing with the Immigrant Inspector. Following the hearing, Louis F. Post, Assistant Secretary of Labor issued a warrant of deportation against Mische on February 16, 1918. On October 30, 1918, Mische filed for a writ of habeas corpus contending that he did not have a fair hearing. He states that he was denied his right to inspect the warrant and the evidence that the warrant was based on. He also argues that he was denied his right to legal counsel and was subject to personal abuse and intimidation which compelled him to give evidence against him. Judge Frank H. Rudkin agreed to hear the writ and ruled that the writ will be denied due to sufficient evidence to support his deportation.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 15, 1903 Joseph Winterhalter petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Winterhalter stated that he had been put on trial for an unnamed charge, and was in custody by virtue of a note from I. S. Claiborn. Claiborn’s note stated that Winterhalter had violated his bond and that he had “made violent threats against and upon the conviction the said court did judge”, and that Winterhalter should be imprisoned until a court authorized his release. Winterhalter stated that he did not know who Claiborn was and believed he did not have the jurisdiction to put him in custody. The outcome of this case and the fate of Winterhalter are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Sheriff O.P. Walter of Kansas City sent a telegram and letter to Sheriff Robert Kyd of Gage County to hold L. M. Hunter until Walter could travel to collect him, claiming that Hunter was wanted in Kansas City for “some offense.” Sheriff Kyd did detain Hunter, and Hunter filed a petition for a writ of Habeas from Judge J. E. Bush and claimed that he was being held with no warrant or other legal process. The result of the petition after the initial application, as well as the specific charges are not stated in the case, but newspaper accounts indicate Hunter was released because there is no legal cause to extradite defendants on misdemeanor charges.

Summary of Proceedings:
Louis Katz, the petitioner, was detained for the alleged crime of being both an alien and importing and bringing to the United States a woman or girl for the purpose of prostitution. Katz was first incarcerated for this, and then set to be deported to Fiume, Hungary after the commencement of his sentence. His petition argued that he was both wrongfully incarcerated for the crime of importing a women for the purpose of prostitution, as well as wrongfully set to be deported. Through Judge Edward Cushman Katz's cause was dismissed without cost and this is the latest judgment included in the case in 1912. Documents are provided afterward in 1919, and it is unclear if they are wrapping up this case or entering a new proceeding. 

It is possible the archive combined two cases into one file, with one case referring to Katz's charged crime and the other regarding his deportation, but this is unclear.

Summary of Proceedings: W.N. Parker was arrested on January 3, 1894 in Ballard, Washington on charges of obtaining money under false pretenses in Salem, Oregon. The Chief of Police of Salem H.P. Minto sent a telegram to James M. Woolery that contained the warrant for Parker’s arrest as well as sent an agent of the state of Oregon to Washington with extradition papers to receive Parker and return him to Oregon. Following his arrest, W.N. Parker’s wife Alice A. Parker filed a writ of Habeas Corpus with the help of the attorney W.T. Scott. The writ was granted but W.N. Parker would remain in custody and eventually be extradited to Salem on January 8, 1894 to stand trial.

Summary of Proceedings: Alvira E. Britton claimed that while in the process of applying for a divorce from her former husband Robert I. Kendall in 1910, she gave over custody of her baby son Robert I. Kendall Jr. to Stephen W, Bryant and Alice Bryant. She was also about to undergo a life-saving surgery. After her divorce was granted, Alvira claimed to have tried to get her son back from the Bryants, but they refused to give him back. Alvira asserted that they neglected to send Robert to school or church consistently. Alvira got remarried to John Britton and felt that she was in a position where she could provide Robert with the proper care and wanted to regain custody of her son again. The writ was allowed and the judge decreed that custody of Robert would go back to Alvira. Robert Jr. apparently wanted to stay with his foster parents, who he had been with since infancy ,crying when he had to leave them.

Summary of Proceedings: On 11 July 1912, Patty McFadon and his attorney, C. L. Hover, submitted this petition which stated that McFadon was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Sheriff Felix J. McShane under § 242 of the Criminal Code of the State of Nebraska. The petition stated that this section was invalid because it was not properly passed by the legislature. It is unclear what exactly this section criminalized as the text is not included in the Case File. Presumably, the proposed section would have criminalized vagrancy; as McFadon was charged with “vagrancy,” and was sentenced to a term of 10 days in county jail. This sentence was issued and signed by Charles E. Foster, the Omaha Police Magistrate, on 8 July 1912.On 11 July 1912, Judge A. L. Sutton of the Douglas County District Court ordered that the writ be allowed, returnable to Sheriff McShane and set a hearing before Judge Charles Leslie for that same day. The Sheriff’s return, which was filed on 15 July 1912, stated that he brought McFadon before Judge Leslie as commanded.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 16, 1864, J. W. Tripp was charged with the murder of Alexander Clarke. On May 18, Justice of the Peace William L. Chalmers ordered the sheriff to commit Tripp. On June 3, 1867, Tripp petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. The next day, Washington Supreme Court Justice Charles B. Darwin delivered the writ and subpoenaed Chalmers. The witnesses were subpoenaed in the following days. On June 10, Justice Darwin denied the writ and remanded Tripp to the custody of the respondent.

Summary of Proceedings: Tom Buras was accused of stealing a Cadillac in St. Joseph, Missouri and was arrested and incarcerated in his hometown of Omaha. However, his father, Josef Buras, assisted by Tom's attorneys John W. Baldwin and James H. Walker, filed a writ of habeas corpus on August 6, 1921, saying that Tom couldn't be guilty of the crime as he wasn't in St. Joseph at the time. Originally, the writ was addressed to police commissioner Henry Dunn, chief of police Michael Dempsey and chief of detectives Charles Van Dusen, but it was only served to Henry Dunn on the advice of Buras's attorneys. By August 8, the writ was served, but on August 12, the case was dismissed "upon motion of attorney for applicant." Census records indicate that Tom was eventually released, however, as in the 1920 census, he is living in his father's house.

Summary of Proceedings: Thomas Ross was indicted by a grand jury on August 7th, 1914, for selling whiskey to a native of the territory of Alaska and ordered to serve three years at McNeil Island Penitentiary. On March 16th, 1916, Ross filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of himself, claiming that he was being deprived of his liberty by Warden Halligan. The petitioner claimed that he had unlawfully been sentenced to three years, when the maximum penalty for the offense he was convicted on was two years and denial of his parole was not according to the "Parole Law." The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 30, 1922, Robert H. Johnson filed a second habeas petition against the sheriff of Douglas County. In his petition, Johnson explained that a complaint had been filed against him under the charge of vagrancy, was found guilty, filed an appeal - which was dismissed - and is now under a new warrant without complaint. Johnson further sought to challenge the vagrancy ordinance, Ordinance No. 10916, and alleged, in a supplemental petition, that his arrests were political. Johnson explained that he had campaigned against City Prosecutor Dineen during an election, and that his vagrancy case and 60 others are now being dismissed. A writ was issued, sustained, and Johnson was ordered to be released on January 24, 1922.

Summary of Proceedings: Sue Sing petitioned for habeas corpus based on his detention on the Steamship Danube by Captain William Meyers. The Collector of Customs, T.J. Black, refused to examine Sue Sam or any of his witnesses or qualifications because he had examined him on a previous trip and judged him as a Chinese laborer. Charles F. Sliter wrote an affidavit swearing to the court that Sue Sing is a merchant and member of the firm Goey Lung Co. located at No. 85 Second Street. The judge granted Sue Sings' writ and discharged him from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 18, 1923 Knud Knudsen was charged with selling milk and cream below the standard contrary to the ordinance of the city of Omaha, and sentenced to serve 15 days in jail. He filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on October 19, arguing that there is no ordinance authorizing a jail sentence for such offense. On this same day Knudsen was discharged, and on October 26 the judge ordered the writ to be returned.

Summary of Proceedings: In late January 1916, Charles John was arrested and charged with possessing morphine and heroin in violation of the 1914 Harrison Act. John either could not or would not pay the $2,000 bail and was therefore placed in the Douglas County jail to await a grand jury hearing. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing among other things that the Harrison Act did not criminalize individual possession of narcotics. John withdrew his petition before the judge could make a determination; his fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
George H Place attempted to regain custody of his children, Zella V. Place and Howard D. Place from Mary A. and Charles E. Dake. Place alleged that the Dakes were not educating his children, moving them from place to place, and having disreputable moral character. Place said that he was married and could provide Zella and Howard an education and take them to church. The writ was allowed, but we do not know the outcome of the children's custody. 
Another point: George H. Place seems to have also been the attorney for in a child custody case later that year- Susan M. Horn.

Summary of Proceedings: In August 1905, the Omaha Nation brought a civil suit against the U.S. Secretary of the Interior, Ethan Hitchcock, and two of his agents, William Beck and John Mackey, in the Thurston County District Court for violating an 1882 act of Congress regulating Omaha monies in the U.S. Treasury. Acting under a 1904 act of Congress, Beck and Mackey had been distributing Omaha funds to individual tribal members contrary to the wishes of the Nation. The Thurston County District Court issued a writ ne exeat compelling the two men to each pay a $500 bond ensuring that they would answer the Omaha complaint and then jailed them when they refused. Beck and Mackey petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, they were released from custody, to which the Omaha Nation excepted.

Summary of Proceedings: In April of 1885, Wilson D. Coyle assaulted Charles Seaman and was sentenced to 60 days in jail and ordered to pay a $200 fine for his crimes in May of 1885. After serving 60 days in jail, Coyle was still being held in jail, as he had not yet paid his fines.Coyle then filed a writ of habeas corpus on July 3, 1885, claiming that he was being unlawfully imprisoned for longer than his term. On the same day, Judge George Turner allowed the writ and ordered Coyle and Sheriff E. J. Whittier to appear in front of him in court. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party is unknown.

The petition is missing from the case file, but newspaper records indicated Linton was being held in the Seattle City Jail. Warren and McBride alleged they arrested Linton under “suspicious circumstances which justified his arrest” and held him originally on an open charge. Summary of Proceedings: On February 10, 1919, Ruth McLane filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming the chief of police, Marshall Eberstein, was unlawfully detaining her of her liberty. Her lawyer, John Berger, had been arrested along with her. He was the former city prosecutor and accused the current prosecutor of falsely accusing him. He filed petitions for Dollie Dean and Nellie Atkins as well, who were arrested with McLane. She claimed that on February 8, she was arrested and charged with being an inmate of a common and ill-governed house and with vagrancy and prostitution. She paid the bond of one hundred dollars, promising that she would appear in court on February 10, which she did, and pled not guilty. However, the courts found her guilty, sentenced her to serve ninety days in the county jail, and pay a one-hundred-dollar fine. She filed a notice of appeal and paid the four-hundred-dollar fixed bond, which the police magistrate accepted and filed. The magistrate told the chief of police and keeper of the jail that they should release McLane. Although they accepted the release, they refused to deliver up to and release her body. This was apparently because she refused to submit to a physical examination by the Health Department. She remained detained at the city jail without being charged with any offense or violation. The judge accepted McLane’s petition and filed a writ of habeas corpus. An Omaha Daily Bee Article states that McLane was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Rooney is charged with the burglarizing of a saloon in the city of Omaha. Specifically, with the taking of cigars, he is given a bail amount of five hundred dollars on July 28th of 1882. He is then found guilty along with Thomas Ruby and Manus Correll by Police Judge Gustave Anderson. He petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus. With this petition, he asserted that the building in question, the saloon, is not protected under Nebraska law because it is a retail liquor saloon. A jury in the courtroom of Judge James Neville allowed the writ and discharged Rooney from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Danish person and resident alien Edward E. McDonald, also known as Anton Jenson and A. George Jensen, filed for a second writ of habeas corpus on February 6, 1919. Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid held McDonald under the authority of immigration officials, including A. F. Richardson and the Secretary of Labor, for advocating the teaching of the unlawful destruction of property. Case similarities related to dates and allegations levied against McDonald point to other arrests of I.W.W. members in the Pacific Northwest. Judge Frank H. Rudkin dismissed the writ because the Department of Labor complaint had “ample evidence to support and sustain the finding complained of.”

Summary of Proceedings: John Brown was charged and arrested for disorderly conduct on July 2nd, 1894. While his hearing went on, it became known that he had threatened the life of his wife, Mary Brown. Upon that, he was acquitted and the judge ordered that he be recharged on the account of his beating of his wife. However, upon being discharged and then rearrested, Brown filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus. The application was granted on the account that his second arrest was illegal and without due process of law. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 29, 1913, J. R. Moore and his attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and alleged that Moore was being detained under a void warrant from British Columbia, falsely charging him with conspiracy to defraud. Moore claimed there was no cause or valid warrant for his arrest, and that he was unlawfully denied bail. Judge Gilliam granted the writ, and allowed Moore bail in the sum of $10,000. Gilliam set the case to be heard in Judge Ronald’s court, who agreed that there was no valid cause for detainment. Ronald approved the petition, and Moore was released.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 24th, 1921, a petition for a writ of habeas corpus was filed on behalf of Agnes Smith. The petition was filed by her mother Mary Foley and step-father Thomas Foley. The Foleys alleged that Agnes was being unlawfully detained at the Institute for Feeble-Minded Youth (Beatrice, NE) by Superintendent S.J. Stewart. The Foleys explained that in 1914, Agnes was committed to the Girls' Industrial School (Geneva, NE) by the Juvenile Court of Douglas County. She was to be detained there for a period of 2 years, but was instead detained for 5 years. Agnes was then committed to the Institute for Feeble-Minded Youth against her will and consent and without the knowledge of her parents. The Foleys asserted that Agnes was not feeble-minded, and wished for Agnes to be released. The judge initially granted the petition, but quickly recalled the sheriff from issuing the writ after a special appearance from S. J. Stewart. In the appearance, Stewart objected to the jurisdictional authority of the court because Agnes was detained in Gage County. The judge agreed with Stewart on the matter, citing case Gillard v. Clark in his decision. The judge dismissed the petition at the cost of the petitioner. The fate of Agnes Smith is unknown. Additionally, the age of Agnes is unclear. She was not referred to as a minor in the case file, and it is possible that she reached the age of majority between 1913 and 1921 but remained detained because of her “feeble-minded” status.

He appealed to the state supreme court, which upheld the decision of the lower court.

Summary of Proceedings: Hans A. Hulke filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on May 24th, 1921, after being arrested with no complaint filed against him. He argued that Michael F. Dempsey was holding him in custody illegally and that no evidence or affidavit had been provided to justify his arrest. The judge agreed to hear his plea and ordered Dempsey to return Hulke to court for a petition hearing. The petition's outcome is unknown; however, the suit was continued in a separate case file. Newspaper coverage indicates Hulke was arrested for extradition on embezzlement charges in his role as a collection agent.

Summary of Proceedings: Lem You held the three bound parties in addition to 40-50 other Chinese women, all of whom he intended to sell. Wah Kim claimed that You was wrongfully imprisoning these three girls and filed a habeas petition on their behalf. Writ was granted for girls to be released "forthwith." You denied every allegation, even denying that the girls concerned were those that Wah Lee claimed. He claimed that the girls were in Omaha for the Trans-Mississippi Exposition to show Chinese customs. Witnesses were called. It appears that the three girls were placed into the sheriff's custody and designated to the care of a Dr. Wycoff. Unknown final result.

On October 13, 1919, William C. Messick filed a writ of habeas corpus for the release of his four-year-old daughter, Dorthey Messick, from the home of George Abshier, her maternal grandfather. Dorthey was living with her mother, Jennie A. Messick and Absheir. 

Judge A. W. Frater allowed the writ and Sheriff John Stringer went to Absheir’s home, obtained Dorothey, and gave her to William on October 14, 1919. Abshier and Jennie returned the writ claiming marital neglect, calling William “a gambler and moral degenerate.” William replied to the return, stating that Jennie was an adulteress and had been living in California for two years in an extramarital relationship with Dan Medinica. William also asked to be granted custody of Dorthey. 

The case file ends with a 1922 order from the King County Superior Court to allow William to withdraw certain “letters, checks, and other papers” as exhibits in the habeas proceedings.

Summary of Proceedings: Sigmond Seaman was arrested for “unlawfully and maliciously keeping and harboring a certain dog without procuring a license and tag.” He appealed thai charge, listing multiple reasons why the ordinance he was being charged under should be null and void. Seaman further alleges that his appeal was unlawfully refused by the police judge, J. A. Callison, who sentenced Seaman to be fined and held in jail by John J. Hursman. Seaman then filed for a writ of habeas corpus from Judge Davis, which was granted and a hearing scheduled for July 16, 1897, but the result of said hearing is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In the summer of 1905, an Omaha Indian man named Louis Dick petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his two children, whom he called Lucy and Emory, claiming the pair were being detained at the Genoa Indian Industrial School. The school's superintendent, W. H. Winslow, responded that Louis had enrolled Lucy for a three-year term in the fall of 1903, and that Emory, whom Winslow said was actually called Emily, was enrolled at Genoa by order of the Thurston County District Court in January 1904. After hearing the evidence, the Dick children were remanded to the custody of the school superintendent.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 7, 1914, Alex Petosky filed for a writ of habeas corpus against Sheriff Edward Cudihee, asserting that he was being held without a charge. Cudihee produced documentation that James M. Cox, the governor of Ohio, Ernest Lister, the governor of Washington, and Justice Fred C. Brown had all called for his arrest on the charge of being a fugitive from justice. Petosky’s original charge was for the crime of deserting, because he was said to have deserted his two children Lulu, age 8, and Leslie, age 7. Petosky claimed that he had previously moved from Ohio to Washington with his (unnamed) wife and children in order to make better money, but that his wife treated him poorly and forced him to move back to Ohio, where her family lived. Petosky said he was unable to make enough money there, so he came back to Washington. He attempted to bring his wife and children, but she repeatedly refused. Petosky filed for divorce and asked for full custody of his children, while his wife asked for alimony. Petosky said he was granted the divorce and full custody. The case indicates that during these proceedings Petosky's now ex-wife illegally maintained custody of his children. He claimed that the desertion and fugitive of justice charges were attempts by his wife and her family to defame him, and gain access to the land he had bought in Ohio. Judge A. W. Frater allowed the writ to be heard. Petosky’s fate and the outcome of this case are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 2, 1913, Glenn E. Hoover, a free speech attorney,  and George H. Hodgdon with their attorney J. Siegfried petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. They claimed that they were being held for contempt of court in the case The State of Washington vs. McNally et al.. They also stated that in that case, the defendants filed affidavits of prejudice against the judge, John E. Humphries. Hoover and Hodgdon said the affidavits void their contempt of court charges, in accordance with state laws. Newspaper coverage indicates that Judge Smith freed both men, along with a variety of other Seattle Socialists held in contempt by Humphries. Humphries attempted to disbar Hoover without a trial. Newspapers also indicate other judges verbally opposed Humphries' apparent abuses of power.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 26, 1901, George E. Daniel and his attorney petitioned for writ of habeas corpus. In the petition, Daniel claimed he was being held illegally by Chief of Police John Sullivan. Daniel stated that he was being held on a warrant from Yukon Territory, Canada, where he was charged with embezzlement, but that the four men who had sued him for embezzlement had dropped the charges. Daniel claimed that Sullivan had the release from the four men, but refused to honor it. Judge Bell issued the writ. The outcome of this case and Daniel’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In December 1913, Gregori Kornilin and 8 other immigrants from Russia arrived in Seattle, Washington via the steamship "Tamba Maru" after being denied from their desired location, Canada. The Russian immigrants were held for special inquiry by the Immigrant Inspector and Board of Special Inquiry. The board rejected the immigrants as they were "persons likely to become a public charge" and that Russian immigrants were common or farm laborers, and stated there is no work for them. 
The Russian immigrants petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus which stated the petitioners were in good health, able bodied, and able to take care of themselves. The petition further stated that the petitioners were not held by the Immigration Commissioner upon any process issued by a court of common jurisdiction. 
In a return to the petition, Henry M. White, Commissioner of Immigration, admitted petitioners were not held upon a process issued by a U.S. or state court but alleged a valid and lawful reason for their detention. Judge Jeremiah Neterer granted the writ of habeas corpus and discharged the petitioners on the grounds that the petitioners were not excluded by provisions of the Immigration Act of Feb. 20, 1907, and the reasons given by the board of special inquiry did not permit the petitioners to become public charges. 
Henry M. White appealed the decision stating that it did not matter whether the immigration authorities erred in their interpretation of the law or finding of their facts, the courts had no authority to interfere. White further stated that the matter is "res adjudicata" unless the case of "In Re Unlawful Detention of Mullah Sing and Seventy-two other Hindu Aliens" has been reversed by the Supreme Court, as that decision ruled the jurisdiction of the court is limited to ascertaining whether the petitioners were denied a hearing. 
The petitioners and their attorney responded in a brief that the petitioners' exclusion was unlawful as they were not excluded upon statutory ground. The brief further stated the claim there is a shortage of farm laborers is absurd. On June 22nd, 1914, the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's decision with instruction to dismiss the writ of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1923, Richard J. Organ filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Charles Flournoy. The petitioner alleged that Flournoy was committed and detained by Michael L. Endres (Sheriff of Douglas County), and the Superintendent of the Douglas County Hospital. Organ states the confinement was without an order or judgment from a civil or criminal jurisdiction, under the pretense that Flournoy was mentally insane. The petition stated the confinement was illegal and contrary to law as Flournoy was of sound mind and capable of "taking care of himself and his business." Judge Charles A. Goss authorized the writ of Habeas Corpus. At trial, Michal L. Endres, stated Flournoy was not in his custody and the writ was returned without further action.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1903, Charles "Chick" Houghton was arrested in Multnomah County, Oregon, convicted of robbery, and sentenced to five years at the state penitentiary. In 1906, Houghton was granted "conditional clemency," or parole, by the governor and released from prison early with the understanding that he would be returned to finish his sentence if convicted of any crime. He was then arrested again in Multnomah County, convicted of larceny, and returned to the state penitentiary. Houghton appealed this decision to the state supreme court and then filed a writ of habeas corpus in the Marion County Circuit Court, which was granted. Houghton argued that his detention was illegitimate since his conviction was under appeal. After hearing the evidence, the Circuit Court dismissed Houghton's petition and remanded him to the custody of the state penitentiary. Houghton immediately appealed this decision to the state supreme court, too. In early 1907, the state supreme court upheld the lower court's ruling.

Summary of Proceedings: Harry Meehan was arrested on February 7th for carrying a concealed weapon. Since he worked seasonally for the police as a dog catcher, he claimed that he was allowed to concealed carry. Harry filed a petition for habeas corpus on February 11th. The petition was approved; however, the response to the writ and outcome are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Domenico Lazzaro, often referred to as Frank Rossi, and his wife, Bambino, were arrested and faced deportation over alleged violations of the Immigration Act of February 5, 1917. Domenico and Bambino were accused of managing a house of prostitution and were ordered to be deported to Italy. In her writ of habeas corpus, Bambino stated that there was not enough evidence to justify deportation, and that she should be deported to Canada and not Italy since she entered the United States from Canada. In Domenico’s case file, the Immigration Inspector, Luther Weedin notes that while Domenico lived in Canada for three years before moving to the United States, Bambino had never lived outside of the United States after migrating in 1900. 

Judge Jeremiah Neterer denied Bambino’s writ for habeas corpus and ordered that she remain in the custody of the Seattle Immigration Inspector and is subject to deportation. Following this ruling, Bambino immediately appealed the decision. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals later affirmed Judge Neterer’s initial ruling and on January 25, 1927 Bambino Lazzaro was deported to Italy from the port of New York.

Summary of Proceedings: John Howard, confined in the Douglas County jail, was facing extradition to Canada for his alleged involvement in several crimes. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming, among other things, that the procedure leading to his arrest and detention were inconsistent with treaty obligations between the United States and Canada. The court consolidated his petition with those of Arthur Wyse, Axel Pierson, and Harry Compton. After hearing the evidence, his writ was denied and Howard remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: Walter Britton and John Trigg filed a joint petition claiming they were being indefinitely imprisoned due to their inability to pay a fine. Subsequent documentation shows that they had been accused and found guilty of being drunk and disorderly and disturbing a religious meeting on December 17, 1899. Britton and Trigg were then ordered to be fined $26.70 and $26.40 respectively and to be held for 13.5 days or until the fine was paid. Judge Jacobs grants their writ and sees them released from their imprisonment.

Summary of Proceedings: Hong Sing petitioned for habeas on behalf of his friend Ah You, who claimed to be a merchant eligible for re-entry into the United States within the terms of the Chinese Exclusion law. Summary of Proceedings: It was November 1924 when James Dolezol petitioned for and received an order of writ of Habeas Corpus after being arrested and held in custody by Dennis H. Cronin and Micheal L, Endres in July of that year. Dolezol had been charged with violation of the National Prohibition Act and had been given a hearing for said charges where he was sentenced to three months imprisonment on two counts and a fine of $400. In his petition he presented that he was being unlawfully depreciated of his liberty and held in custody for longer than the imposed time of imprisonment. In December of the same year the court agreed, and he was discharged. In March of 1925 Cronin and Endres filed for and were allowed an appeal based on assignments of error. They presented that the imprisonment of three months on two accounts was ordered to run consecutively meaning that time of imprisonment would be six months and that the time of imprisonment was imposed until the fine was paid of which Dolezol had not paid. It was February of the following year that the Circuit Court of Appeals made the order to reverse the December 1924 order allowing the writ of Habeas Corpus and to remand Dolezol to custody in compliance with the decision of the case Cronin, U.S. Marshal et al., vs Wiliam J. Fox. which was carried out later that month.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 6th, J. C. Christopher and his attorneys, Bell and Dalton, petitioned for a Writ of Habeas Corpus. Christopher argued that he was held without warrant or due process of law by the King County sheriff, Rober T. Hodge. In his return, Hodge stated that Christopher was in his custody due to a warrant issued by the Governor of Washington, stating that Christopher should have been held until E. E. Harrison could get him. Harrison was a duly authorized agent of Utah, and Christopher was being held to be taken by Harrison back to Utah because he was charged for the crime of neglecting to provide for his wife. The Governor’s warrant for extradition was actually signed on May 4th, and aligns with Hodge’s arguments. It calls for the arrest of Christopher as he is a fugitive from justice from the State of Utah, and that he still stands charged for his crimes charged to him on January 15th, 1912. Judge J. T. Ronald of King County Superior Court allows the writ and sets a court date for May 6th at 1:30 pm, the same day as the petition and respondent’s reply. On May 7th, however, the petitioner’s reply is signed and filed, which reiterated Christopher’s argument that he was not a fugitive from justice and that he has not been charged with an extraditable offense. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
On May 10, 1892, Ludwig Kostrouch was charged with the crime of grave robbery. On June 11, 1892 he was punished with confinement for one year at the County Jail of King County and fined $500. Over a year later, on June 29, 1893, Kostrouch continued to remain in confinement due to being unable to pay the fine. Kostrouch’s attorney, Fred Zick, contended that since Kostrouch did not have the financial ability to pay, the court erred in granting him that punishment. Thus, only the one-year confinement should be honored, and Kostrouch should have his liberty restored from Sheriff James H. Woolery. 

According to the Seattle Post- Intelligencer, printed on April 23, 1892 on page 8, Kostrouch had aided in stealing the body as a part of the Radloffs' conspiracy to collect William Radloff's life insurance.

Hoffman was arrested and tried on court June 10, and fined 100 in costs. On June 13, Hoffman filed for habeas charging that such complaint had not be properly signed, that such complaint did not have sufficient facts to be prosecuted, that liquor in private apartment does not break Nebraska laws, and that he did not have proper access to council before and during trial. The petition was granted, but final outcome and fate of Hoffman unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Loui Won petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Louis Lin Hoon, a partner in his firm, Hop Chung, located at No. 60 Second Street and Pine Street. Louis Lin Hoon was being held on the Steamship Singal by Captain Bendergard after a visit to China, as they believed he was returning in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. The case file contains the trial transcript, including the witness who signed an initial affidavit to his merchant status and the petitioner, Loui Won, as the managing partner of their firm. The Judge granted the writ and released Louis Lin Hoon from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Yellow Sun, Little Wolf, Horse Driver, and Blue Hawk petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus and Judge George Lake released them on bail of six thousand dollars. With this agreement Yellow Sun et al. must later then appear in the District Court for Lancaster County. Interested parties, Eagle Chief and Tera-cowah acknowledged themselves as indebted to the State of Nebraska for five thousand dollars. Then, Samuel M. Janney and Jacob M. Troth also acknowledged themselves indebted in the same manner, but for the sum of one thousand dollars. 
(The portion after this comes from the additional sources, and is not in the document utilized for encoding into air table.) 

This allowed for all of the petitioners to be released as long as they returned to Lancaster for further proceedings in October. Lastly, in October of 1871, Judge Lake released them without bail and struck the case, with the provision that if new evidence is available within 28 months they will be tried again. After 28 months passes they were truly free from proceedings.

Summary of Proceedings: Jessie's mother, Rhoda, filed for a writ of habeas corpus. She placed her son under the care of Louis Figgins, but later claimed that Figgins (Fagan) unlawfully held her son and would not release him into her care. After hearing the evidence, Jessie was remanded to the custody of Figgins. In 1898, the county was ordered to pay the costs of the petition; it is unclear what prompted this payment or the impact it had on Fiandt's position.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 25th, 1912, Carmelo Spezzi petitioned on behalf of Diamico Oct and Vincenzo Perrino for their freedom. According to Spezzi and the bound individuals’ lawyer, Paul W. Houser, Oct and Perrino were employed by Puget Sound Traction, Light and Power Company in San Francisco. In San Francisco, they were promised free transportation to Renton, Washington, where the company had a coal mine, in which they would work. Upon their arrival, they allege that they were told that they then belonged to the company and owed the cost of their transportation, which Oct and Perrino refused to pay, citing that they had been told it would be free. At this point, Oct and Perrino allege that they were threatened with bodily harm, violence, and even death to remain in the stockade outside the mine, and then they were forced to work in the said mine.  Judge J.T. Ronald approved their application for a writ of Habeas Corpus on October 25th, 1912, and on the same day the writ was delivered to the President of the company, Jacob Furth. On October 26th, in court, the company responded to the claims of Oct and Perrino’s lawyer, retorting that they had never held Oct or Perrino and that they were free to sever ties with the company any time they pleased. This statement was given by the Assistant to the Manager George B. Harrington, who continued to say that the company also paid for transportation from the mines to the courtroom for the bound parties, and they were free to offer their opinion. However, the case file concludes there, and thus, the fate of Oct and Perrino remain unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
W. E. Walker, friend of A. Sokolow, attempted to visit Sokolow in Seattle City Jail. City jail staff refused Walker, stating that Sokolow was held by the Department of Justice, and that Walker needed to obtain written permission from the United States Attorney’s office and also the office of the special agent. Walker attempted to obtain these written permissions from the appropriate authorities and “was informed at both places that they had no jurisdiction over said plaintiff.” 

Walker obtained an attorney, Kazis Krazauozunas, to file a petition for Sokolow’s release. Judge John S. Jurey issued the writ on on February 28, 1918. The fate pf Sokolow is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Johnson was a Norwegian migrant that was arrested and subject to deportation on the accusation of advocating for the unlawful destruction of property. In his petition for writ of habeas corpus, Johnson argued that he was denied his right to counsel, his right to examine the warrant and the evidence within, and was subjected to “personal abuse and intimidations” which compelled him to give evidence against himself. Judge Frank H. Rudkin agreed to hear Robinson’s petition for writ of habeas corpus. Rudkin ruled on Charles Johnson, John Perish and Emery Sarracin cases at the same time. In his ruling, Rudkin referenced his opinions in his rulings for In re Holm and In re G. S. Marhow. Rudkin noted that while these migrants were members of the International Workers of the World, there was no evidence that substantiated the claim that they advocated for the unlawful destruction of property. As such, Rudkin ruled that John Perish and the other two migrants were unlawfully restrained of their liberty and ordered their release from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Phillis petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in an attempt to retrieve Julia from the custody of Robert Duncan and Sally Adams. Phillis asserted that she was a free woman, that Julia was her daughter, and that Robert and Sally were illegally enslaving her child. Robert and Sally claimed that they purchased Julia from John Sutton and, although they acknowledged Julia's freedom, cast doubts on Phillis' maternity while claiming that Julia wished to remain with them. Julia's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1919, Jennie Greenwald petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her husband, Harry Greenwald. The petition alleged Harry was imprisoned and detained by F. D. Simons, referred to as the "agent in charge of the department of justice", who was about to extradite Harry to the state of California without any just legal process or authority of law. Simons received a telegraph, the contents unknown to the petitioner, that stated Harry would be immediately removed to California, and charged with an offense which was not disclosed to the petitioner. The writ was not served at the request of Harry's attorney, and in a later order from the judge, it was revealed the petitioner was discharged in said cause and ordered the petition to be dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: S. G. Linton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham. Linton alleged he was being illegally held in the Seattle City Jail with no charge against him and was being denied both bail and access to his friends or attorneys. The outcome of the case and the fate of Linton are unknown. This is the second time Linton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Beckingham. Newspaper coverage links Linton to smuggling alcohol and refers to him as "Peanuts S. G. Linton, underworld character."

Summary of Proceedings: The petitioner, John W Harding, was charged with accessory to murder Peter Gallager. The petitioner filed for habeas corpus on the basis that he was more than 20 miles away from the place where Gallager was killed. However, when he came to court to testify, he was arrested for withholding knowledge about Gallager’s murder and refusing to pay bail at his appearance. The petition and writ were granted on the basis that there was not sufficient grounds for confinement, and the petitioner was released from custody. The county was required to pay the $132.45 in court fees.

Summary of Proceedings: Williams Alfredo petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on May 18th, 1917, claiming that he was being unlawfully detained by Omaha police in the city jail. Alfredo's petition claimed that he was a stranger in the city and had not committed any crime. Judge Willis G. Sears granted his petition and issued a writ commanding Chief of Police Henry W. Dunn, Captain Heitfeldt, and Chief of Detectives Stephan Maloney to appear and show the time and cause of Alfredo's detention. Sheriff Michael L. Clark delivered the writ to Dunn; Heitfeldt and Maloney were not served. The outcome of the proceedings is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 16, 1887, Gus Bendjus, Robert Strangland, Ben Fredericksen, John Blending, Frank Nelson, Andrew Johnson, Leander Brown, John Thompson, Alex Agren, Charles Burke, and Thomas Jacobs met with their comrades in the Gray's Harbor Branch of the Columbia Fisherman's Protective Association at the group's headquarters in Aberdeen, Washington. After some discussion, various groups set out to destroy wealthy businessmen's traps on the river. Bendjus and his friends destroyed Wililam Church's, causing $650 in damage. A warrant for their arrest was filed the same day for one count of rioting and two counts of malicious mischief, and they were found guilty by a grand jury. They petitioned for their freedom, but this was denied on October 17, 1887. However, all of the men were released on a $400 bail on October 19, 1887.

Summary of Proceedings: Hiura originally came to the U.S. as a stowaway on the Tacoma Maru in 1914, and resided in Tacoma until October 1919, when he made a visit to Japan. Upon his return, at the Port of Seattle, Hiura was charged with obtaining a passport under false pretenses and liable of becoming a public charge. The Board of Special Inquiry, consisting of three inspectors, grounded their ruling on the notion the passport should not have been issued. On appeal, Hiura's agent argued no evidence was submitted supporting the notion Hiura would be liable to become a public charge, and regarding the false passport, argued the passport is not the foundation of Hiura's right to be in the United States and the rights of an immigrant must rest upon facts aliunde the passport. The exclusion decision from the Board of Special Inquiry was affirmed and a deportation order was suggested. Hiura then petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in which Hiura's attorney argued the petitioner was arbitrarily excluded and denied admission because of prejudice and the Board of Special Inquiry was not legally constituted. Citing Section 17 of the Immigration Act, the petition argued the Special Inquiry Board needs to consist of three members/officers, whereas in said case the board was composed of two inspectors and a stenographer. Looking at the Board of Special Inquiry minutes, an "Anna Mullen" was named as the stenographer, and later a "Miss Mullen" was noted as the third vote for the exclusion of Hiura. The petition further questions the Board's authority to sit as a court of error and appeal to review the issuance of a passport. Juge Neterer ruled the confinement and restraint of the petitioner was unlawful, and that said petitioner is entitled to be admitted into the United States.

Summary of Proceedings: In May 1872, William Kirkland pled guilty to the murder of Andrew Campbell in Chehalis County, Washington Territory. Newspaper coverage indicated that Kirkland claimed to have killed Campbell in self defense during a land dispute. In August 1872, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, citing procedural and jurisdictional concerns, which was granted. Although his fate is unknown, his petition seems to have compelled Judge Roger Greene to subpoena multiple witnesses.

Summary of Proceedings:
John W. Hall was arrested on May 15, 1890 on a warrant issued by Justice John F. Miller. Hall was held in the King County Jail by Sheriff John Harte McGraw without a hearing. Hall was charged with the crime of "conducting a swindling gambling game of bunco" on May 13th and his first hearing was set for May 19th. Hall submitted a writ of habeas corpus for being restricted of his liberty. Hall’s writ was heard by Judge Thomas J. Humes on May 17. No outcome of the writ is stated in the record. 

James Sanford also filed for habeas corpus after being charged with the same crime. Both men filed on the same day. (See: hc.case.wa.0821)

Summary of Proceedings: On December 24, 1902, Mrs. L Gemmell went to the couple Nelson and Marion Farleigh to ask for the return of her 8-year-old child, Wallace Gemmell. Mrs. Gemmell had not been living with her husband and Wallace’s father, George Gemmell. However, she had retained full control and custody over Wallace. When the Farleighs refused to give up Wallace, Mrs. Gemmell filed for a writ of habeas corpus on December 26, 1902. Her writ was delivered to Judge Bell by Sheriff Cudihee, and accepted the same day.

Reilly and Christy Reilly, the petitioners, adopted Ruth Reilly in October of 1920 with a decree from the Juvenile Divison of the Circuit Court of New Madrid County, Missouri. Martin and Christy Reilly then filed a writ of Habeas Corpus is issued so they could possess sole custody of Ruth. Judge Leslie ordered the writ of Habeas Corpus to be allowed, and Martin and Christy Reilley were issued custody of Ruth.

Summary of Proceedings:
Note that the events discussed in the petition took place in March 1913. Bernard Uphoff’s criminal complaint against Anthony C. Wagner was filed on 22 July 1915. Wagner’s petition for a writ of habeas corpus was filed on 9 August 1915.
On 22 July 1915, Bernard Uphoff made a criminal complaint against Anthony C. Wagner before the Justice of the Peace in Logan County, CO. On 1 August 1915, the Governor of Colorado issued a requisition and demand on the Governor of Nebraska for the arrest and return of Anthony C. Wagner. The NE Governor issued a warrant for Wagner’s arrest, he was taken into custody by Chief Henry Dunn of the Omaha Police Department. The filed complaint alleged a violation of §1849 of the 1908 Colorado Revised Statutes (which concerns the fraudulent taking of another’s personal property), but the actual complaint did not charge any violation of the provisions of said section. 
Anthony Wagner filed a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus on 9 August 1915 stating that he was being unlawfully imprisoned by Omaha Chief of Police Henry Dunn and Michael Dempsey, who was the acting Chief of Police in Omaha. Dempsey is crossed out from further records and a writ was never delivered to him. He also asked that a writ be served to Samuel Patterson who was the Sheriff of Logan County, CO.
Wagner’s petition alleged that his interaction with Bernard Uphoff took place in Platte County, NE. Uphoff’s complaint alleged that he and Wagner had communicated about a mortgage in March 1913 in Logan County, CO. Wagner’s petition stated that neither he nor Uphoff were in Logan County, CO during that month and, further, that they had not even communicated about the mortgage during that month.
The issue was based on a specific parcel of land in Cheyenne County, NE (the Southwest Quarter of Section 31, Township 17, Range 52, West of the 6th Prime Meridian). Wagner stated that he was the true, legal owner of this parcel on 4 March 1913 and for several days thereafter. In early March of 1913, Wagner offered to purchase a “valuable” piece of real estate from Uphoff. Uphoff’s complaint stated that the value of this parcel was part of the deal made between the parties. Uphoff alleged that Wagner stated that the value of the land would grant him the income needed to pay for the real estate that Uphoff was selling. On 4 March 1913, Uphoff and Wagner negotiated a loan of $2,080.00. On 8 March 1913, Wagner conveyed his interest in the parcel to A. E. Butler. This deed was filed on 19 March 1913 in Book 11, Page 308 of the Cheyenne County, NE Deed Records. Wagner’s complaint noted that the parcel was worth at least $3,000 (exceeding the loan value between Uphoff and Wagner). 
Uphoff filed a complaint in Colorado. By removing the complaint from Nebraska and filing in the Colorado court system, Uphoff was able to allege wrongdoing under the aforementioned Colorado Statute (presumably, there was not a parallel statute on the books in Nebraska). At the time the complaint was filed in Colorado, Wagner was incredibly ill with tuberculosis and was unable to travel. Based on improper defense, the Logan County Justice of the Peace David Beattle filed a verdict in favor of Uphoff assessing damages at $7,000.00. Wagner’s complaint stated that, at most, he owed Uphoff $3,600.00. He stated that he would settle to pay that amount, but Uphoff refused and, instead, moved for Wagner to be arrested and made to pay the full amount. 
Uphoff’s complaint asserted that Wagner had fraudulently misrepresented his ownership in the parcel. Wagner’s petition stated that he had never intended to defraud Uphoff and, further, that his actions had not constituted fraud. 
The Appearance Docket notes that on 10 August 1915 Judge James P. English ordered that Wagner’s writ be allowed and that he be dismissed from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 18, 1922, Toney Spaeth was found guilty of violating the National Prohibition Law and ordered to pay a fine of $500. Since Spaeth could not pay the $500, he was ordered to be imprisoned until the fine and costs were discharged. Spaeth was already serving time for another unrelated charge. Due to this, the court ruled that his sentence to pay off the fine would be cumulative and begin after the petitioner was served his sentence for his other charge. Spaeth filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that the court could not make the sentence for his inability to pay his fine cumulative since the other sentence was rendered in a different jurisdiction. Judge J. Stanley Webster denied Spaeth's petition for writ of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings:
On August 9, 1919, Agnes Marshall was arrested without a warrant at No. 1613 North 16th Street, where she says she was working caring for a woman named Mrs. Ashmore. She was taken to the city jail until she paid a bail of $300. After she did, the police judge demanded that she be released, but the head matron at the detention home where she was being held, Alta Burger, refused to let her go until she had been tested for venereal disease. This indicates that Marshall was originally arrested for prostitution, despite it not being explicitly said in the case. However, Marshall refused to be tested unless her doctor was present. Therefore, on August 13, 1919, Marshall filed a writ of habeas corpus against Burger.  While the petition was allowed, the case was eventually dismissed for want of prosecution on January 30, 1920, with Marshall responsible for paying all costs.
Newspaper coverage indicates Marshall was arrested for vagrancy and applied for habeas along with Mamie Allen and Ruth Mathews.

Summary of Proceedings: Doo Woon filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he claimed he was being illegally detained by Portland Chief of Police William Watkinds. Doo Woon was arrested by Chief Watkinds on the suspicion that Doo Woon was a fugitive on the run for a crime committed in California. Judge Matthew Deady disagreed with the imprisonment, and granted the writ and Doo Woon was released from detainment. Included in the case file is Judge Deady’s full legal opinion.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 12, 1889 William Cohrane, sheriff of King County, Washington Territory, arrested and jailed Joseph Mifford. Two days later Mifford and his attorneys filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus claiming that Mifford's arrest was illegal in that Cochrane acted under no legal authority, gave Mifford no reason for his arrest, and in that Mifford was being held in jail without due process of law. The same day as Mifford filed a petition, Thomas Burke, judge of the third judicial district of Washington Territory, granted said petition. The fate of Mifford and the case is unknown following Burke's order granting Mifford's petition.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 11th, 1915, Francis Stephen Medcraf petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being deprived of his liberty by respondent Robert T. Hodge, Sheriff of King County. Medcraf was arrested for violating a Washington statute requiring all practitioners of dentistry to be licensed. The statute, amended in 1901, required applicants to have a diploma from a college of dentistry and pass examination before the board of dentistry. The statute exempted Washington citizens practicing dentistry at the time of passage. Medcraf moved to Seattle in 1908 and opened up his own dental practice, applied to the State Board of Dentistry for a license, and paid the fee for examination but was denied due to not having a diploma from a college of dentistry. The petition stated Medcraf had 22 years of dental experience and alleged the statute violated due process and equal protection as it created a privileged class as it benefited dentists, not on account of merit, but on account of having a diploma or location of residence at time the statute was enacted. Judge Neterer balanced many competing precedents and ultimately sided with the respondents who cited precedents which established provisions for determining the qualifications of those engaging in the practice of medicine was not open to question and cited cases in which requiring a diploma to practice dentistry was upheld and not found to be discriminatory. The writ was denied, and the petitioner was remanded to custody.  Medcraf petitioned for an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court and supplemental research revealed that the Washington statute was upheld and Medcraf was remanded to custody once again.
