Summary of Proceedings: Louie Charles was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Charles was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Charles and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Charles argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. On June 27, the writ of habeas was sustained, and Charles was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Wong Chung petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Wong Ying, who was being held on the Steamship Danube by Captain William Meyers. Wong Ying was not permitted to enter the port because of suspicion that he was a Chinese laborer and arriving in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. Wong Chung argues in the petition that Wong Ying is a merchant and thus exempt from exclusion. Judge Bellinger grants the writ and releases Wong Ying from custody as a verified merchant.

Summary of Proceedings: Harry Compton, confined in the Douglas County jail, was facing extradition to Canada for his alleged involvement in several crimes. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming, among other things, that the procedure leading to his arrest and detention were inconsistent with treaty obligations between the United States and Canada. The court consolidated his petition with those of Arthur Wyse, Axel Pierson, and John Howard. After hearing the evidence, his writ was denied and Compton remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Warren arrested Joe Adometis on July 17, 1919 under suspicion of wife mistreatment and misconduct with another man’s wife in the state of Illinois. Adometis’ lawyer, Van C. Summary of Proceedings: Sometime in 1896, James Murray and “Mrs. Murray” adopted a girl named Violet and introduced her into the family. The Murray couple would frequently quarrel and the two separated, though custody over their beloved child Violet was still an unresolved issue. James Murray made a claim to Violet by establishing himself as an appointed guardian in a court hearing in British Columbia in 1903, and Mr. Murray most probably had Violet in his possession at this time. Sometime near April 14th, 1905, Violet was taken and brought to the United States by Mrs. Murray, and Mrs. Murray’s mother, Mary Jane Durham, filed adoption papers with the Washington State Probate Court recognizing her as the legal caregiver of Violet. James Murray filed a writ of habeas corpus on July 29, 1905 in an attempt to secure custody over his foster daughter, claiming that he had original guardianship. The writ was issued but was later quashed upon hearing by Judge George E. Morris, and James Murray was made to pay the court fees.

Summary of Proceedings: John Owen was sentenced to five years in the Nebraska State Penitentiary in 1909 for unspecified reasons. In September 1910, he was granted parole by the governor. Owen found a job and began working, but was imprisoned the following month after the governor rescinded the parole. Owen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus challenging the rescission, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and Owen remanded to the custody of the penitentiary. He appealed to the state supreme court, which affirmed the decision of the lower court.

Summary of Proceedings: In May 1923, Robert Ross petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Michael L. Endres and Joseph Sherry, Sheriff and Deputy Sheriff of Douglas County, Omaha, respectively. Ross was charged with disorderly conduct and sentenced to serve ninety days in county jail. The petition asserted the ordinances of the city of Omaha only authorizes the municipal court or police court to sentence a person to thirty days for such an offense. Judge Charles A. Goss allowed the writ and ordered the petitioner be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 10, 1905, O.V. Lawson was arrested and charged with practicing medicine and surgery without a license.  He used the title M.D. and assumed an alias under the name of another individual, D. T. Richards.  He allegedly prescribed drugs to treat “wounds, fractures, and bodily injuries, infirmities, and diseases.”  His patients included Frank H. Warren, Frank R. Wallace, and J.A. Havlik. The Fidelity and Deposit Company of Maryland acted as a surety to allow Lawson to pay his bail.  Lawson pleaded not guilty, but the jury ruled that he was guilty as charged.  He was sentenced to 90 days in the King County Jail and fined $100.  Lawson appealed at the Washington Supreme Court, but they affirmed the judgment and denied the appeal.  On January 8, 1906, Lawson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that the statute that criminalized practicing medicine without a license was void.  He stated that it deprived him of his right to an occupation and property.  He added that the Board of Medical Examiners was an illegal board with arbitrary power.  He argued that this board, also known as the State Medical Society, was part of a conspiracy and hired spies to testify against him in court.  Judge A. W. Frater issued the writ.  The respondent, L.C. Smith, submitted a demurrer, arguing that the facts did not justify seeking a legal remedy.  He also stated that Lawson was held in custody based on the judgment of a court, highlighting the existence of due process.  The case file does not indicate the outcome of the petition or Lawson’s fate.  According to the January 12, 1906 issue of the Washington Standard, Lawson’s petition for habeas corpus was denied.  It also reported that Justice Mount of the Washington Supreme Court granted a writ of error and released Lawson on a $500 bail bond.

Summary of Proceedings: Aubrey Pickard petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Leonard Pickard from Genevieve Pickard and two others, which was granted. Although not specified in the documents, it appears likely that Leonard was Aubrey's son and Genevieve his ex-wife, as the judge had the cause "transferred to Judge Morning to be heard in connection with application to modify divorce decree." After hearing the evidence, Judge Morning dismissed the writ, awarded custody of Leonard to Genevieve, and ordered Aubrey to pay her court costs.

Summary of Proceedings:
In October 1915, Edward Krause was arrested in Washington for the alleged crime of kidnapping one William Christie in Alaska. The U.S. Commissioner ruled that Krause be taken to the Territory of Alaska at Juneau to face a grand jury. Krause petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus stating that the illegal acts charged to the petitioner, are not in violation of the law of the United States, only the laws of the territory of Alaska. Judge Neterer authorized the writ. In his final ruling Judge Neterer stated the main question was whether the petitioner shall be removed to the district court of Alaska. Neterer balanced competing precedents regarding the jurisdiction of the district court of Alaska and stated there is a line of demarcation placed by Congress between the local laws affecting the territory and laws affecting all states and territories. The final ruling was that the United States government did not have the power to extradite Krause as the offense charged, kidnapping, was not an offense under any law of the United States. Netererer noted that Alaska was not without remedy, as they had their own extradition laws. 
Supplemental research shows that Krause was eventually extradited to Alaska where he faced trial for a multitude of crimes including kidnapping, murder, robbery, impersonating an officer, and fraudulent use of mail. Krause was convicted of first degree murder for killing J.O Plunkett and was given the death penalty. Before his execution, Krause escaped the Federal Jail in Juneau and was later shot by a local after they recognized him from local media.

Summary of Proceedings: Christian Tjosevig petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against U.S. Marshal John M. Boyle and his deputy F. J. Colligan. Tjosevig claimed he was being held for being a fugitive from justice and for attempting to spread materials through the U.S. Postal System with the intent to defraud, and alleged he was innocent of both charges. Tjosevig was the owner of an Alaskan copper mine, and Boyle and Colligan alleged he and five others were distributing false advertising about the mine’s worth through the U.S. Postal System in order to sell shares. Judge Jerimiah Neterer ruled that writ be dismissed and Tjosevig should remain in the custody of Boyle and Colligan. Tjosevig appealed to the Ninth Circuit, but the appellate court affirmed Neterer’s decision. Another man charged alongside Tjosevig, George Francis Rowe, also petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: Loyd Wassgren was put under the care of H.D. Brown during Anna Berg's hospitalization at the Wayside Mission Hospital in 1903 for the duration of stay. However, H.D. Brown refused to return Wassgren to the Berg family and neglected him. At the same time, H.D. Brown claimed that Anna Berg signed a document giving Wassgren to the Children’s Home Society. Judge Tallman granted the writ on January 30th, 1904. On February 2, 1904, Sheriff Edward Cudihee issued the writ to H.D. Brown. The fate of Wassgren is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 23, 1919, a court case was brought by Mrs. Roy Davis to Polk County District Court in Des Moines, Iowa, alleging that her daughter, Margaret Grundy, had become "incorrigible" and was no longer obeying her. Interestingly, Grundy was already over the age of 18 at the time of the court case. She was originally committed by judge Lawrence De Graff to the Industrial School for Girls in Mitchellville, Iowa, but was transferred to the House of the Good Shepherd in Omaha, Nebraska. However, on September 3, 1919, Mrs. Davis filed a writ of habeas corpus to try to regain custody of her daughter, alleging that the original judgement was obtained through fraud and coercion, and that she was threatened and lied to in order to get her to bring the case. It was served to the Mother Superior of the House of the Good Shepherd, Mother Raphael. Judge William A. Redick allowed the writ of habeas corpus and ordered Grundy's release on September 3, 1919, with court costs paid by the county treasury on February 5, 1920. Interestingly, 1920 census records show that Grundy was still working as a seamstress at the House of the Good Shepherd after she was granted her freedom. Perhaps these were based on outdated records, or Grundy decided to work for pay at the convent after her time as a student there.

Summary of Proceedings: An unknown party petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to challenge the detention of Catiche, Helen, Julie, and Joseph, which was granted. Alexis Amelin responded that he was an agent for Alexander Scott, a steamboat captain and the enslaver of Catiche, Helen, and Julie. Amelin said he had placed those three in jail while awaiting their hearing. He also claimed that he had never had possession of Joseph, who he believed was enslaved by Pierre Chouteau, Sr. The fate of the four bound parties is unclear.

Summary of Proceedings: C. W. Guinn petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Guinn alleged that Warren imprisoned him in the Seattle City Jail with no warrant or due process of law by the authority of a telegram from an unknown sender. Guinn claimed he had broken no laws, either in Washington or anywhere else. Newspaper records indicated Guinn was a fugitive from justice and was charged with larceny in the state of California. The writ was dismissed by motion of the petitioner, and Guinn was released on a bond of $3000. Newspaper records indicated he was eventually taken back to California to face charges there.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 8, 1903 Loran L. Paine petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his eleven-year-old daughter, Katie Paine. Loran’s wife Leslie had died, leaving him with the care of three sons and Katie. The quality of the scans makes it difficult to ascertain many of the details of this case, however, Katie was in the custody of Peter and Nellie McLain, who Loran claimed had no legal claim over her, and were asking for a large sum of money from Loran in order to return Katie to his care. The outcome of this case and the fate of Katie Paine are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 3, 1923, Harry Little, a 17-year old Black teenager, was convicted of vagrancy in the police court of Douglas County, Nebraska. Judge Frank M. Dineen sentenced him to 60 days in the county jail. However, on February 9, 1923, Esther A. Johnson, the chief juvenile probation officer for Douglas County, filed a writ of habeas corpus against Omaha sheriff Michael L. Endres for Little's release. She stated that since Harry Little had already been declared a delinquent minor and was a ward of the juvenile court before his arrest, the juvenile court had complete custody over him and the police court had no jurisdiction to keep him in  jail. The case was dismissed on January 27, 1925, long after the teen's sentence had elapsed.

Summary of Proceedings: Ella Baker petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Grace Baker from the custody of Thelma Falbey, which was granted. Ella was Grace's grandmother and Thelma Falbey was Grace's mother. Ella had custody of the child after Thelma's divorce from Harry Baker, her son and Grace's father. On September 5, Thelma had taken the child, saying she was going to take her to the movies, but they never came back. While the hearing was pending, the sheriff deposited Grace with the matron of the Lincoln Detention Home. After hearing the evidence, Grace was remanded to the custody of Ella.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward F. Hunter filed a writ of Habeas on behalf of Mary Josephine Marshall on account of Mary being a minor. Hunter claimed that Edward Deggeller was appointed guardian of Mary by H. S. Elliot and to place her in the Good Shepherd's Home. Hunter further claimed that this confinement of Mary is illegal and that Mary should be released. The writ was granted. It was found at the following court proceedings that Mary had run away from home, refusing to live in the same house as her mother, Mary Cook, and her stepfather, H. J. Cook. Mary Josephine Marshall went to Eliza Robinson for housing, and Robinson initiated proceedings in the Lewis County Superior Court to become her legal guardian. The court ruled Robinson unfit, and assigned Edward Deggeller as her guardian, and Deggeller placed her in the care of the House of the Good Shepherd until she came of age. Further documentation from Mary Cook granted her consent for Mary Josephine Marshall’s placement there. As a result, Mary Josephine Marshall was left in the care of the House of the Good Shepherd.

Summary of Proceedings: Wong Sing (Lin) Wing petitioned for habeas corpus while being held on the Steamship Signet by Master Bendergard. T. J. Black the Collector of Customs believes that he was a chinese laborer and thus excluded from entry to the United States by the Chinese Exclusion Act. Several witnesses testified that he is a merchant working for Yuen Wah Company with his father at No. 141 Second Street. He worked there for seven to eight years with his father before they returned to China two years ago, and his father remained in China. The Judge accepted that he was a merchant and granted the writ discharging him from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In January 1885, three men were accused of land fraud in the Third Judicial District Court for the Territory of Washington. William Jones, William Doyle, Fred Williams, and Alfred Woods were all subpoenaed to testify in their trial. When the district court recessed, the judge required each of the four witnesses to pay a $500 recognizance guaranteeing that he would return to testify when the court reconvened. The four men refused, citing financial hardship, so the judge had them confined in the McNeil Island Federal Penitentiary. Jones, Doyle, Williams, and Woods petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the Second Judicial District Court, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the four men were remanded to the custody of the US Marshal at the penitentiary and their writ was denied.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 3, 1924, Florence Godly was sentenced by Judge John McGee to 12 months in the Lancaster County Common Jail and ordered to pay a $500 fine for violating the National Prohibition Act. On November 29, 1924, she filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that she should be discharged after serving four months in the Lancaster County Jail because the cumulative sentences imposed upon her did not specify the order in which she needed to serve them. She also cited Sec. 1042 of the Revised Statutes of the U.S. and argued that she had served 30 extra days in replacement of the fine. On December 2, 1924, the petition and writ were allowed and the judge ordered her release from police custody after the hearing on Dec. 3, 1924. On March 13, 1925, the respondents appealed the case to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit in St. Paul, Minnesota. On January 30, 1926, the decision of the lower court was reversed and Chief Justice William Taft remanded Florence to the custody of the respondents. The higher court also refered to the Cronin vs. William J. Fox decision.

Summary of Proceedings: Paul Schuman and Charles Shea petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff Robert T. Hodge. Schuman and Shea alleged that they were charged with accepting the earnings of a common prostitute and that their bail was set at $5,000 for each of them. According to newspaper records, Schuman was a Seattle patrolman offering prostitutes protection from the police in exchange for $5 per week graft. Schuman and Shea claimed that the bail was excessive and in derogation of their constitutional rights. Hodge returned with the warrant confirming the charge and bail amount, and he claimed the bail was not excessive. The case file reveals neither the case outcome nor the fates of Schuman and Shea.

Summary of Proceedings: In August 1883, a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed on behalf of J. S. Roadman on the basis of him being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by P. W. Dillon, Sheriff of Spokane County. The petition alleged the complaint upon which Roadman was arrested did not charge him with the commission of any crime, and the evidence did not prove Roadman guilty of any crime, but asked him to pay three hundred dollars bail. Judge S. C. Wingard allowed the petition, yet the outcome of the writ and Roadman's fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Louisa Celestine (previously Louisa George) filed for a writ of habeas corpus for her five-year old daughter, Annie George, from the unlawful custody of George and Mary Sidwell. Louisa had Annie with her previous husband, John George. When John died, his probate case No. 4302 granted custody of Annie to the Sidwells on April 11, 1902. The probate case was investigated by esquire L. J. Turner, who declared that Louisa had abandoned Annie.

Louisa’s writ was accepted by Judge Griffin and the petition was on May 19, 1902. Louisa claimed to be of the right and nature entitled to the care, custody, control and comforting presence for Annie. She also claimed to be married and living with Josie Celestine in Snohomish county, where they have abundant means and the ability to provide for and educate Annie. In the response, the Sidwells contend that they had no knowledge of Louisa’s marriage or living conditions, and thus deny her fitness. 

In the case, Louisa provides documentation of her marriage with Josie. The marriage had been officiated by P. L. Rouk and endorsed on September 2, 1899. Judge Griffin ruled in favor of Louisa on July 19, 1902. He decided  that although it is true the Sidwells were properly taking care of Annie, that Louisa proved she could also provide for Annie, and that the Sidwells had no evidence of Louisa abandoning Annie.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 11, 1918, J. B. Murray made complaint against Ike Payne. On September 12, Payne was charged and tried in the Omaha Police Court for the unlawful possession and transport of intoxicating liquor. Found guilty, on note of second offense, Payne was fined 300 and to be placed in jail until fine be paid. On September 27, Payne filed for habeas charged that such a fine exceeds the jurisdiction of a police magistrate. Payne's petition was granted, but case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 30, 1920. Note: Payne filed new Habeas petition a week later in 1918.

Summary of Proceedings: The petitioner Brandon W. Wittekopf was arrested by police officer W.G Wilson on January 3rd, 1903. He was accused of engaging in same-sex relations that occurred on January 1, 1903, and was formally charged with vagrancy. Wittekopf was brought to the Seattle City Jail on January 5th, 1903, and was convicted of the charge of vagrancy and ordered to remain in jail for thirty days. A writ of habeas corpus was filed on January 7th, where the petitioner argued he was being unlawfully restrained and deprived of his liberty by the Chief of Police John Sullivan. Judge William R. Bell agreed that the petitioner was being unlawfully held and allowed the writ the same day.

Summary of Proceedings: James Mareskes was arrested on May 14, 1918. Following his arrest, he filed for a writ of habeas corpus alleging that the Chief of Police, Joel Warren, was illegally restraining him of his liberty. The petition contends that Warren was holding Mareskes despite not Mareskes not being charged with any crime. Mareskes further states that he has been refused the opportunity to post bail and is being prevented from contacting any of his friends or an attorney. This case file is only three pages long and does not include the outcome of the writ or the fate of the bound party.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 1st, 1923, John N. Baldwin petitioned for and was given an order allowing a writ of Habeas Corpus for Arthur Williams after he had been arrested by Daniel B Butler and Charles Van Duesen the morning of that same day when they had reason to believe he had committed larceny. In the petition, Baldwin argued that Williams had been detained without justification. In their response, Van Duesen and Butler presented that they arrested Williams on a charge of investigation and that at the time they did not have sufficient time to properly investigate. The court granted Van Duesen and Butler leave to amend their response to the writ. The final order of the writ and the fate of Williams is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Jack Norton, petitioner, was charged with running a saloon in the City of Omaha without a license. Judge Cunningham allowed the writ because he found that two policemen used fraud to entrap Nortion to justify his arrest. According to the Chief of Police, the two policemen knew well that Norton had a license for said saloon which then expired and he had, as per custom, deposited $1000 for a new license with proper authorities and was allowed to operate his saloon pending application for the new license. Norton was released from custody, and the two officers (Martin White and Daniel W. Iler) were ordered to pay the costs of the case.

Dupree returned to Oregon for imprisonment.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Walton petitioned for habeas corpus against Sheriff L. C. Smith on January 10, 1906. Walton had been arrested for the crime of "Barbering on Sunday" after he shaved a guest in the Tourist Hotel. His petition argued that the charged action was not illegal, that the law that he was charged under violated the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees to equal protection and due process, and that the Justice of the Peace had no jurisdiction to issue an arrest warrant. Judge Cornelius H. Hanford ordered that Smith show cause for Walton's detention. On February 9, Hanford stated that the State Supreme Court had decided that the statute was not unconstitutional and stated that a Sunday observance law was not considered invidious discrimination under the Supreme Court case Petit v. Minnesota. Hanford remanded Walton to the custody of Lewis and stated that Walton could appeal to the Supreme Court. In an order from November 20, 1909, Hanford stated that Walton could receive his recognizance by surrendering himself to the custody of the United States Marshal to be remanded to the custody of Lewis.

Summary of Proceedings: Clara A. Lilly, the petitioner, filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus to release her children, Carl A. Herbert, Bessie V. Herbert, and Oscar H. Herbert, from the Nebraska Children's Home Society. The Home Society did not permit her to see her children, who were taken after a complaint that Lilly was unable to care for them due to sickness for a temporary period. After their removal, Lilly re-married, her current husband being David S. Lilly, and claimed she now has a good and sufficient home for the children. The case ends with a stipulation of dismissal without prejudice. The fate of the Herbert children is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Marguerite Volker (also referred to as Margaret Walker) petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on October 30th, 1924. She claimed that she was being unlawfully detained in jail by M. L. Endres, Sheriff of Douglas County. She claimed that she was being held without just cause, she had no proper trial, no charges upon her, and that she had not been given a fair trial. The judge granted her petition. When M. L. Endres responded to her petition, he claimed that he was holding Marguerite by virtue of a mittimus from F. M. Dineen (Municipal Judge of the City of Omaha). Dineen requested that Marguerite be detained at the County Jail. At the Municipal Court, she had been found guilty on charges of vagrancy and prostitution. Endres insisted that because of this, the writ be denied. The case file included no additional information about this case, but the appearance docket noted that on January 25th, 1927 the writ was dismissed for want of prosecution. The fate of Marguerite is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In August 1923, Alma Bushey petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of her son, Harry Cherritt. The writ alleged Cherritt was restrained of his liberty by the respondents and held in jail for more than forty-eight hours without being able to communicate with the petitioner, friends, counsel, and was denied bail. The petition further alleged Cherritt had not committed any crime and was not detained by virtue of any final judgment from a competent tribunal. The appearance docket reveals the writ was denied, and Cherritt remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 20, 1891, Yip Wing Kee and Mack Tung filed for a writ of habeas corpus because they claimed they were unlawfully detained by Captain R. Unsworth of the Steamship Lairhain. Captain Unsworth claimed that he was ordered to detain Yip Wing Kee and Mack Tung by the Collector of the Port of Portland R.P. Earhart. Unsworth wrote that Earhart claimed Yip Wing Kee and Mack Tung were prevented from coming into the United States under the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Matthew Deady disagreed and granted the writ and ordered Yip Wing Kee and Mack Tung released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: John F. Bernard petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Ansel Lucchesi against King County Sheriff Aaron T. Van Devanter. Bernard’s name does not reappear in the case file. Lucchesi was imprisoned by Judge Joseph M. Glasgow when he defaulted on a bond to testify against Jennie Williams, who Lucchesi accused of grand larceny. Summary of Proceedings: Special Constable W. H. Harris said Hutchinson was arrested at Port Blakely and committed to his custody by virtue of an arrest warrant. The warrant by Justice Campbell stated that Hutchinson embezzled money ($240) from W. H. Harris. Hutchinson's attorneys filed a petition and Judge Greene granted it and ordered Hutchinson to be released. After this, an execution was issued in King County to take the defendant's property (2 small horses, 1-4 spring wagon and 1 set of double harness) to be sold, however Mrs. Lena Hutchinson claimed to own the property so Sheriff McGraw could not take it.

Summary of Proceedings: Francis J. Scrivens petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against U.S. Commissioner of Immigration Luther Weeden. Weeden was holding Scrivens at the Immigration Station in Seattle under a warrant to deport Scrivens to Great Britain. Scrivens claimed he was a naturalized citizen of the United States because he had taken out his first naturalization papers and served in the U.S. Army during World War I. Judge Jerimiah Neterer determined that Scrivens was an alien, and ordered the writ to be dismissed and Scrivens to remain in the custody of Weeden while awaiting deportation.

Summary of Proceedings: Loui Gow petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of his business partner Loui Ah Fat, held on the Steamship Signal. They worked together at Pow Chung Lung Company located at No. 183 Second Street before Loui Ah Fat returned to China briefly to visit family. Upon return, T. J. Black refused to allow Loui Ah Fat to enter the port as he believed Loui was a Chinese laborer and was in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. After hearing testimony from several witnesses, the Judge ruled that Loui Ah Fat was a genuine merchant and granted the writ releasing him from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Found guilty of perjury in 1897 and sentenced to four years hard labor in the Nebraska State Penitentiary, in 1900 Leonard Kephart petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was eligible for "commutation for good behavior as provided for by Section 569" of Nebraska's Criminal Code. Therefore, he claimed that warden John H. Hopkins was unlawfully imprisoning him. Judge Holmes granted the petition. After reviewing evidence, Holmes allowed the writ and ordered that Kephart be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Williams was arrested on July 10th, 1912. The next day, he was sentenced to serve 30 days for having "bogus money" in the Snohomish County Jail. Williams was later indicted by a federal grand jury for the same charges on November 23rd, 1912. He filed a writ of habeas corpus on October 25th, 1915, arguing that he was charged with a false charge, as the charge was never proven or substantiated. Williams also argued that his rights were being violated, as he was twice tried, sentenced, and imprisoned for the alleged offense. Judge Cushman dismissed the writ on November 29th, 1915, and ordered Williams to remain in the custody of Warden Halligan.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 25, 1894, Wong Chen How filed a writ of habeas corpus for Ngug Moy Sung and Lee Lun Hip. Wong Chen How claimed that Ngug Moy Sung and Lee Lun Hip were being illegally detained on the Steamship Islander by Captain John Irving. Wong Chen How further claimed that Ngug Moy Sung and Lee Lun Hip were Chinese merchants who were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Act. Judge Bellinger denied the writ for Ngug Moy Sung and Lee Lun Hip. However on appeal, Judge Bellinger reheard the petition for Lee Lun Hip, and granted it. Bellinger then ordered him released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 7th, 1901, William S. Fuller petitioned for his freedom from Ed Cudihee. Cudihee was the Sheriff of King County, and was holding Fuller on a charge of him being a fugitive from justice. Fuller had been arrested by Jack Williams, a deputy sheriff, for having fled from Santa Clara County, California on a charge of embezzlement. Allegedly, on July 16th, Fuller embezzled around $1300 from Standard Oil. He was officially charged by C.W. Cobb, a Justice of the Peace of Santa Clara County, California. On November 7th, the same day as his petition, Judge Arthur Griffin of King County granted the writ and a day in court. However, the case file ends there and the fate of Fuller is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry Reed, an Irish immigrant, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid. Reed alleged that he was being held illegally at Spokane County Jail under the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. He claimed he was denied a hearing for six months, denied his right to counsel, and compelled to give evidence against himself under intimidation. The court’s judgement stated that it appeared Reed had been discharged for unknown reasons, and thus his writ was dismissed.

Judge Frost granted the petition. Skipton later amended his petition, which Judge Frost also accepted. Summary of Proceedings: On October 10th, 1887, Thomas Brown, G. Geods, George Downing, Charles Schubard, C. J. Young, and Peter Wegener were arrested for disobeying the orders of the master of the American ship Ivanhoe. They were jailed at McNeil Island Penitentiary, and one of their attorneys, Junius Rochester, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on their behalf. The petition was granted, and their case was heard by Judge Richard A. Jones. Judge Jones ruled in favor of the petitioners, and they were discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: One June 2, 1917, 23-year old Margaret Holton was arrested without a warrant and incarcerated in the Omaha City Jail. The Omaha Daily Bee states that it was for "forgery in the third degree." However, she was required to testify in St. Louis, Missouri regarding the trial of Paul O. Sommer, who was accused of embezzling $20,000 from the Holman company. Margaret used to be his assistant, making her testimony on his business dealings possibly very valuable. Assisted by her attorney Daniel Horrigan, she filed a writ of habeas corpus on June 4, 1917. She appeared in court on June 6, 1917, and was released on a $600 bail, with one W.N. Mace serving as surety. A continuation of the writ of habeas corpus and return was filed on June 7. The conclusion of the case is unclear, as no more records document Margaret's fate. According to the Omaha Daily Bee article, she was released on bail and went to testify in St. Louis.

Summary of Proceedings: On 19 August 1829, Patrick Henry, respondent, had a petition filed in his stead by his next friend and mother, Maria Whitten. Whitten claimed that Henry was freed following the death of their enslaver, John Whitten, who had fled from Virginia with the two following an instance where they were being sold there. Whitten, with the other two, fled first to Kentucky and then to Illinois where they found themselves in a financially poor situation that necessitated the sale of Maria Whitten’s services to Abraham Granger. After some time there between 1828 and 1829, John Witten passed away and freed Maria Whitten and Patrick Henry. The defendant, Garland Rucker, at some point following this incident allegedly enslaved them and stole away with them to St. Louis where he intended to sell them.

Summary of Proceedings:
John Toria filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he was held without charge in the King County Jail. In his writ, his lawyer stated that Toria was being illegally held by King County Sheriff, John Stringer, “to compel your petitioner to make incriminatory statements regarding an alleged murder that occured in Auburn, Washington, on December 19, 1917, and to compel the petitioner to give information which he does not possess regarding the killing.” The fate of Toria is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 7th, 1912, Jack Sommer petitioned for the freedom of his client, Dave Rubenstein in Seattle, Washington. Rubenstein had been detained on the notion that he had falsely represented himself to obtain money from his wife. Sommer argued that he had received no sum of money whatsoever. This writ was granted, but before the writ could be delivered to Claud Bannick and Charles Tennant, who were holding Rubenstein, he was released from custody. On June 11th and 12th, therefore, Sommer moved to have the writ quashed, which was granted by Judge J.T. Ronald.

Summary of Proceedings: The Appearance Docket stated that the writ application was filed on 27 November 1915 and issued on the same day. The Sheriff's return to the writ was filed on 7 December 1915. The Sheriff's return stated that the writ was issued to Police Chief Henry Dunn, Cheif of Detectives Stephen Maloney, and Jailors Andrew Fahey and John Brady. Newspaper coverage indicates Maloney worked as a janitor in the State Bank of Omaha, when he was wrongly accused of committing a crime there. Maloney would later sue for $10,000 in damages for the wrongful arrest.

Summary of Proceedings: Moy Ham petitioned for habeas corpus for  Wing Wo and Young Lun Coy. Moy Ham claimed they were restrained on the Steamship Signal by Captain M. Bendergard. They were not allowed to depart the ship because he believed they were Chinese laborers, so their entry would be in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. Several witnesses wrote affidavits testifying that Wing Wo and Young Lun Coy were merchants, and John Catlin verified their stories in his investigation and report. After the Judge reviewed the report, he granted their writ and released them from custody. Case File contains notes from John Catlin’s report, including testimony from witnesses and notes on the petitioners

Summary of Proceedings: On July 22, Morris Passovoy filed for Habeas. He charged, in his petition, that his imprisonment was infringing on his constitutional rights as a citizen, that O. Gorman holds a false warrant for his arrest - claiming him as a fugitive from justice from Wisconsin. Passovoy also claimed innocence from charges of embezzlement or other crime in the false warrant. Summary of Proceedings: On November 25, 1887, Alice McKay filed a petition for a second writ of Habeas Corpus in King County Third District Court to receive custody of her eight-year-old daughter, Mary, from the custody of John and Della Keevan. Mary had been living with the Keevans for five years, the Sisters of Charity (Sisters of Providence) having placed Mary with them after Alice placed her daughter into the care of the sisters in 1882 while receiving medical treatment. Shortly after, Alice petitioned for custody of Mary. After having her initial writ denied, Alice utilized a different legal strategy in her second writ. Alice argued to Judge Roger Greene that the Keevans were unfit parents for Mary due to their Catholicism and that they were denying her visitation without reason. The Keevans argued that Alice was a drunk, immoral, abusive, and living in adultery with her neighbor Antone, "a dark Italian." Alice countered by claiming that the Keevans were similarly immoral, and that her previous encounters with the law were due to abuse she faced from her now estranged husband, R. G. McKay. Before the court ordered a decision in the case of Mary's custody, Alice and her daughter, Katie, abducted Mary from the Keevans' home the day after Mary's twelfth birthday in 1891. Shortly after, the court ordered Alice to return Mary to the Keevans and Judge Isaac Lichtenberg, who took the case upon the death of Judge Jones, granted custody of Mary to the Keevans. A month after the ruling, Alice and her attorneys filed evidence to the court showing of Della's purchase of alcohol and personal correspondences indicating alcohol abuse. A year after the decision, the Keevans were granted a divorce on account of "mutual abuse."

Summary of Proceedings: John O. Lee claimed that David Koch was unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Felix J. McShane. Koch was charged with being a fugitive from justice after he escaped Iowa State Hospital for the Insane and traveled to Nebraska. It was ordered that he be extradited back to Iowa and placed back in the care of the hospital. Lee claimed that Koch was of sound mind and placed in the institution under insufficient evidence. The writ was denied by the judge and he remained in custody. Koch then filed an appeal for a new trial for his case to be looked at by the Nebraska Supreme Court. However, it is unknown what the fate of the bound party was after the appeal.

Powell to be heard by Benjamin S. Baker.

Summary of Proceedings:
On various dates in and around 1912, the petitioners arrived in Manilla, Philippines from various points across the world—most in India. The petitioners stayed for various amounts of time ranging from five months to two years long. In 1913, the petitioners, as many other South Asian immigrants did at this time, decided to move from U.S.-controlled Philippines to the Western United States. Upon arrival, the petitioners were searched and charged a head tax. At some point, these petitioners were then charged with having been a public charge at their time of entering the United States. On August 20th, 1913, a petition for a writ of habeas corpus was filed on behalf of seventy-six petitioners claiming that they were not alien immigrants because they had first passed immigration checkpoints by entering the U.S.-controlled Philippines earlier. On August 23rd, 1913, the government sent return to the order to show cause and claimed that the petitioners were rightfully deported by the Secretary of Labor. On August 27th, 1913, Bhagat Singh, Nadham Singh, Nan Singh, and Ballah Singh submitted sworn statements that they were on the steamship with the other "seventy-three" other petitioners before the court had entered lawfully. On August 28th, 1913, a motion to quash the warrants was filed by the petitioners alleging that the substantive error of re-examining the petitioners should warrant the grant of habeas. It further claims that there is ample evidence of legal immigration at Manilla, that institutionalization would be required to support being a public charge, that records exist to prove legal admission, and that the decision of the immigration officers is not final. In a memorandum brief, the respondents claim that the court can only review whether evidence was presented, that the allegation is to being a public charge not illegal entry, and that anyone could have got the documentation they possess. In a memorandum brief of the petitioners in response, they claim that it is illegal to issue a warrant of being a public charge before actually becoming one. The writ was then originally denied stating that the court only has jurisdiction to decide whether a trial was awarded. On September 13th, 1913, the petitioners file a petition for rehearing stating that the decisions of the Supreme Court run counter to the decision made previously and that this case has the potential to impact immigrations in San Fransisco. On September 17th, 1913, Judge Neterer granted the rehearing and allowed the petitioners to amend the petition. The amended petition, submitted on September 27th, stated that Faizand Ali, Papa Singh, and Nizam Din were released by the respondent before the commencement of the original proceedings and that Buran Singh had died prior to the commencement of proceedings. Neterer ruled that the petitioners be remanded to the care of the respondent but that they could not be deported while awaiting appeal. On September 30th, 1913, Neterer grants permission to appeal to the Supreme Court. That same day Chief Justice Edward Douglass White granted the appeal and ordered the respondents to show cause within 60 days.

Note that all documents within the case file are inconsistent as to the name and amount of petitioners. The petitioners listed here are from September 27th, 1913, "order refusing to grant the writs and discharging the government" document. There are possible duplicates, likely misspellings, and likely people entirely omitted. Please see case file to review all instances of petitioners being listed.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 19th, 1901, William Harrison petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Harrison, with his lawyer, Frank B. Wiestling, argued that he was being illegally held in the Seattle City Jail by Chief of Police of Seattle, John Sullivan. Harrison and Wiestling’s argument relied on the fact that Harrison’s conviction of vagrancy was outside the authority of a police judge. Justice of the Superior Court of King County, Arthur E. Griffin approved the writ. However, on November 23rd, 1901, they moved to have the writ quashed on the reasoning that their argument was not sufficient in evidence. Thus, Harrison remained in custody and likely served the remainder of his 6 month sentence.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward Ruck was arrested on November 3, 1917 by the King County Sheriff, John Stringer. Ruck alleges that there was no legal justification for his arrest in his petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Stringer, in his return of respondent, contends that Ruck’s arrest was based on a warrant issued by Judge Otis Brinker. The warrant was issued because Ruck was wanted to stand trial in Cuyahoga County, Ohio to face charges for neglecting the care and needs of his six children.

Summary of Proceedings: Anna R. Oesterreich petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her infant son, Angus, against W. S. Rand. Oesterreich alleged that Angus was being held illegally at the Parental School, of which Rand was the superintendent, under the pretense that he was a delinquent and neglected child. Oesterreich claimed these pretenses were untrue and that she had not been allowed to defend herself in court. Rand returned that Angus had been committed to the Parental School by a judge of the King County Superior Court Juvenile Department, and that Oesterreich had been given due notice of this order. The case file does not reveal the outcome of the case nor the fate of Angus.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 14th, 1920, Henry Bonnemeyer was arrested under the charge of "aiding, abetting, and contributing to the delinquency" of a minor, Ruth Funnel. Upon his arrest, he went to trial, where he was tried without a jury and declared guilty by judge Willis G. Sears. Bonnemeyer and his attorneys disputed the illegality of his 90 day prison sentence by filing a petition of Habeas Corpus. Their argument was based on the fact that Bonnemeyer was an adult tried by a juvenile court and that no county attorney ever filed evidence against him. These facts were enough, they claimed, to warrant his release. After the petition hearing, it appears that their writ was dismissed; however, Bonnemeyer and his attorneys made a plea for demurrer against the respondent's evidence for Bonnemeyer's captivity. Based on the appearance docket, it seems that the judge, again, dismissed their plea and Bonnemeyer remained in captivity.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 1, 1894, Lee Wut Chow filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Lee Chu, Young Sing Lot, Chan Yee Shan, and Young Hing. Lee Wut Chow claimed that they were illegally detained on the Steamship Signal by Captain M. Bendergard. Lee Wut Chow further claimed that Lee Chu, Young Sing Lot, Chan Yee Shan, and Young Hing were merchants who were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Charles Bellinger agreed with the writ and ordered Lee Chu, Young Sing Lot, Chan Yee Shan, and Young Hing released from custody. Included in the case file are signed affidavits, and Special Prosecutor John Catlin’s reports.

Repository: ["[National Archives and Records Administration, Seattle Branch, Washington (Seattle, WA) (Seattle, Washington)](hc.loc.000035)"]
Summary of Proceedings: A mother and daughter, Toy Gum and Ah Gum respectively, were confined by T. J. Black in Steamship Haytian Republic for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Toy Gum’s husband, Me Kim, petitioned for writ of habeas corpus for her and their daughter. The daughter was born in the United States, but she moved to China at 3 years old to live with her grandmother, and her mother went to China to bring her back after 10 years. The writ of habeas corpus was granted, and they were ordered to be released by Charles B. Bellinger. Transcripts of interviews done are included in the case file.

He was alleged to have burned the building with the intent to defraud the Northern Insurance Company of London. He was arrested by Henry W. Dunn and Patrick Mostyn and then later filed a writ alleging that he was deprived of his liberty and is held without warrant, without writ of detention, copy of commitment, and not a fugitive from justice. His writ was allowed but later the case was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 5, 1923, Al Madison was charged with forgery. He was accused in a complaint filed by county attorney Henry J. Beal of forging a State Bank of Omaha check on on September 29, 1923. On March 17, 1924, he pled guilty to the charge, probably hoping to be released on parole. On September 17, 1924, a man named C.S. Nelson, with the help of his attorney, Joseph J. Powers, of the firm O'Brien and Powers, field a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against chief of detectives Charles Van Deusen and a John Doe. It is unknown if Al Madison and C.S. Nelson are the same person, however, there would be little reason for their files to be kept together if they weren't. The petition was allowed in favor of C. S. Nelson and ordered to be returned to the chief of police on Septerber 18, 1924, however the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Mario Lozito filed a petition for writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his wife, Francesca Lozito, on February 16, 1920. Mario Lozito alleged that his wife was being held without an order from a tribunal under the general pretense that she was insane. He stated that she was not congenitally or dangerously insane and that she was taken care of in her home by her husband and mother. A judge ordered that the Superintendent of the Douglas County Hospital come before the Court and show cause for her detention, and this order was delivered to Cora E. Patton, Matron and Acting Superintendent of the Douglas County Hospital. Lozito was discharged from custody following a hearing on February 19, 1920. However, on the same day, Patton filed a motion to quash the writ. The Court, after considering the motion of a complaining witness named Guenn P. Godard, vacated the order allowing the application for writ of habeas corpus. Francesca Lozito was returned to the custody of the superintendent of the Douglas County Hospital by the Court's orders, and her fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Paul Carrigan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of John Soudas. Carrigan claimed that Soudas was being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail without charge, set bail, or access to counsel. Charles L. Beckingham, the Seattle Chief of Police, responded that Soudas was being held on a warrant charging him with murder in the first degree. The case file does not reveal the outcome of the case or Soudas’s fate.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 5, 1891, Watanabe Masa, Taniuchi Takema, Akiyama Naka, Hatsutori Tane, Taniuchi Nobu, Hashimoto Yaya, Kondo Matsu, Yoshida Migo and Aflen Meme filed for a writ of habeas corpus because they claimed they prevented from landing in the U.S. and were detained by Shipmaster Ulrich Johanson on the Steamship Pemptos. Johanson claimed that the petitioners were imported into the United States for immoral purposes. After determining that the petitioners were coming to the United States to join their families and husbands, Judge Matthew Deady granted their petition and ordered them released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Teramoto came to the United States in 1911 through a San Francisco port, where he remained until June 1921, when he began working as a mess boy on a steamship going to Japan and coming back. He returned back to the United States in August 2021 where he was arrested by Acting Commissioner of Immigration Thomas W. Lynch in Seattle and ordered for deportation. Teramoto petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming his arrest to be unlawful.
The writ was denied and Teramoto was deported. Teramoto was advised by his attorneys that he did not have any means to prosecute an appeal or take any further action.

Summary of Proceedings:
After being charged with the murder of her husband Franklin (Frank) Teller, Mary E. Teller petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the hopes of either securing her release or lowering her bail. The judge granted her writ but only to try the question of bail. He elected not to lower the bail and remanded Teller to the custody of her jailer to await trial. Teller would eventually be acquitted of the murder and her case is well documented in newspaper coverage. 

There is an additional set of documents in the archives that details the actual murder case. It includes witness lists, cost lists, and some description of witness testimony.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 28th, 1912, Judge J.T. Ronald granted a Writ of Habeas Corpus to Myrtle Johnson. Johnson’s writ, which was filed on behalf of her three children, was not found in the case files. However, Judge Ronald did order Frank Wright and Mattie Smails, the holding parties, to appear in court with the 3 children on May 1st, 1912. Because the last names of the three children are ‘Wright’, it is presumed that Frank Wright was their father, although Smail’s role is unclear. On May 8th, 1912, a court order from Judge Ronald was found ordering that the case be withdrawn on the motion from Myrtle Johnson and her lawyer. From this order, it is also learned that none of the respondents appeared in court.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 21st, 1912, Judge J.T. Ronald granted Charles Dietrich a Writ of Habeas Corpus. Dietrich was originally charged with the crime of abandonment and desertion of his wife in Manitowoc, Wisconsin. According to Dietrich, he and his wife, Emma, married in July 1911 in Manitowa, Wisconsin. However, since he could not find work there, he moved to Washington to be able to provide and support himself and his wife through steady work. However, Emma did not follow Dietrich to Seattle, and instead stayed in Manitowoc County. According to Emma, Dietrich left suddenly in September 1911 and abandoned and deserted her. Emma undertook legal action and Charles was arrested for the first time in November 1911. During his hearing though, he was released and not charged. He was arrested again at some point in March 1912 for the same crime. This happens after a lengthy legal process that takes place in Manitowoc and Seattle over the course of about 2 months. Eventually, the Governor of Washington places an arrest warrant out for Dietrich, so he can be taken from Seattle back to Manitowoc. Dietrich is held in the custody of Bannick, the Chief of Police of Seattle, specifically under the advice of the Sheriff of Manitowoc, Walter Pellett. On March 23rd, 1912, the case was tried in court, however the specific outcome is unknown. What is known is that on March 30th, Dietrich’s bond was paid off for $200, although it is unclear if he is being taken to Wisconsin to be tried or if he is still in Washington.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney George Olson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his client A. J. Chance. Olson claimed that Chance was being illegally held by Seattle Chief of Police Louis M. Lang in the Seattle City Jail under a false warrant. Lang confirmed that he was holding Chance on a warrant from Oregon which claimed he was a fugitive from justice and that he was wanted in Oregon for the crime of obtaining money by false pretenses. Both the outcome of the case and the fate of Chance are unknown.

He obtained $335 worth of goods of H. W. T. Mall & Company by false pretenses. The writ was allowed but Davis was not discharged from prison.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 16th, 1921, Nick Fort was charged and arraigned for a vagrancy charge for which he plead not guilty but was found by Charles E. Foster, Police Magistrate, to be guilty for. The conviction was appealed to the District Court where Judge L. B. Day denied the appeal for want of jurisdiction by reason of defective bond on appeal. Day ordered that the remainder of the original 30-day sentence be finished. On December 30th, 1921, Fort was arrested again on a state mittimus concerning the previous charge. A petition was then filed on January 3rd, 1922, by Fort which alleged that the mittimus alleges violations of Nebraska State Laws when the original charge was concerned with a City of Omaha Ordinance. On January 4th, 1922, the response from Sheriff Clark was filed and a hearing was scheduled. Judge A. C. Troup found in favor of the petitioner and ordered Fort discharged on January 10th, 1922.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 7, 1913, Margaret Holland and her attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her son, Lawrence. Margaret claimed that Lawrence was being held on a telegram from Oregon which claimed he was insane. Margaret said he was not insane. Judge Humprhies allowed the writ to be heard in Judge Ronald’s court, who deferred it to Judge Frater’s court. Sheriff Edward Cudihee produced the telegrams from R. E. Lee Steiner, superintendent of the Oregon State Hospital for the Insane in Salem, Oregon. The telegrams stated that Lawrence was committed to the hospital due to being declared insane, and that Maragret had taken him from the hospital without the consent or permission of the doctors. Steiner advised that Lawrence was a menace to society and should be detained. Judge Frater ruled against the Hollands, and Lawrence was put back in custody, in order to be eventually taken back to the hospital in Oregon. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, who dismissed the appeal. The hospital failed to send anyone to retrieve Lawrence, so his custody was transferred to the sheriff of Multnomah County, Oregon.

Summary of Proceedings: Ching Chong Quie petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Ham You, Ing Sam, and Ing Yow. All three are detained on the steamship Danube by Captain William Meyers on the orders of T. J. Black, the Collector of Customs. T.J. Black accepted that they previously resided in Portland, Oregon for several years and visited China with the intention of returning, but still denied them entry because he did not accept they were merchants. The petitioner and Ed Kahn, a witness, informed the judge that Ham You is a retail merchant as part of the Tong Duck Chung Co. firm at No. 134 Second Street. Additionally, the petitioner provided that Ing Sam and Ing Yow are in general merchandising at a business at No. 60 Second Street. The Judge accepted these positions as providing merchant status and granted their writ discharging them from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 14th, 1908, Franklin C. Chase was indicted on two counterfeit charges and was sentenced to serve 10 years at McNeil Island Penitentiary. Chase filed a writ of habeas corpus on September 11, 1911, arguing that there was no legal commitment for his imprisonment, his conviction was false, and O. P. Halligan, warden of McNeil Island, was unlawfully restraining him of his liberty. Judge Rudkin denied Chase's writ on September 27th, 1911, and remanded Chase to Halligan's custody at McNeil Island.

Summary of Proceedings: In May 1885, Arthur Powell petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the basis that he was illegally restrained of his liberty by E. J. Whittier, Sheriff of Spokane County. Powell was charged, along with Asa Shuck, with stealing a stallion worth $40. Each man was granted recognizance in the sum of $250, however, both failed to post bond and were thus kept in custody awaiting their court appearances. Powell's petition alleged the charge of "horse stealing" was not an offense against the laws of the Washington Territory and that testimony showed no probable cause that Powell was guilty. The fate of the petition and the fate of Arthur Powell are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Mrs. Inger Hanson filed for a writ of habeas corpus on March 12, 1918 for Addie Hanson. J. S. McBride, respondent and doctor at the Seattle Public Safety Building, claimed that Addie Hanson was in violation of several of Seattle City health ordinances related to communicable venereal disease. Judge John S. Jurey allowed the writ on March 13, 1918. The fate of Addie Hanson is unknown. 

Case file includes alleged descriptions of the conditions inside of the Seattle Public Safety Building.

Stratton allowed his petition and McGraw and Sarvis were summoned to court. Sarvis’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: The Board of Commissioners for Gosper County, Nebraska found that John Wilken was a dipsomaniac, or alcoholic, and had him admitted to the Nebraska State Hospital for the Insane "until cured but not exceeding three years." Wilken petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the judge ruled that while the hospital could admit and detain Wilken, the Board of Commissioners had exceeded their authority in sentencing him for a period of time. The writ was denied and Wilken ordered to be returned to Gosper County to appear a second time before the Board of Commissioners.

Summary of Proceedings: On an unknown date, Otto Rose was originally arrested based on a May 21st, 1920 complaint charging him with delinquency. The complaint alleged that Otto was immoral and took Gertrude Dohse to the Howard Hotel and kept her there for several days and sold some of her jewelry. Otto was then re-arrested on February 13th, 1921 and held without bond. On February 21st, Otto was sentenced to the State Industrial School at Kearney. On March 7th, Otto filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. He claimed he was being unlawfully imprisoned and that his constitutional rights were being violated. Otto claimed that the complaint under which he was arrested did not specify a crime under Nebraska statute and did not state that a crime had been committed or that there had been any violation of any statute or ordinance. Additionally, he claimed that upon his arrest he was not permitted to engage counsel , present evidence, received no notice of hearing, and was not permitted a jury trial. He named August Vosberg, Chief Juvenile Officer, as the respondent. The petition was granted, but on March 8th the writ was denied and bond ordered. Otto began the appeals process almost immediately. On March 11th, documents for a motion for a new trial, notice of appeal, and application for recognizance were filed. In the motion for a new trial, Otto's lawyer alleged that the judgment and findings of the court were not sustained by evidence and were contrary to law. They also alleged that the court erred in not directing the juvenile court to give Otto a fair trial and in overruling Otto's motion to have a physician testify that he was not fit to stand trial. The motion for a new trial and application for recognizance were overruled and denied. The Supreme Court affirmed Otto's claims, finding that the return from Vosberg did not indicate that Otto had been charged with any crime whatsoever nor that he was an appropriate candidate for the industrial school. The Supreme Court reversed the District Court's decision and ordered that Otto be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In July 1918, Ruth Livingston was arrested and convicted with being an inmate of an ill-governed house and sentenced to twenty days in jail, then subsequently committed to the Omaha Detention Home for Girls. Ruth filed a bond for an appeal, which was approved by the Police Magistrate and authorized for her release. The Detention Home for girls refused to recognize the order and did not release Ruth. The petitioner stated she was not charged for the crime of prostitution or being in danger of exposing others to infectious diseases. In addition, Ruth stated she was forced to submit to medical treatment against her will. Judge Willis G. Sears authorized the petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus. The writ was returned and not served as it was recalled by the plaintiff's attorney, likely because Ruth had been released from the Detention Home by that point and the case was dismissed for need of prosecution.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis T. Silvain petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of Elsie Jones and Mrs. E. M. McMillan against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham. Silvain alleged that Jones and McMillan were being illegally held in the Seattle City Jail without any reason given for their confinement, criminal charge brought against them, or valid process of law conducted. Due to the brevity of the case file, the outcome of the case and the fates of Jones and McMillan are unknown. Newspaper coverage indicates Mackintosh had Beckingham arrested on Nov 13, 1917 for refusing to deliver two habeas petitioners before his court in a "vice case," but no names are given. Further coverage explains an anti-vice campaign was in effect, and would be "unmolested by habeas corpus releases."

Summary of Proceedings: On July 13, 1857, Michael Broderick petitioned on behalf of five men (whose names are unknown) who he believed to be subjects of Queen Victoria that were being detained at the U. S. Military Port by Major George Haller. The bound parties were allegedly being held on the charge of desertion of the Satellite (Queen Victoria’s ship). That same day, Judge Chenoweth ordered Major Haller to bring the bound parties before the court. On July 14, Major Haller responded to the petition and alleged that the bound parties deserted the Satellite and that it was his duty to “in the waters of the sound in connection with and as a part of the joint campaign of the governments of Great Britain and the United States to ascertain land determine the boundary between” the two governments. Major Haller further detailed that the Satellite's officer in command asked him to detain the bound parties until he could send for them. The fate of the bound parties is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Thomas Cornwell filed an application for a writ of habeas corpus on June 3, 1924. Naming Peter H. Dillon (Chief of Omaha Police) and Charles H. Van Deusen (Omaha Chief of Detectives) as respondents, Cornwell stated that he had been detained in the Omaha City Jail without any information or "other charges" being filed against him since May 20, 1924. Judge James M. Fitzgerald granted the writ and commanded that Vandeusen and Dillon appear in court and show cause for Cornwell's detention. The Appearance Docket states that Cornwell was discharged on June 3, 1924, which suggests that Cornwell's writ may have been allowed. Newspaper coverage indicates he was arrested as a fugitive from Dubuque, IA, fleeing charges of wife and child abandonment.

Summary of Proceedings: George Richardson was a witness in a case against Daniel O’Leary where O’Leary was charged with disturbing public worship but had not been convicted. So, O’Leary filed a complaint against Richardson accusing his complaint of being “frivolous and malicious”. As a result, Richardson was ordered to remain in jail until he paid $117.40. Richardson then filed a writ of habeas corpus against James H.Woolery,  the sheriff who detained him, to appear in court. The writ was permitted and Woolery was commanded to bring Richardson before the judge, but Richardson’s fate is undisclosed in the case file. Newspaper coverage indicates Richardson was wrongfully arrested in retaliation for his charge against O'Leary and was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Aileen Fales filed for a writ of habeas corpus on April 4, 1918 for her son, Ernest Fales, aged four, from his father, John E. Fales. Aileen obtained “the care, custody and control” of Ernest in her divorce from John on February 7, 1918. John responded to the custody arrangement by abducting Ernest. Aileen claimed that John then submitted a fraudulent agreement to her, transferring custody of Ernest, which she signed under false pretenses. Judge John S. Jurey allowed the writ on April 4, 1918. The fate of Ernest is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Joe Jam filed a petition for habeas corpus on November 9th, 1893, on behalf of Joe John, a merchant who had sailed to China with the intent to come back.  Joe John was gone for a year and came back in October of 1983, and was imprisoned on the steamship Signal by the captain of the ship Bendegard.  Joe Jam believed that this was due to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which barred Chinese laborers from coming into the U.S. C.J. Jaocbs was sworn in as a witness and attested that he knew Joe John before his departure and that he was a Chinese merchant and a member of Joe & Jam Co. The writ was granted, and Joe John was discharged.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 14, 1921, David Patterson pled guilty to two charges in the Multnomah County Circuit Court. He was sentenced to no more than three years in the state penitentiary but was paroled the same day. On December 15, Patterson was arrested on an outstanding warrant from a Marion County justice of the peace for the same crime to which he had already been convicted. On December 16, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Patterson was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: The Donohue family petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve a boy named Bernard Seward from the custody of the Noonan and Seward families, which was granted. Bernard Seward was apparently the nephew of Agnes Donohue and Kittie Noonan. When Bernard had come to Lincoln to see Kittie Noonan and her family, they had kept him there, not returning him to the Donohues in Chicago. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and Bernard was remanded to the custody of the Noonan and Seward families. This was apparently because the judge decided that Lincoln was a better place to raise the boy than Chicago. Bernard was also the heir to a farm in Butler county, Nebraska. Almost two years later, the Donohue family successfully challenged the jurisdiction of the court to hear the earlier proceedings. The outcome of this challenge and the fate of Bernard are unknown. However, 1930 census records show Bernard living with the Donohues in Omaha.

Summary of Proceedings:
Matoba Watari had been a resident of the United States since 1900. On June 1921, he served as a galley man on a ship going from Japan and back. He had a delayed return due to contracting gonorrhea which had him logged as a deserter and stowaway. When he arrived, U. S. Commissioner of Immigration Thomas Lynch had Matoba detained and set for deportation. Matoba petitioned claiming unlawful arrest and refuted the accusations that he was a deserter or stowaway aboard the ship.
The writ was denied and Matoba was put back in the custody of Lynch to be deported.

Summary of Proceedings: Moye Wicks filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 7, 1913 for Mary Conti. Wicks stated that Conti was held at the Spokane County Jail under the authority of Immigration Inspector A. F. Richardson. Richardson alleged that Conti was “an undesirable alien” and “entered the United States for immoral purposes and…followed the life of an immoral person within the United States.” It was alleged that the United States Commissioner of Labor had issued a warrant for her arrest. Wicks claimed Conti’s bail was excessive, in the sum of five-thousand dollars. Judge Frank H. Rudkin denied the writ on October 25, 1913.

Summary of Proceedings:
Marshall Griffin filed for a writ of habeas corpus on April 22, 1918. Seattle Police Chief Joel Warren had held Griffin since April 14, 1918 without charge. Judge John S. Jurey allowed the writ on the same day it was filed. The fate of Griffin is unknown.

According to newspaper coverage, Griffin was eighteen-years-old. He had been arrested on suspicion of “having picked the pockets of Larry Flanagan, deputy U. S. marshal at Tacoma, on a train en route to Bellingham.”

Summary of Proceedings: Peter Williamson Merta, the bound party, entered the United States from Finland to work as a logger in 1903. IN 1917 he joined the IWW, a union organization, and served as the Secretary of the organization in Raymond, Washington. On March 1st, 1918, the bound party was arrested on a warrant issued by the Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson (unnamed in the petition). The bound party was charged with being an alien, advocating or teaching the destruction of property, and being likely to become a public charge. On April 30th, 1918, Thomas M. Fisher, immigration inspector, interrogated the bound party on these issues and found the charges to be substantiated. The attorney for the petitioner does not agree that the questions were relevant. On December 9, 1918, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed. On December 13th, 1918, the Secretary of Labor issued another warrant authorizing the deportation of the bound party. It is also mentioned that he is suspecting in supporting certain anarchic beliefs such as the violent overthrow of government, disbelief in organized government, and unlawful killing of US officers. On December 16th, 1918, Judge Jeremiah Neterer let the writ issue and ordered a heating for the 30th of December. On February 5th, 1919, Judge Neterer denied the writ due to its similarity to two previously adjudicated cases, In re Samuel H. Dixon and In re Charles Bernat. The bound party was returned to the custody of the Commissioner.

Summary of Proceedings: In July 1914, Thomas Thurston and his wife Agnes Thurston were indicted in the District Court of Alaska for detaining, delaying, and embezzling mail matter. Supplemental research revealed that Thomas and Agnes Thurston served as the postmaster and assistant postmaster, respectively, of Iditarod, Alaska. The Thurston's were accused of detaining and delaying the commission of Thomas Thurston's successor as postmaster. The District Court sentenced Agnes to pay a fine of $350 and sentenced Thomas to serve one year and three months at McNeil Island Penitentiary. In October 1915, Thomas Thurston petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus alleging that the detainment was illegal as the charge was not included in the sentence and no proper or legal commitment was delivered to the warden of McNeil Island Penitentiary, O.P. Halligan. The respondent attorney returned by stating the U.S. Marshal delivered a certified copy of the judgement as commitment to the warden. Regarding the other claims of the petition, the respondent attorney cited multiple legal precedents stating that irregularities in manner and form, such as omitting to state the charge in the sentence, have been found immaterial in showing prejudice on part of the defendant. Judge Jeremiah Neterer ruled in favor of the respondent, dismissing the petition, and remanding the petitioner to the custody of the Commissioner of Immigration.

Summary of Proceedings: Golda and Rudolph Maurer were a couple living in Council Bluffs, Iowa. According to his WWI draft card, Rudolph Maurer was an clerk for American Express. On August 7, 1914, they had a baby girl, Marion Lavonne Maurer. However, on September 8, 1917, Rudolph decided to separate from his wife and move to Nebraska (an easy hop across the river), but it was agreed that Golda would retain custody of Marion. But only one day later, Rudolph, with the help of his family, including Julius Maurer, decided to take the girl. They told her mother that they just wanted to take her on a short trip, but, in fact, they absconded with her across state lines and never returned. Less than a month later, on October 2, 1917, Golda issued a writ of habeas corpus against Rudolph and Julius, demanding that they produce Marion in Douglas District Court. They complied, but their attorneys subpoenaed many witnesses to testify on their behalf. The case was dismissed without prejudice on November 10, 1917, although an Omaha Daily Bee claims that the court awarded Rudolph custody of the child, but Golda "secured possession" of the child afterwards. In 1918, Rudolph filed for divorce against Golda, and claimed that he had no idea of the whereabouts of his wife and child.

Summary of Proceedings: A. C. Rankin filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on September 22, 1924. Rankin alleged that he was unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Charles H. Van Dusen, chief of police. That same day, Judge James M. Fitzgerald issued a command that Van Dusen show cause for Rankin's detention to Judge A. C. Troup. After a hearing on September 24, 1924, Rankin's application was denied and he was remanded to custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Nick Evangellos was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Evangellos was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Evangellos and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Evangellos argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. On June 27, the writ of habeas was sustained, and Evangellos was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Mr. Michael Mullaly appeared before Judge A. L. Sutton on 22 February 1912 to submit his petition for a writ of habeas corpus for his minor daughter, Dorothy Mullaly. He states that he took his daughter to St. James Orphanage to be taken care of and that when he returned to pick up his child, Reverend Father Roach refused to allow him to take his child. On 23 February 1912, Judge Leslie ordered that Dorothy Mullaly be discharged from the custody of St. James Orphanage and Reverend Father John Roache.

Summary of Proceedings: Oliver Lachapell was arrested, charged with using "obscene language in the presence of ladies," and jailed for 12 1/2 days after refusing to pay a $25 fine. Lachappel petitioned a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. He argued that cursing in front of women was not a crime, the act making it so having been repealed decades earlier. After hearing the evidence, Lachappel was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Annie Dodd and Benjamin F. Dodd gave away 4 of their 9 children, Clara, Marvel, Rosa, and Minnie Dodd, to the Nebraska Children's Home Society. Annie and Benjamin claimed that Annie was in bad health and could not properly take care of their children at the time. They filed a writ of habeas corpus after they claimed that the Nebraska Children's Home Society refused to tell them where their children were and had placed them each under the custody of different people. The counties kids ended up in included Webster, Harlan, and Washington. Annie and Benjamin claimed to have been misled and were under the impression that would be able to get their children back anytime they wanted to. However, the Nebraska Home Society claimed that Annie and Benjamin knew exactly what they had agreed to and had given full consent to waive their rights as parents. Along with this, many witnesses testified that Benjamin was an alcoholic, the children lived in destitute conditions, and they profited off of one of their disabled children as entertainment to make money. The petition was granted for Annie and Benjamin's case against the Nebraska Home Society moved to court for a trial.
