Summary of Proceedings: On June 26th, 1875, Josephine Sheffler allowed John B. Montague to adopt her daughter, Edna Elenor Edwards, as long as he properly cared for her. Josephine was previously married to Charles A. Edwards and was given custody of their child, Edna Elenor, at the time of their divorce. On November 11th, 1876, Josephine and her husband, J. H. Sheffler filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Edna Elenor. They claimed that Montague was not taking proper care of her and that she was being kept in a saloon where vile language was used and that was associated with women of ill fame. Montague denied these claims, and stated that he and his wife had bonded with Edna, and spent a sizable amount of money to properly care for her. The outcome of the petition and the fate of Edna Elenor is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
On September 25, 1900, Lillie Parker accused John Walker of bastardy in Cass County, Nebraska. Walker was arrested, arraigned in state district court, and ordered to pay a $500 recognizance, but fled to Iowa before doing so. Since bastardy was not an extraditable offense, the court found Walker guilty of bastardy in absentia and ordered him to compensate Lillie, whose child had not survived infancy. Walker was then accused of subornation of perjury, which was an extraditable offense, and returned to Nebraska. He was arrested and released on bail a few times before ultimately being jailed for failure to pay Parker. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, his cause was dismissed without prejudice, as he had not exhausted all his remedies in state court, and he remained in custody.

It is worth noting that Judge William Munger commented directly on habeas corpus law in his opinion, saying: "It is a fundamental rule that a court will not, by proceedings in habeas corpus, review the errors of another tribunal. It is only upon the theory that the judgment, the basis of the imprisonment, is void."

Summary of Proceedings: In September 1920, Harry L. Hunsaker filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his daughter, Genevieve Hunsaker. The petition stated that Harry L. Hunsaker was awarded the custody of Genevieve in 1919 after the divorce to her mother. Harry entered an agreement with Walter W. Hamilton, where Hamilton agreed to keep Harry's three children together in his home. Hamilton violated this agreement and gave Genevive to the Nebraska Children's Home Society, which gave custody to respondent Pearl Beck. The petition alleges Pearl is a woman of bad character and unlawfully restraining Genevieve in her custody. The case was dismissed for want of prosecution in 1922.

Summary of Proceedings: William H. Geary and William Williams were seamen upon a ship called the Barque Cambridge. On May 5, they petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and stated that their voyage concluded at Port Townsend in 1872. After the voyage concluded, they asked to be paid and discharged from the ship. The ship captain filed a complaint to Commissioner Burns and they were charged with mutiny. They argued that the commissioner violated an act authorizing commissioners to superintend the shipping and discharge of seamen by charging them based only on the oral evidence of the captain. On May 7, Judge Orange Jacobs approved the petition. On May 9, Judge Jacobs ordered the respondent to bring Geary and Williams before the court. On May 12, the respondent replied and stated that Commissioner Burns ordered him to detain Geary and Williams until their trial date. The judge then remanded Geary and Williams into the custody of the respondent to await trial.

Hrachovsky’s lawyer, Walter Metzenbaum, stated in a petition for a writ of habeas corpus that Warren had not charged Hrachovsky. According to newspaper coverage, Seattle police arrested preacher Hrachovsky on July 28, 1919 after authorities in Minneapolis, Minnesota issued a warrant for grand larceny. Judge John S. Jurey issued the writ on July 29, 1919 however, newspaper coverage stated that Hrachovsky was returned to Deputies E. J. Gustaison and A. E. Munson for trial in Minneapolis.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 11, 1921, a writ of Habeas Corpus was petitioned for by Harry H. Schiffler on behalf of his child Kathryn Elizabeth Schiffler against Walter N. Halsey. In his petition Harry presented that his daughter Kathryn was in custody of Halsey, a Presbyterian minister in Omaha and dean of UNO, without his consent. In his response, Halsey claimed that his daughter who had passed earlier in the same year was the wife of Harry and mother of Kathryn and that when she died, she requested that Halsey keep and care for Kathryn. It was also stated in his petition that Harry had remarried and together with Erma Nelson had a comfortable and safe home for Kathryn. He had traveled all the way from Los Angeles to be in Omaha for the hearing. It was January of the following year that the petition was dismissed for want of prosecution. In the 1930 census, Katheryn is seen living in Los Angeles with Harry and his new wife, Florence.

Summary of Proceedings: Nathan Finegold filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on December 28, 1923. On the same day, Judge Charles A. Goss issued an order commanding that Sheriff Michael L. Endres show cause for Finegold's detention. Endres submitted a response stating that in November, Finegold had been arrested due to a capias issued by Judge Carroll O. Stauffer for the charge of being in "contempt of court." This charge was connected to an accusation that Finegold had committed perjury as a plaintiff in a suit against the Union Outfitting Company and William Bell. Finegold was sent to the County Jail and was found to be sane in a medical examination by Dr. G. Alexander Young. On November 17th, 1923, the Court found him guilty of contempt of Court in connection with perjury and sentenced him to eight (8) months in prison. The judge for the habeas corpus petition dismissed Finegold's application without prejudice and it is likely that Finegold's detention continued.

Summary of Proceedings: Edgar Robinson was a Canadian citizen that was arrested due to a warrant issued by the acting Secretary of Labor in February 1918. The warrant alleged that Robinson violated American immigration laws by advocating for the unlawful destruction of property. In his petition for writ of habeas corpus, Robinson argued that he was denied his right to counsel, his right to examine the warrant and the evidence within, and was subjected to “personal cruelties and intimidations” which compelled him to give evidence against himself. Robinson also highlights that he has remained imprisoned for more than six months after his hearing with the Immigration Inspector. Judge Frank Rudkin agreed to hear Robinson’s petition for writ of habeas corpus. Following the hearing, Rudkin ruled that there was no testimony that showed that Robinson advocated or taught the unlawful destruction of property and that his detention illegally deprived him of his liberty. As such, Rudkin ordered that Robinson be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
C. S. Riddle applied for a writ of habeas corpus on February 26, 1918, alleging that Seattle County Sheriff John Stringer held him without due process. Stringer countered that Riddle had been charged with grand larceny and was being held within the appropriate sixty-day pre-trial period. 

Of note, a key witness in the case, Fred Hafsrof, a seafaring man, had departed for East Asia and would not return until March 1918, further complicating the case. While the writ was issued, Springer’s amended return challenged Riddle’s petition and asked for a denial. The fate of Riddle is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Mahala filed for a writ of habeas against Martin Mitchell claiming that she was unlawfully held by him and his was attempting to take her from St. Louis to Kentucky. Mahala claimed that she was a free woman born in Illinois in 1812  to a woman who had herself been freed from the service of Elijah Mitchell around 1808-1809. Martin Mitchel claimed that Mahala was instead part of the estate of the now deceased Elijah Mitchell and now his property. Mahala’s case was grouped by the court with a number of other suits, mostly made by explicitly Black litigants, against several members of the Mitchel family. Judge Carr agreed to hear Mahala’s petition, and also allowed her to sue as a poor person, and assigned her the legal counsel of Gustavus Bird. With Bird’s help, Mahala accused Martin of trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment. Further events and the outcome of Mahala’s petition is unknown.

Petitioner Frank Vangart, the father of Willie, then filed for the release of Wilie Vangart to release Willie who has now reached the age of 16. Judge Kennedy finds that Willie is indeed unlawfully deprived of his liberty, and he is released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Frank Smith petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in an attempt to retrieve Mollie Calhoun, a fourteen-year-old girl, from the custody of W. E. Miller and his wife, which was granted. Frank maintained that Mollie's father, Joseph Calhoun, had left Mollie in his charge when he left Oregon for the Indian Territory, now Oklahoma. Although Frank admitted that he had allowed Mollie to live with the Millers in the hope that she receive an education, he asserted that instead they were "making a slave out of her." During the hearing, Frank withdrew his petition. An entry on page 34 of the Marion County Probate Index suggests that Mollie remained with the Millers.

Summary of Proceedings: Yaichiro was held in the Seattle Immigration Station on the offense of moral turpitude within two years after he immigrated into the U.S. and on the offense of entering the U.S. without inspection. He applied for habeas and claimed said imprisonment and deportation to be illegal, that he was denied right to counsel, and did not have a fair hearing. One important aspect of his allegedly unfair hearing is that Yaichiro reportedly did not understand English, and was not able to understand the questions asked of him. The petition was denied, and Yaichiro was returned to the custody of Henry White to be deported.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 22, 1904, a grand jury found evidence that Robert Gillis, aided by Philip Reardon, broke into a warehouse owned by N. A. T. Co and committed larceny by taking several cases of cigars. Gillis escaped to Washington state, followed by the respondent, a Deputy U.S. Marshall, George A. Leckley, who had been given agency by the Governor of Alaska, John G. Brady, to bring Gillis to justice as a fugitive of the law. Thus on December 8, 1904, a petition was filed following Gillis’ apprehension by Leckley for the purpose of securing his freedom. On May 8, 1905, Judge George C. Hatch threw out the writ  and remanded Gillis to the custody of Leckley so that the warrant could be carried into effect.

Summary of Proceedings: Petitioner A. D. Warner used his expertise as a jurist to have the record expunged on November 14, 1898. Newspaper accounts indicated that Warner, five years previous, had been engaged in a child custody dispute with his ex-wife, Evalyn M. Warner, during a divorce. According to newspaper coverage, Warner filed a writ of habeas corpus against Evalyn in order to obtain custody of their son, Dixon Carroll Warner, after Evalyn placed Dixon in the House of the Good Shepherd. According to newspaper coverage, Judge Lichtenberg had “granted an alternative writ, making it returnable” on August 4, 1892.

Summary of Proceedings: Harry Gee petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Gee claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Gee was arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Gee are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 26, 1928 Calorina Merales was sentenced to serve 90 days in the Douglas County jail under a complaint filed against him for carrying concealed weapons in violation of the ordinance of the city of Omaha. Merales was confined to the jail on a state mittimus which listed a violation of the statutes of the state of Nebraska as the reason for confinement. On these grounds, Sam Beber filed for a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus for Calorina Merales, arguing that the state mittimus ordering confinement did not align with the complaint he was found guilty under. The outcome of the case and fate of Calorina Merales are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 30, 1913, Adolph A. Gust and his attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he was being illegally held by Edward Cudihee. Gust stated that he divorced his wife, Sarah A. Gust, and was then ordered to turn over all property and money, and then to pay a fee of $3000 and a fee of $5000. Gust said that he turned over his money and property, but was consequently unable to pay the fees, and was jailed for contempt of court for failing to pay those fees. Gust claimed that the court did not have the jurisdiction to issue the warrant, and that there were not sufficient facts supporting the charge in the warrant. Newspaper coverage indicates that Judge Macintosh approved Gust’s writ, and he was released.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 20, 1917, Roy C. Jordan filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that Chief of Detectives Steve Maloney unlawfully restrained him of his liberty in the Omaha City Jail. He claims that Maloney illegally and unlawfully arrested him on February 17 without a warrant and without a complaint or a criminal charge filed against him. Thus, Maloney detained him without a warrant or authority of law. The same day, the judge accepted the petition and filed a writ of habeas corpus; however, the outcome of this proceeding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: John D. Decora was arrested after a complaint was made by Louise Johnson Bear to Thurston County on March 14, 1910; that Decora had deserted wife Helen Johnson Decora on September 22, 1909, and had been having a sexual affair with an unmarried woman, Grace Graywolf, and has lived with Graywolf since then. Decora was charged with adultery and wife desertion, his trial was held on March 25, 1910, but he refused any legal representation. Decora plead guilty to the charge of adultery and was sentenced to four months in Thurston County jail with only bread and water. On April 15, Decora and attorney, Charles T. Dickinson filed for habeas against Douglas County sheriff, E. F. Brailey; charging that Brailey had no authority to detain Decora in Douglas County. On April 18, Decora was released from Douglas County custody and transferred back to Thurston County authorities.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 12, 1920, Mattie Cahill was arrested on the south side of Omaha, Nebraska, and charged with being an inmate of an ill-governed house. She was found guilty in the South Side Police Court by Omaha Police Magistrate Charles E. Foster. Mattie Cahill then paid the $200.00 appeal bond set by Foster. On September 13, 1920, the case respondents Marshall Eberstein, Omaha Police Chief, and Alta Berger, Matron and Superintendent of the Omaha Detention Hospital, illegally detained Mattie Cahill at the Detention Hospital of Omaha and subjected her to forced physical examinations instead of releasing her to the District Court of Douglas County after the appeal. On September 17, 1920, Mattie Cahill’s attorneys, Jamieson H. Sullivan and Eugene D. Sullivan, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that the respondents violated Amendment 5 of the Constitution by subjecting Mattie Cahill to forced physical examinations. The petition was allowed by Judge Charles Goss that day and the Douglas County Sheriff, Michael L. Clark, delivered the writ to the respondents on September 17, 1920, by judge’s order. On September 20, 1920, Marshall Eberstein and Alta Berger responded to the writ and provided copies of the commitments they received from Foster and Dr. J. F. Edwards, Omaha Health Commissioner, that ordered the respondents to take Mattie to the Detention Hospital of Omaha in order to subject her to forced physical examinations to ascertain whether or not she had contracted a venereal disease. After the hearing, Judge Charles Goss ordered the respondents to release Mattie Cahill from custody and she was released based on the results of the examination.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 24th, 1888, J. R. Snyder issued a warrant of arrest for B. Norman. Snyder claimed that Norman had violated an ordinance that was passed in 1837, which established the fire limits in Spokane. On that same day, Norman filed a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he was being wrongfully imprisoned by J. F. Warren, Spokane Chief of Police. The next day, Judge George Turner ordered Warren to bring Norman to court. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Pat Burns, petitioner and bound party, was allegedly falsely charged with larceny by the State of Washington on 13 June, 1897. Burns filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on 12 July, 1898, alleging that he was being transported to prison after being found guilty of grand larceny in Superior Court of King Count, and while awaiting appeal to the Supreme Court of Washington. The petitioner alleged that his incarceration was invalid on the grounds that grand larceny is a felony which should require a grand jury, which the petitioner alleged he did not receive.

Lee Him petitioned for their writ of habeas corpus. Writ of habeas corpus was denied for Lee Yick and Fook Gue, and they were remanded by Judge Charles B. Bellinger. Petition outcome for Hen Sen Fong is unknown. Case file is incomplete.

Summary of Proceedings: In March 1918, Alson Cole pled guilty to murder in the district court of Howard County, Nebraska and was sentenced to death. In January 1920, he unsuccessfully petitioned for habeas relief in federal court. In August, he petitioned a second time, arguing that he had not pled guilty to murder in the first degree--which is how he was sentenced--and that the trial court had never had a hearing to determine the degree of his guilt. The judge agreed with him and in October that the Howard County district court re-sentence him. In December, the court issued a nunc pro tunc order establishing that they had found Cole guilty of first-degree murder in 1918 but had neglected to record this fact in the trial docket. They once again remanded him to the custody of the warden of the Nebraska State Penitentiary to await his execution. Cole petitioned a third time in federal court for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that the nunc pro tunc order did not remedy the defects in his trial. The court disagreed and denied his petition without a hearing on December 20, 1920. Newspaper reporting reveals that the state of Nebraska executed Alson Cole later that day.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 9, 1876, nine mariners were arrested and charged with desertion after refusing to take the American Ship "War Hawk" to San Francisco. The petitioners claimed they were wrongfully detained for this crime by a deputy US marshal. Instead of proceeding to the ordered location, the mariners landed at the port of discovery in Washington and were arrested there. The nine men petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming neglect was the cause for not proceeding to their ordered location. Their attorneys argued that while the "War Hawk" was able to provide the plaintiffs with suitable food, it neglected to do so and was an "unseaworthy" ship. Marshall Wyckoff responded that the said marines absented themselves without permission from the master or another officer of the said "War Hawk" and before the end of said voyage contract. John R. Lewis, a King County judge, ruled that the said plaintiffs were "illegally restrained and imprisoned of their liberty" and granted their petition.

Summary of Proceedings: Italian Vincent Corella filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 30, 1918. Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid held Corella under the authority of immigration officials, including A. F. Richardson and the Secretary of Labor, for advocating the teaching of the destruction of property. Case similarities related to dates and allegations levied against Corella point to other arrests of I.W.W. members in the Pacific Northwest. Judge Frank H. Rudkin dismissed the writ due to the earlier discharge of Corella from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
According to newspaper coverage, George and his wife had recently divorced and in April 1919, while courts had awarded Mrs. Hansen custody, Lily left her mother’s home in Poulsbo to seek out her father in Seattle.

An April 28, 1919 ruling by Judge King Dykeman had made Lily a ward of the state of Washington and ordered her to stay at the Girls Parental School, with George ordered to pay every month for her support.

George Hansen filed for a writ of habeas corpus on December 17, 1919 for his sixteen-year-old daughter, Lily Hansen, to be released from the Girls Parental School.  The fate of Lilly is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Bound parties Thomas Combs and Charles Ross were arrested for unlawfully collecting and removing garbage without a contract with the City of Omaha in 1901. They were ordered to pay a fine of $5, refused, and were detained; then, Henry Combs filed an application for Habeas Corpus on their behalf. When the case was heard in April of 1901, Judge Dickinson found that they were indeed legally confined as they violated the 4462 Ordinance, yet the first section of the Ordinance is void because it seeks to enforce a civil contract upon the City by the exercise of a criminal ordinance. Therefore, their writ for Habeas Corpus is approved, and while a bill of exceptions is filed the Nebraska Supreme Court affirms the judgment.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 7th, 1890, Marcus Pollasky filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his client, Charles Pollow. On the previous day, November 6th, 1890, Pollow stood trial for the crime of larceny, to which he pled not guilty. Pollasky alleged that the jury returned a verdict of not guilty, but that Pollow was then put back into the custody of Sheriff John H. McGraw without cause or due process of law. Judge J. A. Stanton allowed the petition, and summoned McGraw and Pollow to appear in the court of Judge T. J. Humes on November 8th. The fate of Pollow is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Mike Aboud, a previous resident of Oklahoma, unlawfully claimed to own several items to receive $37 from the Bank of Aline under false pretenses. Afterward, he fled to Nebraska. Thomas B. Ferguson then requested the Governor of Nebraska, John Mickey, to arrest and extradite Aboud. Ferguson specifies that the Governor of Nebraska should place Aboud in the custody of Gus Hadwiger, Sheriff of Woods County, to bring to Oklahoma—Mike Aboud's presumed relative, Elias Aboud, petitions for a writ of Habeas Corpus on his behalf. Judge George Day finds Aboud to be lawfully detained and rejects the writ of Habeas Corpus, and he is then extradited to Oklahoma.

Summary of Proceedings: Alice Bigelow's twin daughters Edith and Edna were placed in the Home of the Good Shepherd under two conditions: 1) they would only be there for six months and she could remove them whenever she wanted, and 2)they would not be taught the Catholic religion. Alice's daughters were there for one year and three months and she was only allowed to see them through bars under the supervision of a woman referred to as "Mother Superior." They were also taught Catholic practices which Alice believed affected them mentally and physically. She refers to them as being "regular prisoners in fact." On March 22, 1899, Alice petitioned to get her children back and was granted custody on that same day.

Summary of Proceedings: Ella M. Crouch petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of her minor son Robert Koch Lynch against Polla A. Lynch. Crouch claimed that her divorce from Robert Lynch’s father awarded her the custody of Robert Lynch for three months each year while Robert Lynch was on summer break from school. Crouch claimed that Robert Lynch had concluded school for the year, but Polla Lynch refused to surrender custody of him to Crouch. Ancestry records indicate Polla Lynch was Charles Lynch’s second wife and Robert Lynch’s stepmother. The petition was allowed, but the case outcome and fate of Robert Lynch are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 11th, 1904, O.J. Watkins, with his lawyer G.M. Emory petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus. Watkins’s petition stated that he was being held illegally by John Doe, Sheriff of King County, Washington, in the King County Jail. It also stated that Watkins believed he was being held on a warrant from H.C. Beach, a Police Judge in Bellingham, Whatcom County, Washington. Watkins argued that the warrant was illegal and void because it was based on a complaint from H.J. Smith that claimed Watkins took money from him under false pretenses, which was therefore outside of the jurisdiction of the police judge. Watkins also complained that he had been held for over a month in King County, despite being discharged after hearing from a Justice of the Peace for King County. Watkins was also a resident of California and had been brought to King County through extradition proceedings, and he could not furnish bail. He claimed in his petition that he believed the sole purpose he was being held was for the payment of $31 back to H.J. Smith. After a full hearing from both sides, in which the attorney for the Sheriff admitted that he was being held for the purpose of the repayment, Judge Frank H. Rudkin released O.J. Watkins.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 30th, 1894, Clarence S. Preston filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his client, Herman Weise. The scans of the actual petition are unclear, and it is subsequently difficult to make out the exact details, but Preston appears to claim that Police Judge W. H. Vernon did not have the jurisdiction to arrest Weise on a charge of maintaining a nuisance. Preston also seems to claim that Ordinance No. 118 for the City of Ballard, which made maintaining a nuisance a crime, was invalid. He claims that Weise’s detainment by Marshall J. D. Diggs is illegal, and subpoenas both the city clerk, E. O. Marsh, and Judge Vernon to court. Judge Richard Osborn allows the writ. Newspaper coverage indicates that Weise was released from prison.

Summary of Proceedings: Richard Lloyd Green was the minor son of Pearl Alma Bentley who on April 14th, 1923, submitted a petition of habeas corpus on his behalf. In this petition, she claimed that Richard was being unlawfully held by his father, Edgar B. Green. Pearl stated that in September 1919 she divorced Edgar and was awarded custody of Richard, and that Richard would be able to visit Edgar during summer vacations. Pearl asserted that she had provided Richard a good home and was ready to continue that upon his return to her. Pearl asserted that Edgar was not a fit parent. He was addicted to alcohol. He would often be very intoxicated and in this state he would become neglectful towards Richard. Pearl alleged that Edgar threatened to remove Richard from Omaha (thus out of the court's jurisdiction). She requested that Edgar produce Richard before the court and that she be granted custody of him. The judge granted Pearl's petition, and the sheriff brought Richard before the court. On April 14, 1923, Richard was turned over to the custody of Pearl on the condition of her appearance at the hearing on April 16th. On April 30th the case was dismissed with prejudice, with parties to pay their own costs. The 1930 census shows Richard living with his father.

Summary of Proceedings: W. A. Kerry petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles L. Beckingham. Kerry claimed he was being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail, as he had not been granted his right to due process and had not been charged with anything in court. Beckingham returned, affirming that Kerry was in his custody and providing a copy of the warrant for Kerry’s arrest, which charged him with possessing an unlawful amount of intoxicating liquor. The case file does not reveal the outcome or Kerry’s fate.

Summary of Proceedings: The Justice of the Peace, John B. Gordon issued a warrant to arrest Albert Sykes on February 25, 1913 on the grounds that Sykes was a fugitive of the state of Oregon. Gordon issued the warrant at the request of W.G. Witzke who wrote to Gordon detailing that Sykes was wanted for assaulting and attempting to rob a person named, W.W. Kofeldt in Multnomak County, Oregon on October 2, 1912. Following Sykes arrest, R.B. Brown filed a write of habeas corpus on February 25, 1913. Brown, acting as Sykes' lawyer, claimed that Sykes' arrest was illegal and that he had no knowledge of any complaint or warrant issued against him. Judge Ronald approved the petition and ordered the Seattle Chief of Police, Claud Bannick to bring the body of Sykes before the court for a hearing on February 28, 1913. The fate of Sykes after the hearing is not stated in the documents.

Summary of Proceedings: According to newspaper coverage on June 16, 1918, James Treanor, D.  S. Deitz, Patrick McGovern, William Baskin, and J. J. Extell were all arrested and charged with being disorderly persons. The group was alleging hosting an I.W.W. meeting in the woods near Lake Washington when they were arrested by the Chief of Police, Joel Warren. In their petition, the petitioners argue that they do not know the nature of their charge and are not guilty of any violations of the law. Further newspaper coverage notes that this writ of habeas corpus was denied by Judge John S. Jurey stating that the petitioners needed to file writs of habeas corpus separately.

Summary of Proceedings: John Grant Lyman, with the help of L. B. Thornet and Charles M. Courtwright, escaped the Alameda County Jail in California on September 24th, 1911. Lyman was quickly indicted, tried, and convicted on the charge of conspiring to aid, abet, assist, and permit John Grant Lyman, himself. He was sentenced to 18 months in the United States Penitentiary at McNeil's Island and his sentence started on December 25th, 1911. On December 13th, 1912, Lyman filed a writ of habeas corpus, stating that he should not be confined to the Penitentiary at McNeil's Island, as there were no federal statutes in place that punished a prisoner for escaping, and therefore he had not committed a crime. The fate of the bound party and the outcome of the petition are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 7th, 1918, the bound party, Madge Weeks, was arrested for keeping an ill-governed house. The case was tried in police court by James F. Fitzgerald who ordered that Weeks be jailed for twenty days. On July 11th, Weeks appealed to the district court for a bond, which was approved. It is then alleged by the bound party that the Chief of Police refused to acknowledge the bond and was held in custody beyond the remainder of her sentence. On July 30th, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed and said writ was granted and called for the discharge of the bound party on August 1st.

Summary of Proceedings: Sam Walton and Lulu Walton got married in October of 1908 and had a son, McKinley Walton. In April of 1909, Lulu Walton deserted Sam Walton for Edward Stanley, taking their son with them. Sam Walton filed a writ of habeas corpus for his son in December of 1918, with the hopes of Lulu Walton and Edward Stanley returning McKinley Walton to him. In January of 1920, the writ was dismissed and the fate of the parties are unknown.

Rudkin dismissed the writ after deportation proceedings against Mirylees were dropped.

Summary of Proceedings:
Franklin Parker petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to challenge the detention of Elizabeth Winteer at the Hospital for the Insane at Ingleside, Nebraska, now the Hastings Regional Center, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Wineteer was released. 

Newspaper coverage indicated that Elizabeth was committed by her husband in order to get access to her land. Franklin, her brother, petitioned for her release. L. M. Parker, Elizabeth's other brother, apparently was also involved. 

N.B. Dr. Sadie C. Doran, witness, was an early woman physician in Nebraska.

Summary of Proceedings: Gussie Goldman Waters, a native of the Russian Empire, immigrated to the United States in 1903. She stated she was a U.S. citizen through her marriage to Fred L. Woods, a natural born citizen of the U.S., which took place on November 1914. In October 1914, Goldman was taken into custody at Skagway, Alaska by an immigrant inspector under a warrant charging her with being an "alien" to the United States of America and entering the U.S. for the purposes of prostitution. Goldman was transferred to Seattle and taken into custody by Henry M. White, Commissioner of Immigration. Goldman petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus alleging that she was not given a fair and impartial trial as she was not given copy of the proceedings, denied her right to cross examine witnesses, and no testimony was taken to show the petitioner was not an alien to the U.S. subsequent of her marriage. The Secretary of the Department of Labor ordered the cancellation of the warrants of arrest and deportation against the petitioner. Subsequently, Judge Cushman ordered the petitioner be discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Tom Weber was an immigrant from Germany, having arrived in the United States in 1903. In 1916 Weber joined the IWW, a union organization. On February 15th, 1918, Tom Weber was arrested under a warrant issued by the U.S. Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson, and was held for multiple months while his case was pending. The charges alleged were that he was an alien, he advocated for and taught the unlawful destruction of property, and that upon entering the country he was a likely public charge. On December 2nd, 1918, a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed stating among other things that while Weber was not in favor of capitalism he did not endorse the destruction of property, he was at no time a beggar, and that a transcript of his hearing was never given to him. A return from the attorneys for the respondent states that the application does not include facts sufficient for a cause of action, does not show entitlement to relief, and that the court had no jurisdiction as the Secretary of Labor was yet to rule on the case. The fate of the petition and the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 10th, 1923, H.S. Lover filed a petition on behalf of his client Frank Monroe, claiming that Frank was unlawfully detained in the county jail by Michael Endres. The judge allowed the petition, and issued the writ to Michael Endres, "commanding him [Endres] to release said Frank H. Monroe from custody upon giving bond in the sum of $100." On February 14th, Lover filed a subpoena requesting the presence of Irvin Stalmaster (Deputy County Attorney) as a witness on behalf of Frank Monroe. On February 15th, Lover submitted an amended petition. This amended petition explained that Frank had been arrested and charged with assault. In court, he had entered a plea of not guilty but the court record a plea of guilty instead. Frank and his lawyer claimed that this was done unlawfully, wrongfully, and without jurisdiction. As a result of this guilty plea, he was sentenced to 90 days in jail. Frank also alleged that at the time of the hearing, he advised the court that he had employed counsel and requested that he be given sufficient time for his counsel to appear. Frank alleged that the court refused to grant him sufficient time for his counsel to be present. Frank requested that the court fix a bail bond in such a sum they deemed appropriate, that they should correct the record of his plea, and that he be granted the chance to appeal. Frank alleged that the court refused to fix the amount of bail or to correct the record, which prevented him from being able to submit an appeal. Michael Endres submitted a return to the writ. The dates of what Endres described were not filled in on the return. But, Endres claimed that, firstly, Frank was released on his own recognizance. He then explained that his authority for detaining Frank in the first place came from a mittimus from Judge Frank Dineen after Frank was sentenced to 90 days after being found guilty of assault. On February 17th, the writ was allowed. Frank Monroe was released from custody and his bond was exonerated.

Summary of Proceedings: John Whitney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his daughter, Mary Whitney, from the custody of his late wife's parents, Nathan and Irena Tharpe, which was granted. This may have been because he remarried in 1906. After hearing the evidence, the writ was allowed and Mary remanded to the custody of her father. The court, however, required that John allow Mary to spend at least ten days with her grandparents at least twice a year in order to keep custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
On July 29th, 1899, Charles W. Nordstrom petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus after being convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death. The petition alleged that since the verdict against Nordstrom, he had become insane and it would have been inhumane to take his life. A commission appointed by the Superior Court found Nordstrom to be sane, and to avoid execution, Nordstrom and his attorneys filed a series of subsequent appeals. Circuit Judge C.H. Hanford denied the writ, and Nordstrom subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court in which the ruling was affirmed. 
Supplementary research shows that since the alleged murder took place in 1892 and Nordstrom was executed in 1901. The case gained national fame at the time for being the longest stay of execution in history.
For other petitions filed by Nordstrom see related petitions.

Summary of Proceedings: Mack Dwyer filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against sheriff Michael L. Clark on August 29, 1919. Dwyer's petition stated that he was charged with vagrancy on August 28, 1919. The Police magistrate found Dwyer guilty, fined him $100, and committed him to the Omaha County Jail until the judgment was complied with. Dwyer's petition stated that the law that he was charged under—Section 290 of the Criminal Code of the State of Nebraska—mandated that the fine for the offense should not exceed $50. Thus, Dwyer stated that the judgment was null, void, and illegal. On August 29, 1919, Judge William A. Redick commanded that Clark bring the body of Dwyer before the court for a hearing on August 30, 1919. Dwyer's application was granted. The appearance docket stated that Dwyer remained in jail but would be discharged upon payment of a $50 fine, suggesting that the judge voided the $100 fine and reduced it to $50.

Summary of Proceedings: Harry Fetterhoff petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. The original petition was lost, but Warren’s reply stated that he was holding Fetterhoff in the Seattle City Jail under a warrant charging Fetterhoff with violating the Explosives Act of 1917. Newspaper records indicate Fetterhoff may have been involved with the I.W.W. Due to the brevity of the case file, the outcome of the case and Fetterhoff’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In March 1924, the Multnomah County Court of Domestic Relations committed seventeen-year-old Ferne Hills to the State Industrial School for Girls for "stealing" and other "immoral conduct." That August, her parents, Marvin and Myrtle Hills, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on her behalf, which was granted. After hearing the evidence. Ferne was remanded to the custody of the school superintendent. The Hills appealed the decision to the state supreme court, which affirmed the decision of the lower court.

Summary of Proceedings: Sam Gum petitioned for habeas after being detained by Immigrant Commissioner Henry M. White on the accusation that he was an illegal immigrant with bonds of $1,000. Sam Gum argued that his deportation and his hearing was unfair and illegal, that he had lived in the United States for many years, and added that he had already had a hearing with a William G. Strench in Ketchikan, Alaska, addressing his work as a cook for a prostitution house. On July 14, 1921, Sam Gum was granted temporary leave of jurisdiction in order to provide his family money in Alaska which they were owed. He then died on March 10, 1922, and his petition was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: Frank Mead petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against W. N. Keller, the superintendent of the Western Hospital for the Insane. Mead claimed that his commitment to the Western Hospital for the Insane was illegal as he was not allowed to testify, gather witnesses, or procure an attorney. He alleged that the trial happened without him present, without his knowledge, without a jury, and with only one witness. Keller brought forth the complaint and commitment paperwork, which claimed Mead experienced auditory hallucinations, paranoia, and the persistent delusion that his neighbors, Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Cavness, were attempting to persecute him. Several witnesses were called, and all testified that Mead was fully sane and that the Cavness’s were persistently violent and aggressive toward him. Keller filed a motion to quash the writ, which was granted. Mead appealed to the Supreme court of the State of Washington, but his fate remains unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: William George Clarke, a man from Chicago, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that his two sons, Holley (19) and Caryl (8), were being deprived of their freedom by Mary E. Lyon and H. E. Wood. The respondents were the half-brother and in-law, respectively, of Annie Carpenter Clarke, the deceased ex-wife of the petitioner and mother of the bound party who had moved to Lancaster County with the children following the divorce in 1901. Judge Holmes granted the petition. The respondents claimed that they were appointed guardians of the bound party and given control of Annie's estate by her request after her death in 1906. They also alleged that the petitioner did not ever financially support his children after the divorce. Additionally, they claimed that he had a violent temper and was addicted to "intoxicating liquors," thus not making him a suitable guardian for his children. After hearing evidence, Judge Holmes denied the writ and ordered that the children remain in custody of Lyon and Wood, but that the petitioner be able to visit them at seasonable times. In the Court's decision, they also mention that the petitioner was currently going through another divorce from his second wife. Clarke then moved for the Court to grant him a new trial, which was overruled. The appearance docket shows that the Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed the Court's decision in 1909.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 22nd, 1923, Harry Miller filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. He claimed that he was being unlawfully detained by Peter Dillon, Charles VanDeusen, Ike Walton, and a John Doe. He said the reason for his detainment was a warrant issued by the governor of Nebraska based off of a requisition by the governor of Missouri. In this warrant, Ike Walton (Kansas City Chief of Police) and the other named respondents were authorized to detain Harry and bring him to the state border to be transported back to Kansas City, where he was alleged to have attempted to acquire property under false pretenses. Harry claimed that this detainment was unlawful for many reasons: 1) All proceedings had and papers issued regarding the requisitions and warrant were null and void 2) The governor of Nebraska had no power to authorize his detainment because the demand and requisition was not authorized by the Constitution or Nebraska or Missouri statute 3) The warrant was issued with no investigation 4) He had never been in Missouri to commit the crimes he was accused of 5) Extradition was not authorized by the Constitution or Nebraska statute 6) The crimes alleged against him were crimes of Missouri and not Nebraska. The respondents submitted a return in which they claimed their authority for detainment came from a warrant issued out of the Municipal Court of Omaha by Judge George Holmes. Neither the governor of Nebraska or Missouri were mentioned in this return. But, the warrant was for the charge of being a fugitive from justice. On November 26th, Judge Arthur Wakely ruled in favor of Harry; he allowed the writ and Harry was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles O’Malley petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on July 24, 1917. O’Malley argues that he was unlawfully imprisoned and restrained of his liberty by the Chief of People Charles Beckingham. He states that the arrest was illegal because there was no warrant, order, or justification for his detainment. Beckingham responds stating that O’Malley’s arrest was based on a warrant issued by John B. Gordon which charged O’Malley with being a fugitive from justice. The case file does not state what O’Malley’s original crime was nor where it was committed. The file also does not state the outcome of the petition or of the bound party.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 19, 1922, Fred Sledge filed for habeas against sheriff, Michael L. Clark. In the petition, Sledge explained that on April 5, 1921, he had been sentenced to 1 to 7 years in the State Penitentiary, to take effect within 30 days. Sledge argued that those 30 days have past and that he had been confined for over 1 year. In returning the writ, Clark explained that the penitentiary had no room for Sledge and was ordered to remain in Douglas County jail until room was opened on April 20, 1922. The writ for habeas was denied on April 24, 1922, and Sledge was ordered to remain in custody. Newspaper coverage indicates Sledge had been convicted of burglary.

Summary of Proceedings: Frank G. Bevans petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that his ten-year-old biological daughter, Gussie Bevans, was being deprived of her liberty by Frank's ex-wife and Gussie's mother, Winnie Crandall. Frank and Winnie had divorced years previously, and the court awarded custody to Mrs. F. L. Knight, Winnie's sister and Gussie's aunt. Judge Holmes granted the petition. In her response, Crandall claimed that Frank should not be given custody because he lives in Wyoming and that Knight was not a proper guardian because he had moved with his family to York, Nebraska—away from Crandall. Frank objected to having his daughter in Winnie's custody, as he didn't want his daughter under her husband's influence. After reviewing the evidence, Judge Holmes ruled that custody of the bound party would be awarded to Louise R. Upton, Matron of the School for Girls (Brownell Hall) in Omaha, Nebraska for five years. Frank G. Bevans filed two additional motions, one in June of 1900 and one in June of 1901, requesting that Gussie Bevans be allowed to spend summer vacation with her parents (equally split between them), which all parties agreed to. The 1910 Census shows that Gussie was living with Frank in Augusta, Wyoming.

Summary of Proceedings: I. E. Spafford, the petitioner, was detained for administrating a drug to Fanse Spafford (relation unknown) for the purpose of causing an abortion during the stage referred to as "quick" in the case text while it was not necessary to save the life of the said mother. In this context, "quick" refers to the stage where a fetus is moving. After Fanse Spafford took the drugs, Fanse died.  I. E. Spafford was then detained, with the bail set to $500. I. E. Spafford's lawyers state that Spafford did not commit any such offense and, therefore, his detention is illegal; additionally, during his hearing, he was without an attorney and therefore was induced to waive his rights to examination. Judge Richards A. James discharged Spafford from custody due to a lack of evidence and probable cause.

Summary of Proceedings:
Around September 1894, nine-year-old Myrtle Watson was given up by her parents G.W. Watson and Mary J. Watson for unknown reasons. She was left in the care of W.H. Snyder. It is unknown how long Snyder was supposed to be in charge of Watson.

Later that same year, Snyder took Watson to Sisters of Good Shepherd - a wellness house for troubled children to seemingly avoid the responsibility of continuous care for the young girl. After Waton’s family heard of this they’ve tried to gain custody of their daughter back from Good Shepherd to no avail because they've refused to give Myrtle Watson back. 

The Watson parents filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Myrtle Waston with her supporting testimony that Good Shepherd has been stripping her of her rights and liberties as an individual and they must release her back into the care of her parents.

On February 19, 1895 the last recorded set of court records show that the writ was granted for the Sisters of Good Shepherd and the fate of Myrtle Watson is unknown.

The 1900 census shows Myrtle Watson as an "inmate" in the State Reform School.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 11, 1913 Frank Lagerquist and his attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Lagerquist claimed that he was being held against his will by Peter A Swanson. Swanson’s relationship to Lagerquist is unclear. Swanson claimed Lagerquist was insane, which Lagerquist denied. Swanson produced documentation from Nome, Alaska, stating that Lagerquist had been declared insane there, and transferred to Morning Side Asylum Company in Portland, Oregon for care. At that point, Swanson said he requested and received custody and care of Lagerquist, as granted to him by the unnamed Secretary of the Interior. Judge Frater allows the writ to be heard, and sends it to Judge Ronald’s court. Ronald deferred the case to Judge Humphries’ court. The court’s medical experts found Lagerquist to be mentally sound. Lagerquist’s writ was allowed, and he was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Anna Sultz, an immigrant from Bohemia, was deprived of her liberty by Andrew Farar, Superintendent of the County Hospital in Douglas County, Nebraska. Sultz was placed in the County Hospital by the Board of Insanity after an application by her husband, Kasper. She alleged that she was of sound mind and was not able to have a hearing or produce witnesses before the board. Newspaper coverage indicated that Anna believed her husband, Kasper, had institutionalized her in order to gain access to her property. Judge Sutton found that she is unlawfully deprived of her liberty, and she is released from custody. The newspapers reported that she was then placed under the guardianship of a neighbor, as she was considered insane, but not enough to require institutionalization.

Summary of Proceedings: The acting chief of police, Henry Spaker, arrested Gus Langston at his place of business and brought him before the police judge, J. A. Callison. Callison found Langston guilty of being in violation of the ordinance that governed the ownership and operation of pool and billiard tables. Langston was found in violation of section 8 specifically, because he allegedly allowed minors under the age of 18 to use his tables. Langston filed for a writ of habeas to see himself released, and Judge Betton agreed to hear his case and ordered a writ be delivered to Spaker, but the events and outcome of the hearing is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 8th, 1919, Nellie Atkins was arrested and charged with vagrancy, prostitution, and maintaining and keeping a common and ill-governed house. On February 10th, she pleaded not guilty in court but was found guilty. She was sentenced to 90 days in jail and a $100 fine. She immediately appealed this decision. She furnished $400 in bonds and the Magistrate issued her release. Nellie claimed that despite the issue from the Magistrate, the Chief of Police and Keeper of the Jail were not releasing her. It was on these grounds which she filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, also on February 10th. The judge granted her petition. A hearing for this writ was scheduled for July; between the issuance of the petition and the hearing Nellie was released on her own recognizance. On July 15th, 1919, the judge allowed Nellie's writ and she was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney John W. Whitham petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of his client Frank Baker against King County Sheriff John Stringer. Whitham alleged that Stringer imprisoned Baker in the King County Jail under no charge or authority of justice. Many documents are missing from the case file, but nine days after Whitham filed the petition, the court ordered Stringer to release Baker. It is unknown how the court came to this outcome.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 4, 1864, Walla Walla county policeman W. F. Tompkins got a letter from an A. Lavor in Montana asking him to arrest a J. M. Burks and William Moore. Lavor incarcerated the men in the Walla Walla jail. On October 3, 1864, the men petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, saying that there was no evidence proving that they had committed a crime. They also claimeed that no formal complaint had been filed against them. Judge Oliphant ordered the men released, stating that he had seen no proof that they should be in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: John Commons, Superintendent and Special Disbursing Agent of the Omaha Nation, was tasked with evicting Thomas Barada from land that belonged to Howard Provost, an Omaha man, under the Dawes Act. Aware of Commons' plans, Barada accused him of preparing to breach the peace in the Thurston County Court. Commons was arrested and jailed when he refused to pay a $200 peace bond and soon petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Commons was released.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 2, 1905, Bertha Kuzek and her attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her nine year-old son Richard Oswald. Kuzek stated that a man named F. G. Rangener was holding Richard without any legal right to. Judge Osborn allowed the petition, and set it to be heard by Judge Morris. Rangener made a return to the petition, stating that Richard was in the custody of Minnie Faust, who Rangener said had been granted custody of Richard because his father, Fred Oswald, was in Dawson, Y. T., and Kuzek was determined by the court to be unfit to care for Richard. Judge Morris approved the writ, and Richard was released from the custody of Faust and Rangener and returned to Kuzek.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 5, 1924, Merle Arlington was discharged from the Douglas County jail after serving a 60-day sentence, and while waiting for transportation to return to her home in Casper, Wyoming, she was compelled to appear as a witness in another case. Upon voluntarily appearing in court as a witness, Arlington was sentenced to serve 60 days in the county jail with no complaint issued against her. After being sentenced, Arlington was then charged with vagrancy and prostitution. On October 15, 1925, Arlington's attorney filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on her behalf. The outcome of the petition and Merle Arlington's fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Elsie Miller Dickinson, a native of the Russian Empire, immigrated to the United States in 1907. She stated she is a U.S. citizen through her marriage to Fred Dickinson, a natural born citizen of the U.S., which took place in November 1914. In October 1914, Miller was taken into custody at Skagway, Alaska by an immigrant inspector under a warrant charging her with being an "alien" to the United States of America and entering the U.S. for the purposes of prostitution. Miller was transferred to Seattle and taken into custody by Henry M. White, Commissioner of Immigration. Miller petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus alleging that she was not given a fair and impartial trial as she was not given copy of the proceedings, denied her right to cross examine witnesses, and no testimony was taken to show the petitioner was not an alien to the U.S. subsequent of her marriage. The Secretary of the Department of Labor ordered the cancellation of the warrants of arrest and deportation against the petitioner. Subsequently, Judge Cushman ordered the petitioner be discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Alberto Sichofsky was found to feloniously and knowingly enter and attempt to the United States from a foreign country, in this case, the Republic of Mexico. Sichofsky came to the Republic of Mexico from Poland, where he was a male citizen of the age of sixteen years and over. Sichofsky was then imprisoned at McNeil Island prison, from which he petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the basis that he had completed his sentence of three years after credit for good conduct and therefore was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty. Judge Neterer found that Sichofsy was indeed unlawfully detained and ordered for his release from McNeil prison.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney A. G. McBride petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his clients Joseph Conrad, John Osolin, and V. Deloff against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. McBride claimed that Conrad, Osolin, and Deloff were all arrested without a warrant and by no legal authority. McBride was allowed to sue on forma pauperis, claiming that any financial property Conrad, Osolin, and Deloff owned was taken from them upon their arrests. Warren alleged that Deloff was not then and was never detained by him, but admitted that Conrad and Osolin were in his custody at the Seattle City Jail. Warren claimed he detained Conrad and Osolin at the request of the United States Commissioner of Immigration and United States Department of Labor and that both men were illegal immigrants to the U. S. Warren alleged they were being charged with being disorderly persons and teaching and advocating for “the unlawful destruction of property and the overthrow by force of violence of the government of the United States.” Newspaper records indicate Conrad and Osolin may have been connected to the International Workers of the World. The petition was denied, and Conrad and Osolin remained in the custody of Warren.

Summary of Proceedings: Sometime in the middle of 1924, Mary Peterson was detained by Seattle Immigration Agents. On December 9th, 1924, Peterson was ordered to be deported because she was "a person liable to become a public charge." Peterson then filed a writ of habeas corpus on December 16th for herself and three other immigrants that were ordered to be deported, J. A. Peterson (no relation to Mary Peterson), Frank Berry, and Margaret Berry. On January 9th, 1925, Judge Cushman granted the writ and ordered the release of Mary Peterson, J. A. Peterson, and the Berrys.

Summary of Proceedings:
Doris Brown, also known as Lou Evans, was taken into custody on June 11, 1918 by the Chief of Police, Joel Warren, and later the Commissioner of Health, John S. McBride under a warrant issued by John B. Warren. The warrant charged that Brown was in violation of Seattle City Ordinance No. 16046 by violating the public morality, peace, safety, or good order of the City of Seattle. Brown stated in her petition that she was being illegally restrained of her liberty since she has not been charged with any crime. 

The City’s Health Commissioner, John S. McBride, wrote in his return to the writ that Brown was held in his custody at the city’s isolation hospital to be treated for a “dangerous, infectious, and contagious disease.” However, McBride does note that he and his assistants were unable to fully investigate whether Brown had any “dangerous, infectious, and contagious diseases” because of “the obstinate refusal of the petitioner to submit to some of the tests.” McBride further claimed that Doris Brown was a “notorious prostitute,” and submitted a section from the city’s rules and regulations on venereal diseases and underlined part of the section on syphilis and gonorrhoea which stated that “among prostitutes, all prostitutes shall be considered as suspected of suffering from such infection and subject to examination by the health officer.” The outcome of the petition and the fate of the bound party are not stated in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: James Simpson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L Reid. Simpson alleged he was a Scottish immigrant and was being held in Spokane County Jail awaiting deportation. He claimed Richardson and Reid had no authority to hold him on the charge of teaching or advocating for the destruction of property. Newspaper records indicated that Simpson may have been associated with the I.W.W. Richardson and Reid provided the warrant for Simpson’s arrest, as well as the warrant authorizing his deportation. Judge Rudkin ruled that the writ should be allowed, and Simpson’s release was set for a later date to give government authorities time to appeal if they wished. There is no evidence that any government authorities did appeal the ruling. This case is related to several other petitions for writs of habeas corpus from immigrants facing deportation on the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property whose hearings fall on the same day as Simpson’s.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 1, 1888, a complaint was filed in Garfield, Whitman County, Washington against Edgar Bunnell and Arthur Bunnell for being drunk and disorderly, which violated section 12 of article 8 of the town ordinances of Garfield, Washington. It is unknown how exactly the Bunnell men were related. On September 8, 1888, they were brought before the town clerk, Thomas Kennedy, and fined $15 each plus court costs of $65.81. Since Garfield was such a small town, the town clerk also acted as a police court judge and justice of the peace. The men petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Garfield town marshal William Isbell on September 10, 1888, claiming it wasn't in Kennedy's jurisdiction as a town clerk to sentence them. On September 11, 1888, the men paid their bond and were released from custody. In his answer to the men's writ, Isbell pointed out that the men had already been released and that Kennedy was a qualified justice of the peace. In the hearing on September 25, 1888, judge William G. Langford denied and quashed the writ, as well as ordering the Bunnells to pay Isbell's court costs.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Duteau was charged, found guilty, and imprisoned for the charge of grand larceny by Judge Reah Mary Whitehead. Duteau was accused of stealing $84 of money given to him by Charles Ballard as a surety for a bond. Following his conviction, Duteau immediately appealed the decision but could not obtain an appeal’s bond. After being unable to appeal the decision, Duteau filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that Judge Reah Whitehead did not have the jurisdiction to try and convict him for the crime of grand larceny. Judge R. B. Albertson agreed to hear the writ of habeas corpus and ruled that Judge Whitehead did not have jurisdiction in this case. Judge Albertson ordered the Duteau be discharged from custody and that his costs incurred during the trials be reimbursed.

Summary of Proceedings: Chung Chew applied for the writ of habeas corpus on January 31st, 1894, on behalf of his new wife, Lum Lin Ying, who was not allowed to land in Portland off the Steamship Signal. Chung Chew was a Chinese merchant in Portland and had been betrothed to Lum Lin Ying when he was 9 and she was 2, and the marriage was officiated according to the laws of China. He has also never seen his wife until she arrived here, and papers were signed back and forth between Portland and China for the marriage. Other Chinese people on the steamer accused her of being a prostitute from California, but had no evidence to prove it. Chung Chew’s attorneys argued that a marriage “valid in the place where it is contracted is valid anywhere”. The petition was granted and she was discharged.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 18th, 1924 John Fenezia filed for and received an order for a writ of Habeas Corpus having been arrested and deprived of his liberty by Dennis Cronin and C. J. Palmer in July of that year. Fenezia was arrested and held in Hall County Jail on accounts of selling liquor in violation of the National Prohibition Act. He had previously been given trial for said accounts where he was sentenced to three months on three counts and a fine of $400. In his petition it was presented that he was entitled to his freedom having been held for longer than the three months imposed as the longest period of imprisonment. The court agreed and ruled for him to be discharged. It was March of the following year that a petition for appeal was made by Cronin and Palmer. They presented that the sentence ordered the three months on the three counts to run consecutively and thus it would be a nine month sentence and that the imposed fine imposed imprisonment until it was paid. This appeal being allowed lead to a mandate order from the Circuit Court of Appeals in February 1926 to discharge the writ of Habeas Corpus and remand Fenezia to custody which was then carried out later that same month.

Summary of Proceedings: S. G. Linton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham. Linton alleged he was being illegally held in the Seattle City Jail with no charge against him and was being refused access to his friends or attorneys. The outcome of the case and the fate of Linton are unknown. Linton would go on to file three more petitions for writs of habeas corpus against Beckingham. Newspaper coverage links Linton's arrest and release to that of former police officer E. J. Margett.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 14, 1905 Milton M. Spear, who had given the name “Martin Von Schlosser” to those his attorney, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. He claimed that he had been arrested without a proper trial or process of law. In the petition, Spear/Schlosser claimed that he had been told he needed to stand trial on a criminal charge brought against Milton M. Spear, whom he maintained he was not. The return from Sheriff L. C. Smith and agents of Michigan Bert E. High and George H. Larkins stated that Schlosser was an alias used by Spear, and that he was a fugitive from justice from Michigan. The return alleged Spear was attempting to avoid the charges he was facing for check fraud and forgery. The return included documentation which pointed to Police Judge Sellers of Detroit originally charging Spear, and that the governors of both Michigan and Washington also issued warrants for his arrest. Newspaper coverage supported the return’s claims, indicating that Spear had been falsely claiming to be Scholsser, a German Baron, but that the authorities had presented evidence that they believed confirmed Schlosser was Spear. The fate of Spear/Scholosser and the outcome of this case are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In June 1899, Salfest A. Sylvester petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus after being arrested by the respondent, an agent appointed by the Governor of North Dakota, who attempted to extradite the petitioner to North Dakota on charges of embezzlement. The petition alleged the arrest was not in accordance with the extradition laws as the agent did not have the required documents, the crime of embezzlement was not defined in statute, and that Sylvester was not in North Dakota at the time of the alleged crime. Wenaas, in the return to the writ, alleged the Sylvester was an employee of the Equitable Life Assurance Society and embezzled possessions and property for his own use. 
Circuit Judge C. H. Hanford ordered the discharge of the Sylvester on the grounds the respondent did not show sufficient cause for restraint. The respondent motioned for a continuance in order to grant time for a new extradition order to be issued from North Dakota. and Hanford agreed to have the Sheriff hold Sylvester for two days. The respondents filed for an extra ten day extension on July fifth, it is unknown if they received it.

Summary of Proceedings: Petitioner D. B. Davidson was a contracted prospector under a Colorado syndicate that granted him supplies and provisions in exchange for a percentage of the claims found in the Canadian Northwest Territory. After a fire burned Davidson’s supplies, he continued his explorations independent of the aid of the syndicate. When he returned to San Francisco, California keeping the entirety of his claims, his contractors filed a civil suit. Davidson traveled to Seattle, Washington in order to find counsel to aid his side of the suit. There, he was jailed on August 27, 1898 by the Chief of Police, Charles Reed. Davidson's attorneys, Andrew Faulk Burleigh and Samuel Henry Piles, claimed that Davidson was arrested for fictitious charges with the purposes of extorting his money.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 9, 1881, Dan Sullivan was convicted of petty larceny in front of justice of the peace V. D. Lay and sentenced to 60 days in jail. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Sheriff David Marsh on June 13, 1881, claiming that his confinement was illegal because the writ of certiorari wasn't directed at the sheriff specifically, it didn't specify the county or jail that Sullivan was to be imprisoned in, and Lay had exceeded his jurisdiction in incarcerating Sullivan. The writ was returned and filed on June 13, 1881, but the outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Alma Zerbst petitioned for the custody of her nine-year-old illegitimate daughter Esther Gieselman on September 28, 1917. The writ of habeas corpus was served to Esther's grandparents and self-appointed guardians, William and Dora Gieselman, on September 29, 1917. They lived on 1458 South 18th Street in Omaha, Nebraska, while Alma, along with her husband Frank Zerbst, lived in Newcastle, Wyoming. According to census records found on familysearch.com, Alma's maiden name was Gieselman, and she was the daughter of William and Dora, two German immigrants. The 1910 census also provides the information that Esther's father was Belgian. The Gieselmans appeared in court on October 2, 1917, claiming that Alma Zerbst had abandoned her child shortly after its birth and was unfit to take care of her daughter. While Alma maintained that she and her husband were capable and willing to take care of the girl, the court dismissed the writ, leaving Esther in her grandparents' custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis J. Urann, a traveling salesman, was arrested by Seattle Police on June 16, 1905 due to an embezzlement charge made against him after his time as a salesman in Boston, MA. While in Boston, he embezzled over $11,000 from his employer, Samuel P. Goodenough & Co. The company filed 101 indictments against him in response to the embezzlement. Urann had thought the debt was cleared up and claimed he did not flee to Washington, but rather traveled after settling the dispute. Urann filed a writ of habeas corpus on June 22, 1905 claiming that he was arrested without due process or a legal warrant, and that the charge was “made with spite and founded upon malice” and was an attempt to extort money from him. The outcome of his writ and his case as a whole is unknown, though there is another linked case in July in which he petitions again refuting the same charge.

The petition was granted, sustained, and Brown was released from custody the same day.

Summary of Proceedings: Adelbert W. Shafer petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his two daughters, Florence M. Shafer (age 9) and Alice M. Shafer (age 5), from the custody of his wife May L. Shafer and co-conspirators S. W. Clark and Mary S. Clark. Adelbert Shafer claimed that May Shafer and the Clarks were holding his daughters illegally in an attempt to induce him into agreeing to obtain a divorce from May Shafer, who he also stated was not fit for custody of the children. After a hearing, the court sided with Adelbert Shafer and ordered that the children be released. Several months later, May Shafer requested a re-hearing. At the re-hearing, the court was ordered to drop all claims of impropriety or immorality against her, and a new custody arrangement was reached. As both parties seemed to be fit for custody, but could not live in the same household without marital strife, it was ruled that Florence Shafer would be placed in the custody of Adelbert Shafer and Alice Shafer would be placed in the custody of May Shafer.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 17th, 1912, W.F. Buchanan was arrested for embezzlement by Seattle Chief of Police Bannick. According to Bannick, he hard received a telegram announcing that Buchanan had committed the offense in New Mexico. On February 19th, Buchanan petitioned for a Writ of Habeas Corpus with the help of his attorneys, claiming that he had not committed any such offense. Judge J.T. Ronald granted the Writ of Habeas Corpus on February 19th and set a court date for February 23rd. On February 27th, Judge Ronald ordered the action be dismissed based on an agreement between Buchanan and his attorneys. According to the order, Buchanan voluntarily waived extradition and gave himself over to the New Mexico authorities.

Summary of Proceedings: Pete Johnson was taken into custody on 8 November 1913 by Chief of Police John Briggs and County Jailer Michael Corcoran. He was charged with “playing at a gambling game for money in a public place.” He was released on a bail bond and his trial was set for 12 November 1913. On 10 November 1913, Briggs filed a complaint against Johnson charging him with the same offense, contrary to the forms and ordinances in such case in the State of Nebraska. On 12 November 1913, Johnson appeared in court before Police Judge James F. Callahan. He was found guilty of the aforementioned offense, contrary to the ordinances of the city. He was sentenced to a fine of $100 and costs or 90 days in county jail. The charge of gambling for money in a public place is not a misdemeanor under the ordinances of South Omaha, NE and that it is not a crime of any kind, degree, or nature. Thus, he was not arraigned according to law. On 12 November 1913, an order allowing the writ of habeas corpus was filed. The writ was returned on 13 November 1913.

Summary of Proceedings:
On August 20, 1898 in Omaha, Nebraska, Henry Tschosanosky (alias J. Martin, alias Andrew J. Smith) was charged with the crime of grand larceny for unlawfully and feloniously taking $2015.80 worth of pelts from Gustave E. Shukert. Nebraska State Attorney Howard H. Haldrige requested the governor of Nebraska, Silas A. Holcomb, to appoint agent Henry Thompson to capture the now fugitive Tschosanosky (who will henceforth be referred to as “Martin'', to reflect the case proceedings). Martin traveled to Seattle, Washington, where the Governor of Washington, John Rogers, assented to Thompson’s pursuit and where C. G.  Augstin, Justice of the Peace for the Seattle Precinct, sent a warrant after Martin. Charles S. Reed, the Chief of Police for Seattle, King County, pursued Martin under this warrant. The process of Martin’s jailing at this time remains unclear through the records, but he was alleged to be under the restraint of Thompson, not Reed, whilst remaining in Washington. 

Martin filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus August 21, 1898 which was then heard on September 10 by Judge Orange Jacobs. Martin’s attorney, Frank E. Sims claimed that the affidavit and warrant (sent from Nebraska and Washington, respectively) used to arrest Martin were vague, defective and uncertain. On September 19, Thompson responded, filing for a motion to quash the writ in accordance with the laws of Nebraska. Sims responded to this action on October 8, further casting doubt on the authenticity of the alleged documents sent by the authorities in Martin’s case.

Summary of Proceedings: J. Charles E. Joy files for a writ of habeas on behalf of Stella S. Joy on June 3rd of 1899 with the claim that Stella is being held unlawfully in her father's house. Charles W. Ogle, Stella's father, is allegedly depriving her of her liberty at 2726 Charles Street in Omaha, Nebraska. Judge Cunningham Scott approves the writ and orders the clerk to send an order to the sheriff and bring Stella Joy before him. Judge Scott finds that Stella Joy is indeed illegally deprived of her liberty by her father and is discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 14, 1903, George Roberts was arrested on a warrant issued by Judge R. R. George. He issued the warrant based on a complaint he received stating that Roberts is being charged for the crime of grand larceny in San Francisco. The complaint alleges that Roberts committed the crime on March 15, 1903 by stealing $80 from W. L. Perry. The same day that Roberts was arrested he filed for a writ of habeas corpus arguing that his arrest and detention were not legal. Judge William R. Bell accepted Roberts' writ of habeas corpus but the outcome of the writ is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 5, 1912 O. R. Bystone (alias J. P. Harcourt) and his attorney, Walter B. Allen, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, stating that he believed the sentences he received in two Grand Jury trials, one for grand larceny and one for forgery, went against Washington State laws. The petition was directed towards Sheriff Robert T. Hodge, the warren of the Washington State Penitentiary C. A. Reed, and two guards Blystone did not know the names of, who were referred to as "Richard Roe" and "John Doe". The writ was denied, and Bystone and Allen appealed to the Washington Supreme court. The previous ruling was confirmed. Bystone remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1884, John Doyle was arrested in Marion County, Washington. Doyle was charged with obstructing the Union River Logging Railroad, an alleged violation of the territorial code, and then jailed in Olympia. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that the Marion County justice of the peace, W. J. Ross, lacked the jurisdiction to try him for this offense. Additionally, he claimed that he had not violated the territorial code, and that his bail was too high. He requested that his bail be lowered from $3000 to $100. After hearing the evidence, the judge ordered that Doyle's bail be lowered to $1500. Doyle made bail with the help of two sureties and was released pending his trial.
