Summary of Proceedings: J. I. Buchanan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff John Stringer. Buchanan alleged Stringer had him detained in the King County Jail under a warrant from the state of Idaho. Newspaper records indicated this warrant charged Buchanan with obtaining money under false pretenses by acting as the mortgagor and mortgagee in a realty transaction. Buchanan claimed Stringer, as an authority of the state of Washington, had no authority to hold Buchanan on a warrant from the state of Idaho. He also claimed he was denied his right to bail, which was afterward set at $1000, according to newspaper records. Due to the brevity of the case file, the outcome of the case and the fate of Buchanan are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 20, 1902, O. D. Moore was convicted of selling liquor without a license. He was fined $25 which he was fully paid and served time in the county jail. He was jailed again by Sheriff Edward Cudihee, presumably for not paying the $143.50 needed to obtain a liquor license. Moore petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on February 4, 1903, arguing that he was being held in jail for having debts, which was not allowed in Washington state. The judge allowed the writ and further ordered that Moore would be able to prosecute his writ without paying anything. The fate of the party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
On February 9, 1903, three French women were removed from the steamship Rosalie, which had arrived at Puget Sound from Victoria, Canada. Their immigration status was determined by a "board of inquiry" formed by Treasury Department officials in Seattle. It was decided that the three were French citizens previously denied entry to the U.S. at New York and were believed to be "imported into the United States, at the port of New York, from France, for the purposes of prostitution... and that they were paupers who would become a public charge." They were placed into the custody of James P. Lavin, Immigration Inspector, who in turn placed them in the custody of Sister Superior M. Angelique of the House of the Good Shepherd.

On February 13, 1903 the women, through their attorney, petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus in State Court. Judge Bell granted their petition. In response, the respondent's attorney filed a motion to move the adjudication to Federal Court as the matter was in regard to immigration law. That writ of certiorari was granted and the case moved to Federal Court under Judge Hanford.

Hanford denied the writ, ruling that the Treasury Department had the right to deny them entry. He further ruled that they were to be returned to Victoria. Shortly after his ruling on February 19, the Assistant Treasury Secretary ordered them deported to France from New York. As a result, the respondent, Lavin, petitioned to have Hanford's order returning the women to Victoria changed. Hanford denied the request on March 3rd and, on March 6th, the women were each granted $500 bail financed by the French consulate.

Lavin, through his attorney, Cushman, appealed the case to the U.S. Circuit Court. On December 10 1903, the Appeal was ruled and Judge Hanford's order that the women be sent to Victoria was overturned as the appeals court found that the Treasury Department had the authority and that the Immigration Act allowed for the women to be returned to France as they had not been away for more than one year.

In June 1904, Georgette surrendered to authorities and was deported to France. On July 22 1904, the other two women were ruled to have forfeited their bail. Their ultimate fates are unknown; it appears they jumped bail and absconded.

Summary of Proceedings: Thomas P. Overnell and Nancy Overnell, the parents of Thomas Nelson Overnell (a 14-month-old child), got into a custody dispute in October of 1862. On October 23, Frances Miller (Nancy's brother) testified as a witness and stated that Mr. Overnell and Ms. Overnell were at his father’s house and barn when the custody dispute occurred. Frances told the Justice of the Peace that he witnessed Mr. Overnell take Thomas and that, “judging from his condition”, he believed Ms. Overnell should, instead, have custody. Mary Bozarth also testified and stated that Mr. Overnell should not have custody of Thomas. On October 27, Caleb N. Miller (Nancy's brother) petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Thomas. He stated that Mr. Overnell forcefully took Thomas out of Ms. Overnell's custody. The couple was separated at the time and Caleb stated that Mr. Overnell threatened to take Thomas out of the county. On October 28, Judge Hewitt ordered the sheriff to arrest Mr. Overnell and either bring Thomas to the court himself or to give Thomas to Ms. Overnell so that she could bring him. The sheriff placed Thomas into Ms. Overnell's custody. On October 30, the judge ruled that Mr. Overnell admitted “that the mother is for the time being the more proper and suitable party to have custody” and decided that Ms. Overnell should have custody of Thomas.

Summary of Proceedings: In the autumn of 1906, William Walker, a member of the Omaha Nation, was arrested on the Omaha Reservation, charged with having repeatedly beaten his wife, Little Girl Walker, also of the Omaha Nation, and sentenced to thirty days. William was processed in the Omaha Court of Indian Offenses and held in an agency jail, both of which were established earlier that year at the request of the Omaha Nation Tribal Council "to deal with members of our tribe who are guilty of violating moral and civil codes"--specifically issues involving alcohol and domestic violence. According to Superintendent of the Omaha Agency, John Commons, this was necessary because Nebraska state authorities were loathe to enforce these laws on Omaha land. William petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, which was largely about the legitimacy and jurisdiction of the Court of Indian Offenses, William was released from custody. Though not noted in the case file, Attorney Thomas Sloan was also a member of the Omaha Nation.

Summary of Proceedings: McLane was convicted of the crime of vagrancy and charged with a ten-dollar fine. The witness, D. L. McCowan, said that McLane was a healthy man who could work but lived an idle life that consisted of wandering around the streets and having an unnamed woman support him. McLane defaulted on his payment and was therefore ordered to hard labor until the fine was paid or ten days had passed. The petitioner’s attorneys, Kalloch, Murphy, and Holcomb, argued that the detention was illegal because Seattle territory law had recently changed and did not give the justice of the peace authority to detain him. Therefore, the detention was illegal under the US Constitution. Judge Greene issued the writ of Habeas Corpus on this basis.

Summary of Proceedings:
On October 23, 1893 Adolph Krug, who was the acting treasurer of the city of Seattle at the time, was convicted on the charge of using $10,000 public money to make a profit for purposes not authorized by the law. On March 26, 1894 Krug's motion for a new trial was denied, and he was sentenced to serve 7 years of hard labor in the Penitentiary of the State of Washington, and to pay all costs. 
Krug appealed to the Supreme Court of the State of Washington, and he alleged that this judgement is contrary to his rights as a citizen of the United States, as enumerated by the constitutions of Washington and the United States. Among other things, Krug claimed he was never made aware of the nature of charges against him, and therefore was not able to adequately defend himself, contrary to his constitutional rights. The Supreme Court of Washington affirmed the judgement of the lower court, and they stated that while citizens maintained the right to know the nature and cause of accusations against them, Krug and people of "his kind" were not afforded that right. 
Krug filed a Habeas petition on February 11, 1897 to prompt an investigation into his rights and to receive a fair trial. On March 8th, 1897, the petition was denied, and Judge Hanford argued that issuing a writ would be an unwarranted interference with the execution of the laws of the state. Krug decided to appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States. The Supreme Court likely affirmed the ruling as supplemental research reveals that in July, 1899 Krug was granted parole from Walla Walla penitentiary.

The outcome of the case and the fate of Kelly are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
On May 31st, 1917, Mike Jamamovich was arrested for the illegal possession of intoxicating liquers in Omaha. Following his arrest, Perry McD. Wheeler "pretended" to file a complaint against him as the self-designated acting city prosecutor for Omaha. Not only this, but McD. Wheeler failed to even sign the complaint before handing it off to H. Glen Meran, the self-designated acting police magistrate for Omaha. The two acting officials held a trial for Jamamovich in which he was testified against by witnesses who had not been sworn in or subscribed to the filed complaint. The trial resulted in a sentence of sixty days in county jail, which, the petitioner's defense argued, was far more excessive than the crime he had been charged for. Additionally, because neither McD. Wheeler or Meran had been officially designated by the mayor of Omaha to serve in either of their self-designated roles, they had no authority to try and sentence Jamamovich. 

Jamamovich filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus and presented these facts to the court in hopes of his freedom. After being heard by Judge Willis G. Sears, he was granted a writ of Habeas Corpus and released from police custody on June 4th, 1917.

Summary of Proceedings:
On October 16th, 1890, James Shay filed for a writ of habeas corpus, written by his lawyer John Wiley. That day, Police Judge Claudius M. Rivers issued a warrant for Shay’s arrest, on the charge of drunkenness. Shay was found guilty, and was charged a $5 fine, plus the costs of the proceedings. Shay was to be held in the Seattle City Jail by Chief of Police George C. Monroe until he paid the fees. In the habeas petition, John Wiley claimed that the Police Court, which had been recently created by the City of Seattle and given jurisdiction from a voted upon charter, was unconstitutional. Because he believed the Court and charter were unconstitutional, he alleged that Judge Rivers did not have the jurisdiction to charge Shay with drunkenness, nor have him detained. The petition was allowed by Judge J. A. Stratton, who set the case to be heard the following day, October 17, by Judge Thomas J. Humes. Newspaper coverage indicated that Shay did not show up to the trial. Chief Monroe stated that Shay paid his fines and was released prior to the filing of the habeas petition. Newspaper coverage indicated that Shay was drunk enough on the night of the October 16 to not realize he was part of the case. The papers state that paid his fine and left, forcing his attorneys to find a different case to use in their challenge of the Police Court. His attorneys then found John Reilly, whose case, “In the matter of the application of John Reilly for a Writ of Habeas Corpus”, was filed by Wiley and his colleagues Hale and Scott, on October 17, using the same legal basis. These cases appear to be attorney led, as the attorneys were attempting to challenge the constitutionality of the Police Court as a whole. 
It is worth noting, the case "In the matter of the application of Harry Brooks for a Writ of Habeas Corpus", in February 1890, is another case that challenged the constitutionality of the Police Court, and subsequently of Judge Rivers.

Summary of Proceedings:
On June 29, 1887, John Dugan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the basis he was unlawfully restrained of his liberty by James Glispin, Sheriff of Spokane County. Dugan was sent to jail by Justice of the Peace Pierce, in default of giving $1,500 bail, on the charge of being an accessory to the crime of murder of Frank Teller. Then Justice of the Peace Booge set additional bail at $1,000 to give testimony at the trial of Mary Teller. Mary Teller, Frank's wife, had been accused of Frank's murder. Newspaper indicated that John was Mary's younger brother. The petition alleged there was no evidence that implicated Dugan in said murder and alleged bail was excessive. Judge Turner authorized the petition, considered the evidence in the case of the Territory v. Mary Teller, and ruled there was not probable cause to sentence Dugan as an accessory to the crime of murder. In addition, Judge Turner reduced bail to $250 to ensure Dugan would appear as a witness in said case. Then Dugan was discharged from custody. 

There is an additional set of documents in the archives that details the actual murder case. It includes witness lists, cost lists, and some description of witness testimony.

Summary of Proceedings: John Reynolds, the petitioner and bound party, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus after his incarceration due to an unspecified violation of the Mann Act. Reynolds was originally sentenced to fifteen months and to pay a fine of one hundred dollars; Reynolds claimed that due to his good behavior during incarceration and fulfillment of his sentence, he should have been released already and is now being unlawfully detained. Additionally, Reynolds stated that he was a pauper and needed an attorney to be appointed to him and for the fine to be excused. In answer, the respondent and holding party, O. P. Halligan, the warden of McNeils Island, stated that Reynolds was not yet due for release. Judge Edward Cushman's decision and the fate of the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
On January 8th, 1912, Esther Crandall was arrested by Robert Hodge. On January 11th, Fred Brown, a justice of the peace, decided that Crandall should remain in custody until she was discharged or released by due process of law. On February 9th, more than 30 days after she was arrested, she applied for a writ of Habeas Corpus. The same day, J. T. Roger, judge of the superior court, based on the facts in the application, granted her the writ and commanded her to be delivered before him the next day  in court, February 10th. What happened on the 10th is unknown on the records. However, on February 13th, Hodge, the Sheriff of King County and respondent in the case, argued with the help of his lawyers that Esther was being held by virtue of a commitment issued by Fred Brown on January 11th and by virtue of an arrest issued on February 10th by D. K. Sickels, a clerk.

According to the Seattle Star, Crandall was charged with having taken the girl to improper places and keeping her in vicious company. It was alleged that the girl, Olive Westbrook, ran away from the Fremont Home for Girls. On February 19th, Crandall was convicted.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis M. Cohn petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus arguing that Sheriff McClay was depriving him of his liberty. Weeks previous, Cohn had successfully petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, was remanded to custody, and filed an appeal in the Supreme Court. While that petition was pending, Cohn successfully petitioned for a writ after he had been remanded into custody again. Judge Tibbetts ruled that because Cohn had been committed a second time for the same offense, Cohn was deprived of his liberty. Tibbetts ordered that Cohn be released.

Summary of Proceedings: Wong Ging, a Chinese national, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigrant inspector Alfred Hampton. Ging claimed Hampton was holding him illegally at the Spokane County Jail. Ging alleged he was arrested alongside Wong Dick, who filed a separate petition for habeas corpus, for the possession of opium. Ging was now being held past his sentence and threatened with deportation. Hampton returned with the warrants for Ging’s rearrest and deportation on the basis of the Immigration Act of 1917. Judge J. Stanley Webster ordered Hampton to release Ging from custody and no longer pursue deportation. Hampton appealed to the Ninth Circuit, claiming Webster stated no real facts entitling Ging to release. The Ninth Circuit court upheld Webster’s ruling. Ging was arrested alongside Wong Dick, who filed a separate petition for habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: James Connell McAvinew petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff John Stringer and agent of the state of Pennsylvania Ira C. McCloskey. McAvinew alleged that he was being charged as a fugitive from justice, but that the proceedings were irregular and illegal as the criminal complaint against him stated no cause of action. Stringer and McCloskey returned with a warrant from Pennsylvania for the arrest of McAvinew which charged him with desertion and non-support of his wife. The outcome of the case and the fate of McAvinew are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Moy You petitioned for Habeas Corpus on behalf of Doug Ah Wing, Chiu Duug Suey, and Moy Woo You, who were detained on the Steamship the Haitian Republic. The collector of customs T.J. Black refused to allow them off the ship because he believed them to be laborers arriving in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. However, they were able to prove merchant status by submitting evidence of their employment as retailers at 128 Second Street. Thus, the writ was granted, and all parties were discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 14, 1916, the petitioner arrived at the port of Seattle on the steamship "Ixion." On June 20, 1916, Assistant Commissioner Sargent made the determination that the petitioner was not the son of the natural born citizen he claimed to be the son of. On July 24, 1916, an order was issued to arrest the petitioner for not being entitled to admission. On August 4, 1916, a petition was filed alleging citizenship by reason of being the natural born son of Yo Bing Goe, a resident of New York. He further alleges that his appeal was not heard by the Secretary of Labor as is required by law. On August 4, 1916, the writ was issued. On August 5, 1916, an order to show cause was issued. On September 13, 1916, a return was filed by the government. On October 13, 1916, the petitioner filed points and authorities as to their claims. The petition alleges issues of parental rights as well as the ability of the judiciary to determine the question of whether parental relationships exist. On November 9, 1916, the petition was denied, writ discharges, and the petitioner was remanded to the custody of the Commissioner of Immigration. On November 25, 1916, an order dismissing the petition was issued and the government withdrew their files.

Summary of Proceedings: This is a three page case that only mentions that case being moved from Spokane to Walla Walla at the request and approval of the attorneys for both the petitioner and the respondent. Newspaper coverage indicates Elsie was "an authoress" who had been scheduled for deportation, but then married U.S. citizen John A. McNeil of Sherman, OR on Mar 12, 1913 and was now challenging her deportation. Elsie also claimed that she had been previously married to a U.S. citizen in 1894, according to the press. Immigration officials responded with charges that Elsie had been connected with the management of a disorderly house and would be deported on those grounds. Despite abundant coverage over the term of Elsie's arrest, there is no clear outcome in the record.

Summary of Proceedings: Mary Marshall and her three children, Lillie, William, and Walter, were forced to enter the Home for the Friendless in 1884 after her husband, Francis Marshall, abandoned them. Shortly afterwards, William was struck ill and referred to Hattie R. Painter, a physician, and her presumed relative, Joseph Painter. His disease apparently involved "eruptions over the head" that were considered so disgusting that William was not allowed to be with the other children. In 1886, Mary Marshall petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that William Marshall was unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Hattie and Joseph Painter. In the same year, she petitioned for a divorce from Francis, claiming abandoment and extreme cruelty. After hearing testimony, Judge Pound declared that William Marshall was not deprived of his liberty. Although he ordered that William remain in the custody of the holding party, Pound ordered that the petitioner be able to visit her son at all reasonable times and that in six months she could petition to modify the custody agreement.

Summary of Proceedings: Alfonso Gagliardi was an Italian migrant that had been living in the United States since 1915. In November 1920, Gagliardi left for temporary visit to his family in Italy. Following his return a few months later, the Immigration Inspector and acting Commissioner of Immigration in Seattle issued a warrant on March 10, 1921 charging Gagliardi with violating U.S. Passport Law by entering the United States without a properly visaed passport and for being a public charge. In October 1921, a warrant for deportation was ordered for Gagliardi. In December 1921, Gagliardi filed for a writ of habeas corpus. This writ was granted by Judge Jeremiah Neterer. This writ was never appealed, however, in March 1922, another warrant for Gagliardi was arrested again accusing him of entering the United States without a properly visaed passport but did not charge Gagliardi with being a public charge. Gagliardi filed for another writ of habeas corpus after another warrant of deportation was filed against him. In this writ, Gagliardi argued that the immigration official violated the previous writ of habeas corpus by re-charging and re-arresting Gagliardi for the same crime. Judge Jeremiah Neterer approved this writ of habeas corpus and ordered Gagliardi be released from custody. In his opinion on the ruling, Judge Neterer stated that a person that had been discharged on a writ of habeas corpus cannot lawfully be arrested again for the same cause. This ruling was appealed by the immigration officials arguing that the Judge Neterer erred in ruling the second case against Alfonso Gagliardi was in legal effect identical to the issues of the first case. The outcome of the appeal is not included in this case file. However, census records show that Gagliardi continued to live in Seattle for several decades following this case.

Summary of Proceedings:
Moy Chong, a resident and business owner in Portland, departed to Hong Kong in 1892 on business and to visit relatives. Prior to departure, Chong appeared before a notary and received a signed certificate as proof of residence and his business to allow for re-entry. 
Nearly a year later, upon return, Chong was denied entry by a deputy collector. The deputy collector confiscated the certificate and refused to return it. Chong was informed he had to board a steamship along with 200 other Chinese passengers to return to Hong Kong. Chong's application for a writ of habeas corpus was granted by the Superior Court of Pierce County and he was discharged by the U.S. Commissioner. An appeal was taken questioning the jurisdiction of the U.S. Commissioner. 
In the District Court, Chong's petition was denied and Chong was placed in the custody of U.S. Marshall, J. C. Drake. 
Chong's attorney gathered multiple affidavits from business partners and those personally acquainted with Chong to establish proof of his residence; one of which stated the reason Chong had difficulty upon entry was that the notarized certificate misspelled Chong's name as "Chung" and that Chong's business was mistakenly referred to as "Won Chem Wo Co." instead of "On Chong Wa & Co." The Circuit Court issued a writ of habeas corpus to stop the deportation yet the results of the proceedings are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 1st, 1897, William E. Baker was charged with committing the crime of larceny by embezzling money from the Adams Express Company. On July 8, 1898, after being informed by Inspector Roger McGarr of the Boston police department that the fugitive was now located in Seattle Washington, a warrant for his arrest was issued and was subsequently carried out by Detective William L. Meredith in the afternoon of July 9, 1898, and was jailed by Charles S. Reed Chief of Police in Seattle. Before he could be transferred to McGarr and taken back to Boston to stand trial his lawyers John F. Dore and Solon T. Williams submitted an application for a writ of Habeas Corpus claiming that his imprisonment was illegal. The application would drag on until finally being granted a court hearing taking place on July 16, 1898. The writ was denied, and Baker’s attorney made an appeal to the Supreme Court of the State of Washington which would eventually affirm the lower court’s initial ruling. Baker would remain in custody. Whether or not he was eventually extradited to Massachusetts is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 5, 1906 Mazie Ziegler petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her three-year-old son William. Mazie stated that her husband, Jacob J. Ziegler, had been abusive and neglectful towards her, and was a habitual drunk who failed to provide for her or her son. She stated that this drove her to leave with William to live with her unnamed sister. Mazie claimed that Jacob violently took William from her after she left, and Mazie believed Jacob intended to take William out of the court’s jurisdiction soon. Judge Frater issued the writ. Jacob applied for a leave to intervene, which was granted. The outcome of this case and the fate of William are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 1st, 1903, B. E. Miller petitioned for his freedom in King County, Washington. Miller was being held by John Sullivan, the Chief of Police of Seattle, in the Seattle City Jail. Miller, with the advice of his lawyer, Edgar Hadley, alleged that he was likely being held on the pretense of a telegram, but on no legal grounds. On April 2nd, Judge W. R. Bell approved the writ. However, the case file ends there, and B. E. Miller’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Alex Boggio was an Italian migrant that was arrested and subject to deportation on the accusation of advocating for the unlawful destruction of property. In his petition for writ of habeas corpus, Boggio argued that he was denied his right to counsel, his right to examine the warrant and the evidence within, and was subjected to “personal abuse and intimidations” which compelled him to give evidence against himself. Boggio’s writ for habeas corpus was dismissed because the immigration officials released Boggio from their custody before the scheduled hearing date for the writ.

Summary of Proceedings: The bound party, Samuel Summers, was issued a warrant in the County of Tallahatchie, Mississippi for the crime of knowingly receiving stolen property over the value of $100 by Justice of the Peace J. B. Ray. On August 23rd 1918, the bound party was arrested upon report of McArthur, K. B., allegedly without an issued warrant. On August 27th 1918, the wife of the bound party, Maggie Summers, and attorney for the petitioner, John M. Macfarland, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus naming Chief of Police Micheal Dempsey and Jailer George Stevens. In response, Geo Holmes, police magistrate, issued a letter detailing the reasoning for confinement and the previous warrant from Mississippi. On August 30th, Justice Geo Holmes issued an arrest warrant for the bound party who was already, at that point, in custody. The following day on August 31st, the application for the writ was granted and Summers is released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 7, 1892 in California, George Sutherland (Alias Gillin) signed on as a seaman on a voyage from the port of San Francisco. Petitioner claimed that he was not informed of where they were going. He further claimed that he was forcibly taken on board in Oregon at the port. The owner of the boat resides in England and sails under English flags. P.L Cherry was the British Vice Consult residing at Astoria Oregon and he wrote to C.R. Thomas a US Commissioner of the US district court of Oregon that Sutherland signed to join the ship and refused to board. An arrest warrant was then issued for Sutherland's arrest. Eventually, Peter Grant filed for a writ of habeas corpus for George Sutherland. It was denied. Sutherland eventually escaped from custody. He was deemed a deserter, and his fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In early 1916, Tom Birbilis, a twenty-eight-year-old Greek immigrant who had been living in the United States since he was a teenager, traveled from Iowa to Nebraska with nineteen-year-old Marie Campbell. Soon thereafter, the US Departments of Labor and Justice investigated him for violating the Mann Act. A district attorney accused Campbell of being a prostitute and Birbilis her pimp, but ultimately dismissed the suit. Campbell admitted that she had worked as a prostitute in Iowa, but had determined to leave that life behind when she agreed to travel to Nebraska with Birbilis, whom she had married. Nevertheless, U.S. immigration officials then decided to deport Birbilis for the alleged violation. Birbilis petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that he was being detained by inspector S. L. Whitfield and had not received a fair hearing. The U.S. District Court judge agreed, setting bail at $1,000 and ordering that Birbilis appear before him so that both he and the U.S. government could subpoena witnesses. Birbilis lost in Omaha but appealed the decision to the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals in St. Louis, which dismissed his case. It is unclear whether or not he was deported. 

It is worth noting the ethnic and gendered dynamics of this case. Birbilis' attorneys, for instance, wrote the following in a brief that survives in the case file: "The alien is a Greek. This American girl will perhaps make him a better citizen and herself a worthy companion for him. She is perhaps the highest type of American womanhood with whom this alien could expect to become associated in marriage. She was a fallen woman.”

Summary of Proceedings: Edna M. Gerould, the mother of Russell G. Watson, had been married to Fred Watson and, shortly after the birth of Russell, put him in the care of his grandmother Susan C. Watson. Later, Edna divorced Fred Watson and married Percy E. Gerould. Edna M. Gerould then filed for a writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of her son, Russell, from Susan. Susan claimed that Edna is a prostitute and of poor character. Several witnesses spoke to the court on the merits of Edna and Percy Gerould's reputation, stating that they were well-equipped to care for children and that Edna was a well-respected lady. Edna M. Gerould was then awarded custody of her child, Russell G. Watson, and it was found that Susan C. Watson was unlawfully in possession of the child. Gerould was then permitted to move said child from the city of Omaha to the city of Hastings.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 9, 1922, Louis Loukas file for habeas against Chief of Police, Micheal F. Dempsey, and acting Chief of Detectives, Ben Danbuam. In his petition, Loukas denied that charge of fugitive from justice, arguing that he had never been or lived in the state of Kansas. On the return of the issued writ, E. E. McKnight refers to a warrant issued by the Governor of Nebraska on behalf of the Governor of Kansas, under the charges of wife desertion and fugitive from justice. The case was later dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924.

Summary of Proceedings: Ah Sing was confined in Steamship Signal by M. Bendegard for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. In his petition for Writ of Habeas Corpus, which was filed by Young Hock Sing, he claims that he is a U.S. Citizen born in 1867 with Chinese descent. However, Judge Charles B. Bellinger denied his writ of habeas corpus because referee John Catlin concluded that Ah Sing is not a U.S. citizen. He was remanded back to the custody of M. Bendegard. The casefile includes an affidavit from two White witnesses claiming that Ah Sing is a Chinese merchant.

Summary of Proceedings: Henri Dachez, a naturalized U. S. citizen from France, was sentenced to Pierce County Jail after he was found connected with the management of a house of prostitution, found receiving, sharing in, and deriving benefit from the earnings of a prostitute, and found assisting a prostitute. On August 7th, 1914, the Commissioner of Immigration at Seattle, Henry M. White, signed a warrant to deport Dachez to France after his jail sentence expired on January 16th, 1915. Dachez filed a writ of habeas corpus on January 15th, 1915, arguing that he should not be deported, since he was a U. S. citizen. Judge Cushman denied and dismissed the petition on February 8th, 1915, and ordered Dachez to remain in the custody of Thomas M. Fisher, an Immigration Inspector. Dachez then appealed Judge Cushman's ruling, and on March 15th, 1915, Judge Neterer allowed the appeal. The outcome of the appeal and the fate of the bound party, Dachez, is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 13, 1891 a warrant for the arrest of one Thomas Fountain was issued by Justice of the Peace Edward Von Tobel after Maud Gardner issued a formal complaint that Thomas Fountain assaulted her with a deadly weapon. Fountain was subsequently arrested by constable Charles Robinson. Following his arrest and detainment with the assistance of his attorney James McCutcheon, Fountain filed a petition of Habeas Corpus against James H. Woolery, Sheriff of King County stating that his imprisonment was illegal because the arrest warrant did not properly state what he was being arrested for. While the case files give no further information on the status of the petition numerous newspaper articles published about the events state that his writ was denied. Outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 11, 1891, Adam Cushing filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he claimed that he was being illegally detained by Multnomah County Sheriff Penumbra Kelly. Kelly responded by claiming that Cushing was a fugitive on the run from the state of Washington. Kelly further claimed that Cushing was charged with the crime of receiving stolen goods that were stolen from the Oregon Short Line and Utah Northern Railway. Judge Matthew Deady disagreed with Kelly, granted the writ of habeas corpus and Cushing was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 3, 1918, a complaint was filed against Flossie Gordon in the Omaha police court, charging Gordon with being a vagrant. The sentence fined Gordon for $100, and if defaulted, Gordon would be placed in jail. On July 6, Gordon filed for habeas with attorney, Daniel Horrigan, claiming that a police judge lacks the authority to give such a sentence. The petition was granted, and on July 8, Judge Redick sustained the writ of habeas and Gordon was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 28, 1924, Samuel R. Thompson was arrested on the charge of being a fugitive from justice from Illinois that was wanted for wife abandonment. On June 6, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that he was being illegally detained for the purposes of extradition to Illinois. The respondent replied the same day and stated his reason for arresting Samuel. On May 31, Illinois Governor Len Small addressed a petition to Nebraska Governor Charles W. Bryan asking him to apprehend and return Samuel to Illinois. On June 3, Governor Bryan issued a warrant for Samuel’s arrest to all law enforcement officers in the state. According to the appearance docket, the hearing for the writ continued on June 7 and the judge discharged Samuel from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Thomas, T. Smith, W. Alexander, and John Kelly were imprisoned by J.H. Lappeus on the charge of deserting from the Bark James A. Falkenberg. On March 31, 1869, they filed a writ of Habeas Corpus contesting the arrest warrant issued by magistrate O. Risley on the grounds that the state of Oregon did not invest him with the jurisdiction to carry out the provisions of the Act of Congress Passed July 20th, 1790 concerning seamen. The writ was denied and the petitioners remained in jail.

Summary of Proceedings: Mike Oumpo was an immigrant from Russia, having entered the United States in 1913. In 1917 Weber joined the IWW, a union organization. On January 16th, 1918, Tom Weber was arrested under a warrant issued by the U.S. Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson, and was held for multiple months while his case was pending. The charges alleged were that he was an alien, he advocated for and taught the unlawful destruction of property, and that upon entering the country he was a likely public charge. On December 2nd, 1918, a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed stating among other things that he joined the IWW because he was told he would not obtain a job if he did not, that he had never destroyed property, and that a transcript of his hearing was never given to him. A return from the attorneys for the respondent states that the application does not include facts sufficient for a cause of action, does not show entitlement to relief, and that the court had no jurisdiction as the Secretary of Labor was yet to rule on the case. The fate of the petition is unknown, but the bound party was released from custody according to a hearing on deportation cases.

Summary of Proceedings:
In May 1891, Sunny Luckey, who also went by the alias Charles Edwards, allegedly murdered Dickson Scott in the Coweta District of the Muskogee Nation(spelling taken directly from case documents), which was then referred to as Indian Territory. Shortly after the alleged murder, Luckey reportedly fled to Washington. Around December 13th, 1893 King County Sheriff James H. Woolery arrested Luckey.
On December 26th, 1893 Luckey’s wife, Sula Edwards, with his lawyer, C. A. Ridenour, filed a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf. In it they claimed that Luckey’s detainment was illegal because they believed no official court judgment put him there. Judge Richard Osborn allowed the petition on December 28th, 1893. 
Woolrey produced documentation that the Indian Agent for the Muskogee Nation, O. B. White, and Judge Sam C. Davis of the Coweta District Court both requested that Luckey be brought back to Indian Territory to be tried there. Additionally, Woolrey produced a letter from Judge William Caldwell confirming Luckey’s original charges. Woolrey also showed that Caldwell issued a warrant for Luckey to be held in custody at least until January 13th, when Caldwell had intended to try him in his court.
Information from ancestry.com points to Luckey being held in Seattle and then released February 6th, 1894. Additionally, newspaper reporting from January 17th, 1894 states that his petition was “dismissed on motion of petitioner”. Luckey's fate beyond this is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles and Mary Marino were arrested for the unlawful sale and possession of intoxicating liquor. On July 3, 1924, Charles was sentenced to nine months in the Lincoln County Jail along with a $400 fine. On December 1, 1924, Charles petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that he served each of the three-month sentences concurrently and should be discharged. On December 3, the judge ordered the respondents to release Charles from custody. The respondents appealed the case to the U.S. Court of Appeals Eighth Circuit (St. Paul, Minnesota) on March 14, 1925. On January 30, 1926, the decision of the lower court was reversed by the higher court and the judge remanded Charles to the custody of the respondents. The higher court also referred to the decision in the Cronin v. William J. Fox case.

Summary of Proceedings:
On March 11, 1913, Earl Thornton filed a petition of habeas corpus on behalf of his wife, Irene Thornton. In the petition, Earl claimed that Mrs. Katherine Murphine was holding Irene in the Western Washington Hospital for the Insane and refusing to let Irene leave or see Earl, despite having been discharged on February 25, 1913. The outcome of this case and the fate of Irene Thornton are not listed in the case file. 
However, newspaper coverage indicated that Irene was released from the institution sometime in March, and returned to live with Earl. In May, Irene and her family reported that Earl was neglecting her. By September they were divorced, and in December Irene remarried.

Summary of Proceedings: Athas Chinis was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and was brought before the Police Court on June 17. Chinis was found guilty in Police Court on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Chinis and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for Habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Chinis argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. On June 27, the writ of habeas was sustained, and Chinis was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Joe Ambrose petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff John Stringer. Ambrose alleged that he pled guilty to a charge of petit larceny and was sentenced to be held for 30 days in the King County Commissioner’s Office, as the King County Jail was declared unfit for human habitation. He claimed that Stringer, in defiance and contempt of court, took him to King County Jail and was detaining him there instead. Stringer responded that Ambrose was being held in the King County Jail to serve a prior sentence for burglary in the second degree and provided a warrant ordering Ambrose’s arrest for burglary. The warrant was dated after the petition for a writ of habeas corpus was filed. Stringer claimed that the sentence for Ambrose’s petit larceny charge had not yet been pronounced. The outcome of the case and the fate of Ambrose are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Irwin A. Medlar claimed that he was unlawfully detained by John F. Boyd and Patrick Horigan. He was charged with being a fugitive from justice after being arrested in Omaha. It was said that Medlar had been charged with a "crime of seduction" in Harvey County, Kansas, but he claimed that he was only there for work and did not commit any crime. The judge determined that he was in fact unlawfully detained and was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward Thacker, father and guardian of Addie Thacker, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that Addie Thacker was being unlawfully detained by Dora Doyle. According to secondary research, Doyle was police matron. Judge Holmes granted the petition. After reviewing evidence, Holmes appointed W. W. Towle, attorney for petitioner, as the guardian of the bound party and ordered that the petitioner pay for the care and maintenance of bound party. All parties agreed to this new custody arrangement. By 1910, the father and daughter had moved to Colorado.

Summary of Proceedings: William H. Martin, the petitioner, was detained on the charge of Grand Larceny by Sheriff William Coburn and filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus arguing he is not guilty. Officer John Sexton's testimony stated that on December 1st at 3:00 am he was told to respond to a robbery in South Omaha at the boarding house of Mrs. Soash of $50.00 and a gold ring. The money was found, but not the ring and Police Judge King found Martin guilty of grand larceny. Martin claimed that no probable cause was found for either theft and files a writ of Habeas. It was then ordered by Judge Joseph Clarkson that Martin's writ be allowed. On January fourth, Martin was officially discharged from custody. In February of 1890 after the filing of a bill of exceptions Martin and his counsel, John H. Pierce are ordered to argue before the Nebraska Supreme Court, indicating that unanswered questions persisted in the case. The outcome and nature of the said argumentation before the Supreme Court are not stated.

Summary of Proceedings: Marl Wray filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that Joel Warren and J. S. McBride have been illegally restraining him of his liberty. In his petition, Wray claimed that he was arrested on a charge of being a disorderly person. He states that the police have refused to try him for such a charge and have refused to allow him to post bail. Furthermore, Wray claimed that the police have refused to allow him to contact or meet with his physician for treatment for his eczema condition. In his return writ, Chief of Police, Joel Warren, claimed that Wray was arrested on a warrant issued by John B. Gordon which charged him with violating public morality, peace, safety, and good order. Warren further stated that Wray was in the custody of J. S. McBride because he suffered from a “dangerous, infectious, and contagious disease,” and that he is currently in the city’s isolation hospital. The outcome of the petition and the fate of the bound party were not stated in this case file.

Summary of Proceedings:
On July 14th, 1904, Lem Shaw petitioned for the freedom of Loy Sen, an approximately 30 years old Chinese woman. The relationship between the bound party and Shaw is unknown. It is known, however, that Thomas R. Delaney was holding her because of a complaint of embezzlement against Sen. The writ of Habeas Corpus was granted on July 14th, 1904 by Judge W. R. Bell, however the outcome of the case is unknown.

According to a Seattle Newspaper at the time, Loy Sen had eluded the San Francisco police for 4 years as an embezzler. On information from Chief of Police Wittman of San Francisco, detectives Tennant and Byrnes of Seattle arrested her. At the time of her arrest, she had a ticket to China on the steamer, Shawmmut. In a telegram delivered to the Seattle police, it was stated that a police officer was already on his way to Seattle with the necessary requisition papers to bring her to San Francisco to face charges. It is unknown how much she allegedly embezzled, but it is known that the man she embezzled from was Wong Fung. She denied the charges and claimed she knew nothing about why the police were arresting her.

Summary of Proceedings: T. Walter V. McGovern petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle chief of police John Sullivan and King County Sheriff Edward Cudihee. McGovern claimed he was being held illegally in King County Jail as the warrant he was arrested under was not issued under any criminal complaint. He recounted how he worked with deputy sheriff James Callaghan and attorney Hughey Bean to file criminal complaints against several men he accused of running a gambling resort. According to McGovern, after the accused were arrested, he was advised by Callaghan and Bean to leave Seattle, and he did so out of fear for his safety. This flight resulted in McGovern being unable to testify against the men. Cudihee claimed that McGovern was arrested with a warrant on the basis of contempt and was held on a bench warrant. Being unable to secure bail, McGovern was sent to King County Jail. A warrant for McGovern's arrest was filed after he filed the petition for habeas corpus. The case file does not reveal any outcome or the fate of McGovern, but newspaper records indicate his writ was allowed and he was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In the spring of 1898, Richard Townsend enlisted in the U.S. Army to help prosecute the Spanish-American War. He deserted in January 1899, a few weeks after the United States signed a peace treaty but before Congress ratified it. In March 1904, Townsend was arrested in St. Louis, Missouri, charged with desertion, and brought to Fort Crook in Nebraska. He was court-martialed in June, found guilty, dishonorably discharged, and sentenced to two years military labor. A few months later, Townsend petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that the statute of limitations had expired. After hearing the evidence, he was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Army. Judge William Hunger, however, declared that Townsend could petition again pending the outcome of a similar case, In re Cadwallader, that was then pending before the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit.

Summary of Proceedings: P. V. Abugadie had previously been arrested by the Chief of Police, Joel Warren, and an unknown John Doe. His petition for writ of habeas corpus from this arrest was successful and Abugadie was released from custody. However, a few days following this successful petition, Abugadie was rearrested by Joel Warren and the unknown John Doe. Following this second arrest, Abugadie filed another petition for a writ of habeas corpus highlighting that he had already been granted a writ of habeas corpus from similar charges. In this new petition, Abugadie again states that he has not been accused of any violations of the law and that his detention is unlawful. Abugadie speculates that the cause of his detention is related to a “controversy” involving the payment for a Willys-Overland Automobile in California. He states that he has a running account for an automobile of around $200.00. Abugadie argues that he had amicably settled the issue with the account and that the automobile is currently in the possession of the Overland Pacific Company in Seattle. The case file for this petition is only four pages long and does not include the outcome of the writ of habeas corpus or the fate of the bound party.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Lopez, identified as “a kanaka of mixed blood” by the Seattle Post Intelligencer, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to gain custody of his two-year-old daughter, Nellie Louisa Lopez, from his former wife Mary McGowan.  In the petition, Lopez argued that McGowan lacked the means to support Nellie Lousia and associated with lewd people.  Lopez also argued that he had the ability to support Nellie Louisa.   The writ was issued on July 17, 1899.  However, rather than serving the writ to McGowan, the sheriff,  A. T. Van De Vanter, served the writ to O.H. Ryther, the custodian of Nellie Louisa.  According to the Seattle Post Intelligencer, McGowan had left her child at the Ryther Home, a house for orphans.   McGowan’s answer to the petition argued that all statements made by Lopez were false.  On August 4, 1899, the Seattle Post Intelligencer reported that Judge Jacobs had put Nellie Louisa in the custody of Ryther. Then, on August 8, 1899, the Seattle Post Intelligencer reported that Lopez took Nellie Louisa from the Ryther Home, committed a heinous crime, and was arrested.

Summary of Proceedings: Mike Miller was arrested near the Omaha Police Department on October 15th, 1916, for allegedly committing assault. A few days later, Miller was officially charged with "Assault with Intent to Commit Great Bodily Harm" and sentenced to 90 days in the county jail. Though the case never made any explicit claims as to why Miller deserved to be set free, the petitioner argued that he was wrongfully being detained and filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on November 14th 1916. Just a day later, his case was heard and a writ was allowed. The court ordered Felix J. McShane and Henry Schroeder, the respondents, to release Miller from their custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 5, 1920, Ruth McLane petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. She claimed that Marshall Eberstein (Chief of Police), Alta Berger (superintendent of Detention Hospital), and Dr. J. F Edwards (Health Commissioner) imprisoned, detained, confined, and restrained her of her liberty. In her petition, she argued her detention was illegal. The police arrested her in Omaha, charged with being the keeper of an ill-governed house, and the police magistrate found her guilty. The police magistrate sentenced her to 30 days in the country and the cost of prosecution. Following the proper process, she appealed the bond cost, and the police magistrate approved the appeal bond. However, instead of releasing her, the Edwards sent her to Detention Hospital, where Berger, the superintendent, confined her without a warrant. Berger wanted to perform physical tests on her, and after she refused, he threatened to use force to conduct the examination. She argued that her detention violated her rights under Article 5 of the Amendment of the Constitution of the United States and Section 11 of Article 1 of the Constitution of the State of Nebraska. The same day, the judge accepted the petition and ordered a writ of habeas corpus. The next day, Alta Burger responded to the writ, citing Ordinance No. 10509 to justify confining McLane. However, the outcome of this proceeding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Moy Gum and Wah Gee were confined in the Steamship Haytian Republic by T. J. Black for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Moy Yuen filed for writ of habeas corpus for Moy Gum and Wah Gee. Writ of Habeas Corpus was denied for Moy Gum, and he was ordered to remain in custody. Wah Gee was granted a writ of Habeas Corpus and was ordered to be free from custody. Case file includes transcripts of cross and direct examinations.

Summary of Proceedings: Tony Branchi claimed to have been unlawfully detained by Felix J. Mcshane, Henry Schroeder, Henry W. Dunn, Stephan Maloney, Michaell O. Dempsey when he filed a writ of habeas corpus on November 23rd, 1915. He was detained under suspicion of violating parole that was given in the State of Pennsylvania. He claimed that he was forcibly removed from the state of his parole by Pennsylvania authorities in order to incriminate him. Therefore he was not a fugitive of the law under Nebraska statutes. The writ was allowed and he was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 11, 1903, H.C. Gill petitioned for the freedom of his clients, Yvonne Le Fevre and Georgette Normand. Gill’s petition alleged that Le Fevre and Normand were being unlawfully restrained by M. Angelique, Sister Superior of the House of the Good Shepherd, in the said House of the Good Shepherd, in Seattle, Washington. Gill’s petition also alleges that to the best of the petitioner’s knowledge, they are being held by the request of the U.S. Immigration Inspector, James P. Lavin. On February 13th, Judge W. R. Day granted the writ of Habeas Corpus to Le Fevre and Normand. In these papers, Marie Le Fevre is also added to the list of bound parties, although her (presumed) relation to Yvonne is unknown. The same day, Sheriff Ed Cudihee served the writ on the Sister Superior personally. On February 14th, 1903, the Chief Justice of the United States of America, Melville W. Fuller, reached out to the court to pause all proceedings and immediately send all records and proceedings to the Supreme Court.

Summary of Proceedings: George Hansen filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Florence Hansen, who was being held by her uncle and aunt, Louis and Bessie Hansen. George's exact relationship to Florence is not stated. While the actual petition is not included in the case file, the petition was allowed by Judge King Dykeman on August 6th, 1914. Judge Everett Smith would hear the case in his court. In May of the same year, Florence’s mother, Christine Hansen, was awarded custody of Florence. According to Christine’s attorney, J. H. Bauer, Christine left Florence with her uncle and aunt for the summer, and intended to pick her up before the school year started, so she and her (unnamed) sibling could attend school. The outcome of this case and fate of Florence are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: W. W. Yager petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police J. F. Warren. Yager alleged that he was arrested without charge or warrant and was being held illegally in Seattle City Jail with no due process. He claimed that he knew of a telegram sent from the San Francisco chief of police to Warren, informing Warren that Yager had abandoned his wife and child in California. Yager maintained that a telegram did not hold the authority that a warrant did, and it gave Warren no legal right to arrest Yager. Warren responded with a warrant from Seattle Justice of the Peace Otis W. Brinker charging Yager with being a fugitive from justice, but no California warrant was present in the case file. The outcome of the case and Yager’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 29, 1916, Richard Casey allegedly carried a concealed weapon. On October 31, 1916, the Police Court of the City of Omaha, Douglas County, charged him with this in violation of statutes of the state of Nebraska. Casey was tried, convicted, and sentenced to pay a fine of twenty-five dollars. However, on the same day, Casey petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the grounds that he was unlawfully deprived of his liberty. He claimed that the police had no jurisdiction to try and sentence him under a charge of carrying concealed weapons. Thus, all the proceedings were unlawful and void, and the police unlawfully deprived him of his liberty. The outcome of this proceeding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: A group of passengers was detained on the steamship “Danube” coming into the Port of Astoria from Vancouver. Their friend Ju Guy petitioned for habeas corpus on May 3rd, 1893, upon receiving notice of their detention. He explained to the court that the individuals were merchants and thus permitted entry despite the Chinese Exclusion Act. William Meyer, master of the steamship, presented the detained individuals, and they were ordered released by Judge Charles B. Bellinger. There are pictures and handwritten accounts of the merchants included in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: William Boward, aged 11, was entrusted to the care of William and Martha Alvord by the child’s parents when he was 15 months old to care for until he reached maturity. Roughly 18 months prior to the petition’s date Theodore Boward, aged 9, was similar entrusted to the Alvords by the boys’ mother on her deathbed, contingent on Solomon Boward, the boys’ father’s, consent. Solomon allegedly gave said consent a few hours following his wife’s death. Solomon began to resist this custody arrangement about 5 months prior to the petition’s date, around the same time he remarried. Solomon eventually filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus to see the boys returned to him. The Alvords claimed Solomon could not properly care for the boys due to his work, and that their step-mother had allegedly abused and mistreated the children before. William Boward also testified on behalf of the Alvords, and against Solomon leading the judge to conclude that William was not illegally and unlawfully restrained, but that Theodore was. This led to a custody arrangement where William and Martha Alvord retained custody of William Boward, but Solomon was given custody of Theodore Boward. Solomon attempted to appeal this result, but the outcome of his attempts is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In August 1885, William C. Swartz petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by E. J. Whittier, Sheriff of Spokane County. Swartz was charged with stealing one red line back cow, valued at $35. The petitioner was given bail in sum of $500 yet failed to give bail and remained in custody awaiting his appearance. The petition alleged there was no probable cause, and the bail amount was excessive. Judge George M. Turner ruled Swartz was not illegally restrained and remanded him to the custody of the Whittier.

Summary of Proceedings: Blanche Folson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to challenge her detention at the "Hospital for the Insane at Hastings," now the Hastings Regional Center, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, which included commitment papers, Folson was remanded to the custody of the superintendent.

Summary of Proceedings: George Bell was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Bell was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Bell and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Summary of Proceedings: William Young was approached by the deputy sheriff John Roberts and Miles E. Clark. Roberts asked Clark if this is the man he wanted arrested and Clark affirmed, Roberts then took Young into custody. After Young filed a writ of habeas corpus, he was released on bail by the judge. Local news coverage indicated Young was among striking workers and Roberts arrested him without cause. Local press coverage also called for Roberts' dismissal and accused him of wrongfully arresting innocents like Young while letting vice criminals go free.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles F. Ireland was arrested for committing arson in Brandon Manitoba Canada. He was detained in Seattle, where he was visiting his brother in law. Ireland then filed a writ of habeas corpus directed at the sheriff J. H. Woolery. On June 21st, 1894 he appeared before the justice of peace and paid a $750 fine, and was asked for a second appearance before the justice of peace on June 27th, 1894. After this initial meeting, he was released from custody, Woolery was not able to locate him for a hearing before Judge Humes on June 22nd, 1894.

Summary of Proceedings: Mary Brabec filed for a writ of habeas corpus in order to gain custody of her children, Annie, Lillie, Willie, Emma, and Arthur Brabec, from their father, Joseph Brabec. She alleged that while Joseph is her husband and father to her children, he was prone to “extreme and repeated cruelty” as well as “habitual drunkenness,” and that she “had been many times threatened by him” leading her to flee their farm and to seek a divorce and sole custody of the children from the Gage County District Court. She claimed to fear that Joseph would hurt the children in the time it would take the divorce and accompanying custody arrangement to process, and that between his drunkenness and refusal to allow the children to attend school except when forced by school authorities that he is unfit to have custody of them. Judge Pemberton agreed to hear the petition, and had Joseph, the children, and additional witnesses all summoned to court, but the outcome of the proceedings is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
At trial on 3 December 1893, Charles Stevens plead guilty to malicious destruction of property valued at less than $100. After the trial before the District Court, Stevens was sentenced to 4 months in the County Jail and was ordered to pay a $100.00 fine plus the costs of the trial which were $43.78 in total. The order was signed by Judge Charles Ogden who, at the time, was one of the District Court Judges. His term concluded at the end of that year as he was filling a temporary vacancy.

A petition was submitted to the District Court on 5 February 1894 which stated that Stevens had been held in the County Jail since 2 December 1893. The petition asserts that the maximum penalty provided by law is imprisonment for a term not exceeding 30 days and that the District Court had no jurisdiction or power to sentence Stevens for a longer term. Judge Cunningham R. Scott ordered that the writ be allowed and that the petitioner and County Attorney appear in Court on 6 February 1894. At that trial, Judge Scott held that Stevens was unlawfully deprived of his liberty and ordered that he be discharged and that costs of these proceedings be taxed to the County.

Summary of Proceedings: Peters was imprisoned by W. G. Malin after it was discovered that he had secretly aided mothers of the Sac and Fox Tribe in taking their children from the American Indian Boarding School at Toledo, IA back to the tribe's reservation. There was a previous trial in this same case which determined that Peters had been wrongfully imprisoned. The judge ruled that Malin's court-appointed guardianship of the children whom Peters had taken from the school was not legal, and therefore void. The judge also ruled that the state did not have the right to interfere in the proceedings of the school, because it was a federal institution and its attendees federal wards. Furthermore, the criminal laws of the state did not apply to the Native Americans and their tribes, and would only apply if a member of the tribe was involved in an act which "brought him within the plane of the legislative jurisdiction of the state." It was argued that this would apply only in a small number of cases. The ruling of this retrial is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 30, 1921, Charles Saap was arrested and accused of having alchohol in his possesion. On August 1, he was found guilty by Police Magistrate Charles Foster and ordered to pay a fine. He appealed the decision, paid the appeal bond, and was released from custody. On September 26, Judge L. B. Day decided that the appeal bond was defective and dismissed it for want of jurisdiction. Charles was then remanded to the custody of the respondents. On September 29, Charles’ wife, Alvina, petitioned on his behalf for a writ of habeas corpus. The writ was dismissed for want of prosecution and Charles’ fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Jim Ryan filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against H. P. Haze (the police officer in charge of the Omaha Work House) on December 20, 1917. Ryan's petition stated that, on November 24, 1917, Ryan was charged by the Police Court with "Unlawful possession of Liquer." The Police Magistrate of Omaha tried Ryan, found him guilty, and sentenced him to sixty days of imprisonment in the Work House and required to do "Hard Labor." Ryan's petition alleged that his sentence and commitment were illegal because the prohibition law that he was charged with violating stated that all imprisonment sentences imposed by magistrates would be served in the County Jail. It was commanded that Haze bring the body of Ryan before judge Willis G. Sears to show cause for Ryan's detention. Ryan's application was denied, and it is likely that he remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 1, 1920, Harry Becker, also known as Isic Feurht, was charged with the crime of "Investigation" and imprisoned in the Omaha City Jail. While there, no other charge was made against him. On November 4, 1920, aided by his attorneys from the firm of Jamieson and O'Sullivan, Becker petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against chief of police Marshall Eberstein. He pointed out that "investigation" was not a crime in the state of Nebraska, and that he was being unlawfully held.  The case was dismissed upon the relator's motion at his costs on November 4, 1920, and a writ and return was filed on November 6, 1920.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 18, 1885, Ah Lit filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he believed he was being illegally detained by the Portland Chief of Police S.B. Parrish. Parrish claimed that he was ordered to detain Ah Lit by Police Judge R.M. Dement on the charge of violating Portland City Ordinance 3983. Portland City Ordinance 3983 stated that opium smoking was disorderly conduct. Judge Deady disagreed with the charge of disorderly conduct, and ordered Ah Lit released from custody. The case file contains Judge Deady's full opinion regarding the ordinance and unlawful imprisonment of Ah Lit.

Summary of Proceedings:
On 25 March 1893, James Plunkett (Mary’s father) committed Mary to the care and custody of Sister Mary Michael (petitioner) along with two other children; Eddie Plunkett and Katie Plunkett. Katie was around 1.5 years older than Mary and Eddie is around 3 years older than Mary. Their mother had passed away and James was “not so situated as to be able to keep house, or suitably care for his said children.” In December of 1895, James passed away without providing any guardian for the children. He did not leave any means or property of any kind which could be used to provide for the children. He in no way revoked his commitment of the children to the care of petitioner.
Sister Mary Michael (petitioner) was in charge of Saint James’ Orphanage. The children were continuously in the care of petitioner until 11 April 1896. The petitioner was under the assumption that the children did not have any living relatives and were not provided or cared for by any person other than said petitioner. On 11 April 1896, the two older children (Katie and Eddie) were placed in the care of Dennis Kane. The petitioner was not aware that Kane was willing to take more than two of the children. Subsequently, petitioner placed Mary Plunkett in the care of the Costello family where she stayed until December of that year. Petitioner was then informed that Kane was willing and ready to take care of Mary as well, allowing all three children to be raised together. Kane and his wife stated that they would legally adopt all three Plunkett children (giving them rights of inheritance). 
Sister Mary Micheal then went to the Costello family’s home and, with their consent, took Mary back to the aforementioned orphanage. She arranged for Mary’s transportation to the Kane’s home. On 19 December 1896, Mrs. McAdo came to the orphanage and asked for Mary to stay with her and her daughter overnight. The two made an agreement that Mrs. McAdo would bring Mary to the Webster St. Depot on the following day to take the train to the Kane home. On the following day, Mrs. McAdo refused to bring Mary to the train and has, ever since, refused to allow her to go to the Kane’s home or return to the petitioner. 
Petitioner believes that Mrs. McAdo is not suitably situated to have the care and custody of said child. It would be in the best interest of Mary to allow her to be raised with her siblings by Dennis Kane and his wife who are well qualified and suited. 
Sister Mary Michael asks that a Writ of Habeas Corpus be granted so that Mary will be released to the custody of petitioner for the purpose of bringing her to Mr. Kane. Sister Mary Michael signed this petition on 12 January 1897. Judge Baker ordered that the writ be allowed, ordering that Mrs. McAdo come to the Court House with Mary Plunkett at 10:00am on 16 January 1897.
Sheriff McDonald signed a statement that the writ was received on 14 January 1897 and that it would be served to Mrs. McAdo on the same day. In a document filed 2 March 1897, Judge Baker stated that the Court found for Sister Mary Michael, stating that said petitioner was “entitled to the care and custody” of Mary Plunkett and that the best interests of the child would be served by awarding her custody to the petitioner. Albyn L. Frank (District Court Clerk) then filed a motion for the costs to be taxed to Douglas County. This motion was sustained by the Court (Judge Baker) on 9 June 1898.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 24th, 1917, a man whose legal name is unknown committed first-degree murder against George Connery in Anoka County, Minnesota. The man whose legal name is unknown used many aliases, including Frank J. Curtis, Frank McCool, and John Doe. He was tried before a Minnesota jury and indicted for his crime. Curtis, as he is referred to in the legal documents regarding his habeas corpus petition, fled the state of Minnesota sometime after the murder or the trial and arrived in Nebraska. After Curtis fled, J. A. A. Burnquist, the Governor of Minnesota, sent a letter to Keith Neville, the Governor of Nebraska, asking for the state of Nebraska to capture Curtis and return him to Minnesota. Sometime between the murder and May 5th, 1917, Curtis was captured by the Omaha Police Department and held in custody by Henry W. Dunn--the Omaha Chief of Police--, Henry Hietfield, and Stephen Maloney--the Omaha Chief of Detectives. Following his arrest, Curtis filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus as he argued that he was held imprisoned for no apparent reason. The judge granted his writ, but ordered that the holding parties return to court the following day, May 8th, 1917. There are no further records to indicate whether Curtis was released or not.

Summary of Proceedings: Blanche Barry was arrested and tried in a Police Court in Omaha on the charge of vagrancy and having a vanereal disease. This charge was successfully appealed on July 6, 1918, and an order of release was issued by Police Judge James M. Fitzgerald. Barry and attorney, John M Macfarland, filed for habeas against City Health Commissioner, Ernest T. Manning, charging that he continues to hold Barry in a detention home without complaint or judgement. The petition was granted, but later denied on July 12th. Barry motioned for a new trial, charging that such judgement was contrary to the evidence, but the motion was overruled on July 16th.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Hajek, the petitioner, files a writ of Habeas Corpus in an effort to regain custody of his son, Frank Hajek, who was eight years of age in 1905. John and Mary Terry of Ravenna had custody of Frank since his mother died in 1903. They were the boy's aunt and uncle. Judge Kennedy denies the writ of habeas corpus. John and Mary Terry were found to be best able to ensure Frank's welfare, and he stayed in their custody, with Joseph never getting in touch with the boy. Joseph Hajek then petitioned again under Judge George A. Day for the custody of his son, likely because he had recently remarried. Judge Day found that Frank is unlawfully detained and Joseph Hajek was awarded custody of Frank.

Summary of Proceedings: W. W. Wingard, the petitioner, was detained with T. W. Gosney for the crime of tampering with witnesses in an action pending before a court of the State of Washington. The case file stated that the crime occurred on August 16th, 1915. Allegedly, Wingard attempted to persuade Rose Smith and Alma Moen, who were subpoenaed, to not appear as ordered in the case "State of Washington, plaintiff, vs. Rose Foster". Afterward, he was ordered to be confined in Pierce County Jail for four months and fined five hundred dollars ($15,461.98, 2024). On the 20th day of October 16th, Wingard filed a petition for a write of habeas corpus with the claims of being deprived of liberty without the due process of law, being denied a public trial, having failed to be informed of the nature and cause of the charges, having been denied constitutional rights under Article 6, and having been denied the right to be confronted with witness. Judge Cushman allowed the writ and Wingard was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Ardula Porter petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of her daughter, thirteen-year-old Clara Barnes, from her brother-in-law, J. C. Barnes, which was granted. Ardula and Joseph Barnes had gotten divorced without establishing custody of their daughter, Clara, who had been living with her father and his family when he died. According to Ardula, Joseph's brother, J. C., was refusing to allow Ardula to take custody of her daughter. The petition was dismissed during the hearing "without costs to any of the parties, the said child having been surrendered to the petitioner."

Summary of Proceedings: The bound party, James Cummings, having allegedly committed Grand Larceny in Yellow Medicine County, Minnesota was issued an arrested warrant. On or about November 5th, 1919, Alfred C. Anderson reported that Cummings was allegedly a fugitive from Justice. This report prompted Police Magistrate James M. Fitzgerald to authorize the arrest of Cummings. The bound party and his attorney then initiated an application for a writ of Habeas Corpus on November 5th. The writ was allowed to issue but was denied and the the petitioner remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
According to newspaper coverage, all petitioners in this case file were “members of the Industrial Workers of the World…held for federal investigation.” Seattle City Police had raided an I.W.W. meeting on May 2, 1918, jailing two-hundred and eleven men on vagrancy charges. Attorney for the petitioners, H. E. Foster “charged that the arrests were a part of a scheme inspired by rival cities to stir up labor troubles, in an effort to discredit [Seattle’s] record in the handling of government contracts in the progress of the war.” Foster also claimed that special representative of the department of justice, Clarence Reames, was “sending letters to judges asking them to suspend operation of habeas corpus.”

Seattle Police Chief charged all petitioners as disorderly persons and fixed bail at two-hundred dollars. Newspaper coverage stated that Commissioner Robert W. McClelland fixed bail for petitioners with draft law violations at two-thousand and five-hundred dollars.

Petitioners experienced a variety of outcomes. James Lacey faced a warrant of arrest issued by the court of  John B. Gordon, Justice of the Peace in Seattle Precinct and sitting Police Judge.

T. Wolf, John Strom, Gus Lundberg, M. Brech, Gus Johnson, Ed Aspelin, A. Kisil, Welgot Peterson were “turned over to the Immigration Officers of the United States Government for the purpose of deportation as undesirable aliens, under Federal deportation warrants.”

Edward Nelson, Edward Hintz, William Smith, Albin Anderson, William Kircher, Henry Stinson, Jim Sorenson, William Swanson, Roy Sample, Axtol Anderson, Alfred Holquist, Oscar Roberg, George Glenert, J. J. Extell, Emel Hummell, James Lacey, H. Lubbert, Allmond Kadgin, Nichillis Gussok, Eric Arthur Peterson, Charles Bolla, Edwin Browning, Adam Turner, Dan Kelley, C. W. Hall, Charles Swelgin- were “turned over to the Department of Justice of the United States for prosecution for violation of the “Draft Laws” or Selective Service Act of the United States, and that complaints have been filed and warrants issued therefor.”

Shiegekagn Hasama and J. S. Weaver were not in custody. Police Chief Warren stated that the two men had already been prosecuted in the above mentioned police court and convicted and their respective judgements satisfied. 

Carl Swelgin was also a defendant in a pending suit over alleged fraudulent naturalization certificate in the District Court of the United States for the District of Oregon.

James Johnson, William Fiele, Thomas Rimmer, Tony Wolf, John Strom, Wilgot Peterson, Gus Lundberg, Michel Brech, Gus Johnson, Ed Aspelin, and Alex Kisil were “unnaturalized aliens  within the United States who were found advocating and teaching the doctrines and principles of anarchy therein and the doctrines and principles of a forcible resistance to the execution of the laws of the United States and Government thereof.” Officers with the Department of Labor issued warrants for this group of petitioners.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 9, 1918, George W. and Elise M. Hahne filed for habeas against Elsie's parents, Fred E. and Mary A. Sawtell for custody over their minor children, George W. and Dale D. Hahne. In the petition the Hahne's claimed that the Sawtells agreed to maintain care of children during certain parts of the year in Hastings, Adams County, Nebraska. Furthermore, full custody and care remained in hands of the Hahnes in Omaha and that the petition comes forth after the Sawtells refused to give the children back. The petition was granted, but the cause was later dismissed by the Hahnes on August 27, 1918. Census records indicate that the family continued to share custody, as the boys appear in both the Hahnes' household in the 1920 census on January 7, 1920, and in the Sawtells' house in Hastings on January 9-10, 1920.
