Summary of Proceedings: On July 6, 1911, Mary A. Dohney placed an advertisement for a room for rent. On July 7, A. T. Cochran and alleged wife responded and co-habituated for five days in the rented room. The supposed wife was identified as Mary J. Carr, but Dohney had believed her to be called Mrs. Cochran. On July 11, Dohney launched a complaint against Carr, charging that she, a married woman, and A. T. Cochran, and single man, lived together in violation of section 11, chapter 38, revised statutes of the state of Illinois. Order of commitment and warrant against Carr was issued July 12, signed by clerk Galpin. On July 15, Carr was said to have departed from Chicago to Omaha, Nebraska. Warrant for Carr was sent to Omaha July 17, which provided a description and photograph of Carr. On July 19, Carr filed Habeas with attorney John G. Kuhn, against John J. Donohue. On July 19, the petition was granted, and a writ was issued; Carr was released on bond of $500 with Maurice Rouch as Surety. On July 26, the writ was sustained, and Carr was discharged.

Davis provided documentation that claimed Peben’s imprisonment in the Gage County Jail was the result of his refusal to appear in court after being subpoenaed in a separate case in which he and P. Summary of Proceedings: Vitan Deloff was a 34 year old migrant from Bulgaria who was arrested on February 5, 1918 by the Immigrant Inspector, A. F. Richardson. Following his arrest, Deloff was given a hearing on April 24, 1918, however, remained in custody until he filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 30, 1918. In the petition, Delof argued that he was not given a fair hearing because he was denied his right to legal counsel and his right to view the warrant and the evidence upon which it was based. Judge Frank H. Rudkin agreed to hear the petition, however, A. F. Richardson agreed to release Deloff from custody before the hearing for a writ of habeas corpus could occur. Due to Deloff being released, the writ of habeas corpus was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: Caroline and John Dyer were adopted by Lewis and Ada Dyer from the Nebraska Children’s Home Society. Caroline and John were eventually ordered to be removed from Lewis and Ada Dryer and returned to the Home Society in Omaha. The Home Society claimed that this change was because the Dyers were not capable of offering the good home that they claimed they would during the adoption process. The Home Society alleged that the Dyers did not own the farm that they claimed to during the adoption process, and that Lewis Dyer was a “man of immoral character” who drank excessively, brewed alcohol in his home, and committed adultery. In response to learning this the Home Society demanded the Dyers return the children to them in Omaha, and after regaining possession of the children the Home Society put them in the care of the respondent, W. F. Lanning. The Dyers filed for a writ of habeas to regain custody of the children, denying most of the Home Society’s claims, and that because of a mutual feeling of attachment between the children and themselves as adoptive parents that the children should be returned to their custody. Judge Kelligar grants the writ and agrees to hear the petition, and the Home Society, on behalf of Lanning object, claiming the court has no jurisdiction in this case. This objection was eventually overruled, and the case heard, though it was eventually dismissed on November 16, 1908.

Summary of Proceedings: The petitioners are a group of Chinese Merchants who departed the US to visit family in China. On their return, William Meyer, Master of Steamship Danube, detained them on the vessel under suspicion of violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Their friend Goey Luug petitioned for habeas corpus and provided proof of their residency in Portland, Oregon. Judge Bellinger approved their writ and granted their release.

Summary of Proceedings: Arrested and convicted in the District Court of Sheridan County on the charge of grand larceny for stealing a cow, Herman Granger petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that Warden of the Nebraska State Penitentiary Leidigh was unlawfully detaining him. He had previously appealed to the Nebraska State Supreme Court, who had upheld the verdict. Granger argued that he was imprisoned under the NE House of Representatives bill no. 87 "an act to punish cattle stealing..." when the bill had not passed, making his incarceration unconstitutional. Judge Holmes granted the petition. After hearing evidence, Holmes denied the writ and remanded Granger back into the custody of the warden.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 3rd, 1919, Albert Larson filed a habeas corpus petition on behalf of his daughter Nellie Larson who was being wrongfully held by Louis and Mollie Saunders. The petition was approved and the Saunders were ordered to appear in court and bring Nellie on April 5th. The hearing found that Nellie was being wrongfully detained by the Saunders and Mr. Larson's writ was approved by the court. Nellie was returned to her father.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph W. Fleming was arrested by the chief and captains of police for Omaha. The sheriff of Cumings County allegedly called them to arrest the petitioner for defrauding Peter Shinstock. Joseph Fleming filed a petition for habeas corpus on June 23rd, 1919 in which he argued that he could not be arrested and charged by officials in another county. The petition was approved and he appeared in court on the same day. The writ was dismissed for "prosecutorial related costs".

Summary of Proceedings: Max Rosenthal, was found maintaining a solicitor without having a license and therefore violating Ordinance number 977 of the City of Omaha. Rosenthal, petitioner, files for a writ of Habeas Corpus on grounds that the City Council of Omaha does not have the authority to enact an ordinance of this kind as it conflicts with the constitution of the United States and Nebraska. Summary of Proceedings: Lucy Stewart filed for a writ of habeas corpus for her child, Chester Stewart, from her husband, George M. Stewart. Summary of Proceedings: Max Tushkeich petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against J. A. Schiller, the chairman of the Spokane Local Board No. 3 for Division No. 2. Tushkeich claimed he was an immigrant from Russia and had no intentions to become a citizen of the United States. He alleged that he filed military draft paperwork stating he was an alien and should be exempt from military service, but was being held at Spokane City Hall in preparation to be sent to Camp Lewis. Schiller claimed that Tushkeich did not claim exemption from military service, to which Tushkeich replied that if he did not claim exemption, it was the result of his lack of fluency in the English language. Tushkeich’s draft registration card stated he was an alien and had parents dependent on him for support, but Tushkeich wrote “None” in response to the question “Do you claim exemption from draft (specify grounds)?” The court ruled that, while Tuchkeich did not claim exemption, he was exempt from military service. The writ was allowed and Tuchkeich was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 26th, 1920, Fred Sailor was arrested and charged with vagrancy. Subsequently, he was allegedly found guilty of these charges before a police magistrate and was sentenced to 60 days in the county jail. On September 8th, 1920, Sailor filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus alleging that the plea of guilty was entered against him and that the magistrate refused to accept an appeal bond as a result of his guilty plea. Originally, the result of this writ was that Judge A. C. Troup denied the writ, ordered a new trial at the lower court with the plea of not guilty, and remanded custody to the police court. on September 9th, 1920, T. B. Murray, Attorney for the City of Omaha, filed a motion to set aside the order of the court claiming that the facts of the petition were false and that he had no notification of the proceedings the day before and thus could not represent the City. On September 10th, 1920, Judge Troup vacated their order, denied the writ, and remanded custody of Sailor to the Sheriff. It is unclear, but likely, that as a result of the Judge vacating their original order, a new trial was not granted.

Summary of Proceedings:
Fifteen men and women filed for habeas corpus on November 10, 1917 while being held in Seattle City Jail. Their lawyer claimed that their arrest for disorderly conduct occurred without a warrant, and that the individuals were not offered bail. Two days later, on November 12, 1917, the return for their writ expressed that the group had been charged, offered bail, and no one in the group was “in the custody of the Chief of Police.”

According to newspaper coverage, the group were associated with a series of vice raids conducted in Seattle in mid-November, 1917. Coverage referred to the petitioners as “underworld characters,” “immoral women found to be a menace to the health of the community." Newspapers also confirmed that several superior courts had dismissed writs of habeas corpus and applied charges to people arrested in the raids, stating they “had…been admitted to bail, and charges placed against them.”


Of note are changes to the list of names on the petition. The petition reflected changes in status during the proceedings, with several people crossed off of some legal forms but included on others.

Summary of Proceedings: It was November 25th, 1942, when Gus A. Fagerberg petitioned for and was allowed an order for writ of Habeas Corpus having been arrested and deprived of his liberty by Dennis H. Cronin and William C. Condit in July of that year. Fagerberg was arrested on the grounds of violating the National Prohibition Act and then sentenced to three months imprisonment on five counts and a fine of $500. In his petition he presented that he had satisfied the longest period of imposed imprisonment and yet was still being held in custody. Later in the same month the court agreed, and he was discharged. It was March of 1925 when an appeal was made and then granted to Cronin and Condit after they presented that the ordered imprisonment of three months on the five counts were to run consecutively and that the imprisonment was justified until the fine was paid, of which Fagerberg had not paid. It was February of the following year that the Circuit Court of Appeals filed a mandate that the decision to discharge Fagerberg be reversed and that he be remanded to custody in compliance with the case Cronin, U.S. Marshal et al., vs William J. Fox. Later that same month the writ of Habeas Corpus was discharged and Fagerberg remanded to custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Augé petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his stepson, Amadee Quevereux, from Joseph Poupenez, which was granted. Augé accused Poupenez of illegally indenturing Quevereux; Poupenez countered that he held Quevereux by virtue of an indenture of apprenticeship agreed to by Quevereux's mother. After hearing the evidence, Quevereux was released.

Summary of Proceedings:
On July 1, 1903 Mary Cowing petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her son, Warren B. Cowing. Mary claimed Warren was being held by his father of the same name, Warren B. Cowing. Mary said she had been given legal custody over her son, but that Warren Senior was refusing to disclose where he was holding Warren Junior within Seattle. The outcome of this case is unknown. However, a second habeas petition was filed the following year that indicated the custody battle continued, and that Warren Senior was given custody, but Mary and Warren Junior attempted to run to California. See: “In the Matter of the Application for Writ Habeas Corpus W. B. Cowing Jr.” 

Junior and Senior are not used in the case language, but used for clarity here.

Summary of Proceedings:
Sometime shortly after his wife's death, Fred O. Lane, a carpenter in Omaha, Nebraska, gave the custody of his then five-year-old daughter, Frances Lane, to a Sarpy County couple, the Brothers, via a "written instrument." The girl lived with the couple for three years, becoming part of their "hearts and home." Frances was the couple's niece, and Andrew was known in his community as a well-to-do foreman. The couple believed that the piece of paper Lane had signed were formal adoption papers, and that he had surrendered parental rights. Andrew R. and Hattie Brothers attested that they had always told the girl who her biological father was, despite his lack of involvement in her life. According to the Omaha Daily News, they lived in boxcars that had been retrofitted into a house. As the Brothers told it, after years of absence, Fred Lane suddenly took the girl back with him to Omaha on June 1, 1916. According to Lane's second wife, when Frances returned to her father's home "her clothes were ragged...and she had learned to use bad language." 

Likely to regain custody of the girl, the Brothers filed for adoption on June 27, 1916 in Sarpy County, and despite Fred Lane's objections at the hearing, which Frances was never present at, Sarpy County approved the adoption on August 2, 1916. However, Fred appealed, and during the long legal process, the girl remained in his home. On January 9, while walking to Walnut Hill School with her friends, Frances was taken by the Brothers and brought back to nearby La Platte, after which Fred Lane filed for a writ of habeas corpus. His appeal of the adoption decision was affirmed by Sarpy County District Court on January 13, 1917. 

Fred had remarried and had another child by this time, and claimed that he had received several wealthy Omaha families wanted to adopt the girl, as she was "an unusually attractive child." He said to the Omaha Daily Bee "Brothers has one baby of his own...I don't see why he should want mine." Apparently, at one point, pieces of evidence about Frances's affection for one side or the other was stricken for the record. During the trial, she curled up on a bench in the corner of the courtroom and played with a doll. According to the Omaha Daily Bee, Judge A.C. Troup consulted with the child privately before making his final decision. Fred was given custody of the child on January 18, in a verdict that elicited tears from onlookers. The Omaha Daily Bee said that "The child, the cynosure of all eyes in a crowded court room when her future was decided by Judge Troup, did not seem to understand what it was all about as her father clasped her to his breast at the dramatic moment when the final decision was made."

Summary of Proceedings:
Francis Williams filed for a writ of habeas corpus at the same time as Sue Belmont and Edward Twitty. In his petition, Williams argued that he was illegally being restrained of his liberty by Joel Warren, the Chief of Police, and J. S. McBride, the City Health Commissioner. Warren and McBride had detained Williams stating that he had a dangerous, contagious, and infectious disease. The case file never states which disease that Williams was claimed to have and Williams denied that he had any disease. Instead, he alleged that he was “the victim of malice and caprice of the Health and Police Departments.” In his return to the writ, J. S. McBride stated that Williams was taken into custody on a warrant issued by John B. Gordon which charged Williams with violating City Ordinance No. 16046 on the preservation of public morality, peace, safety, and good order in the City of Seattle. 

Newspaper coverage notes that the original petition of Francis Williams in the King County Superior Court was denied. Francis Williams reapplied for a writ of habeas corpus and a new judge Boyd Tallman agreed to hear the writ. Tallman ordered that three physicians be assigned to independently examine the petitioners and provide testimony on whether they believe that the Health Commissioner was justified in quarantining them. However, J. S. McBride appealed to the Supreme Court of the State of Washington and was able to receive a writ of prohibition preventing the physicians from examining the petitioners. Newspaper articles show that by the end of 1918, Francis Williams, Sue Belmont, and Edward Twitty remained in quarantine under the custody of J. S. McBride. William’s attorney, Edwin J. Brown wrote several opinion pieces in the Seattle Star detesting the quarantines and the detainment of his clients which he used to jumpstart his mayoral campaign.

Summary of Proceedings: Around 29 Chinese men identified as Chinese according to the petition and due to signature (written in Chinese) were detained by Captain James Carroll aboard the "Ancon" steamship. These petitioners were all residents of the United States for five years or more at "Tongas Landing," which is within present-day Southeast Alaska and at the time, was the Territory of Alaska. They then arrived in Port Townsend in Washington Territory, where they were denied entry by US Customs due to provisions and terms of the "Chinese Exclusion Act," which were updated within the same month of their arrival under the Scott Act of 1888. Caroll is the holding party, and is detaining the men, but is doing so due to enforcement of the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1888 by US Customs in Port Townsend. The outcome is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On behalf of Edward and Martha Shelmidine, William H. Moore petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that they were unlawfully detained by Gable (first name unknown), a marshal in Waverly, Nebraska. Judge Cornish granted the petition. In Gable's response, he alleged that he was holding the couple on orders of the Governor of Texas, Joseph D. Sayers, who issued an extradition warrant. In case files, Martha Shelmidine was also referred to as Mrs. M. M. Claxton. After reviewing evidence, Judge Cornish allowed the writ and ordered that the Shelmidines be released from custody. According to secondary source research, Martha was allegedly previously married in Texas and married Edward in Nebraska. She was allegedly facing charges of bigamy in Texas, which is presumably why Sayers issued an extradition warrant.

Summary of Proceedings:
On September 25, 1906 Celia I. Dougherty petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Dougherty petitioned on behalf of Delloris Nelson, a female child who had been born less than 2 months previously in White Horse, Yukon Territory, Alaska. Celia stated that Delloris was being held illegally by her mother, Edna Nelson, E. E. Dilly, and his unnamed wife in the Seattle Hotel. The Dillys’ relationship to Edna is unknown.
Celia produced documentation of a child custody agreement that gave her and her husband, Oscar M. Dougherty, full legal custody of Delloris. Delloris was to be held by the couple at the “Watsons Home” in White Horse. The agreement also stated that Edna Nelson, Delloris’s mother, was unable to care for her and agreed to hand over custody of her daughter. Nelson was given a dollar by Oscar and Celia in exchange for Delloris. 
Worried that Delloris would soon be taken out of the court’s jurisdiction, Celia filed an affidavit. Judge Frater sent out a warrant asking for Delloris to be brought to court. The outcome of this case and the fate of Delloris are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: A. F. Ryan was arrested on June 2nd, 1919, by two detectives who took him to the Omaha Police Station for "investigation." Ryan's attorney showed, however, that no complaint was ever filed against him. In light of this argument, an application for a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed by Ryan and his attorney and granted by Judge William A. Redick. The judge ordered the bound and holding parties to reappear in court on June 5th, 1919. During the writ hearing in court, John T. Dunn, the Omaha Chief of Detectives and holding party, produced a warrant for Ryan's arrest, citing vagrancy as the charge. Despite this, Judge Redick ruled in Ryan's favor and ordered his immediate release from police custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
William Rusmussen, Charles Lawson, and Clarence Hoyt filed for a writ of habeas corpus on April 8, 1918. Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren held them in the Seattle City jail without a charge. Judge J. T. Ronald allowed the writ on the same day it was filed.

According to newspaper coverage, some of the men were arrested under suspicion of draft registration violations, affiliation with the I.W.W, and desertion.

Summary of Proceedings: The Davis family petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Joseph R. Kimmel from the custody of the Kimmel family, which was granted. The petitioners were Annie Davis, Joseph R.'s grandmother, Carrie Davis, his aunt, and Clarence W. Davis, his uncle. Joseph M. Kimmel intended to take the boy back to his mother's and Joseph R.'s grandmother's house in Portland, Oregon. To faciliate this, he had taken the boy from the Davis's home in August of 1913. Joseph's R.'s mother, Jennie Kimmel, had died on July 5, 1913, but she had apparently agreed with her husband before her death that their son would stay with her family. After hearing the evidence, Joseph was remanded to the custody of the Kimmels. The Davises appealed to the state supreme court, which overturned the decision of the lower court. Ultimately, it was found that the child's father, Joseph M. Kimmel, had "voluntarily relinquished" his right to the boy. The court awarded custody of Joseph R. Kimmel to the Davis family but allowed his father to have him on Sundays as well as "four days in any month, with one week's notice."

Summary of Proceedings: On May 3rd, 1920, Ethel Siefken submitted a petition on behalf of her three children Marvel (9), Elmo (8), and Kennard (7). The children were in the custody of Mr. and Mrs. Wes Conley. The Siefkens also had three other children, Madeleine (5), Eva (4), and Helen (2), who Ethel apparently retained custody of. Mr. and Mrs. Conley claimed custody of these children based off of an agreement with their father, Albert Siefken. Ethel and Albert had filed for divorce in May of 1920. Ethel desired the custody of her children because she believed that they were not receiving proper care, attention, and companionship. The judge granted Ethel’s petition. W. C. Condit, Sheriff of Dodge County, was granted temporary custody of the children for the habeas proceedings. On May 6th, the writ was granted and Ethel was awarded custody of the three children.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 6, 1880, Elmery Seelling complained against Henry A. Carleton to Gage County justice of the peace Peter Shafer, accusing him of bastardy. He was found guilty, with bail set at $500. Carleton could not pay this, and so he was committed to the county jail. Therefore, with the help of the law firm Bush and Richards, Carleton filed a writ of habeas corpus on December 30, 1880 against Gage County sheriff Nathaniel Herron, arguing that he was being unlawfully detained. However, the writ was not issued and served until January 10, 1881. At the hearing on January 11, court officials argued about whether the testimony from the previous hearing in front of the justice of the peace should be allowed, with it ultimately being struck from the record. Judge J.A. Coffey ultimately ruled against Carleton, committing him to jail and ordering him to pay court costs.

Summary of Proceedings: In October 1920, the Umatilla County Circuit Court convicted Elvie Kerby of first degree murder and sentenced him to be hanged from the neck until dead. The following year, his mother, Mrs. D. C. Kerby, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, which was granted. The attorney for the Kerby family argued that the manner in which the state of Oregon had abolished and then reinstated its death penalty, a complex measure involving constitutional amendments and ballot initiatives, was itself unconstitutional. After hearing the evidence, the Marion County Circuit Court remanded Elvie Kerby back into the custody of the warden of the state penitentiary. The Kerbys appealed the decision to the state supreme court, which ultimately affirmed the lower court decision.

Ho claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Summary of Proceedings: On May 2nd, 1923, Anna Cohen filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her 20 year old son, Eddie Toman. She alleged that Eddie was being unlawfully detained by Michael Dempsey (Sheriff) and Pete Dillon (Chief of Police), for the purpose of being handed over to the State Industrial School (Kearney, Nebraska). Anna wished him free. In a return, Dempsey and Dillon explained that Eddie was committed to the State Industrial School on September 10th, 1913 and that he would be held there until he was 21 years old. But, he escaped the school and they had since been holding him for, on behalf, and at the request of the Superintendent of said school. The Superintendent was present in court and was prepared to take Eddie and return him to school. On January 21st, 1924 the writ was dismissed for want of prosecution. The fate of Eddie is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Claus Hubbard filed a writ of habeas after claiming to be unlawfully imprisoned without cause or warning. When Hubbard's lawyers went to the jail and asked what he was incarcerated for, the jailer claimed that he was arrested for vagrancy, but then changed his answer suggesting instead, that he was jailed for being a “suspicious character" which was not an offense of the law. His lawyers claimed that it was common practice for the Omaha police to throw people in jail with the goal of running them out of town. 
Hubbard was characterized as being a black man who had previously protested against the chief of police for throwing other black people in jail without cause and leaving them there for “indefinite lengths of time.” Therefore, Hubbard believed his arrest was retaliation from the chief. He also was experiencing chronic poor health and thought that if he had to stay in jail “it might even cause his death.” 
Ultimately, his petition was granted and he was allowed to have his case brought to the court. According to newspaper coverage, the judge sided with Hubbard, going as far as to say that "Hubbard would have been justified in shooting the officer who arrested him if the use of a pistol had been in defense of his constitutional liberties”. Hubbard was released, and his writ granted.

Summary of Proceedings: E. Stubley was sentenced to serve time at McNeil Island Penitentiary on January 3rd, 1910, after being tried for conspiracy to use the mails to defraud. On August 18th, 1914, Stubley sent a 3-page letter to an attorney, claiming that the Warden of McNeil Island had unjustly taken away his good time served, was holding him past his original sentence, and that he was only allowed Stubley 3 pages to write a letter. The attorney then sent the letter to Judge Cushman, and a writ of habeas corpus was filed in Stubley's name on August 19th, 1914. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Emil Runge petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff Robert T. Hodge. Runge alleged that his imprisonment in the King County Jail was due to a complaint of non-support issued by his wife to King County Justice of the Peace Reah M. Whitehead. Runge claimed that he was not a resident of King County, but of Yakima County, and that he committed no crime in King County. Thus, Runge claimed that Whitehead had no jurisdiction to sentence him to the King County Jail. Hodge filed a motion to quash the petition, but neither the case outcome nor Runge’s fate are revealed in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: Thomas V. Redman was arrested on July 29th, 1911, and charged with attempting to pass counterfeit money. On December 9th, 1912, Redman was sentenced to serve 7 years at McNeil Island Penitentiary after being found guilty of unlawfully having possession of a counterfeit coin with intent to defraud person or persons. While serving his term, Redman filed a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty and that he should not be serving any time. He pointed to the 6th Amendment of the U. S. Constitution, claiming that he was being punished for the same offense twice and was not given a fair or speedy trial, and that no witness could ID him, the police refused to prove his alibi, and many other errors occurred during his trial. Judge Cushman dismissed the case on July 15th, 1916, but Redman refiled the case five days later. On December 7th, 1916, the case was moved to the Supreme Court, but the outcome of the case and the fate of the bound party and petitioner are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Caleb Sykes was charged with fraudulent breach of trust and larceny 
and was a fugitive from justice from the state of Tennessee. 
They said he stole from the three men (Cassleburry, Borum, Roberts) things of the value of three hundred dollars of the proper goods and chattels with the intent to convert to the same to his own use. 
Sykes fled from the state of Tennessee, arrested in Omaha and was being held for Tennessee authorities

Caleb says that he left Tennessee in January when there was no indictment pending when he left, nor any property delivered into his possession. He says he is a resident of Nebraska and married with three children. Rumors were circulating that he had an intimate relationship with a woman in Memphis and then some threats were made against him. They then came to his house and tried to break in so he left because he thought his life was in danger. 

Sykes presented all of this information to court and writ was allowed and he was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Ella Cammenzind, a prisoner in the Douglas County Jail, filed a writ of habeas corpus on January 3, 1919 against the Omaha chief of police, Marshall Eberstein, and the chief of detectives, John Dunn. However, when her attorney, J.B. Randolph, approached John Dunn in order to sign the writ of habeas corpus and talk about the case, he refused to meet with Randolph. Willis G. Sears granted her writ of habeas corpus, and Cammenzind was released on a $100 bail on January 4. An Omaha Daily Bee article indicates that she was accused of kidnapping her 16-year old stepdaughter, Mary Cammenzind, after which she sued for divorce, as well as a $20,000 alimony, against her husband, Charles, a Sioux County rancher. She had taken Mary from her home in Harrison, NE to Omaha on November 7. Ella alleged that Charles abused her and the child, but Charles and Mary said nothing about the matter. On April 1, 1919, district judge A.C. Troup refused to grant Ella's suit for divorce. During the trial, Charles alleged that Ella was the one who had physically intimidated him, and he had only retaliated. Charles also alleged that their marriage was invalid on religious grounds, since Ella had misrepresented herself as a widow when she was, in fact, divorced. If the Catholic Cammenzind had known this, he claimed, he would never have married her.

Reid held Strang under the authority of immigration officials, including A. F. Richardson and the Secretary of Labor, for advocating the teaching of the unlawful destruction of property. Case similarities related to dates and allegations levied against Strang point to other arrests of I.W.W. members in the Pacific Northwest. Judge Frank H. Rudkin dismissed the writ due to the earlier discharge of Strang from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Mary Ann Speaks was born in Alexandria, Virginia--then the District of Columbia--around 1811. In 1836, Speaks claimed, her mother had her bound to Susan Blunt for ten years as an apprentice in housewifery. Blunt promised to free Speaks from her apprenticeship two years early if she agreed to accompany her to St. Louis, to which Speaks agreed. After Speaks had labored nearly eight years as an apprentice in housewifery, Blunt died without making a will. Her administrator, James Quisenberry, acknowledged that Speaks was a free woman, but desired that she pay two years' wages to liberate herself from the Blunt estate. When Speaks refused, Quisenberry had her jailed, and Speaks petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. Her petition invoked the law of apprenticeship, of estates, and of servitude. After hearing the evidence, Speaks was released.

Summary of Proceedings:
On June 25, 1903, Wong Yuen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Lee See, who he claims to be his wife, and Ah Sing and Ah Yuen, who he claims are his son and daughter, respectively. Wong Yuen claimed that his wife and children were being held by Chin Tai Hee in Room 12 of 408 Main Street in Seattle, and that Chin Tai Hee had no legal claim over the three bound parties. Wong Yuen stated that he feared his wife and children would be taken out of the court’s jurisdiction, so Judge Bell had Chin Tai Hee and the three others put in custody. While in custody, Chin Tai Hee petitioned for habeas corpus himself, and was granted his freedom by paying bail, and agreeing to come back to court when summoned. 
Although the actual case file did not give much information beyond this, newspaper coverage illuminated the complexities of this case. Coverage indicated that Wong Yuen had been tried and convicted of forgery against Chin Tai Hee, and that he filed this habeas case from jail. Additionally, newspapers indicated that the Chin family and Wong Yuen were rivals who had a long history of fighting with each other, to the degree that Chin Tai Hee had promised a reward to anyone who could kill Wong Yuen. Newspaper coverage also indicated that Chin Tai Hee and Wong Yuen were both claiming that Lee See was their wife, and that they were the father of the two children. The newspapers indicated that Judge Bell eventually sided with Chin Tai Hee, proclaiming him the rightful husband and father, which was seemingly confirmed by the testimony of Lee See. Wong Yuen’s writ appears to have been denied, and Lee See and the children remained with Chin Tai Hee.

Summary of Proceedings: Leong Yuk Tong petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus for Look Quon because he was detained on the Steamship Danube. He was being held by Master William Meyers under the order of T. J. Black, the Collector of Customs. They argued that Look Quon was not allowed to enter the port because he was a Chinese laborer and thus would violate the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. However, several witnesses testified that he was a merchant working at the Hung Dock Chung Firm located at No. 134 Second Street. The Judge accepted the testimony and granted the writ releasing Look Quon from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Bernard Patrick Morris, the petitioner, failed to report for military service with intent to evade service and was therefore charged with desertion and detained by the Seattle police department. In response, Morris claimed that he was a subject of Canada and was given an exemption by Dominion officials through an Exemption Certificate. Yet, several Military officers and officials responded to the Court, stating they have no trace of a "Bernard Patrick Morris" as enlisted or been drafted. Nonetheless, he was able to eventually produce a certificate from the Canadian Registration Board that he was registered for the Canadian Draft. The Canadian government stated that he was made exempt because of his status as a married man and father. Later on in the case are attached proceedings from a divorce; it is unclear how this played a role in the case and what Morris's fate was.

Summary of Proceedings: It was June 9th, 1913, Mac Fock petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus. Fock believed was being held by Ellis De Bruler for deportation. Fock had returned from China in March of that year and was denied admission. Fock then appealed to the Secretary of Labor.  Fock presented them with certificate he received in 1896 discharging him from prison for being charged with unlawful entry in the U.S. In return, De Bruler claimed that he held Fock under order of deportation to the Republic of China. It was also presented that Fock had applied for admission as a returning native born citizen, when there existed documented evidence that he was born in China. In his reply, Fock argued that an investigation of the immigration office pronounced the certificate genuine and thus he perceived he had the right to re-enter the United States. The court determined that the certificate could not be considered evidence and was issued fraudulently. In August of 1913, the court granted the respondent's motion to discharge the writ. The writ was then denied and Fock remanded to custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Egnatz Weiss petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff Robert T. Hodge and Bernard A. Flood, an agent of the state of New York. Weiss claimed he was being illegally held in King County Jail by Hodge under order of a warrant from New York directing Flood to transport Weiss to the state to face charges for abandonment. Weiss alleged that the warrant was made out for an Ignatz Wise, which he said was not his name. He maintained that he did not abandon his family, but left New York to find better work and sent money back to his wife and children. Hodge and Flood both confirmed that Weiss was in their custody and brought forth the warrant ordering his arrest. The outcome of the case and Weiss’s fate are both unknown. This is the second petition for a writ of habeas corpus Weiss filed in relation to this arrest.

Summary of Proceedings:
Patrick McDonald, a thirteen year old boy, was arrested, accused of being a vagrant, and sent to the St. Louis House of Refuge. Bail was set at $100. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, contending that minors who had parents and homes could not be vagrants, which was granted. Michael McDonald, likely his father, witnessed the petition. After hearing the evidence, Patrick was remanded to the custody of F. S. W. Gleason, superintendent of the House of Refuge.

Summary of Proceedings: Belden Finley petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his son, Verne Finley, from the custody of Verne's grandparents, Jesse and May Carter, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and Verne remanded into the custody of his grandparents. The judge ordered that Belden pay the Carters $3 per week, that the Carters teach Verne to "love and respect" Belden, that Belden be allowed to take temporary custody of Verne at "seasonable times," and that Belden be allowed to re-apply for custody of his son when he could better demonstrate his ability to care for him.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 28, 1898, Edson Sturgeon was awarded a divorce with his then wife Emma A. Harrison. In addition, Sturgeon was awarded the sole custody of his child and minor Zeta Myrtle Sturgeon. On March 13, 1901, Emma Harrison “enticed” Zeta from Edson Sturgeon, and was holding her in Ballard, Washington. On April 1, 1901, Edson Sturgeon filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of his child Zeta, claiming that he had a legal claim to his child as well as that Emma Harrison was unfit to have custody of said child. Within his petition, he also urged the court to move quickly in their action as he was concerned that Harrison would move Zeta out of the jurisdiction of the court. A warrant was issued, Zeta was removed from the custody of Emma Harrison and placed in the House of the Good Shepherd while the court concluded its proceedings. On April 6, 1901, the court awarded full custody to Edson Sturgeon as well as ordered Emma A. Harrison returned to Sturgeon all of Zeta’s personal belongings that she took with her when Emma came into possession of the child.

Summary of Proceedings: In October of 1913, Sukutaro Kuwahara, petitioner and husband of the bound party, entered the country from Japan illegally as a stowaway. On December 11th 1914, the petitioner began working for the Eatonville Lumber Company where he worked for five year paying taxes and earning a stable living. On September 29th, 1919, Hisayo Kuwahara, the bound party and wife of the petitioner, entered the country via the S.S. Africa Maru. On October 3rd, 1919, the bound party was denied entry into the Untied States on an appeal to a Board of Special Inquiry. The status of her husband as a stowaway was cited in the decision and was formally denied on the grounds that she would become a public charge. On January 21st, 1920, the petitioner filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of his wife, the bound party. In the period between the hearing for the case and the filing of the writ, the attorney for the petitioner gathered testimony as to the financial well-being of the petitioner to provide evidence for his ability to support his wife, the bound party. The respondents made a motion to quash the hearing and show cause claiming that the petitioner was part of some "excluded class", possibly referring to the Chinese Exclusion Act. On February 4th, 1920, the Judge, Jeremiah Neterer, ruled that the action should not be quashed and issued the writ the next day. On February 7th, 1920, the writ was granted and the bound party was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 19, 1894, George P. Van Dyke petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his son, W. D. Van Dyke.  Van Dyke was arrested for robbery on March 16, 1894.  The petition argued that no information, charge, or complaint was filed against Van Dyke. On March 19, 1894, Judge Langley issued the writ.  He stated that Van Dyke had been held for a longer amount of time than allowed by the law and that there were no efforts to prosecute him.  While the fate of Van Dyke was not included in the case file, Page 5 of the March 20, 1894 issue of the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reported that Van Dyke remained in custody.  It explained that George P. Van Dyke had asked that no complaint be filed until George Williamson, an accomplice, was also captured. This is because he wanted to show that Van Dyke was influenced by Williamson.  Chief Willard had originally complied with this request, but Judge Langley ordered the complaint be filed immediately.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 21st, 1921, Hans A. Hulke was arrested in the City of Omaha to be held until his extradition to the state of Indiana. Initially, Hulke and his counsel were unaware of his extradition; however, on May 25th, during his hearing for his petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus, the petitioner was made aware of this fact. Following this revelation, Hulke filed a motion for continuance to better prepare his case for freedom. The judge granted the motion and scheduled the return for June 4th, 1921. During this time, the respondents obtained an order from the Governor of Nebraska to arrest Hulke and hold him to be extradited to Indiana. The court was informed that Hulke had committed grand larceny in Indiana against the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, which sought to press charges against Hulke. Despite this, because he was arrested with no warrant or mittimus, the judge ruled in favor of Hulke and deemed that his detainment was illegal and that he would be set free immediately.

Summary of Proceedings: Andrew Rogers petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his young daughter, Lucy Rogers, from Francis Resser, which was granted. Rogers accused his wife of absconding with Lucy to Resser's home; Resser responded that Lucy and her mother were boarders and that he asserted no claim over the child. After hearing the evidence, Lucy was released into her father's custody.

Summary of Proceedings: J.G. Jeffreys (G.L. Jeffrey), a black man, was arrested and charged with assault and battery and mayhem after resisting the commands of constable Richard Diamond and biting his hand. Jeffreys was found guilty and was levied a fine of ninety-nine dollars plus the court costs of Diamond, and was committed without bail until his fees were paid. Jeffreys and his petitioner Allen A. Garner, an attorney and prominent Black community leader, asserted that he was held illegally as his charge was not one that could be punished "by the laws of the States” and that the ruling was “excessive of the jurisdiction" of Judge Cousins. Jeffreys’ writ of habeas corpus was granted and he would later be released. This case is most probably the same as that of G.L Jeffrey, but the the cases remain distinct in a couple minute ways.

Summary of Proceedings:
On February 1 1904, a criminal complaint was formally filed against Ernest Hutchinson, a native of Michigan doing business in Seattle. Hutchinson was charged with violating Seattle City Ordinance 6036, which imposed licensing on the sale and trade of stamps in the city. Hutchinson apparently sold stamps (a system of warehouse coupons which provided a holder with the equivalent value of goods from a storehouse) without securing either the $600 license to trade stamps, nor requiring the purchasers of stamps to secure their $100 stamp licenses.

In his petition, filed on April 12, 1904, Hutchinson claimed the ordinance violated both his rights under the US Constitution and under the Washington State Constitution. In numerous filings between April and May, Hutchinson's petition was granted and he was released on his own recognizance. His lawyers submitted numerous briefs on his behalf, both to secure his initial petition costs (which was ordered by Judge Hanford on May 25) and to claim that the entire ordinance licensing the stamps was unlawful. Citing many cases, both at the state and federal levels, Hutchinson claimed the licensing was "an interference with private property” and that, under the state constitution, licensing was restricted as a police power and was therefore limited to items related to the “peace, happiness and prosperity” of its citizens. Judge Hanford ruled in favor of Hutchinson, and declared the ordinance unconstitutional. Eleven years after it was first filed, Hutchinson's company, The Sperry and Hutchinson Company sued in regards to this case, and were successful, in 1915.

Summary of Proceedings:
Antonio Bojar was charged with the crime of assault with a deadly weapon with the intent to inflict upon the person of another a bodily injury, with no considerable provocation appearing from said assault, against Adrian Obel. Bojar was judged guilty, and ordered to stay in the Penitentiary of the State of Washington for nine months and pay the cost of the prosecution. 

John Fairfield, the attorney for Bojar, claimed that Bojar had acted in self-defense. The case was appealed, but Bojar lacked the money or friends to perfect his case, which included filing a transcript or Statement of Facts of the case to the state Supreme Court. Bojar asked to withdraw this appeal, but was denied and his guilt maintained by Judge Thomas J. Hume. During this entire process, which lasted from June 2, 1892 to June 20, 1893, when the Writ of Habeas Corpus was sent, Bojar had been unable to procure bonds and was imprisoned longer than his original sentencing of nine months. The Writ was accepted , and Bojar was taken to court by Sheriff Woolery on July 11, 1893.


 On January 9, 1894, the guilty judgment of the Superior Court was affirmed once again.

Summary of Proceedings: Elinor Olsen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren and Commissioner of Health J. S. McBride. Olsen’s petition is not included in the case file, but it was granted by Judge John S. Jurey. McBride claimed that Olsen was at no time detained by Warren and was immediately transferred into his own custody after her arrest. He alleged she was infected with a dangerously contagious disease, namely gonorrhea and syphilis, and was now under quarantine at the city isolation hospital. The outcome of the case and Olsen’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In July 1922, 19-year-old Czech immigrant Henry Patera and Mary Poulicek met and started dating. A few months later, on December 6, 1922, he proposed to her with a diamond ring. This was against the wishes of his parents, Jacob and Agnes Patera, who promised to kill him if he married Mary. Thus, in January, he fled to San Francisco and joined the navy. Mary's father, James Poulicek, somehow found him and paid for his passage back to Nebraska to stand trial for the crime of seduction. On June 19, 1923, he stood on trial in the court of Charles A. Goss for parole in this offense, pleading guilty to the crime. Mary testified in this trial, and weeping, showed the jury her ring and proclaimed that she forgave Patera and still loved him. At this, Patera stopped the trial and proclaimed that he would marry Poulicek. The ceremony took place immediately in the courtroom: Judge Goss officiated, the bride and groom's lawyers formed the wedding party, and the jurors were witnesses. Goss ordered the couple to live apart from the parents and for Patera to compensate his new father-in-law for the travel costs of his return from California. After the ceremony, Henry kissed Mary and promised to be the "bestest husband ever." He would not keep this promise: on their wedding night, he refused to sleep in the same bed as Poulicek and left her again only one day after they had been married. He was returned to Omaha shortly after and arrested for violating his parole on August 1, 1923. On August 7, Patera and his lawyer, Julius J. Zitnik, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against sheriff Michael L. Endres and jailer Joe Sherry. Zitnik was also part of the Omaha Czech community. He claimed that since he had already been placed on probation, he could not be confined in jail. Judge Charles Leslie denied his petition on August 9, 1923, and Patera remained in the custody of the court. He was later sentenced to a reformatory for two years. On August 23, 1923, Mary had Henry Patera's daughter—this means that she would have been heavily pregnant during the June 1919 courtroom wedding, a factor that likely encouraged Judge Goss to allow this unusual procedure. A few months later, in October 23, Mary sued Henry's parents, Jacob and Agnes Patera, for $15,000, claiming that their persecution of the couple had Henry's "loss of affection." Two years after Henry got out of prison, Henry married another Czech immigrant named Silvera. He worked as a laborer in a steel works to support his wife and daughter Silvia, born in 1928. Mary ended up marrying another man with the surname of Shada before her death in 1984.

Summary of Proceedings: At an unspecified date, the bound party, Edward Falconer, was alleged to have committed the crimes of conspiracy and falsely assuming to be an officer in Pottawattamie County, Iowa. On September 10th, 1919, a grand jury in Pottawattamie County found standing for Falconer to be charged with the crime. After the commission of the alleged crime, Falconer allegedly fled to Omaha, Douglas County, Nebraska. On September 19th, the Governor of Iowa, W. L. Harding demanded the extradition of Falconer to the aforementioned county. The following day, the Governor of Nebraska, Samuel R. McKelvie, issued a warrant for the arrest of Falconer. Sheriff of the County of Pottawattamie, William Greneweg, then took custody of Falconer within the jurisdiction of Nebraska and returned him to the aforementioned county. On September 24th, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed by the bound party's attorneys making claims including but not limited to: the warrant from the Governor of Nebraska to Sheriff Greneweg was null and void, all proceedings related to the warrant were null and void, the Governor of Nebraska had no authority to transport the bound party, the warrant was issued without investigation, the bound party was not present in Iowa when the times were committed, the alleged crimes are not crimes against Nebraska, and as a result of at the time of arrest being on bail for grand larceny, was ineligible to be extradited. On September 26th, the writ is denied and the bound party was released on bail for twenty days in order to prepare a writ of error to the Nebraska Supreme Court. On September 30th, a motion for a new trial was filed alleging, among the allegations in the petition, that: the court erred in finding the indictment valid, the court erred in ruling the bound party could be removed, the court erred in allowing an extradition not certified by the Chief Magistrate to be allowed, the court erred in not allowing the writ of Habeas Corpus, and the court erred in not squashing an answer and return motion. On October 8th, the motion for a new trial was overruled as a result of an agreement reached by both parties. On October 18th, the writ of error was filed with the Supreme Court. On May 6th, 1921, the Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the lower court at the cost of the plaintiff. Fate of the bound party outside Nebraska is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 6, 1912, A. E. Ream and his attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Ream claimed that he was being held without an official charge and without process of law. He stated that he was told he was being held based on a charge of a crime that occurred in Portland Oregon, which he denied being involved in. The return from Chief of Police Bannick stated that he was acting on a warrant from Washington Governor Hay, who had an extradition request from Oregon. The outcome of this case and the fate of Ream are unknown.  This case appears to be tied to the case “Habeas Corpus of F. M. Mitchell against Claude Bannick (Chief of Police)”, which was filed on the same day and involved the same attorney and petition type.

Summary of Proceedings:
On August 19, 1902. C.C. Smith went to trial before John F. Miller for violating a city ordinance defining the crime of being a disorderly person. Miller judged Smith guilty and sentenced him to a $50 fine, which Smith could not pay. Smith was thus kept in the King County jail. Smith, represented by attorney John C. Calhain, petitioned against his imprisonment, alleging that Miller did not have the legal authority to handle the case as Miller was not a legitimate police judge.

The respondent, Chief of Police John Sullivan, and his counsel, attorney Ellis DeBruler, argued that Miller was made a temporary judge under the orders of Judge Thomas Humes. To which, they identity official paperwork by Judge Humes dated August 18, 1902. Judge Robert R. George, the current acting police judge and judge during the time of the proceedings, responded himself, stating that although he was on vacation for the days of August 18 and 19, that he remained within the city. He did not see any motive or reason for why he would need a temporary replacement. 

Judge Arthur Griffin heard Smith’s writ on August 26, 1902, and sided with Smith, granting his writ of habeas corpus. DeBruler filed a notice of appeal for the case September 8, 1902, with the motion to file an appeal on December 18, 1902.

Summary of Proceedings: Prosfrio Deffillipps and Filip Perill were seamen on the "Bark Eldorado," a ship that arrived at the port of Tacoma, Washington, on June 29th, 1886, from San Francisco, California. After the ship's arrival, the two men left the vessel, leading the shipmaster, L. S. Humphrey, to file a complaint against the seamen for breaching their contract to work on the boat. Authorities detained Deffillipps and Perill the next day and held them in county jail for their alleged crime. The two proceeded to file a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus that same day, June 30th, 1886. Their attorney argued that the local police had no authority over the dispute between an employer and his employees. Unfortunately, no document clearly shows whether the two men were granted their freedom.

Summary of Proceedings: In December of 1921, Joe Strilka was arrested for contempt of court and taken in front of Honor Carroll O. Stauffer, who sentenced Strilka to 15 days. On February 10, 1922, Strilka filed for habeas, arguing that after an arranged appeal to the Supreme Court on January 28, 1922, Stauffer reduced Strilka's sentence to 13 days, which have now passed. In addition, Strilka argued that he had been charged taxed costs, which were retaxed at a high rate, without any legal authority, and that the judge had not sentenced Strilka to costs or taxed costs. A writ was issued and Strilka was released.

Summary of Proceedings:
Anna B. Nemitz filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 22, 1919, claiming she was held without a warrant or charge.
 
According to newspaper coverage, her son, William Fay Ealy, a twenty-two year-old painter, allegedly murdered Elizabeth Bryan on October 21, 1919. Formal charges were filed against both Ealy and his mother, Anna B. Nemitz, for first-degree murder in the same week that they each applied for habeas corpus. The case was widely reported on in contemporary newspapers.

This case file contains documents from the habeas corpus petition of Nemitz’s son, William Fay Ealy.

Summary of Proceedings: Mayor of South Omaha, Allen R. Kelly, was allegedly found taking bribes from several individuals and brewing companies (Omaha Brewing Association, Jos. Schlits Brewing Company, W. M. J. Lemp Brewing Company, Fred Krug Brewing Company, Metz Brewing Company, South Omaha Brewing Company, Anheuser-Busch Brewing Association, Pabst Brewing Company) to the sum of twenty-five hundred dollars. Allen R. Kelly accepted and received said money as a reason to veto any ordinance from the city council that would increase the liquor license tax above and beyond the sum of five hundred dollars. Additionally, Kelly prevented the arrest of those breaking codes related to alcohol serving. In response, Kelly claimed he was not guilty and not eligible for prosecution because he is not a ministerial officer but an executive one, making him a class of officer that is not included in the bribery codes. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, and it was found that Kelly should remain in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Tom Boulias was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Boulias was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Boulias and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Boulias argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. On June 27, the writ of habeas was sustained, and Boulias was released.

Summary of Proceedings:
Following the removal of the Ponca tribe from their homelands in Nebraska to poor lands in Indian Territory (Oklahoma) and the death of Standing Bear's son, Standing Bear and 29 Ponca left the Oklahoma reservation without the permission of their Indian agent. The group made their way up through Kansas and into Nebraska on foot and stopped at the Omaha Reservation. The Omaha welcomed them as they had long been allies, but orders were issued for the thirty Poncas arrest. A newspaper editor extensively published columns about the proceedings and gathered the two attorneys to make Standing Bear's case. A writ of habeas corpus was issued by Judge Elmer Dundy, and in the trial proceedings, the United States government argued that writs of habeas corpus could only be utilized by citizens of the United States or those considered "human." According to this argument, Standing Bear and Indigenous peoples at large were not considered human and therefore should not be able to use writs of habeas corpus to defend themselves in court. Standing Bear's attorneys argued that their clients had cut ties with the Ponca tribe in Oklahoma, had made their intentions known to the Indian agent, that their return to Nebraska was legal and they had not broken any laws. Judge Dundy found for Standing Bear and the group of thirty was to be released. Following the trial, Standing Bear's group was not immediately allowed to return to their homelands as the land had been given to the Lakota nor could they return to the Omaha Reservation for fear of further arrest. 

A report published on the trial and the Ponca ordeal indicates that there were "eight men, seven women, and eleven children" among the band that accompanied Standing Bear in this petition.

Summary of Proceedings:
Petitioner, George Gumm, stated that he was unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Douglas County Sheriff F. J. McShane. On 8 May 1916, a complaint was filed against Gumm, charging him with Vagrancy. Gumm claimed that the Police Magistrate did not have jurisdiction to try and sentence him The complaint filed by City Prosecutor T. J. McGuire referenced “Dope” and “Opium” and the Vagrant Complaint which lists Rick & Pszauowski (first names not listed) as Witnesses for the State has a note which says “Peddling Dope.” Judge Willis G. Sears ordered that the writ be issued, returnable on 24 June 1916. An Amended Petition was filed on 28 June 1916. This petition stated that the aforementioned conviction was obtained without a trial by jury and was therefore void. This petition also stated that on 3 June 1916, a pardon was issued by the Mayor of Omaha, “remitting the penalty and costs imposed upon him by said Police Magistrate, and ordering his release from custody.” Daniel Horrigan, Gumm’s attorney, stated that this petition was presented to Sheriff McShane but McShane refused to release Gumm from custody. Thus, this amended petition asked for a Writ of Habeas Corpus to be issued such that McShane abides by the Mayor’s pardon. The outcome of this amended petition is not noted. 

Newspaper accounts cite a Maud Gumm associated with "peddling dope" earlier in 1916.

Summary of Proceedings: Ichitara Matsutsuyu entered the United States from Japan in 1906. On June 13, 1917, Matsutsuyu was arrested on a warrant from the Secretary of Labor alleging that had become a public charge. On August 27, 1919, a hearing was held on McNeil Island in which the petitioner charges that no questions were asked about the nature of his alleged indigence and an additional charge of smuggling Japanese boys from Mexico was added. On December 2, 1919 a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed and an addendum was added on December 12, 1919. On December 18, 1919, Judge Neterer issued an opinion stating that a fair trial was given on the charge of smuggling Japanese boys. An April 12, 1920, record indicates that the writ was denied, but the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 11, 1919, Grafton W. Coffin file petition for habeas against the chief of police, Marshall Eberstein, and chief of detectives, John Dunn, after a complaint for larceny by bailee had been made on March 4 and a warrant issued March 7. Coffin argued that he had been in the state of Iowa working for the Nelson-Zarp Co. when the offense occurred, the he was unaware of property missing, and had left Iowa for Kansas City, Missouri, before being brought to Omaha on March 9. In addition, Coffin argued that he had not been provided council in his proceedings and that he had not received demand for the missing property. A writ was issued but the cause was dismissed upon motion by Coffin, the relator.

Iwamatsu was ordered for arrest and deportation on the basis that he violated Section 11 of the Immigrated Act of 1917. Summary of Proceedings: In March 24, James T. English petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of his client Stanley Nielson on the basis Nielson was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty. Three days prior, Nielson was charged and found guilty of drunkenness and carrying concealed weapons and subsequently sentenced to sixty days in County Jail. The petition alleges that Nebraska State Statutes, Section 9829, outlines that the offense of carrying a concealed weapon was a felony providing for imprisonment in the penitentiary. The petition further alleged inferior courts had no jurisdiction to sentence or imprison for such an offense, and the sentence of sixty days was illegal. The outcome of the petition and the fate of English is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 30, 1913, W. J. Harvey and his lawyer filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, stating that J. Howard Shattuck, sheriff of Kitsap County, was illegally detaining him. They claimed no valid warrant or charge existed against Harvey. Harvey also mentioned that he believed he would soon be removed from the court’s jurisdiction. Shattuck produced a hand written warrant on the same pages as his return, which alleged that Justice W. B. Crook of California ordered Frank Harvey’s arrest on the charge of grand larceny. It is unclear if Frank is another name of W. J. Harvey’s, or if it is someone different entirely. The fate of Harvey and the outcome of this case are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 15, 1922, J. H. Walker filed for habeas on behalf of Luis Digilo, against Chief of Detectives, Charles Van Duesen, Chief of Police, Michael Dempsey, and City Commissioner, Henry Dunn. In the petition, Walker explained that Digilo was being held without warrant under the suspicion of being a fugitive from Justice in the state of Iowa. Walker further argued that Digilo had not been in Iowa at the time of the alleged offense and that the respondents had threatened to kidnap Digilo and bring him outside court jurisdictions. On the return of the writ, the respondents argued to be holding Digilo, since November 9, under the authority of a telegram received from Sheriff of Polk County, Iowa, W. F. Robb. A writ was issued but the case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924.

Summary of Proceedings:
Moy Wah, a resident and business owner in Portland, departed to Hong Kong in 1892 on business and to visit relatives. Prior to departure, Moy Wah appeared before a notary and received a signed certificate as proof of residence and his business to allow for re-entry. 
Nearly a year later, upon return, Moy Wah was denied entry by a deputy collector. The deputy collector confiscated the certificate and refused to return it. Moy Wah was informed he had to board a steamship along with 200 other Chinese passengers to return to Hong Kong. Moy Wah's application for a writ of habeas corpus was granted by the Superior Court of Pierce County and he was ordered deported by the U.S. Commissioner. 
An appeal was taken questioning the jurisdiction of the U.S. Commissioner.  External research shows that one of the witnesses for the government, Charles Moy, testified that he was member of the firm that Moy Wah claimed to be partner in, but knew nothing of Moy Wah. Originally, Moy Wah's petition was denied and he was placed in the custody of U. S. Marshall, J. C. Drake. Moy Wah's attorney gathered multiple affidavits from business partners and those personally acquainted with Ni to establish proof of his residence. The Circuit Court issued a writ of habeas corpus to stop the deportation, yet the result of the proceedings are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: William Chapman petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of his wife, Mildred Chapman, on October 13th, 1922. He alleged that his wife was not of sound mind and that her sister, Ruth Podrawzek, was unduly influencing her. Ruth allegedly convinced Mildred to file for divorce from her husband. The petition was approved and a hearing was ordered; however, the events of the hearing are unknown. The appearance docket indicated the case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21st, 1924.

Summary of Proceedings: Max Cohen, the petitioner and bound party, was convicted of suborning, trying to bribe, Esther Woods in a case against Jake Gronish, her husband, for violation of the White Slave Act on May 7th of 1912. Gronish was arrested for this due to his alleged transport of Woods from Ohio to Oregon for the purpose of prostitution, and as attorney in that case for Woods, Cohen had her testify falsely before the court in an effort to protect Gronish. Cohen stated in his defense that Oregon Law Section 1535, C. 21 provides that "neither husband nor wife, in such cases, shall be compelled or allowed to testify in each case unless by consent of both of them" unless the case is related to personal violence.

Summary of Proceedings: Leong Jang Get, Leong Fook Chee, Leong Shar Jung, Chin Wang Gin, and Leong Fook Lung were confined by T. J. Black in the steamship named Haytian Republic for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. A petition for writ of Habeas Corpus was filed by Twin Wo Charley. Writ of habeas corpus was granted to Leong Fook Hing, Leong Jang Get, and Leong Fook Chee, and they were ordered to be released. Chin Wang Sin and Leong Shar Gung were denied writ of Habeas Corpus and were remanded. The case file includes testimonies from bound parties and a witness.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 18, 1884, Daniel Ainsworth petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. In September, Ainsworth had been accused of fraud and Grand Larceny, and was convicted of Grand Larceny. Records show that he was employed at Spokane Country Bank and gave bills of up-charge and exchange to W. H. Whitney, costing Whitney hundreds of dollars. Ainsworth and J. S. Sanford allegedly tried to cash these checks at the Seaboard Bank of New York. In his petition, Ainsworth claimed that he did not knowingly defraud Whitney, and that there was no testimony presented at his trial. He also argued that the complainant, Hoyt, had complained under false pretenses. Furthermore, Ainsworth alleged that the complaint did not indicate that he had ever possessed Whitney’s money. Judge Wingard allowed the writ, and Ainsworth was moved from Spokane County Jail to Walla Walla County jail because there were concerns for his safety. Ainsworth, however, failed to show up to the trial. Telegrams in this case file state that Ainsworth had malaria, was disabled, and could not leave his room, though it remains unclear if that is the reason for his absence from court. Judge Wingard ordered the forfeit of Ainsworth’s bail. The outcome of this case and Ainsworth’s fate are unknown, but it is likely that the writ was ultimately denied due to his failure to appear in court.

Brandon stated that the charge brought against him was illegal and oppressive.  After the hearing, Fred Brandon was found guilty of adultery and was jailed by the Sheriff John H. McGraw.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 4th, 1922, Gladys Jackson petitioned the court for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Paul Epperson. The nature of the relationship between Gladys and Paul is unknown. Gladys alleged that Paul was being unlawfully detained because he was not being held by virtue of any warrant, commitment, mittimus, or court order. She also claimed that he was held for more than seventy-two hours without the filing of any complaint or information against him. She named Michael Dempsey as the respondent. The judge issued the petition. Michael Dempsey filed a return, citing that he detained Paul Epperson at the request of Governor Samuel McKelvie, the governor of Nebraska. McKelvie issued a warrant for Paul's arrest on behalf of the governor of Illinois, Len Small. Paul Epperson was charged with burglary in Illinois and considered to be a fugitive from justice. On March 6th, the writ was denied and Paul remained in the custody of Michael Dempsey. He presumably returned to Illinois.

Summary of Proceedings:
Based on newspaper coverage, Attorney John Wiley and his associates Scott and Hale set out to challenge the constitutionality of the Police Court of Seattle, and consequently the rulings of Judge Claudius M. Rivers. Originally, they tried to use the case of James Shay (see: "In the Matter of the application of James Shay for a Writ of Habeas Corpus). Following the release of James Shay from custody on October 16th 1890,  Wiley needed a new case to use to challenge the Police Court. 
On October 17th, 1890, Wiley found John Reilley. That day, Reilly had been arrested for and found guilty of drunkenness. Judge Claudius M. Rivers ordered that Reilly be placed in the custody of Chief of Police George C. Monroe. Wiley and Reilly filed a petition for a writ habeas corpus. In Reilly's petition, just as in Shay's case, John Wiley claimed that the Police Court was unconstitutional. The City of Seattle had recently created and given jurisdiction to the Police Court via a charter. Because Wiley believed the Court and charter were unconstitutional, he alleged that Judge Rivers did not have the jurisdiction to charge Reilly with drunkenness, nor to have him detained. The petition was allowed by Judge Thomas J. Humes, and was heard in his court. 
Newspaper coverage of this case indicates that City Attorney Lyon was the attorney for the respondent, and argued that the court was constitutional and subsequently Reilly was not being illegally detained. The newspapers indicate that Judge Humes ruled in favor of Lyon and Monroe, and Reilly remained in custody. 
It is worth noting, the case "In the matter of the application of Harry Brooks for a Writ of Habeas Corpus", in February 1890, is another case that challenged the constitutionality of the Police Court, and subsequently of Judge Rivers.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 17, 1913, A. H. Hubbard and his lawyers petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. In the petition, they alleged that Claude G. Bannick, chief of police, was holding Hubbard without a proper warrant. Bannick was holding Hubbard on a telegram from Alberta Canada that stated Hubbard had been charged with “obtaining money under false pretenses”, a charge that Hubbard denied and also stated was not an extraditable offense. Charles Sullivan, acting chief of police while Bannick was out of town, was served the writ. Hubbard paid bail, and Judge Ronald released him with the stipulation that he had to return to court for his hearing. The outcome of the petition is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Pearl Dils had taken her son, Willard Dils, to Boyd County, Nebraska while in the processing of divorcing her husband, James Dils. James petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Willard, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the court ordered that James and Pearl share custody of Willard while their divorce was pending. Each was to have custody of Willard for one week at a time, dropping the boy off at the office of James' attorney, E. E. Spencer, on Saturday afternoons. Neither was to remove Willard from Lancaster County nor take him to their relatives' homes without permission of the other. Once this was decided, James withdrew his petition.

Reid held McDonald under the authority of immigration officials, including A. F. Richardson and the Secretary of Labor, for advocating the teaching of the unlawful destruction of property. Rudkin dismissed the writ because the Department of Labor issued a warrant for McDonald’s arrest.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 1, 1894, Ung Coey filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Gunne Sun Jew, Ung You, Gunne Sin Chuck, Gunne Sin, and Young Hin Yee. Ung Coey claimed they were being illegally detained on the Steamship Signal by Captain Pendergast. Ung Coey further claimed that they were Chinese merchants who were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Bellinger partially agreed and granted the writ for Gunne Sin and Young Hin Wee. The fate of Gunne Sin Chuck, Gunne Sun Jew, and Ung You is unknown. Included in the case files is signed affidavits, and Special Prosecutor John Catlin’s reports.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 17, 1919, Judge King Dykeman presided over a petition about the welfare of a minor, Lowell Raddue. In this case, Dykeman ruled that Lowell is a dependent child of the state and ordered that he be placed in the custody of the Washington State Training School in Chehalis, Washington until he was twenty-one years old. During the trial, Lowell was in the custody of the matron of the Juvenile Detention Home in Seattle, Francette P. Maring. Lowell’s mother, May Raddue, filed a writ of habeas corpus against Maring on February 21 arguing that the detention of her son was illegal. In her petition, May noted that Section 4382 of the 1915 Remington Code stated that only children between the ages of six and sixteen. She argues that the King County Juvenile Court had no jurisdiction to rule against her son because he was seventeen years old. In her return to the writ, Maring notes that before having May’s writ of habeas corpus delivered to her, the custody of Lowell was transferred over the Washington State Training School. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party are not included in this case.

Summary of Proceedings:
Nora Dixson filed this petition on 6 May 1912. The petition stated that David Moore was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by John Briggs (Chief of Police), James Sheehan (Chief of Detectives), Joseph Clark (Jailor for South Omaha), and William Corrigan (Jailor for South Omaha). The petition stated that Moore had been confined in the jail without an order of commitment or other process authorizing such detention, no complaint had been filed against him charging him of a crime, and that the arrest had been made without warrant or other process. Judge Willis G. Sears ordered that the writ be allowed. 
Chief of Police John Briggs and Chief of Detectives James Sheehan filed a return which stated that on 19 April 1912 Martha Widdis, a teacher in the Lincoln School, was on her way home carrying a handbag containing a small sum of money and a watch. At 22nd and I streets, she was “accosted by a colored man who snatched her handbag and ran south through the alley.” The man was seen entering the alley by John Walliker, who claims that the party he saw is the defendant and that he was wearing a white hat, but Miss Widdis stated with equal certainty that the man who snatched her purse was wearing a black hat. Mrs. Anna Peterson also saw the man running through the alley and stated that he “had the appearance” of Moore, but could not positively identify him. William Sires saw the man further on in the alley, Sires stated that he saw him take the contents from the handbag and then throw the bag into a small ravine. Like Mrs. Peterson, Mr. Sires stated that he “had the appearance” of Moore but also could not identify him positively. John Wade saw him coming out of the ravine after throwing away the handbag, but also could not identify him. Someone by the surname Altman stated that he had seen Moore on 18 April 1912 in the vicinity of 22nd and I streets. Detective Sheehan investigated the case and on 1 May 1912, was informed that David Moore had been seen on the afternoon of 19 April 1912 taking a watch, fitting the description of the one stolen from Miss Widdis, from his pocket. After this, Moore was placed in custody and had been retained in the city jail at South Omaha since that time. No complaint had been filed because the South Omaha Police thought the evidence was not sufficiently conclusive as to Moore’s identity  and guilt. He was being held “as a suspicious character awaiting further development in the case.”
On 9 May 1912, Judge A. L. Sutton ordered that Moore be given a proper trial within three days or be discharged from custody.
