Summary of Proceedings: H. E. Spence petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Morris Rabinvich. Spence alleged that Rabinvich was being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail by Chief of Police Louis M. Lang. Rabinvich was charged with being a fugitive from justice fleeing from San Francisco, CA. Spence denied this, claiming Rabinvich was enlisted in the United States Army in San Francisco and ordered to be stationed at Fort Lawton, WA. Lang returned with an extradition warrant ordering Rabinvich’s arrest. The warrant was dated after Spence’s petition was filed. The case file does not reveal an outcome, nor the fate of Rabinvich.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 28, 1919, B. E. Atherton filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that Marshall Eberstein unlawfully deprived him of his liberty. He stated that the police held him in the Omaha City Jail for a complaint filed against him in Minneapolis, Minnesota, charging him with wife and child abandonment in the state. However, he claimed that he had been a resident of Omaha for the past twelve years. Additionally, on the contrary, his wife abandoned him in Omaha about three years ago. The same day, the judge accepted the petition and filed a writ of habeas corpus. The writ was granted the next. However, judge Willis G. Sears overruled the decision in April, dismissing the writ for “wants of prosecution at relator’s costs.” He found that Atherton did, in fact, have a wife and child in Minnesota, and ordered him taken back to Minneapolis at once.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 19, 1916, Mary Seung was arrested by Robert T. Hodge and placed in the King County Jail after being declared an "insane person." Mary Seung was declared insane by J. T. Ronald after a complaint was filed by a person named Jane M. Skiff. In her petition for habeas corpus, Mary Seung claims that since she did not speak or understand English she was unable to offer a defense to the charges made against her. She also states that she believed that her husband, John Seung, was behind the initial complaint because she had discussed obtaining a divorce from him. She believed that he wanted to have her declared legally insane so she could be deported back to China. Newspaper reports of the trial noted that John and Mary originally married in China over thirty years before this trial. While Mary only moved to the United States in 1913, the newspapers highlighted that John moved to the United States decades ago without Mary. During his time in the United States, John started a canning company and was reported to have four children with a two different women. One of the children that John had in the United States years before Mary arrived acted as the interpreter for her initial trial that declared her insane. While the conclusion to the petition is not included in the case file, the Seattle Star reported that the J. T. Ronald approved the writ of habeas corpus and ordered that a new psychological evaluation be taken with a new interpreter. Following this new evaluation, Mary Seung was declared sane and released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
On December 21st, 1884, Sterling P. White (alias Bud White), shot Amos Light Bearden. Bearden died two days later from the gunshot wound. On December 25th of the same year, White was found guilty of killing Bearden by a Coroner's Jury. White filed a petition of habeas corpus on February 2nd, 1885, claiming that he was being unlawfully held because he had never committed a crime, he was never charged with a crime, he was never given a fixed bail, that he was wounded and being in jail was dangerous to his health, and that J. W. Carpenter had unlawfully acted as Justice of the Peace, prosecuting attorney and deputy sheriff in his case. In April of 1885, White was convicted of manslaughter, and sentenced to two years hard labor in a penitentiary by Judge George Turner. Additionally, his writ of habeas corpus was dismissed. 

In October of the same year, a second habeas corpus petition was filed on White's behalf, but the purpose of that petition was to allow him as a witness in a different court case. (See: Writ of Habeas Corpus for Sterling P. White, an Important Witness)

Summary of Proceedings:
Blanche A. Bradley was the 11 year old daughter of petitioner, Jacob S. Bradley. Jacob claims that Blanche is being unlawfully deprived of her liberty by Arah Dickey. Arah and Jacob were previously married, they were divorced while living in Louisville, KY and Arah now lived in Omaha, NE. She claimed to be married to a man with the last name Dickey, but the petitioner states that the pair is not actually married. The pair operated a saloon with furnished rooms available for rent. Arah and Blanche resided in one of the rooms. The place is “of bad reputation” and is “an improper and dangerous place for any child.” Jacob is asking for Arah to summoned to show cause for her detention of Blanche and hopes that Blanche may be discharged from the unlawful detention. 
Jacob S. Bradley and his attorney, Charles V. Miles, presented the petition on 8 July 1899 to Judge Jacob Fawcett. Judge Fawcett ordered that the writ be allowed. Sheriff John W. McDonald recognized the receipt of the writ and stated that he would appear in court, bringing along Arah Dickey and Blanche Bradley. John D. Ware, Arah’s attorney, filed their motions on 10 July 1899. They asked that the Court set aside the order for the following reasons; (1) the petition was insufficient in law to justify the court in making the order, (2) the petition was insufficient in manner and form to confer jurisdiction upon the court to make the order, (3) the petition does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, and (4) the petition does not state facts in regard to the alleged unlawful imprisonment, but states conclusions of law. They also asserted that Arah was cganted custody in their divorce proceedings. Jacob and his attorney, Charles, submitted a response on 10 July 1899 stating that they concede that custody was awarded to Arah but that simple fact does not serve as a defense to the petition which is specific to Arah and Blanche’s current living situation.
On 10 July 1899, the parties appeared in court where Judge Baker concluded that it would be in the best interests of the child that she be withdrawn from Arah’s custody. Arah apparently wept when it was announced that her daughter would be taken away from her. Costs of the proceedings were taxed to the county.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 6, 1892, G. W. Crowell was convicted of being a disorderly person for distributing business cards that falsely indicated he was a representative of the government land office.   Crowell petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on April 9, 1892. In his petition, he argued that Ordinance No. 1818 of the City of Seattle, which defined who was a disorderly person, was null and void. This is because it conflicted with the Washington State laws for being a disorderly person.  He also stated that he did not fit the definition of being a disorderly person according to the ordinance.  Judge T.J. Humes ordered for Crowell to appear before the court, but the outcomes of Crowell’s petition and case are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
M. J. Costello applied for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of James E. Traynor on December 1, 1919.

Authorities arrested Traynor at 6:00 PM on November 28, 1919 and held him in the King County Jail for federal investigation. According to Costello, federal authorities declared that they no longer required Traynor. Once released, Traynor was rearrested on November 28, 1919 for vagrancy. Costello paid a two hundred and fifty dollar bail to Justice Brinker for the release of Traynor. After this second release, Traynor was rearrested and held in Seattle City Jail. While Judge A. W. Frater ordered a writ for Traynor on December 1, 1919, the fate of Traynor is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Although the original petition for a writ of habeas corpus is missing in the case file, based on the docket, Carol Williams filed a petition against Alta Berger on December 9, 1919. Judge George A. Day allowed this to issue. However, included in the case file was Berger's return to writ. Her return to writ states that, on December 8, 1919, the courts prosecuted Williams on a charge of vagrancy and prostitution. She was found guilty and sentenced to thirty days in county jail. Berger claimed that she managed the Detention Hospital and that, by an Omaha ordinance, certain venereal diseases, such as "syphilis, gonorrhea, and chancroid" were "declared to be contagious, infectious, communicable and a menace to public health." She claimed that the law declared that it was unlawful for any person with such disease(s) to knowingly expose other people and required the Health Commissioner and their deputies and assistants to examine all persons convicted in a court for prosecution for the diseases. If said person was said to have a venereal disease, the person must be detained at the hospital. They had examined Williams, and her result was positive for venereal disease, so they committed her to the Girls' Detention Home for examination and treatment. On December 13, 1919, Williams requested a continuance (it is unclear why), and the judge ordered a five-day continuance. However, on December 18, 1919, the judge dismissed the proceeding because Williams failed to appear by counsel or otherwise in court.

In his petition, Ronneburg charged that he had been arrested on September 30 without warrant or complaint and, had since, not been brought to appear in any court. Newspaper coverage indicates Ronneburg was found with an unclaimed diamond in his possession, suggesting theft was the charge.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 20, 1903, a subpoena was served upon Branch directing him to appear before Calvin C. Valentine, a notary public in Douglas county. Branch was the secretary for the Business Men’s Association and was subpoenaed to provide insight into the case of William Halsted, et al. vs. the Omaha Waiters Union. He appeared but he did not produce the books and papers called in for the subpoena because he alleged they were taken from his possession by T. J. Mahoney (attorney for the Business Men’s Association) to investigate for the trial that Branch was subpoenaed for. Valentine issued a mittimus for his arrest and Branch petitioned that he was unlawfully detained because the notary public Valentine had no authority to arrest him for such a reason. Branch was later discharged from prison.

Summary of Proceedings: James O’Bryan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. O’Bryan claimed Warren was detaining him at the Seattle City Jail with no color of authority or right. Warren replied that O’Bryan was an unnaturalized alien found teaching and advocating for the principles of anarchy, which Warren claimed was an arrestable offense during wartime. Newspaper records also indicated that O’Bryan was a member of the I.W.W. Warren alleged he transferred O’Bryan into the custody of the Department of Labor for deportation. The case outcome and fate of O’Bryan are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 10, 1901 Cicero Newell petitioned the superior court of King County claiming that the children Patrick Quinn, Leo Quinn, and Mary Ann Quinn (ages ten, eight, and five respectively) be removed from the custody of their parents Daniel Quinn and May Quinn for reasons of severe child abuse and neglect. Both Daniel and May were described as being “habitual drunkards” with May at the time of the petition being imprisoned for some unknown crime. On November 11, 1901 an order was issued by the judge Boyd J. Tallman for the Sheriff of King County to seize the children and deliver to Daniel and May to present themselves in court on Friday, November 1, 1901 to argue why they should retain custody of the children. Ultimatley the custody of the children would be awarded to the County, and placed in the care of Cicero Newell at the Boys' and Girls' Aid Society that he operated with his wife.

Summary of Proceedings: In April 1920, H.J. Finch petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully detained of his liberty by Michael L. Clark, and E,J. West, Sheriffs of Douglas County, Nebraska, and Osceola, Iowa, respectively. Finch was indicted by a grand jury for cheating by fraud and being a fugitive of justice from Iowa. Finch represented he was a member of the commission firm, Jackson-Signall, and engaged in an agreement with S.R. Bell for the purchase of 400 sheep. Upon receiving the sheep, Finch alleged they were not as represented and rejected the sale. The petitioner asserted that Bell agreed Finch would take the sheep into his possession, sell them for what he could and remit the best possible price to Bell. The grand jury found that the notion Finch was a member of Jackson-Signall was untrue, and Finch attempted to defraud Bell. Judge A.C. Troup denied the writ and ruled Finch was confined in a legal manner be re-committed to custody. Attorneys for the petitioner motioned for a new trial on the grounds the judgment was contrary to evidence and law. On appeal to the Nebraska Supreme Court, the judgment was affirmed.

Summary of Proceedings: Michel Koseris, the petitioner, is a drafted soldier in training at Camp Lewis seeking to be discharged by writ of Habeas Corpus. He filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus after being drafted into the army despite having a dependent wife who is unable to work and needs extensive care due to her health conditions. Koseris states that he made an application to his Local Board of the County of Bannock, State of Idaho, for his right to exemption or discharge but was denied. Koseris states that if he is not discharged, his wife will become a public charge and that in his county, all married men with a dependent wife or children were exempted except him. According to the case file, after the matter was argued, "the demurrer was sustained by the court, and the rule to show cause was discharged to which the petitioner excepted and his exceptions were allowed," and so it is indicated that Koseris remained a soldier.

Summary of Proceedings:
French alien Edmund Rusla filed for a writ of habeas corpus on November 15, 1922. Immigration inspector Luther Weedin held Rusla in King County Jail for violating the Immigration Act of 1917. The Republic of France refused “to receive or issue a passport for petitioner.” Judge Jeremiah Neterer allowed Rusla’s writ after immigration officials were unable to deport him. Rusla was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Wong Fat and Wong Fong are merchants working at the firm Kwong Chung Lung located at 89 Second Street. All the petitioners traveled together on the Steamship Haytian Republic and were refused entry by the Collector of Customs T. J. Black. The case file includes a trial transcript for Wong Fong, providing information on the relationship between some of the petitioners. However, the fate of Louis Ye Hong, Law Bock, Wong Ah Fi, Louis Yee Ling and Wap So Jau is unknown as they are not explicitly released in the decision, unlike the other three petitioners. Wong Fat and Louis Chin were released with granted petitions on July 20th, 1893. Wong Fong was released with a granted petition on July 27th, 1893.

Summary of Proceedings: Howard L. Rucker was arrested because of a warrant issued by the governor of Iowa, Albert B. Cummins. This was ordered because Rucker was charged with the crime of cheating by false pretenses as a fugitive from justice in Iowa. John H. Mickey, the governor of Nebraska, orders his arrest. Rucker was charged with cheating because he told J. W. Martin and P. P. Louck that a town named Morris had been laid out in the territory of Oklahoma and that it was in a flourishing condition. He told them there was a store, other buildings were in construction, the railway system had a line close to town and that the railroad into town was nearly completed. The two men purchased ten lots and later found out that all statements were false. This case stretched through three more years before “Nolle” was entered by order of the court.

Summary of Proceedings: Lewis Johnson, a black man, was arrested in Washington afterd being accused of stealing $1880 dollars from John Pritchard in a hotel in Vancouver, Canada while Pritchard was intoxicated. Witnesses Tate, Russel, and Garnett attest that Johnson had a lot of money with him around the time Pritchard's money was taken, around June 4th or 5th of 1915. While Kennedy declared cause for extradition so Johnson could be tried in Canada, Johnson petitioned for writ of habeas corpus, arguing the statements against him to be untrue and without probable cause or legal evidence. The outcome of this case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Tom Weber was an immigrant from Austria, having arrived in the United States in 1912. In 1916 Weber joined the IWW, a union organization. On January 4th, 1918, Tom Weber was arrested under a warrant issued by the U.S. Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson, and was held for multiple months while his case was pending. The charges alleged were that he was an alien, he advocated for and taught the unlawful destruction of property, and that upon entering the country he was a likely public charge. On December 2nd, 1918, a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed stating among other things that he did not know English and thus did not read IWW literature, was never a beggar, did not want to destroy property, and that a transcript of his hearing was never given to him. The fate of the petition and the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Blanche Masse Pouliot, a Canadian immigrant, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against A. F. Richardson, an Immigrant Inspector and alleged that she was being illegally held at the Spokane County Jail. She claimed she had been served a warrant for her deportation from the United States issued by the U.S. Department of Commerce and Labor for entering the country with the intention to practice prostitution. Pouliot admitted that she had been a prostitute, but did not enter the country with the intention to practice prostitution and had, in fact, quit the profession to become an honorable wife to Adelard Pouliot. Richardson submitted several testimonies revealing that Blanche Pouliot was practicing prostitution in Washington state and that Adelard Pouliot was assisting her with building a house of prostitution in Ione, WA. Adelard Pouliot petitioned separately for a writ of habeas corpus, but as the warrants for arrest and deportation listed both him and Blanche Pouliot, his case was merged with this one. The court determined that the Immigration Act of 1907 denied immigration to prostitutes and those involved in managing houses of prostitution. As such, the court ruled that the writs of both Blanche and Adelard Pouliot were denied, and both were to be deported to Canada.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 24th, 1912, George Cornwall petitioned for his freedom with the help of his attorney, O. E. Sauter. Sauter and Cornwall argued that when he was sentenced on a charge of attempted rape in 1907, his 5-20 year sentence had no legal jurisdiction. Upon review, Judge King Dykeman of the King County Superior Court granted the writ. The respondent, Charles F. Reed, the Warden of the State Penitentiary, with the help of his attorneys Caldwell and Ketteran, argued in response that Cornwall and Sauter’s argument had no legal jurisdiction itself. At some point, the Supreme Court of Washington got involved, in which Judge Crow ruled in favor of Cornwall and Sauter, affirming Dykeman’s decision to grant the writ. Therefore, the date in court was set for August 31st in Dykeman’s courtroom, but the outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Louise Murphy, Bertha Graves, Bessie Hanson, Agnes McDonald, Dot Kelly, Billie Anderson, and J. B. Lloyd filed a petition of writ of habeas corpus arguing that they were illegally confined and restrained of their liberty in the Seattle City Jail. The petition states that the women were arrested several weeks prior likely during the vice raids happening across Seattle at this time. They were then being quarantined in the City Jail for an alleged infectious and contagious disease which each petitioner denied having. The petition further states while the women were originally arrested on a complaint of “Being a Disorderly Person,” they had not been formally charged with any crime nor have they been allowed to have a hearing for their charges. Furthermore, every petitioner in the case states that they have been denied the possibility of bail. Louise Murphy makes an additional claim in the petition arguing that she had been recently engaged and her detention is causing her to be restrained of her “right of engaging in Holy wedlock with her fiancee.” Judge Kenneth Mackintosh agreed to hear the women’s case. The original respondent of the case was the Chief of Police Joel Warren, however, in his return to the writ, Warren claims that the women were no longer in his jurisdiction by the time he received the petition. He states that Dot Kelly had been released because she did not have signs of having an infectious disease and that Louise Murphy was granted bail by the police court. Warren notes that Bertha Graves, Bessie Hanson, Agnes McDonald, and J. B. Lloyd were transferred to the jurisdiction of J. S. McBride, the Seattle Health Commission and were staying at the city hospital. Billie Anderson disappears from the file following this point. It is unknown if she was released with Dot Kelly and Louise Murphy or not. 

Following Warren’s return, the petition was adjusted to be directed at J. S. McBride and the judge overseeing the petition was changed to A. W. Frater. In his return to the petition, McBride argued that Bertha Graves, Bessie Hanson, Agnes McDonald, and J. B. Lloyd were found to have syphilis and were being detained and treated at the city hospital. McBride argues that several city ordinances allowed him to detain these women and forcibly treat them of their disease. The case file does not include any documentation past McBride’s return so the outcome of the petition is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 29, 1921, police officers arrived at the home of Mabel McKillip and her husband, and compelled her to accompany them to the jail where she was forcibly imprisoned. Charges for vagrancy and prostitution were brought against her, and on September 30th, McKillip was fined $15.00 and costs for vagrancy. McKillip paid this amount and was not released, but instead held in the Detention Home. McKillip subsequently filed a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus, arguing that the charge of vagrancy does not authorize a commitment to the Detention Home. On January 21, 1924, the petition for a Writ was dismissed for want of prosecution.

Summary of Proceedings:
Attorney John E. Costello filed the petition on behalf of his client, Jimmy Jardini (aka Jimmy Russell), claiming he was being held unlawfully. Jardini was confined, beginning December 1, 1888, to await a Grand Jury to be impaneled on February 1, 1889 to indict him for the crime of attempt to commit rape. It is not known why he was still in jail a month later, and it is not known whether he was indicted (presumably he was not.) 
In an unusual ruling, Judge Thomas Burke, rather than ruling on the petition itself and ordering the jail to produce Jardini, ruled (on the same day in fact) that the writ be granted.

Summary of Proceedings:
Robin and Polly Holmes, a married slave couple, moved from Missouri to the territory of Oregon (a free territory) with their owner, Nathaniel Ford, in 1844. Ford promised that if the couple helped him move and set up a new home, he would free them and their children. In 1850, the Holmes and Ford came to an agreement that Robin, Polly, and their newly born child would be set free, while the rest of the Holmes children would remain with Ford until they came of age. Robin filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his three children, Mary Jane (Jenny), Roxanna, and James, on April 16th, 1852. Over a year later, the case reached the Oregon Supreme Court in July of 1853. Chief Justice George A. Williams ruled in favor of the Holmes, and the children were ordered to be released. This decision made it clear that slavery was unlawful in the Oregon territory. 
Roxanna and James returned to their parents, who moved to Marion County, OR and opened a plant nursery. However, Jenny remained with Ford, likely to earn funds to support the rest of her family. Four years later, Jenny left Ford to marry Ruben Shipley, a freed slave. Despite the Supreme Case ruling that came from this habeas corpus case, Ford demanded Ruben pay $700 for Jenny's freedom, which he did. The two got married, moved to Corvallis, Oregon, and had six kids.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Lewis filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on grounds that a bond was never accepted by Police Chief Donahue to prevent his release from custody. Lewis had been arrested on the complain of a dissatisfied customer on the charge of "obstructing the street." Since he was denied the option of paying a bond for his release, Lewis claimed that a writ of habeas should be issued and he should be discharged from unlawful imprisonment. Eventually, the writ was dismissed due to his lack of ability to pay costs by Joseph Lewis.

Summary of Proceedings:
Gladys French filed for habeas corpus through her lawyer, claiming she was held without a charge or bail. The similarities in her case file, including relevant dates and outcome, indicate that she was jailed during Seattle vice raids of mid-November 1917. 

In response to the writ, Police Chief Charles Beckingham issued  a warrant for her arrest in the Seattle Police Court based on her violation of city municipal health ordinance No. 32444. 

According to newspaper coverage, Gladis was later detained in a “women’s internment station” and unsuccessfully attempted to escape on December 26, 1917.

Summary of Proceedings: Malinda, a free person of color, is suing Robert Wilburn for trespassing, assault and battery, and false imprisonment with the use of force and arms. Wilburn allegedly beat, bruised and mistreated Malinda and her child Nelly while she was enslaved by him. He kept her without any probable cause. Wilburn moved across state lines and Malinda is arguing that this should constitute her freedom. She is attempting to sue as a poor person via her friend Beriah Cleland for the amount of $500. The court found that Wilburn was only passing through Illinois and had no intention of residing there with Malinda, denying her status as a free woman and that Nelly may follow her mothers status.

Summary of Proceedings: James Stephenson filed a complaint that charged Ben Shear of the offense of infamous crime against nature with a beast. Stevenson alleged that he had “certain carnal and venereal intercourse” with a mare. After the preliminary examination, Shear said that there was no charge or offense against the laws of Nebraska against him. He also said there was no evidence against him that showed that there was probably cause to believe he had committed any offense. Bail was set for Shear at fifteen hundred dollars. The last information in the files say that the hearing was continued and the outcome of Shear’s petition is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Walter Versteeg claimed that he was deprived of his liberty by Martin J. White and H. P. Haze in the city jail in Omaha. He had been detained in the jail but there was no complaint against him whatsoever. Judge Baker affirmed an original writ of Habeas Corpus, ordering that he be discharged from being restrained of his personal liberty. The state recognized that they had received copies of the writ and that they had personally delivered the writ to H. P. Haze. The District Court Judge, W. W. Slabaugh, under the Clerk Albyn L. Frank and the Deputy A. Steere, Jr., ordered that White and Haze bring both Versteeg and documentation of their cause for his detention to court on 29 September 1898. According to the Appearance Docket, the writ was returned on 7 October 1898, signed by John W. McDonald (Sheriff).

Summary of Proceedings: In October of 1921 Harry Dragoun petitioned for and was given an order allowing for a writ of Habeas Corpus having claimed he was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by sheriff Micheal L. Clark after being arrested for a second time. It was June 1921 when Dragoun was arrested and charged with reckless driving of an automobile upon which he was tried for and discharged. Then in October of the same year, Dragoun was arrested again and charged with seriously maiming and disfiguring while exceeding the speed limit. In his petition he argued that the second arrest was based upon the same facts and circumstances that the first arrest was made on and thus was put twice in jeopardy for the same offense contrary to Constitution of the State of Nebraska Article I section12. Sheriff Clark, in his response, presented that he held Dragoun in custody by virtue of a warrant by a police magistrate. It was January 1924 that the writ was dismissed for want of prosecution. The fate of Dragoun is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Petitioner, Morris Yost, filed this Application for a Writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Emma Yost - alias Emma Urlas - stating that she had been arrested and placed into custody of Chief Henry Dunn, Chief Stephan Maloney, and two jailors with real names unknown on 14 December 1912. The application was filed on 28 December 1912. The application stated that Emma had been taken into custody without any order of commitment or other process authorizing the detention. No complaint had been filed against her charging her with the commission of any crime or offense against the laws of the State of Nebraska; thus, the detention was without any legal authority. Judge Sutton dismissed the case on 17 January 1913.

Summary of Proceedings: O. J. Vallecott, relationship to bound party unknown, petitioned on behalf of Benjamin D. Mills claiming that an unidentified John Doe had illegally deprived Mills of his liberty. Arrested on the charge of embezzlement and sentenced to serve time in the state penitentiary, Mills had appealed his case to the NE Supreme Court, who suspended his sentence and allowed him to enter into bail. Vallecott claimed that the order from the Supreme Court supersedes any order that John Doe was acting upon. Judge Holmes granted the petition. Half a year later, the court ordered that the action be dismissed. Fate of bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 13, 1905, Thomas Ball and his attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, stating that Ball was being illegally held by L. C. Smith. They stated that the commitment, issued by Justice Wright, that put him in custody was not issued during a criminal procedure. Furthermore, they asserted that the charge brought against him of “Not Paying a Board Bill and Expense Charges” was not a crime under Washington state laws, and therefore not within the court’s jurisdiction. Judge Morris allowed the petition to be heard in Judge Griffin’s court. Griffins approved the writ and Ball was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Jim Jones was arrested for drunkenness and disturbing the peace on January 26th, 1916. He was ordered to stay in jail for 60 days and pay a $200 fine. The Police Magistrate asked for an extra $3.50 to assure his appeal was submitted. Jim Jones petitioned for Habeas corpus on February 3rd, 1916, due to the extra money demanded. The petition was approved on February 7th, 1916, and appearance in court was ordered. There is no information about the hearing or outcome.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis M. Davenport was the owner and operator of Davenport's Restaurant in Spokane Washington. He was arrested by the Spokane County Sheriff on March 1, 1900 charged with having a quail in his possession which he intended to sell. During this period, Washington had a law which made it illegal to sell any grouse, pheasant, ptarmigan, partridge, sage hen, prairie chicken, or quail in the state. Davenport filed for a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he purchased the quail legally in St. Louis, Missouri and that the law he was arrested over was unconstitutional because it restricted inter-state trade. Judge C. H. Hanford took the case and ruled that the state law was unconstitutional and void due to its restriction of inter-state trade and the Louis Davenport should be discharged from the Spokane County Jail.

Summary of Proceedings: Frederick Jacobsen filed a petition of for a writ of Habeas Corpus on December 29th, 1919, in hope of gaining custody of his daughter, Helen Jacobsen. Helen was, at the time, in the custody of her mother, Florence Jacobsen, and her maternal grandparents, Roy T. and May Earley. Florence Jacobsen had been living in her parents home since she and Frederick Jacobsen divorced. Frederick Jacobsen's petition was specifically against the Earley's, claiming that they were keeping his daughter away from him, even refusing visits. The Judge called for the pair of grandparents to produce young Helen in court to determine whether or not F. Jacobsen's writ would be allowed. The respondents argued that their daughter, Florence Jacobsen, had taken care of and been the sole provider for Helen Jacobsen since her birth, and that the father did not deserve custody. According to the Douglas County Court appearance docket, F. Jacobsen's writ was dismissed on January 6th, 1920, and Helen remained in her mother's and grandparents' custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Archie B. Kelly, the petitioner and bound party, filed a Writ of Habeas Corpus to be released from McNeil Island on the charge of stealing a team of black mares from James Hall. This occurred after Johnny Augustus (sometimes called John Battiste), an indigenous man from the Colville Reservation, paid the team of mares to Kelly due to his debt of $285 on May 20th, 1914. 

Afterward, James Hall, whose position is not clear but is identified as an "Indian Farmer," questioned Kelly on his possession of the houses and insisted they "belonged to the government" and took them from his possession when he was gone. After the theft, Kelly sought advice from lawyers about how to move forward and was advised to "go and get the said horses, but in doing so, not to 'break into' any enclosure" and did that. This led to his arrest for larceny. During the initial trial,l Johnny Agustus testified to Kelly's account, but Mr. Hall did argue that Augustus could not testify due to his status as an indigenous person, though the Writ does explain that Augustus was speaking "good, understandable English" in his testimony. The latter is an argument of Mr. Hall, who also went on to say that his duty is to "reform the Indians and to restore such property as they might dispose of," making Augustus not eligible to do with his property as he pleases to atone for his debt. Augustus was then not present for further proceedings because he died during the time of the trials. In the initial case the US Commissioner dismissed it, the horses were returned to Kelly, and there was no evidence of the government ownership of the horses on June 8, 1915. 

But, on April 14, 1915, Kelly was arrested again for the same crime and was charged with horse stealing before a Federal Grand Jury. In cross-examination, Kelly explained that he did not intend to steal but instead thought the horses were his and did not make any attempt to conceal them. 

Throughout the case, Kelly did not have consistent legal representation; he sought advice from different lawyers over time but did not have consistent representation but Raymond W. Clifford did act as attorney for petitioner at times. Additonally, he pursued appealing the case to the Supreme Court of the United States, where he explained that he was impoverished but believed that he was entitled to redress and discharge through habeas corpus. The case files do not provide an outcome but do indicate that the writ of habeas corpus was issued and Kelly was ordered to be brought before Judge Edward Cushman.

Summary of Proceedings: S. G. Linton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham. Linton alleged he was being illegally held in the Seattle City Jail with no charge against him and was being denied access to his friends or attorneys. The outcome of the case and the fate of Linton are unknown. This is the fourth time Linton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Beckingham. Newspaper coverage indicates Linton's nickname is "Peanuts" and that he runs a rooming house and regularly provides bail for women arrested on charges of being "disorderly."

Summary of Proceedings: Allan Young claimed to be unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Ed Simpson, a constable for Douglas County Nebraska. He was arrested upon a warrant for bastardy, issued by Justice of the Peace, Ed Leeder. According to Young, Careline Peterson made the complaint that she was pregnant with his bastard child and was accordingly arrested on December 29, 1914. However, on that same day they were able to come up with an agreeable and satisfactory settlement to both parties, agreeing to dismiss persecution. She then again, filed another complaint by herself, charging him again with being the father of a bastard child on January 18, 1915 and Young again was arrested by Ed Leeder. Young showed a copy of the agreement that said he was willing to “pay for inlaying expenses, support, and maintenance of said child…[and] for all damages on account for her alleged pregnancy.” The writ was allowed and he was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Allen Shears filed for a writ of habeas corpus on January 20, 1920. King County Sheriff John Stringer held Shears in the King County Jail after Shears was extradited from New York on charges of grand larceny. A New York Grand Jury had indicted Shears in relation to a far-ranging fraud scheme involving mining investments. Accomplices to the scheme operated in Alaska, Oregon, Washington, and New York. 


Judge Jeremiah Neterer dismissed the writ on July 3, 1920.

Summary of Proceedings: Anna Tatum petitioned with a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Glen Hull who was detained in the Omaha City Jail. Glen Hull was arrested on January 19th, 1917, and the petition states there was no reason given for his arrest. After the hearing the writ was approved and Glen Hull was ordered to be released from police custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Francisco and Carolina Marino petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that their minor son, Joseph, was being held unlawfully on the U.S. naval vessel the "Wisconsin." They were represented by the law firm Preston, Carr, and Gilman, but their individual attorney is not named in the documents. The respondent, Lieutenant Commander H. T. Mayo of the Wisconsin claimed and provided evidence that Joseph claimed to be "eighteen years and one month" and swore an oath to that effect at his enlistment. The respondent also stated that they would return Joseph if it was demonstrated that he was a minor, but that he would then be "liable for punishment by a Naval Court Martial" for fraudulent enlistment.
Judge Hanford ruled that Joseph was a minor and canceled his enlistment. It is unknown whether Joseph did face a naval proceeding.

Summary of Proceedings: John Batlos was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Batlos was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Batlos and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Batlos argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. On June 25, the writ of habeas was sustained and Batlos was released.

Summary of Proceedings: On or around September 1st, 1866, fourteen year-old Louisa Jane Derrick began to stay at Mary J. Whitesides' house. Her father and only parent, Andrew H. Derrick, claimed to not have knowledge of this and that he did not consent to her leaving. On December 31st, 1866, Andrew Derrick filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Louisa, claiming that Whitesides was depriving her of her freedom and that she was teaching Louisa to renounce her religion, despise all Christians, and to disobey her father. In return, Whitesides claimed that Andrew was not in the territory of Washington when his daughter left and that he did not have a home to provide Louisa with. Judge Wyche ruled that Andrew was a fit parent and gave him care and custody of Louisa.

Summary of Proceedings: In late 1918, the Department of Labor ordered that Andy Pappas be deported for violating the U.S. Immigration Act of 1917, accusing him of assisting a prostitute and being liable to become a public charge. In March 1919, he was placed in the Douglas County jail to await deportation, unable or unwilling to pay a $1000 bond. Pappas petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on September 13, arguing that he was being detained indefinitely and that the amount of his bond was unconscionable. His petition was "denied on the merits" but "conditionally sustained"; the judge agreed that his detention was unlawful (since the Department of Labor was struggling to find a ship to return him to Greece) and ordered that his bond be reduced to $100. Pappas made bail on September 23, agreeing to remain in Dawson County until his deportation hearing. When he failed to show up for his hearing in December, he forfeited his bond. While his fate is unknown, the appearance docket record of his case concludes with a line saying that the a U.S. marshal was forced to return a writ of capias in November 1921 because Pappas was "not found."

Summary of Proceedings: C. V. Stortz and a second petitioner with the surname Stortz claimed they were unlawfully arrested with no legal warrant and had not committed larceny or a felony. Their attorney demanded to know the nature of the charges and be admitted to bail. However, their jailers claimed that they were not accused of any offense and therefore not to be brought in court to meet with their attorney or allowed bail. Newspaper coverage indicates the married couple had been arrested on suspicion of being accomplices to a burglary.

Summary of Proceedings: Chin Duck petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Duck claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Duck was arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Duck are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: In July 1919, George W. Willett filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of James Gannon. The petition alleged Gannon was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by John T. Dunn, Chief of Detectives, without warrant or complaint, and that said restraint is without due process of law. In the answer and return to the writ, John T. Dunn stated that the Seward County Attorney, through the Chief of Police of Lincoln, directed him to arrest and apprehend Gannon for the purpose of turning him over to Gus A. Hyers, Chief Agent of the Governor of Nebraska. The answer and writ further alleged that Gannon was accused of bootlegging in Seward County in violation of state liquor laws and fled to Douglas County. Judge Willis G. Sears authorized the petition and rued that there was no charge filed in Seward against Gannon, therefore John T. Dunn was ordered to discharge Gannon from his custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 28, 1919, Mack Sterns was found guilty of vagrancy by police magistrate Charles E. Foster. He was fined $100 and confined to the county jail until he could pay the money. However, Paragraph 8865 of Section 290 of the Revised Statues of Nebraska for 1913 stated that one could not order someone charged with vagrancy to pay more than a $50 fine or jail them for more than three months. Therefore, on August 29, Sterns and his attorney, George A. Lee filed a writ of habeas corpus against sheriff Michael L. Clark, which was allowed by judge Lee S. Estelle. On August 30, 1919, judge William A. Redick found in the favor of the petitioners, but Sterns still had to pay a $50 fine and the costs of his stay in jail. On September 4, 1919, the writ of habeas corpus and return was filed.

Summary of Proceedings: Allen H. Shears was arrested by the King County Sheriff, John Stringer, based on a warrant issued by the Governor of the State of New York. The warrant accused Shears of embezzling $3,000 between December 1, 1917 and September 22, 1918 from the Fire Association of Philadelphia and the Insurance Company of North America. Shears filed a writ of habeas corpus and argued that the Governor’s warrant was illegal and without due process. Shears claims that since no complaint or affidavit had ever been filed against him the warrant is illegal. The petition further claims that this matter was brought before the King County Prosecuting Attorney in 1916 and the attorney refused to file any charges based on the information and facts given to him. Judge A. W. Frater allowed the writ of habeas corpus because the respondent parties missed the deadline to file their return and granted the petitioner’s request to have the late return exempted.

Strigulas was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Strigulas and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. On June 27, the writ of habeas was sustained, and Strigulas was released.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 10, 1914, Mrs. Orlando Terrell Byington (whose first name is not given) files a petition of habeas corpus on behalf of her husband, Orlando Terrell Byington. Chief of Police Austin E. Griffiths held Orlando in jail. On July 14, 1913 Orlando went to court on the charge of grand larceny in Fresno, California. However, Mrs. Byington’s petition alleges that the case was dropped because the prosecuting witnesses did not show up. On October 13, 1914, a complaint from Ben Cornelison and a warrant from Judge John B. Gordon alleged that Orlando actually had been charged with larceny and was a fugitive from justice. Judge Boyd J. Tallman called all parties to court. The outcome of this case and the fate of Orlando Terrell Byington are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1862, James Robinson was arrested for the crime of grand larceny. Robinson was believed to be guilty of feloniously taking four horses and one mule valued at $450 from Peter Riffs. Robinson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus stating his innocence and that he repeatedly asked what he was charged with and requesting a hearing. Robinson stated that he wished to be confronted with the witnesses and evidence against him, but was denied. Justice W. P. Horton authorized the writ. A later document from Deputy Sheriff George H. Porter revealed that Robinson escaped custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Angelo Rose traveled from Ohio to Omaha to visit relatives. He stated that he planned to return to Ohio within 2-3 weeks and had not left Ohio for the purpose of avoiding arrest. He was arrested 28 August 1899 and had been held for two days without a hearing and had not yet been scheduled for a hearing. Further, he states that he is not guilty of any crime in any jurisdiction. It was reported that he embezzled money from individuals in Ohio but he had not yet been found guilty. The individuals who filed that report were aware that the petitioner was leaving Ohio and intended to visit Omaha, NE. 

A complaint was filed on 11 August 1899 stating that Rose left Cuyahoga County, Ohio on or around 1 August 1899 and was a fugitive of justice for embezzlement. This document was signed by George C. Cockrell, Justice of the Peace. On 31 August 1899, the writ was allowed and Judge Baker wrote to Sheriff McDonald and asked that Rose be released to the custody of the State of Ohio. On 1 September 1899, Rose was ordered to be released from the custody of Douglas County to the custody of the State of Ohio. A supplemental petition was filed on 1 September 1899 stating that the representative of the Governor of Ohio did not have authority and, further, that Rose was not a fugitive from justice per the requisition papers from the State of Ohio and that no affidavit or indictment had been produced by the Governor of Ohio stating that Mr. E. D. Barry had authority to arrest Rose. The proceedings following this second petition are detailed in case file (hc.case.ne.1449).

Summary of Proceedings: In early August 1913, Edward Blackfish was arrested and charged with assaulting Lydia Chief on the Winnebago Reservation. Both Blackfish and Chief were members of the Winnebago nation who had accepted land allotments under the Dawes Act. The U.S. District Court for the Omaha Division of the District of Nebraska set his bail at $2,000 and placed him in the Douglas County jail. Blackfish petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that he was a citizen of Nebraska and could only be tried in state court. The respondents demurred, arguing the federal jurisdiction applied. After hearing the evidence, the court sustained the demurrer and remanded Blackfish to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: Accused of embezzlement, Thomas Van Sciever was arrested on the order of Lorenzo Crouse, governor of Nebraska. Crouse received orders for extradition from W. H. Auble, agent of the state of California on behalf of W. H. Markham, governor of California. Thomas Van Sciever, and his agent and wife Addie Van Sciever, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that chief of police P. H. Cooper and agent W. H. Auble were depriving him of his liberty. Judge Hall granted the petition. After hearing evidence, Judge Tibbetts remanded him to the custody of Sherriff Miller. Van Sciever filed a writ of error and appealed to the Nebraska Supreme Court, who in 1897 affirmed the decision.

Summary of Proceedings:
At 3-4am on May 14th, 1891, Bolton Rogers, the Chief of Police of Seattle, arrested George W. Loomis. Loomis was arrested when landing from the steamer “Eastern Oregon”. When questioned, Rogers apparently stated he was arrested for being a suspicious character. Loomis petitioned on May 14th, his writ was allowed by Judge Thomas J. Humes, and Sheriff James H. Woolery served it about 1:40 pm in the afternoon to Bolton Rogers. The allowed writ was to have Loomis brought before Humes at 5pm that afternoon of the 14th. However, Rogers had transferred Loomis from the city jail to the county jail about 11:50 am on the 14th, and thus Loomis was then in the custody of the Sheriff of King County, J.H. Woolery. 

According to the Seattle Post Intelligencer, before the hearing, Loomis was liberated on the order of Chief Rogers.

Summary of Proceedings: Why How Sin and Why Yuk Tong left the United States for China in November 1891. Then, after approximately a year, they returned to Portland, Oregon, on the Steamship Haytian Republic. However, the Master of the Haytian Republic detained them on January 28th, 1893, due to suspicion of violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. The petitioners provided written accounts, photos, and witnesses proving their eligibility to re-enter the United States. Thus, their writ was granted, and they were released from captivity on January 30th, 1893.

Summary of Proceedings: Following the death of his parents when he was about ten years old, John Heo had lived with a white family away from the Indian reservations that his parents belonged to. He had severed his tribal relations for nearly twenty-five years. R. H. Milroy, the Indian Agent of the Nisqually and Puyallup Agency, arrested Heo when he refused to return to the agency and cohabitate with an Indian woman, presumably his wife. Heo petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus which was granted, and the trial was heard by Judge Hoyt. Milroy argued that all Indians living in or coming to the agency were under his jurisdiction. He stated that he was justified in requiring Heo to return to the reservation to live with his wife and child. Heo argued that because he had severed ties with his nation, had never lived on a reservation since his parents' death, and had adopted a Western lifestyle, Milroy did not have sufficient justification to arrest him. Judge Hoyt, after hearing the evidence, ruled in favor of Milroy, and Heo remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 23rd, 1916, Jesse Fowler, Mamie Cole, and Arthur Haynes were arraigned and tried by the police magistrate for vagrancy in the Police Court of the City of Omaha. On August 24th, 1916, with the help of their lawyer Daniel H. Horrigan, Jesse Fowler and Mamie Cole filed a Writ of Habeas Corpus against Sheriff F. J. McShane Jr.. They claimed the complaint they received was not sworn to by the city prosecutor or signed by police magistrate and that the police magistrate did not have jurisdiction to try and sentence people, so therefore all proceedings were then unlawful and void. On the same day, Judge Willis G. Sears allowed the petitioner's Writ of Habeas Corpus and ordered Jess Fowler, Mamie Cole, and F. J. McShane Jr. to appear in court the next day. On August 28th, 1916, Judge A. C. Troup ruled in favor of the petitioners, stating that they were unlawfully deprived of their liberty and ordered their release.

Summary of Proceedings: John Alperson was arrested by Michael Whalen for giving away and allowing to be taken, cigarettes and material for their composition known as cigarette paper. His legal team argued that his charge was unconstitutional because it was a subject not sufficiently expressed in the title of the act. They argued that the object of the constitutional limitation is “to prevent the legislature from passing a law under the guise of one name, which might affect some other interests or rights,” and it is contended that the right to give away cigarettes can not be abridged in a law where the title does not specify an intention to prohibit a gift. They also argued that the subject of the legislation is disguised so that legislators would not be sufficiently notified by the title that it was intended to discourage the use of and prevent all traffic of said articles. Alperson was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 10, 1894, Charles P Bishop was charged with malicious prosecution against Charles Lett and E. E. Staples. He was put into King County Jail on the same day. On April 11, Bishop filed for an application for a Writ of Habeas Corpus with the help of his Attorney, L Gilman. Justice TJ Humes granted this application, and ordered Woolery, the holding party and Sheriff of King county, to bring him into the court. Woolery brought Bishop into the court, but the outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Mary Charlotte filed for her and her four children's freedom in St. Louis on May 1, 1843, claiming that she had been born to Rose, a Black woman in Montreal, Canada who had been wrongly traded into slavery and that therefore she herself should be free. This extremely long case file narrates Mary Charlotte's transnational and intergenerational claim to freedom with documents and testimony dating back to the 1780s and spanning French and British Canada as well as the Northwest Territory and Missouri Territory in the U.S. This case blurs the line between freedom suits and habeas petitions in Missouri Courts, so the file references habeas but does not contain a labeled petition. The case went to Missouri's Supreme Court in 1859, which upheld the lower court ruling in favor of Mary Charlotte's freedom. The case file includes disputed jury instructions regarding juror interpretation of slavery law in Canada and in the Northwestern Territory.

Summary of Proceedings:
On October 7, 1904, Tom Sing filed a habeas corpus petition against Thomas M. Fisher (the Chinese Inspector at Port Townsend) on behalf of his twelve-year-old son Ham Hung Wah. Sing and his wife Na Lay were described as being "alien" Chinese residents of Montana, while the twelve-year-old Wah was described as a native-born citizen born in Montana in 1893. The petition alleged that Wah had been arrested and detained by Fisher for being an "alien Chinese person" after returning from a visit to China. The petition stated that attempts to deport Wah were illegitimate because Wah was a citizen entitled to the same rights as other American citizens, which meant that he was entitled to judicial due process instead of an arbitrary decision by executive officials. Sing also submitted a document signed by five white witnesses testifying to his trustworthiness, his Presbyterian Christian practices, and his adoption of the "habits of western civilization." 
Judge Cornelius H. Hanford commanded that Fisher show cause for his detention of Wah on October 25, 1904. On that same day, Judge Hanford dismissed the petition at the request of Wah's attorney for unknown reasons; external scholarship states that Wah's application for entry was rejected by the Montana Chinese Inspector and Lay was later deported in 1908.

Summary of Proceedings: Emma Westman petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren, City Health Commissioner J. S. McBride, and State Health Commissioner Thomas D. Tuttle. Westman alleged Dry Squad officers arrested her for possessing alcoholic liquors. At the police department, she was forced to submit to a blood test before she was charged with disorderly conduct and was told that she was infected with syphilis. Westman claimed she was physically restrained for the blood test and since been receiving forcible injections for treatment of syphilis, which she believed had been injurious to her health. She claimed that she did not, in fact, have syphilis and was being illegally detained in the quarantine department of the Seattle City Jail. Warren, McBride, and Tuttle replied that Westman’s arrest was ordered by several city ordinances pertaining to public health and infectious disease. Judge John S. Jurey ruled that the writ was denied and Westman should remain in custody of McBride and Warren. Westman appealed to the Washington State Supreme Court, but the ruling was upheld.

Summary of Proceedings:
A. F. Richardson arrested Li Chi Nin for violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act and started deportation proceedings. Nin filed an appeal on May 6, 1905. Nin mounted a test case against the Chinese Exclusion Act through both legal challenges to his deportation in the United States District Court in Spokane, as well as newspaper opinion pieces against the law. 

Judge Edward Whitson released Nin after Tai Gee, Eug Hong, Louis Den, Sum Lu Yick, and W. D. Vincent paid his bond. In 1907, immigration officials deported Nin to China.

The case file does not contain the writ of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings:
On April 16, 1902, H. Armstrong, the Chief of Police of the city of Denver, Colorado issued a telegram to John Sullivan, the Chief of Police of Seattle. The telegram read:

“Hold Frances Palmer; officer will start today to return with her
H. Armstrong, Chief of Police”

Because the telegram did not mention a charge or commission of crime of any kind, nature, or description, Palmer argued that she was illegally detained. In the brief filed by her attorneys, Humphries and Bostwick, it was also mentioned that Palmer had recently recovered from scarlet fever and thus her health was in a delicate state that would worsen should she be continuously detained. Sheriff Edward Cudihee delivered the Writ of Habeas Corpus to Sullivan on April 18, 1902. Judge W. R. Bell heard the case the same day.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 2nd, 1921, Mary Foley and Thomas Foley petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of their daughter, Agnes Smith. The petition revealed that in 1913 Agnes was committed to the Girls' Industrial School for a period of two years, but was detained for five years. She was then committed to the Institute for Feeble-Minded Youth against her will and without proper noticed to her parents. Mary and Thomas Foley asserted that Agnes was not feeble-minded. The Foleys named S. J. Stewart, the superintendent of the Institute for Feeble-Minded Youth, and members of the Board of Control as respondents. The petition was granted. In a return, S. J. Stewart assured the court that he was legally detaining Agnes due to a decree made by W. R. Fulton, a Fillmore county judge. The decree ordered Agnes detained to the Institute for Feeble-Minded Youth because it was what was best for her and society. On May 14th, the writ was denied and Agnes remained in custody. Judge L. W. Colby affirmed that Agnes was duly committed and a "fit and proper subject" for the Institution.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 19, 1901, Fred Harris and Charles Eick petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. The petition stated that the two men had been arrested in September on the charge of rape. They claimed their bail was set unreasonably high, and they were held in jail while awaiting their trial, which occurred in early October. The men claimed that no indictment had been found against either of them, and no information had been filed, but they were still being held in jail by Sheriff Edward Cudihee. The outcome of this case, and the fate of Harris and Eick are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 8, 1909, Thomas Johnson was arrested by E. F. Brailey for vagrancy and arraigned in the police court on a plea of guilty. Thomas’ petition charged that the intent was not to plead guilty - which was made known on June 11, 1909, that he had no representation, that he was not given time to secure witnesses, and that he did not waive his right to trial by jury. He was sentenced to 90 days in county jail by the police court. Johnson also claimed to have been denied his U.S. Constitutional rights in Articles 5 and 6 and denied his rights in Article 1, Sections 3, 5, and 11 of the Constitution of the State of Nebraska. A writ was issued on June 17 but later denied on June 18, 1909.

Edith was described as "incompetent," and Oscar worried that she was being deprived of liberty by her son, Cassius and Sheriff Anderson of Phelps County. She was later placed in the Ingleside state hospital for the insane in Hastings.

Summary of Proceedings: Sam Greer was arrested on October 21st, 1916, in Omaha, after being charged with "carrying concealed weapons." Sears granted Greer the writ, and the petitioner was released from the Douglas County sheriff's custody.

Judge Frost granted the petition. When Walton was judged insane by a commission, they ruled that he was not dangerous and could be released. Summary of Proceedings: In October 1890, M. O. Ricketts petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of a young man named Till, which was granted. Ricketts claimed that Till was being "held as a slave" in Fillmore County, Nebraska by a farmer named Milton Willerford. Willerford denied this, maintaining that he had not purchased Till and that he did not detain him against his will. Rather, Willeford asserted that Till, whose history the case file does not elucidate, had chosen to live with his family the past seven years. The cause was eventually dismissed by the mutual agreement of both parties. Till's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Daniel O'Connell, the petitioner, was prosecuted in District Court for the violation of Section 3 of Title 1 of the Espionage Act of June 15, 1917, by conspiring to obstruct recruiting and enlisting, and alleging a conspiracy to evade the provisions of the Draft Act of May 18, 1917, in violation of Section 37 of the United States Penal Code. O'Connell's petition for Mandamus and Habeas Corpus states that both violations were the same and based on the same facts and evidence and, therefore, invalid. In reality, the petition stated O'Connell had not committed a crime but instead was targeted because of his association with the corporation American Patriots. The purpose of this was to raise money to test in the courts the constitutionality of the use of the Draft Act and the draft army in Europe to carry out the war objects of the Allies.

Summary of Proceedings: Gross S. Edison was caught with counterfeit bank notes on December 31st, 1910. He was indicted on four counts of fraud in 1911 in a Missouri court and sentenced to five years in the United States Federal Penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas. On September 9th, 1915, Edison, filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of himself, arguing that the judgement and sentences he received were invalid and illegal. On October 6th, 1915, Judge Pollock ruled in favor of Edison, claiming that the Missouri Court failed to charge Edison with any offense against the laws of the United States and the judgment and the sentence were illegal. Edison was then released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 21st, 1919, the bound party, John Sullivan, was arrested for fast and reckless driving. After being formally charged, the bound party was found guilty and sent to jail for 30 days. On February 27th, a petition was filed alleging that the government attorney, Murray, altered documents in the course of the trial without re-swearing testifiers or re-arraigning Sullivan. The writ was issued and on March, 3rd the realtor was discharged on a bond.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 18, 1903, Frank Richards and his attorney P. D. Hughes petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Richards had been jailed in January 1903, but no indictment or information had since been filed against him. Richards alleged it had been over thirty days since his arrest and no action had been taken regarding his case, which rendered his continued imprisonment illegal. The outcome of this case and the fate of Richards are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In December 1919, James Douglas petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Henry M. White, Commissioner of Immigration. Douglas was a citizen of Canada and was arrested and charged with being a person who was likely to become a public charge. At a hearing before the Department of Labor, Commissioner White issued an order directing Douglas to be deported from the United States. The petition alleged the evidence was insufficient, and Douglas did not violate the Immigration Act of Feb. 5th, 1917. Judge Neterer initially denied the petition, on account that the Court's jurisdiction was limited to determining whether a fair hearing was accorded, and the Immigration Acts makes the hearing before the Department of Labor Final. However, a couple days later, Judge Neterer dismissed the proceedings. The fate of James Douglas is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 21, 1918, a complaint was made by Arthur E. Volkmeier against James H. Parsons on the charge of Grand Larceny made, originally, in Bannock County, Idaho. Parsons was arrested and brought to the Police Court in Omaha on warrant by Judge Terrel in Bannock, and on the charge of being a fugitive from justice. Parsons filed for habeas against police chief, Micheal Dempsey, and police captain, Anton Vanous, charging that at the time of his arrest no warrant or complaint had been made against him. A writ of habeas was issued, but denied on September 4.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 24, 1894, Lee Tong filed for a writ of habeas for Ah Din, Chew Chow, Chew Tai, and Chew You. Lee Tong claimed that they were being illegally detained on the Steamship Signal by Captain M. Bendergard. Lee Tong further claimed that Ah Din, Chew Chow, Chew Tai, and Chew You were Chinese Merchants who were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Bellinger granted the writ for Chew You and ordered him released from custody. Judge Bellinger denied the writ for Ah Din, Chew Chow, and Chew Tai and ordered them to be remanded back to custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Sarah D. Bassett, was the petitioner for Florence May Mitchell, a 14 year old girl from Dawes County, Nebraska. Bassett filed a petition for Mitchell to Judge Irving F. Baxter alleging that she had been unlawfully imprisoned for two months by Margaret Duffy who was in charge of the Salvation Army Home in Douglas County. Florence May Mitchell was born in Michigan and her father relinquished custody to the Children’s Home Society of Michigan, then subsequently, of Nebraska. From there she was taken into the home of C. D. Tyler seven years ago. Then, Mitchell was kidnapped and removed from possession of Sarah D. Bassett on their way to Sioux County, Nebraska to care and provide for her after she had been “debauched” and was approaching maternity. Allegedly, Mitchell was taken by the father and friends of James Sullenberg (the party accused of her abuse) and kept confined for ten days where she was then transferred to Omaha and put in the hands of Margaret Duffy. Duffy motioned to quash the writ because she said that Bassett did not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action and that she did not have the legal capacity to sue out said writ. Yet, there was an order overruling the motion of Duffy to quash the writ. The writ was allowed and Florence May Mitchell was discharged from imprisonment in May.

Summary of Proceedings: In December 1903, W. L. Lafferty, an employee of the Kansas City-based L. B. Price Mercantile Company, was fined $50 for violating a Fremont, Nebraska city ordinance against peddling samples without first paying a fee to the city treasurer. When he did not pay, he was confined to the Dodge County jail. Lafferty petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court, arguing that his right to conduct interstate commerce had been violated. The City of Fremont responded that Lafferty erred in filing in federal court since he had not exhausted his remedies in state court, namely appeal. After hearing the evidence, Lafferty was remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Tebo, a Native American on the Winnebago Reservation, was taken to the court in Thurston County following his Habeas Corpus release in April by judge Estelle of Douglas County on charge of fornication with an unmarried woman, Martha Walker beginning March 15, 1909. On April 19, 1910, Tebo was said to have plead guilty to the charge and sentenced to 90 days in jail, with last 15 days alternating 5 on 5 off, bread and water only, along with a $50.00 fine, and costs of trial. Tebo was placed in the Douglas County jail under conditions that Thurston County did not have safe facilities. Tebo and attorney, Julius S. Cooley, presented petition against E. F. Brailey, sheriff of Douglas County, charging that he had no jurisdiction to hold Tebo in Douglas County. In addition, they asserted that Tebo was tried twice for the same crime, against the constitution, that the alleged crime was not a felony, that his sentence was inhumane according to statues of Nebraska, that the alleged crime was committed on the Reservation, that as a ward (Indian) to the federal government state courts have no jurisdiction over his case, and that according to unwritten tribal custom his sexual relationship and cohabitation with Martha Walker made her his wife. E. F. Brailey, and attorneys, motioned for the petition to be quashed. On June 15, 1910, judge Estelle denied the writ and Tebo remained in the custody of Douglas County.

Petition or Case Title: In the Matter of the Application of W. M. McPhay for Writ of Habeas Corpus
Primary field: In the Matter of the Application of W. M. McPhay for Writ of Habeas Corpus
Repository: ["[Washington State Archives, Puget Sound Regional Branch (Bellevue, Washington)](hc.loc.000032)"]
Summary of Proceedings:
On November 16th, 1902, William McPhay, a black man, killed a popular policeman, Walter J. Morris, within the town of Summit, Mississippi. The reasons for this are unclear and contested: Mississippi publications suggested McPhay was drunk and belligerent, while McPhay says he was acting in self defense. Swarms of vengeful citizens sought out McPhay, who quickly fled west. The Leader (Mississippi) claimed that this case and the racist sentiments arising with it “furnished the chief foundations” of stories that Black people were rising against white supremacy in Mississippi. These fears were played upon by "white cap leaders" to strengthen their movement, influence, and freedom in abusing and destroying Black peoples and communities in the nearby area.

On February 28th, 1905 McPhay was arrested and charged with murder after being found in Ballard, Washington by Seattle deputies. This charge was based on the warrant that was filed against McPhay in Mississippi three years prior, and Washington officials were able to locate McPhay after his family moved from Mississippi to join him in Washington. William McPhay then filed a writ of habeas corpus, alleging the warrant is not sufficient in legal authority for the arrest, as Seattle police made the arrest completely upon “hearsay” from information originating from another state. McPhay’s writ is denied, but he quickly appeals to the Washington Supreme Court. The outcome of this appeal is not explicitly stated in the case files, but it seems likely that the appeal was also denied. McPhay was to be extradited to Mississippi, but Washington residents and officials alike grew worried as to what McPhay’s future would be in the southern state. 

According to newspaper coverage, Washington Governor Albert E. Mead personally corresponded with the Governor of Mississippi and noted white supremacist, James Vardeman, to guarantee William McPhay’s right to a free and fair trial away from fears of extrajudicial violence. He presented these concerns after worries were shared to him by “friends” of McPhay and due to the virtue of his “public duties” as a public official. During his stay in Ballard, Washington, it seems William McPhay crafted an excellent reputation for himself and was thought of by his community as a man of “good repute and standing.” The Seattle Republican is most concerned with McPhay’s life as they heard word of Amit county running out Black people from nearby communities and burning their homes. In this article, they claim the reason McPhay killed the policeman was because the policeman was at the head of a lynch mob. The article further states this mob came together as the officer intended to lynch McPhay for his “association” with a Black woman whom the officer also associated with as a “paramore,” or lover. These worries seem entirely justified as an article from a Mississippi paper at the time of the killing promised that if McPhay was found “there is little doubt that short work will be made of him.” A fundraiser social event was held for “Mrs. William McPhay” to secure the funds needed to travel back to Mississippi and be with her husband. She left Washington after “some 40 odd dollars” were collected for her benefit. William McPhay was tried in Summit, Mississippi and found guilty of murder. Much to the chagrin of many Mississippians, he was sentenced to life in prison rather than the death penalty. 

A “Will McPhay” who was serving a life sentence was pardoned and released from the Pike county jail in February of 1914.

Summary of Proceedings: Poon Sea petitioned on behalf of Low Fon, who was detained on the Steamship Haytian Republic by T. J. Black, who refused him entry to port because of the Chinese Exclusion Act. Low Fon lived in the United States for several years before returning to China to visit his mom on October 23rd, 1892. Before this visit, he raised, bought, and sold fruit in Mount Tabor, a neighborhood in Portland, Oregon; thus, the petitioner claims he should be exempt as a merchant. The Customs Collector denied this claim, arguing that selling fruit is not a merchant job, leading Poon Sea to seek a writ of habeas corpus. William Danbar, an agent of the Steamship Haytian Republic, replied to the court that they could not produce the body of Low Fon as the ship was seized by collectors at the port and now in the possession of the Marshals. The court then ordered the Marshal to produce the body, and upon hearing, granted the writ and released Low Fon from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: D. J. Needham’s petition stated that he was being unlawfully held by Omaha Police Chief Henry W. Dunn. He stated that he was being held upon a warrant of the Chief of Police of Milwaukee, Wisconsin upon the charge of wife and child abandonment. He was asking for a writ to be issued because he claimed that he was going to be removed from the Omaha jurisdiction and taken back to Wisconsin without extradition papers. On 13 November 1915, Judge James P. English ordered that the writ be allowed and a writ be issued to Chief Dunn. In the Writ Return filed on 22 November 1915, Sheriff McShane stated that he was unable to deliver the writ because Needham had already left the state.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 29, 1902, Herman Schwingler and two men broke into the house of Maud Schwingler to kidnap their 6-year-old child Urban Schwingler. Maud and Herman were married, but had not been living with each other; Maud left due to the continued cruel and inhuman treatment that made her life burdensome. Since leaving, she had remained peaceable and quiet, and viewed herself as a suitable parent for Urban. She filed a writ of habeas corpus for Urban on December 30, 1902, with the help of her attorney Herbert E. Snook. Judge Tallman accepted the writ, and sent the order to Judge Arthur Griffin to hear the petition on January 3, 1903.

Summary of Proceedings: May Andrews petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff Edward Cudihee, and claimed she was being illegally held in King County Jail. Andrews attested that she was arrested for grand larceny in the summer of 1901 and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted, and she was briefly discharged. She was immediately rearrested and charged with “larceny from the person”. The state admitted that the charge was a mistake, and Andrews’s charge was changed to grand larceny. Andrews claimed that, since she had already been found not guilty of grand larceny in her first habeas corpus trial, she was being held without cause. Her writ was granted and she was released from jail, but there is evidence in the case file that Cudihee appealed to the Supreme Court of Washington.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 19, 1906 John O’Day and his attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. The petition stated that no legal judgment or complaint had been filed against O’Day, and therefore his imprisonment by Sheriff L. C. Smith was illegal. No proposed charge was listed in the case file. Judge Frater agreed to hear the case. The outcome of this case and the fate of O’Day are unknown.
