Summary of Proceedings: E. A. Bullock made a complaint to C. F. Eiseley, which stated that Frank E. Waring committed the crime of forgery. John J. Donahue and Patrick Harvey, sheriff and jailor respectively, were told to arrest him. J. L. Greene, the superintendent of the Nebraska Hospital for the insane alleged that Frank E. Waring was adjudged insane by the board of commissioners of insanity and was committed to the custody of the hospital. Green filed a case to gain custody of Waring back into the hospital. On April 20, 1903, Waring was committed to J. L. Green and the Nebraska Hospital for the insane.

Summary of Proceedings: Gen Men petitioned on behalf of his son, See Loon, who was detained aboard the Steamship Danube. William Meyers, Master of the Steamship, believed the child to be a Chinese laborer and thus not allowed entry to the port by the Chinese Exclusion Act. However, his father is a merchant and was educating See Loon as a merchant; thus, he argued they were both exempt. Judge Belliger agreed and granted the writ releasing See Loon from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 15, 1922, attorney John N. Baldwin petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Willian Maier (alias Maher). The petition was against John Pszanowski, acting Chief of Detectives, Michael Demsey, Chief of Police, and Henry Dunn, Commissioner of Police. Baldwin claimed they unlawfully detained Maier for "implicitly in the transportation of liquor." He had previously stolen a Cadillac in Omaha and jumped a bond in South Dakota, where he was arrested for smuggling liquor. There was no probable cause for his detention. Maier claimed that he had no connection with the transportation of the said liquor because he was not physically present at the time of the crime the police accused him of committing. Additionally, Maier had no connection in any manner to any person associated with said transportation of liquor. On August 16, 1922, the Judge accepted the petition and filed a writ of habeas corpus. On January 21, 1924, the Judge dismissed the case "for want of prosecution."

Summary of Proceedings: On 20 January 1914, Marcus Glassman was charged with being an inebriate. On 14 January 1914, petitioner was arrested on a charge of being insane and was placed in the County Jail, he has been detained there since that date. He was not granted a hearing until 28 January 1914. At that hearing, no person testified to any facts that would prove that he was either insane or an inebriate. The petition states that the “insanity board of Douglas County, Nebraska” has not made a finding as to whether he was an inebriate or insane, but has continued to confine the petitioner. Glassman filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on 3 February 1914 asserting that he was being unlawfully detained. Judge James P. English ordered that the writ be issued and directed to Sheriff McShane. Sheriff McShane received the writ on 3 February 1914.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1919, Thomas Kelley, James Cosgrove, Henry Wedgworth, Frank or James Keating, and Patrick Burkery were arrested for bootlegging in Omaha, Nebraska, where they lived. This scheme allegedly allowed 3,000 cases of whiskey to cross the Nebraska-Iowa border via the use of motor boats. According to the Omaha Daily Bee, it was organized by a group of Omaha Italians. However, this was done on the orders of the sheriff of Pottawattamie County, Iowa, and he ordered the men to be taken to the state line. Because of this, they filed for a writ of habeas corpus on March 29, 1919, arguing that they were innocent of the crime and that the Iowa sheriff had no constitutional right to have them arrested in another state and then taken back to Iowa. Although their writ was allowed, the case was eventually dismissed on June 30, 1920, for a want of prosecution, and the petitioners had to pay all court costs. The Omaha Daily Bee says that the men were all released on bond on March 24, 1919. However, he was arrested again, allegedly for the 28th time, in the February of 1920.

Summary of Proceedings: In September 1913, Joseph Kopf was arrested in California and extradited to Nebraska to answer a charge of first degree murder in Nehama County. Kopf was accused of having bludgeoned a man to death during a robbery gone wrong in 1899 and subsequently fleeing the state in 1902. Kopf petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, he was remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings:
Petitioner, Ms. Gertrude Bloomfield, asserts that Chief Sigwart is unlawfully holding Pearl Proto (a five year old child). Petitioner states that she was granted custody by the mother of said child and that Pearl was forcibly taken from Ms. Bloomfield on 29 August 1896 and has since been held, unlawfully, by Chief Sigwart. This statement was sworn and signed in front of Notary Public Wilbur M. Lemon on 31 August 1896. Ms. Bloomfield and her attorney, Mr. Lee Helsley, appeared before Judge Fawcett on 31 August 1896. He stated that the writ should not be allowed to Ms. Bloomfield as it was written in her petition. Instead, he asked that Ms. Bloomfield and Sheriff Sigwart appear in court before District Court Judge Baker on 5 September 1896. A document filed on 2 June 1898 notes that this case was remanded for costs to the trial court. The motion to tax the costs of the trial to the county was filed that same day by Albyn L. Frank (Clerk for the District Court), the motion was sustained by Judge Fawcett on 14 June 1898. 
It is not clear what the conclusion of the case heard before Judge Baker was. Judge Fawcett simply states that the writ should not be allowed and lists a time and place for a further trial, there is no further information.

Summary of Proceedings:
On June 10, 1913, W. S. Matthews and his lawyers filed for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his seven minor children, Marion Stoddert Matthews, ten and a half, Catherine Saville Matthews, Maria Devereux Matthews, Virginia Chambers Matthews, Nancy Matthews, Elizabeth Lawrence Matthews and Frances Key Matthews, two years old. The children are listed from oldest to youngest, but the two ages listed are the only ones given. 
In the petition, W. S. asserted that his wife, Maria, left their home in Vancouver, British Columbia, and took their children to Seattle, Washington without his knowledge or consent. He stated that she then took them to the House of the Good Shepherd. W. S. claimed that he was, and remains, ill at the time she took the children. He claimed he had the means and desire to care for the children. Additionally, he believed Maria intended to file for divorce and to take the children to San Diego soon, leaving the court’s jurisdiction. Judge Everett Smith allowed the writ to be heard, and sent a warrant to both the Mother Superior of the House of the Good Shepherd and to Maria. Maria filed a motion for continuance in the case, which was granted by Everett. During this period, the temporary custody of the children was given to an unrelated and unnamed third party.
 Maria responded to the petition, and said she did take the children, but that W. S. asked her to leave and was aware she was leaving. Further, she claimed that W. S. often failed to provide for their children, forcing her to ask her family for money. Additionally, she stated that W. S. allowed a man named R. L. Packard to stay in their house, along with her mother in-law. Maria claimed that both W. S. and R. L. created unbearable living conditions. She stated she had, on the advice of her brother A. Y. Greene, left the children in the House of the Good Shepherd temporarily in order to attempt reconciliation with W. S. in British Columbia. She requested full custody of her children and child support payments. W. S. denied all of her claims, and added that the laws of British Columbia gave the father the legal authority over children, rather than the mother.
The outcome of this case and the fate of the children is unknown, though local newspaper coverage indicates all daughters remained with their mother.

Summary of Proceedings: Irish national, John Duffy, filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 31, 1918. Spokane County Sheriff, George L. Reid held Duffy under the authority of immigration officials, including A. F. Richardson and the Secretary of Labor, for advocating the teaching of the destruction of property. Case similarities related to dates and allegations levied against Duffy point to other arrests of I.W.W. members in the Pacific Northwest. Judge Frank H. Rudkin denied the writ on October 31, 1918. The fate of Duffy is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Nelson Davis married Sarah Magdalene Fryer on July 23, 1874 in Columbia County, Washington. Four years later, they had a daughter, Maggie M. Davis. While the couple was living with Nelson's four children from a previous marriage, Maggie was Sarah and Nelson's only child. However, on November 19, 1888, Sarah left Nelson, taking the 11-year old Maggie with her. On November 27, 1888, Nelson filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against Sarah, stating that he should have custody of Maggie, as he had a house and the resources to care for her. Judge William A. Langford allowed the writ, which was returnable December 14, 1888. No further records exist of the case, although by 1910 Nelson was living at his son-in-law's house.

Summary of Proceedings: Getchie was arrested for vagrancy. After the evidence was announced, he was convicted and sentenced to thirty days and for the last six days he could only eat bread and water. No formal entry was made in the records of the judgment or the sentence in the police records. The court decided that forgetting to record was simply an error that did not affect the process under which Getchie was held. Therefore, the judge ruled that Getchie should remain in jail for the rest of his sentence.

Summary of Proceedings: In September 1919, Joseph O'Hare filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the basis he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Michael L. Clark, Sheriff of Douglas County, Nebraska. O'Hare was charged with assault with intent to commit rape and allowed to give bail in the sum of $2,500 in default of said bail he would be committed to jail. The petition alleged at the preliminary hearing, witnesses were examined, and the evidence showed there was not probable cause for holding O'Hare. The petition also stated that O'Hare was 17 years of age, and under state law cannot be charged with assault with intent to commit rape. At trial, the court ruled against O'Hare, and the petitioner's attorney motioned for a new trial on the grounds the judgment was not sustained by sufficient evidence and contrary to law.

Summary of Proceedings: G. W. Gardner, petitioner, along with James Nethesny, E. Neale, & Mayo C.  Boyd, was found riding a bicycle without a lighted lamp on June 23rd of 1899. Gardner filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds that the findings of the court were not backed by evidence or in line with the law. Furthermore, Gardner argued that the ordinance in question is void, impartial, unjust, and contrary to the United States and Nebraska Constitution. Additionally claiming that the City Council of the City of Omaha had no authority to pass such an ordinance.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 8, 1906, Martha Morrison petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her husband, Al Morrison.  Her petition states that he had been arrested by Earnest LaCount, a police officer, out of spite and without cause.  She stated that there were no charges against her husband and argued that he had not violated any laws.  Judge Forster heard the writ, but the outcome of the petition and Morrison’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Sixteen-year-old Virgie La Grand was arrested in Portland, Oregon on November 6, 1914, accused of being a "common prostitute" and charged with vagrancy, and sent to the State Industrial School for Girls in Salem. The following April, her husband, James La Grand, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. James unsuccessfully argued that the Portland municipal court that had sentenced his wife lacked the jurisdiction to do so. After hearing the evidence, Virgie was remanded back into the custody of the school superintendent.

Summary of Proceedings:
After being ordered to be detained and deported by Commissioner of Immigration Henry M. White, Moy Hing Hun petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Moy Hin Hun alleged that he was the lawful son of American citizen Moy You Jin and that the reason to which he was detained and his appeal denied by the Secretary of Labor was that he was accused of being a illegal Chinese Immigrant, due to allegedly having a wife he married in China before coming to the United States.
Judge Cushman made the final decision that Moy Hing Hun and his witnesses failed to prove to the Secretary of Labor that Moy You Jin was his father, and thus ordered the courts to take no control.

Summary of Proceedings: Jacob Penner petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was unlawfully detained by James L. Greene, Superintendent of the Nebraska Hospital for the Insane. Judge Cornish granted the petition. When Penner came before the court, Cornish ruled that Penner be released on his own recognizance. Cornish also set the hearing date for March 10th, 1906. The writ outcome and fate of the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Harm Dirksen was being imprisoned for unspecified reasons. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. Newspaper coverage indicates he was arrested for statutory assault against his stepdaughter. and held in Lancaster County because Boyd County had no jail. Boyd County officials also reported that they feared a lynch mob in Boyd County and had no means to deter such violence. Judge Frost ordered Dirksen returned to Boyd County since there was no agreement to hold county prisoners in a state penitentiary wo the prisoner's consent.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 7, 1924, Daisy Cattleman was detained in the Douglas County jail on charges unknown to her and without a proper trial. On October 30 she filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. The proceedings revealed that the municipal judge of the city of Omaha ordered Cattleman's detention on charges of vagrancy, sentencing her to 30 days in county jail and payment of prosecution costs. The writ was dismissed for want of prosecution. Cattleman's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: T. Judson Ferguson was arrested, charged with forging a "contract or order on the Township of Alma, Harlan County, Nebraska for the sum of $50.00," and jailed. Bail was set at $350. Ferguson asserted that he was not guilty but did not post bail. He then asserted that the writ of mittimus was unlawful and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Ferguson was remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Quivey, and "the Nebraska Childrens' Home Society, a corporation." Summary of Proceedings: On June 20, 1922, Marie Philbrick filed habeas against the superintendent and manager of the St. James Orphanage, Julius J. Hettwer, over the custody of her three children, Beatrice, Robert, and Kathleen. In her petition, Philbrick argued that she has and continues to hold full custody over the children, according to a divorce decree, and that the children were placed with the Orphanage under the condition that Philbrick maintains all legal and full custody over the children. Furthermore, Philbrick argues that Hettwer is refusing visitation with and access to the children. A writ was issued and sustained, and on June 21, 1922, the judge ordered the children to be released into custody of Philbrick.

Summary of Proceedings: On Friday evening, September 12, 1919, Seattle Police Officer J. O’Neill arrested Edna Shields near her home for being a disorderly person. Shields filed for, and was granted, a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that she had not been charged with a crime. In the return for this writ, Seattle Chief of Police J. F. Warren stated that he had transferred custody of Shields to Health Commissioner, H. M. Reed. Reed claimed that he was quarantining Shields in an isolation hospital under suspicion of “suffering from an infectious and contagious disease.” The fate of Shields is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry McCullough petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of his five year old daughter, Gladys. McCullough claimed that Gladys’s mother placed her in the custody of the Washington Children’s Home Society under duress and without permission. McCullough filed the writ against the superintendent of the Washington Children’s Home Society, Harrison D. Brown. Brown responded that Gladys had been freely given up to the Washington Children’s Home Society and adopted by Thomas W. and Emma Reamer. McCullough included the Reamers as respondents in a supplemental petition, claiming they had no legal right to adopt Gladys. The Reamers filed a motion to quash the writ, which was denied, and McCullough testified that he was fit to be a guardian as he had a steady job as an engineer. McCullough and his attorneys later moved that the case be dismissed, though the fate of Gladys is unknown. McCullough filed a separate petition for writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of his other child, John.

Summary of Proceedings: Albert Weston and John Surra managed and operated a soft drink bar and fruit store in Omaha that allegedly sold alcohol. On June 26, 1924, their bond was set for $5,000 after they were found guilty on the charges of unlawful sale and possession of intoxicating liquor and maintaining a common nuisance. On July 3, 1924, Judge McGee sentenced John Surra to two six-month sentences for the alcohol charge and a one-year sentence for the maintenance of a common nuisance charge to be served in the Madison County Jail (along with a $500 fine). On December 18, 1924, John petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that he served both six-month sentences concurrently, was entitled to a shortened sentence for good behavior, and that the maintenance of a common nuisance charge was void because it was unconstitutional. The writ was allowed and delivered to the respondents on December 20, 1924. However, the petition was withdrawn by John on December 26 and he was returned to the custody of jailor C. S. Smith. It is possible that he saw other cases filed during the same time frame go to the U.S. Court of Appeals and did not want to prolong the case if the decision would be reversed in a higher court (see Cronin vs. William J. Fox and related cases). Additionally, the writ for Fred Totoro’s case is included in this case file.

Summary of Proceedings:
Columbia George was convicted of murdering Anna Edna, a Cayuse woman living on the Umatilla Indian Reservation in Oregon, and was sentenced to life imprisonment. First, he was sent to the Oregon State Penitentiary at Salem, Oregon. Then, he was transferred to the custody of C. B. Hopkins at the Federal Penitentiary on McNeil's Island in Puget Sound, Washington. 
George appealed the decision, and argued that because he had faced injustice by the hands of the judge. The case initially went to the Supreme Court of Oregon. The judge denied his writ of Habeas Corpus and ruled that a state court did not have the authority to rule in the case. The case was then sent to a US circuit court. 
George argued that the Supreme Court jurists had judged him as an Indian ward, and not a U.S. citizen who was subject to both federal and state law (whereas an Indian ward would have been strictly subject to federal statute), and therefore should have granted his petition and heard the case. This was due to his receipt of an allotment of land by the U.S. government under the Dawes Act, which when accepted, changed his legal status to a U.S. citizen, and no longer an Indian Ward of the United States government. 
The case went to the United States District Court where the jury convicted him guilty of murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment. George appealed, and was reportedly tried again, and was once more convicted of murder. The archives lack these documents, but the case is referenced in this case, no. 1390, in Judge Hanford’s denial and dismissal of George’s petition for wrongful imprisonment by Charles E. Hopkins at the US Penitentiary at McNeil Island. George appealed a fourth time and was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: On the 15th of September, 1891, Henry Howard sold a bottle of liquor to an Indian, a citizen of British Columbia, Great Britton. Howard was arrested due to it being illegal to sell to this Indian. On the 17th day of September, Howard petitions for a writ of Habeas Corpus with his attorney, Frank Hartley Jones. The petition is based on the fact that under the Jay treaty between the US and Great Britton, it is legal to sell the liquor and therefore he was wrongfully jailed by the Honorable Von Tobel. On the 18th, his writ was granted by T.J. Humes and he was to be delivered the courthouse on the 19th by the Sheriff, J.H. Woolery. Woolery delivers Howard to the courthouse on September 19th, 1891 at 9:30 am. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Lee Young petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Young claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Young was likely arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct, though no newspaper article listed his name. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Young are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Myers, the petitioner and bound party, filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus to be released from McNeil Island Penitentiary and be transferred to the custody of Morningside Sanitarium. Further, Myers filed an appeal in forma pauperis in accordance with a previous poverty affidavit he had filed. Myers states that he was a patient at Morningside Hospital (at the time, Sanitarium) in Oregon and that he escaped from the hospital during a period when he was not well. Myers was incarcerated for the crimes of obtaining goods under false pretences from J. A. Donald and Aubrey Pinkiert (two separate counts), and for obtaining money under false pretenses from Joe Anichich during his time in Alaska. In his argument, Myers stated that because he was not discharged from the hospital but escaped, he should still be seen as legally "insane" and should stay in Morningside until he can be legally discharged by the hospital. Additonally, Myers stated that at the Penitentiary, he was put into involuntary servitude, not as punishment for any crime, and therefore, it was a violation of his rights. Judge Edward Cushman found that Myers was provided a fair trial and indicted fairly and was, therefore, legally convicted, and the petition was forever dismissed in 1916, but further documents are in the case file from 1917, so the fate of the party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 6, 1920, Mae and Charles Smith were married in Omaha, Nebraska. Their marriage did not last long: Mae filed for divorce in the October of 1921. She must have been heavily pregnant at the time, as she gave birth to Charles's son, Delbert Dean Smith, on January 8, 1921. Despite being summoned to court repeatedly, Charles never showed up. Finally, on July 12, 1921, judge Charles A. Goss granted Mae Smith a divorce "on the grounds of extreme cruelty." He also gave her complete custody of Delbert. Despite this, around June 1, 1922, Charles came to Mae's house and asked to take the child on a short visit. She acquiesced, but Charles and her son never returned. She believed he had taken him back to Sterling in Johnson County, Nebraska, where Charles now lived. In an attempt to regain custody of her son, Mae filed a writ of habeas corpus on November 6, 1922, but it was returned unserved—presumably because, like the earlier divorce trial, Charles refused to answer summons and evaded legal authorities. She filed another writ on April 2, 1923, but 11 days later, this writ was returned unserved as well. Finally, the case was dismissed for a want of prosecution on January 21, 1924. Census and Social Security records indicate that Delbert spent the rest of his childhood with Charles and his second wife, Lola. The family even moved back to Omaha in time for the 1930 census. It is unknown if either Delbert or Mae knew that the other lived in the same city during this period of time.

Summary of Proceedings:
E. F. Humason filed for a writ of habeas corpus from the Spokane County Jail on April 20, 1891. His legal representation alleged that his imprisonment was illegal because he “was held to answer for an infamous crime without presentation of indictment by a grand jury,” and that the information brought against him was illegal, as well as his conviction. Humason had been convicted of grand larceny in a well-known case of cattle theft. Overall, his case tested the statutory code and state constitution of the newly-established State of Washington.

Judge C. H. Hanford denied Humason’s writ on the grounds that he had received adequate due process in relation to his conviction.

Summary of Proceedings: In April 1878, Henry Palm was arrested in Olympia, Washington, charged with murder, and jailed to await a grand jury trial. In May 1878, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that he should not be jailed for eight months to await the next convening of the grand jury. The judge granted his petition, but the fate of Palm is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: John Bowler and Edward McCrink (called McCrinkle in the petition) were arrested for the charge of perjury after they testified at trial that they were beaten with brass knuckles by James H. Bennett. They filed for a habeas petition on the basis that the commissioner who arrested them did not have jurisdiction or probable cause to detain them. The petition was granted, and upon hearing the evidence, the judge granted the writ of Habeas Corpus as well. Following the writ, the judge returned to the original trial of assault and the petitioner’s attorney called multiple witnesses.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 28, 1895, Lai Kwong filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Chee Chung Quock. Lai Kwong claimed that Chee Chung Quock was being illegally detained on the Steamship Signal by Captain M. Bendergard. Lai Kwong further claimed that Chee Chung Quock was born in San Francisco and traveled to China for an education. Lai Kwong stated that Chee Chung Quock was a US Citizen who was exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Bellinger granted the writ and ordered Chee Chung Quock released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: One May 13, 1918, a complaint was brought against eighteen-year-old, Harold Kent, for disorderly conduct. In the municipal court, Kent was sentenced to 90 days of service in the county jail. On May 16, 1918, Kent's father, J. W. Kent, filed for habeas against the county sheriff, Michael Clark, arguing that no offense for such charge can be found under the statutes of Nebraska. A writ was issued and sustained; Kent was released same day.

Summary of Proceedings: In April, 1894, Ah Jack was arrested on the grounds of being unlawfully in the United States and was subsequently ordered deported to China. Ah was held by an unnamed "Keeper of the Jail of King County". Ah Jack petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus stating he was not informed he had to register his name in accordance with laws of the United States. This was likely a provision of one of the many Chinese Exclusion laws that were passed during this time requiring Chinese laborers in the US to register with the government and receive a certificate of their lawful presence. In a petition of intervention, the United States attorney stated that Ah Jack's petition should be denied as he has been arrested for being unlawfully in the United States and ordered deported to British Columbia and China multiple times prior. The result of the proceedings and fate of Ah Jack are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
S. L. Fowler filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he was held without charge in the King County Jail. In his writ, his lawyer stated that Fowler was being illegally held by King County Sheriff, John Stringer, “to compel your petitioner to make incriminatory statements regarding an alleged murder that occured in Auburn, Washington, on December 19, 1917, and to compel the petitioner to give information which he does not possess regarding the killing.” According to newspaper coverage, Fowler was “in jail as a suspect” for a murder in Auburn. 

The fate of Fowler is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In January of 1874, Han Lee filed a petition on behalf of Seo Kim, a Chinese woman who was allegedly being held by Ah Chow in the Seattle area. Han Lee believed that Ah Chow intended to cross the border into Victoria and sell Seo Kim. It was also known that a man named Ah Ying had obtained a marriage license to marry Seo Kim, which Han Lee believed Seo Kim desired. Han Lee previously bought Seo Kim in China and believed that he was losing his property. Ah Chow denied that he was detaining Seo Kim. When ordered by the court to bring her in, he claimed that he had never held her captive nor had he any intent on selling her across the border. Even after a court order was issued, he refused to appear before Judge Orange Jacobs. The sheriff, H.G. Thornton was ordered to arrest and bring Seo Kim into custody. He brought her in but was not able to bring Ah Chow in at that time. A warrant was then issued for Ah Chow’s arrest, but Thornton could not find him, claiming he must have been hiding out somewhere in Seattle. Seo Kim was discharged from custody and the petition was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: Alex Kisil, the bound party, entered the country 5 to 6 years prior to his arrest from Austria-Poland and joined the IWW, a union organization. On May 8th, 1918, the bound party was arrested on a warrant issued by the Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson (unnamed in the petition). The bound party was charged with being an alien, advocating or teaching the destruction of property, and being likely to become a public charge. On July 5th, 1918,S. J. Burford, immigration inspector, interrogated the bound party on these issues and found the charges to be substantiated. The attorney for the petitioner does not agree that the questions were relevant. On January 8th, 1919, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed. The fate of the petition and the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 21, 1887, Moses Cline (also known as BM Cline or Moses Brown Cline) filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of his four-year-old daughter, Elnora Cline, in the Third Judicial District Court in King County, Washington. Elnora had been living with her mother and Moses' wife, Ella Cline, in Seattle since April 15, 1887. Moses claimed that as a single mother, Ella would be unable to maintain the best interest of Elnora and that as a caring and capable father he not only possessed a legal right to custody of his child, but that Elnora would benefit from being in his custody. In response, Ella maintained that she had a legal right to custody of Elnora and that Elnora's age required the care of her mother. While the remaining files for the case are missing following Ella's return to the writ, Elnora seems to have gone into Moses' custody for a brief period, given that Moses listed Elnora as the sole other member of his household on the 1889 Kitsap County Census.

Summary of Proceedings: Sylvia and Audrey Brewer were allegedly concealing Edna May Smith without the legal right to custody. They were not given custody rights by any court order or judgement. The petitioner, M. E. Smith, was the father of Edna and asserts that he was able to care for her and that he is entitled to legal custody of the child. On 3 September 1914, Judge A. L. Sutton ordered that a writ be issued in favor of Merle E. Smith, directed to Sylvia and Audrey Brewer. The defendants, Sylvia and Audrey Brewer, were the sisters of Prudence A. Smith, who was the mother of Edna M. Smith. On 23 March 1906, “Prudence A. Smith against Merle E. Smith” was filed in Fremont County, Iowa. This petition for divorce between the two parties granted Prudence A. Smith the sole and absolute custody of Edna M. Smith. Following the divorce, Prudence moved to Nebraska to find employment. She lived with her two sisters, both of whom were employed. M. A. Stephenson, one of Edna’s guardians, was a man of high standing whose worth exceeded $50,000. The sisters jointly owned 295 acres of land in Fremont County, Iowa which grossed $1,000/year in income. Merle Smith visited Edna in Nebraska one year after the divorce, but had not seen or contacted the child since that time. Prudence died on 11 July 1914. “In the Matter of the Guardianship of the Person and Property of Edna M. Smith, minor heir of Prudence Smith,” was filed on 15 July 1914 granting guardianship of Edna M. Smith to Sylvia Brewer and M. A. Stephenson. They had been the guardians of Edna since that date. Merle Smith had not contributed to support the child in any way since the divorce. He did not make any effort to contact her until 2 September 1914 when he demanded that Audrey Brewer tell him where Edna was. The defendants were returning home when they were accosted by Frank Smith, brother of Merle E. Smith, Frank called for Merle who arrived with three police officers. Smith demanded the child, but the defendants refused to turn Edna over to Merle. The defendants asserted that they had reason to fear that Frank and Merle intended to kidnap Edna and to harass and disturb the defendants. On 8 September 1914, the cause was dismissed without prejudice.

Summary of Proceedings: Howard M. Findley, an attorney for the Washington State Board of Law Examiners, petitioned for writs of habeas corpus ad testificandum on the behalf of Earl and Cecil Jordan, who were being held in the Washington State Penitentiary. Findley claimed the two Jordans were necessary witnesses against Homer E. Turner, who was facing disbarment for committing acts involving moral turpitude, dishonesty, and corruption. The court granted the petition, but the case outcome and fates of Earl and Cecil Jordan are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Ah Fook and Billie Louie petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham and Mayor Hiram C. Gill. Fook and Louie claimed that they were being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail without warrant or due legal process. The case file does not reveal a charge, but newspaper records indicate the men were affiliated with the Hip Sing tong, an organization of Chinese immigrants allegedly tied to criminal activity, and were arrested in connection to the shooting of a man affiliated with a rival tong. The case outcome and the fates of Fook and Louie are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In Boston, Massachusetts John E. Foye was accused of corrupting a juror, Charles H. Milliken, via bribery. Allegedly, this happened during the February 3rd, 1899 court case in which V. J. Richard Mulrey and Thomas J. Scollans were accused of fraud. Based on newspaper coverage and the transcripts of Milliken’s testimony during his own trial for accepting bribery, Foye, Scollans, and their acquaintance Oliver Downing were thought to have been conspiring together to corrupt multiple jurors. Foye’s alleged bribe was quickly discovered, and Judge T. H. Cann issued a warrant for Foye’s arrest. Despite Foye seemingly not appearing in court, a trial was held in Judge Albert Mason’s court beginning on March 11th. By April 3rd, Foye, still seemingly not present, was indicted. A second warrant was then issued for his arrest by Judge Mason. On April 21st, Boston police officer Michael J. Morrissey reported that he was unable to find Foye, who he believed left town for Washington around February 7th. The source of Morrissey's information was a telegram he received from C.S. Reed, Chief of Police in Washington. 
On April 21st, a requisition was issued from Massachusetts governor Roger Wolcott to Washington governor John Rankin Rogers asking for Foye to be apprehended, and recommending Morrissey for the job. On April 29th, Governor Rogers ordered Foye’s arrest. Over the next few days, Morrissey went to Washington to find and arrest Foye. On May 1st, Foye and his lawyer John F. Dore, along with colleagues Solen T. Williams and Jenner, filed a petition of habeas corpus claiming Foye never committed the crime of which he was accused, and that the original charges were unclear. They felt Morrissey and Reed detained Foye unlawfully. The petition was allowed by Judge Orange Jacobs of the King County Superior Court. On the same day, Sheriff A. T. Van De Vanter came and took Foye into his custody in preparation for the hearing of his petition. Foye paid his bail, and Van de Vanter released Foye to his sureties, Ole Anderson and Benjamin J. Bernhardt. The hearing date, originally the 5th of May, was pushed back to May 8th. 
On May 8th, Foye and his lawyers then reapplied for a petition of habeas corpus, arguing that Foye did not leave Massachusetts to flee the charges against him. The said Foye had been living and working in Washington for a year, and subsequently should not be detained. They again claimed that Foye did not commit any crime, nor did the indictment made against him include any punishable offense based on the laws of Massachusetts or Washington. They also argued that the indictment by clerks John P. Manning and John R. Campbell was invalid due to them not being the proper people to certify to an indictment. They next claimed he was not in Massachusetts for the end of the trial in which he was accused of bribing the jury, nor was he in the state at the time of his indictment. Finally, they stated that the testimony of David C. Sullivan, the evidence used to connect him to the bribery case, was invalid due to Sullivan soon after being charged with perjury for his statements. Judge Orange Jacobs heard the petition in court and ruled against Foye, ordering that Foye be remanded to the custody of Morrissey. Foye’s lawyers then appealed his decision to the Washington Supreme Court. The Supreme Court quickly confirmed Judge Jacob’s ruling. Judge Jacobs then called Foye to surrender himself to the jurisdiction of the Superior Court, but Foye was unable to be found, and was presumed to be on the run from the law once more. Foye’s sureties were then ordered to pay his bail, or have their property seized. Foye’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1920, David Goertzen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that he was being illegally detained by the U.S. Army at Fort Omaha on a pretended charge of desertion. Goertzen claimed that two years earlier he had received permission from his local draft board in Hamilton County, Nebraska to travel to Saskatchewan for harvesting season since he was exempt from combatant service and unlikely to be called up. He remained in Canada until some time after Armistice Day in 1918, and was arrested back in Nebraska in March 1920. Goertzen was court-martialed in May, dishonorably discharged, and sentenced to two years hard labor at Fort Leavenworth, which was reduced to one year's confinement at Fort Omaha. Upon hearing the evidence, his petition was denied, and Goertzen presumably remanded into military custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Nora Sullivan, an Irish born immigrant, came to the United States through New York City in 1916. Sullivan then moved to Butte, Montana, and the next year stayed at the Montana State Hospital for the Insane for a few months to cure her rheumatism. In April of 1919, Sullivan moved to Seattle, Washington. Shortly after, she was taken to the Bureau of Immigration Detention Station, where officials were attempting to deport her for being "an insane alien". On August 17, 1919, Sullivan filed a writ of habeas corpus in an attempt to be released from the station and to remain in the United States. Judge Jeremiah Netherer allowed the writ and ordered Nora Sullivan and Henry M. White, the Commissioner of Immigration at Seattle, to court. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 28, 1916, J. Sidney Smith was convicted of conspiracy to use the United States mails for a defrauding scheme and was sentenced to two years in the United States Penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas along with a fine of $10,000. On September 29, 1921, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that newspaper coverage of the trial made the jurors biased and unable to be fair and impartial. He cited the 5th and 6th Amendments of the Constitution in his petition. His writ was denied and his fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 3, 1917, Franklin Kapps, a Chicago man taking the train through Nebraska with his wife and child, was arrested without a warrant. According to the Omaha Daily Bee, he was accused of larceny after he had taken some documents from his former office. With the help of his attorney, Daniel H. Horrigan, he filed a writ of habeas corpus for his freedom against the Omaha chief of police Henry W. Dunn on February 5. Judge Willis S. Sears not only allowed the writ, but ordered his release on February 6th of that year.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 25th, 1917, the Omaha Police Department filed a complaint against and arrested E. C. Smeeth for allegedly obtaining goods under false pretenses. He was charged for acquiring $25 worth of goods and sentenced to thirty days in county jail. A few days after his sentencing, he filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus claiming that his actions did not violate any ordinances of the City of Omaha. Unfortunately, the case file does not show whether or not the petition resulted in an allowance or denial for a writ of Habeas.

Summary of Proceedings: Fred Neff claimed to have been unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Henry Dunn and Steve Maloney. He claimed to have been taken before Vince Hasacall (Police Magistrate) and was given an appeal bond to the sum of $300. Neff was waiting to see if Hascall would take a cash bond or would require a personal bond. However, twenty four hours later, Hascall came to the conclusion that he wouldn’t take a cash bond and that his chance for a personal bond had expired. Therefore he claimed to be illegally restrained of his liberty. The petition was granted, however the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In October 1924, Perry Hartness petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully detained of his liberty by Michael L. Endres, Sheriff of Douglas County, The petition alleged that Hartness was placed under arrest on October 11th, 1924, released on a cash bond of $25, to appear in Court on the on the 13th. Hartness stated he was placed in county jail for no known reason, and he has not committed any crime nor violated any law. Judge Stauffer allowed the writ, and the appearance docket states the application was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 26th, 1918, Edwin Ekstrom was arrested by an Immigration Inspector on charges issued by the Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson, alleging that he was an alien, had advocated or taught the unlawful destruction of property, and was likely to become a public charge. On July 5th, 1918, Ekstrom was brought before another Immigration Inspector, S. J. Burford, who took testimony from Ekstrom in which he claimed to not believe in the I.W.W anymore. On November 14th, 1918, a petition was filed which alleged that the questions in the hearing were not material, claims that the Secretary of Labor was taking too long with his immigration status, that there was no evidence for the charges, and that a copy of the hearing transcripts were not being produced for the defense. On November 3rd, 1918, Judge Neterer denied the writ but allowed for resubmission on December 3rd or if being threatened with deportation. On February 10th, 1919, the writ was again denied.

Summary of Proceedings: Fred E. Beers petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his daughter, Gladys Irene Beers, against former wife Irene Frallicciardi, her father Horace J. Walker, and his wife Gertrude J. Walker. Fred Beers alleged that the three respondents were holding Gladys Beers illegally, as Fred Beers had been granted full custody in the divorce proceedings Frallicciardi and himself. Frallicciardi denied this and claimed that she was originally granted custody of Gladys Beers in the divorce proceedings, but that custody was given to Fred Beers after he motioned to modify the divorce agreement. She also claimed that Fred Beers only paid alimony for two months before leaving the state of Washington. Fred Beers admitted that he left Washington during a period of mental illness, but claimed he did pay his alimony. He alleged that, upon his return to Washington, he found that Gladys Beers was living with the Walkers, whom Fred Beers claimed were show people, spiritualists, and free-lovers. The writ was allowed, and the judge ruled that Fred Beers was able to regain custody of Gladys Beers. Frallicciardi and the Walkers appealed to the Supreme Court of the State of Washington, but the original judgement was upheld.

Summary of Proceedings: Kate E. Cusack petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her daughter, Annie Regar. Cusack claimed Regar was being withheld from her custody against her will by Margaret D. Hendricks and her husband G. A. Hendricks, and that they were planning to take Regar with them to California. Margaret Hendricks returned claiming that Cusack placed Regar in her care in a state of destitution, that Hendricks had provided care for Regar for many years, and that Cusack had never been denied access to Regar. Hendricks maintained that she cared for Regar like she was her own child and feared returning her to the custody of Cusack and her husband. Judge Osborn allowed the writ and ordered that Regar be returned to the custody of Cusack.

Summary of Proceedings:
On January 9, 1918, a group of men filed for habeas corpus while held in the Seattle City Jail. Their petition revealed a complicated series of legal conflicts related to I.W.W activity. Of the seventeen people in the bound party, there were a total of eight separate outcomes based on a variety of charges involving state and federal authorities. 

Federal authorities indicted James H. Manning during a grand jury that took place in Chicago, Illinois between April 6 and September 28, 1917. The Grand Jury found Manning had violated federal statutes in relation to the “execution of U.S. law in carrying on war” and also incitied “disloyalty in the military.” The U.S Marshal of the Western District of Washington State, Northern Division, issued a warrant for Manning on January 10, 1918. The U.S Marshal of the Western District of Washington State, Northern Division, also issued a warrant for J. Mills, also known as Jackson Leonard on January 8, 1918, for failure “to register for military service of the United States as required by law.” 

Joel Warren, Seattle Chief of Police, held Oscar Johnson after Johnson’s conviction of being a disorderly person. 

Federal officials were investigating several  members of the group, including Antone Schmid, under suspicion of being “a German alien,” J O’Brien for “his violation of the Selective Service Act,” and Sergio (Sergig) Fedorouo, Sam Rovinson, E. Ludwig, Sol Ehrlich and H. Lea for “violation of the Emigration Act of February, 1917.”

Warren stated in the return of the writ that H. Burns, George Pitkin, A. J. Helin, Peter Keenan, J. Wamese, and H. Lasky were no longer in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Austin Campbell was arrested on June 23, by Chief of Police, John Briggs. Mary Campbell and attorney John M. Macfarland, petitioned on behalf of her husband, Austin Campbell, on June 28 for habeas against John Briggs. Mary Campbell argued to Judge Lee S. Estelle that no charge has been brought against her husband since arrest and that he is being held too long under suspicious character - claiming this to be a violation of the statute of the State of Nebraska. A different judge, Willis G. Sears, issues writ. On June 29, the writ was sustained, and Austin Campbell was released.

Summary of Proceedings: James Ryan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid. Ryan alleged that he was being held illegally at Spokane County Jail under the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. He claimed he was denied a hearing for six months, denied his right to counsel, and compelled to give evidence against himself under intimidation. The court’s judgement stated that it appeared Ryan had been discharged for unknown reasons, and thus his writ was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: Marian L. Burton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Commissioner of Health J. S. McBride. Burton alleged she was being quarantined in the City Emergency Hospital against her will and was ready and able to pay for a private physician should she be released. McBride responded, confirming he had Burton in custody in accordance with city ordinances and that she was infected with a dangerously contagious form of syphilis. Due to the brevity of the case file, the outcome of the case and the fate of Burton are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Oh Chow petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of  Ung Sin, Ung Hung Hing, and Ung Doon. They are confined on the Steamship Signal, seized by T. J. Black, after a voyage from the Port of Victoria to the Port of Portland. Oh Chow appeared as their witness at the port and obtained affidavits certifying their merchant status before they returned to China for a visit. However, T. J. Black, the Collector of Customs, refused to accept the witness of certificates, insisting they were laborers and in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. The judge accepted Oh Chow as a witness and verified the certificates of merchant status, granting the writ and releasing all three from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 27th, 1921, Harold Savage filed for and received an order allowing for a writ of Habeas Corpus after being arrested and held in custody by Marshall Eberstein and Charles Van Dusen. In his petition Savage presented that he had been arrested on suspicion of him having committed a crime in Texas, but he had no knowledge of indictment or complaint against him in either Texas or Nebraska. It was the same day that the response of Eberstein and Van Dusen was presented in court. They presented that they had Savage in custody on the basis of an issued warrant from Nebraska charging him with being a fugitive from justice. It was also presented that there was an indictment in Texas that charged him with robbery with a firearm. It was May 1921 that the court dismissed the cause. The fate of Savage is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: George Rigby was arrested for vagrancy by Sheriff E. F. Brailey and brought to the Police Court. Under the testimony of Detective Savage, who claimed Rigby to be a thief with a bad record, Rigby was sentenced to 90 days in jail. On November 2, Rigby and attorneys, M. L. Beckwith and John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas. Rigby claimed that there was no evidence to support the charge, and that he was at home with money during the time of his arrest. His petition was granted by Judge Lee S. Estelle, but Rigby's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Rainbow, James Fisher, and Peter Decora were Native police officers on the Winnebago Reservation in Thurston County, Nebraska. The three men were charged with enforcing a Department of the Interior regulation prohibiting anyone from conducting business on the Reservation on days that federal officers were distributing lease payments. On October 18, 1906, an attorney and member of the Omaha Nation named Thomas Sloan tried collecting fees on a payment distribution day, and so Rainbow, Fisher, and Decora escorted him off of the Reservation. Sloan sued the officers for assault in the Thurston County District Court. Once jailed, the trio refused to pay bail, petitioning instead for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the judge concluded that Rainbow, Fisher, and Decora had no right to enforce the Department of the Interior regulation without congressional authorization and remanded them to the custody of their jailer. The officers appealed the decision to the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit in St. Louis, Missouri, which overturned the circuit court decision and ordered the release of the three men.

Summary of Proceedings:
Barney Slomen and Harry Smith were arrested by John H. Boyle for possessing an alleged grains of morphine, a derivative of opium and coca leaves, and he and Smith were indicted separately and both sentenced to five months of jail time. Slomen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, alleging unfair trial and the sentencing was without authority of law. Judge Neterer sides with Slomen. Newspaper coverage indicated that Slomen was released. 
Interestingly, the newspapers also reported that Barney had previously been arrested for morphine related charges. 
Prison records list him as residing in McNeil Island Penitentiary for "dope" possession in February of 1917, indicating this was a recurring issue for Slomen.

Summary of Proceedings: Andrew Anderson was arrested by Hudson, a policeman of Spokane, Washington, from the order of the sheriff of Spokane, charging Anderson with being a fugitive from justice of the state of Washington. He was imprisoned without any complaint for said offense or warrant being issued from Omaha. He made a petition alleging he was unlawfully deprived for vagrancy charges. It was found that the vagrancy charges were not issued in good faith but were made to subterfuge to aid the requisition from Washington. He was released and then arrested again in the courthouse corridor upon a complaint ordered by the judge of the Omaha police court for having opposed and resisted a police officer in May. C. R. Scott decided that the warrant of commitment was contrary to the state's law and was illegal. The judge, Scott, decided that Anderson was unlawfully deprived of his liberty, so Anderson was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Evelyn Burress Miller died of the measles on May 18, 1882. She was survived by her husband, Louis Miller; her infant daughter, also named Evelyn Miller; and her parents, Thomas and Catherine Burress. In the wake of his wife's death, Louis left his daughter with her grandparents for several months. When he tried to retrieve Evelyn, Thomas and Catherine refused to surrender her. In the summer of 1883, he unsuccessfully petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the Nemaha County and district courts. Louis remarried a few years later and resumed his attempt to re-establish custody of Evelyn. When the Burresses refused, Louis, now living in Ohio, petitioned for habeas relief in federal district court in 1889. After a lengthy hearing, which the newspapers covered in salacious detail, the court determined that Louis should have custody of his daughter, who was now eight years old. Thomas and Catherine appealed in federal circuit court to no avail. Eventually, the parties agreed that Louis would have custody of Evelyn but that her grandparents could visit at reasonable times. However, when Louis tried to board an eastbound train with his daughter in Council Bluffs, Iowa, Catherine assaulted him. She and Thomas seized their granddaughter and returned to Nebraska. The case file makes no mention of Evelyn's ultimate fate.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 24, 1923, Aurellio Coliginna submitted a petition for a writ of habeas corpus for the unlawful imprisonment of his 11-year-old daughter, Vincenzzina Coliginna. His petition alleged that, without informing him, his unnamed wife (who was also Vincenzzina Coliginna's mother) had eloped to Illinois two years ago with a man named Capizza and taken the child with her. He further alleged that the Acting Chief of Police and the Chief of Detectives of Omaha were illegally holding Vincenzzina Coliginna at the mother's request while refusing to allow him "care and custody and control" of the child. He also stated that the mother was unfit to have custody of the child because she was living unlawfully with Capizza. In turn, Vincenzzina's mother accused Aurellio of kidnapping his daughter from Joliet, Illinois. She said that he had lured both of them into a car, then thrown her out of the speeding car as they drove towards Lemont, Illinois. Judge Charles A. Goss issued an order on the same day commanding P. F. Dillon and Charles F. Van Deusen to show cause for the child's detention. The outcome of the petition and the fate of the child are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 9, 1913, George Roy Wood and his attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which alleged that Wood was being held by Edward Cudihee without a warrant or official charge, and that Wood was being denied bail. Cudihee produced a warrant dated June 11, 1913, and documentation which alleged that Wood was a fugitive from justice from Indiana. In Indiana, Wood had been charged with “feloniously causing and encouraging” Nola Daniels, 16 years old, to “have sexual intercourse” with him. The documents stated that Wood was over twenty years old at the time, but did not specifically list his age. Frater set bail, which Wood paid. Wood failed to show up to court on June 11 as ordered, and was charged with contempt of court. He then surrendered himself on June 12. Wood and his attorney filed several exceptions to Cudihee’s returns, one of which stated that he should not be in Cudihee’s custody due to there not being an extradition warrant from Indiana. Frater allowed that exception, but denied that he should not be in custody at all. Frater denied his petition, and Wood's custody was transferred to Edward R. Nichols, an agent from the state of Indiana. Wood and his attorney stated their intention to appeal to the Supreme Court.

After hearing the evidence, Hansen was remanded to the custody of the superintendent of the state institution.

Summary of Proceedings:
On July 13th, 1904, W.H. Harris petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus in the King County Superior Court, State of Washington. Harris had been arrested on May 26th and held until June 7th, when he was taken before the court of J.B. Gordon Justice of the Peace for Seattle Precinct, where he was charged with “living with a prostitute”. On July 5th, he was taken into the courthouse before Boy J. Tallman and a jury of 12 men, where the jury returned a verdict of “guilty as charged”. He was sentenced to one year at the State Prison and a $1000 fine. However, Harris pointed out in his petition that his case was irregular and illegal as the jury that had returned the verdict had been selected for June 1904, but returned that said verdict in July 1904. Judge Bell granted the writ of Habeas Corpus. Ed Cudihee, the holding party and respondent, argued that Harris was still found guilty and should still be charged. 

According to a Seattle newspaper at the time, Harris was not released from jail by Bell. It was apparently revealed that Harris had pressured the court into using June’s jury as he would not have otherwise received a hearing until July, and thus his argument was invalid.

Summary of Proceedings: C. W. Benson accused Allen Sharp of being insane and reported him as such in an attempt to have Sharp committed to the Nebraska Hospital for the Insane. Sharp was detained by Sheriff Trude and taken to be examined by the hospital. Dr. C. W. Walden examined Sharp and concluded that Sharp was not insane, but he was an inebriate and addicted to alcohol, and petitioned the hospital board to commit Sharp, and the board agreed to commit him for 3 years. Sharp filed for a writ of habeas in order to escape detainment at the hospital, claiming that, without evidence, the hospital board had “pretended to make a finding that your petitioner was an inebriate” in order to justify detaining him. Judge Pemberton granted Sharp’s petition, and eventually found that he was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty and should be released.

Summary of Proceedings: Evaline L. Young, petitioner, filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her daughter, Mertie L. Young, against her former husband, Samuel J. Young. He had left her to move to Omaha, but apparently missed his young daughter so much that he decided to kidnap her from her mother's home in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Omaha Daily Bee suspected that his impulsive behavior was the result of "mental paroxysm." Judge Melville Hopewell allowed the writ due to the "tender age and delicate health" of Mertie Young, who is sixteen months old and had an "enfeebled constitution." The judge determined that Evaline was the proper caretaker in this scenario.

Sam Pong was arrested and jailed in Olympia, Washington on charges of embezzlement. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. The petition itself is nearly eight pages. N.B. Witness testimony notes included in this case file contain several signatures employing Chinese characters.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 28, 1919, a complaint was filed accusing Gussie Burns of 808 N 16th St. of vagrancy by J.B. Murray, the city prosecutor. Gussie was tried before James M. Fitzgerald, a Douglas County police magistrate on the next day, found guilty, and sentenced to 30 days in the county jail. However, she had also been inspected by Omaha's health commissioner and diagnosed with a venereal disease, and was thus confined to the Women's Detention Home at 1915 Dodge St. This was not the first time that this had happened to Gussie—in fact, she was discharged from the detention home as having been cured of a venereal disease shortly before her arrest on November 29. She points out that it was unlikely that she would have caught another disease in such a short period of time. According to Gussie, Alta Berger, the superintendent, and other authorities at the detention home refused to release her until she had "an operation for the removal of certain tubes"—perhaps sterilization. Gussie refused to undergo the surgery unless she could pick the surgeon performing it, which the Detention Home did not allow. Thus, on March 2, 1919, long after her 30-day sentence had elapsed and she had responded well to the treatment for venereal disease, she filed a writ of habeas corpus with the assistance of her attorney William E. Lovely of the firm Lovely and Lovely. It was allowed to issue by judge Lee S. Estelle. The writ was initially addressed to Berger, chief of police Marshall Eberstein and health commissioner Dr. J.F. Edwards, although it was only served to Berger. There was a hearing before judge Charles A. Goss on March 4, 1920, and the writ and return was filed on March 9, 1920. Surviving records do not indicate the outcome of the case, but an Omaha Bee article from January 10, 1919 describes Gussie Burns being held down by doctors at the Detention Home until she "quieted down." According to that same paper, she was again arrested on May 3, 1919 for the same charge of vagrancy after being found in a "Dope House" with cocaine on the premises.

Summary of Proceedings: Clifford B. Smith was arrested in Lancaster County on a warrant from Dakota Territory, which claimed he was guilty of grand larceny. Police Judge A. F. Parsons ordered Smith's detention with the intention of keeping him in police custody until he could be delivered to Dakota Territory authorities. Smith petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against the jailer A. C. Langdon, which was unsuccessful. The verdict was later overturned in the Nebraska Supreme Court in April 1887 by Chief Justice Samuel Maxwell.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 12th, 1916, Robert Morrison was arrested and charged with vagrancy by the Omaha Police Department. He was originally sentenced to be held in county jail for thirty days, however, after his thirty days expired, the Sheriff refused to release him. On May 15th, Morrison filed a Habeas Corpus petition with the hopes of being released. Judge Willis G. Sears heard his case, and allowed Morrison's writ. Soon following, Morrison was granted freedom from his incarceration.

Summary of Proceedings: William Gerald was indicted on 44 total counts for violating Sec. 9 of the Act of Sept. 13, 1888, and Sec. 8 of the Act of Feb. 20, 1907, by attempting to smuggle 22 alien Chinese persons into the United States through Mexico. On October 19th, 1914, Gerald filed a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he had only committed one offense, not 44, as he attempted to import one vessel or boat, and that he was entitled to a deduction in his sentence for good behavior. In response, Warden Halligan stated that he had forfeited his good time by fighting during a ball game. Judge Cushman dismissed the writ on November 9th, 1914, and ruled that Gerald would remain in the custody of Warden Halligan at McNeil Island Penitentiary.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 23, 1920, Nellie P. Christy, neé Crother, asked for a divorce from her husband of 15 years, Robert E. Christy. She accused him of committing repeated acts of adultery with their maid, Beulah Shepherd. Robert had become infatuated with the 17-year-old, and continually defied Nellie's attempts to fire her. He also refused to support his wife or their six children, so Nellie had been forced to take in roomers and work in a laundry. At some point, he had moved away from the family's home in Fullerton to live in Omaha with Beulah. The divorce was granted, and Nellie was given custody of the three older children, with Robert maintaining custody of the three younger. Robert continued coming around Nellie's household after the divorce to verbally abuse and swear at her, as evidenced by a restraining order issued against him in September 1920. Robert filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, presumably against Nellie, for his daughter, Ruth Christy on July 12, 1923. Apparently, sometime before 1923, custody of all six children had been given to Robert after Nellie was accused of living with another man. This did not dissuade Nellie from visiting her children, and she violated a court order to do so. She accused Robert of poisoning her children's minds against her, and said that the gifts of hand-knitted stockings that she had mailed to them were returned to sender. On January 21, 1924, the case was dismissed for want of prosecution. This may be because the Christy family was involved in another legal case at the time—Ruth and Vera had danced in a public theater, which was illegal for girls under 14. Both had been sent to a reform school in Riverview on July 13, 1923.

Summary of Proceedings: In the fall of 1921, Willard Mathews negotiated a deal in the Douglas County district court whereby he would plead guilty to having embezzled funds from the Pioneer State Bank in Omaha, Nebraska, if the state would drop related charges against two of his colleagues. He was sentenced to between one and ten years at the state penitentiary. After unsuccessfully appealing his conviction in the state supreme court, Mathews petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court. He argued that he had embezzled funds during a window in which Nebraska had repealed one set of criminal statutes but not yet replaced them, and that therefore he had violated no law. After hearing the evidence, he was remanded to the custody of the warden.

Summary of Proceedings: Carrie Schastale filed this petition asserting that Sister Florida was being unlawfully deprived of her liberty by Sister Holdwig And St. Joseph Hospital in Douglas County, NE. “Sister Florida,” whose real name was unknown, was 14 or 15 years old at the time of the petition. She entered the institution for short-term care but was being held against her will for over a year, she was being deprived of her natural rights to “go and come” from the institution. Schastale filed the petition on behalf of “Sister Florida” because she was detained and unable to apply for the writ on her own. On 16 July 1914, Judge Sutton ordered that the writ be allowed.

Summary of Proceedings:
F. Vetter was a tailor who lived in Walla Walla, Washington. He was born in Prussia, and was married to another immigrant, Lina Vetter. He was described as a "quiet, industrious man." They had two children, Minnie, born in 1860, and Susannah, born in 1864. A saloon keeper in Walla Walla named Eugene Crowne would visit the house frequently. However, over time, Mr. Vetter became suspicious of his friend's relationship with Lina and forbade him from visiting the house. Eugene continued visiting Lina while Mr. Vetter was away, and eventually, on May 27, 1869, the two ran away together, taking Minnie and Susannah with them. Mr. Vetter immediately filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Susannah, and sheriff James McAuliff caught the family in Wallula, Washington on a boat headed to Oregon. Crowne also filed a habeas writ (See: Eugene Crowne v. James McAuliff) Crowne then filed a motion for dismissal on May 31, 1869, but it was denied. 
On June 1, 1869, Judge Joseph E. Wyche determined that the children should stay with the Sisters of Charity in Walla Walla until the divorce suit that Mr. Vetter initiated in the beginning of June was completed. Crowne was characterized as a serial philanderer, and Judge Wyche expressed contempt for him, saying that "no jury in the country would convict the slayer of the destroyer [of the family].” Crowne was to face a later trial for his adultery. Eugene and Lina got married in Walla Walla in September 1869, and the 1870 census reveals that Minnie and Susannah were still in the custody of the Sisters of Charity.

Summary of Proceedings: Eugene Ladd, a US Army officer in charge of the Fort Robinson post exchange, was arrested by the sheriff of Dawes County, Nebraska and charged with violating a state law against selling intoxicating liquors without a license. After making bail, Ladd petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. He argued that he had only sold wine and beer, which was expressly permitted by federal regulations, and that the state of Nebraska lacked the jurisdiction to prosecute him. After hearing the evidence, Ladd was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney H. Sylvester Garvin petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus ad testificandum on the behalf of Louie Zackary against Benewah County Sheriff C. A. Gregory. Garvin claimed that Gregory was detaining Zackary in the Benewah County Jail, but that Zackary was needed to testify in an ongoing criminal trial. The defendant of said trial, Nick Noce, was accused of selling intoxicating liquor in the form of vanilla extract to Zackary, an Indigenous person. Judge J. Stanley Webster allowed the petition, but no further information is revealed in the case file. The case outcome and the fate of Zackary are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Robert H. Robinson came to the court alleging that his six year old child, George G. P. Robinson, was deprived of his liberty by Mrs. William Kruse. After the death of the child's mother in 1890, Robert had employed Mrs. Kruse to care for George, as he traveled frequently in his job as a Pullman porter. While he never visited, he sent $2.50 a week for the child's care. He had asked for custody of the boy back as he had recently remarried—to a white woman, as the Evening World-Herald points out. George was also described as a "mulatto" in an Evening World-Herald article. Mrs. Kruse maintained that he owed her $200 for the child, and traveled from Council Bluffs to Omaha to try to avoid him. The writ was allowed and ultimately the child was ordered to be returned to his father, although the Evening World-Herald claims that he cried for Mrs. Kruse, who he saw as his mother, while exiting the courtroom.

Summary of Proceedings: He was charged with the crime of receiving and aiding in the concealment of stolen property, namely, diamonds of the value of $18,000. They were taken and carried away by Sherman W. Morris (Frank Sharcliffe) and stolen from William C. Pollack. The governor of Iowa,Albert B. Cummins, ordered the extradition of Thomas Dennison from Omaha on the grounds that he was a fugitive from justice. Dennison argued that the warrants of arrest and extradition were unlawful, that he was innocent and not related to the charge referred to, and that the constitutions of the states of Iowa, Nebraska, and the United States do not allow for his extradition back to Iowa. Dennison also argued that Elmer Thomas, the respondent attorney, conspired with people for the sole purpose of bringing Dennison into disrepute. The writ of Habeas Corpus was denied, Dennison requested a new trial on July 5th, a month after the case started, and it was denied.

Summary of Proceedings: In May 1924, a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus was issued for James Farrar on the basis he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Michael L. Endres, Sheriff of Douglas County. Farrar was sentenced to ninety days in jail under a complaint of vagrancy, and the petition alleged the mittimus was void and of no force as the authority, J.F. Powers, was not a state officer empowered to prosecute on behalf of the state of Nebraska, and that complaint failed to state a cause of action. The appearance docket stated the writ was denied and Farrar was remanded to custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1903, Olive Anderson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that minor children Walter and Edna Gross were being deprived of their liberty by Minnie Gross and Henry Smalley. Walter and Edna were the children of Olive Anderson's daughter, Freida Gross. Freida and the children's father, John Gross, had been divorced in 1902. Allegedly, John had left her because she was a vaudeville dancer. Freida left for Los Angeles, but John followed her, took the children, and placed them in  the custody of Minnie Gross, his sister-in-law. Judge Cornish granted the petition. In 1904, the court dismissed the cause "for want of prosecution." The next month, the petitioner showed in court and Judge Holmes reinstated the case. In 1906, the court again dismissed the cause. The fate of the bound party is unknown. However, a Lincoln Journal Star article implies that, as Freida didn't show up in Lincoln for the trial, since she worked in L.A., the judge simply asked John to take care of his children.

Summary of Proceedings: J. B. and Sarah Montgomery divorced in 1871. The Douglas County Circuit Court ordered that J. B., not Sarah, should have custody of their daughter, Mary Montgomery. Sarah refused to comply with the court order, prompting J. B. to petition for a writ of habeas corpus in Marion County, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the Marion County Circuit Court awarded custody of Mary to J. B., found Sarah to be in contempt, and ordered her to pay all court fees.

Summary of Proceedings:
On February 5, 1919, J. A. Kelly was arrested and placed in the Seattle City Jail. Five days after his arrest, Ralph S. Pierce assisted Kelly in filing a writ of habeas corpus. The writ argued that Kelly has no knowledge or idea why he was arrested and that he has been denied the right to speak with his attorney or any of his friends. Newspaper coverage of Kelly’s arrest notes that he was one of several I.W.W. members that were arrested in a wave of arrests on February 5, 1919. The Seattle Star states that these arrests were due to the King County Prosecuting Attorney, Fred C. Brown, declaring that the I.W.W. was illegal in King County and announcing that he will arrest and prosecute every member “who adheres to the organization, on a felony or criminal anarchy charge.” 

The case file does not state the outcome of this writ of habeas corpus, however, newspaper coverage followed the trial of J. A. Kelly and the other I.W.W. members for several months. In May, the papers highlight that J. A. Kelly received additional charges after a witness accused him and another I.W.W. member of plotting to murder the Seattle Chief of Police, Joel F. Warren. However, on June 5, the majority of the I.W.W. had their anarchy cases dropped and were released. J. A. Kelly was not released with this initial group due to having the extra charge for plotting to murder the Chief of Police. However, the following day the County Prosecuting Attorney dropped the remaining charges against Kelly and released him from custody. Brown stated in the paper that he did not believe he could get a jury to prosecute Kelly on the statements of one informant.

Summary of Proceedings:
This supplemental petition was filed because Rose claimed that no “proper or legal complaint” had been filed against him as required by law. He states that he is not a fugitive from justice but was visiting relatives in Omaha and had not left Ohio for the purpose of avoiding arrest. This file offers a restatement of the facts from the prior file; Rose was arrested wrongly, he was held without trial and no news of a trial being scheduled, he claims to have not committed any crime in Ohio and, thus, cannot be a fugitive from the law.

The form from the Justice of the Peace (George C. Cockrell) states that a complaint was submitted by Deputy Sheriff Louis Grebe on 31 August 1899 stating that on or about 1 August 1899, Rose was a fugitive from justice from Common Court in Cuyahoga County, Ohio. Deputy Grebe claims that Rose stood accused of the crime of embezzlement (a sum of $300), committed in Cuyahoga County, Ohio. 

George C. Cockrell (Justice of the Peace) signed an order on 1 September 1899 to the Keeper of the Common Jail to keep Angelo Rose for “further examination,” as he had been charged with committing the offence of Fugitive from Justice. An order that the Sheriff release Rose to allow him to appear in court on 1 September 1899 was submitted on 31 August 1899 by Coblyn L. Frank (Clerk). 

Judge B. S. Baker ordered that Rose’s writ be allowed and ordered that a writ of habeas corpus be issued in favor of Angelo Rose, returnable on 1 September 1899 at 2:00pm directed to Sheriff John McDonald.
