Summary of Proceedings: On February 14th, 1912, Jennie Columbia filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of her son, Robert Columbia. Robert was arrested five days prior to the writ and nothing was charged or filed against him in that time. Robert was stated to be 20 years old and in the bond of the applicant, his mother. On February 14th, Judge Gay approved the writ and commanded that Robert be in court the next day, February 15th. However, on the 15th, Judge Gay found that in between the filing of the application for the writ and the court session, charges had been filed and the custody of Robert was remanded to the sheriff of King County, Washington, Robert Hodge. The charges filed against him are unknown and his conviction is also unknown. The case seems to conclude on February 15th, but filing is not completed until April 26, 1912.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 27, 1827, Peter Jackson, the petitioner, brought a petition to the St. Louis County Court for the purpose of gaining his freedom from the Walton family. He had been moved throughout the United States alongside his enslavers William Walton, Henry Walton, and Elizabeth Langford; most recently between Missouri and Illinois. Citing his time in a free state, he sought to petition for his freedom from the Walton family after being beaten by James Walton, respondent, and brought back to Missouri from Illinois by George Walton, other respondent. It is unclear what the outcome of the case was, but further case records between Peter and the Waltons and documentation inside of the case file indicate the possibility of a mistrial caused by poor testimony on the part of Henry Walton.

Summary of Proceedings:
Former deputy sheriff of Milan, Washington, Charles A. Palmer filed for a writ of habeas corpus on November 18, 1922. John W. Pace held Palmer in the Washington State Penitentiary on a conviction of second-degree murder. Palmer shot and killed two men during an altercation in 1917. First, a jury in the Superior Court of Spokane County acquitted Palmer of first-degree murder. A second trial resulted in a guilty verdict for murder in the second degree.

The Federal District Court in Spokane dismissed Palmer’s application for a writ of habeas corpus on November 15, 1922.

“Slayer Charges Trial Injustice, Murderer, in Prison, Asks for a Writ of Habeas, Corpus,” The Spokesman-Review, November 1, 1922, Page 12.

Summary of Proceedings: Frederick Jacobsen filed a petition of for a writ of habeas corpus on August 20th, 1919, in hope of gaining custody of his daughter, Helen Jacobsen. Helen was, at the time, in the custody of her mother, Florence Jacobsen, and her maternal grandparents, Roy T. and May Earley. Florence Jacobsen had been living in her parents' home since she and Frederick Jacobsen divorced. Frederick Jacobsen's petition was specifically against the Earleys, claiming that they were keeping his daughter away from him, even refusing visits. The judge called for the pair of grandparents to produce young Helen in court to determine whether or not F. Jacobsen's writ would be allowed. The respondents argued that their daughter, Florence Jacobsen, had taken care of and been the sole provider for Helen Jacobsen since her birth, and that the father did not deserve custody. The case's outcome is unknown, but based on the appearance docket, it is evident that Helen remained in her mother's and grandparents' custody.

Summary of Proceedings: P. V. Abugadie was arrested on June 7, 1918. A week after his initial arrest, Abugadie filed for a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he is being illegally restrained of his liberty. In the petition, Abugadie claims that he is being held against his will by the Chief of Police, Joel Warren, and an unknown person, referred to as John Doe, at the Seattle City Jail. The petition states that the detention is unlawful because no charges have been brought against Abugadie. A second petition from P. V. Abugadie notes that Judge John S. Jurey approved Abugadie's writ of habeas corpus and ordered his release from custody. However, that second petition mentions that Abugadie would be rearrested a few days later by Joel Warren and the unknown, John Doe. Newspaper coverage indicates Abugadie was arrested on California charges of auto theft.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 5, 1924 Edward Ryan filed for a petition of a Writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Eva Ryan. The petition alleged that Eva Ryan was being detained in a Douglas County jail without a warrant on a pretended complaint from Kansas City Missouri. The petition also states that Eva Ryan is a resident of Nebraska and was not present in the state of Missouri when the alleged crime is believed to have taken place. After allegedly being deceived into signing a waiver of extradition to Missouri, the petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus was filed. On April 9, 1924 the application was granted and Eva Ryan was discharged.

Summary of Proceedings: James B. Palmer, the petitioner, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus to receive the custody of his 9-year-old daughter, Flora Palmer, from Victoria (Jennie) Hogan, the aunt of Flora. Victoria Hogan alleged that James Palmer and Flora's mother never married and that the mother of Flora is Hogan's sister (possibly cousin). Before her death, Hogan's sister gave custody of Flora Palmer to her. Further, Hogan alleged that James Palmer was a man of "vulgar and vicious" habits and financially unable to care for Flora. Palmer accused Hogan of kidnapping Flora on September 30, 1907 and threatening to shoot him if he tried to reclaim her. This was all complicated by the fact that, according to an Omaha Daily Bee article, Hogan was not only James's in-law, but also his ex-wife—while living with Victoria, James had grown attracted to her cousin, Flora's mother. It was then found that Palmer should be in the custody of Hogan, but the details of the new custody arrangement were not provided. Related to this case seems to be a proceeding that alludes to James B. Palmer stealing money from Victoria Hogan.

Summary of Proceedings: Ah Sing petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Sing claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Sing was arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Sing are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 22, 1905, Hugh J. O’Neill and his attorneys petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. While the actual petition is not included in the case file, the return and response to the return indicated that Hugh J. O’Neill was accused of owning a business that sold railroad tickets without the proper authority to do so. Additionally, O’Neill and his attorneys felt the warrant which imprisoned him, not included in the case file, was void and that the charge violated both the Washington state and United States constitutions. Judge Giliam denied the writ. O’Neill and his attorneys appealed to the Washington Supreme Court, who affirmed the previous ruling. O’Neill remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
James Marcil, an inmate at McNeil Island Penitentiary, was released on parole on August 12, 1911, but was returned to the penitentiary on May 19, 1912, for violating his parole. Marcil filed a writ of habeas corpus on September 5, 1913, claiming he was being restrained of his liberty. Marcil argued that he should have been released on September 4 due to good time. However, O. P. Halligan, the Warden of McNeil Island Penitentiary, claimed that the good time earned by Marcil at the time of his parole was forfeited and canceled when Marcil violated his parole. 
On September 19, 1913, Judge Cushman allowed the writ and ordered Marcil to be discharged from McNeil Island. The next day, the state appealed the case, and the decision was reversed on October 29th, 1913. Marcil was ordered to remain in custody at McNeil Island until he finished serving his sentence, which was expected to end on December 28, 1914.

Summary of Proceedings: The petition alleges that Mr. James Sparks is being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Sheriff John Drexel. Sparks pled guilty to the charge of maliciously destroying property of a less value than $100.00 during the September 1893 term of the District Court. On 2 December 1893, petitioner was sentenced to imprisonment in the County Jail for a term of 4 months and to pay a fine of $100.00 plus the costs of the trial. The petition states that the maximum penalty provided by law for said offense is imprisonment for 30 days. Therefore, petitioner is being unlawfully deprived of his liberty. Judge Cunningham R. Scott ordered that the Writ be allowed, returnable before the Court on 8 February 1894. Judge Scott determined that Sparks was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Sheriff Drexel and ordered that he be discharged. He further ordered that the costs of the proceedings be taxed to the County.

Summary of Proceedings: Dorothy Voelger petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle chief of police Louis M. Lang. Voleger alleged she had been arrested without a warrant and with no criminal charges filed against her. She suspected her arrest was to hold her as a witness for the separate criminal trial, State of Washington vs. Louis Steuernagel et al. Lang responded affirming that Voleger was being held on bond to secure her attendance as a witness in said trial. The case file reveals neither an outcome nor Voelger’s fate.

Summary of Proceedings: Leung Mon Hong petitioned for writ of habeas for Leung Ah Kung Huie Gar Hing, Wing Hing, Ah Sing, Chin Wah, and Chin Shong Chung, and Hue Gar Hing that were confined in Steamship Signal by Master Bendegard for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. The case file includes affidavits as well as the involvement of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in respect to the aforementioned Chinese immigrants. Judge Charles B. Bellinger granted writ of habeas corpus for Ah Sing, but denied the rest, and they were remanded back to confinement.

Summary of Proceedings: Arthur Treichel was born on Christmas Day, 1917, to Maude P. and August Treichel. Census records indicate that he had an older brother named Julius, but we know even less about his fate than we do about Arthur's. He was born into a fractured family: Although his parents were still married, they lived separately. A few years after his son's birth, in May 1919, August left his wife and children for "parts unknown." In that same month, Maud gave Arthur to his aunt and uncle, Adolph and Marie Holz, and set off for California. Both were immigrants from Germany. But little Arthur's troubles didn't end there: In February 1919, Adolph Holz fell ill, confined to his bed and unable to work. As census records indicate the family survived off of odd jobs Adolph did around the neighborhood, this must have plunged the family into desperation. Feeling that she could no longer support the child, Marie surrendered her nephew to the Child's Saving Institute. However, when Adolph recovered, Marie went to ask for her ward back, but the officials at the Institute refused. Time and again, Marie returned, but each time they refused, giving a different reason each time. Finally, on October 4, 1919, the couple filed a writ of habeas corpus, demanding that the Institute and its leaders produce Treichel in court on October 6. The Douglas County sheriff and his deputy went to the Institute, but there was no Arthur Treichel to be found, and so the case was dismissed—to add insult to injury, the Holzes also had to pay the court costs.

Summary of Proceedings: Back Gee, Lop Woo, Ah Lee, and Ah Hin boarded the steamship Haytian Republic in June 1893, traveling to Portland, Oregon. When they arrived on July 17th, T.J. Black ordered them to be held on the steamship by Master H.K. Struve, as their entrance to the US would be in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. All four petitioners presented evidence of their merchant status, including written accounts, photos, and witnesses to T.J. Black. However, he rejected all their evidence due to “inconsistent testimony between papers and witnesses”. The petitioners presented evidence of their work and investment in Chee Lee Wah Co. at a hearing, and only Back Gee and Lop Woo had their writ granted and their incarceration discharged. Ah Lee and Ah Hin were denied and remanded for unknown reasons. However, on motion from their attorneys, Watson and Beekman, Judge Bellinger reversed his decision and approved Ah Lee on July 29th and Ah Hin on August 7th. The case includes a full trial transcript of questioning and cross-examination of all four petitioners and their witnesses. Also included in the case are certificates proving the four petitioners are residents of Portland, including photos and signed by a judge, that their partner Lee Kop obtained before they left for $5 as he anticipated they might have issues upon return.

Summary of Proceedings: Wong Mon Oak petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Wong Yue Doy and his wife, who were held on the Steamship Signal by Captain Eugene Hayden. T. J. Black, the Collector of Customs, refused them entry to port because he believed they were in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. However, Wong Yue Doy was a merchant in Portland before he returned to China to get married, and his wife was born in San Francisco and therefore a U.S. citizen. The Judge granted the writ and released them both from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: A. C. Hallam, agent for the United States under the Secretary of the Navy and manager and operator of the Puget Sound Navy Yard Hotel, was charged with maintaining a dance hall without paying for a city license of $150.00 per year. Judge Cushman sided with Hallam, and ordered the petitioner be discharged.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 7th, 1922, Gertie Folden filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her minor daughter Adean. She named her ex-husband and Adean's father, Homer Folden, as respondent. She explained that she divorced Homer in October 1921 and was granted custody of Adean. On July 22nd, she claimed Homer obtained possession of Adean through deception and had since refused to return Adean, thus she was being unlawfully detained by Homer. The petition was granted, and the writ allowed. Adean was to be returned to the custody of her mother.

Summary of Proceedings: On several occasions between December 20th, 1888, and May 10th, 1889, Jeremiah Mangan used threating language and destroyed property of Flora E. Mangan, his assumed wife. On May 18th, 1889, Jeremiah was sentenced to one year in jail because of these actions. That same day, he filed a writ of habeas corpus, claiming he was being unlawfully detained by Sheriff McGraw. A week later, on May 25th, Judge Hanford ruled in favor of Jeremiah and he was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Lum Hue, Yuet Wo, Fong Vin, Evon Kook, Chin Hop, Tye Fat, Mark Ging, Lee Chung, Mar Chew, Lee Kee, Yee Hop, Chin Bock, Chin Chuen, Ham Suey, Lee You Jo, Leong Kuan, Song Hop, Louis Bo, and Fong Yuep were confined by Captain John Ross in the Steamship Haytian Republic because of the Chinese Exclusion Act. They petitioned for a write of habeas corpus, which was granted, and they were released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Jesus Garcia was accused of carrying a concealed weapon on March 17, 1917,  found guilty by police magistrate James M. Fitzgerald, and sentenced to pay a fine of $25 and court costs on March 19. He was to be held in custody until he could produce the money. He filed for a writ of habeas corpus on March 20, 1917, to be served against the sheriff, Michael L. Clark. The sheriff's return to writ was filed on March 26, 1917, but no further information about the outcome of the petition or Garcia's fate is in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: Roy Suratt petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Mayor Hiram C. Gill, Chief of Police Louis Lang, and Chief of Detectives Charles Tennant. Suratt claimed he was being held in the Seattle city jail without due process for obtaining money under false circumstances. He alleged that he had a metal polishing business in Portland, OR with one Thacher Jones, but sold all his rights, title, and interest in the business to Jones after several months. Suratt alleged that Jones sold a potential partner, Stewart, a half interest for $125, that Suratt saw none of that money, and that Stewart was also the complainant against Suratt. The case file does not reveal the outcome or the fate of Suratt.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 29, 1867, A. N. Jones was fined in a case with an unknown charge. On April 21, 1869, Justice of the Peace W. L. Chalmers issued a writ of execution ordering the sheriff to apprehend and detain Jones until the fine was paid. On May 8, 1869, Judge B. F. Dennison ordered the sheriff to bring Jones before the court. The case file mentioned that this was a habeas corpus case, but the petition date is not clear. It is also unclear if Jones' himself petitioned, or if someone else petitioned on his behalf. Jones’ fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry Siemer petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he had been illegally restrained and restricted of his liberty by the Seattle Chief of Police, Bolton Rogers. Siemer contends that all he knows about his arrest is that it was requested by someone from the State of California. Bolton Rogers clarifies that he placed Siemer in jail at the request of Judge William Caldwell who issued a warrant for Siemer’s arrest. Caldwell issued the warrant because Siemer had been charged for the crime of raping a fifteen year old girl in Oakland California. The outcome of the petition is unknown from the case file, however, newspaper coverage of the case note that Siemer was extradited to California to face trial for his charges.

Summary of Proceedings: Chin Chew petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Chew claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Chew was arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Chew are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: Vera Baker petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Thomas Smiley from the custody of William and Pearl Smiley, which was granted. At the hearing, counsel for the petitioner requested a recess to gather evidence in support of the "character of the home of the petitioner and its surroundings," which was also granted. Summary of Proceedings: On October 30, 1903 Fred B. Goldman, with his attorneys, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Goldman claimed that he was being held illegally by Sheriff Edward Cudihee. The petition detailed many potential charges and unusual circumstances. Goldman was first jailed on the complaint of E. P. Gaffney, for obtaining money under false pretenses from Gaffney’s hotel. The petition said Goldman paid him back, and Gaffney dropped the charges. Then, Goldman was informed he was being held as he awaited an extradition charge from California. Next, John Cudihee, deputy sheriff, made a complaint against Goldman which stated that Goldman assaulted a fellow prisoner, C. M. Keene, with a deadly weapon. Keene reportedly declined to push that charge. Finally, Goldman stated that his wife Bonita died of heartbreak because he was in jail, and he wanted to go with her body to California, where it was to be buried. Newspaper coverage confirms this death. The outcome of this case and the fate of Fred B. Goldman are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis S. Lathrop, the parent of Clara Lathrop, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus to regain custody of his daughter who was nine years old from his sister, Maria M. Bradway et. al. Lathrop had placed Clara in the custody of Bradway when she was two years of age. Bradway claimed that Lathrop was an inadequate guardian because of his second marriage to Nelle Patterson. Bradway characterized this individual as a "common prostitute" and presented documents that showcased her history of prostitution, vagrancy, and disturbance. Louis S. Lathrop was denied the writ and custody continued to be granted to Mary Chambers, Maria M. Bradway, and P. A. Whitlock. Lathrop was permitted to see the said Clara Lathrop at all "suitable and reasonable times for a reasonable period at each time" by Judge Joseph R. Clarkson.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 19, 1916, Roy Walker was arrested and imprisoned without a warrant. With the help of his attorney Amos P. Scruggs, a prominent Black attorney in Omaha and future candidate for the House of Representatives, he filed a writ of habeas corpus on June 23, 1916, against the chief of police, chief of detectives, and the captain of police. Willis G. Sears allowed the writ, as he had been held without any legal proceedings actually being formally initiated against him, but the legal documents provide little insight into his fate. Newspaper coverage indicates Walker was also Black and that he was charged with burglary, but was released on his habeas petition.

Summary of Proceedings: In February, 1911, Kichitaro Kubota entered the United States as a sailor. He would eventually build a life in San Fransisco, part-owning a hotel and restaurant. In January of 1919, he left the United States to visit Japan. In July 1920, Kichitaro returned with his new-found wife, Ise Kubota, but they were denied admission under the charges that Kichitaro never had a legal residence and that they were both likely to become public charges. This decision was appealed, but on August 18th, 1920, the Secretary of Labor denied this appeal. On September 4th, 1920, a writ was filed which alleged, among other things, that the testimony and evidence provided on behalf of the petitioners were not taken into consideration and that Kichitaro had the means to support the couple. On September 4th, 1920, an order was issued to show cause for the detention. On September 8th, 1920, the writ was issued and later that day an order was filed discharging the petitioners.

Summary of Proceedings: Martin D. Reilly and Christy Reilly, the petitioners, adopted Ruth Reilly in October of 1920 with a decree from the Juvenile Divison of the Circuit Court of New Madrid County, Missouri. Ruth Reilly was then unlawfully detained by Mrs. Elizabeth Reilly, Martin's mother, and Mrs. Ellen Dennett, his sister. Martin and Christy Reilly then filed a writ of Habeas Corpus so they could possess sole custody of Ruth. Judge Leslie ordered the writ of Habeas Corpus to be allowed, and Martin and Christy Reilly were issued custody of Ruth in 1922. In 1923, Judge Day oversaw the case and approved the writ of Habeas Corpus, ordering Ruth to be returned to the custody of Martin and Christy Reilly. In 1924 the case is dismissed for want of prosecution. In 1924, Martin and Christy Reilly filed another petition before Judge Day and then Judge Fitzgerald stating that Elizabeth Reilly and Ellen Dennett continue to refuse to comply with the previous orders. Elizabeth Reilly and Ellen Dennett tell the court that they deny that the other Reillys' are the lawful parents of Ruth. Ellen and Elizabeth then claimed that they asked the other Reillys' to procure the adoption on their behalf and expected to have the exclusive custody of Ruth. Further, Ellen and Elizabeth claimed that the previous petitions in 1922 and 1923 were rejected and stated that they should continue to have exclusive custody of Ruth. In 1925 the cause was dismissed, and Ruth is living with her adoptive parents in the 1930 census.

Repository: ["[Washington State Archives, Puget Sound Regional Branch (Bellevue, Washington)](hc.loc.000032)"]
Summary of Proceedings: On May 20, 1914, Harry Brewer and his lawyer F. B. Carpenter filed for a writ of habeas corpus. They claimed Sheriff Edward Cudihee and his agent John W. Roberts arrested Brewer without a formal accusation or charge of a crime. Judge A. W. Frater allowed the petition.  Roberts claimed Brewer, along with Herbert Wolff, robbed August Reets, stealing $235 from Reets. Wolff also filed a petition of habeas corpus (see: Habeas Corpus of Herbert Wolff against Edward Cudihee, Sheriff). Newspaper coverage indicated that Brewer and Wolff beat and drugged Reets before robbing him. Roberts produced a warrant for Brewer's arrest that was dated May 21, 1914, the day after the petition was filed. The outcome of the petition and Brewer’s fate are unknown.

Black, the collector of customs, believed Chong Jung Fong was a Chinese laborer and ordered Captain Beudegard to keep him on the ship. Summary of Proceedings: Mary Louise Deverchere petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve her two sons, John Edward White (age 3 years 6 months) and Harry William Lindsley White (age 18 months), from John Lindsley White, who Deverchere claimed was the boys’ illegitimate father. John White countered that the boys were not in his custody, but with his sister, Julia M. Eagles, in Portland, OR, and that Deverchere was not fit to have custody of the children due to past adulterous behavior. He also provided a marriage certificate stating that he and Deverchere were married, granting him paternal rights to the children. Deverchere claimed that the marriage certificate was a forgery, and that she was legally married to one Geneross Napoleon but had been cohabitating with White for seven years, during which time she planned to divorce Napoleon but never did. Despite an abundance of subpoenas and evidence, the case outcome is not stated in the file. Available newspaper coverage suggests that Eagles retained custody of the children.

Summary of Proceedings: Chin Lung petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Chinese inspector A. F. Richardson. Lung’s petition is not included in the case file, but he alleged he was held in the Spokane County Jail awaiting deportation to China. Newspaper records indicate that Lung claimed he was a minor born in Seattle, WA and was a birthright citizen of the United States who travelled to China for an education. Richardson claimed that Lung was in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 by being unlawfully in the United States without the required certificate. It is inferred that the unknown initial court ruled in favor of Richardson, as Lung appealed. The U.S. District Court ruled that Lung should be deported, and his writ was denied.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 24, 1920, Earl Thomas Beni petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. In his petition, he claimed that on August 12th, the police arrested him and charged him with impersonating an officer and disorderly conduct. The next day, the police magistrate, Charles E. Foster, tried his case and sentenced him to 30 days in the county jail. However, Beni argued Foster lacked jurisdiction, and the court’s judgment was void because his charge does not exist in the state of Nebraska statutes. He does not specify which charge he referred to. The same day, the judge accepted and ordered a writ of habeas corpus. However, the outcome of this proceeding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Golf S. Marham was a 37 year old Bulgarian migrant who moved to the United States in 1913. On June 28, 1917, Marham was arrested by the A. F. Richardson, Immigrant Inspector, based on a warrant issued by Louis F. Post, Assistant Secretary of Labor. The warrant broadly accused Marham of advocating for the unlawful destruction of property or the overthrow of the United States government and asserted that Marham was an anarchist. Marham was granted a hearing with Richardson on November 26, 1917 and following the hearing Richardson recommended Marham’s deportation based on Marham's admission to being a member of the Industrial Workers of the World and being employed to teach the tenets of the organization. 

Marham filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 30, 1918 arguing that his detention was illegally restraining him of his liberty. In the petition, Marham argued that he was subjected to personal abuse and intimidation which compelled him to give evidence against himself. Furthermore, he stated that he was denied a fair hearing because he did not have a right to inspect the warrant or the evidence that the warrant was based on. He also argued that he was denied his right to counsel at the hearing. Judge Frank H. Rudkin agreed to hear the writ of habeas corpus. In his written opinion, Rudkin stated that it seemed that the grounds for Marham’s deportation is that the immigration inspectors believe that he is an undesirable citizen which is not an excluded class in immigration law. Rudkin thus ruled that Marham’s detention was unlawful and ordered that he be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On Sunday, March 10 1901, Press Evans was arrested for assault in the precinct of Franklin. He was jailed by Sheriff Edward Cudihee under the orders of Justice of the Peace, F. M. Tucker. In the petition by Evans’s attorney, A. C. MacDonald, it was claimed that Evans was arrested by a man not in uniform and his case was decided on a Sunday, which was not a legal holiday. Evans was ordered to pay a fine of $25 and $12, which he did not have the means to pay and was thus imprisoned. On March 12, 1901, Judge George Emory heard and issued Evans’s Writ for Habeas Corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: Sherman Hall, age 6, was being held at St. James Orphanage after his father, Louis Hall, placed him in their care in October, 1913. Petitioner, Minnie Hall Riley, is Sherman’s mother. Petitioner stated that Louis was a man of immoral character, a habitual drunkard, and unfit to care for a child. At the time the petition was filed, Louis had not contacted petitioner or the child for a month. Minnie attempted to retrieve Sherman from the orphanage but they refused her request. She submitted this petition for a writ of habeas corpus on 23 November 1914, asking that Sherman Hall be discharged from the unlawful imprisonment. Judge James P. English ordered that the writ be allowed, returnable on 24 November 1914. Judge English ordered that custody of Sherman Hall be granted to Minnie Hall Riley.

Summary of Proceedings:
On June 6, 1897, Henry Craemer petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus after he was charged with murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, and manslaughter. Craemer was convicted of murdering a woman named Philipina Mueller and her baby. Newspaper reports indicated that Craemer was set to be executed the following month. The newspapers also His petition alleged the death warrant was without jurisdiction and authority of law as the jury had found Craemer guilty of "nothing more than murder in the second degree", which carries a sentence of 10-20 years imprisonment, but not death. Craemer appealed the decision to the Supreme Court of the United States which dismissed the appeal. Circuit Court judge C. H. Hanford denied the writ. On the notice of appeal, the Governor of Washington stayed the execution for ninety days. 
Supplementary research reveals in that, during following years, Craemer and his attorneys' filed motions and appeals to delay the execution. All evidence was, allegedly, circumstantial, so there were questions as to Craemer's guilt. 
In 1898 Judge Orange Jacobs, the Superior Court judge who heard Craemer's case, authored a letter to Governor Rogers recommending the commutation of Craemer's sentence to life imprisonment, and subsequently Governor Rogers did as such sixteen hours before Craemer's execution. Ten years later, in 1908, a witness who confirmed Craemer's alibi was discovered and Governor Mead pardoned Craemer.

Summary of Proceedings: Oscar Collins petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren and Commissioner of Health J. S. McBride. Collins claimed that he was arrested for being a disorderly person and was being held illegally in a quarantine unit of the Seattle City Jail without trial or bail fixed upon him. Warren alleged that, while Collins was in fact arrested, authority over his detainment had been handed over completely to McBride. McBride alleged that Collins was being quarantined for an infectious and contagious disease, and that Collins was too sick to be brought into court. Collins denied that he was sick and claimed the quarantine was a means to conceal his unjust imprisonment. He motioned to command McBride to allow up to four third-party medical examinations to determine if he was, in fact, ill. Newspaper records indicate that Collins had to re-file with a second judge, and that his second petition was denied. His fate remains unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: May 12th, 1911, D. A. Hatfield was confined and held in the King County Jail on a charge, conviction, and sentence of a felony for forgery in the first degree (Case number 5589). Hatfield and another prisoner, George W. Workman, attempted to escape from prison by "obtaining from outside said prison, through means which are to the prosecuting attorney unknown, acid, saws, and blow pipe, and by then and there using and attempting to use said acid blow pipe and saws in sawing and cutting the iron bolts and bars of said prison, for the purpose of making an aperture therein, through or by means of which they, or either of them might escape". D. A. Hatfield was found guilty by a jury and sentenced to at least 2 years of prison. Hatfield's attorney argued that the attempt to charge Hatfield with attempted escape from prison does not charge him with a crime against the laws of the state of Washington. The attorney also stated that it "fails to show that your petitioner was imprisoned by virtue of a written commitment". The application was denied.

Summary of Proceedings:
In December 1916, Irene Steward filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Charles Bird and Josephine Bird, also known as Jack Lewis. The petition was filed on the basis of Charles and Josephine being unlawfully deprived of their liberty by being confined in the City Jail of Omaha by Henry W. Dunn, Chief of Police of Omaha, and Michael F. Dempsey, Captain of the Police of Omaha. Judge Willis G. Sears allowed the writ of Habeas Corpus and discharged the bound parties. 

Newspaper coverage indicates Josephine Bird was the Black owner of a brothel and her husband Charles was a bartender, and that Josephine claimed the police extorted her and assaulted both her and her husband while they were in jail. The press also reported that the Birds faced "white slavery" charges, but that Josephine filed a complaint against police officials. Josephine's actions continue to appear in local press coverage well into 1916.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney D. C. Conover petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren on the behalf of his client Laura B. Johnson. Conover alleged that Warren had jailed Johnson in the Seattle City Jail on the charge of being a fugitive from justice from Kittitas County, WA. Conover claimed Johnson’s imprisonment was illegal as Warren had no warrant or authority to jail her. Warren’s response was not included in the case file. The writ was dismissed by motion of Conover and Johnson because Johnson had already been released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Ling Lew petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Lew claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Lew was likely arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct, though no newspaper article listed his name. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Lew are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Smith without a warrant or proper charge. Smith responded stating that Judge Gordon had issued a warrant for Smith’s arrest, which stated that LeWald was a fugitive from justice from Illinois, where he had been charged with embezzlement. No outcome is stated in this case file, but LeWald filed a second habeas case later that month, indicating that he was not released.

Summary of Proceedings:
Ichitaro Akagi was ordered for arrest and deportation on the basis that he was a Japanese laborer in the United States without a passport.  He was taken into the immigration detention center in Seattle. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he was illegally restrained. In the petition, he alleged that the law that was the grounds for the warrant did not apply to him because there was no law requiring a passport from someone coming directly from Japan to the U.S. He added that as a seaman, he was entitled to enter and remain in the United States until he took another ship.
On March 21st, 1922 Ichitaro Akagi escaped from the detention center and from the custody of Weedin, becoming a fugitive from justice.
All exhibits were withdrawn.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis Seiffer, alias David S. Berman, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that warden of the State Penitentiary Leidigh was depriving him of his freedom. Seiffer had been arrested on the charge of forgery, fined, and sentenced to five years imprisonment "and kept at hard labor." Seiffer claimed that before his initial trial in Furnas County's District Court, deputy sheriff A. E. Peterson insinuated that Seiffer would be lynched and hung and that the gathered crowd joined in the intimidation. Additionally, he claimed that he was told that if he pled guilty, he would only receive one year in prison. Judge Hall allowed the petition. After hearing evidence, Hall granted a Seiffer a "writ of relief" from the custody of Leidigh and ordered that Seiffer be transferred into the custody of Furnas County sheriff to await additional legal action. According to the August 11, 1895, Chicago Chronicle, Seiffer (spelled Seiffert) was a well-known forger throughout the United States.

Summary of Proceedings: Benjamin Wise was arrested on suspicion of having committed arson, arraigned before the Justice Court of Salem, and jailed to await a grand jury trial. Bail was set at $2,000. Wise paid his bail and was released only to be promptly re-arrested and jailed to answer a second charge related to the arson. Bail was set at $3,000. Wise petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. He contended that the bail was excessive. After hearing the evidence, Wise was remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: Euphemia Eastwick petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve her son, Benjamin Eastwick, from the Oregon State Hospital in Salem, which was granted. Benjamin was adjudicated to be an insane person in 1911 and committed to the Mountain View Sanitarium in Portland. In 1912, Euphemia unsuccessfully petitioned for habeas to retrieve Benjamin from Mountain View, but succeeded in having him transferred to the state hospital. At the hearing, Euphemia claimed that she was able to care for her son "without the assistance of the State," citing wealth that Benjamin had inherited from family in Philadelphia. However, multiple physician witnesses, as well as Benjamin's state-assigned guardian, Harrison Platt, asserted that Benjamin suffered from incurable "dementia praecox," or what we now call schizophrenia, and was "unfit to be at large, except with a constant male attendant." After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and Benjamin remanded back into the custody of the state hospital superintendent.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 29, 1913 John Schmidt and his attorneys Faster and Worthington petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. In the petition, they stated that Schmidt was being held by Chief of Police Claude G. Bannick and that Schmidt was not charged with any crime. Bannick was out of town for part of the case, and so Acting Chief of Police L. J. Stuart received the writ. Justice Everett Smith granted the writ to be heard in John E. Humphries’ court. Humprhies stated that Schmidt’s bail was paid, and additionally that prosecution failed to show up to court. Humphries agreed that there was no charge against Schmidt, approving his petition. He ordered Schmidt released, and returned the bail money to him. Newspaper coverage indicates Schmidt had threatened a woman and then broke into her room with the intent to assault her.

Dickey was arrested for failing to file a certificate of partnership with the county clerk of Douglas County for more than 20 days prior thereto doing business as W. Cook & co. In September 1893, Mary Lanenville, filed a writ of habeas corpus stating that Sister Mary unlawfully confined and imprisoned her in the house of the Good Shepherd. Sister Mary mentioned that a man took  Mary Laneuville away from the care of her husband in July 1893 and cohabited with her until she became an inmate. The judge granted the petition, however the outcome of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Celia Berg O'Neill, a native of the Russian Empire, immigrated to the United States in 1904. She stated she is a U.S. citizen through her marriage to Fred O'Neill, a natural born citizen of the U.S., which took place in November 1914. In October 1914, Berg was taken into custody at Skagway, Alaska by an immigrant inspector under a warrant charging her with being an "alien" to the United States of America and entering the U.S. for the purposes of prostitution. Berg was transferred to Seattle and taken into custody by Henry M. White, Commissioner of Immigration. Berg petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus alleging that she was not given a fair and impartial trial as she was not given copy of the proceedings, denied her right to cross examine witnesses, and no testimony was taken to show the petitioner was not an alien to the U.S. subsequent of her marriage. The Secretary of the Department of Labor ordered the cancellation of the warrants of arrest and deportation against the petitioner. Subsequently, Judge Cushman ordered the petitioner be discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
On March 1, 1911, Catherine Guignon was arrested while entering Ellis Island. Inspector Thomas M. Fisher alleged that Catherine Guignon was “an alien, a citizen of Belgium” and “was at that time one of the inadmissible classes in that she was a prostitute.” Fisher and J. B. Densmore, Acting Secretary of Labor, ordered her to be deported back to Belgium on August 15, 1913.

Several immigration inspectors in Spokane, Washington interviewed Guignon and her associates, including her partner, Charles Guignon. Catherine and Charles alleged that they ran his hotel, the Plastino Hotel, and lived as common law spouses on his ranch for twelve or thirteen years. Other townspeople countered that Catherine was a prostitute and Charles was her pimp. 

Judge Frank H, Rudkin ordered Catherine’s discharge from custody on September 29, 1913.

Summary of Proceedings:
Elizabeth Crashul filed a writ of habeas corpus in an attempt to regain custody of her children after they were taken from her and her husband in November of 1914. The children were taken because the Chief Probation Officer of the Pierce County Juvenile Court filed a complaint that their children were not being raised in a proper environment and at risk of growing up to live an idel, dissolute, and immoral life. The complaint also claimed that Elizabeth was living separately from her husband Michael, however, Elizabeth denied this claim multiple times in the petition. 

Elizabeth's petition of habeas corpus claimed that she had not been able to contact her children for several months and argues that her and her husband did not know about their summon to court to defend their right to the custody of their children. One of the pieces of evidence submitted during the trial is a letter written to the Humane Officer of Pierce County asking him to provide "Austrian or Polish" interpreters for Elizabeth and Michael Crashul because they little to no English and were struggling to navigate the American legal system. 

In the end, the petition was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. The Judge, John S. Jurey argues that since the decision to remove the custody from Elizabeth and Michael Crashul came from the Superior Court of Pierce County the Superior Court of King County had no jurisdiction to change or rectify their decision.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 2, 1922, Effie Norland filed for habeas against Margaret Moriarty over the custody of "Baby Norland," known as "Jack Moriarty." In the petitions Norland explained that the child had been the product of her wedlock to Louis Norland, and that the couple Charles T. Moriarty and Katherine Moriarty tried to adopt the child from a Salvation Army home in September of 1914. Norland argued that because her husband, alive during the proceedings, was not present and did not consent to the adoption, that such adoption was void. With the adoptive parents now deceased, Norland further argues that Margaret Moriarty, sister to the now-deceased couple, does not hold any legal grounds of custody over the child. A writ was issued, and a demurrer sustained on May 6, 1922. In 1922, another couple, the Van Nesses, attempted to adopt Jack, as they had cared for the child after Charles and Katherine's death, although Jack wanted to stay with the Van Nesses. They were denied, since Maggie contested the adoption. This may have been a religious clash: the Van Nesses were Catholic, while Maggie was Protestant. However, the case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924. By the 1930 census, Jack Moriarty was in the house of Margaret Moriarty's sister, Genevieve Creigh.

Summary of Proceedings: Patrick McGinn petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles L. Beckingham. McGinn alleged that he was arrested without a warrant or criminal complaint against him and was being held without due legal process in the Seattle City Jail. He also claimed he was being denied the right to consult his attorney. McGinn alleged that Beckingham was attempting to compel him into making a statement, admission, or confession that would incriminate McGinn of murder. The outcome of the case and the fate of McGinn are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Peter Leopold petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Leopold claimed Warren was holding him in the Seattle City Jail under a warrant delivered via telegraph from Bellingham, WA, but alleged he was not a fugitive from justice. Summary of Proceedings: On December 3, 1914, Hugh Bronson and his lawyer Edwin James Brown filed a petition of habeas corpus. They claimed that Bronson was being held without a charged crime, and that Judge Hanks, who ordered his detainment, didn’t report the court proceedings to the clerk in the required time frame. In his commitment statement, Hanks reported that he charged Bronson with “Threatening to Kill”, based on the oath of the alleged victim, Joseph Ladne. Bronson had been held for thirty-three days by Sheriff Edward Cudihee. Judge Boyd J. Tallman allowed the writ, and ordered Bronson’s release on December 5, 1914.

Summary of Proceedings:
Carl Holm filed for a writ of habeas corpus on October 24, 1918. Max Anderson, jailer of the Spokane County Jail, held Holmes on behalf of Immigration Inspector, A. F. Richardson, for advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. This case file includes a transcript of Immigration Inspector Thomas M. Fisher’s interrogation of Holm in relation to I.W.W literature.

Judge Frank H. Rudkin found that Holm’s testimony did not prove that he advocated for the teaching of the destruction of property, and ordered Holm to be released on October 25, 1918. According to newspaper coverage, Holm was the only member of a group of seven Swedish men, detained by Richardson, to be released. Immigration officials deported the other six people.

Summary of Proceedings: William Johnson was detained on suspicion of having committed a crime on February 24th, 1920. There was a complaint filed against him the next day for statutory rape. A preliminary trial was held and Nettie Vacirca, a 14-year-old girl and alleged victim, testified along with Vosburgh and Hopkins who both work in the police station and heard William Johnson allegedly voluntarily admitted to the crime. Johnson petitioned for habeas corpus on February 27th, 1920, arguing that there was insufficient evidence for a sustained trial and that the alleged confession was extrajudicial and coerced. His petition was denied so he motioned for a new trial on March 4th, 1920. On March 6th, 1920, he filed again for habeas corpus. The second petition was allowed and a return was sent, but the outcome of the second petition is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1906, Ike Zemansky was working as an auctioneer selling jewelry and watches.  E. R. Marsh filed a complaint to Police Judge John B. Gordon stating that Zemansky sold a watch chain and braid for one dollar without a license.  Judge T. H. Cann issued a warrant for Zemansky’s arrest.  On March 1, 1906, J.W. Goldstein, Zemansky’s employer, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on Zemansky’s behalf. He stated that Zemansky had already paid $200 to the City of Seattle to receive his license for auctioneering. Under Ordinance No. 11141 of Seattle, Zemansky was required to pay an additional fee of $270.    The petition indicates that Zemansky was arrested because he did not pay this additional fee.  The petition argued that Ordinance No. 11141 was unconstitutional, as it “[prevented] the exercise of business” and “imposed an unjust burden.”  While the petition was directed to Judge A. W. Frater, Judge Geo. G. Hatch issued the writ.  While the case file does not indicate an outcome, Page 3 of the March 2, 1902 issue of the Seattle Star reported that the writ was granted.  However, Zemansky’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 28th, 1917, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed in the name of Jennie E. Turkington for unspecified reasons. The outcome of the petition and the fate of the bound party are unknown. Census records indicate that by 1920 Turkington is an inmate in the Nebraska Hospital for the Insane based in Lancaster County, NE. Newspaper accounts indicate Jennie's husband George, "a known real estate dealer," initiated the insanity diagnosis to have her committed after Jennie filed for divorce on April 3 for "cruelty and non-support." Newspapers also reveal that Jennie's friends initiated a challenge to the insanity ruling in 1918 suggesting that George bribed their children to testify against their mother and that the insanity ruling was spiteful. 1919 press coverage indicates Jennie remained in the asylum, but that her oldest daughter moved into a boarding house and George was investigated for requiring his 11 year-old daughter to manage his household.

Summary of Proceedings: On the 25th of November 1924, William J. Fox filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds of being unlawfully in confinement and deprived of his liberty by Dennis H. Cronin and William C. Condit. He was being held in custody on the basis of having sold liquor in violation of the National Prohibition Act with a sentence of three months and a fine of $400. In his petition, Fox presented that he had been held longer than the three months, the court agreed and discharged him from custody. In December 1924 an appeal was made by Cronin and Condit, filing assignments of error within it and then was granted. In February 1926 it was ordered by the Circuit Court of Appeals that the order made in November 1924 allowing the discharge of Fox be reversed with recommendation to discharge the writ for habeas corpus and remand Fox to custody which was carried out three days later.

Summary of Proceedings: Bessie Berry was arrested and tried in a Police Court in Omaha on the charge of vagrancy. This charge was successfully appealed on July 6, 1918, and an order of release was issued by Police Judge James M. Fitzgerald. Berry was then transferred to a detention home, when Berry, by attorney John M Macfarland filed for habeas against Police Captain, Henrey Heitfeld who refused to release Berry, C. C. Tomlinson who is in charge of the detention home and refused to grant Macfarland consultation with Berry, as well as Ernest T. Manning. The petition was granted, and the writ allowed; Berry was discharged on July 9th.

Summary of Proceedings: In June of 1920, Chung Him and Seid Yam were arrested by an Immigration Inspector, Henry M. White, in Ketchikan, Alaska. Both men were charged with being employed in or in connection with a house of prostitution. The men, cooks aged 59 and 65, said they had lived in the United States for thirty to forty years. They also said that if their place of employment was a house of prostitution, they were unaware of that fact. Due to this charge, Him and Yam were ordered to be deported from the United Stated and back to China. In response, the men filed a writ of habeas corpus on December 6th, 1920. On the same day, Judge Neterer ruled in favor of the petitioners. However, a month later, the decision was overruled by the Washington Court of Appeals. Him and Yam then resubmitted their writ of habeas corpus. The outcome of this second writ of habeas corpus and the fate of the bound parties is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: B. E. Weldon also known as E. D. Strong was arrested on July 24th, 1891 by the Sheriff of Multnomah County, Penumbra Kelly. He petitioned for writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was arrested without a warrant. He believes that he may have been arrested because of a charge against him in Alabama for forgery and defrauding a corporation. His petition for writ of habeas corpus was denied by Judge Matthew P. Deady, and he was remanded to custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Ora Billingsley petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles L. Beckingham. As the petition is missing from the case file, it is unclear for what offense Billingsley was held in Seattle City Jail or for what reason he found his jailing to be illegal. Newspaper records suggest that Billingsley was arrested for shooting and killing two police officers. The outcome of the case and the fate of Billingsley are both unknown. Billingsley’s petition was connected to that of three other men, two of whom were his brothers.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry Imhof was charged with selling, giving, and disposing of beer to “certain Indians” in Sitka in the territory of Alaska. It is unclear from this case why the judicial proceedings occurred in the Territory of Washington. Imhof was put into detention and held by Louis V. Wycoff in the third territory of Washington, but the order for his arrest came from James P. Ludlow, the commissioner of the third district of Alaska. Though the original petition was sent to Roger Green in the third judicial district, Green was called away on business and the petition was heard by John Hoyt in the second judicial district. After the petition was granted, the writ was heard by Greene, who ordered that the petitioner’s detention was illegal and that Henry Imhoff should be discharged from custody.

Williams's sister, acted as Kathleen L. Williams's "attorney-in-fact" who was allowed to act legally on behalf of her sister. Kathleen Williams's petition alleged that on July 3, 1923, she had allowed Roger H. Williams to visit his grandmother Elisabeth S. Williams. However, Kathleen stated that Elisabeth S. Williams refused to return Roger, claiming that her son had sent her telegrams telling her not to. The petition also stated that Kathleen L. Williams was of competence and fitness to take care of the child, and that nobody else had been awarded care of the child. Judge Charles Leslie granted the writ and commanded that Elizabeth Williams come before the court and show cause for her detention of Roger Williams. After the hearing, the application was granted and the appearance docket states that Roger H. Williams was to be delivered to a "named party," presumably Kathleen, to be returned to New York. Judge Leslie said that Elisabeth was a perfectly competent guardian, but the boy should be in New York with his parents, even if they were estranged. Elisabeth said when the verdict was announced, "I don't care what these lawyers and the judge say, this is unfair to take this boy from me. It's not right." Later, Kathleen sent a letter to the Omaha Bee claiming that Elisabeth had mistreated Roger while he was in her care, and that he needed to be placed in a hospital to recover after he returned to New York.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 14, 1919, Ruth Morrisson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that the chief of police, Marshall Eberstein, was unlawfully detaining her of her liberty. She stated that on January 3, she was arrested and placed in the Omaha City Jail and subsequently, the Omaha Detention Hospital. While in the Detention Home, she protested publicly against the harsh treatment of superintendent Alta Gerber. However, no charges were filed against her, and no fixed bond for her release was set. The same day, the Judge accepted the petition and filed a writ of habeas corpus. On January 16, Ernest T. Manning, City Health Commissioner, sent an answer and return of the writ, claiming that he determined that Morrison was infected with a communicable venereal virus, and for that reason, he ordered that she be isolated and quarantined in the Detention Home for treatment. The outcome of this proceeding is unknown. However, in July 1919, she was again arrested for vagrancy and being an inmate of a "disorderly house," a euphemism for prostitution. Two other women, Ruth McLane and Bessie Weinberger, as well as former city prosecutor John M. Berger, were arrested with her, although he alleged that he had been set up.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 14, 1864, C.M. Bradshaw petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Nicholas Adams and Thomas Gould. Bradshaw stated that Adams and Gould were being held captive by an armed group of over thirty people that referred to themselves as the “Vigilance Committee”. The group allegedly threatened to expel Adams and Gould from the territory by force and execute them by mob law before the writ could be issued. Bradshaw also asked for a warrant to be issued for the group’s apprehension. The judge accepted the application for the writ and issued the warrant. Adams’ and Gould’s fates are unknown. Bradshaw wrote a letter outlining the event that was published roughly a month later indicating that he believed the vigilance committee were secessionist Democrats seeking to punish Republican voters and secure a political stronghold on the county.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1870, Samuel and Edwina Montgomery married. Together they had two children, George Clarence and Myra Bell Montgomery. On October 1st, 1876, Edwina left Samuel. In May of 1877, Samuel allowed Edwina to take the children to a different city to look for work. Edwina then did not return the children to Samuel. Samuel claimed that Edwina threatened to kill Samuel if he tried to take Myra. Samuel filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Myra Bell Montgomery on May 30th, 1877. The following day, Judge Wingard granted custody of Myra to Samuel.

Summary of Proceedings: Alson Cole pled guilty to murder in the Howard County, Nebraska district court in March 1918. According to his petition for a writ of habeas corpus, Cole was then convicted of murder in the first degree and sentenced to death without a trial. After unsuccessfully applying for habeas relief in federal district court, Cole appealed the decision to the eighth circuit. The court of appeals dismissed the case as frivolous and remanded Cole to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 26, 1903, Jennie Du Bois petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Ed Cudihee, sheriff of King County, alleging to be held without a warrant. The judge allowed the writ on the same day, but the fate of the bound party is unknown. Newspaper coverage indicates Du Bois was charged with robbery and was also suspected of being brought into the country from France for "immoral purposes" and would be prosecuted under the Mann Act. Du Bois was released on her own recognizance and disappeared before federal charges could be filed.

Summary of Proceedings: The three petitioners, George Walker, John San Francisco, and Pedro O’Brien were seamen on the vessel Hattie E. Tafley, which was sailing from Hong Kong to Victoria and then to Sidney. The petitioners were underfed, and the captain of the ship, George Finleyson, voluntarily deviated from the voyage plans to come to Port Blakely in Washington. The petitioners left the ship at the port and libeled the barque for their wages in the District Court of the 3rd Judicial District, but the libel failed, and the seamen went on board to collect their clothing that they left on board. When they went back on board,  Finleyson placed them in chains and held them against their will. Because they were held on board when the petition was filed, the petition was filed by their next friend Jeremiah Macauley. Upon hearing the evidence, Judge Roger Greene granted the writ and commanded Finleyson to release the petitioners.

Summary of Proceedings: On 21 April 1913, Ethel Allen and Nellie Roberts were arrested and and charged with prostitution. They were convicted of said charge and committed by the Judge of the Police Court of the City of Omaha to the County Jail. The complaint, submitted by A. M. Wirt, stated that the two women engaged in prostitution on 21 April 1913 “contrary to the ordinances of the City of Omaha, aforesaid, and statutes of said State in that behalf provided and against the peace and dignity of the people of the State of Nebraska.” This complaint was submitted to Charles E. Foster, Police Magistrate for the City of Omaha. On 22 April 1913, Roberts and Allen appeared in court and pled guilty. Costs were assessed at $95.00 each. The State had two witnesses, one whose name is illegible and the other by the last name Holden. On 30 April 1913, Allen and Roberts along with their attorney, F. W. Driscoll, submitted a petition for a writ of habeas corpus which stated that the charge was not a state offense and “not contrary to the form of the statutes of the State of Nebraska.” The Appearance Docket noted that their application was denied on 1 May 1913.

Summary of Proceedings: William Bird was dishonorably discharged from military service on January 23rd, 1870, Court Martialed, and sentenced to hard labor for the murder of Lieutenant Cowan. Then he was moved to the Multnomah County Jail, where he petitioned for habeas corpus. The writ was originally sent to the jailor, but James H. Lappeus, the chief of police, replied that the person ultimately in charge of his custody was the General Commanding the Department of Columbia. So the writ was sent to First Lieutenant Louis V. Caziarc, who replied and provided information on the legitimacy of military discipline. The Judge confirmed the legality of the incarceration and dismissed the petition for habeas corpus, remanding William Bird to custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
In early November 1899, Samuel Morgan, a soldier imprisoned at Fort Crook to await trial for desertion, assaulted his guard and escaped to the nearby town of La Platte. A sergeant ordered two enlisted men, John Fair and Henry Jockens, to track down Morgan, order him to halt twice, and to shoot him if he did not comply, which is what they did. Morgan died from his wound after five minutes. Fair and Jockens were court-martialed and found not guilty of manslaughter. One month later, the pair were arrested and charged with murder under Nebraska law in the Sarpy County District Court. In January 1900, Fair and Jockens petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court, arguing, among other things, that Nebraska lacked the jurisdiction to try them and that they were just following orders. After hearing the evidence, they were released from custody. Nebraska declared that it would appeal and bail was set at $1,000 apiece. However, the state dropped the appeal later that year and Fair and Jockens successfully petitioned to have their bail discharged.

It is worth noting that Judge William Munger commented directly on habeas corpus law in his opinion, saying: "I am mindful of the rule of law that in a habeas corpus proceeding the Court will not examine the evidence for the purpose of determining whether the party should be pronounced guilty or innocent of the offense for which he is imprisoned; yet in a case of this character it is not only proper, but necessary, for the Court to determine whether the parties acted wantonly and with criminal intent, or whether their acts, though wrongful, were errors of judgment only."

Summary of Proceedings:
Don E. DeBow filed a petition for habeas corpus against Douglas County Sheriff and Jailer Michael L. Clark on September 25, 1917. His petition stated that, on September 19, 1917, DeBow had been arrested and charged with selling securities of an association called "The Farmers Oil & Gas Company" without a permit from the Nebraska State Railway Commission, which allegedly violated Section 808 of the Revised Statutes of Nebraska, otherwise known as the "Blue Sky Law." 

DeBow pled not guilty in an arraignment in front of Omaha Police Magistrate James M. Fitzgerald. Fitzgerald found probable cause, set DeBow's bail at $400.00, and directed a mittimus for Fitzgerald to Sheriff Clark on September 22, 1917. DeBow did not pay the bail and was taken into custody. DeBow's petition asserted that the process used to justify his detention was illegitimate. Judge Willis G. Sears allowed the writ to be issued and commanded that Clark appear with the body of DeBow and justify DeBow's detention on September 27, 1917. On October 2, 1917, after hearing the evidence, judge Willis G. Sears denied and dismissed DeBow's application, and it is likely that DeBow stayed in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward L. Dodder filed a petition to acquire the custody of Ruthie Ewart from his sister, Mrs. Dodder, who intended to take Ruthie to California, where she lived asn an invalid. This was after her ex-husband and Ruthie's father, J.S. Ewart, kidnapped Ruthie on February 2, 1902, while she was on her way to dinner at her grandfather's house. The girl was understandably alarmed at first, but was happy to realize that she was with her father. A writ was also served to J.S. Ewart, but since a writ couldn't be served on a Sunday, court authorities had to wait until after midnight to serve him the writ. The judge denied the writ, and Mrs. Dodder was allowed to take Ruthie on a temporary visit due to her illness. However, she ultimately ended up in the custody of her grandmother, Mrs. Ruth Dodder.

Archie Malott filed for a writ of habeas corpus ad testificandum on January 18, 1922. Malott was a key witness in the grand jury proceedings against Edward C. Davis, Edward Miller, and John Martindale for violating the Prohibition Act, as well as conspiracy to impersonate United States officials.  

Judge Frank H. Rudkin released Malott, requesting that he be returned to Seattle, Washington into the custody of the King County Sheriff.

Summary of Proceedings: Adam Treger filed for a writ claiming that he had been unlawfully imprisoned by Charles S. Reed with no warrant and with no clear indication of what crime he is being confined for. Judge Jacobs granted the petition, and the sheriff’s office under A. T. Van De Vanter responded that the writ had been served two days later, but there was no further documentation of the proceedings or specific charges against Treger. Summary of Proceedings: Ung On, a Chinese immigrant and laborer, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Chinese inspector A. F. Richardson. On’s petition is lost, but he alleged he was held in the Spokane County Jail awaiting deportation to China. Richardson claimed that On was in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 by being unlawfully in the United States without the required certificate. It can be inferred that the initial court ruled in favor of On, as Richardson appealed. The U.S. District Court also ruled in favor of On. His writ was approved and he was released on bail.

Additional Sources:
Fred Soggs was arrested in Bremerton, Kitsap county, for the crime of rape. He had a preliminary hearing by the Justice of the Peace for the Sidney Precinct, John Bishop, in June 1900. There, Soggs was commanded to answer to the Superior Court of Washington on July 25 1900. Soggs was released on bond until the next trial date. This next original trial date would be delayed three times. 

The first delay occurred when on the original hearing date, Soggs’s attorney, John F. Dore could not make the trial. Dore had sent a letter to the judge, Frank J. Heed, mentioning that he was out of town hearing a different trial and could not make the November 12, 1900 trial. Soggs’s case was not heard, and delayed to the court’s next term. Almost a year later, Soggs was once again scheduled to have his case heard on September 23, 1901. However, Dore also could not make the trial held by Judge John C. Denny, causing another delay. On September 25, 1901, Soggs and Dore would appear in court and ask for the order forfeiting bail be put aside. Then, on November 26, 1901, the trial was once again delayed following the agreement of Judge Denny and Soggs. 

The Prosecuting Attorney of Kitsap County, J. B. Yakey would have to file another warrant for Soggs due to the delays in trial. Soggs would once again be charged with the crime of rape on April 17, 1902. 

In his writ of habeas corpus, Soggs argued that his constitutional right for a speedy trial was violated (6th amendment) from what would be an almost two year delay. During which, he paid bail three times amounting to a sum of $3,000. 

On April 18, 1902, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court at Olympia, J. B. Reavis, ordered Superior Court Judge William R. Bell to hear Soggs’s case. To which, judge Bell ordered the holding party, sheriff of Kitsap county, D. H. Sackman to bring Soggs for a hearing. Sheriff Sackman responded that Soggs was not currently in his possession, nor was in his possession at the time of the writ. It is likely that after filing the writ, Soggs had decided to skip bail.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis Way Seah filed for a petition of habeas corpus on November 10th, 1893, on behalf of Louis Sam, a Chinese merchant coming back into the U.S. from a year-long trip from China. Sam had been a resident of Portland for many years, working as a merchant, not a laborer. He was being restrained on the steamship Signal by the captain of the ship, George Beudegard. He believed this was due to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 which prohibited laborers from entering the U.S. The Writ was granted on November 13th ,1893.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney Paul Carrigan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of his clients Harry Toy, Ah Juat, and Ah Suey against King County Sheriff John Stringer. Carrigan alleged that Toy, Juat, and Suey were arrested without a warrant and were being held illegally at King County Jail with no due process, charge, or fixed bail. Stringer responded with a warrant which charged the three men with carrying concealed weapons. The warrant was dated after the petition was filed. The case outcome and the fates of Toy, Juat, and Suey are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Nelson, Smith, Elsner, Whaley, Mattson, Lundblad, Coffey, and Annir were hired by L. E. Gray as mariners aboard the Bark Gem of the Ocean, going from San Francisco, California, to Seattle, Washington, carrying cargo. As Gray did not sign their shipping contracts or agreements in writing or print, Nelson and others demanded that they were entitled to be discharged and paid off in wages of $37.50 each. Gray refused, and Nelson and others were arrested by Sheriff Lewis Wycoff for disobedience. Nelson and others applied for habeas, claiming said imprisonment to be illegal, there was no proper charge, they were not examined or held on bail, and there was not any definite offense. The petition was granted.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 25, 1913, E. N. Roberts along with his attorney Vince H Faben, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. In the petition, Roberts claimed he was being held illegally by Claude G. Bannick as there was no proper warrant and he was unaware of what charge he was facing. Judge Gilliam granted the writ, to be heard in the court of J. T. Ronald. Bannick produced a warrant from Justice Fred C. Brown, dated February 26, 1913. The warrant stated that Roberts was charged with Burglary in the Second Degree for attempting to burgle a freight car on February 22, 1913. The fate of Roberts and the outcome of this case are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Albert and Loretta Sheldon divorced in 1888. Five years later, Loretta, who had remarried, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to establish custody of their son, Hallie. Loretta claimed that the divorce settlement had not determined custody; Albert countered that the settlement had granted custody of Hallie and his brother, Olliver, to himself and custody of a third son, Walter, to Loretta. After hearing the evidence, Hallie was remanded to the custody of Albert and Loretta ordered to pay his court fees.

Summary of Proceedings:
George Steward and Irene Baker were married on February 15, 1911, after Irene had an affair with him while married to Norman C. Baker. They had a son named George W. Steward Jr. on January 18, 1917. However, there was controversy about the child's parentage, as George Steward traveled frequently in his job as a waiter. Irene claimed that the child's father was her common-law husband, John L. Stewart, and thus referred to the child as John L. Stewart Jr. According to Irene's friend Mrs. M. Elliott, Irene visited her for a month shortly before her death from tuberculosis on March 18, 1918. She told her that if she died, she wanted Mrs. Elliott to take custody of her son. Despite this, after Irene's death, George Sr. took his son to Battle Creek, Michigan briefly. However, through correspondence, he and Elliott decided that Mrs. Elliott would take care of the child until Steward had settled into a comfortable home in Michigan.
 
They met in Chicago to exchange the child in May 1918. While they did not have a formal child support agreement, George Steward gave Mrs. Elliott $385 over the period in which she had custody of the child and Steward took out an $800 life insurance policy for George Jr. Once Steward had established a life in Battle Creek and remarried, he sent for the child, but Mrs. Elliott refused to surrender him. Because of this, he filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on June 4, 1924. The sheriff and his deputy could not find Mrs. Elliott or George, however, and thus served the writ to her husband, Donald C. Elliott. 

During a hearing on June 13, 1924, custody was granted to George Steward Sr., despite Mrs. Elliott's protests. She claimed that George was not the child's father—she believed Irene's claims that John L. Stewart, who she had lived with since 1914,  was her son's father. She also said that George had not taken a fatherly role in George (or John) Jr.'s life, and while Irene and John Stewart were living in Chicago, he had represented himself as Irene's brother. In fact, Mrs. Elliott said that George and Irene had never lived together at all. Because Mrs. Elliott intended to appeal, the court agreed to leave the boy in her custody until the legal processes concluded. The Supreme Court filed their opinion on the case on April 16, 1925. They claimed that, while George Steward was the boy's father, Mrs. Elliot should retain custody of the child, as it was in George Jr.'s best interests. They had no idea if George would be welcomed into his father's new family, and giving him into George Sr.'s custody would require him to leave the court's jurisdiction. However, they left the case open for a potential further appeal by George Sr. if he could prove that he was capable of caring for the child.

Summary of Proceedings: Harry Ferguson filed a writ claiming that he was imprisoned by Sheriff A. T. Van De Vanter after being arrested under no warrant or specific charge, just that it was some crime committed in the State of Colorado. It was further clarified he was arrested by James L. Wilson, a deputy sheriff of King County, in Snohomish County on the 5th of November and taken to the county jail. On the 28th of November Ferguson was formally charged with grand larceny for the theft of the property of George Conner, but said charge was only made after the writ had already been issued by Judge Orange Jacobs. Wilson further showed that he did have a warrant filed on November 9 for Ferguson’s arrest, but the warrant was never properly shown or explained to Ferguson, and the sheriff refused to allow Ferguson to consult with an attorney or anyone who might do so on his behalf. After the writ was granted, Ferguson and his lawyer argued that there was no evidence of the theft, and filed for both Ferguson’s release and the return of his confiscated property, which was granted.
