Summary of Proceedings:
Isaaiah Miller (representing himself) filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his two minor children, Eva L. Miller (16) and Jessie M. Miller (12). Their petition was filed alleging that both children were being unlawfully detained by Mother Superior Raphael of the Convent of the Good Shepherd in South Omaha, Nebraska. Neither their mother or father placed the children in the care of the Mother Superior, they were placed in the care of said convent by an unknown person while their father was sick. Once Mr. Miller was well and was made aware of the children’s location, he went to the Convent and demanded that the Mother Superior permit him to take the children back into his care. The Mother Superior denied his request and ordered him to not attempt to see the children anymore. He was informed that he would not be permitted to see or visit his children and would not be allowed to take the children from the Convent. They assert further that the Mother Superior forced the children to perform “hard and medial work … without any compensation” and that those under her control suffered “many and great indignities against their will.” The Writ was submitted by Eva, Jessie, and Isaaiah Miller on 4 June 1895 and was signed and sworn by Mr. Miller and George W. Covell (notary public)
The District Court, led by Judge Cunningham R. Scott, issued a writ in favor of Mr. Miller and his children, directed at Mother Superior Raphael returnable on 20 June 1895.
Mother Superior Raphael asserted that she took control and custody of the minor children because their parents were not able to care for them. She states further that she took custody at the request of the “Women’s Christian Association of Davenport, Iowa” on the grounds that the parents weren’t capable of bringing up the children. She asserted that Mr. Miller could regain custody of his children if he brought documentation identifying them as his children and showing that he had a cause for custody. District Court Clerk Frank E. Moore filed a document showing cause for custody on 20 June 1895, the day that the parties were ordered to appear in Court. The fate of the bound parties is not directly listed.

Summary of Proceedings: Claimed that Lynka Thomas was deprived of her liberty Mitchell Mark (Alias’s include “Glass,” “Green”) and Katherine Mark. According to Anthasso, 12 year old Lynka, and was kidnapped by Mark in California from her father, John Thomas and Mary Thomas, her grandmother. Katherine and Mitchell requested that the case be dismissed on insufficient evidence. They claimed that Lynka was not 12 years of age, she was in fact 15 and had no lawfully appointed guardian in the state of Nebraska. For two years she had been a member of Mark's family and was treated in the same way as all their other children. They claimed that she came to Nebraska with them willingly, desired to stay with them, and had no knowledge of the petition filed for her. It was determined that Mary Thomas, Lynka’s grandmother, gave her to Mark's family. Katherine and Mithchell were said to have paid $1,125 to Mary. Jonathan Anthasso and Mary Thomas offered to settle the case with Mitchell, if they paid him $3000 to no longer claim Lynka. Ultimately the judge ordered that Lynka be released from Douglas County sheriff custody and be allowed to choose either to live with the Marks or her grandmother.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 20, 1922, Edgar I. Fuller filed for habeas against his wife, Helen S. Fuller, and her mother, Mrs. Stina Sorensen, over the custody of their 4 1/2-year-old daughter, Helen Dorothy Fuller. Mr. Fuller argued that he and Mrs. Fuller had married in Utah in June of 1915 and are current residents of California, and on November 5, 1922, Mrs. Fuller took the child to her mother's in Omaha and is refusing Mr. Fuller access to the child. Upon return of the issued writ, Mrs. Fuller argued that Mr. Fuller had treated her cruelly and in an inhumane manner, that she had issued a divorce in Omaha, and that Mr. Fuller had never provided support for their child. On November 21, the writ was dismissed upon an agreement made, and the 1930 census shows Helen living with her mother and grandmother. Note: Mr. Fuller was a officer in the KKK.

Summary of Proceedings: W. H. Mahan, the petitioner, was detained for having corn whiskey at his home by officers Ballinger and Chilberg and then charged with violating the National Prohibition Act. Mahan later filed a petition of Habeas Corpus and made the argument that he was being unlawfully detained because he was arrested by an illegal warrant and that no evidence was introduced to establish probable cause that he had committed a crime. After his initial arrest, he was imprisoned due to his inability to pay bail. He then said that no sufficient legal cause had been shown to keep him in custody. The petition outcome and fate of the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 1st, 1912, Rose baker committed the crime of being willfully idle, as charged by G.W. Humphrey, a Seattle police officer. On June 4th, during her trial, she entered a plea of ‘Not Guilty’, but her attorney, Herbert Snook, entered a plea of ‘Guilty’. After that, G.W. Humphrey attempted to appear as a witness for the plaintiff, however his testimony was rejected for the objection of hearsay. Therein, the plaintiff’s attorney, Ralph Pierce, moved for a continuance, which was granted until June 18th, 1912, for the purpose of securing witnesses capable of testimony. On June 4th, the defendant, Rose Baker, petitioned for her freedom from the Chief of Police. Her petition was granted by Judge Everett Smith, and she was to go before Judge Gilliam on the 5th. On the 5th, there was an affidavit with the witness deposition of Otis Brinker, who was present during the original court session, which he described in full. The Chief of Police’s return was also signed and filed that day, saying that the warrant for her arrest was still valid from the day prior, as signed by Justice of the Peace Gordon. Attached was the arrest warrant, which certified the information already given.

Summary of Proceedings: Molly Martin petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve her son, Earl Martin, from his grandmother, Susie Harris, which was granted. Mary had obtained a divorce from Mrs. Harris's son, Joe Martin. After hearing the evidence, the writ was allowed and Earl released into his mother's custody. The court, however, determined that both women were "fit and proper persons to have custody of said child," and allowed Susie to have custody of Earl one day each month and one month each summer. Molly petitioned to modify the custody arrangement a few times over the next several years, but was unsuccessful.

Summary of Proceedings: Clara McLellan Northberg petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of her son Wilfred McLellan, age 13, and daughter Alva McLellan, age 10. Summary of Proceedings: On December 18, 1923, the governor of Nebraska issued a warrant for the arrest of Nettie Goodwin and George Armstrong on the charges of adultery and being fugitives from justice. This was based on a request from the governor of Iowa, N.E. Kendall, where the accused were from. Interestingly, the writ was directed both at the deputy sheriff of Woodbury County, Iowa, Frank Jibb,  and his wife. The couple were soon arrested and were confined by Douglas County sheriff Michael L. Endres, Frank Jibb, and an unknown man, called John Doe in court papers. They filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on December 20, 1923, claiming that they were being confined unlawfully since their arrest wasn't based on an affidavit or indictment from a magistrate, they weren't charged with a crime in the warrant for their arrest, there was no date specified for when this adultery was committed, and they had not left Iowa to escape prosecution. Interestingly, Goodwin and Armstrong believed that they were being confined based on a warrant from Iowa, not Douglas County. In turn, the defendants presented the warrant from the governor and said that John Doe didn't exist and there was no third man confining the couple. On December 21, 1923, an answer and return to the writ was issued and the case was continued until further order. At a hearing on Christmas Eve 1923, the application was granted and the relators were ordered released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Peter Lievo, the bound party and Finnish immigrant, joined the IWW, a union organization, in 1916. On February 5th, 1918, the bound party was arrested on a warrant issued by the Secretary of Labor, William B. Wilson (unnamed in the petition). The bound party was charged with being an alien, advocating or teaching the destruction of property, and being likely to become a public charge. On March 28th, 1918, W.P. Callahan, immigration inspector, interrogated the bound party on these issues and found the charges to be substantiated. The attorney for the petitioner does not agree that the questions were relevant. On December 17, 1918, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed. The fate of the petition and the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 1st, 1924, Lee Holmes petitioned for and was given an order allowing a writ of Habeas Corpus after he had been arrested and imprisoned in Omaha, Nebraska, in January of that year. He had been arrested on the charge of issuing a check with insufficient funds to meet same. He was given a hearing on said charges in January where he was bound over to the district court under $1500. The Municiple court ordered his release but the bond having been filed with surety guaranteed his appearance in a district court. In his petition Holmes presented that since the time of his arrest to the release order from the Municipal court he had been held in custody by Charles H Van Deusen who refused to allow him his liberty and thus he was being imprisoned without legal authority. It was the 2nd of February that the writ was denied, and Holmes was remanded to custody.

Matthews, alleging that he was unlawfully restrained of his liberty in the military at or near Lewiston. Lunkin claimed that he had enlisted in Oregon on February 23, 1861, but that he was only seventeen years old and that he had enlisted without the permission of his parents. He also stated that he had been promised $31 a month but that he had not been paid. Judge E. P. Oliphant allowed the writ to be heard, but the outcome of the case and Lunkin's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 13, 1862, W. M. Kerby was arrested by Walla Walla county sheriff James Buckley. He was accused of having killed a man named Maples in late July of 1862. The alleged crime occured in Lewiston, Nez Perce county in what is now Idaho. He was taken into custody by Nez Perce County Constable Alexander shortly at the time, but escaped to Walla Walla. He was being held in Walla Walla County Jail on the orders of Justice of the Peace E. B. Stone. In his petition for a writ of habeas corpus, filed on August 15, 1862, Kerby argued that there had been no trial, nor had a formal complaint been made. Judge E.P. Oliphant allowed a writ to issue, and Kerby was produced in court on August 16, 1862. Just under a week later, it was reported in the Walla Walla Statesman that Kerby had escaped once again.

Summary of Proceedings: Arrested after giving his customer trading stamps which could be redeemed at his company for merchandise, James H. Flaherty petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that the ordinance used to convict him in Police Court was unconstitutional, therefore, he was being deprived of his liberty. Judge Holmes granted the petition. In his statement, Holmes claimed that the charge and arrest dealt with public morality, not public safety, thus it was not a valid exercise of police power. He also ruled that Flaherty's method of advertising was not improper, and that the ordinance he was charged with violating was unconstitutional. He cites rulings in several other states. He allowed the writ and ordered that Flaherty be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On the night of December 30, 1894, W.P. Book was arrested at his brother-in-law’s home. The Seattle Post-Intelligencer notes that Book was arrested on the accusation of improperly assessing the price of a house during his tenure as the president of the Aberdeen Bank. The next morning, Book petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus arguing that Bolton Rogers, the Police Chief of the city of Seattle, unlawfully restrained him of his liberty by detaining him without cause. Book contends that Rogers did not have any warrant, charge, or court order giving him the legal justification to detain him. Available newspaper coverage states that Book was released on $2,000 bond. The newspapers later note that there was a case against W.P. Book which was eventually discharged in late January by Judge Irwin after finding that the property that Book's Aberdeen Bank was properly assessed.

Summary of Proceedings: A complaint was made by J. B. Murray on October 22, 1918, against Charles Ferguson for possession of intoxicating liquor. Ferguson was found guilty and charged $100 and costs of prosecution or to stand committed until fine be paid. Ferguson filed for habeas with attorney Daniel Horrigan on October 24, charging that the court does not have a charge for such offense under Nebraska laws. Douglas Co District Court Judge William Redick was named in the writ, but Douglas Co District Court Judge Lee Estelle oversaw the proceedings. The petition was granted and the writ sustained; Ferguson was released from custody October 26.

Summary of Proceedings: Mary V. Cunningham filed for a writ of habeas corpus in an effort to regain custody of her approximately 15 year old daughter, Ruby L. Lanham, from William and Flossie Prine. Judge Pemberton granted Mary’s petition and ordered the Prines to appear in court with Ruby. The Prines denied that they had in any way deprived Ruby of her liberty, or ever induced Ruby to remain with them rather than her mother. William further claimed that Mary was not fit to have care and custody of “this or any female child” because she was a “person of bad repute and unchaste.” The court ruled in favor of the Prines, finding that Ruby was not being deprived of her liberty, and denying Mary’s writ.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 14, 1896, Ernest Kinloch enlisted in the U.S. Army. Two days later, he was arrested on his way to the train station, charged with insanity, and jailed to await a hearing. He quickly petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Kinloch was remanded to the custody "proper military authorities."

Summary of Proceedings: Jear Chong, Gear Ling Ding, Lee Sing Tong were confined in Steamship Signal by M. Bendergard for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Each individual had two non-Chinese affiants claim that they are Chinese merchants, not in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. Lai Chen filed writ of habeas corpus, which was granted for Lee Sing Tong, but was denied for Jear Chong and Jear Lin Ding. Per Judge Charles B. Bellinger, Lee Sing Tong was released while the two others were remanded to custody of M. Bendegard. The case file includes an arrest warrant for Wah Hing for not appearing as a witness after there was a subpoena commanding him to appear. The case file also includes signed affidavits and special prosecutor John Catlin’s investigative reports.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 9th, 1913, Charles Gerrish filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his wife, Bell Leaper Gerrish. Charles explained that they were married on August 14th, 1913, and alleged that on the same day George Leaper, Bell's presumed brother, Albert Leaper, Bell's father, and Bell's unnamed mother forcibly removed Bell from his custody, against his and Bell's will. He alleged that the Leapers refused to allow Bell to leave or to talk with him, and that they threatened to kill him if he attempted to remove Bell from their care. On September 12th, the judge found that Bell was not unlawfully detained and the writ was denied. The appearance docket seems to indicate that Bell testified in open court that she was not being held against her will.

Summary of Proceedings: Yuzuoka Mutsu, the petitioner, petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus after she was detained by Ellis DeBruler, Commissioner of immigration in Seattle, Washington. Mutsu was detained with Nakagawa Hatsu in August of 1910; both women were detained and charged with practicing prostitution subsequent to entry to the United States. In the petition, Mutsu is identified as a resident of Washington, an inhabitant of the state for the past nine years, and a subject of the Japanese Empire. Her petition made the argument that her confinement was in violation of the United States Consititue and Treaty of the United States with the Japanese Empire, specifically in relation to the sections pertaining to discrimination because she was not given equal protection under the law. Judge Donworth denied the writ and ordered Mutsu to be remanded to the custody of DeBruler.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 22, 1924, Herlinda Diaz was taken into custody and charged with being a "vagrant and prostitute" in Douglas County. A hearing took place on January 23 and witnesses examined by the state and the evidence the presented showed that Diaz was neither a vagrant or a prostitute. However, a testimony given at the hearing stated that Diaz was meeting Jose Carillo at various times and places against the wishes of her husband and mother. Diaz's lawyers argued that Diaz is a married woman with a home, and therefore not a vagrant, and that the said testimony does not establish her guilt of prostitution. Diaz subsequently filed a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus against Douglas County sheriff Michael Endres. On January 27, 1925 the case was dismissed. The fate of Herlinda Diaz is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 25, 1919, Stella Williams was detained by police officers of the city of Omaha, and on January 27th, she was charged with being an inmate of an ill-governed house. Williams was taken to trial on that day, found guilty, and sentenced to serve 20 days in the Douglas County jail. She immediately provided the appeal bond necessary to file an appeal, which was approved by the Police Magistrate, who then notified the keeper of the Omaha city jail to release Williams. The keeper of the jail refused to release Stella Williams due to an order issued by Omaha Health Commissioner E. T. Manning, who ordered Williams to be quarantined and isolated in the jail due to her infection with a communicable venereal virus. On October 31, 1919, the application was dismissed at the cost of the county. Williams' fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Initially charged with vagrancy, William Shooks failed to appear at his court hearing on July 23, 1893. This prompted a bench warrant to be issued. Judge Glasglow proceeded to commit Shooks to jail following Shooks’ reappearance in Seattle on October 12, 1893. The following day, Shooks filed his petition. Judge Langley allowed the writ and released Shooks. 

The first names of the petitioner's attorneys were never mentioned or found in newspaper clippings.

Summary of Proceedings: Yip Back and Yip Bong are being detained on the Haytian Republic Steamship under the orders of the collector of customs T. J. Black. The customs collector does not believe they are merchants and thus their arrival would be in violation of the Chinese Immigration Act. The petitioner, Hong Fay, argues that they are merchants working at Wah Hing Co, a tailoring company located at No. 30 Alder Street. This information is verified by a white witness who works on the railroad, Charles J. Whelan. Judge Bellinger agrees they are merchants and thus their writ is granted, and both individuals are released from custody. The case file includes a trial transcript.

Summary of Proceedings: Ah Sue, alias Chin Shee, a Chinese immigrant, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against U.S. Commissioner of Immigration Henry M. White and Chinese Inspector Henry A. Monroe. Sue claimed she was being held illegally in the Detention House at the Immigration Station in Seattle awaiting deportation. She alleged she was arrested on a warrant for practicing prostitution as an alien, a violation of the Immigrant Act of 1917. Sue denied this claim, stating that the warrant was not based in fact and that she was denied a fair trial as well as her right to counsel. She claimed White and Monroe used illegal and unfair methods of procuring evidence against her, and that they stated conclusions, not facts. The court denied Sue’s writ and ordered she continue to be held by immigration authorities for deportation. Sue appealed to the Ninth Circuit, which affirmed the court’s original ruling that the writ be denied and Sue be held for deportation.

The petition was granted, but the case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 26, 1920.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 16th, 1920, Marie Paulson Hislop petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her children Herbert and Robert. She alleged that Herbert and Robert were being unlawfully deprived of their liberty by the Child Saving Institute and their secretary, A. A. McGraw. Marie explained that she initially relinquished custody and control of her children to the Child Saving Institute (January 1920) because she did not believe she could properly care for them, and that she was to have an operation which she did not believe she would recover from. Because of this, the Juvenile Court of Omaha granted custody of Herbert and Robert to the Child Saving Institute. At the time of the petition, Marie claimed that she had since recovered from the operation and was fully capable of properly caring for her children. She did not believe her children had been adopted out yet and revoked any previously signed papers of relinquishment and consent to adoption. On August 17th, the Judge granted her petition, and the writ was served both to A. A. McGraw personally and to the Child Saving Institute. While serving this writ, the Sheriff was supposed to take and bring before the court Herbert and Robert but he was unable to locate them. On August 18th,  A. A. McGraw responded to the petition, asserting that the Child Saving Institute was acting within their legal rights and responsibilities. This return also revealed that the children had already been adopted out to a family outside of Douglas County, and that the Institute would not reveal the family’s identity or location. The writ was dismissed and fate of bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 1st, 1884, Sam Hing, John Sam, Joe Chinaman, Jim Kee, Ah Kee, Ah Sing, Ah Him, and James D. Patterson were all arrested at Sam Hing's house and charged by a justice of the peace for opium use. The court sentenced the eight men to a fine of ten dollars plus court costs for "inhaling and smoking" opium. Following their imprisonment for failing to pay their fine, Sam Hing filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of the entire group and was represented by the attorney Edward Everice. The group had their case heard by Judge Roger S. Greene on July 7th, 1884; however the outcome of their petition is not revealed in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: In May 1921, W.B. Mitchell filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Benjamin Henry Greenwood. Greenwood had been arrested, court martialed, and sentenced to seven years in a military prison for desertion. Greenwood argued in the petition that he did not flee after being drafted into the United States Military. Instead, he claimed he did not have any knowledge of being drafted and was never informed of it because he had moved to Charlestown, South Carolina, to work at a shipping terminal. The petition argued that since Greenwood never received his mobilization papers he is not subject to a military court martial. However, Mitchell and Greenwood’s petition for a writ of habeas corpus was denied by Judge Frank H. Rudkin.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 24, 1907, T. Katioka and his attorney Walter A. Keene petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. They alleged that Katioka was being held by Chief of Police C. W. Wappenstein without charge or warrant and that he had been denied bail. Bail was set by Judge Tallman, and Katioka and Keene paid it. The bail documentation indicated that Katioka had originally been charged with assault with a deadly weapon. That charge was changed to assault and battery. Katioka paid a ten dollar fine and was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Wah Sing petitioned for the writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his cousin Young Hing on January 23rd of 1893, after he was restrained on the ship Wimington by Captain E.J. Moody following his attempt to return to Oregon. Wah Sing and Young Hing had been residents of America for 12 years and were merchants in Portland. Young Hing left for a trip to China in March of 1891 with the intention of returning, and left the business to his partner. Upon his return, he was denied landing in Oregon, with the reasoning from Captain E.J. Moody being the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, denying the entry of Chinese laborers. After proving Young Hing was a merchant and not a laborer, the writ was allowed and he was discharged from the ship.

Summary of Proceedings: George Leib was indicted for forgery charges and sentenced to five years in prison, which he began serving on February 14th, 1913. Leib filed a writ of habeas corpus on October 26th, 1915, claiming that he had been wrongfully imprisoned. Judge Cushman dismissed the case and ordered Leib to remain in custody at McNeil Island Penitentiary on November 2nd, 1915. In response, Leib filed an appeal on May 1st, 1916. In his appeal, Leib cited a similar case involving Gross S. Edison, who was also indicted for forgery and was released on habeas corpus. Leib argued that both cases should be ruled the same way and that a precedent in appellant’s favor had been established by a Federal Court of equal rank, in a parallel case and this precedent was ignored in the petitioner's case. Judge White affirmed the lower court's ruling on November 9th, 1916, and Leib was ordered to finish serving his sentence at McNeil Island.

Summary of Proceedings: Sarah and Daniel Dee got divorced in February of 1901 and Sara was given sole custody of Harry Dee, their child, by Lake County in Colorado. Three years prior, Harry had been taken by force and without the consent of Sarah. Daniel took their child, Harry, and kept him hidden away in a ranch. Then Daniel relocated Harry to Leadville, Colorado and left him with Daniel’s sister. Sarah did not have steady employment at the time and arranged with the sister, Mrs. Carr, to take care of Harry until she was able to care for him. Then she lost contact with Harry and tried to ascertain where he was located to no avail. Therefore, Sarah alleged that Harry, her child, was in the unlawful care of Mary Walters, Daniel's sister. After months of continuing the case, the case was dismissed at the costs of the relator. An Evening World-Herald article indicates that the parents reached an agreement outside of court to give custody to Sarah.

Summary of Proceedings: In March 1919, Wendell Phillips Herrick filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty. Herrick's wife, Ethel, alleged in the Municipal Court of Chicago that on September 10th, 1918, Wendell neglected and refused to maintain and provide for her. Herrick was charged with non-support of his wife and charged as a fugitive from justice from Illinois. The Governor of Nebraska, at the request of the Governor of Illinois, issued an order of extradition to Illinois. The amended petition alleged the extradition was illegal and the fugitive from justice claim was overcame by multiple affidavits from Herrick's colleagues in Nebraska at the Western Union Telegraph Company stating Herrick was not in Illinois at the time and did not leave the state of Nebraska during September 1918. The respondent's attorney gathered a conflicting deposition from Herrick's colleague in Illinois at the Western Union Telegraph which stated he saw Herrick in Illinois during the month of September 1918. The court allowed the petition but denied the writ of Habeas Corpus. Herrick's attorney motioned for a new trial on the grounds the judgment was contrary to both the evidence and the law, and the court erred in receiving the deposition offered by the respondent. The motion for a new trial was denied, on appeal to the Supreme Court of Nebraska, the judgment was affirmed.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 26, 1922, George Painter filed for habeas against sheriff, Michael Clark. In the petition, Painter explained that his arrest came of April 17 in Sarpy County, Nebraska, after violating Section 16, Chapter 186, Laws of Nebraska 1917 as amended by Section 16, Chapter 156, Laws of Nebraska, 1921 (Section Laws 1921, Page 639), which prohibits the manufacture of intoxicating liquor. Painter was sentenced to a $500, costs, and 30 days. Painter argued that such confinement was unconstitutional and that the law was designed to deprive petitioner of due process. In addition, Painter argued that he had not been informed or arraigned for this charge, that as an uneducated man, Painter had no knowledge of law or legal proceedings, was not provided presentation, and agreed to plead guilty to pretend charges. The case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924.

Summary of Proceedings: E. I. Chamberlin petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of Frank Gibson against Seattle Chief of Police J. F. Warren. Chamberlin alleged that Gibson committed no crime and that Warren had no authority to imprison Gibson. Warren responded that he had a warrant charging Gibson with being a disorderly person and that Gibson was being held for defaulting on his bail, set at $200. Newspaper records indicate Gibson was a member of the I.W.W. and that his writ was denied. The fate of Gibson is unknown. This is one of several petitions for habeas corpus that involve Gibson.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 26, 1878, S. L. Morse accused John Morrissey, Joseph Bartlett, and C. C. Thomas, Richard Roe, and John Doe of grand larceny. Morrissey, Bartlett, and Thomas were charged with committing grand larceny in Uwatilla County, Oregon. Justice of the Peace O. P. Lacy found probable cause to detain them and set their bail at $5000. As none of the men could pay the sum, they were put into the custody of Walla Walla county sheriff George F. Thomas on August 29. They were to remain in custody until their next hearing on September 26. The same day, John Morrissey petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that he was being detained illegally. Judge Samuel C. Wingard allowed his writ on August 28, and Sheriff Thomas filed his return to the writ on August 31, citing the writ of commitment signed by Justice Lacy, but no more is known of Morrissey's fate or the outcome of this case.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 20, 1922, Robert Johnson filed for habeas against the sheriff of Douglas County. In his petition, Johnson explained that a false complaint was made against him by the City Prosecutor, Frank M. Dineen, under the charge of vagrancy on July 13, 1922 and that following his sentence in Police Court, an appeal in pending. Johnson argues that under such appeal the jurisdiction of the police court, which issued a new warrant without complaint while out on bond, had no authority to commit Johnson. A writ was issued, sustained, and Johnson was ordered to be released on October 27, 1922.

Summary of Proceedings: Chango Kim was a migrant from Korea that arrived in Seattle in 1904. After nearly a decade in the United States, Kim was arrested by the Seattle Immigration Inspector, A. F. Richardson for violating Section 3 of the Immigration Act of 1907 which outlawed migrants from having any connections with a house of prostitution. Kim argued that he cannot be deported for violating the Act because his employment came more than three years after his arrival in the United States. Judge Frank H. Rudkin ruled that deportations under Section 3 of the Act are not subject to such a rule and denied Kim’s writ of habeas corpus and remanded him to the custody of the Immigration Inspector.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 24th, 1924, a warrant was created for William, Helena, and Albert Wilhelm Richter, an immigrant family, on the charge that all persons were likely to become public charges. The Richter family filed a writ of habeas corpus on March 9th, 1925, with hopes of remaining in the United States instead of being deported to Canada. The next day, Judge Neterer ordered the family to not be deported, but stated they must stay inside their house until further notice. On May 19th, the family was given 10 days to file a brief with Judge Cushman. The outcome of the petition and the fate of the bound parties is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
On April 3rd, 1897, Charles W. Nordstrom petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus after being charged with murder in the first degree, murder in the second degree, and manslaughter, and having been set to be executed later that month. The petition alleged that the jury in the Superior Court of King County found Nordstrom guilty of "nothing more than murder in the second degree", a sentence of 10-20 years of imprisonment but not the death penalty. Circuit Judge C. H. Hanford denied the petition and Nordstrom subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, where the lower court's ruling was affirmed. 
Supplementary research shows that since the alleged murder took place in 1892, Nordstrom and his attorneys issued a number of appeals to avoid the death penalty. A year after this petition, Nordstrom's attorneys successfully delayed his execution by appealing the decision on the grounds Nordstrom was insane. A commission of physicians unanimously decided that Nordstrom was sane, and he was later executed in 1901. 
For other petitions filed by Charles W. Nordstrom, see related petitions.

Summary of Proceedings: Moy Share Park, the bound party and an individual of Chinese descent, was charged under the Chinese Exclusion Act. This charge was appealed and subsequently denied on the 2nd of April 1920. On April 5, 1920, a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed alleging that his father was a Native Born U.S. Citizen and thus derived an exemption from the Act. On April 6th, 1920, Judge Cushman orders the holding party to respond to the application and explain why the writ should not be issued. On April 30th, 1920, Judge Neterer rules that the Chinese Exclusion Act stipulates that the decisions of immigration officials are final unless there was an unfair trial. By virtue of there being testimony present in the original appeal, the Neterer does not find this to be the case and finds that the court does not have jurisdiction to hear the writ. The writ was denied and the bound party was remanded to the custody of the Commissioner of Immigration.

Summary of Proceedings: Robert Geslin filed for a petition of Habeas Corpus December of 1921 on the grounds that he was being held in custody and deprived of his liberty by William M. Basher, an immigration inspector, in Douglas County, Nebraska. Basher was holding Geslin in custody under the claim that he was an alien. Geslin, having been born in the Empire of Russia, made his way to New York in 1920 where he applied for and was given papers of naturalization and after had and was residing in Lincoln, Nebraska. It was November of the following year that he was arrested, charged and given a hearing. After the hearing, he was informed that there would be nothing more of the matter until he received information that Brasher had a warrant for deportation. When Brasher appeared in court he denied all allegations and asked that Geslin be remanded for deportation. It was January 1925 that in trial it was decided the writ of Habeas Corpus be allowed and Geslin be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Mary Odalovich was detained in a house by her father, V. Odalovich. V. Odalovich claimed Mary owed him three hundred dollars. Her next friend, John Tomich, applied for a writ of habeas corpus on her behalf on August 17, 1917. Judge John S. Jurey issued the writ the same day. The fate of Mary is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Gerasimos Nicolovinis, the petitioner, was born in Kalovata, Kepal, Greece, in 1892 and moved to the United States in 1910. Nicolovinis was drafted, but because of his lack of understanding of English and knowing the facts, he failed to make a claim of exemption and is certified by the Local Board No. 2 as a deserter. Afterward, he was apprehended and taken in front of the board and then put into custody at Camp Lewis and inducted into the army. The petitioner stated he was being restrained from his liberty because he was an alien and not subject to the draft. The petition was dismissed with prejudice, reasoning not included in case files.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 30, 1906, Katie Christner petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her ten-year-old son, Loy Willmer Christner. Katie and her husband J. L. Christner had Loy and four-year-old Mona Marie Christner together. In her petition, Katie stated that J. L. had been abusive to her, so she left Illinois with her children and came to Georgetown, Washington. She stated that J. L. followed her, threatened her, and enticed Loy to come with him, whom he now prohibits from returning to her. Frater issued the writ. J. L.’s return denied Katie’s claims, and stated that he was the only fit person to have custody over Loy. The outcome of this case and the fate of Loy Willmer Christner are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: John Musser petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his young son, Clayton Musser, from Anna Musser, which was granted. Although not stated, it seems likely that Anna was the child's mother. Anna did not respond to the writ, and so after hearing the evidence, Clayton was released into his father's custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Nineteen people jointly petitioned against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. They claimed they were being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail under no legal authority. Newspaper records indicated that at least 12 of the 19 petitioners may have been involved with the I. W. W. The outcome of the case and the fates of all nineteen petitioners remain unknown due to the brevity of the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 6, 1894, Jong Ling filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Jung Ming and Ung Chung. Jong Ling claimed that they were being illegally detained on the Steamship Signal by Captain George Beudegard. Jong Ling claimed that they were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Act because Jung Ming and Ung Chung were merchants and not laborers. Judge Charles Bellinger granted the writ and ordered them released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 4, 1890, Alexander Vachon was jailed by H.G. Thornton for the charged crime of bigamy. On July 8, 1890, Vachon filed a Writ of Habeas Corpus with the assistance of his attorney V.B. Duvall claiming that he was being illegally deprived of his liberty in the Seattle City Jail. The writ of Habeas was granted and a hearing before Judge Thomas Humes was set for July 9, 1890. Outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Al Atkinson, confined in the Douglas County jail, was facing extradition to Canada for his alleged involvement in the violent theft of liquor, a firearm, and other items belonging to one Robert Andrist. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming, among other things, that the procedure leading to his arrest and detention were inconsistent with treaty obligations between the United States and Canada. After hearing the evidence, his writ was denied and Atkinson remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1913, D. L. Anderson took his young son, Cecil Anderson, from his and his wife's house in Kansas to his parents' house in Oregon. When three years had passed and D. L. had not returned with Cecil, his then-wife, Ina Anderson, secured a divorce in a Kansas district court. Ina then traveled to Oregon and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the Marion County Circuit Court, which was granted. She initially named D. L.'s parents, William and Nancy Anderson, as the respondents. William and Nancy refused to cooperate, arguing that it was D. L., not them, who had custody. Ina then amended her petition to include D. L. as a respondent, forcing him to appear in court. After some back and forth, the two parties resolved the dispute outside of court, and the cause was dismissed without prejudice. The case file does not specify what happened to Cecil.

Summary of Proceedings: Ethel Johnson was arrested on February 9, 1919 for keeping a "Common Illgoverned House" based on the accusation of a man named J.B. Murray. She was tried at police court under magistrate Charles E. Foster on the tenth and sentenced to thirty days in prison plus court costs. She filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against Omaha sheriff Michael L. Clark on February 14, which was issued by judge William A. Redick. In her petition, she argued that she should be set free because the ordinance outlawing prostitution in the city of Omaha did not provide for prison sentences above ten days. She had also tried to pay an appeal bond on February 13, and although she had the money and a surety, the court refused to allow the bond, as it had been more than 24 hours since the judgement. Clark merely stated that he had the authority to imprison her based on the writ of mittimus submitted by police magistrate Charles E. Foster. On March 21, 1919, her application was granted and she was set free.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 18, 1914, Tony Sullivan and Tony Broski filed for a writ of habeas corpus against Chief of Police Claude C. Bannick. They claimed they had received no official charge, and no warrant had been issued for their arrest. They also claimed they were innocent of Assault in the First Degree, which was the pretense of their arrest. Bannick produced a warrant, also dated February 18, 1914, from Justice Fred C. Brown. The warrant and related documents indicated that Broski, Sullivan, and Joe Alfonso had assaulted F. H. Risley with a knife on January 31, 1914. Newspaper coverage referred to the men as thugs and a gang, and said they were using foul language around one in the morning near Risley’s home. The same article said that Risley, a police officer, ordered the men to leave and then they attacked him. The outcome of this case and Sullivan and Broski’s fates are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Logan Billingsley petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles L. Beckingham. As the petition is missing from the case file, it is unclear for what offense Billingsley was held in Seattle City Jail or for what reason he found his jailing to be illegal. Newspaper records suggest that Billingsley was arrested for shooting and killing two police officers. The outcome of the case and the fate of Billingsley are both unknown. Billingsley’s petition was connected to that of three other men, two of whom were his brothers.

Summary of Proceedings:
George A. Tarrant filed a petition to receive custody of his daughter, Eva, from his former wife, Lila Daniels, and her current husband, Ed Daniels. George Tarrant alleged that his wife left him in 1898 with their three children, the youngest being Eva at 13 and the others around 17 and 18, to marry Ed Daniels and that he did not know her or the children's whereabouts until recently. George found that they were residing in Washington County, Nebraska. He stated that Eva is being abused in every way, and it 
 was known in the neighborhood that the Daniels lived in that they were unfit to care for children. The outcome of the case is unclear.

Summary of Proceedings: In May 1923, the Umatilla County Circuit Court had seventeen-year-old Myrtle O'Grady transferred from the St. Rose Industrial School in Portland to the State Hospital for the Feeble Minded in Salem. In November 1923, Myrtle's mother, Harriet O'Grady, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on her behalf, which was granted. Harriet's petition raised questions about the qualifications of the medical authorities who examined her daughter. After hearing the evidence, Myrtle was remanded back into the custody of the hospital superintendent.

Summary of Proceedings: Albert Schiessl claimed that Wilma Schiessl, his 2-year-old daughter, was unlawfully detained by Gussie Maloney. Gussie was the wife of Albert and the mother of Wilma. Albert claimed that Gussie left him for another man and that she was "morally unfit" to take care of the child properly. His wish was that Wilma be placed under his custody and not Gussie's. The writ was allowed and he was released from jail.

Repository: ["[History Nebraska (Lincoln, Nebraska)](hc.loc.000039)", "[Douglas County District Court (Omaha, Nebraska)](hc.loc.000020)"]
Summary of Proceedings: Frank Brandt petitioned on behalf of his 14 year old daughter for custody. Frank was married to Emma Brandt and they had a daughter, Pearl in 1891. Three years later, Emma passed away. In 1897, Frank remarried Martha Dorhmann. In 1904 Frank's sister, Emma Becker, solicited the custody of Pearl for the purpose of assisting her in and about her household duties, alleging that her mother was ill and she could not do it all herself. Frank permitted Pearl to go with Emma until he sent for her to come back. Frank filed the writ because he demanded Pearl back three months later and Emma refused. Emma argued against this accusation and said that she was in the process of getting custody of Pearl because Frank and Martha were unfit to take care of Pearl themselves. The court ended up giving custody back to Frank and Martha after Emma did not appear for the hearings.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry Orlofsky petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle chief of police Claude G. Bennick. Orlofsky claimed his detention in the Seattle City Jail was illegal as Bennick arrested him without knowledge of a warrant being issued. Bennick responded that he had received a telegraph from New Mexico wherein a warrant was issued charging Orlofsky with being a fugitive from justice. The warrant was dated after Orlofsky’s petition was filed. The court denied the writ and ordered Orlofsky to be sent to New Mexico with an agent of the state. Orlofsky attempted to appeal to the Supreme Court of Washington, but his appeal was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 29th, 1918, Lena Heaton was taken into custody under suspicion of prostitution. She was transported first to St. Joseph Hospital where she received initial inspections, and then to a building on 22nd & St. Mary's Avenue where she was bound to prevent the spread of diseases that she was allegedly confirmed to have. The bound party, Heaton, alleged that she was not allowed to speak to anyone until her sister, Camille Schultz, was allowed to visit on July 13th, 1918. On July 20th, 1918, a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus was filed. A hearing was held in which the holding party, Health Commissioner Ernest C. Manning, filed a return and was subpoenaed to appear before the court. On July 23rd, 1918, the bound party's application was denied, which, based on the timeline, was interpreted to mean that the writ was denied. The costs of the officers involved in the case were taxed to the county whereas other costs were taxed to the bound party. On July 26th, 1918, the bound party filed for a new trial on the basis that the judgment was not sustained by sufficient evidence, the judgment was contrary to the evidence, errors of law were committed, the court erred in allowing testimony of physicians in relation to physical examinations, and that the court erred in allowing testimony of physicians in relation to conversations had with the bound party. The status of the appeal and fate of the bound party are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 24th, 1913, Willis Kelly filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his minor son, Phillip Kelly. Willis named Jessie Kelly as the respondent. The petition revealed Jessie to be the ex-wife of Willis and mother of Phillip. Willis claimed that Jessie was unlawfully holding Phillip. In September of 1913, Willis and Jessie divorced; and Willis was awarded custody of their two children, George and Phillip. Willis alleged that Jessie was an unfit mother as she was addicted to alcohol, would use profane language in front of the children, and would frequently entertain men in their home and maintained improper and immoral relationships with them. Willis alleged that on October 23rd he made a formal request to Jessie for her to release their children but she refused.  Jessie replied to the petition, denying all of the allegations against her. She claimed, rather, that Willis was a man of vile and vicious habits. She claimed that in July 1912, he forced her to sign a paper admitting that she was intimate with other men and that he then used that paper to get $500 from a Banker at Snyder Nebraska. He said that using that paper, he would be able to get enough money to put him on "Easy Street". Jessie claimed that Willis was addicted to alcohol, and that he would frequently come home drunk and when he did he would abuse her. Jessie claimed that they parted August 1912 and that Jessie had custody of the children, but then in June 1913 they lived together and as a result of that living together she was now pregnant. Jessie further claimed that Willis wanted Jessie and the children to live with him in July, but then soon after Willis brought a man home to stay with Jessie while he went to South Dakota. On October 23rd, Willis returned and forcibly removed George from Jessie. Jessie claimed that on November 3rd, Willis called Jessie and promised that he would drop the habeas proceedings and marry her. She claimed that was a scheme to keep her out of court. Willis responded and denied any allegations of force, but that he did have Jessie sign the paper of infidelity and did remove George from Jessie's care. In the end, Judge Pemberton decided in favor of Willis, allowing the writ and demanding that Phillip should be released from Jessie's custody. The decision was made by virtue of the divorce settlement.

Summary of Proceedings:
On November 5, 1829, Vincent Duncan petitioned the court to release him from James Duncan whom Vincent alleged had wrongfully enslaved him following the death of James Duncan's father, Jesse Duncan. Vincent had been leased to the Saline Salt Works of southeastern Illinois following the stipulations listed in the 1818 Constitution of the state that banned slavery everywhere except in the Saline Salt Works where it could continue given that slaves were contracted in periods of no more than a year and only until 1825. Any contract in voidance of such terms would free the individual involved. James Duncan came to collect Vincent sometime following the death of James' father and found Vincent unwilling to leave, causing James to reenslave Vincent. Sometime later, Vincent and James found themselves in St. Louis where Vincent went to court to seek his freedom.

The Duncan family sought witnesses from Illinois and their home county in Kentucky to verify their claims of ownership and deny any claims of wrongful enslavement. Taking place over the course of several years and several trials, the jury finally decided against Vincent's claims that he had been wrongfully enslaved, stating , "We the jury find the plaintiff a slave."

Summary of Proceedings: On December 20, 1906, Fred Schneiderwind stole one dozen plates, according to H.S. Daniel. On January 21, 1907, Fred was sentenced to 90 days being absolutely void, on the charge of petit-larceny. The habeas file was entered January 22 and filed on January 30. On January 30, the writ was allowed, returnable January 31, 1907. However, on January 31, the writ was denied, and the case was to remain undecided until February 22, 1907. On October 3, 1907 the case dismissed due to a court motion for warrant of prosecution. Note the case file ends on January 30 without documentation reflected in the docket.

Summary of Proceedings: This petition is the third petition for writ of habeas corpus filed by George Roberts. Similar to the previous petitions, Roberts argued that he was being illegally held by Thomas L. Ryan. This petition also states that Ryan is conspiring with a Seattle Police Officer named J. Barok to remove Roberts from the jurisdiction of King County and extradite Roberts to San Francisco to face trial for the crime of grand larceny for stealing $80 from W. L. Perry. Following the hearing for the writ of habeas corpus, Judge W. R. Bell denied Roberts' petition and ordered its dismissal. Roberts claimed that he will appeal the decision but the court documents state that Roberts did not appeal within the five day limit and ordered that he remain in the custody of Thomas L. Ryan. Newspaper reports of this case note that following this decision Thomas L. Ryan was able to extradite George Roberts to California to face his charges. Roberts would later be convicted for grand larceny and be sentenced to nine years in prison.

Summary of Proceedings: Chinese merchant She Kimm petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of his minor son Wah Kee against F. D. Huestis, the Collector of Customs for the District of Puget Sound. Kimm alleged that Kee was being detained illegally by Huestis at the Customs House in Port Townsend under the suspicion that Kee was not a U.S. citizen. Kimm claimed that Kee had been in China for over a decade for the purposes of education, but was born in the United States, making him a citizen. Kimm was unable to provide a birth certificate for Kee, claiming it was destroyed in a fire that burned his storefront down several years prior. The doctor who delivered Kee testified that he was born in Spokane, and several patrons of Kimm’s store testified that they had seen Kimm’s children. H. L. Clark, an agent for the Northern Pacific Steamship Company, alleged that Huestis had ordered the company to hold Kee in preparation for his deportation to China. The court ruled that Kee was born in China and, thus, was not a native citizen of the United States. Kee remained in the custody of Huestis and Clark.

Summary of Proceedings: C. Sing applied for the writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his friend Leong Chung Tick on July 29th, 1893, who was being unlawfully imprisoned on the steamship Haytain Republic by the T.J. Black Collector of Customs at the port of Portland.  According to C. Sing, Black believed Leong Chung Tick was a Chinese person prohibited from landing in the United States, referring to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, and denied Tick’s application after he made a “pretend examination.” Sing mentions that Tick has been a resident of Portland for 10 years and a merchant at Feng Yuen and Co., and had offered to produce “respectable” white witnesses to testify on his behalf.  This was also denied along with his request to have an attorney present at his examination. Judge C.B. Bellinger issued the writ directed at T.J. Black and ordered him to present the body of Leong Chuck Tick with the reasoning for his detainment. Bellinger transferred the case to E.J. Lake and outcome is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: The 27-year-old John L. Allsman had married the 14-year old Hazel Smith in Council Bluffs, Iowa on July 15, 1913. Hazel's mother, Tessie Smith, had managed to catch the couple in Omaha as they were about to leave by train. Allsman was charged with child stealing and Hazel was taken back to her parents' home. On July 25, 1913, Allsman petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to challenge Hazel's detention by her parents, which was granted. While her hearing was pending, Hazel, who was a minor, was placed into the custody of Emily Hornberger, the county probation officer. Jesse Strode, the Lancaster County attorney, successfully motioned to have himself added to the case as a "party defendant on behalf of the State of Nebraska." After hearing the evidence, Allsman's writ was allowed and Hazel was released from the custody of her family. The couple went on to settle in Omaha and have 9 children.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 20, 1904, Gideon W. Morley petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his sixteen-year-old daughter, Edith Morley. Gideon’s petition claimed that he had divorced Frances K. Morley and that he was given full custody over Edith. However, Gideon asserted that Frances had taken Edith from him and he believed she intended to remove Edith from the court’s jurisdiction in the near future. The outcome of this case and the fate of Edith Morley are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Neil MacDonald, the petitioner and bound party, was charged with violating Section 3 of the Espionage Act for wilfully making false statements with intent to interfere with the operation and success of the military and naval forces of the United States and to promote the success of the enemies of the United States. On April 16th, 1918, it was found that there was probable cause that MacDonald was guilty, and he was given a one thousand dollar bond ($19,923.18 in 2024). On the 3rd of July 1918, MacDonald filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus stating that he was a Canadian by birth, was illegally confined, and not present when the Grand Jury convened on June 11, 1918, and was not indicted or confronted by witnesses. MacDonald asked for a hearing concerning his detention and to be restored of his liberty. The petition outcome is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 7th, 1888, Justice of the Peace J. R. Snyder sent Joseph Deveriske to prison for the crime of larceny. On April 19th, 1888, Betty Deveriske, Joseph's wife, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Joseph. Betty claimed that Joseph was being illegally imprisoned, and that J. R. Snyder did not have the jurisdiction to imprison him. Judge Nash allowed the petition, setting the court date for the following day. The outcome of the writ and Joseph's fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Dry Squad Sergeant George Comstock petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff John Stringer. Comstock alleged that Stringer was holding him illegally in King County Jail without charge, warrant, or bail. Comstock also claimed he was being prevented from consulting with his lawyer. Stringer made no return to the writ, so said writ was allowed and Comstock was released from custody. Newspaper records indicate Comstock was rearrested on federal charges for conspiring with bootleggers soon after his release.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis Gar Han, Tung Wing, Louis Him, and Ung Wong were confined in Steamship Islander by Master John Irving for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Louis Gar Han, Tung Wing, and Louis Him are U.S. Citizens of Chinese descent and below 21 years of age according to their petition. Ung Wong claims that he is a Chinese merchant. Judge Charles B. Bellinger granted writ of habeas corpus to Louis Him, Tung Wing, Ung Wong, and they were discharged from custody. Louis Gar Han was denied writ of habeas corpus, and he was remanded to the custody of John Irving.

Summary of Proceedings: Estella Lyell of Eagle, Nebraska petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Samuel Prey, her nephew, from the custody of Martha Prey, his grandmother, which was granted. She claimed that Martha was unable to care for Samuel due to her advanced age. The custody of the boy was in question due to his parents' divorce. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and Samuel remanded to the custody of Martha. However, the 1920 census shows a now 18-year-old Samuel living with his mother, Nellie, in Eagle, Nebraska.

Summary of Proceedings:
On November 4th, 1913, police conducted a raid in a residential building in Portland as it was believed to be a place of prostitution. Yut Yow was one of the women arrested on the charge of being an "alien" and a prostitute in connection with a house of prostitution. An order of deportation was issued based upon the testimony of the two arresting officers, thereafter in January of 1914, Harry Gong petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Yut Yow. The petition alleged Yut Yow was a native-born citizen of the United States as she was born in San Francisco and that she was deprived of due process and a full and fair hearing as she had no opportunity to be present during police testimony. The petition further alleged that Chinese Inspector Barbour, through an interpreter, exacted a pretended statement from Yut Yow on the day of her arrest confessing she had been a prostitute for 15 years. Yut Yow's testimony from a later hearing revealed she denied being a prostitute, did not know what a prostitute was, and did not remember if she admitted to being a prostitute during previous testimony. Judge Neterer authorized the writ, yet by the time it was served to immigration authorities, Yut Yow was not in their custody as she had already been delivered to a ship and likely deported. The petitioner's attorney agreed to have the cause dismissed.  
For related case of another women arrested during the same police raid, see related petition of Gwoo Shee Ah Look.

Summary of Proceedings: Luige Gargono was drafted for the service and held at Camp Lewis. His brother, Joe Gargono, filed a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf to free him from service on the grounds that he was a citizen and subject of Italy and never had taken out his papers for citizenship in the United States and therefore was exempt due to alienage. As proof, the petitioner presents Luige's certificate of honorable discharge from the Italian army and states that his passport is being held by the local board (along with the English translation), but after it is received should be considered when deciding his release. The petition outcome and fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: John Martin served two years at the Nebraska State Penitentiary on a burglary conviction. The day he was released, he was arrested and charged with having committed an attempted robbery in Iowa several years prior. Martin claimed he had been in a different state at the time of the attempted robbery and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the writ was allowed and Martin released from custody.

Sears granted the petition but there was no outcome on any of the documents.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 22, 1914, James Dermott and his attorneys Bell and Turner filed a petition of habeas corpus, asserting that Dermott was being held illegally and without warrant or official complaint against him. Shortly after, Austin E. Griffiths, Chief of Police, produced documentation that California governor, Hiram W. Johnson had sent word to Washington governor, Ernest Lister, that Dermott was charged with abandonment of wife, and was a fugitive from justice. Judge Mitchell Gilliam denied Dermott’s writ. Dermott was given the option of paying part of his bail, and having to report to court if called. Dermott accepted these conditions, but failed to show up to court when summoned, so Judge Archibald W. Frater ordered that his bail be forfeited. Frater also stated that Dermott left the jurisdiction of the court, and evaded custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles E. McHugh fled from Iowa to Nebraska in order to escape a charge of seduction. Francis M. Drake, the governor of Iowa, wrote to Silas A. Holcomb, the governor of Nebraska, in order to ensure that P. R. Schaap, a sheriff from Iowa, has the documentation and authority to pursue and arrest McHugh and take him back to Iowa to answer the charges against him. After being arrested McHugh filed for a writ of Habeas denying all of the accusations against him. He also asks for a re-hearing and new trial because of a variety of irregularities that he alleged took place in his previous trial, including the burden of proof being put on him rather than the prosecution. Judge L. B. Letton agreed to hear the petition and granted the writ, but the outcome of the hearing is unknown.

Repository: ["[History Nebraska (Lincoln, Nebraska)](hc.loc.000039)", "[Douglas County District Court (Omaha, Nebraska)](hc.loc.000020)"]
Summary of Proceedings:
The petition submitted by Mr. James H. Howard alleges that Police Judge Louis Berka issued a complaint against him, accusing him of a crime that does not allow a “preliminary examination before an examining magistrate can be had.” Nonetheless, the complaint was issued based on a preliminary examination. No other complaints were filed against Mr. Howard, meaning that this examination was not allowed under the law. 
This case involves a group of co-defendants; William F. Herman, James H. Howard (Petitioner), N. D. Coleman, and Harry Voorhees. Police Judge Berka submitted his complaint to the Court as an exhibit. This complaint commanded Sheriff John Drexel to take co-defendant William Herman into custody until he could be “charged by due course of law.” The crime alleged his “obtaining money under false pretenses.” His bail was set at one thousand dollars. In this complaint, Berka refers to himself as an examining magistrate.
Another exhibit submitted with this petition is the case of the State of Nebraska v. Herman, Howard, Coleman, and Voorhees which was tried before the Police Court of the City of Omaha on 17 February 1894. The group was accused of conspiring to cheat and defraud the United States National Bank of Omaha, the First National Bank of Omaha, Union National Bank of Omaha, and Omaha Savings Bank. They scammed these banks by saying that there was an organization called the Omaha and Council Bluffs Railway Employee Association, that they were planning to throw a charity ball, and that the funds of the Charity Ball would be used to establish and maintain a free hospital for the railway workers and their families. Each of these banks purchased tickets to this ball totaling to $40.00 transferred to the co-defendants.
In response to the Petition, Judge Ambrose allowed the writ, returnable on 6 March 1894. The District Court commanded Sheriff Drexel to appear in court on 6 March 1894, bringing Mr. Howard with him along with their cause for detaining him. At trial Judge Ambrose determined that, based on the case presented, Mr. Howard was lawfully imprisoned and was ordered to return to custody and pay the costs of the proceeding.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 6, 1912, Winnie Mitchell petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her husband, F. M. Mitchell. Winnie stated that F. M. was being held by Claude G. Bannick as a fugitive from justice from Vancouver, British Columbia for a supposed crime committed there. Winnie claimed that F. M. had committed no crime in Vancouver and that no proper warrant was issued for his arrest. Judge Ronald issued the writ. The outcome of this petition and the fate of F. M. Mitchell are unknown. Summary of Proceedings: John Perish was an Austrian migrant that was arrested and subject to deportation on the accusation of advocating for the unlawful destruction of property. In his petition for writ of habeas corpus, Perish argued that he was denied his right to counsel, his right to examine the warrant and the evidence within, and was subjected to “personal abuse and intimidations” which compelled him to give evidence against himself. Judge Frank H. Rudkin agreed to hear Robinson’s petition for writ of habeas corpus. Rudkin ruled on John Perish’s, Charles Johnson, and Emery Sarracin’s cases at the same time. In his ruling, Rudkin referenced his opinions in his rulings for In re Holm and In re G. S. Marhow. Rudkin noted that while these migrants were members of the International Workers of the World, there was no evidence that substantiated the claim that they advocated for the unlawful destruction of property. As such, Rudkin ruled that John Perish and the other two migrants were unlawfully restrained of their liberty and ordered their release from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: W. C. Donovan filed for habeas corpus on behalf of W. B. Detcher, Nels Christofferson and Ed Callow. George E. Stone held Detcher, Christofferson, and Callow in the Spokane County Jail as witness for two other cases. Detcher and Christofferson were witnesses in the case of Abraham Hacker, accused of manslaughter. Callow was a witness in the case of John Cavanaugh, accused of grand larceny. None of the three petitioners could afford to pay the bail set by Judge George W. Stocker. Judge Frank H. Rudkin denied their writ on August 8, 1914 on the grounds that they had not exhausted their legal remedies in state courts.

Summary of Proceedings: Upon arrival at port on the Steamship Danube, Leong Ling was denied entry to Portland, Oregon, by T. J. Black, the Collector of Customs, as he decided the individual was not a merchant and therefore excluded under the Chinese Exclusion Act. Thus, Captain William Meyer held the individual on the steamship in accordance with the instructions of customs. Leong Ling's business partner, Seong Youk Tong, petitioned for habeas corpus on his behalf. After demonstrating merchant status before Judge C. B. Bellinger, Seong Youk Tong’s petition was granted, and Leong Ling was released from custody and allowed to enter the city.

Primary field: In the matter of the application of Jennie Miller Powers for a writ of Habeas Corpus vs Mary Elizabeth Miller and R.J. Miller her husband
Repository: ["[Washington State Archives, Puget Sound Regional Branch (Bellevue, Washington)](hc.loc.000032)"]
Summary of Proceedings: Jennie Miller filed a petition for her five year old daughter, Mary Alice Powers, who has been held against her will by R. J. Miller and Mary Elizabeth Miller, a married couple living in Seattle. The child was held by the Millers because Jennie Powers had divorced from her husband John Powers on the 6th of April from the same court as this petition. The petition was granted on April 9th and a court time was set for a custody hearing on behalf of Mary Alice Powers. At the hearing, Mary Elizabeth Miller argued that she is the grandmother of Mary Alice Powers and the mother of Jennie Miller Powers and she should have custody of Mary Alice Powers because the petitioner abandoned her on November 3rd, 1884, leaving her daughter, the bound party, wholly in the care of the respondents and that she is unfit physically and mentally to support the child. Jennie Miller Powers argued that while the child had been in the care of the Millers, she had not abandoned the child and is not unfit to care for the infant, as the child was only in the care of the Millers while the divorce suit was pending as an agreement between herself and her husband. Jennie Miller Powers alleged that the respondents had been paid for their care of the child and that they were conspiring with John Powers to keep Mary Alice Powers from her mother out of ill will and malice towards the petitioner. She further alleged that they were unfit in their care for the child because they are “immoral in their talk and extremely lewd”. The court’s decision stalled until May 1888, when Judge Jones ruled that the custody of Mary Alice Powers should be returned to her mother, the petitioner Jennie Miller Powers.

Summary of Proceedings: Esther Hilderbrand submitted a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus on 23 September 1912, stating that her friend Margaret Carr (whose assumed Convent name is Catherine) was being unlawfully detained and deprived of her liberty by the Mother Superior of the Good Shepherd Convent (whose first and real name is unknown) despite being over the age of 21. He stated that the petition and “proofs” showed that Margaret Carr was being unlawfully detained and deprived of her liberty.

Summary of Proceedings: Fred Lowry petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Henry Drum, warden of the Washington State Penitentiary. Lowry alleged he was serving 2 to 10 years at the State Penitentiary on a charge of criminal anarchy, but claimed that state courts had no jurisdiction to sentence him. Lowry claimed his offence amounted to treason, which the federal government has exclusive jurisdiction over. Lowry’s initial proceedings claimed he promoted and attempted to overthrow and overturn the government with the I.W.W. After much debate over which court’s jurisdiction Lowry’s offense fell under, Judge Frank H. Rudkin ruled that the writ be denied, and Lowry was ordered to remain in the custody of Drum.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 31, 1901, May Andrews petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Andrews stated that she had gone through arraignment for the charge of Grand Larceny, but that no court date was set within sixty days of the information being filed against her by State Prosecuting Attorney Fulton, and thus her imprisonment was illegal. Deputy State Prosecuting Attorney Faben filed an affidavit stating that Andrew and her attorney, John F. Dore, had requested that the courts wait to set the trial date until Dore got back from trying a murder case in another county. Dore and Andrews denied that they ever requested a continuance in this case. The outcome of this case and the fate of Andrews are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 3, Pierce H. O’Dell petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to Judge L.B. Day, arguing Sheriff Michael L. Clark was unlawfully depriving him of his liberty. He claimed that on September 27, 1922, the police arrested him, and the court tried him in the municipal court before Judge George Holmes. He was bound over to the district court of Douglas County under a $2000 bond. However, O’Dell argued that the clerk had not filed a transcript of the proceeding. He contended that a complaint was filed against him without the knowledge or consent of the county attorney of Douglas County or any office forces under the county attorney. Yet the court charged him with a felony. The next day Judge Day accepted and filed a writ of habeas corpus to Sheriff Clark. However, the outcome of this proceeding is unknown.  Newspaper records indicate O'Dell operated in real estate and a year after this petition faced charges for real estate fraud.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 17th 1893, Kate and John Lovell filed their third writ of habeas corpus which was the final attempt in a series of efforts to regain custody of Maggie Lovell, the biological daughter of Kate Lovell and adopted daughter of John Lovell. Maggie was being held by the House of the Good Shepherd in Seattle by Sister Mary of the Nativity, the Mother Superior of the institution. Maggie (9 years old) was dropped off by Kate Lovell to Sister Mary sometime in 1890, with Kate Lovell understanding this to be a temporary arrangement until she could adequately care for all her children. Sister Mary alleges that part of the conversation included the fact that Maggie would be retained by Good Shepherd until she was eighteen years old. After returning for her daughter, Kate was denied visitation by the institution various times, and allegedly assaulted another sister in an attempt to see her daughter. Sister Mary and her legal team used violent instances like these along with the general reputation of Kate as an unfit mother to depict Kate as someone that would be unable to care for Maggie and therefore should not receive custody. The Lovell family denies all these allegations, and during the court case contrary evidence was brought to light depicting Kate as either an impassioned and capable caregiver or as absent and abusive mother who forced her children to beg for food and clothing. Evidence was also brought against John Lovell that showcased his arrest on suspicion of abuse of Mary, another one of the Lovell daughters, though he also stated no abuse took place and that he was appealing the decision in another case. Ultimately, this negative evidence surrounding the Lovells proved too overwhelming and they lost the case, which was then promptly appealed. During the appeal, the Lovells’ attorney argued that the evidence brought up against John was irrelevant and that in the original case Good Shepherd failed to establish why they had legal custody to retain Maggie. On July 18th, 1894, they won their appeal and it was found that Maggie was “wrongfully and illegally deprived of her liberty” by Good Shepherd and she was promptly released after about three years in the institution.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 30, 1914, Louis T Sullivan accused Lucille and Vernon Lee Goldy, husband and wife of murdering Quong Chew. The alleged murder occurred on December 25, 1914, and the Goldys’, along with Serafine Villaflor and L. F. Oesear, were accused of beating Chew to death with a brush. On December 30, the Goldys’ and their attorneys John Stringer and Geroge F. Hannan applied for a writ of habeas corpus. In the writ, they claimed that they were being held without a warrant by L. M. Lang and Charles M. Tennant and that prosecuting attorney John F. Murphy had given orders to Lang and Tennant to not let the Goldys’ talk with their lawyers. A warrant for their arrest was produced on December 30, the same day that the petition was filed. The outcome of this case and the fate of the Goldys’ are unknown, although newspaper coverage indicates that Lucille was later sentenced to one year in jail for manslaughter, and that her sentence was immediately suspended by the judge, freeing her from jail.

Summary of Proceedings:
C.P. Bishop and N.H. McLean were imprisoned by Bolton Rogers, the Chief of Police of Seattle, and thus filed an application for a writ of Habeas Corpus on June 6th, 1894. Their lawyer, Charles F. Repath tried to speak with Rogers, but Rogers refused and was rude, and denied him access to talking to his clients. When the application for writ of Habeas Corpus was filed, judge JW Langley grants the writ on June 6th. J.H. Woolery then tries to deliver the writ, however he is unable to find him after searching and inquiry, and thus delivers the writ to George W. Hogle, a captain under Chief Rogers. 

According to the Seattle Post Intelligencer, Repath was denied any ability to speak with his clients due to the likelihood that he was involved in the conspiracy and that was so assumed by the police. However, Judge Langley concluded that unless there were more objections, Repath should be able to see his clients. Judge Langley also concluded that Rogers was just in arresting the men, and thus he remanded custody of them back to Chief Rogers.
