Summary of Proceedings: Oscar J. Quinn was charged with "drunkenness and reckless driving" by Police Magistrate Charles E. Foster on August 5, 1920 after he allegedly became drunk in public before recklessly driving a car on the highway. Quinn plead guilty and was sentenced to 15 days in county jail on August 6, 1920. Quinn filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against Sheriff and Jailer Michael L. Clark, alleging in the petition that he was being wrongfully detained. His principal argument was that the mittimus issued to jail him stated that he was detained for violating Nebraska state statutes, when in reality he was found guilty of violating the ordinances of Omaha. He also alleged that the Police Magistrate had wrongfully substituted city ordinances for Nebraska state statutes on the complaint against him. Judge A. C. Troup commanded Michael L. Clark to show cause before the Court for Quinn's detention and also issued subpoenas to city clerks to bring the original complaint against Quinn and city ordinances 10192 and 10370 to the Court. The outcome is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Kozo Koyama petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Kiku Furuta. Koyama believed Furuta was being held against her will by her disputed husband, Kiichi Furuta, and H. T. Satow. Koyama claimed that Kiku Furuta had filed for a divorce from Kiichi Furuta and that the action was served. Koyama claimed that Kiichi Furuta then forcibly took Kiku Furuta back to his home and told her attorney that they were living together as husband and wife. Koyama expressed his belief that Kiku Furuta was at risk of bodily harm or being removed from Seattle against her will. The case file reveals neither the outcome nor the fate of Kiku Furuta.

Summary of Proceedings: Around September 18, 1923, Duncan Burrage was arrested on the charge of vagrancy based on a complaint signed by the city prosecutor, D.E. O'Brien, and a writ of mittimus signed by police magistrate Frank M. Dineen. He was then sentenced to be confined for 60 days in the Criminal Division of Central Station of the Municipal Court of the City of Omaha. On October 29, 1923, his attorney, J.D. Cranny, of the firm Cranny & Moore, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, demanding that sheriff M. L. Endres produce Burrage in front of judge Charles A. Goss. He claimed that the complaint for vagrancy was invalid because it was signed by the city prosecutor, who did not have the authority to make such a claim, the Douglas County municipal court didn't have the jurisdiction to imprison him and the complaint was not sworn to by a judge or clerk or filed for record in Omaha's municipal court. A hearing was held that same day in which the petition was granted and Burrage was discharged.

On August 18, 1892, William Priedo was arrested by a Mr. Cave (first name unknown), under the orders of John Roberts, the acting captain of the police of the City of Seattle, County of King, State of Washington. Priedo petitioned for a Writ of Habeas Corpus, which was accepted on August 19, 1892 by Judge Isaac J. Lichtenberg. His case was to be heard August 20, 1982. 

According to the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, August 21, 1892 print, page 5, Priedo had stolen a span a mules and his writ was denied.

Summary of Proceedings: A. Lon Parks was convicted of assault and battery against M.L. McCan in October 1892 by Edward Von Tobel. Summary of Proceedings: Thornton Kinney was arrested while working on a boat in St. Louis on the suspicion of being a fugitive from slavery. Judge Johnstone ordered Thornton be held at the county jail until his master picked him up or discharged in due course of law. Thornton filed for a writ of habeas claiming that he as a free person, and had been for many years at that point detailing his life moving from Virginia, spending time in Liberia, and working as a free laborer along the Mississippi, and living as a free man on and off for roughly 10 years in St. Louis. He also claimed to have a copy of his papers proving that he was free dating to March of 1838. Charles C. Bridges, an agent of Hatcher, claimed that Thornton was lying, and that he knew Thornton to be a slave as recently as 3-4 years prior. An additional witness produced a bill of sale for an enslaved man named Kinney who was sold from the owners of the steamboat Thornton Kinney worked on to John T. Hatcher dating to December of 1851. The case was eventually dismissed, though Thornton’s attorneys filed to set aside the dismissal and reinstate it, but the outcome of said appeal is unknown.

Macdonald from the firm of Gordon & Resterday, filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his eleven year old daughter, Hollis Estella Ralph. Oscar stated that Hollis’s mother (unnamed) passed away August 8, 1903. At some point, John J. Golliet and Rebecca A. Golliet, a married couple, took Hollis into their custody. Oscar claimed the custody transfer happened unlawfully. Oscar stated he had a stable job as a farmer and was willing and able to provide and care for Hollis. The outcome of the petition and Hollis’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 21, 1903, Lavinia Heron petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her infant son, Clifford Heron. Clifford was being held by Edward K. Heron, whose exact relationship to Clifford is unstated. Lavinia said Edward had no legal claim to the custody of Clifford, and she was willing and able to care for him herself. She also stated that Edward had threatened Clifford’s life and intended to remove him from the court’s jurisdiction. Judge William R. Bell issued both the writ and a warrant for Edward’s arrest. H. J. McGee, whose relationship to all parties is unknown, was paid by the court to care for Clifford while awaiting the outcome of the case. The outcome of this case and the fate of Clifford Heron are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 12, 1920, Opal Rogers was arrested on the south side of Omaha, Nebraska, and charged with being an inmate of an ill-governed house. She was found guilty in the South Side Police Court by Omaha Police Magistrate Charles E. Foster. Opal Rogers then paid the $200.00 appeal bond set by Foster. On September 13, 1920, the case respondents Marshall Eberstein, Omaha Police Chief, and Alta Berger, Matron and Superintendent of the Omaha Detention Hospital, illegally detained Opal Rogers at the Detention Hospital of Omaha and subjected her to forced physical examinations instead of releasing her to the District Court of Douglas County after the appeal. On September 16, 1920, Opal Rogers’ attorneys, Jamieson H. Sullivan and Eugene D. Sullivan, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that the respondents violated Amendment 5 of the Constitution by subjecting Opal Rogers to forced physical examinations. The petition was allowed by Judge Charles Goss that day and the Douglas County Sheriff, Michael L. Clark, delivered the writ to the respondents on September 17, 1920, by judge’s order. On September 20, 1920, Marshall Eberstein and Alta Berger responded to the writ and provided copies of the commitments they received from Foster and Dr. J. F. Edwards, Omaha Health Commissioner, that ordered the respondents to take Opal to the Detention Hospital of Omaha in order to subject her to forced physical examinations to ascertain whether or not she had contracted a venereal disease. After the hearing, Judge A. C. Troup ordered the respondents to release Opal Rogers from custody and she was released based on the results of the examination.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 7th, 1921, John C. Mischnick submitted a petition on behalf of his four year old son, John Robert. John C. claimed that John Robert was being unlawfully detained by Fred and Minnie Nissen. He explained that around August 1st, 1921, Fred and Minnie visited his residence and requested that John C. let John Robert visit their home, agreeing to bring John Robert back whenever John C. desired. John C. then explained that he went to their house on October 28th to retrieve John Robert but Fred and Minnie refused to release John Robert. The petition was granted and on November 22nd the writ was allowed. The judge found that John Robert was being unlawfully detained and that he should be returned to his father.

Summary of Proceedings: The justice of the peace, D. S. Smith, ordered Hughes and his fellow petitioners to pay a peace bond of $500 ($300 for the other petitioners) to maintain the peace with Josiah Gellerson and the community as a whole. The petitioners were jailed indefinitely until they paid the bond, so they filed for a writ of habeas corpus on the grounds that they never threatened to destroy the property of Gellerson. The writ was issued by Judge Lewis.

Summary of Proceedings: Frank O'Neill, Dave Gillinsky, A.F. Pirson, Art Williams, and William Larsen, were arrested for reportedly breaking and entering into the home of Katherin C. Allisen on 410 S. 39th St. on December 5, 1919. They were taken into custody the same day at the Electric Garage on 40th and Farnam, where they stopped to repair their car. A preliminary hearing occurred on December 6 in front of police magistrate Charles E. Foster. The men said that at this hearing it was found that there was not probable cause to hold the men for a further trial, but Foster submitted writs of mittimus allowing sheriff Michael L. Clark to hold the men in the county jail nonetheless. Thus, the men filed a habeas corpus petition on December 18, 1919, which was allowed. A hearing on the petition occurred on December 19, but it was taken under advisement until the 22nd. On that day, O'Neill, Gillinsky, Pierson, and Williams were granted their freedom, but not Larsen for some unstated reason. An Omaha Daily Bee article indicates that Frank O'Neill was arrested for another robbery on January 24, 1920, and that somehow, the men were tried again and found guilty for the the Allison robbery on March 29, 1920. This was reversed and remanded, however, by the Nebraska Supreme Court on March 26, 1921.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney C. J. Smith petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of his client Mable Morgan, alias Grace Revore. The original petition was made against Seattle Commissioner of Health J. S. McBride and his assistant Dr. Simpson, as Smith believed Morgan was detained at the Public Safety Building under quarantine for a venereal disease. Smith amended the petition to address Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren when he discovered Morgan had been moved to the Seattle City Jail under the charge of being a disorderly person. Warren claimed he jailed Morgan on the behalf of Seda Hauser. Hauser was a parole officer for the State School for Girls and claimed Morgan was an unruly and delinquent parole violator. Custody of Morgan was transferred from Warren to Hauser, despite Smith claiming Morgan was an adult and could no longer be confined to the State School for Girls. Hauser failed to appear with Morgan in court, and was ordered to prove why Hauser shouldn’t be charged with contempt of court. Hauser alleged that the case had been dismissed and she was never served an order to appear with Morgan in court. The last page of the case file is dated nearly two months later and includes a deponent’s testimony that she served Hauser an order to appear. The outcome of the case and the fate of Morgan are unknown

Summary of Proceedings: Carl G. Benson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of Marie Belmont against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Benson claimed Warren had no warrant or authority to arrest Belmont, and that her detainment in the Seattle City Jail was illegal. Warren responded with a warrant charging Belmont with “wilfully and unlawfully being idle and having no lawful means of support, and wandering about with no visible calling or business to maintain himself.” The warrant was dated after the petition was filed. The case file does not reveal anything further about the case, but newspaper records indicate Belmont was a stenographer for the I.W.W., that her writ was dismissed, and that she was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: M. C. Gray petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff John Stringer and Earl P. Harper, an agent of the state of Colorado. Gray claimed Stringer and Harper imprisoned him on a warrant charging him with being a fugitive from justice, but alleged he was innocent and should not be detained. Gray did not state where he was being held, but the King County Jail can be inferred from Stringer’s role as sheriff. Stringer and Harper responded with a warrant from Colorado charging Gray with obtaining property by false pretenses. The warrant was dated after the petition was filed. The outcome the case and fate of Gray are unknown. This is the second petition for writ of habeas corpus related to Gray allegedly being a fugitive from justice.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 4, 1874, Francois Lafontaisis allegedly sold two bottles of whisky to an Indian named Nee Shore, a member of the Walla Wallas. They met at a creek on the Uwatilla reservation, where Shore paid $2 for two bottles of whiskey and gave Lafontaisis a $1 tip. Before Shore could drink the liquor, Indian agent A. Seitel took the bottles away from him and arrested Lafontaisis. On May 11, 1874, Lafontaisis was brought before a grand jury and judge Joseph R. Lewis. Several witnesses testified that they had seen him buy the bottles at Joe Bentley's saloon, then resell them to Shore. He was sentenced to 18 months in the Walla Walla County Jail. On May 21, 1875, a year after he was incarcerated, Lafontaisis petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Walla Walla county sheriff George F. Thomas. He argued that the law against selling liquor to Indians had been repealed by the time he was arrested, and his confinement was thus illegal. It is unknown what the result of the writ was, but Lafontaisis was transferred at some point to the U.S. Penitentiary in Washington Territory. He was freed on August 14, 1875 in compliance with an act of Congress passed on March 3, 1875, which allowed for some US prisoners to be released.

Summary of Proceedings: Axel Pierson, confined in the Douglas County jail, was facing extradition to Canada for his alleged involvement in several crimes. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming, among other things, that the procedure leading to his arrest and detention were inconsistent with treaty obligations between the United States and Canada. The court consolidated his petition with those of Arthur Wyse, Harry Compton, and John Howard.After hearing the evidence, his writ was denied and Pierson remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Marr traveled on the Steamship Alice Blanchard from Seattle to San Fransisco. However the ship was towed into Yaquina Bay in Oregon because of ship “distress”. William Johnson, the Master of the Steamship Alice Blanchard, alleged that Joseph Marr staged a mutiny which violated section 5360 of Revised Statutes of the United States. However the act does not apply to coast wide voyages, so his writ was granted and he was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Arrested on the charge of grand larceny, Daniel S. Conroy petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that Sherriff Miller was depriving him of his freedom. Judge Holmes granted the petition; however, after hearing evidence, he remanded Conroy back into custody. One month later, Conroy filed a motion to amend the record after Sherriff Miller admitted guilt. The motion was granted, but presumably Conroy remained in custody. Two years later, a Supreme Court decision affirmed the court's decision.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 10, 1921, Robert McCullough was taken in by Omaha police officers Graham and Franks and confined to the city jail. He was later moved to the Omaha Detention Home, an institution designed to treat those with "social diseases," but which bore many resemblances to a jail. On July 11, 1921, McCullough filed a writ of habeas corpus against the commissioner of police, health, and sanitation Henry W. Dunn, chief of police Michael F. Dempsey, and health officers Dr. Thomas D. Boler and Dr. A.S. Pinto, who worked at the Detention Home. On the 12th, the application was dismissed on the motion of the petitioner.

Summary of Proceedings: Pearl Lyles filed this petition on 22 September 1914 stating that she was being unlawfully deprived of her liberty by Sheriff McShane based on a commitment issued by the Police Magistrate on 8 August 1914. On 29 July 1914, a complaint was filed against Lyles charging her with vagrancy. She was convicted on that charge and sentenced to 90 days in the County Jail. On 7 August 1914, she appealed the judgement but was not discharged from custody. A duplicate vagrancy complaint was filed on 29 July 1914. She was tried and convicted for this duplicate complaint on 8 August 1914. The petition states that the duplicate complaint and all following proceedings were unlawful and that she was being unjustly and unlawfully deprived of her liberty. Judge James P. English commanded Sheriff McShane to bring Lyles to Court on 23 September 1914. The application for the writ was sustained and Lyles was discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In the spring of 1922, James Ingoldsby was extradited from Texas to Otoe County, Nebraska to respond to accusations that he had forged and uttered a check two years earlier. He was convicted of both charges and sentenced to a minimum of ten years in the state penitentiary in accordance with recent changes to state law. When Ingoldsby's appeal to the state supreme court was unsuccessful, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court. He argued that his trial, and especially his sentencing, had been marred by ex post facto applications of new statutes. After hearing the evidence, he was remanded to the custody of the warden.

Summary of Proceedings:
Sakaguchi immigrated to the U.S. from Japan to visit her husband, a resident of the U.S. for twenty-two years at the time. She was denied upon landing for contracting hookworm, and after she was treated, she was further refused admission for the following reasons: an accusation of becoming a public charge, that her passport was not in order, and reported trouble between herself and her husband. Sakaguchi petitioned on the account that the accusations were false and alleged that she was refused a fair and impartial trial. She also claimed that her sister lived in Seattle and could care for her if she were to become a public charge.
The writ was denied and the proceedings were dismissed, so Sakaguchi appealed to the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The initial order was reversed and Sakaguchi was discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Julia Wheeler, aka Frances Roberts, filed for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming she had been arrested but not charged by Seattle City Police. Police Chief Charles Beckingham countered that Wheeler had been charged through the police court with idleness. In his return of her writ, he added that Wheeler was “suffering from contagious and infectious disease dangerous to public health.” On November 20, 1917, Seattle’s health commissioner “removed her to an isolation hospital and placed her under quarantine.”The similarities in her case file, including relevant dates and outcome, indicate that she was jailed during Seattle vice raids of mid-November 1917.

Summary of Proceedings:
On August 21st, 1917, Harry Davis and Morris (or George) Meyer stole 161 men's suits from Moon Clothing Co. in Onawa, Iowa. The duo stashed their stolen goods at the house of Frank Kellerman at 2636 Franklin Street in Omaha, Nebraska. While several men witnessed the pair of thieves store the boxes in the basement, no one knew what the two were scheming, and the burglars refused to disclose what they had in the boxes. Davis and Morris attempted to sell their products to Max Sundheiner, a local merchant; however, Sundheimer refused to purchase the goods as he was suspicious of how the suits had been acquired. He tipped off the police and distanced himself from the two men. 

Sometime between the heist and September 6th of the same year, Davis and Morris were caught by the Omaha police and detained under an arrest order issued by the Governor of Nebraska in compliance with a request from the Governor of Iowa. The two burglars each filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus. Morris argued that he had not left Omaha, Nebraska, for over twenty years, which, in turn, would have made his involvement in the heist impossible. He also claimed that because the executive warrant for his arrest was issued without any prior investigation, his arrest was unconstitutional as both a Nebraska and US citizen. The judge, however, did not agree with his argument and denied his writ of Habeas Corpus. 

Meyer and his attorney attempted to appeal the case in the Supreme Court of Nebraska following their defeat. The appeal was permitted, and the petitioning party began to work on their case. They were granted an extension in March of 1918 to prepare and file Bill of Exceptions. Despite their efforts and nearly two years of being on trial, the Supreme Court of Nebraska ruled against Morris on April 15th, 1919, and affirmed the decision of the lower court. Morris remained in custody for his crime.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 12, 1914, Joseph H. Abbott and his attorneys Robert Welch and John Dore filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. They claimed Michael T. Powers, acting Chief of Police, and Austin E. Griffiths, Chief of Police, were holding Abbotts without proper process of law or a warrant. Griffiths and Powers produced a warrant from Utah judge Otis W. Brinker dated September 12, 1914, which stated that Abbott was a fugitive from justice and therefore should be arrested. On September 11th, 1914 Abbott was charged on complaint of passing a fictitious check in Utah. Welch and Dore filed a motion to quash the return of the respondents, on the grounds that it didn’t satisfy the legal requirements for the continued detainment of Abbott. The outcome of this case and Abbott’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Virginia Farmer petitions for a writ of habeas corpus to have her children returned to her custody. Her three children were in the custody and care of her husband’s mother, Eva Farmer after a Snohomish County Juvenile Court made the children wards of the court and granted Eva temporary custody. Kenneth Mackintosh initially presided over the case but it was transferred over to Everett Smith for the hearing. Before the hearing, Virginia and her attorney filed a motion to have the judge changed since they believed that Everett Smith could not provide a fair and impartial trial. Newspaper coverage of the trial not that the hearing of the petition was conducted by Judge J. T. Ronald. The coverage also notes that Virginia Farmer lost the petition and the children remained in the custody of Eva Farmer.

Summary of Proceedings: Chin Chong Quie applied for the writ of habeas corpus on July 26th of 1893, on behalf of Yee Lock and Wong Fong Yuen, who were both merchants with different companies in Portland. Yee Lock with Sam Yick Wah Co and Wong Fong Yuen, a partner in the firm of Kee and Co.. Both left Portland for two years for China with the intention to return in two years. Both of them were detained on the Steamship Haytain Republic by the Collector of Customs, T.J. Black, because he believed them to be laborers who were forbidden to enter the U.S due to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.

Summary of Proceedings: Pearl Wilson filed a habeas corpus petition on December 2, 1918, stating that Omaha police had arrested her without a warrant in her house around December 1, 1918. Wilson also stated that—without description of why she was allegedly guilty—she was charged with disorderly conduct and prostitution. The case file includes a vagrancy and prostitution complaint form signed by Police Magistrate C. W. Britt and City Prosecutor John M. Berger, with witnesses listed as "Various Handymen." Wilson was then tried before the Omaha Police Magistrate on December 2, 1918 and sentenced to thirty (30) days in the Douglas County jail. Wilson stated that the written sentence did not specify which offense she was being sentenced to jail for, which violated the requirements of the law. Judge William A. Reddick issued an order allowing writ of habeas corpus and commanded that Sheriff Michael L. Clark appear before the court. Clark received the writ but returned it "Not served by direction of Attorney for Defendant," which could suggest that the claim was resolved outside of court. The fate of Wilson is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 18, 1909, Kelso was released from jail on an alleged charge of vagrancy where he had been held for fifteen days. When he was released from the county jail he was immediately rearrested illegally and unlawfully without warrant. The respondent, Donahue, argued that he was lawfully rearrested because he was a fugitive from justice. His petition was granted but there are no results or outcomes in the case files. Which jail he was held in during second arrest is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: George McBride, the father of Margarie McBride (3 yo), lost custody of Margarie after a divorce proceeding by Lillian McBride, her mother, on the grounds of cruelty and nonsupport. Judge Estelle denied the divorce, but Lillian did succeed in separating herself from George. George McBride argues that he has a pleasant home with his parents, Robert McBride and Mary McBride. The court ruled that Lillian McBride, as the mother, is most capable of raising Margarie. This decision is informed by Sarah McPerrin, the mother of Lillian, who was aware of the cruelty of George and is capable of providing for the child. George McBride was allowed to see the child once a week, care for her once a month, and purchase clothing and necessities for the child. George was also ordered to conduct himself peacefully and to not interfere with or molest Lillian McBride during his visits. However, by 1910 George and Lillian had made up and were living together in Omaha, according to the census that year.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1911, the Yamhill County Court found William Gardner to be insane and committed him to the Oregon State Hospital. In 1913, Edwin Cady, whose relationship to Gardner is unclear, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on Gardner's behalf, which was granted. Records from both the insanity and habeas hearings reveal that Gardner believed his wife and daughter were being unfaithful in their marriages and that he had threatened violence against all parties as well as himself. After hearing the evidence, Gardner was remanded to the custody of the superintendent of the state hospital. In 1915, another party petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Gardner.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 12, 1895, B.D. Wright alleged to the Municipal Court of the City of Seattle, King County, Washington that Frank Barnes committed assault and battery against him during the previous day . On July 17, 1895, the Municipal Court of the City of Seattle, King County found Frank Barnes guilty of assault and battery and ordered that he pay a fine of $10 and the costs of prosecution (total of $21.80). Frank Barnes was then ruled in default of the fine and costs and imprisoned in the Seattle City Jail by Bolton Rogers for a period of ten days. On July 19th, John G. Bernard submitted a writ of habeas corpus arguing that Frank Barnes has been unlawfully restricted of his liberty with his imprisonment in the City Jail by Bolton Rogers. Judge Thomas J. Humes agreed to hear the petition for habeas corpus, however, the outcome of the hearing is not mentioned in the court files. Newspaper coverage of the trial notes that the petition was denied.

Summary of Proceedings:
Coley Harris was arrested and jailed on suspicion of being a fugitive from slavery. She declared that she was a free woman and petitioned the St. Louis Criminal Court for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted by one Judge Lackland. After hearing the evidence, she was released. However, Harris, in consultation with her attorney, was then arrested and jailed for a second time in an attempt to prevent her original kidnapper, Rueben Bartlett, from seizing her again. This time she petitioned the St. Louis Commissioner's Court for a writ of habeas corpus, which was also granted. Upon hearing the evidence, Harris was once again released.

Mark Twain believed that Harris had been posing as a slave to avoid punishment for having entered the state as a free Black woman without proper license. See Mark Twain's Letters, vol. 1, 1853 to 1866, eds. Edgar Marquez Branch et al (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1988), 51. (https://books.google.com/books?id=IPgkDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA51)

Summary of Proceedings:
On June 29th, 1897, John Considine petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus after being charged with employing females in a place where intoxicating liquors were sold, a prostitution reform law. Considine alleged that the statute deprived persons engaged in the liquor business of the right to employ women and alleged it deprived women of freedom of choice in vocation. The petition alleged that the law was unconstitutional.
In his ruling, Judge Hanford cited precedent holding the judiciary should not strike down state statues, especially statutes that have a direct connection to social order, health, and morals of the people. Judge Hanford further stated the statute was general in scope and not arbitrary and denied the petition. This case was appealed to the Washington Supreme Court, who affirmed the ruling of the Judge Hanford.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 21, 1923, Hazel Dillon filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against the Child Saving Institute for detaining her three children: Emily, Earnest, and Mabel McCarty. She explained that she left her children under the care of the Child Saving Institute on June 30, 1923, while recovering from a serious illness and operation. On July 12, 1923, H. A. Collins filed a petition alleging that Hazel was “incompetent, without means of support, and not a proper person” to care for her children. She argued that this person swore under oath that they were a Douglas County resident, but they were actually a Sarpy County resident. Additionally, she argued that the Child Saving Institute did not make her aware of any petition asking for custody of her children. Lastly, she explained that she signed documents consenting to the adoption of her children because they were misrepresented as documents that would prevent the adoption. The President of the Child Saving Institute, Howard Sexton, denied these allegations. After the court hearing on September 12, 1923, her writ was denied and the fate of her children is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Gust Christensen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Louis M. Lang. Christensen alleged that he was arrested on a warrant for keeping intoxicating liquor with the intent to sell, but that City Ordinance No. 35503 rendered the violation null and void, thus making his imprisonment in the Seattle City Jail unconstitutional. After the judge ordered the writ, he retroactively denied the application and claimed that the constitutionality of the violation couldn’t be tested by application. Newspaper coverage indicated that Christensen attempted to appeal and was ultimately pardoned, but ordered to return to Sweden and to never re-enter the United States.

Summary of Proceedings: Fred V. Larson was a wealthy landowner from Kansas who conducted business across several states. In December 1916, he sold 390 acres in Graham County, Kansas, while still owing $1500 to a mortgage on that land. He took out a second mortgage for $760 on what he already owed and traded it to H. V. Stiller for $400 and three mules. On April 8th, 1917, he left the State of Kansas and informed his acquaintances that he was going to Nebraska. The Government of Kansas, fearing that he had fled to avoid paying his debt, issued a warrant for his arrest and sent it to the Governor of Nebraska. On the evening of April 16th, 1917, Larson was arrested and imprisoned by the Omaha Chief of Police and Chief of Detectives. This led Larson to apply for a writ of Habeas Corpus. On April 21st, 1917, his writ was allowed, and his captors were ordered to bring him and appear before the court on April 24th of the same year. It remains unclear whether or not Larson was released from their custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In April 1901, the Canton Bridge Company, an Ohio corporation, sued Thomas Ratcliff and several co-defendants for money owed in the U.S. Circuit Court for the District of Nebraska. Ratcliff was subpoenaed to give at a deposition, but refused to cooperate with the notary public, Thomas Maddison, who had Ratcliff jailed for contempt. Ratcliff petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that while Nebraska notaries could exercise this authority, Maddison had been acting under the color of federal law and had no such authority. After hearing the evidence, the judge agreed and Ratcliff was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In the spring of 1875, John Gordon led a group of nearly 140 colonists from Sioux City, Iowa into northern Nebraska with the intention of eventually settling in the Black Hills of South Dakota. He was arrested by U.S. military authorities for violating an order against trespassing on "unceded Indian territory" belonging to the Sioux and consequently confined at Camp Sheridan. Military authorities offered to release him if he agreed in writing not to continue with his plans, but he refused, demanding a civil trial. Gordon then petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that he and his fellow colonists had not actually crossed into Indian territory. Judge Elmer Dundy agreed, writing an opinion declaring that the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie did not reserve any land within the state of Nebraska to the Sioux. He ordered that General Crook turn Gordon over to the U.S. marshal for Nebraska to be dealt with according to civil law.

Summary of Proceedings: Joe Lacorte, the petitioner and bound party, petitioned for release from Camp Lewis and exemption from the draft. Lacorte argued that because he was born in Peglia, Italy, arrived in the US in 1906, and has never since declared intention become a citizen, he is a citizen and subject of Italy. Additonally, Lacorte stated that he is engaged in agriculture as a dairy rancher and that the site relies on his ability to be present and milk the 51 milk cows on the ranch. The petition further states that the petitioner does not have a full knowledge of the English language, and he was entirely ignorant of what was required of him for the board questionnaire, but he had filled it out correctly, and he was exempt from military service on the ground and nondeclarant alien. Judge Edward Cushman found Lacorte to be illegally drafted into the military and, therefore, ordered his release.

Summary of Proceedings:
On December 21, 1898, Salfest Sylvester was arrested at the request of Sheriff Stener S. Wanaas of Traill County, North Dakota. Sylvester was a former manager of the Equitable Life Insurance Company in North Dakota and was accused of embezzling $500 from the company before fleeing to Seattle. Newspaper coverage of the arrest noted that Sylvester denied that he stole or embezzled any money from the life insurance agency but admitted to owing the company around $500. 

A few days after his arrest but before he could be extradited back to North Dakota, Sylvester applied for a writ of habeas corpus. In this writ, Sylvester argued that the complaint made against him and calling for his arrest did not show he was charged with a crime in North Dakota and as such he was not a fugitive. Furthermore, he argued that the governor of North Dakota never certified that an affidavit existed or stated that Sylvester had committed a crime. The Superior Court of King County accepted Sylvester’s writ of habeas corpus but ruled that Sylvester was not illegally restrained of his liberty and allowed for Sheriff Stener S. Wanaas to extradite Sylvester back to North Dakota to face his charges of embezzlement. 

Following this ruling, Sylvester appealed this decision where it eventually made its way to the Supreme Court of the State of Washington. The Washington State Supreme Court ruled that the Superior Court of King County was correct in its initial ruling and ordered that the Sheriff can return the petitioner to North Dakota. Before Sheriff Wanaas was able to extradite Sylvester, he further appealed to the federal courts. While the federal court appeal is not included in this collection of court documents, newspaper coverage of the trial mentions that the Federal Judge Cornelius H. Hanford overruled the Supreme Court’s decision. He argued that the initial warrant from the North Dakotan governor was not sufficient to justify Sylvester’s extradition. Judge Hanford asked the respondent party to produce requisition records to justify the extradition. After these records were not produced, Hanford ordered the release of Sylvester. Shortly after his release, North Dakota issued a new warrant for Sylvester’s arrest after this clerical error, but the newspapers note that Sylvester had not been found in the days following the issuing of the new warrant.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney Wilmon Tucker submitted a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his client, Louis Garfinkle, whom he claimed was being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail by police chief John Sullivan. Garfinkle had been convicted of peddling without a license, but Tucker maintained that the city ordinances which made peddling without a license illegal were unconstitutional. The licensing fee had recently been increased to such a high sum that Tucker claimed it practically prohibited peddling, and was thus unconstitutional trade legislation. He submitted the transcripts of several witness testimonies wherein other Seattle peddlers admitted it would be impossible to pay the licensing fee and still turn a profit. The judge allowed the writ to stand and ordered Garfinkle to be released from prison, but there is evidence that Sullivan’s attorney planned to appeal to the Supreme Court of Washington.

Summary of Proceedings: Louis W. R. Beaty was arrested March 17, 1910, for mixing garbage with refuse material in the City of Omaha. On March 17, Beaty and attorney, M. O. Cunningham, filed a petition of habeas against Police Force Captain, Henry W. Dunn, and Patrick Mostyn. Beaty argued that no statute exists in Omaha or Nebraska regarding the charge. Judge Lee. S. Estelle denied the writ and gave Beaty 40 days to prepare a bill of exceptions on March 22. Beaty made an appeal and motioned for new trial on March 23. Judge Estelle overruled a new trial, 40 days to prepare appeal was maintained.

Summary of Proceedings: Casper Krallman was arrested and charged with unlawful possession and transport of intoxicating liquor in police court on September 16, 1918, following a complaint made by John M. Burger. Krallman was found guilty and charged $200 and costs of prosecution. On September 24, 1918, Krallman filed for habeas with attorney Daniel Hoorigan, charging that police magistrate has no jurisdiction to try and fine on such charges. Krallman's petition was granted and the writ was allowed on September 30, 1918; Krallman was ordered to be released from custody.

The petition was granted October 1, but later dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: Gaston Akoun, Madroche Zitoune, Abraham L. Reed, and S. B. Wadley worked for the Oriental Exhibition Company and were in a separate court with the Company. Akoun et al. were unlawfully detained after a violation of a pretended order of injunction in the original case against the Trans-Missisippi and International and Oriental Exhibition Company. They alleged there was no process according and that they were denied the right to be separately tried for the alleged violation of the injunction. After that trial ended, they were arrested because they had not paid their fines. After filing for the writ of habeas corpus, the writ was allowed, the case was heard, and it was determined they were being unlawfully held so they were released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Ida Johnson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle chief of police Thomas R. Delaney. Johnson claimed she was being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail as she was not granted her right to due process. The outcome of the case and Johnson’s fate are both unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: George Alexander Mirianon, a resident of France, was charged with insubordination to a superior officer and conduct prejudicial to the good order of the vessel while aboard the French Bark, General Faidherbe. Mirianon was brought before the U.S. Commissioner and ordered to be placed aboard the French Bark, Anna de Bretagne, and deported to France. Mirianon petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus which alleged his restraint and order for deportation deprived him of due process and was a violation of the U.S. Constitution and treaty regulations with France. The outcome of the proceedings and fate of Miranon is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Lung Dock Foo petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of his business partner, Loui Yee Wai, who was being held on the Steamship Signal by Captain Bendergard. They both work at the Kung Wo Firm at No. 131 Second Street. Loui Yee Wai had an affidavit from A. W. Rayburn, a white worker with Northern Pacific Railroad, testifying that he was a genuine merchant. However, T. J. Black rejected the certificate and witnesses and decided he was a Chinese laborer arriving in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. The Judge ruled Loui Yee Wai was a genuine Chinese merchant and granted his writ discharging him from custody. The case file contains a trial transcript.

Summary of Proceedings:
On September 6, 1894, Nathan Sanguinette was convicted of burglary.  He was identified as “West Indian” on page 12 of the September 16 issue of the Seattle Post-Intelligencer and as “mulatto” on  page 5 of the September 7 issue of the Seattle Post-Intelligencer.  Sanguinette pleaded not guilty, but he had no defense. He was sentenced to 30 days of hard labor in the state penitentiary, charged $3.00 per day, and had to pay an additional $20.75.  The case file states that Sanguinette appealed his case, and he voluntarily left the county jail.  He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on October 22, 1894, arguing that he served 30 days in the county jail rather than the penitentiary.  He also argued that he should not be kept in prison because he appealed.  However, upon hearing the writ, Judge Humes affirmed the conviction and dismissed the writ and appeal.  He ordered that Sanguinette be taken to the penitentiary. 

Page 12 of the September 16 issue of the Seattle Post-Intelligencer indicates that there were also political considerations in the case involving the governor's pardon.

Summary of Proceedings:
On September 27, 1898, Frank Hazelton was arrested for vagrancy and held by the Chief of Police of Seattle, King County, Charles S. Reed. Reed acted under the orders of C. G. Austin, the Justice of the Peace for the police court. Frank E. Sims, the attorney of Hazelton, gave the Superior Court of Seattle of King County three offenses why Hazelton should be freed on a Writ of Habeas Corpus. First, against the Ordinance used to arrest Hazelton. Secondly, against the authority that the Justice of Peace used to enforce the ordinance. Thirdly, against the length that Hazelton was jailed for. Hazelton was ordered 30 days in jail, and should have been freed by October 27. 

Superior Court Judge Orange Jacobs heard the Writ, and granted Hazelton his freedom December 13, 1898. According to the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, Judge Jacobs reprimanded the police court for using ordinances to redefine "vagrancy".

Summary of Proceedings: Frances Fidler petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to establish who should have custody of her daughter, Mary Thomas, then living with her grandmother, which was granted. By the mutual consent of both parties, they recessed for thirty days. At the hearing, Frances, alongside Mary's father, Archie Thomas, asked that custody of Mary be given to the child's grandmother, also named Mary Thomas. Archie and Frances had divorced on June 9, 1913 on the grounds of extreme cruelty and non-support. The judge agreed to this new arrangement, and Mary was remanded to the custody of her grandmother and namesake.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry Frank filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus immediately following his arrest by the Seattle Chief of Police, Louis M. Lang  on September 28, 1915. Frank claimed in his petition that he did not know the reason or justification for his arrest. Lang claimed that he arrested Frank because of a warrant issued by Judge John B. Gordon. Gordon’s warrant included a complaint from Cook County, Illinois that charged Frank with the crime of larceny and declared him a fugitive from justice. Judge Mitchell Gilliam allowed Frank’s writ of habeas corpus and set his habeas hearing for September 29, 1915. The outcome of the hearing is not included in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 20th, 1913, T. Toda was arrested in Washington for having stolen from a U. S. Post Office in Montana, in the sum of $2,500.00. Toda filed a writ of habeas corpus on January 24th, 1913, claiming that U. S. Marshal Jacoby, the person that was holding him, had no lawful authority to restrain him. In response, Jacoby argued that Toda needed to stay in his custody until a judge in Montana ordered his removal. On February 3rd, 1913, Judge Cushman ordered Toda out of the custody of Marshal Jacoby and into the custody of a Montana Marshal or any other proper authority to answer for his crimes.

Summary of Proceedings: George G. Perry filed a complaint in the office of R.R. George, a justice of the peace.  He reported that on April 18, 1906 in Valdez, Alaska, Frank D. Steel had committed embezzlement by bailee in appropriating $650 from John Doe McMullen.  The complaint stated that Steel had fled to Seattle and was arrested. The complaint noted that Steel could face extradition.  In addition, R. R. George issued a warrant for Steel’s arrest based on this complaint.  On April 25, 1906, Steel petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that the arrest warrant and complaint were the sole reasons why he was arrested.  Judge A.W. Frater issued the writ.  However, on April 26, 1906, Steel submitted an amended petition that explained that according to Section 47 of Carter’s Annotated Alaska Codes, an indictment had to be presented by a grand jury to punish him.  He also stated that Perry lacked knowledge of the truth in this case.  The outcome of Steel’s petition and his fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Ike Payne is also present in the database in a set of cases from 1918. Payne filed another petition for a writ of habeas corpus against Sheriff Michael L. Clark on January 31, 1919. On October 10, 1918, the police magistrate had found Ike Payne guilty of a complaint alleging that he had possessed intoxicating liquor (Payne's second offense) and transported intoxicating liquor. Payne was sentenced to a fine of $100 and detention in jail until the fine was paid. Payne's petition argued that the complaint did not charge Payne with an offense under Nebraska law, that the police magistrate had no power to impose fines or to try Payne for what he was accused of, and that the finding of the Court was invalid because it did not specify which of the two alleged crimes Payne was being found guilty and sentenced for. Judge Arthur Wakely issued a writ commanding that Payne come before the Court and justify his detention of Payne; a hearing was held and Judge William A. Redick denied his application. A motion for a new trial arguing that the judge had erred in denying the habeas petition is also included in the case file. Payne was remanded to custody of the sheriff with supersedeas bond fixed at $200. Payne was released on recognizance on February 19, 1919, with Peter Lafagis as surety.

Summary of Proceedings:
George Desmond filed for a writ of habeas corpus on September 2, 1919. Seattle City Police Chief Joel Warren held Desmond on a charge of bank robbery. Desmond’s lawyer, H. M. Dalton, stated in the petition that Desmond was "innocent of any connection, either direct or indirect, with any such crime.”

According to newspaper coverage, on June 2, 1919, Desmond and two others, John Laird and Claude Cosman, robbed “the bank at Sultan” of twelve thousand dollars “in cash, bonds and war savings stamps.” Desmond allegedly “deposited $3,000 in the Seaboard Bank” and then “went to Montana.” 

Judge J. A. Frater issued the writ on September 2, 1919 but newspaper coverage stated that Desmond remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In October 1915, S. Yoshida petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of F. Ota who was restrained on a Japanese boat, the S. S. Aki Maru, at the Great Northern Dock at Smith Cove. The petition alleged that Ota was arrested, taken into custody, and threatened with deportation by S. Takahasha and a man whose name was unknown, "John Doe", without a warrant, on the grounds that he held anarchistic views. Judge Neterer authorized the writ, however, six days later the petitioner and attorney for the petitioner motioned for the court to dismiss the writ of habeas corpus. F. Ota's fate is unknown.

Gustav Rittmaster, the petitioner, was charged with obtaining money under false pretenses in Iowa. Found to be in Nebraska, the State of Iowa filed to extradite him. Rittmaster filled for a writ of Habeas Corpus in an effort to stay in Nebraska. Judge Hopewell allowed a writ to be issued and ordered Rittmaster to be brought before the court on the 24th day of March in 1891. The final result of this hearing is unknown.

According to a second round of habeas (case B), Gustav Rittmaster was ordered to be detained by Sherrif John F. Boyd for the alleged cause of being a fugitive from justice from Arapahoe County, Colorado.

Summary of Proceedings:
Since November 3, 1884, following a divorce suit between Jennie Miller and John Powers, Mary Elizabeth and R.J. Miller were in custody of granddaughter Mary Alice Powers. Then on April 6, 1888, parents Jennie Miller and John Powers divorced, to which Miller Powers was awarded custody of her daughter by the court, which the grandparents have refused. Powers applies for habeas, claiming that she is lawfully entitled to the custody of her daughter.
Mary Elizabeth and R.J. Miller respond claiming that since they've had custody of their granddaughter, said custody has been exclusive, and that the mother abandoned, refused to recognize child, was deemed physically and mentally unfit to parent, and they have supported all expenses having the child under their care. 
Miller Powers refutes these claims, reporting that custody and support for the child's care had not been taken by solely one party, she isn't physically and mentally unfit or dependent to maintain herself, and accuses her parents of conspiring with her former husband against her.
Writ was granted and custody of the child was returned to Jennie Miller Powers.

Summary of Proceedings: Albert Weston and John Surra managed and operated a soft drink bar and fruit store in Omaha that allegedly sold alcohol. On June 26, 1924, their bond was set for $5,000 after they were found guilty on the charges of unlawful sale and possession of intoxicating liquor and maintaining a common nuisance. On July 3, 1924, Judge McGee sentenced Albert Weston to two six-month sentences for the alcohol charge and a one-year sentence for the maintenance of a common nuisance charge to be served in the Lincoln County Jail (along with a $500 fine). On December 18, 1924, Albert petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that he served both six-month sentences concurrently, was entitled to a shortened sentence for good behavior, and that the maintenance of a common nuisance charge was void because it was unconstitutional. The writ was allowed and delivered to the respondents on December 20, 1924. However, the petition was withdrawn by Albert on December 26 and he was returned to the custody of jailor L. L. Berthe. It is possible that he saw other cases filed during the same time frame go to the U.S. Court of Appeals and did not want to prolong the case if the decision would be reversed in a higher court (see Cronin vs. William J. Fox and related cases).

Summary of Proceedings: Fred and Sarah Totoro were arrested for the unlawful sale and possession of intoxicating liquor. On July 3, 1924, Judge McGee sentenced Fred to two six-month sentences in the Lincoln County Jail along with a $500 fine. On December 18, 1924, Fred petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and argued that he served both six-month sentences concurrently, was entitled to a shortened sentence for good behavior, and should be discharged. On December 20, the judge ordered the respondents to release Fred from custody upon the payment of a $250 bond. The respondents appealed the case to the U.S. Court of Appeals Eighth Circuit (St. Louis, Missouri). On January 30, 1926, the decision of the lower court was reversed by the higher court and the judge remanded Fred to the custody of the respondents. Additionally, Fred forfeited the bond on March 6, 1926.

Summary of Proceedings: Attorney John J. Sullivan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his client Yee Bow. Sullivan claimed Bow was being held at the Seattle Police Station, and that Chief of Police Louis M. Lang and Chief of Detectives Charles Tennant denied Sullivan the ability to talk with Bow and prepare his legal defense. The writ was allowed, and though Bow remained in custody, Lang and Tennant were ordered to allow Sullivan and a Chinese interpreter to interview Bow. Newspaper coverage indicates Yee Bow was arrested as the suspected murderer in a feud between Tongs.

Summary of Proceedings: Sam Plastino came to the United States in 1897 with his parents from Italy and applied for citizenship in March 1911. In January 1912, Plastino was arrested under the charge that he was unlawfully within the US and found receiving, sharing, or deriving benefits from the earnings of prostitution and was ordered deported. Plastino was convicted for violating the Mann Act, by having transported one Goldie Cardiff from Seattle to San Francisco for the purposes of prostitution. The conviction rested on Cardiff's testimony stating that she had given Plastino everything she had earned since September 1910 and later brokered a deal where she would get half of all her future earnings, with Plastino receiving the other half. Supplementary research shows that Cardiff later recanted her statements under pressure and a marriage proposal from Plastino, yet the jury was told to disregard her denial as she was "obviously perjuring herself." Plastino petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus stating he was in custody and about to be deported. The petition stated Plastino did not receive a fair trial and alleged misconduct against Immigration Inspector, T.M. Fisher. Plastino stated that he was never informed such a charge was issued against him, never given an opportunity to inspect the warrant or evidence, never offered counsel, and never informed about the proceedings for his deportation. The petitioner further stated that the transcription of the examination contains forged questions and answers written into the record, as the transcription depicted Plastino waiving his right to an attorney if his brother, Joe Plastino, did not retain one for him. Both Sam and Joe Plastino refuted this in an affidavit. Judge Neterer authorized the petition and committed Plastino to bail in the sum of $1,000 and later ruled the petitioner to be discharged. Judge Neterer based his decision on the fact that Plastino did not have a fair trial and the evidence produced does not support the charge. His decision stated that the testimony raised to question in the petition regarding counsel was bound in a different colored ribbon and raises a doubt as to whether the statement was made by the petitioner or added later to the record. Judge Neterer further stated that while the petitioner may be a "moral degenerate" likely pointing to Plastino's multiple past charges of rape, larceny, and vagrancy, it was the right of the accused to be advised of the privilege of counsel before he was examined. A few weeks after Judge Neterer's decision, by an oral motion of the U.S. attorney, the files of the original records of the Department of Commerce were removed from the record.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 6, 1901, a warrant for the arrest of G.M. Briggs was issued by Justice of the Peace J.A. Taggard of Yakima County on the complaint of Charles A. Bryant that Briggs was selling farm, dairy, orchard, and garden produce on commission without a license to do so. Briggs was subsequently arrested in Seattle, Washington and three days later with the assistance of his lawyers Roberts & Leehey, would file a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. His argument being that his imprisonment was illegal on the grounds that the warrant for his arrest was issued by a judge in a county that was not the same as the one in which he was arrested. His writ was ultimately denied and ordered to stand trial in Yakima, he would be released on bail. Outcome of his case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In July of 1887, Louis Leiberman, a Jewish naturalized U.S. citizen, was arrested on the charge of violating the city of Lincoln's Sunday ordinance. He argued in his habeas corpus petition that police judge Albert F. Parsons violated his right to due process and that his business, a general goods store, exempted him from following the ordinance; therefore, he was being deprived of his liberty by Marshall P. H. Cooper. In April of 1888, Judge Allen Field remanded Leiberman into custody until he was released on bond on April 24th on the sum of $100.

Summary of Proceedings: Wong petitioned for the writ of habeas corpus on October 11th, 1894, on behalf of Young Ah Ning, who was restrained on the steamship Signal by its master, Captain Elder. Wong stated that this was due to the collector of customs at the Port of Portland not allowing Young Ah Ning to land. Young Ah Ning, a Chinese merchant in Portland, according to Wong, left for China in July of 1893 with the intent of coming back. B. Phillippe signed for his identification before he left and was sworn in as a witness, and attested that he knew Young Ah Ning as a merchant. After the court referee reviewed the evidence, the writ was denied, and Young Ah Ning was remanded to the prior custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 8, 1918, Edward Twitty was arrested by a police officer without being told of his charge or reason for detainment. He notes that he was later informed that he was being held by the Police Department at the request of the City Health Department because they believed he was infected with some dangerous, contagious and infectious disease. Twitty later filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he is not infected with any disease and that his arrest is a part of a conspiracy within a Police Department to deprive him of his liberty. The case file does not include the outcome of the petition. Newspaper coverage of the case notes that the case was brought before the Supreme Court of the State of Washington in July of 1918.

Summary of Proceedings: Rittmaster was taken into custody due to the oral order of Hon. Melville R. Hopewell, District Court Judge. Judge Hopewell did this based on claims that Rittmaster was a fugitive of justice from the state of Colorado for obtaining money under false pretenses. Rittmaster claimed that no affidavit was filed against him for being a fugitive of justice or committing any criminal offense. Additionally, Rittmaster claimed that despite being innocent he had been treated cruelly and inhumanly in close confinement, denied bail, and imprisoned without evidence. Judge Hopewell and Judge George W. Doane ordered a writ to be issued in favor of Rittmaster. However, upon return of the writ, the Sheriff said that Rittmaster had been released from jail under due process of law. Due to Rittmaster's supposed release, the final outcome is unclear.

Summary of Proceedings: Alfio DeGeorge was arrested on December 19th, 1923, after fleeing the scene of the murder of a man named Gibilterra. Following a preliminary hearing for the trial of Gibilterra's murder, DeGeorge filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus for being unlawfully detained by the Douglas County Sheriff, Michael Endres, as a suspect in the murder case. DeGeorge claimed that the witness examinations in the preliminary hearing had cleared him of guilt. Despite the Habeas Corpus petition being granted, his writ was denied as the judge deemed that he was still at risk of conviction as an accomplice in the murder of Gibilterra. DeGeorge remained in the custody of the Douglas Country Sheriff.

Summary of Proceedings: In December 1874, J. J. Johnson pled guilty to "Selling liquor to Indians" and was sentenced to three months in jail. Johnson was ordered to pay a $300 fine, and threatened with an additional three months in jail if he did not pay the fine. In March 1875, Henry Struve, secretary of the Washington Territory, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, arguing that Johnson had not conducted the transaction in Indian Country. The writ was issued. The result of the hearing and Johnson's fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In November 1918, Carl Berg petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Henry M. White, U.S. Commissioner of Labor. Berg was a subject of the King of Sweden, and was arrested by an Immigration Inspector, charged with being an alien and having advocated or taught the unlawful destruction of property. The petition alleged Berg demanded a copy of said evidence against him to attach to the petition but was denied by the respondent. Judge Neterer denied the writ, and Berg was remanded to the custody of the Commissioner of Immigration.

Summary of Proceedings: The City of Spokane passed a city ordinance that deemed slaughterhouses deleterious to public health and forbid their operation within two miles of the city limits. William R. Tuttle operated a slaughterhouse within two miles of the city limits and on December 23, 1905, the Police Court Judge J. D. Hinkle issued a warrant for Tuttle's arrest charging him with illegally operating a slaughterhouse. On January 12, 1906, the Police Court found William R. Tuttle guilty and fined him $10 plus costs. Tuttle was also ordered to remain in jail until the fine and costs were paid. Following the judgement, Tuttle filed for a writ of habeas corpus with the Federal Circuit Court arguing that his detainment is illegal because the city ordinance violates the Fourteenth Amendment and the Washington State Charter by forbidding the operation of a slaughterhouse two miles outside of the city limits. Judge. However, since Tuttle never appealed the decision through the state courts, Judge Whiting dismissed the writ stating that the federal courts did not have a proper case for intervention.

Summary of Proceedings: Leah filed for a writ of habeas in order to regain her freedom from Arthur Mitchel. She claimed that she had been taken to Ohio multiple times in the past by Arthur back in 1817 and 1826. In 1826 she filed for habeas in Ohio to gain her freedom and succeeded in being discharged from the custody of Arthur Mitchel. As a result, Arthur is in violation of her freedom as established by the Ohio court system. Judge Carr agreed to hear Leah’s petition, and also allowed her to sue as a poor person and assigned Gustavus Bird as her attorney. With Bird’s help, Leah charged Arthur with trespass, assault and battery, and false imprisonment. Arthur pled not guilty to these charges, and a few witnesses were summoned to the court to help resolve the controversy. Further events within the case, as well as the final outcome, is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 7, 1886, Young John filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he claimed that he was being illegally detained by the Superintendent of the Oregon State Penitentiary George Collins. Young John was arrested and charged with violating the Oregon Act of 1885 to Regulate the Sale of Opium. Young John claimed the Act was unconstitutional because it violated the obligations of contracts and deprived persons of their property. Judge Deady disagreed with Young John and denied his writ of habeas corpus. Included in the case file is Judge Deady’s full legal opinion.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 1, 1916, the Douglas County Circuit Court found Roy Stearns to be insane due to his use of "alcohol to excess" and had him committed to the Oregon State Hospital. On July 18, 1916, Stearns' attorney, Albert Abraham, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, which was granted. Stearns maintained that there had been no physician present in the circuit court as required by law, a claim seemingly at odds with the order of commitment. By mutual assent, the two parties postponed the habeas proceedings to a later date, during which time the hospital released Stearns. With Stearns no longer bound, the judge dismissed the cause.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 27, 1919, Mamie Allen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, and the next day it was filed. Her attorney John M. Berger was also helping two other women file petitions to be released from the Detention Home, Agnes Marshall and Ruth Matthews. In her petition, Allen claimed she was unlawfully imprisoned in the Detention Home. She was arrested on August 23 and charged with vagrancy contrary to the statute of the state of Nebraska. On August 25, the court sentenced her to thirty days in county jail. Although she offered to pay the bonds for the appeal, Judge Charles E. Foster refused to accept. Because of the conviction for vagrancy, the Health Department held her on mittimus for an examination for any venereal diseases under the custody of Elizabeth Hardy, the keeper of the Detention Home. On August 29, 1919, the judge accepted the petition and filed a writ of habeas corpus. The same day, Elizabeth Hardy responded to the writ, claiming that she was authorized to hold Allen because the state of Nebraska Ordinance No. 10222 mandated her to do so. An Omaha Daily Bee Article states that Judge William A. Redick ruled the detention illegal and ordered that the women be released.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 23rd, 1919, William Braniff was tried and charged in Omaha's police court for the offense of assault and battery. He was subsequently arrested, though the complaint for his arrest contained almost no details about the nature of his crime or who the victim was. Braniff took his case to court and filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus. He showed that he was being held based on a complaint that was defective, insufficient, and void of a timeframe for when the crime was allegedly committed. Judge Estelle heard his case and granted Braniff a writ of Habeas Corpus, ordering Sheriff Michael L. Clark to release him from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: F. B. Counort petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Spokane County Sheriff George E. Stone. Counort claimed that he was arrested and tried for neglecting to send his children to school by the Superior Court of Spokane County. He pled not guilty and alleged that his actions did not constitute a crime, but was adjudged guilty and imprisoned by Stone in the Spokane County Court House. Stone’s response recounted Counort’s original trial in the Justice Court, where he was found guilty, and his appeals to the Superior and Supreme Courts, both of which upheld the Justice Court’s ruling of guilty. The federal circuit court ruled that the final judgement of a competent state court could not be reversed by a federal court in the case of Counort’s petition. The judge determined that the matter discussed in Counort’s petition was a case of local law and should stay in local jurisdiction. The court denied the writ, and Counort remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Edward Roberts filed a writ of habeas corpus on February 13, 1897. His attorney, J. C. Whitlock, argued that Roberts was being held without a charge. 

According to newspaper coverage, Roberts “was recently tried for exhibiting dangerous weapons.” Whitlock filed a writ of review in the court of Judge Orange Jacobs, which was dismissed. However, Jacobs later allowed the writ of habeas corpus, “sustained the allegation of the petitioner and ordered his discharge.”

Summary of Proceedings: Al Lake was arrested and detained by the Sheriff of King County L.C. Smith under an unspecified charge. Lake petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was not properly informed of the reason of his detention and that he was detained without lawful warrant and was not provided due process. Judge R.B. Albertson granted the petition, but the outcome of the petitioner is unknown. Lake was represented by the legal firm Morris, Southard, & Shipley, but there is no indication in the case files nor the newspaper accounts as to which attorney in particular represented him and what their role in the case was.

Summary of Proceedings: D. O. Belt, the petitioner, filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus, as he was deprived of his liberty due to extradition papers from Kentucky stating that he had obtained money by false pretenses. Belt states that the documents do not say he is a fugitive from justice or charge a crime against him. Belt states that he agreed with a company to sell them hemp for a specific amount but then decided not to sell or take money from the company. R.C. Morgan & Company members state that Belt had indicated that he owned lots of hemp and was willing to deliver to Lexington and that they had paid $712 and then received no hemp. Judge Troup of Nebraska finds D. O. Belt to be deprived of his liberty.

Summary of Proceedings: James Riley, the petitioner, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus after he was detained for assaulting John McCloud with intent to kill and for killing another man who is not named. Both men are described as indigenous and Snohomish. Riley allegedly assaulted John McCloud, one of the indigenous men, with intent to kill, caused "malicious mayhem," and killed the other man with a knife. According to the Bradleys, the owners of the residence where the assault and murder took place, these incidents all occurred in the same evening during correspondence between Riley and a group of at least 2-3 indigenous women and 2 indigenous men. Almost all of the witnesses in this case state that James Riley is a dangerous man and/or of bad character. Further, both Thomas Horn and Allen McLeod state that they were with the man killed by Riley moments before his death and that he had told them that Riley was his killer. Additonally, H. E. Bradley states that Riley told him that he had murdered the indigenous man who was found by Horn and McLeod.

Summary of Proceedings: In January 1896, Spafford Woodhull was arrested and charged in federal court with having murdered Amos La Prentis on the Omaha Indian Reservation the previous September. Woodhull, who was "born a member of the Omaha tribe of Indians," petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that he was a US citizen living apart from the Omaha, that the alleged murder occurred in Thurston County, Nebraska, and that the federal government therefore lacked the jurisdiction to charge him. His fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Elmer MacNalley and Charles Byers operated and managed a soft drink bar in Omaha that allegedly sold alcohol. On June 24, 1924, Elmer MacNalley’s bond was set for $5,000 after he was found guilty on the charges of unlawful sale and possession of intoxicating liquor and maintaining a common nuisance. On July 2, Elmer was examined by a government physician to see if he was able to attend court. On July 3, 1924, Judge McGee sentenced Elmer to two six-month sentences for the alcohol charge and a one-year sentence for the maintenance of a common nuisance charge to be served in the Lincoln County Jail. On December 26, 1924, Elmer petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. The court documents include notes that the production of his body was waived. On January 5, 1925 he amended his application and argued that Judge McGee had fixed rules for certain charges that did not take into account the circumstances or reputations of the defendants. Judge McGee ordered that the respondents release Elmer from custody upon payment of a bond and the respondents appealed this decision. On January 30, 1926 the decision of the lower court was reversed in the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals and Elmer was remanded to the custody of the respondents.

Summary of Proceedings: William L. Huffman was charged with possessing two forms of drugs (morphine and cocaine) in Arizona and was sentenced to McNeil Island Penitentiary. Huffman filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of himself on December 22nd, 1916, claiming that Warden Halligan, the respondent, was depriving him of his liberty. The petition stated that his liberties were being violated as there was no statute up which his indictment rested on for validity during his criminal trial. Judge Cushman allowed the writ and order Huffman to be released from Warden Halligan's custody on January 22nd, 1917.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 9th, 1891, Chin Hoy and Le Chin Sing filed a writ of habeas corpus because they claimed they were being illegally detained by the Steamship Granholm Captain John Mason. Mason claimed that Collector of the Port of Portland E.P. Earhart ordered him to detain Chin Hoy and Le Chin Sing. Earhart claimed that Chin Hoy and Le Chin Sing were prevented from entering the United States by the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Matthew P. Deady disagree with Earhart and granted the writ and ordered Chin Hoy and Le Chin Sing to be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Wu Kao was arrested for deportation by an order issued by Immigrant Commissioner Henry M. White. He petitioned claiming that he was previously a student and was now a merchant of China, his investigations alongside his secretary in the U.S. were legal, and a passport given to him by the Commissioner of Foreign Affairs allowed him to proceed.
His writ was denied with the argument that Wu Kao didn't carry a certificate required by Section 6 of the Act of 1884 in order for his mercantile status to be accepted and his admittance to the U.S. It was further claimed that Wu Kao didn't investigate industrial conditions as granted by China, but opened up a local merchant shop, and his secretary has left and forfeited a $1,000 bond.

Summary of Proceedings: H. Ray Desch petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his daughter, Margaret Desch, from Katherine Krummack, which was granted. Katherine was the girl's grandmother, being the mother of Ray Desch's late wife. Ray had left the girl with her after his wife's death in January 1917, as he had no home at the time, but managed to pay Mrs. Krummack $10 a month to take care of the girl and bought all of his daughter's clothes. After Ray got back on his feet and remarried, he asked his mother-in-law for custody of Margaret. After hearing the evidence, Margaret was remanded into the custody of her father, with the stipulation that Krummack could see her granddaughter whenever she wanted. Margaret apparently protested against the decision, as she had grown quite attached to her grandmother while living with her.

Summary of Proceedings:
This case is the second writ of habeas corpus filed by Allen H. Shears. The first writ was filed after Shears was arrested by the King County Sheriff, John Stringer, based on a warrant issued by the Governor of the State of New York. The warrant accused Shears of embezzling $3,000 between December 1, 1917 and September 22, 1918 from the Fire Association of Philadelphia and the Insurance Company of North America. Shears filed a writ of habeas corpus and argued that the Governor’s warrant was illegal and without due process. Shears claims that since no complaint or affidavit had ever been filed against him the warrant is illegal. The petition further claims that this matter was brought before the King County Prosecuting Attorney in 1916 and the attorney refused to file any charges based on the information and facts given to him. Judge A. W. Frater allowed the writ of habeas corpus because the respondent parties missed the deadline to file their return and granted the petitioner’s request to have the late return exempted. 

The day following Shears’ first writ of habeas corpus was accepted, the King County Prosecuting Attorney, Fred C. Brown, filed information for a new warrant to arrest Shears. This warrant was issued by Justice of Peace John B. Gordon and Shears was rearrested by Sheriff John Stringer on December 12, 1919. Immediately following this rearrest, Shears filed for a new writ of habeas corpus. Judge A. W. Frater accepted this new writ of habeas corpus stating that that this new warrant was null and void since it was based on the same information as the first warrant that led to the first habeas corpus petition. Fred C. Brown would go on to appeal this decision to the Supreme Court of the State of Washington. The state’s Supreme Court would dismiss Brown’s appeal on December 18, 1920.

Summary of Proceedings:
On February 10, 1902, Edward Ladd was arrested under the orders of the Chief of Police, John Sullivan. In his brief, Ladd is described by his attorney, Richard Gowan, as being held in the King County jail for five days without warrant. In the response, Sullivan claims that he had given orders over the telephone to arrest Ladd after Ladd was charged with a felony in the Pacific County of Washington and became a fugitive of justice. 

The petition was heard by Judge Emory and decided on February 11, 1902. According to newspaper reporting from the Seattle Star on February 12, 1902, Ladd’s petition was denied.
