Summary of Proceedings: Yee Bing petitioned for habeas corpus on December 7th, 1892, on behalf of his friend and coworker Ye Mok, who was not being allowed to land in Portland after a trip to China. Ye Mok was being deprived of disembarking by the Captain of the Steamer Haytian Republic, H.K. Struve. Ye Mok had left for Hong Kong on May 7th, 1892, at the port of San Francisco, on business for the Pow Chung Lung & Co., with the intent to return. On November 18th, the same year, he made his trip back on the Steamer Empress of China from the port of Hong Kong to Vancouver, where he boarded the Steamer Haytain Republic on the 23rd of November. After landing in Portland, Captain Struve did not let him disembark, and Yee Bing believed this was due to the Collector of Customs, James Lotan, refusing to allow him to land, claiming he was a Chinese subject. This is most likely referring to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. Judge Deady commanded that Struve be served the writ and to appear in court the next day, December 8th, with Ye Mok and the reasoning for his detention. At the court date, Struve confirms that the only reason he has Ye Mok in custody is that James Lotan, the collector of customs, would not allow him to land. As evidence, Ye Mok had an affidavit showing his identity as a resident of Portland and left for business with the intent to return, as well as witnesses. The writ was granted and Ye Mok was ordered to be freed.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 14, 1893, Long Yin and Long Soy filed for a writ of habeas corpus. They claimed that they were merchants who were being illegally detained by the Steamship Signal Captain Eugene Hayden. Hayden claimed that he was ordered by the Collector of the Port of Oregon T.J. Black to detain Long Yin and Long Soy. Black believed that Long Ying and Long Soy were Chinese laborers who were not allowed to enter the United States under the Chinese Exclusion Act. Judge Charles Bellinger disagreed and granted the writ of habeas and ordered Long Yin and Long Soy to be released. Included in the case file is Long Yin and Long Soy’s travel documents and testimony they provided to the court.

Summary of Proceedings: C. E. Clay was arrested and tried on police court under an order of mittimus issued July 16, 1918, by police magistrate James M. Fitzgerald, for unlawful possession and transport of intoxicating liquor. Clay was found guilty and charged $100 and costs of prosecution. On August 22, 1918, Clay, with attorney Ed F. Morearty, filed a petition of habeas against sheriff, Michael L. Clark. Clay charged that he had served 37 days in jail, and on day 21, attempted to pay remaining balance of fine, which was refused by Clark. The petition was granted, a writ was issued and sustained; Clay was discharged on August 28.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 27, 1893, Billy Phillips petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his wife, Ellen Phillips, identified as Indigenous by the Seattle Post Intelligencer.  His petition argued that there was no reason or process that justified her detainment.  The case file does not indicate a cause for detainment.  However, page 5 of the September 28, 1893 issue of the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reported that Phillips was detained because she was a witness in A.L. Hick’s liquor selling case.   She was also brought before a grand jury to testify in an assault case, but was returned to the city jail.  Judge Humes issued a writ of habeas corpus.  While the case file did not provide an outcome, the newspaper reported that Humes released Phillips.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 22, 1907, M. L. Volwiler and his attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his children, Robert (7) and Lillian (5). M. L. Volwiler stated that he was awarded full custody of both children in August of 1906, and he then placed both children in an unnamed children’s home, run by a Mrs. Ryther. He alleged that Hattie Volwile took the children from the home on November 2, 1906, without M. L.’s consent. Hattie’s exact relationship to M. L. and the children was not stated. M. L. stated he had been unable to find Hattie, but believed she was in Seattle. The writ was unable to be delivered as Hattie could not be found. However, M. L. moved to dismiss the writ because he had found his children and regained custody of them from Hattie. The motion to dismiss was granted.

Summary of Proceedings: Lucia Martinez filed for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her two daughter, Clara A and Johana Martinez who were being held by one of the defendants, Thomas Barman. The hearing was postponed to August 30 1871 so the defendants had time to collect their evidence and witnesses. Before the hearing took place, Martinez approached the judge and requested the dismissal of the case, and both parties agreed to drop the case. By order of Judge Alsop Clara and Johana were to stay in the custody of the sheriff until the August hearing had ended.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 24th, 1919, a petition was filed by Nellie E. Hurt for her minor daughter of 4 years, June Lucile Hurt, who was allegedly taken by some sort of fraud and false representation to South Dakota by Sula Hurt and Henry Hurt whose relation to the petitioner is unknown. Her husband had recently obtained a divorce from her on the grounds of desertion. On January 27th, the writ was sustained and custody of the bound party was granted to the maternal grandparents of the bound party, Frantz S. Wilson and Jennie Wilson. Interestingly, the 1920 census records show that Frantz and Jennie represented June as their daughter, not their granddaughter. Nellie also apparently remarried by 1920 and was living with her husband and mother-in-law.

Summary of Proceedings: In February 1908, fourteen-year-old Nebraska resident Albert Anderton enlisted in the U.S. Army while visiting relatives in Missouri. He had obtained an order from the probate court of Cowley County, Kansas, designating one Thomas Hawkins as his legal guardian and enlisted with his permission. In April, Albert's father, William Anderton, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his son, which was granted. In his return to the writ, Brigadier General Charles Morton explained that Albert had been court-martialed for fraudulent enlistment and that it would be a bureaucratic hassle to present him before the court since he was technically detained by the authority of the Secretary of War. The judge dismissed the cause and Albert remained in the custody of the U.S. Army.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 13, 1912, Tung Kee arrived in a U.S. port and was taken into custody of the U.S. Commissioner of Immigration, set for deportation. Ben Wa filed for habeas against the commissioner, arguing that Tung Kee was a native-born resident of the U.S. and that deportation would be a denial of his constitutional rights. Wa, with attorneys, motioned for a stay of deportation, which was granted, but later cancelled on August 1, 1912 at the request of petitioner. The outcome of this case the the fate of Tung Kee are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Russell and Nettie Matson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve their children, Mary Alice Matson and Roscoe Brown, from the custody of chief probation officer of the juvenile court Sarah B. Gregory, police matron Dora Doyle, and probation officer Ida Pearce, which was granted. The two children had been held in a detention home since October 26 without a warrant or committment. The parties agreed to merge the cause with a related proceeding in the juvenile court. After hearing the evidence, the judge denied the Matsons' writ and remanded their children to the custody of the respondents.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward L. Twitty petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren and Commissioner of Health J. S. McBride. Twitty claimed Warren and McBride were holding him under the false claim he was infected with a contagious disease. He described the conditions of his detainment quarters as “unsanitary, filthy and poorly ventilated,” with inmates sharing soap and drinking cups, being fed “unwholesome” food. Warren and McBride claimed that Twitty was indeed infected with syphilis and was now under quarantine at the city isolation hospital in accordance with several city ordinances. Newspaper records indicated the writ was denied, and Twitty remained in custody. Newspaper records also indicated that he may have appealed to the Washington State Supreme Court, but did not state an outcome of that appeal.

Summary of Proceedings: John F. Decker petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was unlawfully detained by Sheriff Nicholas Ress. Judge Holmes granted the petition and allowed him bail at the sum of 300 dollars. Decker had been arrested on the charge of perjury after he falsely claimed during a divorce trial that he was a resident of Lancaster County, Nebraska. After hearing evidence, Judge Holmes ruled that Decker had not committed perjury and therefore was being illegally detained. He ordered that Decker be released from custody. However, he ordered that the County Attorney, James L. Caldwell, prosecute Decker for the charge of contempt of court and punish him accordingly. Caldwell immediately followed through in State of Nebraska vs John F. Decker where again Decker was released on bail. The outcome of this case is unknown. Weeks later, Caldwell produced a motion for a re-hearing and a new trial for Decker's habeas corpus case, which the court overruled. In 1906, Caldwell's appeal was tried in the Nebraska Supreme Court, who later dismissed his petition in error.

Summary of Proceedings: Thomas W. Cross petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against the sheriff of King County. Cross did not name the sheriff in his petition, but John Stringer was the King County Sheriff at the time, and it can be inferred he was the one detaining Cross. Cross claimed that he had been ordered to serve a prior sentence in the custody of Stringer for an unspecified charge, but that the sentence had expired and Stringer was unwilling to release him. Cross did not specify where Stringer was holding him, but it can be inferred that Cross was detained in King County Jail. The outcome of the case and Cross’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 8th, 1903 Sarah B. Leray petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus for her husband, J. S. Leray. According to Sarah, J.S. was being held by John Sullivan, the Chief of Police of Seattle in the Seattle City Jail on account of a telegraphic or telephonic message from an unknown person in Spokane. Sarah also stated that this restraint was without warrant or authority of law and without reasonable suspicion. The petition for the writ was granted by Judge W. R. Bell of the Seattle Superior Court and was served upon John Sullivan by Ed Cudihee, the Sheriff of King County. In John Sullivan’s return, he claimed that he was holding J. S. Leray on a warrant of arrest issued out of the Justice Court in and for Spokane County, Washington. The warrant was issued based on the account of William T. H. Lawrence, who complained that J. S. Leray stole $9000 from him. This warrant was issued by J. H. Hinkle, and after it was signed Leray apparently escaped from Spokane to Seattle, where Sullivan was messaged and Leray was caught. He was to be held there until a police officer from Spokane could get there with the warrant and take him back to Spokane where he would be tried for larceny charges. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: James A. Marcil, a prisoner at McNeil Island Penitentiary, filed a writ of habeas corpus on April 21st, 1914. Marcil argued that he should have been released on April 8th of that year, rather than at the end of his original sentence on December 28th, 1914. Marcil claimed that at some point, the Warden of the penitentiary gave him a slip that said his good conduct term would expire on April 8th. Additionally, Marcil argued that he should still be able to earn good time, as in his last petition, it was only stated that he could not keep the good time he lost for violating his parole. Judge Cushman denied this petition on May 4th, 1914, and Marcil was ordered to remain at McNeil Island Penitentiary.

Summary of Proceedings: Mary and T. LeFebvre were married in 1884, and sometime before this petition in 1888 she filed for divorce. Mary filed for divorce on the grounds that her husband does not make suitable provisions for her family and for cruel treatment. T took their 3 year-old child Henry "by force" at a restaurant and had been traveling around. Mary petitioned for custody of their child. Henry was hidden in Seattle at the point of this petition. Her petition included points about how the child has contracted a disease since he is being neglected by the father and needed to be in his mother's care. Mary believed he took the child to stop the divorce. The petition also stated that Mary has been supporting herself and Henry long before the divorce proceedings and still supported herself. The petition was granted, this file only holds the petition and the writ of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 27, 1915, Albert Erickson was arrested by Robert T. Hodge and placed in the King County Jail. Erickson was arrested on a warrant issued by the Superior Court of Spokane County for the charge of contempt of court. Following his arrest, Albert Erickson filed for a writ of habeas corpus. In the petition, Erickson states that the warrant is likely related to the divorce proceedings between him and his former wife, Ida S. M. Baxter (formerly Erickson). He also argues his arrest is illegal because the warrant for his arrest does not specify the nature of his charge of contempt of court or when the crime occurred. Judge Kenneth Mackintosh heard Erickson’s petition and ruled that he is to remain in custody and be transferred to the custody of the Sheriff of Spokane County. Immediately following this ruling, Erickson announced he will be appealing the ruling and paid $500 for a supersedeas bond. Information about the appeal was not included in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: Ray Rickard petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his daughter, Dorothy Rickard, from the custody of Catherine Kleeman and Martha Peer, which was granted. Martha responded that although her mother, Catherine, had Dorothy, who was her granddaughter, in her possession, neither woman claimed custody of the girl. Margaret had apparently left Dorothy with her mother on June 7, 1915. Apparently, Ray and Catherine made up over the month of June, since Catherine was apparently living with Ray in Kansas when he filed the petition.  After hearing the evidence, the judge ordered that Catherine either deliver Dorothy to her father or demonstrate in court why she should not have to do so. A few months later, Ray withdrew his petition, suggesting he had secured custody of Dorothy.  This is confirmed by the 1930 census, which shows that Margaret and Ray were still together with Dorothy in their custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Frank O'Neill, Dave Gillinsky, A.F. Pirson, Art Williams, and William Larsen, were arrested for reportedly breaking and entering into the home of Katherine C. Allisen and her daughter, Grace Allisen on 410 S. 39th St. on December 5, 1919 around 2 AM. They were taken into custody, held on bonds of $2,000 each, the same day at the Electric Garage on 40th and Farnam, where they stopped to repair their car. Upon searching their car, police officer Fred H. Peterson found three loaded guns and a crowbar. The men claimed that none of the guns were theirs and that the crowbar was only in the car to aid in changing tires. The men claimed that they were on their way to Benson, an Omaha neighborhood, to play cards with a friend of Dave Gillinsky's. On that same morning, the five men were taken back to the Allisens' house, but Katherine was unable to positively identify any of them, and she in fact said that one of the policemen bore a stronger similarity to the man she saw than any of the accused men. 
A preliminary hearing occurred on December 6 in front of police magistrate Charles E. Foster. In this trial, all of the men claimed alibis for the night of Thursday, December 4 and Friday, December 5. All of the men were out drinking in downtown Omaha, and several witnesses, including friends of theirs and employees of establishments they visited, testified that the men were with them that night. Notably, it came out in the trial that William Earl Adams, the Allisens' neighbor, had heard someone yell "Harold" during the robbery—none of the men were named Harold. In addition, the men's lawyer, John Battin, pointed out that the short coat that was the most recognizable attribute of the man that Mrs. Allisen saw was in fact a coat that had been issued to every man honorably discharged from the navy, and thus would have been a common sight only a year after WWI. Thus, the men filed a habeas corpus petition on December 18, 1919, which was allowed. A hearing on the petition occurred on December 19, but it was denied on the 22nd. This is perhaps because another habeas corpus petition the men filed, also against Michael L. Clark, had succeeded, allowing all of the men except Larson, for an unknown reason, to be freed. A return to writ was filed on December 27, 1919. An Omaha Daily Bee article indicates that Frank O'Neill was arrested for another robbery on January 24, 1920, and that somehow, the men were tried again and found guilty for the the Allison robbery on March 29, 1920. This was reversed and remanded, however, by the Nebraska Supreme Court on March 26, 1921.

Summary of Proceedings:
George Harlow was arrested for vagrancy and sentenced to 90 days in jail, but the term was suspended. Depite that suspension, Harlow was imprisoned anyways under orders from the Police Court. Harlow argued he was wrongfully imprisoned and his writ was granted. In fact, the judge in the cases ordered the county to assume the costs for his release. 
This case is also connected to George Harris, as Harris seems to have been imprisoned under similar circumstances.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 13th, 1921, Loren Laughlin submitted a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his clients Thomas Wyatt Robinson and Bessie Kraus. The petition alleged that they were being unlawfully detained in jail by William Lytle (City Marshal) and a John Doe. The petition alleged that Thomas and Bessie had not been presented with any copy of commitment, warrant, or other cause of detention although they had asked for them. The petition was granted, and the writ allowed. The judge ordered that Thomas and Bessie be released from police custody. Newspaper accounts indicate that Robinson and Kraus did not know each other or know why they had been arrested together, and Kraus explained she had been recently abandoned by her husband and her arrest separated her from her young son. No charges were filed and both were released.

Summary of Proceedings: In October 1895, William Garrett and John Meyers were arrested on the Winnebago Reservation in northeastern Nebraska and indicted on multiple counts including obstruction and assault. Both men paid a $500 bond and were released. The pair were involved with the Flournoy Live Stock and Real Estate Company, which had been illegally leasing Reservation land, and had resisted the efforts of the US government, including Winnebago police officers, to evict them. After having been released on bail but before their trial date, Garrett and Meyers petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. They claimed that the Winnebago Reservation had been effectively dissolved and that federal authorities had no jurisdiction to arrest them on state land. The respondents countered that the Reservation remained, that federal authorities retained jurisdiction, and that, in any case, Garrett and Meyers were not being detained. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and the petitioners ordered to pay the costs.

Summary of Proceedings:
On August 21, 1913, J. B. Densmore authorized the deportation of Young and Sugiura, both of Japanese descent, for violating the Immigration Act of 1910 and the White Slave Traffic Act, which targeted human trafficking for sexual exploitation. Young and Sugiura contested the warrant, claiming it lacked specific charges and that they were denied a fair trial.

Testimonies from June to November 1913, which included those of former accomplices K. Ito, K. Umeda, Shotaro Washio, and victim Hana Saito, alleged that Saito was taken to Sacramento against her will to provide sexual services. Saito escaped, and Washio enlisted Umeda and Ito to get her back, who involved Sugiura, who then hired Young. Pretending to be police officers, Young and Sugiura allegedly abducted Saito and detained her in a hotel, later returning her to Washio after a series of financial disputes.

The details of this case’s prosecution are largely missing, however the petitioners allegedly encouraged Washio to commit perjury in a previous trial. A writ of habeas corpus was filed and issued on December 12, 1913. The petition argued that assisting a person labeled a prostitute is legally distinct from promoting prostitution. The respondents argued that the court lacked jurisdiction to try this habeas case, even if there is any evidence.

The petitioners argued there was no evidence presented, no charge specified, and that their actions were in good faith to return Saito, who they believed to be Washio's wife. On February 18, 1914, it was recorded that they had previously been tried and acquitted twice for “transporting a Japanese girl”. The writ was denied. A motion for a new trial was filed on February 24, 1914, but no record of its outcome exists, suggesting the petitioners remained in custody for deportation.

Summary of Proceedings: In early December 1919, Katherine and Peter Hulm left their daughter, Frances, in the care of the Benedictine Sisters of Mt. Angel, Oregon. A few weeks later, Katherine petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Frances from the Benedictine Sisters, which was granted. The Benedictine Sisters, responding as a corporation, answered that they did not release Frances because her father, Peter, had written them a letter stating that they were not to permit Katherine to be alone with the child. They made it clear that they were not detaining Frances for any other reason and would comply with the order of the court. After hearing the evidence, which included testimony that Peter had fled Oregon, Frances was released into the custody of her mother.

Summary of Proceedings: Tony Butera, brother of Sam Butera, filed this petition on 8 July 1914 which stated that Sam was being held in the jail of the City of Omaha by Henry W. Dunn (Chief of Police), Steve Maloney (Chief of Detectives), and Edward Morris (Fire Warden) without any warrant or legal authority. The petition states that the aforementioned parties would not allow anyone to see Sam and they would not fix a bond amount. Judge Charles Leslie ordered that the writ be issued and directed at the aforementioned parties (Dunn, Maloney, and Morris). Sheriff McShane stated that he delivered the writ to Dunn and Maloney, but was unable to locate Morris. On 8 July 1914, Judge Leslie stated that Sam Butera was being held on the charge of arson. He ordered that Sam be released from imprisonment on a $2,000.00 “hand in sum,” with the promise to appear in Court the following day. Sebastian Salerno was listed as the surety of this bond. NOTE: The Butera case file erroneously contains two documents from an unrelated case that was tried before a Nebraska juvenile court in the late 1930s.

As the petition is missing from the case file, it is unclear for what offense Billingsley was held in Seattle City Jail or for what reason he found his jailing to be illegal. Summary of Proceedings: In August of 1882, Alice McKay placed her daughter, Mary, into the care of the Sisters of Charity for Mary to receive care as she recovered from Scarlet Fever. A month later, the Sisters placed Mary into the care of John and Della Keevan, telling Alice that they were doing so for Mary to receive "fresh country air." Alice argued that she had frequently attempted to visit Mary and retrieve her from the Keevan but was prevented from doing so after the Keevans threatened to shoot her. Alice claimed that the Keevans "unlawfully and cruelly bed, abuse, and otherwise ill-treat" Mary and that the Keevans had no legitimate legal claim to the custody of Mary. The Keevans responded by claiming that Alice abandoned Mary and left her in a poor physical condition and that "by reason of this poverty and indigent circumstances, she was unable to support and maintain it." The Keevans further argued that they were financially and mentally capable of providing Mary with a moral education and superior material means. While the case file itself does not contain a case outcome, it is indicated in Alice's second petition for custody of Mary in 1887 that this writ was denied on account of Alice's poverty.

Summary of Proceedings: Robert Welts was convicted of selling liquor without a license in Kearney County, Nebraska and fined $100. Since Welts could not pay, he was jailed. After serving for some time, he was released, only to be jailed again in Adams County. Welts declared that he was insolvent and had served long enough to satisfy his debt under state law. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Welts was released.

Summary of Proceedings: After being institutionalized in Lincoln's Hospital for the Insane, William Golden initially petitioned for the appointment of a commission to determine his sanity. His petition was denied because he had not been admitted six months prior to the application. A week later, Golden petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that Supt. H. W. Mathewson had illegally deprived him of his liberty. Dr. Hay, S. J. Tuttle, A. C. RIcketts, and T. J. Fuller were subpoenaed. After hearing evidence, Judge Pound ordered that he be returned to Mathewson's custody.

Summary of Proceedings: William Gerald was indicted on 44 total counts in 1913, for violating Sec. 9 of the Act of Sept. 13, 1888, and Sec. 8 of the Act of Feb. 20, 1907, by attempting to smuggle 22 alien Chinese persons into the United States through Mexico. Gerald unsuccessfully filed a writ of habeas corpus in 1914, then filed a new writ of habeas corpus on July 3rd, 1916. The petitioner claimed that he should have received a single sentence with a maximum sentence of 2 years, cited 21 similar cases to prove precedent was not followed during sentencing, and claimed that his sentence should have been reduced due to good behavior. Judge Cushman denied the writ on July 8th, 1916, claiming that the matter needed to be dealt with through an Appeal Court, rather than a writ of habeas corpus, and Gerald remained in Warden Halligan's custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 13th, 1922 Oliver Watson was arrested for reckless driving. On March 14th, a complaint in writing was drawn by John T. Marcell charging Oliver with reckless driving contrary to the statutes of the state of Nebraska. Oliver was tried and was sentenced by the court to pay a fine of $100 and the costs of prosecution. Police Magistrate Charles Foster issued a mittimus to detain Oliver until fines and costs were paid. The same day, Oliver petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was being unlawfully detained and fined because the complaint against him was void because no such reckless driving statute existed in Nebraska. He named Michael Clark, sheriff, as the respondent. Frank M Dineen responded on behalf of the state, citing that Michael Clark was lawfully detaining Oliver due to the mittimus issued by Charles Foster. The petition was granted and writ eventually allowed. Charles Leslie, the judge who oversaw the habeas proceedings, agreed that there was no reckless driving crime in the Nebraska statutes. Oliver Watson was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
H. C. Littooy, a U.S. citizen who practiced dentistry, applied for a writ of habeas corpus on June 11, 1904. Littooy stated that he had been repeatedly arrested and detained for the offense of practicing dentistry without being licensed by the State Board of Dental Examiners, an offense that violated a 1901 Washington law. His petition claimed that, despite his experience in dentistry, the Board would not allow him an examination because he had no diploma from a dental college. The petition claimed that the licensing law was a violation of Section One of the 14th Amendment because it was "class legislation" and because it infringed upon his right to "equal protection." 
Judge Hanford commanded that Sheriff Edward Cudihee show cause for Littooy's detention. Prosecuting Attorney W. J. Scott and Washington State Counsel Samuel R. Stern responded for Cudihee and stated that the petition should be dismissed because Littooy should instead seek remedy in the Superior Court of the State of Washington. Judge Hanford denied and dismissed the petition, stating that the lack of blatant unconstitutionality of the licensing law meant that directly appealing to a higher court would be more appropriate than habeas corpus. 
Newspaper articles stated that Littooy was fined $200 and was part of a larger group of dentists that were challenging the law; it is unclear if he remained in detention.

Summary of Proceedings: Leo Yan Bang petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Bang claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Bang was arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Bang are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 19, 1913 M. H. Crawford, along with his attorney George McKay, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, saying that he was being held illegally by Claude G. Bannick. In the petition, they alleged that Crawford was incorrectly charged with being a fugitive from justice from Montana and that there was no proper warrant issued for his arrest. Crawford then responded to a return that is not included in the case file, and said that he had not been in Montana for some time and therefore could not have been charged with anything in Montana or be a fugitive from justice. Crawford also mentioned in his response that at the time of birth of an otherwise unmentioned child, he was not in Montana. The outcome of this case and Crawford’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 1, 1923, the petitioner J. C. A. Houselighter, Helen Victoria, May Young, and seven other people were arrested at Houselighter's residence. Houselighter was charged with keeping a disorderly house, while the others arrested were charged with being inmates of a disorderly house. On December 3 Houselighter, Victoria, and Young were fined $10.00 each while the others arrested were released, and Houselighter paid $37.50 as fines on their behalfs. Houselighter was released, but Victoria and Young were sent back to jail to perform blood tests as part of an examination for venereal diseases. After being detained for three weeks without any examination, Houselighter filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Victoria, his stepdaughter, and Young, his friend. The writ was denied, Helen Victoria and Mary Young were remanded to the custody of the respondents.

Summary of Proceedings: William Giles, petitioner and father, filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus in an effort to gain custody of Haeckel Humboldt Giles. Mary A. Giles was granted a full divorce in Illinois from William Giles in July of 1889. In this divorce, William apparently allowed Mary to keep their son temporarily, but that William would have full control of the child. He accused her of kidnapping the child on December 7, 1889. Since the divorce agreement did not contain a provision allowing Mary full custody of Haeckel, due to this William argues he has rightful and full custody of the child. The writ is denied by Judge Joseph B. Clarkson, and the mother, Mary A. Giles, retained custody of the child in Omaha.

Summary of Proceedings: Englishman Herbert Brown entered the United States from Eastport, Idaho with his wife and child around February 1, 1920. Immigrant Inspector B. E. Gowen alleged that the family was in violation of the Immigration Act of 1917, were potentially public charges, and ordered deportation for Herbert Brown with detention in the Spokane County Jail. Richard B. Harris, attorney for the Brown, argued that “the order of deportation was made and the warrant issued on an entire misconception of the law as to what constitutes a person ‘likely to become a public charge.’” Judge Edward C. Cushman denied the writ and returned Brown to the custody of B. E. Gowen on December 10, 1921.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 16, 1868, an order had been issued by Charles E. Mix, the U.S. Commissioner of Indian Affairs, that stated that Native peoples would not be allowed to visit Washington D.C. due to lack of federal funding. Moses Keokuk, the Chief of the Sac & Fox Indians, used his own money to leave the reservation and visit Washington. On his way out of Kansas, he was arrested on November 23, 1868 by Albert Wiley, the Indian Agent for the Sac & Fox Indians.  On this order, Keokuk was transported to the county jail of Douglas County and held there for two days. Keokuk petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus which was granted. He continue to sue for damages against Wiley. After hearing the evidence, the jury found for Keokuk. Wiley filed for a new trial, and appealed to the Kansas Supreme Court. After reviewing the evidence, the Supreme Court of Kansas upheld the decision of the District Court.

The case file reveals neither the outcome of the case nor the fates of Irene and Beryl.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 27, 1919, the Acting Governor of the State of Washington, Louis F. Hart issued a warrant ordering John Stringer, the King County Sheriff to take Joseph Rheinstrom into custody and hand him over to J. I. Kirby who was acting as an agent for the State of Wyoming. The warrant alleged that Rheinstrom was a fugitive from justice that was wanted in the State of Wyoming for the crime of obtaining money by false representation. Following his arrest, Joseph Rheinstrom filed for a writ of habeas corpus. Rheinstrom argued in his petition that his detention was illegal and denied that he had committed any crimes in the State of Wyoming. Rheinstrom’s first writ of habeas corpus was denied by Judge J. T. Ronald. Following its dismissal, Rheinstrom filed for a second writ of habeas corpus which listed J. I. Kirby as the respondent instead of John Stringer. The outcome of this second writ of habeas corpus is not mentioned in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1915, immigration officials denied Chin Sheung Wing entry into the United States and ordered him to be deported. Wing's father, Chin Kim, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his son's behalf which stated that Chin Kim was born in the US and therefore a citizen. In 1901 a proceeding was held to determine the status of Chin Kim, and district judge H.C. Hanford found that Chin Kim was a citizen of the United States. Immigration officials denied the nativity of Chin Kim and believed Chin Sheung Wing was not his son. Judge Neterer authorized the writ, however, upon motion by the attorney of the petitioner, the writ of habeas corpus was dismissed. The fate of Chin Sheung Wing and cause for dismissing the writ is unknown. Subsequently, the U.S. attorney ordered that the government permanently withdraw exhibits and files of the Bureau of Immigration from the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: Samuel Coulter was a federal tax collector in Washington Territory. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the second judicial district after refusing to supply copies of tax records to Judge Jacobs in the third judicial district, for which said judge held him in contempt and ordered his arrest. After hearing the evidence Judge Greene in the second judicial district ordered him to be discharged. It is unclear from the case file whether he had been arrested, or if he filed for habeas relief preemptively.

Summary of Proceedings: John M. Wilson filed for a writ of habeas against his ex-wife, Margaret Wilson, in an attempt to secure custody of their three children Virgil, Laverne, and Frances Wilson.. John alleged that on July 25, 1887 he filed for divorce on grounds of adultery and petitioned for custody of the children in South Dakota, at which point Margaret fled to Nebraska. Margaret denied most of John’s claims, save that he was the father of her children and that they were married, claiming that John only secured the divorce and legal custody by fraud and that prior to the divorce it was agreed she would have custody. Judge Letton granted the petition for a writ, but ruled in favor of Margaret, a decision which J. N. Rickards, John’s attorney, appealed, though the results of the appeal are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1894, M. L. Abbott, uncle and next friend of minor, Hazel Blanche Abbott, aged three years old, filed for a writ of habeas corpus, seeking her return from the household of Joseph and Ida Quirk. Hazel’s parents, Charles and Georgie Abbott, divorced in 1892. M. L. Abbott sought to recover Hazel on behalf of her father, Charles, with plans to take the child to California to stay with her aunt, Mrs. J. D. Allen. Charles Abbott resided in San Francisco, California at the time of the petition. The Quirks refused to forfeit custody of Hazel without reimbursement for boarding. The fate of Hazel is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 15, 1887, two sisters named Hilma and Ida Lundvall were adopted from the Portland Orphans' Home. Hilma, born in 1881, was adopted by Leuvica and William Hume. Her sister Ida, born in 1879, was adopted by Leuvica's mother, Leuvica O. Hamilton. Both families lived in Chehalis County, Oregon. On September 11, 1888, the children's mother, Maria Kristina Peterson, filed a writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of the children. She claimed that the children had not been given into their adoptive parents' custody by any kind of due process of law. After the hearing being delayed several times, Judge Frank Allyn determined that the children should stay with their adoptive parents and that Maria would have no contact with them.

Summary of Proceedings: Joe Jan filed a writ of habeas under the name of Do Gin claiming to be a citizen of Canada and that he was unlawfully held by Sheriff A. T. Van De Vanter in the King County Jail. The writ was granted by Judge Jacobs, but Van De Vanter claimed that he had no prisoner by that name. Three days later, Van De Vanter adds that he believes Do Gin is the same person as a prisoner being held in the county jail under direction of the Marshall and by the authority of Judge C. H. Hanford under the name of Joe Jan, and that Van De Vanter does not have legal custody of the petitioner. He then forwards documentation showing that Joe Jan was found guilty of being illegally in the country and was to be deported, but  Judge Hanford stayed his deportation so that he could also be tried by a Grand Jury to answer charges related to a forged certificate of residence.

Summary of Proceedings: H. G. Martin filed a writ of habeas against Sheriff A. T. Van De Vanter for unlawful imprisonment and claimed that the judge pro tempore who ordered his imprisonment, Walter S. Fulton, was illegitimate. Judge Orange Jacobs granted the petition. Van De Vanter claimed the imprisonment was just, as Martin was being held due to him being held in contempt of court. The contempt of court charge was in regards to his refusal to pay alimony to his ex-wife, Josie Martin, for two months in a row when he had the financial means to do so. Judge Jacobs decides that the purpose of alimony is for a father to support his children, but as there are no children the court has no power to force Martin to pay alimony to his ex-wife. Jacobs further elaborates, however, that to properly change the previous court decree would require a formal appeal of said decree, as overturning it is not the place of a court of habeas corpus. The writ was allowed, and Martin was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Flora Ohler and Joseph Gielday divorced in January 1893. Custody of their two young daughters, Naomi and Leona Gielday, was awarded to Flora. According to Flora, she moved to Iowa and re-married, while Joseph moved to Red Willow County, Nebraska, and took ill. Flora allowed Naomi and Leona to visit Joseph in order to help take care of him. At some point, Leona returned to her mother while Naomi remained with her father. When Joseph died in February 1898, a pair of brothers named Charles and George Shafer contrived to have custody of Naomi awarded to Charles, arguing that she had no relatives living in the state. Flora petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Naomi, which was granted. Flora argued that she was Naomi's rightful guardian and that Charles "only desires the custody of said minor child to gratify his own licentious designs and to accommodate the lust of his single brother George." Charles countered that Flora was an abusive mother, that Naomi remained with the Shafers of her own volition, and that the District Court of Lancaster County, Nebraska had no jurisdiction over Red Willow County. After hearing the evidence, fourteen-year-old Naomi Gielday was remanded to the custody of Charles Shafer.

Summary of Proceedings: Hannah Segerholm was the servant of Hannah and Per A. Anderson. While she was working for them, she had her daughter, Mabel. One witness alleged that Per A. Anderson was the father and another said that Nels Johnson was the father. Hannah Segerholm gave her daughter away to Melissa and Louis Potts to take care of her until she was an adult. She had been in their custody since she was 3 1/2 months old, although no official adoption papers were ever signed. Some witnesses said that Louis took Mabel in his covered wagon to Oklahoma and everyone was unable to find them. Because of this, Hannah Segerholm filed a writ that said she wanted child custody to be given back to Hannah Anderson. Then, this writ was filed with the Potts claiming the Andersons and Hannah Segerholm were unfit to care for Mabel. The battle in the courtroom got physical at points, according to the Evening World-Herald. The court decided that Mabel should stay with the Potts family.

Summary of Proceedings:
Petitioner claimed that he is unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Chief Gallagher in Omaha. He stated that he did not know the cause of his detention and that no complaint had been filed against him anywhere in the state of Nebraska which would charge him with “the commission of any crime or being a fugitive from justice.” The petitioner was informed that Gallagher arrested him at the request of an officer from Oklahoma based on a request being sent by telegram. The petitioner has not seen the telegrams and has no means of procuring a copy. Therefore, he asked that a writ of habeas corpus be issued so he can be discharged from the unlawful imprisonment. 
Judge Simpson (?) allowed the writ on 23 March 1898. On 25 March 1898 Judge Slabaugh dismissed the cause and sustained the motion of the writ, ordering that Douglas be released.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 5, 1896 Oscar Miller was arrested and charged with the crime of assault with the intent to commit murder. His original case was before Justice of the Peace Charles Weatherbee, the county judge for the town of Franklin. Miller and his attorney argue that his charge of assault with the intent to commit murder was dismissed and that Weatherbee instead changed the charge to assault and battery. Mill agreed to plea guilty to the charge of assault and battery, and after his plea, Justice Charles Weatherbee bound him in prison and set his bond at $1,000. However, Miller and his attorney now argue that no complaint of assault and battery existed against Miller and Weatherbee charged him of the crime “on his own notion” after dismissing his original charge. As such Miller and his attorney contend that Weatherbee was illegally holding Miller and restricting him of his liberty. Judge T.J. allowed the writ to stand and agreed to hear the petitioner’s case, however, the fate of Oscar Miller is not stated in the court documents.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 21, 1886, Emilius Hanson filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he claimed that he was being illegally detained by the Portland Chief of Police Sammuel Parrish. Parrish arrested Hanson because he believed that Hanson was violating Portland City Ordinance 4817. The ordinance required licenses for traveling merchants who were selling goods in Portland. On June 26, 1886, Judge Deady ruled that the detention was lawful and denied the petition. Included in the case file is Judge Deady’s full legal opinion.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 14, 1918, J. B. Murray made a complaint in the Omaha Police Court against Frank Diblasco. Diblasco was charged with the possession of intoxicating liquor, his second offense, found guilty, and sentenced to 90 days in jail. On November 1, 1918, Diblasco filed for habeas, arguing that such a charge was not under Nebraska law, that a police judge could not charge second offense, that his first conviction was not complete, and that the judge also had not authority to issue a sentence of 90 days. A writ was issued and later sustained on November 8, 1918, and Diblasco was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry Carlton was arrested by N. Soderberg, the Justice of the Peace for Seattle, in April 1888 and was convicted of the crime of vagrancy by gambling. Carlton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that the commitment from N. Soderberg did not show Carlton had been convicted, that the court who issued the commitment did not have jurisdiction over the issue, and that it was not a commitment at all. R. A. Jones, a District Judge, ordered that the defendant should remain in custody on April 28, 1888, and Carlton returned to the custody of William Cochrane, the sheriff of King County, Washington Territory.

Summary of Proceedings: George W. Vail filed a writ of habeas in forma pauperis against Sheriff Van De Vanter claiming that he was falsely charged with assault and battery in a “pretended trail” under Judge C. G. Austin. He argued that not only were the charges false, but no real evidence was provided, except that which proved him innocent, but despite this C. G. Auston refused to rule him either guilty or innocent, but simply held him under a bail of $250, a sum he was incapable of paying. Sheriff Van De Vanter responded to the writ by claiming and providing supporting documents that Vail was found guilty of assault and battery in a valid court of law by C. G. Austin, who legally bound him to answer for the charge. As a result, Vail remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Marseleno Cardosa was born on June 28, 1918, to parents Rosalio Cardosa and Maria Cardosa. He is referred to by multiple different names throughout the case, but Marceleno Cardosa is the most common one. His parents lived in Oreapolis, Cass County, Nebraska, and worked for the Burlington Railroad construction crew there. Unfortunately, shortly after their son's birth, on November 10, 1918, the couple died of influenza—likely the Spanish flu epidemic. Shortly after, Omaha woman Gerarda de Sauseda took up guardianship of the child, as she had no children of her own. It is unknown how she was linked to the Cardosa family. Her husband lived in Mexico, but Gerarda had not heard from him for over a year, and she was illiterate, signing her name with a cross in court documents. She petitioned to adopt the child on December 5, 1918, and after publishing a notice of the adoption in The Omaha Nebraskan, de Sauseda formally adopted the child under judge Bryce Crawford. She claimed that while Marceleno had living relatives, they had refused to care for him, and that she would care for and educate the child just as his parents would have. She had also grown to love the child while caring for it for months. However, Apolonio and Apolonia Trugillo, Marceleno's aunt and uncle, filed a writ of habeas corpus against de Sauseda on May 13, 1919, claiming that the adoption was null and void, as Douglas County never had the jurisdiction to authorize it. They claimed that Marceleno was being unlawfully detained by someone who wasn't even related to him. Notably, they called him Marceleno Cardosa, not Marceleno Sauseda, as he was referred to in court documents after the adoption. Sauseda retorted that the Trugillos already had children and weren't capable of caring for any more. She also made the point that she intended to stay in the US and educate her son in the American system of law and order. Eventually, on May 20, 1919, the Trugillos' writ was denied and dismissed, and Marceleno was remanded to de Sauseda's custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Paul E. Nelson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff Aaron T. Van Devanter in an effort to be freed from King County Jail. Nelson claimed that when he was arrested for having sexual intercourse with his daughter, incest was not a punishable offense in King County. Van Devanter returned recounting Nelson’s legal proceedings, wherein he was found guilty by courts at the municipal, county, and state level, and concluded that he felt fully justified in Nelson’s imprisonment. The case file does not reveal the outcome or Nelson’s fate.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Maki petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid. Maki alleged that he was being held illegally at Spokane County Jail under the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. He claimed he was denied a hearing for six months and denied his right to counsel. The court’s judgement stated that it appeared Maki had been discharged for unknown reasons, and thus his writ was dismissed. Newspaper records indicate that Maki was arrested the next day for a violation of draft laws.

Summary of Proceedings: Paul Webster was sentenced to two years imprisonment at McNeil Island Penitentiary on July 10th, 1910, for the crime of smuggling goods. On March 18th, 1914, Webster filed a writ of habeas corpus, claiming he should have been released that day on good time according to the Act of Congress approved on June 21st, 1902. Judge Cushman dismissed the writ on March 31st, 1914, and ordered Webster to remain at McNeil Island Penitentiary to serve out the rest of his sentence.

Summary of Proceedings: A telegram was received by Chief of Police (Butterfield) from Vancouver, Canada's Chief of Police, which asked him to arrest Edward Crofery (and a Howard McMillan) for stealing jewelry. Chief did so. Attorney filed for petition of Habeas Corpus on the grounds that there was no illegality on file by any court in the Territory. Writ was granted. The same day, they realized the U. S. Marshall already came with a warrant from U.S. Commissioners Court saying they smuggled goods into the U.S.. Crofery was no longer in custody and couldn't be produced to the court so writ was discharged.

Summary of Proceedings: Petitioner G. D. Huie, who was a business partner of Lawrence Bock, stated that Bock was arrested without warrant or authority. Huie applied to Steven Maloney, Chief of Detectives in Omaha, for permission to see Lawrence Bock and have a bail bond fixed for his release until trial but the Chief refused to allow him to see Bock and refused to fix a bail bond. Huie submitted this petition on behalf of Bock as the Chief Detective would not allow the petitioner or their attorney to visit Bock. Petitioner asserted that Bock was not committing a crime or offense at the time of his arrest. Chief Maloney was detaining Bock under the name “Lawrence Brock” so there is no official record of the detainment of Bock. Judge James P. English ordered that the writ be allowed, returnable on 24 September 1914. Between the hours of 4 and 5 P.M. on 23 September 1914, authorities turned Lawrence Bock over to Deputy United States Marshall Hayes. The writ was served between the hours of 6 and 7 P.M on the same day.

Summary of Proceedings: Frank Moore pled guilty to rape of an eight-year-old in Alliance, NE in 1916 and was sentenced to twenty years. Because state statute set the maximum sentence for the crime at fifteen years, Marguerite Moore petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Frank was remanded to the custody of his jailer.

Summary of Proceedings: Frank Timmons, the petitioner, was detained for violation of a statute regulating Barbery in Washington after practicing the profession for the past 17 years in the area for not having a license or certificate from the Board of State Barber Examiners. Timmons stated that he applied three times to practice his trade, each time paying the $5.00 fee to apply, and each time the Board did not grant it and threatened him with prosecution and imprisonment. In his petition, Timmons stated that the Board exercised arbitrary power and violated the 14th Amendment of the Consitution of the United States through its actions. Judge Cushman ruled that the State Barber's Law is indeed contrary to the constitution of the United States and that Timmons should be discharged from custody and his bond discharged as well.

Summary of Proceedings: Hermann Reiter alleged that his wife, Johanna Reiter, had left him and taken their four children, Johnnie, Hermann, Rosa, and Lilly. They ranged from 2 1/2 to 12 years old. He said that Johanna could not care for them, and was a woman of "vicious and vulgar habits." Both accused the other of infidelity. He asked the children be returned to his custody. When Johanna presented her case the judge could see no issue with the state or cleanliness of the children and reported they chose to stay with their mother initially. In the courtroom, Johanna threatened to kill Hermann's new lover, Lena Peters, if she and Hermann got custody of their children. The case outcome was that Hermann regained custody of the four children after the final day of trial. However, Johanna tried to take the children with her after leaving the courtroom. She said in her defense: "Judge, you may send me to jail if you want to, but I must have my children. I love them and cannot be separated from them."

Summary of Proceedings: Rose Baker was forcibly arrested when she was asleep in her room by a police officer without a warrant on June 3rd, 1912. The petition said no complaint had been filed in any court nor any warrants. The next day, Rose was taken before a judge and they filed a complaint charging her with being willfully idle, which constituted a misdemeanor under city ordinances. Baker entered a plea of guilty and asked the court to pronounce judgement, which they did not do. The petition alleged that she was being kept without due process of law. An affidavit in forma pauperis was also filed for Rose Baker. Sullivan and his lawyers claimed the petition did not state sufficient facts to warrant habeas, and that the District Court did not have jurisdiction. The fate of the writ and Rose Baker is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: John Van Ormer, father and next friend of Rose Van Ormer, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against his presumed wife or ex-wife Christina Van Ormer. Christina had divorced him on the allegations that he was an abusive alcoholic who failed to support his family. She had left with Rose for Colorado in 1889. She stayed there for about some time before returning to Omaha to live with her son from a previous marriage, Phillip Summerlad. In November 1889, John was convicted of assaulting Phillip, perhaps to regain control of Rose. He had also tried to kidnap Rose once before. The struggle became physical again on February 3, 1890, with Christina and John literally fighting over the child in the streets, pulling her between them. This was after John had tried to kidnap her, but Christina managed to regain the child. Rose clearly preferred Christina, and even claimed that her surname was Summerlad, not Van Ormer. Roughly two months later, the cause was dismissed by petitioner. According to an 1890 Lincoln Journal Star article, the custody of Rose was given to her mother in the divorce proceedings.

Around May 18th or 19th, Fred and Anna experienced domestic difficulties, leading to Anna making an oral complaint. On May 19th, the Commissioners of Insanity caused a finding to be made without any hearing or trial and Fred Busch was arrested and confined in the Douglas County Jail. On June 5, 1924, the writ of habeas corpus and return was filed. The outcome of the case and the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Izora I., petitioner, and Frank H. Goldsborough, respondent, married in 1888 and had their son, Claude H. Goldsborough, the bound party, in March 1889. In September of 1889, Frank agreed that if he were to mistreat either Izora or Claude in any way, he would give up all claims to Claude and give Izora all right to take him, with the process of law. Due to Frank's cruel treatment of both Izora and Claude, they left Frank, returned in May of 1889, and left again for Izora's mother's house in Albright, Nebraska in June of 1890 due to Izora's fear that her and Claude's lives were in danger. Afterward, Izora left for her parent's home with Claude, and on the 22nd day of August 22nd of 1890, while Claude was playing in the yard of Izora's home, Frank came on horseback and seized him. He carried the child to Springfield, Nebraska, from Omaha. During this time, Claude was only dressed in underclothing, a treatment that Izora alleges was inhumane. Additionally, Izora alleges that Frank had no clothing for the infant with him and had no inclination or ability to clothe him. Then, Frank left the child with his parents, Henry and Sophranne Goldsborough, who supported the child, while Frank returned to Omaha. On the 28th of August 1890, Izora filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Claude. Judge Joseph Clarkson allowed the writ of habeas corpus and ordered it to be returnable to Frank, Henry, and Sophranne. During the trial, Frank threatened to kill Izora if she received custody of Claude. Judge Clarkson also ruled that Izora should have full custody of Claude, and Frank must be allowed to visit Claude at the home of Mrs. I. J. Lucas each Sunday afternoon in the presence of an adult. Judge George N. Doane, who hears the case in his courtroom as well, came to the same conclusion as Judge Clarkson.

Summary of Proceedings: Matt Puryear, a black man and miner, was arrested for interfering with an officer, assault and battery, and carrying concealed weapons. Puryear was tried and given sixty days in jail by Judge C.S. Cousins. Allen Garner, Puryear’s attorney and a prominent Black community leader, petitioned on behalf of his client pleading that Puryear was being held illegally as no formal charge had been made against him and that Puryear’s judgment was “excessive of the jurisdiction of Justices of the Peace in the State of Washington.” His petition for a writ of habeas corpus was granted but it seems Puryear would eventually have to pay off his $60 to be freed.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles Broadwick was arrested by Robert T. Hodge and placed in the King County Jail. Broadwick contended in his petition for writ of habeas corpus that his arrest was illegal and that there was no warrant for his arrest. In his reply to the writ, the Sheriff, Robert T. Hodge, stated that he arrested Broadwick based on a warrant issued by John B. Gordon. The warrant was dated the day after Broadwick’s petition for habeas corpus and alleged that Broadwick was a fugitive from justice and wanted in the State of California. The case file does not include the conclusion to the petition or the outcome of the case.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 12, 1920, Daisy Hartman was arrested in Omaha and charged with being an inmate of a common ill-governed house. Hartman was found guilty and sentenced to pay a fine of $25.00 and costs. Hartman subsequently provided $200.00 for an appeal bond which was approved by Charles E. Foster, the police magistrate, who then signed an order issuing Hartman's release from prison but mandated that she be held at the Detention Hospital of the city of Omaha if found to be infected with a venereal disease upon examination. On September 13 Hartman was taken to the Detention Hospital and subjected to physical examinations she did not consent to. Hartman and her attorney's filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus, arguing that her confinement in the Detention Hospital and the forced examinations constituted a violation of her rights under Article 5 of the Amendments to the Constitution of the United States. Hartman was released on bond, but her fate and the outcome of the trial are unknown.

Peterson was discharged on January 31.

Summary of Proceedings: C. R. Anderson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of Clara Morris against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham. Anderson alleged that Morris was being illegally held in the Seattle City Jail with no charge or bail fixed against her. Beckingham replied that he had charged Morris with being a disorderly person and fixed her bail, but that she was no longer in his custody at the Seattle City Jail. The writ was dismissed. Newspaper records indicate it is possible that Morris’s arrest was related to vice raids.

Summary of Proceedings: Tassos Tourtas was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Tourtas was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Tourtas and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Tourtas argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. The writ of habeas was sustained, and Tourtas was released.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 30th, 1912, C.W. Skutt, a 63 year old resident of King County, Washington, petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus. Skutt alleged that he was being held illegally by the Sheriff of King County in the County Jail. Hodge and Skutt agreed that he was being held due to an incident on September 22nd, but they disagreed on the details. Skutt alleged that a “Simpson”, with his wife, attacked himself and his minor grandson for no reason, and in self-defense, Skutt pulled out his pocket knife. At this point, Skutt alleged, his attacker struck Skutt’s hand, which caused him to inflict a stab wound on the attacker. John F. Murphy, the prosecuting attorney, instead argued that Skutt stabbed T.J. Stinson, with the intent to kill, and was thus charged with 1st Degree Assault. Hodge also provided an arrest warrant from the county clerk that verified that Skutt was being held in the county jail legally. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Petitioner, George Compton, was arrested on 21 April 1898 on a vagrancy charge. On that same day, he was assigned to the county jail for 30 days. He was not granted a trial at this point. 
Police Judge Gordon issued a mittimus, stating that this 30 day sentence had been imposed at an earlier date but was suspended based on the condition that Compton leave the city and not return. The initial sentence had been imposed on 6 December 1897. The Police Judge asserts that he failed to comply with these terms; leading to his arrest in Omaha on the charge of vagrancy, and was placed in the County Jail to complete his initial sentence. On 21 April 1898, a writ for the offense of vagrancy was submitted by Police Judge Gordon and signed by Sheriff McDonald and Deputy Sheriff Lewis detailing these claims. 
The District Court (Judge Slabaugh) heard the case on 6 May 1898. During this trial, Judge Slabaugh determined that no offense had been committed, that Compton was unlawfully being deprived of his liberty, and that Sheriff McDonald should release him from custody. On 7 May 1898, Judge Slabaugh signed an Order to Discharge the Prisoner on Writ of Habeas Corpus. 
On 17 May 1898, a document was submitted by the Albyn L. Frank (District Court Clerk) motioning for Douglas County to pay the costs of the trial.

Summary of Proceedings: John W. Brennan, the petitioner, was detained in California for the forgery of a post office money order. He was then imprisoned at McNeil's Island after a guilty plea to the indictment charging him. Brennan petitions on the basis that the guilty plea he entered was for an indictment that stated no offense against the government, with the contention that no copies of the orders allegedly forged are set out in the indictment or a reason for his action. Judge Cushman judged that the court had jurisdiction over him and stated that after a judgment of conviction, a prisoner cannot be released by Habeas because the indictment does not constitute a crime within the meaning of the statute.

Summary of Proceedings: James Nesladek and Anna Nesladek petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against A. H. Vosberg (Chief of the Juvenile Department), Michael L. Clark (Sheriff) and Sherman Clayton (Chief Deputy Sheriff and Jailer) for detaining their 17-year-old son, William Nesladek, who was suspected of stealing a car and kidnapping a 16-year old girl with the help of four others. The Nesladeks claimed that they first learned that William was accused of a crime when they were served summons to appear before the Juvenile Court, which meant that Nesladek did not have counsel when he was tried in a trial without a jury. Therefore, they argued that he was convicted and sentenced to the state reformatory without due process of law. Judge Charles Goss commanded that Vosberg, Clark, and Clayton bring the body of Nesladek before the court, and Nesladek was released on recognizance of $1,000 with his parents are sureties while the trial was under advisement. The petition was granted and Nesladek was released from custody of the sheriff upon his sentencing to Kearney, but he was remanded to the custody of the juvenile court. It is unknown what Nesladek's ultimate fate was.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 13th, 1919, Thomas Sullivan was taken into police custody on suspicion of having committed "some crime". Two days later, he was charged with statutory rape. Sullivan filed a writ of habeas corpus on September 18th, 1919, claiming he was being unlawfully held in Douglas County Jail and was being falsely accused. After witness statements in court from the two victims, Bertha Anderson and Elvira Turnquist, the writ was denied on September 24th, and Sullivan remained in police custody. Sullivan then filed for a new trial three days later, however, the fate of this new trial is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 6, 1922, around 4 PM, Peter Nelson was taken into custody by the Omaha police, without knowing why. His attorney, B.W. Gill, could find no warrant for his arrest, although the police claimed that they were detaining him for further investigation. On July 9, his attorney filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus demanding that chief of police Michael J. Dempsey, police commissioner Henry W. Dunn, and captain of detectives Charles Van Deusen produce Nelson in front of judge Carroll O. Stauffer. The writ was served to Dempsey, but not Dunn or Van Deusen. On that same day, a hearing was held, and Gill's petition was denied, with Nelson responsible for court costs. Whether Nelson ultimately remained in prison is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 9, 1888, M. Cross filed a complaint against S. M. McFarland. He filed the complaint with Justice of the Peace W. H. Kuhn for leaving the county with property that he had filed a chattel mortgage on, which Cross had financed on May 15, 1886. The property in question included two 7-year-old mules, a harness, and a wagon. Kuhn ordered county sheriff N. R. Marquiss to put McFarland in the county jail, as he did not pay a $300 bail. This was apparently the second time McFarland had been arrested for breaking his agreement with Cross. On the same day, McFarland filed for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that violating his mortgage wasn't a crime. At a hearing on May 10, 1888, Judge William G. Langford agreed and ordered McFarland to be released.

Summary of Proceedings: H.W. Hull was previously tried and convicted for "keeping a house of ill repute." The judge set a fine of $300 or an unspecified amount of jail time at the King County Jail. When he did not pay the fine, Hull was placed in the custody of the King County Sherriff at the King County Jail. Hull filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he should be entitled to bail and was being illegally kept without a set bail. Judge Greene granted the writ and set a bail amount of $500 to go into effect on July 1, 1884, the first day of the Supreme Court of Washington Territory's new session. In Olympia, WA, he could be let out of jail before the territorial Supreme Court with a payment of $500. Hull's fate following the April 25, 1884 ruling is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 25, 1874, John A. Carr, the Deputy Collector of Customs of Alaska Territory, was arrested by J.A. Campbell, The Commander of the District of Alaska, for introducing alcohol into Indian Territory. On November 12, 1874, Carr filed for a writ of habeas corpus charging that his detention was illegal because the charges were unclear and Campbell did not have the authority to issue an arrest warrant. On January 7, 1875, Judge Matthew Deady agreed with Carr and approved his writ and ordered Carr to be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 9th, 1893, Ah Wing petitioned for the writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Yue Fong, Jun Back Wo, Moy Mine Tie, and Wong Won, who were imprisoned on the steamship Danube by the captain William Myers. According to Ah Wing, he believes they are restrained due to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which banned Chinese laborers from entering the U.S. Yue Fong, Jun Back Wo, Moy Mine Tie, and Wong Won all left for China within the past two years with the intent of coming back to their merchant business, which was left in the charge of their partners during their absence. After looking at the evidence and cross-examining the bound parties and witnesses, the writ was granted to all four on the 24th of August.

Summary of Proceedings: Miles W. Newby, the County Attorney for Monona Iowa accused Harry Davis, Morris Meyer, and George Meyer of robbing Moon Clothing Company in Onawa, Iowa. He had three witness statements corroborating that the three men stored clothes in the basement of their friend Kellerman's house and tried to sell clothes to Moe Sundheiner with the tags still on them. The Governor of the state of Iowa filed a warrant that the Governor of Nebraska approved. Harry Davis filed a petition for habeas corpus on September 13th, claiming that he hasn't left Omaha Nebraska in 20 years and there is no justification for the warrant or his arrest. The petition was approved and an order of return was received. There is no more information about the hearing or case outcome.

Summary of Proceedings: Tsunetaro Machida was arrested and set for deportation to Japan for having become a public charge, and having been likely to become a public charge at the time he entered the United States. He petitioned for habeas corpus. In the petition, Machida denied the charge, and described himself as a hard-working and frugal person. Machida added that he was given improper counsel, who lead to plead guilty. The writ was dismissed, and Machida appealed to the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The cause was dismissed in a letter from the Chief Justice of the United States, William Howard Taft. Machida was returned to the custody of the U. S. Commissioner of Immigration, Harry White.

Summary of Proceedings:
Antonio Bisegna entered the U.S. on February 14th, 1908, from Italy, and stayed until April 1910 when he departed to British Columbia. Bisegna returned to the U.S. on October 22nd, 1913, via the SS Princess Victoria. Bisegna was then held by the Commissioner of Immigration on the grounds he was a "member of the excluded classes" and a person likely to become a public charge under suspicion of committing a crime involving moral turpitude. Bisegna petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus stating he had not been convicted of said crime. The petitioner believed the immigration officials based their charge in the commission of an assault in the third degree by Bisegna after entry into the U.S. Bisegna stated that assault in the third degree was a misdemeanor not involving moral turpitude and he entered the U.S. more than three years prior to the issuance of the arrest warrant. The petition further stated that Bisegna was not given a fair trial and inspectors were biased and prejudiced as they "attempted to do indirectly what they could not to directly." 
Judge Neterer authorized the writ. In a motion for discharge, the petitioner and his attorneys stated the Secretary of Labor and examining inspector exceeded their authority and the alleged reasons for detaining the petitioner are insufficient causes that did not exist prior to the landing of the petitioner and are not supported by the evidence. The motion further stated that deportation is illegal as it provided for the return of the petitioner to Italy instead of the country whence, he came, most likely British Columbia, Canada. Judge Jeremiah Neterer ruled the writ to be dismissed and the defendant remanded to the commissioner of Immigration. Weeks later on March 28th, 1914, upon an oral motion by the U.S. attorney, the government withdrew the Bureau of Immigration transcript as part of the government's return to the writ in the matter.

Summary of Proceedings:
On September 2, 1902, Lee Fong petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Fong, a Chinese immigrant, was denied his request to build a laundry and was jailed for violating Seattle Ordinance No. 710, which outlined the city's safety and licensing requirements for laundries. 
Fong, through his lawyer, claimed that the city ordinance was invalid and arbitrary and that his detainment violated the 14th and 5th Amendments.
In addition, Fong's petition claimed intentional racial discrimination by the Seattle City Council and fire department. 
According to Fong's petition, he sought initial approval for his laundry through his lessor, the building's owner, John Miller. Despite a minor safety concern expressed by the fire inspector, the city health and plumbing inspector approved the laundry, as did the city council. Fong claimed he then spent over $600 to renovate the building. Soon after, members of the public petitioned the government to rescind its approval of "the Chinese laundry." City Council did so on July 21 1902.
J.M. Weistling, in his role as Fong's lawyer, pointed to various court decisions related to similar city licensing and regulation and demonstrated that courts had found that, specifically in the case of ordinances like Seattle's regarding laundries, had been found unconstitutional, as they provided the cities "arbitrary powers" that allowed for unequal treatment under the laws. In addition, Weistling claimed that the Council's decision was based solely on Fong's racial identity: "real objection to the granting of council’s consent for the maintenance of said laundry was the ascertainment of the fact that it was to be conducted by a Chinaman.”
In their response, the Respondent's attorney sought to claim that the cited cases Weistling claimed demonstrated Fong's claims were incorrect as clauses 2 and 3 of the ordinance made clause 6 not an arbitrary power. 
On September 25, 1902 the judge ruled for Fong's writ. There is no documentation of his release, though he may have been released on bail earlier. It is not known whether the Council allowed Fong to run his laundry.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1827, John Singleton, a man of color, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. His counsel, Isaac C. McGirk, also petitioned the court for permission to institute the suit as a poor person. Singleton alleges that he was born in Illinois to an enslaved mother who was emancipated by his enslaver before his birth thusly guaranteeing him as a free man, and then kidnapped by J. Lamkins and trafficked to the south as a slave where he was further enslaved by Zachariah Neal, Henry Byron, and finally Robert Lewis, the respondent. During his enslavement by Lewis, Singleton made his way north to St. Louis for an errand, using the opportunity to seek freedom. Alexander Scott, the other respondent, caught and bound Singleton attempting to secure freedom. The outcome of this petition and the fate of Singleton are unknown based on the case file. Information on this case from the Digital Library of American Slavery indicates the petition was granted and a plea of trespass was filed.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1907, Hyman Stein, a salesman for the Rockford, Illinois-based firm, Chandler Brothers, secured an order for some "lace curtains and rugs" in Schuyler, Nebraska. He was charged in the local police court with peddling without a license, a municipal violation, and fined $25. When he refused to pay, he was charged with contempt of court and placed in the Colfax County jail. Stein petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, he was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 5, 1903, Ada Wilson filed a writ of habeas corpus against sheriff Edward Cudihee. She was arrested for larceny and had been held in King County jail since January 5, 1903. The petition argued that because thirty days had passed since her arrest and no indictment had been found nor had anything been filed against Wilson, her detainment was unsound and thus she should be released. The case files do not state what happens after the judge approves the petition to hear the writ, but newspaper coverage of the case says the writ was denied.
