Summary of Proceedings: In November 1918, Martin de Wal petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Herny M. White, U.S. Commissioner of Labor. Martin was a subject of the Kingdom of Holland and was arrested by an Immigration Inspector charging de Wal with being an alien and having advocated or taught the unlawful destruction of property. At the initial hearing, de Wal stated he had never sold any book on sabotage and that he was against German militarism. The petition stated de Wal demanded a copy of said evidence against him in order to attach it to the petition but was refused by respondent Henry M. White. Judge Neterer denied the writ stating de Wal's case was similar to that of Samuel H. Dixon and Charles Bernat, whose writs were also denied.

Summary of Proceedings: Gin Kato was arrested by Inspector William G. Strench for working as a cook in a prostitution house for seven months in Ketchikan, Alaska, upon a warrant issued by the Department of Labor. Kato was a Japanese immigrant who had left Japan around 35 years previously, who legally arrived at San Francisco on 1884. Kato had a wife in Japan. Gin Kato was charged with a bond of $500 that became $1,000 which, if not paid, resulted in deportation. Gin Kato petitioned claiming that said deportation was a violation of his rights as as a lawful immigrant and resident of the United States. He also later plead a five-year limitation on his deportation and claimed that he was unaware working for a prostitution house was illegal. His writ was denied and a deportation order was issued.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 21, 1905, James Plymate and his attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, and alleged that Thomas R. Delaney, Chief of Police was holding him without charge or due process of law. D. F. Willard, acting chief of police in Delaney’s absence, responded and stated that his officers had been instructed to arrest a man, Thompson, on the charge of assault with a deadly weapon or intent to commit robbery, for the stabbing of Charles Gray. Plymate was also on the scene, and was arrested as well. After being taken to the hospital, Gray stated that Plymate was the one who stabbed him, rather than Thompson. Willard says they were holding Plymate until Gray was well enough to file an official complaint against Plymate. Willard also stated that Plymate had told everyone his name was James Wendt, and admitted guilt to several officers. Plymate claimed that his actions were in self defense after being attacked himself. The outcome of this case and Plymate’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 24th, 1921, Robert Swinney petitioned for and received an order allowing a writ of habeas corpus having been held in unlawful detainment under Marshal Eberstein and Charles Van Duesen following a request from George Robb. All of whom held Swinney by virtue of a warrant from the governor of Nebraska to have Swinney transported to Iowa to be charged with wife desertion. In his petition, Swinney presented that the issued warrant was void as he had been residing in Nebraska since 1919 and had been a citizen for two years. It was argued that there was a failure and want for evidence that would establish the connection of Swinney to the alleged crime. Later that same month the court ordered the writ be granted and Swinney was discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Gladys Frederika Fuson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus by her next friend, Lona McMasters, which was granted. Gladys testified that she had been institutionalized as a dependent minor and the superintendent approved her underage marriage to Harold Fuson against her consent. Gladys claimed she left Fuson at the age of seventeen because she did not want to marry him and then she was arrested in Port Townsend (Jefferson County, Washington) and charged with delinquency for deserting her husband. She was then transported to the King County Juvenile Detention Home in Seattle. Gladys claimed her husband Harold Fuson was seeking a divorce and had orchestrated her detention as retribution for her leaving his household and in order to prevent her from defending herself in the divorce suit. The respondents countered, citing jurisdictional and procedural reasons why the writ of habeas corpus should not lie. After hearing the evidence, Gladys was remanded back into the custody of the superintendent of the King County Juvenile Detention Home.

Summary of Proceedings:
Warren and Mary Cowing divorced in 1903. During their divorce, Mary allegedly relinquished her parental rights to their son, Warren B. Cowing Junior The following year, Warren Senior gave Mary an opportunity to see her son out of “sympathy and respect for her feelings.” Following this opportunity, Mary refused to return Warren Junior to Warren Senior. In his petition, Warren Senior stated that Mary was a “drunkard” and “a woman of loose morals.” Judge Tallman granted Warren Senior a writ of habeas corpus on November 13, 1904. 

In a newspaper article about the case, Mary denied Warren Senior's claims. She proceeded to say, “I will never give the boy up, and if he gets him back, he will have to take him over my dead body.” Newspaper coverage of the case reported that Walter Junior and Mary were located in California a week later. 

Junior and Senior are not used in the case language, but used for clarity here.

Summary of Proceedings:
Marie Robina, a native of the Republic of France, came to the United States in December 1902, via the Steamship La Champagne. Robina married William Grayson on April 1st, 1912, and became a naturalized U.S. citizen. She cohabited with Grayson for seven months. After leaving him she intermittently pursued the vocation of prostitution. Robina was arrested in January 1914 by an immigrant inspector who possessed a warrant charging her with being an alien to the U.S. and a prostitute. A warrant of deportation was issued. 
Robina petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. In the petition, she alleged that during her hearing before immigration inspectors, it appeared conclusively that the petitioner had been a resident and citizen of the United States upon her marriage. The petition further alleged she was denied the right to cross examine witnesses and meet them face to face. In a brief on behalf of the petitioner, her attorneys argued that the Act of February 20, 1907 provides for the deportation of aliens connected with prostitution, yet as Robina was a naturalized U.S. citizen prior to her arrest, the statute is not applicable. Her attorneys further argued that the rights of American citizens should not be infringed upon by an executive committee. The Commissioner of Immigration alleged that the petitioner had a prior arrest in March 1912, and married Grayson less than a month later to prevent being deported. 
Judge Jeremiah Neterer stated that there was no evidence that the petitioner was a prostitute upon entering the United States and stated that citizenship is a valuable right and when acquired it cannot be taken away without due process of law. Neterer ruled that the department was without jurisdiction to order deportation until citizenship was revoked and ruled Robina be discharged. Commissioner of Immigration, Henry White, appealed to the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, and upon a motion by the appellant's counsel the appeal was dismissed. Upon oral motion by the U. S. attorney, the exhibits and files of the bureau of immigration were permanently withdrawn from the file.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 22nd, 1921, Minnie Preis petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her 18 month child Lucile Preis. She had left the child with Martha Johnson after her husband died. Minnie claimed that Martha Johnson and Rilda Goff were withholding Lucile from her without just cause. The judge granted the petition. On the same day, Sheriff Michael Clark served the writ to Rilda Goff and Martha Johnson, as well as presented Lucile to the court. Writ was allowed and Minnie was awarded custody of Lucile. Soon after, Minnie married a man named Myron Evans in Omaha.

Summary of Proceedings: Lee Gar and Lee Dow Seng were returning to Portland, Oregon, from a visit to China on the Steamship Danube. However, when they arrived, William Meyer, the Master of the Steamship, refused to allow them off the ship as he believed they were laborers and thus violating the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. Charley Tong petitioned for habeas corpus on their behalf, and a large number of witnesses testified that the two were indeed genuine merchants. Thus, their writ was granted, and both individuals were released from custody. The case file includes several written witness statements and a list of individuals who knew the defendants for a significant time in the United States.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 28th, 1919, Sol Margultz filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus by his attorneys in the District Court in Douglas County of Nebraska, saying that he was unlawfully detained and deprived of liberty. Margultz maintained that he was being held in the custody of D. Berenberg in Douglas County, Nebraska on a criminal offense allegedly committed in April of 1917 in St. Joseph, Missouri and a warrant for arrest issued in July 1917 based on the charge of grand larceny. Being confined in Douglas County was pursuant to a writ of extradition that was granted by the acting Governor of Nebraska at the time. However it was stated in Margultz’s petition that for the previous 29 years he did reside in Douglas County and that his home address shared with a wife and children had been printed in the Directory of the Nebraska Telephone Company for the previous 2 years. The writ of extradition was then held void and of no force as the application presented did not comply with practices of the Interstate Extradition Conference of 1887. The original warrant that was filed by a justice of the peace in Missouri had been tampered with and thus Margultz was filing for a writ of Habeas Corpus from the mentioned unlawful imprisonment. It is unknown how the judge ruled on Margultz' petition and his ultimate fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 31, 1887, William Tinkham filed a complaint to the Justice of the Peace, John Mason. In this complaint, he alleged that, on August 28, David Kimble and A. B. Corriell used a weapon to threaten to harm and kill William and Annie Tinkham. Mason ordered the sheriff to apprehend Kimble and Corriell and bring them before the court. On September 1, the sheriff apprehended Kimble and Corriell. On the same day, Mason subpoenaed the witnesses. The next day, the defendants pled not guilty and motioned to dismiss the trial, which was granted. Mason then ordered that William Tinkham be committed to the King County Jail, as they believed his original complaint to be false and unfounded. Tinkham was to be held until he paid $40.25 in court costs. William appealed this decision and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. On September 14, Judge and Chief Justice R. A. Jones ruled that Mason had “no jurisdiction or legal authority” to commit William and ordered that William be released from custody. Upon hearing the evidence, an order granting the writ was issued and the Tinkham was released on bail.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 4th, 1886, G. W. Caufield committed Charles Barnes to the jail of King County, Washington Territory for 35 days or until Barnes paid a total of $104.55 in fines for his involvement in the breaking and entering of the house of Charles Forger and the shooting of Eugene Cote by John Barnes on January 3, 1886 in a dispute over a child. On January 6, 1886, Barnes and his lawyers filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus to Judge Roger S. Greene in King County claiming that Barnes had not received due process under the law and was being held without a trial or the court filing any charges against him. Greene granted the petition and the writ of Habeas Corpus was filed, however, the case files following the writ are missing. A newspaper article covering the case on January 7, 1886, states that Barnes was released from custody on the evening of the 6th and would be required to come before a jury regarding his January 4th charges. The fate of Charles following his release is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Moses Phillips complained to the court that John Herring was a public nuisance after allegedly allowing his hogs to roam the streets. On April 27, John was found guilty and detained. On April 28, he motioned for a retrial on these grounds: new evidence, admission of illegal evidence, and the court's refusal to provide counsel. He also argued that his detention was illegal because no verdict was recorded, he was not called upon for sentencing, and there was no judgment ordering for his detention. On May 4, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. His writ was allowed and he was discharged from custody after paying his bond on May 6.

He petitioned for habeas and claimed to be the son of Ng Kum, born in Boston, Masschusetts. In the peitition, he also alleged that he was not given a fair trial, was denied right of counsel, and false evidence was used against him at his hearing. Summary of Proceedings:
On 29 December, 1896, it was alleged that bound party, Antoine Michel, assaulted Indian John Whil-Ochen with a deadly weapon leading to death. On 12 January, 1898, a writ for habeas corpus was filed alleging that Deputy Marshall Felix Pugh charged Michel with a killing that did not occur within the modern confines of the Colville Indian Reservation, but instead in the County of Stevens and of the State of Washington. 
Upon return, Ide admitted that he did not know the specific facts of the case but believed that the action did occur on the Colville Indian Reservation. 
On 31 January, 1898, Judge Hanford found that the land upon which the alleged incident occurred had been relinquished by an act of Congress on July 1, 1892, and ordered that the body of the bound party be transferred to the Sheriff of Stevens County, Washington, if the sheriff so wished to pursue charges. Hanford's ruling stipulated that Ide was to release Michel if the sheriff did not take action within five days, so it is not certain whether or not Michel remained in custody following this case.

Summary of Proceedings: On  October 27th, Myrtle and John Benson filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of their 17 year old daughter, Georgia Benson. In the petition they claimed that Georgia was being unlawfully detained by Clara Pallesen. Myrtle asserted that Georgia had always resided with the family, and that their home had always been comfortable, decent, and respectable, and that the same would be true when Georgia returned home. Georgia had been with Clara since April 1921. Myrtle requested that Clara be presented in court and that custody and control of Georgia be returned to herself and her husband. The judge granted the petition, and the writ was served and Georgia was collected for court. Clara responded to the writ on October 29th, asserting that Georgia was not detained unlawfully or against her will, rather that Georgia had asked to stay with her and was residing with her of her own free will. On the 29th the judge allowed the writ, in so far as any rights that may be claimed by virtue of the alleged guardianship. No documents regarding guardianship are within the case file. The fate of Georgia Benson is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In 1891, Albert Friedrich was found guilty by the Superior Court of Washington for murder in the first degree and sentenced to death. Upon appeal, the Supreme Court of Washington reversed the judgment and remanded the case back to the Superior Court with a mandate to sentence Friedrich to murder in the second degree and sentence him to 20 years of hard labor at the state penitentiary. 
Friedrich's petition alleges that the judgment is a violation of due process as he was not legally convicted in a court or before a jury for the sentence, and that the higher court decision to commute the sentence should not guide the lower court in rendering their final judgment. 
In his ruling, Judge Hanford conceded that Friedrich's imprisonment was a violation of due process, yet found Friedrich was nonetheless guilty of intentional murder and therefore not entitled to be set at liberty. In addition, Hanford stated "his imprisonment under the sentence passed upon him, is no more lawful than his discharge would be." Friedrich's writ was denied, and he likely served his sentence of 20 years hard labor at the state penitentiary.

Summary of Proceedings: Rudolph Tschahle was arrested by an immigration officer on January 25th, 1918. Tschale, originally from Russia, was a self proclaimed socialist and rug factory worker. He was arrested for being likely to become a public charge and advocating for the unlawful destruction of property. He filed a petition for habeas corpus on December 23rd,1918, claiming no warrant or official complaint was made against him. After a hearing his writ was granted, and he was released on January 4th, 1919.

Summary of Proceedings: In December 1917, several dozen people were accused of having conspired to violate the Espionage Act earlier that year and jailed to await a grand jury hearing the following April. Bail was set at $5,000. In August 1918, nine individuals petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that they were still being detained despite never having been indicted. The respondents countered that the April 1918 term of the court was still ongoing and therefore the confinement was legal, adding that none of them had posted bail. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and the nine petitioners remanded to the custody of their jailers.

Summary of Proceedings:
In a previous case, Rudolph H. Gerber petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to have his daughter, Anael Gerber, returned to his custody. In 1915, the Superior Court of the City and County of San Francisco ruled that Rudolph Gerber had custody of Anael, however, shortly before that ruling Rudolph's ex-wife, Dorothy Alden Gerber, took Anael and moved to Seattle, Washington. The previous petition concluded with Judge King Dykeman refusing to give Rudolph Gerber custody of the child and making Anael a ward of the state. Anael was then placed under the care of Sister Superior Mary Leontine at the Holy Names Academy and Normal School and ordered that Rudolph Gerber pay $25 to the Academy for keeping the child. 

On June 7, 1917, Rudolph filed another writ of habeas corpus to try have the custody of his child returned to him from the Holy Names Academy and Normal School. Rudolph's ex-wife, now going by Dorothy Alden de Bit, involved herself in this case as an intervenor attempting to keep the child in the custody of the Holy Names Academy. While the Sister Superior of the Holy Names Academy is written as the respondent of the case, the majority of the documents in this case file are from Rudolph Gerber and Dorothy Alden de Bit and their attorneys. Dorothy and her attorney argued that Rudolph was not qualified to raise a child and contended that the Holy Names Academy was the best place to raise Anael. Rudolph argued that Dorothy and her new husband were too immoral to raise Anael. Rudolph accused Dorothy and Ralph of cohabitation and adultery before their marriage and being involved in lewd and lascivious acts while being a part of a "Christian Yogi" movement. 

In this new habeas corpus petition, Rudolph argued the order to make Anael a ward of the state was illegal because it ignored a previous order of the Superior Court of the City and County of San Francisco which gave Rudolph custody of the child. The writ for the petition was approved by Judge Everett Smith, however, the hearing for the petition was repeated pushed back after the child's mother, Dorothy Alden de Bit, became extremely sick after the birth of another child with her new husband, Ralph de Bit. The delays of the hearing continued. At one point, Judge Kenneth Mackintosh took over the case and was to preside over the hearing, but the hearing was further delayed until December of 1917 and given to another judge, Ben Sheeks. At this hearing, Judge Sheeks approved Rudolph's petition to gain custody of his child, however, he also ruled that Rudolph cannot take Anael back to California with him for one year. He also ordered that Dorothy Alden de Bit must be given visitation rights to her daughter twice a week. 

After five months of staying in Seattle under Judge Ben Sheeks orders, Rudolph Gerber filed a motion to amend the judge's ruling. Rudolph argued that during the months since the December ruling, Anael's mother had not contacted or visited the child once. Rudolph further argued that as a licensed physician and oculist in the state of California, he could more easily make money to care for the child in that state. Dorothy Alden de Bit and her attorney immediately asked to have the motion dismissed, however, Judge Sheeks ruled that Rudolph can be allowed to return to California with Anael and removed the stipulation that he must remain in Seattle with the child for a year.

Summary of Proceedings: James Hallahan was brought into custody on 21 September 1913 on the complaint and information of E. R. Leigh who charged him with the crime of disturbing the peace. He was confined until 23 September 1913, at which point he was brought before Police Judge James Callahan and sentenced to 30 days in County Jail. This petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus argues that the imprisonment is wrongful because the Court doesn’t have jurisdiction as Hallahan is a 17 year old minor. As such, the case should be in the Juvenile Court of Douglas County. Judge Lee Estelle allowed the writ on 24 September 1913.

Summary of Proceedings:
Meyer Green, the petitioner, was prosecuted for trying to avoid business regulations by Police Judge Gordon and petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on grounds that the state statute was unconstitutional. Green's petition was evaluated and rejected by Judge Baker. Green's petition was then evaluated by the Supreme Court, which found an error with the district court decision siding with him and reversed the opinion under Chief Justice Sullivan. 

During the litigation process, likely before the decision by Judge Baker, the case was seen by Judge Estelle, who approved the writ and found Green to be unlawfully detained. It is unclear precisely when this occurred in reference to litigation.

Summary of Proceedings: Hugh G. Durham petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his daughter, Sylvia May Durham, claiming that Frank and Corey Drury illegally deprived Sylvia of her freedom. When Silvia was a baby, her mother died, and Hugh delivered her into the custody of Cory Drewery, Hugh's sister. He filed the writ of habeas corpus because he had remarried and wished to start a family. The holding party produced the body of Sylvia, but there is no record of testimony. Months later, the petitioner moved to dismiss the case, which the unnamed judge granted. This was apparently so that he could start a new action against Sylvia's foster parents. The fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In the summer of 1920, Alson Cole was awaiting execution for first-degree murder in the Nebraska State Penitentiary in Lincoln. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in federal court, alleging numerous violations of his rights by the Howard County district court. The state countered that Cole had already been denied habeas relief in federal court. The judge, however, found that the state district court had erred by sentencing Cole to death after he pled guilty to murder without having had a hearing to determine the degree of the guilt--in other words, that Cole had only pled guilty to murder, not murder in the first degree. Cole was remanded to the custody of the Howard County sheriff for re-sentencing.

Summary of Proceedings: George Bryant petitioned for habeas corpus from the Multnomah County Jail, where he was being held based on a warrant from Levie Anderson, a Justice of the Peace. The warrant was issued after William Cathcart, the Master of the Barkentine Ship W.B. Scranton, alleged that he deserted the ship in violation of a contract of service. George Bryant joined the ship in San Fransico, California, as a cook or steward going towards Portland, Oregon, and argues he did not sign any ship articles and was entitled to leave and be paid $52. The Judge M.P. Deady granted the writ, and George Bryant was released.

Summary of Proceedings:
In September 1914, Chin Quock Wah, a native of China, was denied entry to the United States, detained, and subjected to deportation. Chin Quock Wah petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus which stated three main claims: the petitioner was denied a right to appeal, denied right to counsel, and his detainment and deportation was illegal as the petitioner's father was an American citizen. The petition stated that Chin Quock Wah wished to be with his father, who was a merchant in Boston. 
Regarding the denial of appeal claim, the petition stated that the Solicitor of the Department of Labor was the one who denied the appeal, and as the solicitor was not authorized to perform the duties of the Secretary of Labor, the petitioner was denied the right to appeal. 
Regarding the citizenship of the petitioner's father, Chin Wing Hin was found to be a citizen before a U.S. Commissioner and issued a signed certificate stating so. Immigration officials denied this certificate as sufficient proof of citizenship in the case of Chin Quock Wah. In a memorandum, the petitioner cited precedents supporting the use of signed certificates as proof of residence and citizenship. In a separate memorandum, the respondent refuted the denial of counsel argument by stating the Chinese Exclusion Act does not entitle immigrants to representation to counsel and stated that statues give the Secretary of Labor power to allow subordinates to rule on appeals. 
Judge Jeremiah Neterer ruled against the petitioner and agreed with the respondent arguments, therefore discharging the writ and remanding the petitioner to the custody of the Department of Immigration. The petitioner appealed up to the US Supreme Court where the decision was affirmed.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 23, 1888, Michael Shrek was committed to the Whitman County Jail in Colfax, Washington for six months. Justice of the Peace William A. German had Shrek committed in order to "keep the peace" and because he had defaulted on his bail. The commitment specifically stated that a man named Frank Poshner's peace would be disturbed if Shrek were released. On December 19, 1888, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Sheriff Lewis P. Berry. He claimed that the prison was an "unhealthy and unwholesome place,". Shrek also alleged that the damp conditions of the prison had caused him to contract an illness that required a doctor's care. During the hearing on December 20, 1888, he subpoenaed several doctors to support his case. Berry claimed that he tried to keep the prison in the best conditions possible, and that if it was unhealthy, it was due to how it was constructed and where it was located, rather than any fault of his own. The outcome of this case is unclear, but according to the Pullman Herald, Shrek sued the county in February of 1889 for $10,000 in damages as a result of his confinement.

Summary of Proceedings: John Brown was arrested on August 4th, 1917 by Omaha police for the crime of vagrancy. Shortly after, a complaint was filed against him and he was tried and convicted by the court. His sentence was a fine of $100, however, Brown would be imprisoned for not being able to pay the fine. Because the maximum fine for vagrancy was $50, Brown petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus citing the illegality of his sentence. The judge ruled in his favor, and ordered his immediate release from captivity.

Summary of Proceedings: Arrested and jailed for selling liquor without a valid license, Mark J. Wilbur petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that his license was valid, therefore, he was being unlawfully detained by sheriff Ress. Judge Holmes granted the petition. After reviewing evidence, he denied the petition and ordered that Wilbur be remanded back into custody. Wilbur moved the Court for a rehearing, which was overruled. Wilbur then appealed to the NE Supreme Court, who ruled in favor of Wilbur and ordered that he be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Edwin S. Douglas petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren and King County Sheriff John Stringer on the behalf of M. C. Gray. Douglas alleged that Gray’s imprisonment was illegal because he was not guilty of his accused crime of larceny or of being a fugitive from justice. Douglas did not state where Gray was being held. Stringer responded with a warrant stating that Gray was a fugitive from justice from Colorado. The warrant was dated after the petition was filed. The outcome of the case and fate of Gray are unknown, but Gray petitioned for a second writ of habeas corpus immediately after this case file concluded.

Summary of Proceedings: Stella Williams petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve her son, Horace Godden, from the custody of Charles and Frances Pollard, which was granted. The Pollards were Horace's aunt and uncle, as Frances was the sister of Horace's deceased father. They had assumed custody of Horace after his father's death, with Stella signing a contract allowing the Pollards' custody and education of her son. Stella had now remarried and said she had a comfortable home for her son. After hearing the evidence, Godden was remanded to the custody of the Pollards and Williams ordered to pay the court costs, although Horace was to be allowed to visit his mother every summer.

Summary of Proceedings:
On February 27, 1919, the Acting Governor of the State of Washington, Louis F. Hart issued a warrant ordering John Stringer, the King County Sheriff to take Joseph Rheinstrom into custody and hand him over to J. I. Kirby who was acting as an agent for the State of Wyoming. The warrant alleged that Rheinstrom was a fugitive from justice that was wanted in the State of Wyoming for the crime of obtaining money by false representation. Following his arrest, Joseph Rheinstrom filed for a writ of habeas corpus. Rheinstrom argued in his petition that his detention was illegal and denied that he had committed any crimes in the State of Wyoming. 

Judge J. T. Ronald denied Rheinstrom’s writ of habeas corpus. Rheinstrom immediately appealed the decision. Joseph Rheinstrom also filed for a second writ of habeas corpus shortly after appealing. This second appeal lists Wyoming agent, J. I. Kirby, has the respondent instead of the King County Sheriff, John Stringer. This second petition is listed under Case No. 134038 (hc.case.wa.1347). Rheinstrom’s appeal of the dismissal of the first writ of habeas corpus was heard by the Supreme Court of the State of Washington on May 29, 1919. The Supreme Court denied his appeal. 

Before the Supreme Court heard Rheinstrom’s case, the Acting Governor of the State of Washington, Louis F. Hart issued an executive order recalling the warrant for Rheinstrom’s arrest. In the executive order, Hart stated that the testimony of Charles Jacob Schreibels which the warrant was based on was found to have been made in bad faith. Hart did state this recall does not prevent the Governor of the State of Wyoming or his authorized agents from making another application for a warrant. Following Hart's recalling of the warrant, Rheinstrom was released from the custody of John Stringer on April 30, 1919.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1888, Mary Ellen Lyts left her husband, William D. Lyts, and took their five-year-old son Francis with her. According to Mary Ellen's petition, William "forcibly removed" Francis from her custody on the 20th of March 1889. The next day, Mary Ellen filed a writ of habeas corpus to have Francis returned to her custody, claiming that he was being "unlawfully imprisoned, detained, confined, and restrained of his liberty" by William. The petition was granted and William was ordered to produce Francis in court the following day. Later that same day, William's lawyer responded with a letter claiming that Francis is being held to "secure proper maintenance and education" for the child and that Mary Ellen is "unfit" and lacks the means to support his well-being. The letter also claims that Mary Ellen "abandoned and deserted" William and moved in with a man named Fred Brooks. The day after the petition, letters were exchanged where Mary Ellen's lawyers denied William's claim. William's lawyer responded, requesting a delay to the proceedings until April 2 and offering to allow Francis to live with a third party until the proceedings. On April 2nd, the judge ruled for Mary Ellen, giving her primary custody of Francis while allowing visitation and up to one week per month of custody for William. Mary Ellen was ordered to pay for the costs of the proceeding.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 23, 1922, Joe Vacarro filed for habeas against Chief of Police, Michael Dempsey, Chief of Detectives, C. H. Van Deusen, and Detective, John J. Pazanowski. In his petition, Vacarro explains that on March 22, 1922, he was arrested without complaint or warrant, and that a written complaint must be brought a district, court, or police judge, required by Sec. 8940 of the Rev. Statutes of Nebraska, 1915. Vacarro further suspected that the respondents are holding him at the sole request of an employee of the Savage Tires Company. A writ was issued but the case was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1914.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 3, 1867, Robert Ross testified as a witness in another case titled "Territory vs. Michael Williams". On September 13, he was accused of perjury by the foreman of the jury. On September 18, he was ordered by Justice of the Peace William L. Chalmers to pay a $1000 fine and was committed to the Jefferson County Jail in Port Townsend after not paying the fine. On September 25, Robert petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. His writ was delivered to the respondents. Robert's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: William Wiggins was charged with grand larceny for taking money from the Occidental Hotel safe through a complaint brought by the petitioner, William Fox. After Wiggins was found not guilty in his case, William Fox was charged with the court costs. Fox was unable to pay and detained and sentenced to forty-one (41) days of hard labor for refusal to pay a fine. Afterward, Fox filed for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing his complaint against Wiggins was not frivolous, and, therefore he should not be charged with the court costs. Judge J. R. Lewis granted the writ, and Fox was released.

Dr. Veronica Jackiewicz was arrested alongside several other professional midwives and doctors in Spokane, Washington in November 1912. Jackiewicz was accused and later indicted by a Grand Jury for unlawfully and knowingly depositing an evelope containing information about how to obtain or procure an abortion. On January 11, 1913, Dr. Jackiewicz pleaded guilty to the charges and was fined $50. 

No habeas corpus application was included in this case file.

Summary of Proceedings: H. H. Harding petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff William H. Moyer. Harding claimed he was being illegally held in King County Jail, as his right to due process was denied. Moyer responded by submitting documents of Harding’s trial which found him guilty of forgery and sentenced him to be kept in the county jail until he could be transferred to the state penitentiary to serve 5 years. The case outcome and fate of Harding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: G.L. Jeffrey (J.G. Jeffreys), a black man, was arrested and charged with assault and battery and mayhem after resisting the commands of constable Richard Diamond and biting his hand. Jeffreys was found guilty and was levied a fine of ninety-nine dollars plus the court costs of Diamond, and was committed without bail until his fees were paid. Jeffreys and his petitioner Allen A. Garner, an attorney and prominent Black community leader, asserted that he was held illegally as his charge was not one that could be punished "by the laws of the States” and that the ruling was “excessive of the jurisdiction" of Judge Cousins. Jeffreys’ writ of habeas corpus was granted and he would later be released. This case is most probably the same as that of J.G. Jeffreys, but the the cases remain distinct in a couple minute ways.

Summary of Proceedings:
Carl Martin filed for a writ of habeas corpus at the same time as Francis Williams, Sue Belmont and Edward Twitty. In his petition, Carl Martin argued that he was illegally being restrained of his liberty by Joel Warren, the Chief of Police, and J. S. McBride, the City Health Commissioner. Warren and McBride had detained Martin stating that he had a dangerous, contagious, and infectious disease. The case file never states which disease that Martin was claimed to have and Martin denied that he had any disease. Instead, he alleged that he was “the victim of malice and caprice of the Health and Police Departments.” In his return to the writ, J. S. McBride stated that Martin was taken into custody on a warrant issued by John B. Gordon. The warrant charged Martin with violating City Ordinance No. 16046 on the preservation of public morality, peace, safety, and good order in the City of Seattle. 

Carl Martin’s case was included in Judge Boyd J. Tallman order which required that three physicians be assigned to independently examine the petitioners and provide testimony on whether they believe that the Health Commissioner was justified in quarantining Carl Martin, Sue Belmont, Francis Williams, and Edward Twitty. This order was appealed by J. S. McBride to the Supreme Court of the State of Washington. The Supreme Court granted McBride a writ of prohibition preventing the physicians from examining the petitioners. Newspaper articles show that by the end of 1918, Carl Marin, Francis Williams, Sue Belmont, and Edward Twitty remained in quarantine under the custody of J. S. McBride. William’s attorney, Edwin J. Brown wrote several opinion pieces in the Seattle Star detesting the quarantines and the detainment of his clients which he used to jump start his mayoral campaign. 

The last pages of the case file show at the April of 1921, Carl Martin’s writ of habeas corpus was dismissed for a want of prosecution. Newspaper coverage does note that by April of 1919, Carl Martin was no longer in custody of the city’s health department and was acting as a witness in a city council investigation of Seattle’s quarantines in 1918.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 15th, 1884, George R. Daly petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus after being detained by John Harte McGraw in Washington for stealing a horse in Oregon. Daly petitioned for Habeas Corpus on the basis that he was not imprisoned under any commitment by any authority of law or court authorized to issue the warrant for his arrest and that he was innocent of the crime he had been accused of. The writ of Habeas Corpus was issued because Judge Roger Greene recognized that neither Washington nor Oregon had the jurisdiction to arrest and detain the petitioner and that the warrant for his arrest was not issued according to the law.

Summary of Proceedings: Thomas Franklin Romaini filed for a writ of habeas corpus on December 11, 1919. According to his application, Seattle city police held Romaini without charge or bail under alleged information from a person or persons from California. Judge A. W. Frater ordered a writ on December 11, 1919 and newspaper coverage indicates Romaini, who taught night classes for electricians, was released when Sacramento officials failed to produce documentation to justify their claim he was charged there with grand larceny.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 23, 1919, Ruth Mathews was arrested at her home, and on August 25, 1919, Mathews was convicted of being a vagrant and a prostitute and sentenced to 30 days in the Douglas County jail. On this same day, Omaha police magistrate Charles Foster signed a mittimus committing Mathews for an examination of venereal disease at the County Jail, and she was sent to a Detention Home for women as authorized by Omaha City Ordinance No. 10222. Mathews alleged that she offered bond, but Foster refused to accept it due to the mittimus that placed her in the custody of the Detention Home. 2 days later, Ruth Mathews filed a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus, stating that she was not and has never been afflicted with a venereal disease, and there is no well-founded suspicion that she is afflicted. On August 29th, Mathews was released on recognizance in the sum of $500.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 11th, 1919, Nellie Atkins was removed from her Omaha home by three men claiming to be detectives. She was arrested and taken to jail without being served any warrants. On the following day she was, against her will, subject to a physical examination. She was then moved to the Detention Home on St. Mary's Avenue. She submitted a petition for habeas corpus on January 16th, claiming that she was being unlawfully detained because she had never been charged with a crime, no complaint was ever filed against her, she was deprived of the privilege of furnishing a bond, and had been held in the Detention home against her will. She named Marshall Eberstein and Ernest E. Manning as respondents in her petition. Her petition was granted. In his return to the petition, Manning expressed that he was acting within his rights as health commissioner. He determined that Nellie had a venereal disease and then requested she be isolated and quarantined so as to not spread disease. He did this based on Ordinance No. 9852. The order remanding her to the Detention Home is dated January 12th. It is unclear under what authority she was arrested. On January 18th, the writ was denied at costs of county. The fate of Nellie Atkins is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In September 1912, George Marlowe and Edith DePugh were indicted and convicted by a grand jury on four counts of violation of the Act of June 25, 1910, or the White Slave Traffic Act (Mann Act). Their intended victims, Pearl Stevenson, and Freda Kuhl, were minors living in St. Marie’s, Idaho. Marlowe and DePugh wrote letters and sent telegrams to the girls, encouraging them to travel from St. Maries, Idaho, to Spokane Washington. 

E. C. Macdonald held Stevenson and Kuhl as material witnesses under bail. During the grand jury proceedings, Stevenson and Kuhl filed for a writ of habeas corpus ad testificandum. Matron of the Spokane Juvenile Detention Home, Mrs. Carrie E. Tucker held them until they could give testimony for the grand jury. Judge Frank H. Rudkin allowed the writ, taking testimony beginning on September 12, 1912. The fate of Stevenson and Kuhl is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 14, 1916, based on the facts in the complaint, Acting City Prosecutor T. J. McGuire filed a vagrancy complaint, charging Leon Angus with carrying a concealed weapon. Previously, in March 1916, he had been accused of killing a man named Carl Rudman, but it was found that the shooting was in self-defense. He had shot Rudman, an Austrian mechanic, while already on parole from the Nebraska State Penitentiary, where he was serving a life sentence for killing a saloon keeper named Nels Lausten. On July 22, 1916, Angus petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that Sheriff McShane and County Jailer Schroeder unlawfully imprisoned and restrained him of his liberty. In the petition, he stated that on June 2, 1916, the police arrested him for "suspicious character." On June 14, 1916, William Ramsey (acting in the place of McGuire) drew up a vagrancy complaint, charging Angus with being a "vagrant." Instead of Ramsey signing a complaint, he used the McGuire's rubber stamp to fill the blank space for the complaining witness and wrote McGuire's name where the complaining witness was required to sign. McGuire was not present or sworn by the Police Magistrate Foster as required by the law, so no complaining witness was present or swore to the complaint. Without a complaining witness, Angus was arraigned, where he pleaded not guilty. He was tried for vagrancy, found guilty, and sentenced to ninety days in county jail. In his petition, Angus claimed that there was a misrepresentation of the charges in the vagrancy complaint. The complaint stated that Angus was charged with "carrying a concealed weapon," and there was a drawn line under the words "form of the statutes." As a result, he was sent to county jail on a state mittimus instead of a city mittimus. The petition was received on July 28, 1916, and on the same day, the judge accepted the petition. On August 1, 1916, the judge filed a writ of habeas corpus and the next day, Sheriff McShane responded to the writ, claiming that the charge was not illegal for the following three reasons. First, he claimed that Angus was convicted of vagrancy and carrying a concealed weapon. Second, although Ramsey drew the charges, he did it with the consent of McGuire. Third, it was the judge, with the approval of Ramsey, who included carrying concealed weapons and the line under the word on the complaint. He concluded that Angus should have made a complaint during the trial and asked that the Courts uphold the charges. However, on August 4, 1916, the judge ruled that Angus was illegally detained and should be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
On January 5, 1879, S. W. Hall, who may also be named George Holliday, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the grounds that he was not George Holliday, the person described in the arrest warrant. What Hall was charged with was not mentioned in the case file. However, newspaper coverage indicated that Hall/Holliday was imprisoned on the charge of embezzlement, and had left his original home of Illinois, where he was clerk, to avoid being caught. The newspaper implied that he had been known as George H. Holliday in Illinois, but was known as Hall in Washington. Hall claimed that he was not George Holliday. Hall's fate is unknown.

Portions of this case can be found under each of the two given citations.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 10, 1893, Lee Wing filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Lee Quan Cho, Lee Choon, Lee Cheong, and Lee Hip. Lee Wing claimed that Lee Quan Cho, Lee Choon, Lee Cheong, and Lee Hip were being illegally detained on the Steamship Signal by Captain George Beudegard. They were prohibited from landing because Beudegard believed they were Chinese laborers who were prevented from entering the United States under the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Charles Bellinger determined that Lee Quan Cho, Lee Choon, Lee Cheong, and Lee Hip were Chinese merchants, granted the writ and ordered them released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Rachael (Ray) Cohen claims to have married Albert Rosenbloom (petitioner) on 7 April 1908 in Russia. Rosenbloom stated that he was pressured by force and threat by “matrimonial agents” to consent to marriage. The marriage was completed according to the Jewish rights and customs of the area and was in violation of Russian law. The petition stated that the marriage had no legally binding force and was never consummated. He paid Cohen 400 rubles soon after the ceremony and then left Russia for America. While he lived in America from that point forward, he remained a citizen of Russia. On 20 February 1910, Cohen followed Rosenbloom and filed petitions which led to his arrest in New York. He was compelled by reason of the arrest and imprisonment to pay Cohen $5/week in support. Cohen continuously harassed and annoyed Rosenbloom in his place of work, so much so that he decided to stop paying her support, left New York, and became a resident of Missouri. On 11 November 1911, Rosenbloom moved to Douglas County. On 9 December 1912, Cohen filed a complaint against Rosenbloom at the solicitation of the Jewish Society in Omaha. In the petition, she claimed to be Rosenbloom’s wife and used the name “Rachael Rosenbloom.” She claimed that Albert had neglected his duties to her beginning on 1 March 1911. A warrant was issued for his arrest in Douglas County, he was taken into custody and placed in jail. On 16 December 1912, Albert Rosenbloom was sentenced to 90 days in county jail. This petition asked for a writ of habeas corpus to be issued to release him from his unlawful imprisonment, it hinged on the claim that Nebraska had no jurisdiction over the affairs of Rachael Cohen and Albert Rosenbloom as they were both Russian citizens and were residing in New York at the date listed in the complaint. Judge Leslie allowed the writ on 16 December 1912. The Appearance Docket for the case notes that the application was denied on 18 December 1912, there is no reason stated.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 23, 1918, Genevieve Shoemaker filed for habeas against health commissioner, Ernest T. Manning, and chief of police, Michael Dempsey, claiming that she was being held under no complaint and sleeping on the floor in an inhumane manner of detention. The petition was granted, and Shoemaker was temporarily released from the detention home prior to the return of the writ. During the return, Manning explained that Shoemaker was being detained under evidence of a venereal virus during physical exam and had been quarantined in the detention house on 22nd and St. Mary's Avenue according to Ordinance #9852. In 1920, it was dismissed for want of prosecution; fate of Shoemaker is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 23, 1919, Agnes Marshall was arrested for vagrancy and prostitution. A few days later, on the 25th, police judge Charles E. Foster sentenced her to 30 days in the city jail and signed a mittimus requiring Marshall to be examined for venereal disease. Therefore, she was held by Elizabeth Hardy, keeper of a detention home, to be examined for venereal disease, although Marshall maintained that she didn't have venereal disease and there was no reason to suspect that she did. Another petition filed by her around the same time states that she refused to be examined unless her doctor was present, which the hospital didn't allow. Marshall attempted to post a bond for her release, but the court refused to allow it because of the aforementioned writ of mittimus. Therefore, on August 28, 1919, Marshall filed a writ of habeas corpus for her freedom against Elizabeth Hardy, arguing that she did not have the authority to detain her. An Omaha Bee article says that this petition was filed along with similar petitions from other Detention Home inmates named Mamie Allen and Ruth Matthews. After hearings stretching into the first week of September, Marshall was released on a $500 bond. An answer and return was filed on September 9, and Douglas County paid the sheriff's fees for serving the writ of habeas corpus on November 19.

Summary of Proceedings: Theodore Somski, also known as William H. Alson, Paul Dorman, and Paul Arnold, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel F. Warren. Somski alleged Warren imprisoned him in the Seattle City Jail under the authority of a telegraph from Vancouver, BC. Somski claimed this imprisonment was illegal because he had been in the jail for over 24 hours with no charge laid against him. Newspaper records indicate Somski was wanted for fraud in the state of California. Warren produced the warrant of arrest, which stated Somski was charged with being a fugitive from justice. The warrant was dated after the petition was filed. The outcome of the case is unknown, but newspaper records indicate custody of Somski was transferred to a third party as he was taken back to California.

Summary of Proceedings: A complaint was made on October 3 by Rob Blich against Nick Glavich of assault and battery that happened October 2. Glavich was found guilty in the Police Court and fined $50, costs, and sentenced to 30 days hard labor. On October 17, Glavich and attorney, Louis Berka, filed petition of habeas against the sheriff, charging that his punishment is unlawful - that a Police Judge is unauthorized to pass such a judgment. On October 18, Glavich’s petition and writ was upheld and he was released from custody.

The petition states that due to this status, Menzies is privileged from arrest on civil process. Despite this, Thomas Morris, sheriff of the county of Pierce, State of Washington for Kittitas County, and not within this district, threatens to take said Menzies beyond the jurisdiction of the court. Summary of Proceedings:
On the morning of June 26th, 1886, Ray Raymond shot James Finch in her home, which also served as an alleged brothel known as the "Bay Windows." County Coroner C.S. Penfield held an inquisition later that day.
Raymond stated she was in her parlor with her roommate Ruby Stanley and two other gentlemen, when James Finch forcefully entered her home. Raymond ordered Finch to leave, he refused and struck her. She pulled out her revolver and asked him to leave for the second time, upon refusal, Raymond fatally shot Finch. Raymond stated she did not intend to shoot Finch as she believed there were blanks in the revolver. Ruby Stanley's testimony aligns with Raymond's telling of events. The transcript stated, "witness refused to answer the question of her business was not that of having sexual intercourse with men at that house." 
Sheriff W. D. Gillespie arrived one minute after the shooting and stated he saw Raymond visibly shaken, wringing her hands, trying to give relief to Finch. Raymond made no attempt to escape and gave up the revolver when asked. In addition, Gillespie testified he knew the house was one of "public character" and "gentleman frequent at all times of the night." James B. Barnes testified he was the keeper of the saloon Finch went to prior, and detailed Finch to be quite drunk but "more pleasant than quarrelsome." Francis Snitzinger, a neighbor of Raymond's, testified that Finch entered her house that same night, under the impression his friend was there. Finch, seemingly intoxicated, called her a number of expletives and threatened violence. 

After the shooting, Raymond was under medical treatment for nervous prostration and could not appear in court. An affidavit from the defense alleged a crowd formed outside the defendant's home, and she was a prisoner therein. Prosecuting Attorney S. C. Hyde moved to discharge Pearl Worthington and Ruby Stanley, Raymond's roommates, as witnesses, and both were dismissed despite objections from the defense. From testimony, the court found probable cause to charge the defendant and Raymond was committed to jail without bail. An affidavit from the defense stated the courtroom was filled with spectators and the crowd stomped their feet in approval of the decision. 
On July 5th, 1886, Raymond's attorney Thomas C. Griffits petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on account of Raymond being unlawfully restrained of her liberty by E.J. Whittier, Sheriff of Spokane County. The petition stated Raymond is entitled to bail on said charge and that Raymond's physician, J.M. Morgan had advised that further confinement would greatly endanger her life and render her open to insanity and even death. Three days later the defendant was admitted to bail in the amount of $5,000, an affidavit from the defense alleged that citizens threatened to burn or hang the judge in effigy as a result of this decision. 

In December of 1886 as the trial approached, the defense motioned for a change of venue and a continuance, one of the reasons being prejudice against the defendant by citizens in Spokane Falls. An affidavit from the defense alleged that the citizens of Spokane Falls attempted to employ special counsel to assist her prosecution, George M. Forster. The affidavit further alleged that the crowd that formed outside Raymond's home after the shooting stated "she should be hung" and demanded that Raymond be placed in the city jail, "a nasty, dirty, filthy place." Citing further prejudice, the affidavit alleged that a rumor was brewing that Raymond murdered her previous husbands and was a "dangerous and quarrelsome woman of her kind." Griffits alleged that during trial prosecuting attorney S.C. Hyde denounced the defendant and the "class of women she belonged" and stated she shot Finch only because he was wearing blue overalls, which enraged many of the working men in the courtroom as many were engaged in railroad building and wore blue overalls. 
The defense alleged further prejudice was exacerbated by the current election of prohibition. Advocates of prohibition had a public meeting addressed by temperance worker Narcissa Edith White Kinney, who pointed to the guilt of defendant and killing of Finch as an example of the evils of saloons. Affidavits from prosecuting attorney S.C. Hyde and multiple other Spokane Falls residents refute this and state they had no knowledge of prejudice against the defendant, and she would be able to have a fair trial in Spokane Falls. 

Another reason for continuance cited by the defense was to acquire a key witness, Charles Wilson. In a December affidavit, Raymond stated she did not know Wilson was at the house but was later informed that said witness was there and in a position to see and hear all that occurred. Defendant stated that Wilson was the only other eyewitness to the transaction except Ruby Stanley. This was refuted by testimony from Geroge Wycoff and T. Donaldson who both stated they were present at the time of the shooting. An affidavit from the defense stated they had a conversation with Donaldson in August who told them he was present at the time of the house but did not know Wycoff was present. In addition, they stated Donaldson did not tell the defense he had witnessed the shooting. 

The third reason for continuance cited by the defense was to acquire witnesses to prove the defendant was insane at the time of the killing. A counsel statement from December alleged that the defendant for many years had been affiliated with a species of "insanity and mental disorder," "same is hereditary in her family." Defense expected to prove this by W.J. Woods, the former spouse of Raymond. A letter from Woods revealed that he was married to defendant, Josie Woods, 14 years prior and had two children. Woods stated defendant was afflicted with the "disease of emotional and nervous hereditary insanity." Defense stated they could also prove this with a deposition from Willian McDermott, brother-in-law of defendant, but needed continuance as all of the said witnesses did not reside in the territory. 

On March 20th, 1887, an indictment against Raymond was returned to Court by the Grand Jury, and the defense filed a motion to quash in May 1887. It is likely a continuance was granted as there are a number of subpoenas dating from May 1887 to June 1887, yet the outcome of the proceedings and the fate of Ray Raymond/Josie Woods is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
R. D Watson had been soliciting the sales of ‘Designer” magazines in Black Diamond, King County. Along with a $1, yearly subscription for the magazine, Watson also promised a special offer of premium four yards of silk. Those who bought subscriptions from Watson would also be mailed the address of a dry good house which contained cuts of standard dress patterns that the customer could buy from. On April 2, 1902, Watson was arrested by Sheriff Cudihee on the pretenses of obtaining money under false pretenses. The following day he was judged by Justice Tucker. 

Watson was detained with a bound of $500, of which he could not pay. Watson’s attorneys, Stafford and Dawes, claimed that Watson has the ability and willingness to pay back those who bought his subscription and wanted refund.

Summary of Proceedings: Sing Hi filed a petition for writ of habeas corpus on October 3, 1921, claiming that the process of his jailing by Sheriff Michael L. Clark was illegal and in violation of the Fifth Amendment and Section One of the Fourteenth Amendment. Hi, described in his petition as a resident of Omaha, claimed that he was arrested on October 1, 1921 and charged with disorderly conduct in violation of the city ordinances of Omaha. Hi was then found guilty and sentenced to thirty days in the Douglas County Jail.  Hi also alleged that his detention lacked a legal basis in the laws of Nebraska, the United States, and Omaha. A judge, William A. Redick, issued a Writ of Habeas Corpus in favor of Sing Hi directed to Sheriff Clark. Clark then appeared with Sing Hi before judge A. C. Troup on October 4, 1921. The outcome of the hearing is unknown, and the petition was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924. The fate of Sing Hi is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: General Osip, a subject of Russia, entered the United States on April 30th, 1914. Osip then had a hearing before the Immigration Board about remaining in the United States on May 2nd, 1914. Immigration Services concluded that Osip was likely to become a public charge and ordered him to be deported. Osip responded by filing a writ of habeas corpus on May 4th, 1914, arguing that the was being deprived of his liberties and that he should not be deported. Judge Cushman denied the petition on May 11th, 1914, and ruled that Osip was to remain in the custody of Alexander Fulton, a United States Immigration Officer.

Summary of Proceedings: Petitioner Emma Clifton asserts that her children (Charles, Roy, and Clarice) were being unlawfully restrained of their liberty by Charles Clifton, Sr. in Douglas County. She explained that a court order from 16 November 1892, modified on 28 November 1892, assigned custody of the aformentioned children to her and that Charles Clifton refused to uphold this decree. Because of this, she asked for a writ of habeas corpus so that the children can be “discharged from said unlawful imprisonment.” The custody agreement was attatched to the court files as Exhibit A. This document finalized the divorce of Charles and Emma Clifton, concluded that Charles must pay allimony, and that the custody of the children shoul be assigned to Emma. Judge Scott ordered that the writ be allowed. On 2 December 1892, Judge Scott stated that the children were being unlawfully restrained and ordered that they be discharged from the custody of Charles Clifton.

Summary of Proceedings: Elmer Estes petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his daughter, Rosa May Estes, from the custody of John Kent and a person whom he only as Major Davis, which was granted. Both of the men worked for the Christian Volunteers of America. Rosa May had run away from her home in Kansas City because of trouble with her stepfather, and wanted to stay in Lincoln to do religious work. During the proceedings, Elmer withdrew his petition. This may be because he had tried to secretly take her away on a train to Kansas City the night before, but was caught because his daughter began to scream for help. The fate of Rosa May is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Anderson Steward left the service of Lt. Col. Loomis of the U.S. Army on June 22, 1844. He did so with a certificate of character written by Loomis and in search of work as a servant of another army officer at a government fort further up the Mississippi. He traveled from New Orleans aboard the steamboat Jm. White and, upon coming ashore in St. Louis, Steward was detained and sent to John M. Jamison to be jailed in the county jail. Steward then filed for a writ of habeas to secure his freedom, claiming he was a free man, that there were no charges or warrant against him, and he was being jailed solely on the basis of his race. Judge John M. Krum granted Steward’s petition, and Jamison was forced to bring Steward before the court where he admitted that Steward was not jailed under any warrant or charges, but because he was delivered to Jamison “by the officers of the Steamboat J. M. White , for safe keeping, until satisfactory proof should be had of his freedom.” The events and outcome of the petition beyond that admission is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 9, 1919, Carson (Carlson) Titus was arrested upon a report that he had failed or provide for his wife, Emelia (Amelia) Titus. On June 10th, 1919 he appeared before a police judge where he pleaded not guilty and was placed on a $200 bail. On June 13th, 1919, he was arrested again under allegedly suspect pretenses. At that subsequent hearing, the bound party was ordered to pay Emilia $8 per week and was ordered to be imprisoned until he performed. On June 14th, 1919, a petition was filed on behalf of the bound party by his father, Frank Titus, who alleged that as a minor of 17 years of age, Carson was unable to marry and thus his marriage and any obligations to it are void. The application for the writ was granted on June 16th, but the fate of the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: McDonough reapplied for petition alongside attorney Richard Osborn, claiming convicted imprisonment to be "an act of passion and prejudice" by Soderberg. In a docket entry, it's revealed a Georgia Willimsin charged McDonough with threatening to burn down Willimson's dwelling house, to which McDonough pleaded not guilty and was charged with a bail sum of $1500, which was claimed to be excessively unjust and oppressive. Soderberg is accused through the reapplication to have criminal proceedings against him as a result and should no longer be allowed to act as Justice of the Peace, thus losing all jurisdiction over the petitioner. It's also claimed that McDonough was not mentally or physically fit to be guilty of the charges made against her. Thus McDonough wasn't given a proper trial or hearing and was later discharged from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 9, 1915, A. E. LeBallister filed for a writ of habeas corpus asking for his release from the custody of William R. Bryon and John M. Boyle. Bryon and Boyle had detained LeBallister at the Seattle General Hospital to extradite him back to the Fairbanks Precinct of the Alaska Territory to face trial for the charge of forgery. Bryon and Boyle claimed that LeBallister fled Alaska after being accused of defrauding a man named E. White by forging a receipt worth $100 for the salary of a second mate of a steamboat named the Robert Kerr. In LeBallister’s petition for habeas corpus, he denies the charges against him but also argues that he does not have the health to travel back to Alaska. His petition notes that he was suffering from an advanced stage of Bright’s disease (historical name of kidney diseases). Judge King Dykeman accepted LeBallister’s writ of habeas corpus and allowed for LeBallister to be released from the custody of Bryon and Boyle if he could pay $3,000 for bail. With the assistance of Joseph Blethen and E. L. Webster, LeBallister was able to pay his bail and be released.

Summary of Proceedings: William Reitman was arrested with a warrent issued by the secretary of labor issued on January 16th, 1918. He was questioned by an immigration inspector about his involvement with the I.W.W. William explained that he had been a member of the group for many years, but did not agree with all their beliefs or teach the destruction of property. Despite this, he was detained in an immigration detention station by Henry M. White. William Reitman petitioned for habeas corpus on November 29th, 1918 claiming he was being illegally detained without cause. The judge approved his petition however the outcome of the writ is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: According to Albert Davidson, Lizzie B. Cruse pretended to be an unmarried woman and pretended to be a resident of Douglas county and made a complaint to Edgar S. Bradley (justice of the peace for Douglas County), that she was pregnant with a bastard child and that Davidson was the father of said child. Bradley issued a warrant and delivered the same to B. F. Ford, a constable in Douglas County, commanding the arrest of Davidson. Ford arrested Davidson in his home city of Wymore and brought him to Douglas County and left him in the custody of George A. Bennett, the sheriff, and Joe Miller, the jailor. Cruse never presented her own side of the story, but the writ is allowed. Yet, a week later, the case was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: Alma Oharra was born to Mary J. Harmon and her husband in 1884. At some point she was committed to the House of the Good Shepherd, a home for "delinquent girls" in Omaha, as well as a convent. Her mother filed a writ of habeas corpus for her daughter on January 24, 1918, when Alma was 34. Mary did not share a surname with her daughter because at some point before the filing of the writ, her marriage with Alma's father dissolved. The writ of habeas corpus, set to be executed "forthwith," was directed at the Mother Superior, Sister M. Raphael Moran. (This is her religious name, not the one she was born with, as it is stated multiple times throughout the case that her real name remains unknown.) The writ was approved by judge Willis S. Sears, and Alma appeared before Judge George S. Day in the Douglas County District Court, but the result of the case is unknown. However, 1930 census records indicate that an Alma O'Hara, born the same year as the Alma Oharra mentioned in this case, was still an "inmate" at the House of the Good Shepherd in Omaha, indicating that Harmon was unsuccessful in reclaiming her daughter.

Summary of Proceedings: In September 1914, A. M. Long was convicted of larceny by the Multnomah County Circuit Court and sentenced to between one and seven years in the Oregon State Penitentiary in Salem. In February 1916, Long's attorney, Thomas Garland, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, which was granted. In the petition, Garland named the "Board of Control, and the Warden and Officers of the Penitentiary of the State of Oregon" as respondent. He argued that the circuit court judge had neglected to sign Long's commitment order and that, moreover, Long had been denied his state constitutional right to a private meeting with Garland. Warden John Minto, representing the respondents, denied these charges. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and Long remanded into the custody of the warden. Garland appealed the decision to the Oregon Supreme Court, which upheld the decision of the lower court.

Writ for habeas corpus was initially granted to Moy Bow and Moy For Gwong on June 7th, 1893. Writ for habeas corpus was later granted to Chin Gin Let, Chin Wee Dung, Chin Kaen Dung, and How Ling Quong on June 13th, 1893. Those granted writ were ordered to be released from custody. The case file does not include an order for writ of habeas corpus granted to How Yot, Moy Lun, Huey Chang Yuk, so their fate is unknown. Affidavits for Moy For Gwong and Moy Bow are in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: Otto Koerner immigrated with his wife and two children to the United States in April 1909 and settled in Spokane, Washington. Only a few months after his arrival on November 9, 1909, Otto was arrested by the Spokane County Sheriff, Francis McKay Pugh, and the Seattle Chinese and Immigrant Inspector, A. F. Richardson. His arrest was based on a warrant issued by the Department of Commerce and Labor. The warrant alleged that Otto Koerner and his family violated U.S. Immigration Law by having committed a felony or crime involving “moral turpitude” prior to their entry into the United States. The warrant was based on a letter sent to the department by the Austria-Hungarian Consulate which stated that Otto Koerner was charged and sentenced to three months in the penitentiary for his wife allegedly embezzling 8,000 Crowns from the Rudelsdorf-Moravia Post Office. The letter states that Otto’s wife Valerie was also charged but does not state if she was sentenced. Otto’s charge and sentencing came in October 1909 nearly six months after he had emigrated to the United States. Since the verdict and sentencing came several months after Otto and his family arrived in the United States, Judge Edward Whitson stated that the Immigration Law that forbade the migration of people charged with crimes of “moral turpitude” did not apply to this case. Whitson ruled that Otto Koerner’s detention was unlawful and ordered his release from the custody of the Sheriff.

Summary of Proceedings: In June 1910, Arthur B. Martin was arrested for violation for the Mann Act and subsequently tried, convicted, and sentenced to McNeil Island Penitentiary for five years. Martin fully completed his sentence and was discharged in September 1914, yet upon release was taken into custody by an immigration inspector and placed in the Immigration Detention Station. Martin authored a petition for a writ of habeas corpus and stated he was a native of the United States from the parish of Orleans in Louisiana. Judge Jeremiah ordered the writ to be issued. Immigration Commissioner, Henry M. White, in his return to the writ, alleged that the petitioner was an alien to the U.S. who brought a woman into the U.S. for the purposes of prostitution. White alleged that at a hearing after Martin's initial arrest before the immigration commission, Martin stated under oath he was born in Montreal Canada and came to the U.S. after fourteen years without inspection, and has never been naturalized, but always understood he was a citizen as his father had been naturalized. Martin was unable to swear to the fact that his father had been naturalized, and the return to writ contained a redacted line stating Martin swore under oath he was born in the city of New Orleans. Judge Jeremiah Neterer discharged and dismissed the petition and writ of habeas corpus and Martin was remanded to the custody of immigration authorities and likely deported.

Summary of Proceedings: Huie Sam petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Oh Dick and Ah Yam, held on the Steamship Signal by Captain George Bendergard. Captain Bendergard refused to allow them to enter the port as he believed they were arriving in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. However, several witnesses signed affidavits that Oh Dick and Ah Yam were Chinese Merchants with the firm of Wing Wah and Lung located at No. 181 Second Street. Mr. John Catlin investigated the case and confirmed the witnesses' stories. After reading this report, the Judge granted their writ and discharged them from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Ella Epps, mother of Georgia A. Risch, petitioned on behalf of her grandson Henry Laverne Risch. Georgia and Arthur A. Risch had started proceedings for a divorce around the time of the petition, but had agreed to leave Henry with Ella while the divorce was going on. Ella described Arthur as an alcoholic, "a man of violent temper" and often used "vile, violent and obscene language" towards Georgia. Georgia was also only 17, meaning that Arthur must have married and impregnated her at the age of 15 or 16 at the latest. Epps then claimed that Arthur violently took Henry from her on August 5, 1913 and placed him in the care of two individuals referred to as Mr. and Mrs. Lyons. Henry was sick and in need of certain medications and care. Ella stated that they refused to let Georgia see him or provide him with necessary medication. The writ was allowed and Henry was placed in the immediate custody of Georgia.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 28, 1922, the justice of the peace for Council Bluffs, Iowa issued an order accusing Viola McAtee Jacobson of the crime of conspiracy, and requesting that she either be brought before him or the nearest magistrate. On this order Omaha Chief of Police Michael Dempsey detained Jacobson and held her at the police headquarters. On this same day, William G. Hastings filed for a petition of a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Viola McAtee Jacobson, alleging that she is a resident and citizen of Nebraska and has not been charged with committing any crime against the state of Nebraska. On this same day Jacobson was released under a written bond for $750.00, the bond was later exonerated on December 1 and the application for a writ of Habeas Corpus was granted.

Summary of Proceedings:
On February 7, 1880, a $500 reward was posted for the capture of a man named J. Wallack in Shackleford County, Texas. He was accused of forgery. He managed to evade the authorities in Texas and escape to Columbia County, Washington, where he seemingly began going by the name Julius Leiffman. 
On May 17, 1880, a man named Mr. Boyles arrived at County Sheriff R.P. Steen's house to ask if he could arrest someone without a warrant. Steen said that he could, but was reluctant to. Boyles accused town newcomer Julius Leiffman of stealing $30 from his brother-in-law, J. E. Jackson. Jackson later revealed that there was a $500 bounty on Leiffman's head, and that Washington Governor Elisha P. Ferry had appointed the aptly named John G. Justice to bring the "slippery dog" back to Texas. Based on this, Steen arrested Leiffman and kept him in the county jail, although he continued to ask Boyles to file a formal complaint with the county prosecutor and to give him the papers authorizing Leiffman's arrest. 
From May 17 to June 6, Leiffman was incarcerated without a warrant, with Jackson presenting some mysterious "papers" to Steen on the 6th, but disappearing soon after that. John G. Justice seemingly wanted no part in the case. On June 9, 1880, he told Boyles that he didn't have the money to take Leiffman back to Texas. On June 7, 1880, Leiffman filed a writ of habeas corpus against R. P. Steen for unlawfully confining him. Judge Samuel Wingard allowed the writ and ordered him discharged from the county jail on June 9, 1880.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 20, 1923, Fannie Green was arrested in a raid on an alleged disorderly house on charges of being either an inmate or keeper of said house and confined to the Omaha city jail. Green remained in jail marked as "hold", with no charges filed against her and unable to pay a bond. H. Miller filed a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus on Fannie Green's behalf. The respondent, Chief of Police P. F. Dillon, stated that Fannie Green was in charge of the alleged disorderly house at the time of her arrest and that she was being held in custody pending an investigation on a charge that would be a felony. Dillon denied that Green was arrested on charges of being either an inmate or keeper of the house and that she was marked as "hold". On September 29, 1923, the application was granted, and Fannie Green was discharged.
