Summary of Proceedings:
George Hawkins sought a writ of habeas corpus to challenge his detainment at McNeill Island in Washington State after the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned his conviction for robbery in Nome, Alaska in 1900. Bail was sought for $1,000, but the US District Attorneys for Alaska sought $3,000. On October 14 1902, after the writ of error was approved, Judge Alfred Moore in Alaska issued an order for a new trial, set to happen almost a year later on September 7, 1903. Judge Moore also ordered that Hawkins remain incarcerated until that trial date. 
Being of ill health and without the means to meet the bail, Hawkins claimed that he was being deprived of his liberty and a speedy trial by the refusal to relocate him to Alaska after the appeal.
Judge Hanford agreed, freeing Hawkins under the condition he returns to Alaska to face retrial. He approved the writ and ordered Hawkins's release.

Summary of Proceedings: Sue Bellmont petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren and Commissioner of Health J. S. McBride. Bellmont claimed Warren and McBride were holding her under the false claim she was infected with a contagious disease. She described the conditions of her detainment quarters as “unsanitary, filthy and poorly ventilated,” with inmates sharing soap and drinking cups, being fed “unwholesome” food, and being forced to submit to unnecessary medical treatment. Warren and McBride claimed that Bellmont was indeed infected with a dangerously contagious disease and was now under quarantine at the city isolation hospital. Bellmont alleged her detainment was not in good faith and that she was not infected with any such disease. Newspaper records indicated the writ was denied, and Bellmont remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Charlie (or Charles) Mitchell, Edith Brown, and Alice Ennis operated and managed a residence that allegedly sold alcohol. On July 3, 1924, Charlie Mitchell was sentenced to five six-month sentences (30 months) for the unlawful sale of intoxicating liquor, a year sentence for maintaining a common nuisance, and a $500 fine for the unlawful possession of intoxicating liquor. On December 23, 1924, Charlie petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Judge McGee ordered the respondents to release Charlie from custody upon the payment of a bond and the respondents appealed this decision. On January 30, 1926, the decision of the lower court was reversed and Charlie was remanded to the custody of the respondents.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 13, 1869, Snelling petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Sheriff James McAuliff. He claimed McAuliff had unlawfully detained him at the county jail. Snelling said that he did not know the cause of his restraint. He argued that he had not committed any crimes or violated the statutes of Washington Territory. Snelling said there was no order for the police to hold him by any court or police magistrate of the Washington Territory. Sheriff McAuliff replied that he had been informed that Snelling was convicted of grand larceny was was sent to jail in Oregon, but escaped from jail and became a fugitive from justice. Judge Kennedy allowed his petition. While the outcome of this proceeding is not clear from the case file, Washington press coverage indicates Snelling was returned to Oregon to face charges and Oregon press coverage seems to confirm that. The federal 1870 census shows Snelling as a Native laborer in Walla Walla, WA however.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 10, 1893, Haug Ming filed for a writ of habeas corpus for his business partner Wah May York. Haug Ming claimed that Wah May York was being illegally detained on the Steamship Signal by Captain Eugene Beudegard. Beudegard claimed that he detained Wah May York because he believed that Wah May York was a Chinese laborer prevented from entering the United States under the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Charles Bellinger disagreed, and granted the petition and ordered Wah May York to be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Alfred Bradden, a retired US Army sergeant who was employed at the Fort Robinson post exchange, was arrested by the sheriff of Dawes County, Nebraska and charged with violating a state law against selling intoxicating liquors without a license. After making bail, Bradden petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. He argued that he had only sold wine and beer, which was expressly permitted by federal regulations, and that the state of Nebraska lacked the jurisdiction to prosecute him. After hearing the evidence, Bradden was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1886 Can- ah- couqua filed for a writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of her son who had been at the Indian Training School at Sitka, AK for three years without leave. The defendants argued that Can-ah-couqua had signed an agreement with the school in 1883-when her son was five years old- to relinquish her parental custody for a period of five years. They argued that it was for the well being and education of the boy, Con-ca-bach, that he remain in the school and not be allowed to return to his "uncivilized" mother. Can-ah-couqua argued that she had never been presented any sort of contract or verbally agreed to give- up custody of her son to the school. She further asserted that Con-ca-dach was suffering physically from the poor conditions of the school building, overworked, and unfed. He was also frequent physically and verbally abused by teachers and other staff members of the school. Furthermore, she had not been able to see her son in three years, since he had been taken from her. As part of the petitioner's evidence, Can-ah-couqua;'s attorney submitted a letter that had been written by Con-ca-dach to the governor of Alaska, A. P. Swineford, saying that he wished to be taken out of the school, and returned to his mother. Judge Dawson ruled in favor of the defendants, writing that Can-ah-couqua had relinquished custody for five years in her "agreement" with the school, and it was in the best interest of the child to continue to receive a proper education. Can-ah-couqua was, however, allowed to occasionally visit Con-ca-dach at the school, provided that the there was adequate supervisor by school officials.

Summary of Proceedings:
On 21 January 1915 George L. German filed a complaint stating that Joseph Miller, Bernard Miller, and Peter Miller committed the offense of breaching stolen property on 18 January 1915. They were brought before the Police Judge for South Omaha, H. W. Reed were they pled not guilty. As such, the cause was continued to 3 February 1915. 
On 26 February 1915, F. C. Hagerman, George Christ, John Laininger, J. F. Anderson, and L. L. Fuller gave testimony in the Police Court while the defendants were not present and were not able to hear or respond to the testimony made against them. This right was not waived, expressly or implicitly, by any of the men or their attorneys.
Joseph, Bernard, and Peter Miller and Ed Mazone submitted a petition that stated that they were being unlawfully restrained of their liberty by South Omaha Chief of Police, John Briggs, and a city jailer, Michael Corcoran. The four men were convicted of concealing stolen property in the South Omaha Police Court on 26 March 1915. The charges were under § 8635 of the 1913 Revised Statutes of Nebraska. The issue they cited was that this section was repealed by House Roll No. 47 which was approved by the Governor on 16 March 1915. Despite this repeal, the four men were charged with the aforementioned crime, fined $17.00 each, and costs were assessed at $3.00 each. After that conviction, the men were confined in the City Jail “without authority of law.” 
The petition thus asserted that the petitioner’s constitutional rights were violated during the trial and that their conviction and detention were not made under current law. Therefore, they asked for a writ of Habeas Corpus. 
Judge William A. Redick ordered that a writ be allowed, returnable 27 March 1915. Sheriff Felix J. McShane, Jr. filed his writ return on 5 April 1915, it stated that the writ was received on 26 March 1915 and was served the same day to John Briggs and Michael Corcoran. 
E. R. Leigh, Attorney for Respondents, filed Briggs and Corcoran’s answer on 31 March 1915; it stated that the four petitioners were convicted upon the charge of concealing stolen property with a value less than $35.00, fined $20.00 each, and committed to the county jail until they paid those fines. They also submitted the Mittimi as Exhibits, these documents were each signed by H. W. Reed, the South Omaha Police Court Judge, on 26 March 1915. These Mittimi stated that on 21 January 1915, George L. German had observed Ed Magnus, Joseph Miller, Bernard Miller, and Peter Miller concealing stolen property. 
The Appearance Docket noted that, at the hearing on 27 March 1915, realtors were released “on own recognizance by agreement of counsel.”

Summary of Proceedings: In 1900 Maude Cooper, petitioner, left Kenneth in the care of the Child Savings Institute in Omaha temporarily. John Silas, the defendant, claimed that Kenneth Cooper was then legally adopted in 1901 and he and his wife, Mary, have legal custody of the child. Maude stated she never consented to a change in custody of Kenneth to John Silas. She was also not contacted with a notice of Kenneth's adoption by John Silas. Maude then, in 1903, filed for a writ of habeas corpus so that Kenneth Cooper can return to her care. An order allowing writ of habeas corpus in favor of Maude Cooper and her son, Kenneth Cooper, is provided by Judge Read in 1903.

Summary of Proceedings: Jennie Pickerell filed for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Nell Pickerell. Seattle Health Officer J. S. McBride held Nell Pickerell in the Public Safety Building under suspicion of having communicable venereal disease. Jennie Pickerell claimed that conditions in the Public Safety Building were “unsanitary and overcrowded with occupants many of whom are suffering with chronic communicable diseases.”  Despite Sheriff John Stringer affirming that he delivered the writ, McBride stated that he both wanted to quash the writ and had never received it. The fate of Nell Pickerell is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On 5 April 1912, Sarah Younsum presented a petition for a writ of habeas corpus to Judge A. L. Sutton who then ordered that a writ be issued in favor of Minne Boxter, the daughter of Younsum, returnable on 6 April 1912. The writ was directed to Bessie Early, who Younsum had stated was unlawfully depriving Boxter of her liberty. Younsum’s original petition only states that Boxter was “allowed to go to said Bessie Early,” and has been detained and “deprived of her right to go to her mother” since that time. The date at which Boxter went to Early is not stated. Sheriff McShane’s writ return, which was filed 17 April 1912, stated that he served the writ to Early on 6 April 1912. The Appearance Docket notes that the parties appeared in court before Judge Leslie on 6 April 1912 and then the trial continued on 13 April 1912. The Docket states that the writ was denied and the case dismissed on 20 April 1912. The "custody" of Boxter is not directly stated in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 2, 1904, James O’Donnell petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. The names Sweeny and Steiner are mentioned as attorneys, but it is not clear which party they represent. James claimed that he was being illegally held by Sheriff Edward Cudihee, who had no proper warrant. Cudihee’s return stated that James was being held on a writ of no exeat issued as a result of the divorce hearing between James and Catherine O’Donnell, as Catherine had reason to believe James would be leaving the court’s jurisdiction to avoid paying alimony for the care of their seven children. Newspaper coverage indicated that James said he was traveling for work, but Catherine believed he intended to escape to Canada. Interestingly, Judge Boyd J. Tallman appeared to be both the person who issued the writ of no exeat and the one who heard the habeas corpus case. The outcome of this case and the fate of James are unknown. Newspaper coverage indicates the couple were arrested for fighting on the street and that Catherine was granted the divorce she requested.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 31, 1894 Frank Williams was convicted of breaking the peace after whipping his wife on May 30, 1894. He was sentenced to the county jail for 90 days. On May 31, Williams applied for a writ of Habeas Corpus based on the fact that his wife was not named in the original mittimus by the Judge John Tutt. His application for a writ of Habeas Corpus was granted by the Judge J. W. Langley of the King County Superior Court. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Grace LaVonne petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve her daughter, Virginia LaVonne, from the custody of chief probation officer Sarah Gregory, which was granted. Sarah Gregory wanted a birth certificate before the child was released, which Grace couldn't produce. In their response to the writ, Sarah's counsel requested further time to prepare their defense, which was allowed, during which time the judge determined that Grace should have temporary custody of Virginia. At the hearing, Sarah's counsel mounted no defense, and Virginia was remanded to the custody of her mother.

Summary of Proceedings: Julius Cohen was arrested by the Spokane County Sheriff, George E. Stone, and C. A. Fluegel. Cohen was arrested on a warrant of extradition which charged him with being a fugitive from justice. The warrant was based on a Grand Jury ruling which found enough evidence to charge Julius Cohen with the charge of defrauding Mary Kaminsky of $10 through “the confidence game.” Cohen and his attorneys argued that charge and warrant violate Cohen’s Fourteenth Amendment rights by failing to inform him of the nature of the charge against him. Cohen had attempted to file for a writ of habeas corpus in the Spokane County Superior Court but was denied by Judge E. H. Sullivan. After his appeal was denied, Cohen filed for a writ of habeas corpus in the Federal Circuit Court of the Eastern District of Washington. Judge Frank H. Rudkin denied this new writ of habeas corpus and allowed C. A. Fluegel to begin the extradition of Cohen back to Illinois.

Summary of Proceedings:
William B. Ten Eyck filed a complaint on 5 October 1896 that Jim Smith committed the offense of “Drunk & Disorderly” the prior day (4 October 1896). He was sentenced by Police Judge Gordon to 30 days in County Jail and to pay the $2.00 Cost and $1.00 Mittimus. The same day, William Harrington filed a complaint stating that Mr. Smith had committed the crime of Larceny on 22 September 1896. For this charge, Police Judge Gordon sentenced him to 30 days in County Jail along with a $2.50 Cost and $1.00 Mittimus. He plead “not guilty” to both counts.
Pas O. Hawes, the Attorney for Petitioner, submitted an application for a writ of Habeas Corpus stating that Jim Smith was unlawfully deprived of his liberty, having served both of his sentences yet still being held in the County Jail. On 9 November 1896, Judge Baker ordered that the writ be allowed. A subpoena was sent on 9 November 1896 ordering Pete Schenk (witness) to appear in court on 10 November 1896, bringing all records pertaining to Jim Smith’s case. 
On 9 June 1898, Judge Baker signed an order re-taxing the costs of the proceeding to the County.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 20, 1922, Frank Sellers filed for habeas against Sheriff, Michael L. Clark. In the petition, Sellers explained that he had plead guilty to grand larceny on March 5, 1919, and placed on probation. Such probation was later revoked on March 27, 1920, and a new sentence placed Sellers in the State Penitentiary at Lincoln, NE, for 1 to 7 years. Sellers' attorneys argued that the second sentence was void and that habeas was the correct legal action to get Sellers released. A writ was issued, a demurrer was motioned, and on February 4, 1922, the writ was denied, and Sellers remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 8th, 1919, Dollie Dean was arrested and charged with vagrancy, prostitution, and with being an inmate of a common and ill-governed house. On February 10th, Dollie was found guilty of these charges and sentenced to 90 days in the county jail. She appealed this ruling. After she furnished a $400 bond, the magistrate issued her release. Dollie alleged that the Keeper of the Jail and the Chief of Police refused to release her and that she had since been detained without cause. It was on these grounds that she petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. On February 15th, the writ was granted and Dollie was released.

Summary of Proceedings: Dennis Griffin files for a writ of Habeas Corpus to regain custody of his daughter, Julia Griffin. Julia G. was put in the custody of Julia and John Sullivan after Dennis Griffin's wife, the daughter of Julia and John Sullivan, was institutionalized in 1893, and later died. Since 1893, custody of said child changed many times between the Sullivans, Catharine Griffin (sister of Dennis), Ellen Koons, and Dennis Griffin. Griffin accused Ellen Koons, the girl's aunt, of kidnapping her from Dennis's sister while she was in her custody in Ottumway, Iowa. Dennis sought to place Julia G. in a convent near Ottumwa so that he could see her more frequently. Judge Baker found that it was in the best interest of Julia Griffin to remain in the custody of her grandparents. Dennis Griffin is afforded the ability to visit Julia Griffin at all reasonable times at the Sullivan residence. During the trial, Julia G. displayed a clear preference for her father, running up to him and kissing him as the verdict was read out. There was a class difference between the parties, as, according to the Omaha Evening Bee, the Sullivans "incline[d] towards the aristocratic," while Griffin was "a brawny laborer who can scarcely sign his name."

Summary of Proceedings: Lee Wing petitioned Habeas Corpus on behalf of Lay Deat, Pon Chan Hen, Leon Salt, Wong Tai Ling, and Cheng Wing, as they were being detained on the Steamship Haytian Republic by Harry Struve. Master Struve did not believe they were merchants, and thus their arrival at port violated the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. However, the individuals provided documentation proving themselves as merchants, and therefore their writ was granted, and they were released.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 5, 1893, Louis Chapman was convicted of exhibiting and flourishing a dangerous weapon.  On August 7, 1893, Justice of the Peace C.C. Todd ordered for Chapman to be taken into custody. Chapman petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on October 10, 1893. He explained that he had been held in jail since August 8, 1893 due to his inability to post bail.  He argued that his right to a speedy trial had been violated, as he had been held for more than sixty days without due process of law.  Additionally, he stated that Todd failed to file the transcript of the proceedings in accordance with Section 1597 of Hill’s Code.  Finally, Chapman argued that Section 1368 of Hill’s Code was violated because there was no indictment or additional information filed against him within 30 days of the preliminary hearing.  Judge T.J. Humes issued the writ. However, the outcome of the petition and Chapman’s fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In February 1916, Max Selicow filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the basis that he was unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Henry W. Dunn, the Chief of Police in Omaha. The petitioner owned a "moving picture theater" and was arrested for disobeying the Health Commissioner's order mandating no children under the age of 12 gain entry to such establishments. The petitioner alleged he had no notice of the order, and any such order is unconstitutional and void as it deprives him of equal protection of the laws. Judge Day allowed the petition. The petitioner gave bail for his appearance, then voluntarily withdrew the bail and surrendered himself to the police. The District Court ruled against the defendant, and the petitioner motioned for a new trial on the grounds the ruling was contrary to law and not supported by sufficient evidence. On appeal to the Supreme Court of Nebraska, the court affirmed the ruling against the plaintiff.

Summary of Proceedings: Lelah Puc-Ka-Chee (Meskwaki) was detained by Indian Agent, W. G. Malin and brought to a the American Indian Boarding School at Toledo, Iowa. She was brought there under the guardianship of her court-appointed guardian, Malin. Her husband petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus under his and her name. Circuit judge, O. P. Shiras, ruled that Malin had no right to guardianship over Lelah Puc-Ka-Chee, who was released from his custody and was granted her freedom. Furthermore, Shiras asserted that as a married woman, and therefore a legal adult, Puc-Ka-Chee had the right to decide whether or not she would remain enrolled at the school.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 23rd, 1904, Ben Gabriel petitioned for his freedom. Gabriel was being held in the King County Jail by the Sheriff, Edward Cudihee. In his petition, he informed the court that he was being held on a complaint from May 31st by H.C. Adams. He also informed the court that on June 14th, after the testimonies from two witnesses, Gabriel was held due to their being probable cause to believe he was guilty, and he was held for $1000 bail. His lawyers, Humes, Millers, and Lysons, argued that the two witnesses were not sufficient evidence. In their testimonies, the witnesses were revealed to be teenagers who were not in school and often stole junk to sell at a junk shop. In this particular instance, the two boys argued that they two, along with two others, were told where to steal some junk by Ben Gabriel, who worked in the junk shop. The state argued that these two witnesses were reliable enough to have Gabriel held, which was upheld by Judge John F. Gordon, Justice of the Peace. On June 23rd, the same day that Gabriel petitioned, Judge Boyd J. Tallman approved the writ, which was also served the same day to Edward Cudihee, the Sheriff of King County. The court date was set for July 1st, however the case file ends there, and Gabriel’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Lena Constance Shoemaker Loman petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of her daughter, Udena Marie Shoemaker. Loman claimed that Udena Shoemaker was being withheld from her by her ex-husband, Claude Franklin Shoemaker, despite Loman having been awarded sole custody during their divorce proceedings. Loman alleged that Claude Shoemaker was unfit to care for Udena Shoemaker, as he worked at night and slept most of the day, leaving Udena Shoemaker in the care of strangers. Loman also claimed that she still had custody of their other child, Victor Burton Shoemaker, and felt it was best that the children be raised together. The case file revealed neither the outcome of the case nor the fate of Udena Marie Shoemaker.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 16, 1914, R. T. Davison petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Charles L. Swan, along with lawyers Bell and McNeil. Davison’s relationship to Swan is unknown. Davison claimed that Swan’s detainment was illegal because Swan was not a fugitive from justice, as chief of police Austin E. Griffiths claimed. Griffiths produced documentation showing that Swan had been charged with embezzlement in Jackson County, Oregon, and that the acting Oregon governor Ben W. Olcott, and the Washington governor, Ernest Lister, had both ordered his arrest on the charge of fugitive from justice. The outcome of this case and Swan’s fate are unknown

Summary of Proceedings: On February 8, 1886, L. T. Savacool allegedly forged a property deed. On February 18, C. A. McCabe and James Robinson formally accused him, and Savacool was brought before Garfield County Justice of the Peace William Newland. Newland found him guilty and set bail at $1,000. As he could not pay this, Savacool was confined to the Columbia County Jail in Dayton, Washington Territory. The same day, Savacool petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Columbia County Sheriff J. H. Hosler, saying that he was being unlawfully detained. He claimed that the writ of commitment that Newland had signed did not allow Hosler to lawfully imprison him and that forgery was not a crime in the ordinances of Washington Territory. He subpoenaed many witnesses to speak in his defense, including his wife, Florence Savacool. Hosler cited an order made in 1884 by Columbia County District Court judge S. C. Wingard stating that everyone awaiting trial in Columbia County District Court should be held in the Columbia County Jail. The hearing took place on February 23, 1886. Judge William G. Langford found that there was no probable cause to find Savacool guilty of forgery and ordered him released, with the county paying all court costs.

Summary of Proceedings:
On August 17 1829, Maria Whitten, the plaintiff, filed a freedom petition and on August 20 the petitioner’s lawyer, George Strothers, filed for a writ of  habeas corpus for the bodies of Whitten and her son, Patrick Henry. It is unclear what the role the defendant, Garland Rucker, had in this, but what is clear from the transcriptions of the depositions included in this case file is that efforts were made to examine how exactly Whitten arrived in St. Louis from her stated birth place of Virginia. In these depositions, figures from Equality County, Illinois, and Bedford County, Virginia, testified as to the situation that Whitten was in, having seemingly escaped from a slave market where she was bought and sold by her enslavers, Abraham Patrick Powell and Abel B. Nichols, respectively, in Virginia to Jesse (John) Whitten’s home and then fleeing with him to Kentucky and on from there to Illinois where he ultimately passed away. 
The petition came about as a result of Rucker allegedly assaulting and trespassing against Whitten, but is unclear what the final verdict on the plea was.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph Bowers was arrested by Sheriff William Cochrane for the charge of assault and battery, and he was subsequently sentenced by a justice of the peace to 500 days in jail. He filed for a petition of Habeas Corpus on the basis that the justice of the peace was not acting within his jurisdiction when he sentenced the petitioner. Upon hearing the evidence, the judge allowed the petition, but the fate of the petitioner remains unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Jesse Cain was jailed for contempt and refusing to pay the alimony established in a prior divorce proceeding. He petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. In the meantime, Cain posted a $500 bail and was released. After hearing the evidence, Cain was remanded to the custody of his jailer. Cain appealed this decision to the state supreme court, which affirmed the lower court's ruling.

Summary of Proceedings: Earl Barringer was arrested on January 24 for seduction. On the same day, Barringer filed Habeas with attorneys William F. Curley and Lesley Woodrough, charging that police chief, John J Donahue, and detective, Charles H. Van Deusen, had no commitment to arrest him. The order for arrest came from William M. Sawyer and G. H. Whitmore of Iowa and was issued for a Jacob Barringer on January 23 and 24. A writ was issued and Barringer was released on bond for $500 with C.C. Barringer and O. D. Paudall as Sureties. The writ was sustained and Barringer was officially released from custody on February 4.

Summary of Proceedings: Charles H. Gaydou filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of his son, Charles Gaydou, to receive full custody of said child from Fannie Gaydou and John Marketan. Fannie Gaydou was the mother of Charles Gaydou and the former wife of Charles H. Gaydou. Charles and Fannie Gaydou had annulled their marriage at the time of this case, and Charles Gaydou alleged that Fannie Gaydou had committed adultery against him with John Marketan. Judge Joseph B. Clarkson found Fannie Gaydou to be an unfit person to have the care, custody, education, and maintenance of the said Charles Gaydou and Charles H. Gaydou as a fit guardian for the infant. Accordingly, the final order stated that Charles H. Gaydou was to be given full custody, and Fannie Gaydou was entitled to visit the infant once a week.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 13th 1890, the state of Washington issued a warrant of arrest for Bert Lockerby, on the criminal charge of bastardy. The request for the warrant originally came from the Governor of Minnesota, Lockerby fled the Minnesota, and was considered a fugitive of justice. Governor William Merriam authorized John Vogil to detain Lockerby and return him to Minnesota. Lockerby then petitioned for a writ of habeas, stating that John Doe (as John Vogil was unknown to him) is pretending to be an officer of the state of Minnesota and is illegally restraining him of his liberty. However Vogil stated that he has a legal right to custody of Lockerby, and has a requisition from the Governor. While the case file does not reveal the fate of the bound party, a Seattle newspaper clarified that the case was disposed of due to, bastardy not being a crime under Minnesota laws.

Summary of Proceedings: Shortly after her husband's death, Lizzie Branson of Lincoln, Nebraska, was approached by J.A. Murray, an agent of the Nebraska Children's Home Finding Society, who, the petitioner alleges, "unlawfully secured the possession and custody" of her three children, George Craig, Olie Williamson, and Mabel Williamson by "force, intimidation, and threats" during her time of grief. After Branson signed a waiver, the children were taken from Lancaster County to the Nebraska Children's Home in Omaha, Nebraska. On February 7, 1916, the children's brother-in-law, G.W. Beard, filed a writ of habeas corpus for the children served to the superintendent of the Nebraska Children's Home, Reverend E.P. Quivey, and J.A. Murray. F.J. McShane, the Douglas County sheriff, served the writ to Quivey, but could not find Murray. A return to writ was filed on February 14, but nothing more is known about the fate of the children.

Summary of Proceedings: Fannie Fowle's lawyer (Lewis, James H.) stated in the petition that she was unlawfully restrained against her will by George J. Finleyson (a British citizen). The petitioner believed there was no other cause of her restraint "other than unkindness and willful desire to make a slave" of her. They also cited in the petition that George called her his slave and that she could not leave. Fannie "frequent made attempts to get away" which resulted in the respondent catching her and "severely beat and wound her" for attempting to leave. It is stated she was being held "in the County of King on a Street of said City known as Third Street between what is known as Columbia and Madison Street, just one door from the said Columbia street next to the certain hotel known as the Columbia House." The petition was granted and the writ was served on Finleyson, but there is no further information about her release.

Summary of Proceedings: Elihu Schooner was arrested and jailed as a fugitive from slavery. George Denison, his attorney, asserted that Schooner was a free man and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Schooner was released. Evidence included a sworn statement from his 65yo grandfather Gordon Ockery (born in CT and married to Betsy Pierce of Rhode Island; both Black) that explains Eli's father, John Schooner, was "half-Indian" and had married Gordon's daughter Louisa, but both of Eli's parents died by the time Eli was four years old. An 1840 census shows Gordon's household with minor male children, perhaps including Eli.

Summary of Proceedings:
Millie Kentzler filed a writ of habeas corpus against her ex-husband, Joseph Kentzler, for her two oldest children, Charles and Laura, aged six and four. After the dissolution of their marriage in 1889 amid shared allegations of abuse and neglect, Millie was granted custody by a local probate court in Montana. In the meantime, Joseph had moved to Seattle, Washington. He returned to Montana and kidnapped Charles and Laura, taking them back to Seattle. Millie followed him to Seattle and, according to newspaper coverage, was able to secure a lawyer and file a writ of habeas corpus. Judge Lichtenberg gave Joseph custody while permitting Millie visitation. 

On November 20, 1890, Millie took Charles and Laura from Joseph’s residence. She was found in contempt of court for her action. At some point after this, Charles and Laura were placed in the Orphans Home. Judge Lichtenberg denied both Millie and Joseph visitation at the Orphans Home due to disorderly conduct, although newspaper coverage indicated that Joseph was the main offender. Ultimately, the case file showed that Joseph was granted custody. However, newspaper coverage from 1891 provided evidence that when Millie attempted to visit her two oldest children, Joseph apprehended their youngest child using violence, prompting an arrest and an eventual return of the children to her.

Summary of Proceedings: Rose Dodson filed a petition after claiming that her husband George Dodson unlawfully entered the home of her parents and "forcibly and with great violence" took their daughter, Louisa Dodson from her. Rose claimed that she was sick and was in need of her mother's care and that is why she had went to her parents house. However, George Dodson claimed that Rose unlawfully took the child from their home and was conspiring with her parents to keep Louisa away from him. He also refers to Rose as being of “fiery temper without provocation and in fits of anger she [had] frequently beaten the infant child brutally and unremorsefully.” The writ was originally approved, but then both George and Rose amicably decided they wanted the writ dismissed. It is unknown what the end result of the custody agreement.

Summary of Proceedings: Ah Lee petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was illegally detained on the charge of first degree murder. In the petition, Ah Lee claimed that the Justices of the Supreme Court of Oregon, the Governor of Oregon, and Circuit Court Judge Charles Bellinger were all involved in what he claimed was an illegal detainment because he was a subject of the Emperor of China and U.S. laws did not apply to him. Ah Lee’s writ was denied and he remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: In the summer of 1919, Marie Shelton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the Marion County Circuit Court to retrieve her daughter, referred to as both Josephine Shelton and Josephine Matlock, from Florence and Lloyd Weeks, which was granted. Marie was Josephine's "natural" mother as well as her mother "by virtue of adoption." In 1909, after divorcing Josephine's father, Clyde Maulding, Marie permitted Josephine to be adopted by Clyde's sister, meaning Josephine's aunt, Cora Matlock. Florence Weeks was Cora's daughter, making her Josephine's first cousin as well as foster sister during this time period. Then, in 1916, Cora died, and her husband, C. N., permitted Marie to adopt Josephine, which proceeding was carried out in the Multnomah County Court of Domestic Relations. The Weeks, who had become de facto guardians of Josephine after Cora's death, refused to relinquish the child to Marie. Marie accused the Weeks of holding Josephine for financial gain, making her do "house work and other drudgery" and holding out on her eventual inheritance. The Weeks accused Marie of being an unfit mother, citing her precarious finances, multiple divorces, and general character. After hearing the evidence, the court denied Marie's writ and awarded custody of Josephine to Lloyd and Florence Weeks.

Summary of Proceedings: January 7th, 1913 the Secretary of Commerce and Labor issued a warrant for Marie Miler. She was arrested by an officer of immigration on the 8th and was charged with "being an alien found in the United States in violation of the Act of Congress of February 20, 1907, as amended by the Act approved March 26, 1910, to-wit: That she is an was a member of one of the classes of aliens required to be deported under the laws of the United States, to-wit: (That the said alien was connected with a house of prostitution, and practiced prostitution and derived benefits therefrom after she entered the United States." However the petition states that Marie was not able to defend herself because they only notified her of her right to an attorney after the immigration office examined her, as well as her attorney did not show up to court. The immigration office said they contacted the attorney Roger Marchetti and that he said he would show up but did not. Marie's new attorney believes it is the immigration office's fault for not getting him there and also not conveying that he was being resistant to Marie Miler. Marie also believes that her former partner or husband (both are used) is trying to get rid of her and take her property with other men in town. Marie says their affidavits are fake testimony because they are all conspiring to get her property (these men are referred to as the Italians). Marie seeks to be discharged because she was not represented by counsel, she paid him and he did not appear. The Immigration office believes the "petitioner alone is responsible for the neglect of her attorney". The new attorney working with Marie is Elias A Wright for her habeas petition. The petition is granted and the writ follows but her writ is subsequently denied ("quashed") because there are laws saying only the immigration officer has to be "satisfied" with proceedings for them to be valid (among other laws stated in both defendant and petitioner's briefs).

Summary of Proceedings: The husband of Emma E. Howard, Clark W. Howard absented himself and deserted her, and they remained separate. She was took care of their child, Lillian Violet, but without her consent, Clark stole the child. Emma claimed that he had vicious habits and not a suitable person to care for the child. Then he placed the child in the care of Julia Moore, Mother of Mary Michael, mother superior of St. James Orphanage in Benson in Omaha. Emma proved her character and ability to take care of her daughter, and Lillian was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 14, 1862, Abner S. Nancy petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Captain William M. Matthews. Nancy explained that he had enlisted at the age of seventeen without the consent of his parents and therefore Captain Matthews was unlawfully detaining him at or near Lewiston Washington. Nancy also claimed he had not been paid as promised for his enlistment. Judge Oliphant allowed the petition, but the outcome of this case and Nancy's fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 12, 1916, Festino Ranurez was arrested on a mittimus signed by Vincent C. Hascall, a justice of the peace in Douglas County, Nebraska. There was no charge stated, and he was incarcerated in the Douglas County jail simply to be "held for further investigation." On January 20, 1917, with no formal legal proceedings begun against him, Joseph O. Burger, Ranurez's attorney, filed a writ of habeas corpus against the Douglas County sheriff, Michael L. Clark, who produced Ranurez in court on January 24 in front of judge Willis G. Sears. A writ of return was filed on January 26, 1917, but the fate of Ranurez is unknown, except for the fact that a man with his name was buried in Omaha on March 27, 1918.

Summary of Proceedings: On December 12, 1885, Ella Hibbs filed for a writ of habeas corpus for her husband I.N. Hibbs because she claimed that he was being illegally detained by U.S. Marshal Fred Dubois. Marshal Dubois claimed that Hibbs was a fugitive from justice from Idaho Territory. In the files it shows that Hibbs was charged with the crime of forgery in Idaho Territory, and was found not guilty. Hibbs was the postmaster of Lewiston, Idaho, and illegally used postal money orders. Eventually, Hibbs went to British Columbia and was extradited to be tried in Idaho again for another charge of writing forged postal orders. When the habeas petition was filed, Hibbs was in Oregon and was awaiting transportation to Idaho for another trial. Judge Deady denied the writ and remanded Hibbs to the custody of Marshal Dubois. The Case File contains the Idaho Court proceedings, Judge Deady's full opinion, and other extradition documents.

Summary of Proceedings:
Gladys Brown filed for a writ of habeas corpus after she was arrested on December 5, 1921 on a warrant of deportation issued by E. J. Henning. In her petition, Brown argued that the Spokane Immigrant Inspector, B. E. Gowen was illegally restraining her of her liberty by holding her in the Salvation Army Detention Home. Brown further argued that she was denied her right to a hearing and to due process. In his return to the writ, Gowen noted that Gladys Brown was granted several hearings dating back to April of 1920 and that the information from those hearings lead to Henning issuing a warrant of deportation on September 23, 1921. Judge. Edward E. Cushman ordered that Brown's petition for a writ of habeas corpus be denied and ordered that Gladys Brown will remain in the custody of B. E. Gowen. 

Gladys Brown was also formerly married to Herbert Brown who appears in another Habeas Corpus petition submitted at the same time. Herbert and Gladys divorced between the initial hearings with the Immigrant Inspector and their arrests in December 1921. Herbert Brown and their young child are not mentioned anywhere in this case file.

Summary of Proceedings: Minnie and Norberg were married, living with their daughter, Corine. Minnie and Norberg stopped living together on May 28, 1900 and Norberg deserted Minnie and Corine with no support. Norberg threatened to abduct the child. Abducted the child on January 31, 1901. Minnie got Corine again and put her somewhere safe, visiting her daily. Minnie wanted a divorce and had another case pending for that. In that case she asked for custody of the child. In this case, Minnie is asking for a Writ of Habeas Corpus to get her child discharged from Norberg’s custody. Case filed on March 7, 1901. Corine was in custody of Norberg during the habeas trial. Writ allowed, returnable on March 9th. After “diligent searching,” the police could not find Corine Bradley in Douglas County. On March 7, 1901 the State of Nebraska commanded Sheriff to summon Norberg to appear before judge B.S. Baker to show the cause of taking and detaining Corine Bradley. Filed June 4, 1901.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 16, 1886, notary public William J. Houston was tasked with receiving a deposition from Bertha Dogge on a civil case, Hart Bros., et al vs. Otto Dogge, Bertha Dogge, and Christian G. Herald. Bertha Dogge refused, and Houston found her in contempt of court and ordered her arrest. On July 22, 1886, Bertha Dogge petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that sheriff Samuel Melick had unlawfully deprived her of her freedom. After examining the evidence, Judge Pound remanded her into the custody of Melick. The next day, Supreme Court Judge Amasa Cobb upheld the decision, but he allowed Bertha to file a writ of error and ruled that Bertha be able to be released on her own recognizance provided that she pay a sum of $250.

Summary of Proceedings:
George Coffey and attorney, A. J. Kinseley, filed petition against John J. Donahoe on October 27 claiming that Coffey was being held without any commitment. It was further charged that Coffey had been held since September 8, and was still being held after found innocent of charges. His charge is left unspecified. Petition was granted, but the fate of Coffey is unknown.

Newspaper coverage indicates Coffey had been acquitted of highway robbery charges, but remained accused of assisting in a jail break at Leavenworth Prison in Kansas.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 5th, 1887, George Woodard was arrested by Sheriff James Glispin for unlawfully selling intoxicating liquor. Justice of the Peace J. R. Yildea then tried Woodard for the alleged crime. Woodard filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on July 8th, 1887, claiming that he was being unlawfully imprisoned and being held on excessive bail. Judge George Turner heard the writ and ordered J. R. Yildea, James Glispin, George Woodard, and two other witnesses to appear in court on July 9th, 1887. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the Woodard are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward Gibbons claimed to have been unlawfully detained by Felix J. McShane and Henry Schroeder. The witnesses called in to testify for the case described Gibbons as attempting to steal a car and then running away, yet none of the witnesses saw Gibbon's face. Through witness testimony, people explain that Gibbons was not at the scene of the crime and was at work during the time and then was arrested at work.  Edward was accused of grand larceny and was eventually released from custody because of insufficient evidence of his guilt.

Summary of Proceedings: A Native mother, Ah- lit- quah, allegedly signed an agreement with the Friends Mission School for Indians on Douglas Island that placed her 3 year old daughter, Nu- Shukk (Sarah Woodard) in the school. According to the document signed by a representative from the school and Ah- lit- quah, Nu-Shukk was also placed in the custody of Charles N. Replogle until she reach 18 years of age, or was discharged by Replogle for whatever reason. Ah- Lit- Quah took her daughter out of school shortly after enrollment and refused to return the child to the superintendent. Replogle filed a writ of habeas corpus for the child. The writ was granted and Judge Warren Truitt ordered Ah- lit- quah to bring Nu- Shukk to court. When she did not comply with the order, a warrant for her arrest was issued. Ah- lit- quah was arrested and Nu- Shukk was returned to the boarding school under the custody of Replogle.

Summary of Proceedings: In January 1919, Pete Jolett filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the ground he was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Michael L. Clark, Sheriff of Douglas County. Jelott was charged with having possession of intoxicating liquor, found guilty, and sentenced to pay a fine of $100 and the costs of prosecution. The petition alleged the complaint does not charge Jelott with an offense illegal under the laws of the State of Nebraska. Judge Arthur C. Wakeley allowed the petition but denied the writ. Jelott's attorney filed a motion for a new trial on the grounds the decision of the court was not sustained by sufficient evidence, contrary to law, and the court erred in refusing to discharge Jelott as the complaint did not state an offense cognizable under the laws of the State of Nebraska. It is likely this motion was denied, as the appearance docket states Jelott was later released on recognizance in sum of $200.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 28, 1844, Martha Drusilla filed both a plea of trespass against Richmond Curle and a writ of habeas against both Curle and William Isbell. In her petitions she alleged that she was born free in Alabama, but appears to have become enslaved or at least indentured at some point. She files the writ of habeas in order to win her freedom and be released from the custody of Curle and Isbell. Witnesses are called on both sides, and the case progresses until eventually escalating into a proper court case before a jury. The last documents are the judge’s instructions to the jury dated to February of 1846, but the jury’s verdict is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Petitioner Henry Burman was married to Ida in 1879. They had a twelve-year-old daughter named May. When they divorced they agreed that May would remain in the custody of her grandparents, Mary and Stephan Goodell. Petitioner learned that May was in Deadwood, SD with Ida and a man named Walter Steinspring whom she had married and divorced. She remained in Deadwood after their divorce and “entered upon a life of easy virtue,” working in saloons and keeping the child with her. She allowed the child to “act and play” at places known as “Saloon Theaters.” According to the petition, this is where the “lowest of the demimonde congregate” in the city. Ida temporarily placed May in the care of Mary and Stephan Goodell while she remained in Deadwood. Petitioner stated that he was remarried, had a business and property, and was able to give May a good life. 
Henry alleged that his daughter, May, was being unlawfully deprived of her liberty by Ida Steinspring, Mary Goodell, or Stephan Goodell. Judge Scott determined that Mary and Stephan are suitable people to be entrusted with the care and custody of May Burman but that the listed Ida Steinspring was not a fit or suitable person. The Court ordered that May Burman be remanded back to the custody of Mary and Stephan Goodell and that Henry Burman had the right to visit her. They further ordered that Henry Burman pay the costs of the trial.

Summary of Proceedings: David A. and Mary C. McKay petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against L. J. Covington, the superintendent of the Washington Children’s Home Society. The McKays argued that Covington was illegally detaining their son, Kenneth, at his institution. They recounted that they had placed Kenneth into the care and custody of Winifred McGrath while they went to California, and claimed that McGrath had placed Kenneth in the care of the Washington Children’s Home Society without their permission and under the false assumption that the McKay’s had abandoned Kenneth. Covington admitted that Kenneth had been housed with the Washington Children’s Home Society but had since been adopted. A witness was called to testify for the good character of Mary McKay, that she did not intend to abandon Kenneth, and that she had contacted Covington in an attempt to retrieve him. The case file does not reveal the outcome nor Kenneth’s fate.

Summary of Proceedings:
Vincenzo Ubaldino was, prior to this case, deported to Canada where he had resided for over ten years, for attempting to 'procure a woman for immoral purposes." After attempting to re-enter the United States in violation of the Immigration Act of February 5, 1917, Ubaldino, whose father was from Italy, was set to be deported to Italy. Ubaldino petitioned for habeas corpus and ordered a show of cause.
Because there was no evidence that Ubandino was native to Italy outside of his father living in the country, he was ordered for re-deportation to Canada instead.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 7, 1919, Iris Jones left her common-law husband, Frank Jones, taking their two children, Ray, age 5, and Madeleine, age 3, with her. Iris relocated from the family's previous home at 2812 Davenport St. in Omaha to the home of one Antone Paulsen at 2769 Capitol Avenue, who she soon married. She also took Thelma West, her daughter from a previous marriage. While the couple was living in Omaha with the children, their home was investigated by the Juvenile Authorities of the City of Omaha, after which they skipped town for St. Louis, leaving Ray in the custody of Iris's brother, Clyde McNamet, in Davenport, Iowa. However, on June 1, 1919, Iris and Antone returned to Omaha with the children, placing them in the custody of Etta Jackson, a widow who ran a children's home. Iris continued to support the children by working at a restaurant. Frank visited Mrs. Jackson's home many times asking for custody of his children, but she refused, even though Frank maintained that he was entirely capable and had the resources to take care of his children. Apparently, one time when Frank came to retrieve his children, a crowd of around 30 of Jackson's neighbors tried to stop him, chasing after him and throwing stones, because they thought he was trying to kidnap the children. Therefore, Jones filed a writ of habeas corpus on July 24, 1919. The next day, a subpoena was filed against a man named Tony Loggia who presumably had some relation to Mrs. Jackson. While on the stand, both parties accused the other of adultery, and Iris accused Ray of cruelty. She said to the court, "Them children is all I have to live for." The writ was denied on July 30, and, for reasons unclear, the children were placed in the home of an Omaha couple, Mr. and Mrs. Herman Bianchi of 4702 N 37th St. in Omaha on May 10 of the next year. Perhaps these were distant relatives or the proprietors of another children's home. Additionally, Mr. Jones had to pay the couple $8 per week for the children's maintenance. Both Frank and Iris disapproved of this decision, filing separate motions to have the writ vacated, which it was on August 1, 1921. Mr. Jones and his new wife, Ella sued for custody on August 24, 1921, supported by a motion by Iris stating that he should receive custody, and after an extended hearing, he was granted custody on October 1 of that year. The couple reached a custody agreement where Frank would write his ex-wife frequently to let her know how the children were doing and she could visit once every three months.

Summary of Proceedings:
Petitioner alleged that on 19 April 1894, Elmer P. Quivey of the Nebraska Children’s Home Society unlawfully entered her home and took her three children. The three children were Daniel Jones, 7 years old, John Loyal Jones, 3.5 years old, and Bessie Jean Jones, 1.5 years old. Petitioner claimed that she was the lawful mother of the children and was entitled to their custody. Petitioner, Maggie Jones, married a man named Daniel Jones on 7 June 1875. On 12 April 1894, Daniel Jones abandoned Maggie and the three children, leaving them in her care, custody, and control. Petitioner sent requests directly to Mr. Quivey but he has refused to surrender the children to her custody. 

Judge Cunningham R. Scott reviewed the petition and allowed the writ, returnable on 25 July 1894. Sheriff John Drexel served the writ to Mr. Quivey on 19 July 1894, requesting that he appear in court on the aforementioned date, bringing with him the three children and his cause for custody. Mr. Quivey submitted his case, denying the allegations submitted by Petitioner and asserting that Ms. Jones was fully aware of what would happen upon relinquishing the children to the Nebraska Children’s Home Society. He produced a paper, signed by Ms. Jones, which relinquished the custody of the three children. He explains that the paper was fully explained to Ms. Jones by Mr. C. S. Benawa, a member of the Children’s Home Society. He explained that if she placed the children in the custody of the home, they would have the right to place them in homes and that she would have to relinquish all rights to the children. She agreed to these terms. The Court documents include scanned copies of the forms signed by Ms. Jones showing the terms of the agreement, explicitly stated, along with her assent to each of these terms.

In her response, Ms. Jones admits to signing this paper but asserts that she was not fully aware of the terms of the paper. She claims that she did not realize that the paper would preclude her from knowing where the children were or from having the right to visit them. She explains that, at the time she signed the paper, she was in a period of “extreme anguish” following the departure of Mr. Daniel Jones. She feared that the family would go hungry and was “under the influence of extreme distress,” so she signed the paper. Due to the nature of the situation, she claims that singing the paper was not truly a voluntary act. She was not made aware of the terms of the paper until some time later when she attempted to visit the children and learn of their whereabouts.
Ms. Jones and her attorneys ask that, if she is not allowed custody of her children, she at least be allowed visitation rights and the privilege of knowing their whereabouts. 

Mr. Quivey motioned for the cause to be dismissed on the grounds that Ms. Jones was aware of the terms of the contract and assented to relinquishing custody of her children to the Children’s Home Society. Judge Scott dismissed the cause on 26 July 1894, upholding the motion submitted by Mr. Quivey but ordering that the costs of the trial be paid by respondent.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 13, 1894, George Matson whipped his wife, Mary Matson, and choked her. On June 19th, 1894, he was convicted with disturbing the peace for these actions by Judge John Tutt. He was sentenced to pay 500 dollars and hard labor in county jail for 80 days. On June 20, 1894, he filed for an application for a writ of Habeas Corpus with his attorney, Allen Garner, on the grounds that the commitment is “wholly defective and void and inoperative”. This writ was addressed to the Honorable T. J. Humes, but was granted by R. Osborn. The writ was delivered to J. H. Woolery, the Sheriff of King County, who brought Matson to the courthouse. The outcome of the case is unknown.

The affidavits have signatures from individuals in Rockford Illinois, and Boise City, Idaho.

Summary of Proceedings: Louie Young petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Joel Warren. Young claimed he was arrested alongside 28 others in their hotel on an open charge and was now being held in the Seattle City Jail. Newspaper records indicated Young was arrested during a raid on a Chinese gambling house and charged with disorderly conduct. He alleged he was forced by the Seattle Health Commission to undergo a blood test and was declared free of disease, but was not released. Due to the brevity of the case file, the case outcome and the fate of Young are unknown. Several of the other arrested persons petitioned separately for writs of habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: Wong Dick, a Chinese national, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigrant inspector Alfred Hampton. Dick claimed Hampton was holding him illegally at the Spokane County Jail. Dick alleged he was arrested alongside Wong Ging, who filed a separate petition for habeas corpus, for the possession of opium. Dick was sentenced to 90 days in the county jail, but was now being held past his sentence and threatened with deportation. Hampton returned with the warrants for Dick’s rearrest and deportation on the basis of the Immigration Act of 1917. Judge J. Stanley Webster ordered Hampton to release Dick from custody and no longer pursue deportation. Hampton appealed to the Ninth Circuit, claiming Webster stated no real facts entitling Dick to release. The Ninth Circuit court upheld Webster’s ruling.

Summary of Proceedings: Lulu Dawson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to establish custody of her daughter, Lucile Dawson, which was granted. At the hearing, the respondents, William and Myrtle Headrick, asserted that they made "no claim" to Lucile. They apparently ran a boarding house where Lulu had placed her daughter until she secured her a place at an orthopedic hospital. Lulu therefore withdrew her petition on the advice of her attorney and paid the court costs.

Summary of Proceedings: Bughi Michele was an Italian migrant who moved to Walla Walla, Washington in March of 1910. On July 2, 1910, the acting Secretary of Labor, Charles Earl, issued a warrant for Michele’s arrest. The warrant alleged that Michele was in violation of the Immigration Act of February 20, 1907 due to being a contract laborer that was enticed to migrate to the United States on the promise of employment. To try and prevent his deportation in October, Michele filed for a writ of habeas corpus. In his petition, Michele argued that the warrant against him did not have enough information to justify deportation. Judge George Donworth was the original judge for this case but stated he was too busy to rule on it and asked Frank H. Rudkin to preside over it. Rudkin ordered that the writ be denied and that the Immigration Inspector can start the deportation process of Bughi Michele. NARA records indicate a related case on 11-14-1910 in the Circuit Court located in Spokane, but that case folder is empty.

Summary of Proceedings: May Snyder petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to have her son, Augustus Milton Fleming returned to her custody. Augustus was under the watch and car of Mrs. Frank Thompson when May alleges that William Fleming illegally took the child. Mrs. Thompson had been arranged to watch the child so May could have time to work and earn money to properly care for her child. May Snyder notes that this arrangement was a part of her divorce arrangement with William Fleming which had William paying for Mrs. Thompson for watching and caring for Augustus. On November 6, 1893, Judge Robert Osborn approved the writ of habeas corpus and ordered that William Fleming return Augustus Milton Fleming to the custody and care of May Snyder.

Summary of Proceedings: In the summer of 1884, Herman Hadlan was arrested and charged with violating a pair of Olympia, Washington city ordinances prohibiting the sale of liquor without a license. He was found guilty, ordered to pay $5 and court costs, and sent to jail until he could pay. Hadlan petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, claiming that he had received permission from the city to keep his beer hall and, in any case, that the relevant city ordinances were void. His fate is unclear.

Summary of Proceedings:
On the June 23, 1901, petitioner J. T. Brown submitted a petition of habeas corpus on behalf of Forest McLean, alleging that he had been wrongfully taken into custody by his mother, respondent Helen McLean. Attached as evidence on behalf of the respondent were the proceedings of Helen McLean's  divorce J. S. McLean which established a custodial arrangement for Forest McLean involving the mother of J. S. McLean, Nancy Ann McLean and J. T. Brown. Under the custodial conditions, Forest McLean would stay with J. T. Brown until Nancy Ann McLean had moved to a certain location and was found to be a capable caregiver, at which point custody of Forest would transfer to her.
Helen McLean made several visits to see Forest at Nancy's and allegedly found him in a state of malnourishment and mistreatment, causing her to flee with him, breaking the arrangement stipulated in the divorce proceedings. J. T. Brown filed a habeas corpus petition to regain custody of Forest. This writ was allowed but it was found that Helen was a capable caregiver and could retain custody over Forest.
Attached is a case involving J. S. McLean, Forest McLean, and Helen McLean a year later after J. S. McLean had kidnapped Forest and found himself in contempt of the court. Once again it was found that Helen could retain custody over Forest.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward Rosewater, the petitioner, was charged with bribery to influence the republican legislative ticket of Douglas County, Nebraska, to secure votes by representatives elected if he secures the US senate seat. Rosewater then filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus because the State did not allow him to waive examination and refused to fix an amount for bond. He then walked out of the courtroom to waive the inspection, and a warrant was issued for his arrest. Furthermore, Rosewater stated that the police judge and the State's attorney are both of the same political party and, on this basis, sought to annoy, harass, and disgrace him before the next election. Finally, Rosewater stated that he is innocent and can prove it. Judge Benjamin Baker hears the writer and allows it, and Rosewater is released.

Summary of Proceedings: Anna Krim was born on February 17th, 1905 to Anna Elizabeth Krim, a single mother. Anna Elizabeth Krim soon after called the Washington Children's Home Society with the intention to give up the child as she was worried she would not be able to provide for her as a single mother. The Washington Children's Home Society had Krim sign a contract giving up her full claim of custody over the child, and the Society said their task was to find the baby a new home. About three weeks later, on March 10, 1905, Anna Elizabeth Krim filed a writ of habeas corpus in an attempt to regain custody of her daughter. She claimed that the details of the contract were not sufficiently explained to her and that she was not in the condition after giving birth to sign any legally binding documents. Judge Gilliam agreed with her on both these counts, and added that it seemed she had an “ignorance” of the English language that would also make the contract void. Unfortunately two days prior to Krim’s petition, the Society gave her baby away to a foster family in Ellensburg, Washington. Judge Gilliam ruled that the King County Superior Court had no jurisdiction to execute this writ as the bound party was not with the respondent, and the case was dismissed. The Washington Children's Home Society was represented by the legal firm Smith and Cole, but there is no indication in the case files nor the newspaper accounts as to which attorney in particular represented the Society and what their role in the case was.

After hearing the evidence, the writ was allowed and Burks released from custody. Since Burks had submitted his petition to the state district court, however, he had been detained on federal charges. The state district court found that the federal court should have "awaited the determination of this action" before commencing its proceedings, confirming that Burks should be released.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 12, 1862, William Smith was found guilty of grand larceny, specifically horse theft, by Justice of the Peace A. Dagget. He was put in jail in Walla Walla awaiting trial. The next day, he petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Walla Walla county sheriff James Buckley, claiming that there was no evidence to prove he commited the crime. He subpoenaed multiple witnesses on August 14, 1862. Buckley returned the writ of habeas corpus on August 15, stating that he produced Smith in front of Judge E. P. Oliphant. The state also subpoenaed several witnesses on August 16, 1862. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In 1885, Prosecuting Attorney S. C. Hyde, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to produce the body of Sterling P. White. White had been convicted and being held in the Seatco Territorial Penitentiary for the crime of manslaughter. Hyde petitioned in order for White to appear as a material witness in the case of the Territory of Washington v. Franklin Beander. Judge George M. Turner allowed the writ and commanded the Keepers of the Penitentiary to produce the body of White and bring him before the District Court of the Territory of Washington, with instructions to return White to the penitentiary after testifying. 

White had also petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus eight months earlier. (See: Sterling P. White v. John Cody)

Summary of Proceedings: D.L. Crowder was arrested on September 26th due to a warrant issued by Paul R. Deady, U.S. commissioner for the district, and put in the county jail on the 27th. He petitioned for the writ of habeas corpus against  L.T. Barin, U.S. Marshal, on October 2nd of 1890, due to an indictment filed by the grand jury in Kansas, the United States vs. D. Crowder, on April 14th, of the same year. The indictment was due to a charge of falsely impersonating a United States Officer “under 23 statutes, at large eleven.” Crowder claimed that the indictment failed to state facts to show a crime has been committed, and he had violated no laws. Kansas official statements show the charge was due to  “fraud” committed by Crowder on the Missouri Pacific Railway Company. They claimed he had pretended to be an employee of the Post Office and got a free ticket worth $3.21 for a voyage from Conway Springs, Kansas, to Larned, Kansas. The writ was granted to Crowder with no further details in the existing case. More information was seen from the Newspaper, The Oregonian, in February of 1891, claiming that he was, in fact, a postal inspector and that their fares are typically free.

Summary of Proceedings: Arch was an enslaved person that lived and worked for that of Eusebius Hubbard in the county of St. Louis, MO until August 1870. Around this time, Eusebius died and Arch petitioned a writ of habeas corpus for freedom indicating that he should be freed due to his enslaver dying. But Barnabas Harris still wants to recognize Arch as a slave and claims that he has no status as a free person. Judge N.B Tucker has ruled that he cannot try the case because law and Magna Charta only applies to free persons rather than the enslaved. Judge N.B. Tucker has ruled since he is unsure of the law and only wishes to abide by Organic constitutionality he will leave Arch in the possession of Barnabas Harris .

Summary of Proceedings: On April 26th, 1912, J.C. Christopher applied for a writ of habeas corpus with the help of his attorneys, Dalton and Bell. Christopher argued that he was illegally held in the county jail by Robert T. Hodge because he was arrested without warrant or due process. J. T. Ronald approves this writ and sets the date in court for April 30th, 1912. On the 29th, the return of Hodge is filed. Hodge argues that there was a warrant issued by John B. Gordon Justice of the Peace of King County, which came with the charge that Christopher was a fugitive from Justice of Utah. Under oath, John Lenes, whose role is otherwise unknown, says that on January 15th, 1912, Christopher was charged with the crime of neglecting to provide for his wife in Ogden, Utah. The charge was brought before him by his wife, Louisa Christopher, and he was charged by W.H. Roeder, Jr., of the Municipal Court of Ogden. At this point, Lenes says, Christopher fled Utah, and became a fugitive from justice in Washington. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: In July 1916, Chin Wah Hing petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his son Chin Doe Tung, an 18-year-old Chinese immigrant, who was denied entry to the United States and faced deportation. The decision was appealed and denied on the grounds that Chin Doe Tung was married before coming to the United States and had a wife in China. Judge Neterer authorized the writ but in his final ruling stated that the court's jurisdiction was limited to ascertaining whether the petitioner was denied an impartial hearing and ruled that Chin Doe Tung was not. Chin Doe Tung's petition was dismissed and writ discharged.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 28, 1894, Juok Joe filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Quack Ming, Chin Silk, Chin Gow and Chung Chong. Juok Joe claimed that Quack Ming, Chin Silk, Chin Gow and Chung Chong were being illegally detained on the Steamship Islander by Captain John Irving. Juok Joe further claimed that Quack Ming, Chin Silk, Chin Gow and Chung Chong were Chinese merchants who were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Act. Judge Bellinger granted the writ for Quack Ming, and Chung Chong. Judge Bellinger denied the writ for Chin Silk and Chin Gow.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 27, 1887, Jacob Schuman, a German immigrant, was accused of selling a pint of lager beer to A.L. McCauley. That same day, McCaulay filed a complaint with Justice of the Peace J. C. Dorr. After several delays, during which he was released on a $500 bond, Schuman was called in front of a grand jury. Dorr confined Schuman to the county jail on August 11, 1886. On August 16, 1886, Schuman filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against sheriff J.H. Hosler, stating that the law restricting liquor sales in Washington Territory, the Local Option Act, was unconstitutional and that he had a license to sell liquor from both Columbia County and the city of Dayton. His saloon had apparently been damaged as well, and he had not been offered any compensation for this. According to The Spokesman-Review out of Spokane, Judge William G. Langford agreed that Schuman's confinement was illegal, saying that the law wasn't on the books yet and that the state had an obligation to protect its licensees. The Washington Standard expressed relief that the law was ruled unconstitutional since it had proved counterproductive, "[resulting] literally in free whiskey in each precinct that voted for prohibition." Schuman was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Michal Kennedy filed for a writ to regain custody of his daughter, Zella Kennedy, from his wife, Anna Kennedy. He claimed that he and Ana lived separately, that Anna was destitute and incapable of taking care of Zella, and that he had originally held custody of Zella, only placing Zella in Anna’s care temporarily when Anna was sick “Out of pity and sympathy for Anna.” He further claimed that Anna had not returned Zella in the months since her sickness despite frequent requests to do so. The judge agreed to grant the writ and hear the petition, but the events of the hearing and the outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Jay D. Crary, the petitioner, was charged alongside four other men for defrauding many people by obtaining from the victims their money and property through fraudulent pretenses for the purpose of executing such a scheme through the use of US mail. Crary and his fellow defendants defrauded others through the purchase of shares of the capital stock of 
Clarinda Copper Mining Company in exchange for money and property with about $2,500 ($39,258.86 in 2023) owed to the United States. One of the victims of the alleged scheme is Rev. Aloysius Monsignor Pozzi of Vineland, New Jersey. The petition for Habeas Corpus by Crary states that he has been a longtime resident of Washington and is therefore not in contact with those in the States mentioned as connected to the fraud case (NY, AZ, CO) and that no probable cause was established pertaining to his guilt in his hearings. Judge Cushman reviewed the case and evidence and found that Crary should be discharged.

Summary of Proceedings: Antonio Seston petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus in March of 1924 after he had been arrested and then deprived of his liberty by Frank Hays Jr. in the previous year, Seston, having been born in Italy, made his way to New York where he applied for and received papers of naturalization, after which he had been and was residing in Omaha, Nebraska. When arrested, he was charged with violating the Immigration Act of 1917, with the prosecution arguing that he was dealing and having relations with prostitutes. Seston presented that he was being deprived of his liberty and held for the purpose of deportation and the court ruled for him to be discharged. It was April of the following year that Hays filed and was granted an appeal based upon assignments of error. It was June 1926, that a mandate from the Circuit Court of Appeals was filed reversing the decision to discharge Seston along with instruction to discharge the writ of Habeas Corpus and remand Seston for deportation.

Summary of Proceedings: Ethel Johnson was arrested on February 9, 1919 for keeping a "Common Illgoverned House." She was tried at police court under magistrate Charles E. Foster on the tenth and sentenced to thirty days in prison plus court costs. While she was sentenced to city jail, she was moved to county jail on February 12, which Johnson claimed in her case was irregular and not what the magistrate had ordered. She filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on February 13, which was issued. In her petition, she argued that the charges against her were not specific enough to charge her with a crime—a bold claim, given the shyness about sex in the early 20th century—and that the ordinance outlawing prostitution in the city of Omaha did not provide for prison sentences above ten days. However, in court on the 14th, she asked for her own case to be dismissed, likely because she had just filed another writ of habeas corpus against Clark.

Davenport claimed that he had been held in King County Jail for over 60 days without being brought to trial, and thus that Hodge was violating Davenport’s right to speedy legal proceedings. Hodge presented the warrant issuing Davenport’s arrest on the charge of indecent assault of a female minor. The case file does not state the outcome of the case or Davenport’s fate.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 2, 1903, Ida King petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. King had originally been arrested on the charge of larceny, accused of stealing $30. King asserted that she had been tried by a grand jury, and they had not found any indictment against her, and thus her continued imprisonment was illegal. Newspaper coverage indicated that King was a woman of color, but did not specify beyond that. Additionally, the newspapers stated that she was released and her writ was approved.

Summary of Proceedings: Eli Batten petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of his presumed relative, Delia Batten, with his attorney. Delia Batten was being held by J. J. Neligh (position or relation not specified). The writ was allowed and J. J. Neligh commanded to appear in court and show the cause of taking and detaining Delia Batten. Local newspaper coverage indicates that Delia McArdle, aged 14, married James Batten, aged 20, against the consent of Delia's family. Sheriff J. J. Neligh intervened with a mob of men and persuaded Delia to leave the Batten ranch where James had taken her to live with his father, Eli. Although newspaper accounts suggest the marriage was dissolved, census records indicate Delia and James married in 1887 and by 1900 had four living children (two did not survive).

Summary of Proceedings: Theofarius Mastoros, the petitioner, was a soldier in the United States serving in Company I, 361st Infantry at Camp Lewis, American Lake, in Pierce County, State of Washington. Mastoros never filed a claim for exemption, but the petition implies that an attempt was made to file a claim for discharge after arrival at the mobilization camp. Mastoros was a subject of Greece while within the United States and argued that he was not liable for compulsory service in the military or naval forces of the U.S. and could not be compelled to serve, especially as Greece was a foreign and neutral country. The petition outcome and fate of the petitioner are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: C. T. Fenner petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Spokane County Sheriff LeRoy C. Waller and immigrant inspector James E. McGovern. Fenner alleged that he was a Canadian immigrant being held in the Spokane County Jail for over 90 days awaiting deportation. He claimed that he would willingly return to Canada, but was being refused because proceedings for his deportation were already underway. Fenner motioned to file his petition forma pauperis. The warrant of deportation claimed that Fenner and two presumed relatives were in violation of the Immigration Act of February 20th, 1907 because they were “likely to become public charges at the time of their entry into the United States.” The court dismissed the writ, claiming that deportment procedures were complete, and Fenner was deported to Canada.
