Summary of Proceedings: Joe Hill filed a petition for writ of habeas corpus for his wife, Vera Hill. Both Joe and Vera were arrested by police officers and later charged with being disorderly persons. Joe Hill was eventually released and had his charge dropped, however Vera Hill remained in custody. In his petition, Joe argues that Vera is being held without any hearing and has been refused the possibility of bail. The Chief of Police in his response to the writ noted that Vera is being held for having the “infectious and contagious disease” of syphilis and has been transferred to the custody of the City Health Commissioner, J. S. McBride at the city’s isolation hospital. The outcome of the petition and the fate of the bound party are not included in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 5th, 1914, petitioner arrived from China. On August 27th, the petitioner was presented evidence on their allegedly illegal presence in the country. On September 28th, 1914, an order was issued which allowed J.B. Densmore to execute the powers of the Secretary of Labor in their absence and ordered deportation of the petitioner. On September 29th, 1914, Staten & Stewart administered an appeal to the Secretary of Labor on behalf of the petitioner claiming that a fair trial was not given and Densmore did not have the authority to review the case. A case was then opened in the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia under Justice Gould as to whether the respondents should be compelled to be deposed. The Judge ruled that being deposed would not be prejudicial to the public interest. On September 29th, 1914, a writ was issued. On October 16th, 1914, a return to writ was issued claiming that Ching Hing was a Chinese native and that the denial of entry was correct. On October 20th, 1914, the petitioners filed a stipulation as to the deposition of Louis F. Post, Assistant Secretary of State, as to their status on the day that the review was conducted. On March 24th, 1915, an order was issued to allow a bond of $15,000. On April 2nd, 1915, a return to petition was filed by the petitioners asking the deposition order to not be vacated. On April 10th, 1915, a return to writ was filed. On April 21st, 1915, a memorandum brief was issued stating that the petitioner should be discharged unless the deportation order was made by someone with the authority to do so. On April 27th, 1915, the government filed a memorandum brief which claimed that the questions presented by the petitioner are moot points and asks that the case be dismissed. On May 11, 1915, the writ was discharged and the petitioner was remanded to the custody of the Department of Immigration. The judge rules that the argument was technical and the petitioners could hope for a delay at best. The judge further ruled that the requested depositions are disposed of and that the petitioner did not have a right to an attorney before the Secretary of Labor. On May 29th, 1915, Judge Neterer dismissed the writ and remanded the petitioner to custody. On June 1st, 1915, an appeal was entered to the 9th Circuit Court.

Summary of Proceedings: Christ Antonopulous was arrested for disturbing the peace in South Omaha on June 13 by Chief of Police, John Briggs, and brought before the Police Court on June 17. Antonopulous was found guilty on June 20 and fined $100, costs, and held to 30 days of hard labor. Antonopulous and attorney, John M. Macfarland, petitioned for habeas against John Briggs, E. F. Brailey, and Frank F. Osborn on June 22. Antonopulous argued that he played no part in the disturbance and was being unlawfully detained. On June 27, the writ of habeas was sustained and Antonopulous was released.

Summary of Proceedings:
Jerome E. Corbin filed a writ of habeas corpus to release his son, Frank E. Corbin, a minor who wrongfully represented to military recruiters that he was twenty-one when he was only eighteen. Jerome claimed to have sent numerous letters to the War Department in 1903 to request his son's release.

Judge Hanford approved the petition and ordered the Army to produce Corbin in a week, by January 18. The writ was served on Colonel J. F. Huston, the officer in charge of Company D, 9th Infantry. 

In their response, the government -- represented by three attorneys -- claimed that the young man was already subject to a military court proceeding for fraudulent enrollment. Claiming congressional supremacy and citing precedent that in cases involving courts martial, the military stated they retained jurisdiction over claims of habeas corpus and that their proceedings were in advance of any other proceedings. Jerome Corbin filed a response, claiming that the Army proceedings came after the writ was filed. Judge Hanford agreed with the government's position and returned Corbin to Colonel Huston for the military preceding.

Summary of Proceedings:
Janet Mackay, formerly Janet Roy, a Scottish woman residing in the US was arrested on June 24th, 1918 for plotting to overthrow the US government and holding materials advocating sedition and socialism. She and her sister initially immigrated to New York in October of 1916, where they worked as housekeepers. They then headed to Chicago where they found work in bindery for the newly formed Industrial Workers of the World.​​ In October 1918 the Roy sisters moved to Seattle, Washington despite investigation into their ties to the IWW. The were arrested shortly after. The sisters were held in custody by Henry M. White, US Commissioner of Immigration for Seattle. The case was heard by judge Jeremiah Neterer in the US District Court for Washington. 
While temporarily out on bond and while awaiting deportation, Janet married Ivan Valentine Mackay, a fellow Scottish immigrant who believed he was a naturalized citizen. The court dismissed his claim of citizenship and said the marriage did not certify Janet as a citizen who could not be deported. Mackay's attorney repeatedly asked about the fairness of the case, in part because of the relationship between Judge Neterer and defendant White. In March of 1919 the case was decided and Janet’s application for a writ of habeas was denied. Janet Mackay was officially ordered to be deported.

Summary of Proceedings: John N. Baldwin, the petitioner and petitioner attorney, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on behalf of Anna Walter in 1922 after her incarceration for being an alleged fugitive from justice from the state of Maine. The warrant from Maine stated to arrest Margaret Sterling, aliases Mrs. A. Willard and Mrs. Robert Walter, for fraud. Anna Walter's petition stated that she was not in Portland, Maine, during the time of the crime. Furthermore, Robert Walter, husband of Anna, verified that he is her husband and can verify that she was not in the state of Maine during the time of the alleged offense. The petitioner team filed for a new trial and appealed to the Supreme Court; the appeal to the Supreme Court of Nebraska was dismissed at the cost of the petitioner. A new writ of Habeas was filed in February of 1922 after the Supreme Court dismissal; the outcome is unclear.

Summary of Proceedings: L. J. Urann petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff L. C. Smith and Massachusetts agent Morris Wolf on July 1, 1905. He claimed that he was imprisoned without due process or warrant as a fugitive from justice because he was falsely accused of larceny under Massachusetts law. He claimed that a witness had falsely accused him in order to extort money from him to pay a civil debt. Smith responded that the detention of Urann was legal because Washington State governor Albert Mead had ordered the detention so that Urann could be returned to Massachusetts. Judge Cornelius H. Hanford ordered that Smith and Wolf show cause for Urann's detention. Hanford denied Urann's petition and remanded him to Smith's custody. Urann petitioned for appeal, and his ultimate fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
Minnie Sprouse was a young girl  born to Carrie Sprouse and Edward Sprouse. Emma Voorhes was Minnie’s maternal grandmother, and one day Ms. Voorhes took her away from her parents and brought her to the Voorhes residence to stay. Minnie’s parents became frustrated and demanded that she be returned to them as soon as possible but Ms. Voorhes refused and stated that she would kill both Edward and Carrie if they ever tried to take Minnie away from her. It was speculated by the Parents that they must act fast or Ms. Voorhes will flee with Minnie out of the jurisdiction and to the state of Missouri making the case harder to navigate.

In June of 1896 both Sprouse parents filed a petition of habeas corpus in an attempt to regain custody of Minnie. After the processing of the writ and hearing of the petition, Minnie Sprouse was found to belong to the legal custody of her parents and ordered to be returned.

Summary of Proceedings: Adelard Pouliot petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against A. F. Richardson, an Immigrant Inspector. Pouliot claimed that he was a Canadian immigrant who had filed paperwork toward naturalization in the United States. He claimed that he and his wife, Blanche Masse Pouliot, visited Canada by train and were allowed to return with no issue, but that a warrant for his deportation from the U.S. was issued soon after by the U.S. Department of Commerce and Labor. Adelard Pouliot alleged that the warrant accused him of bringing a prostitute with him from Canada to the U.S., which he denied. He claimed the U.S. Department of Commerce and Labor had no authority to arrest him, and that his imprisonment at the Spokane County Jail was illegal. Richardson responded with several testimonies that claimed Blanche Pouliot, AKA Blanche Robinson, ran a house of prostitution in Ione, WA and that Adelard Pouliot was a regular customer. Richardson also claimed that Adelard Pouliot was not a naturalized citizen as he did not show up to his naturalization hearing, to which Pouliot replied that he had not been made aware of his hearing. Blanche Pouliot filed a separate petition for a writ of habeas corpus wherein the court ruled both writs were denied and both Adelard and Blanche Pouliot were to be deported to Canada.

Summary of Proceedings:
Ah Quong filed a petition on behalf of six Chinese individuals detained by E. V. Rugar. Quong claims that Rugar has no legitimate cause or claim to detain and imprison the Chinamen. The petition was granted and a writ of habeas corpus was issued. The fate of the six Chinamen is unknown.

Local newspaper coverage indicates that Wong Hing, Wong Sam, Fook Gee/Zee, and Ah Moke were allowed to stay in Seattle while Ah Gee and Ah Sam were deported via Vancouver, B.C. (not all names align perfectly between the case and the newspaper report, which is typical in cases involving Chinese petitioners).

Summary of Proceedings:
Bell was held by Sheriff McDonald for over a week, the cause of his detention unknown to him. Petitioner Henry Bell asked for a writ of habeas corpus to be issued on the grounds of unlawful imprisonment (deprivation of liberty). The writ was filed and granted on 2 April 1898. Judge Slabaugh ordered that Bell be returned on 4 April 1898, directing that order to Sheriff McDonald. A copy of the writ was officially filed with the Sheriff on 2 April 1898. A document was entered to the record stating that Henry Bell should be kept in custody for further examination as he had been charged with drunkenness on 26 March 1898; this record was signed and ordered by Police Judge Samuel I. Gordon. 

Bell appeared in court on 4 April 1898 and Judge Slambaugh signed an order releasing him on that same day stating, “it is therefore ordered that said Henry Bell be discharged from the custody of John McDonald Sheriff and from said unlawful detention."

On 17 May 1898, a motion was filed by Ablyn L. Frank (Clerk for the District Court) asking that the costs be taxed to Douglas County and paid out of the County Treasury. The motion was sustained and the County was ordered to pay the sum.

Summary of Proceedings: Rhoda McNamira alleged that he was unlawfully restrained of his liberty by Martin White and that no complaint had been brought against him, nor had he received a trial upon his charge. White charged McNamira with grand larceny and said the complaint was filed and a bond was issued for $600 and never paid and thus explains why McNamira is imprisoned. Judge Slabaugh decided that McNamira was unlawfully held. However the fate of the bound party is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: H. E. Lusher petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of S. Stradley against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham and Captain of Detectives Charles Tennant. Lusher alleged that Stradley was arrested without warrant and with no charge brought against him, and thus that he was being illegally held in the Seattle City Jail. The outcome of the petition and the fate of Hart are unknown. Lusher filed petitions for writs of habeas corpus on the behalf of three other men who were arrested on the same day by the same detectives.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 27th, 1912, James Fitzpatrick was charged with Second Degree Burglary. On June 5th, Fitzpatrick was found “Not Guilty”. Judge J. T. Ronald immediately ordered Fitzpatrick to be held by Robert T. Hodge, Sheriff of King County, on the purported order that there was a warrant for his arrest in California. Fitzpatrick argued that there was no warrant, and that he suspected he was being held maliciously by two detectives of the Seattle police, Tennant and Barton. The writ was granted by judge J. T. Ronald and asked that Hodge appear with Fitzpatrick in court on the 10th. On the 10th, during Hodge’s return, he said he was holding Fitzpatrick on a warrant for arrest issued by Fred C. Brown, a Justice of the Peace for the City of Seattle. Attached to this return is the said warrant from Justice Brown, which stated that Fitzpatrick, alias J. E. Summary of Proceedings: On December 20, 1913, Fred Boughton and his attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, and stated that Boughton was being held without a warrant. Sheriff Edward Cudihee denied his claims, and produced a warrant dated December 22, 1913 from Judge Fred Brown. The warrant stated that Boughton was a fugitive from justice from Iowa. Boughton had originally been charged with grand larceny, and left Iowa while on parole. The writ was dismissed with prejudice, and Boughton remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
Catherine Paulint filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on May 6, 1892 for the custody of Josephine Anna Boynton, aged ten, from her father, Frank F. Boynton. Josephine had been in the care of Catherine, living in Tewksbury, Massachusetts, since the death of Josephine’s mother, Rosalie Adeline Boynton, in 1891. 

After his second marriage, Frank returned to Massachusetts from Seattle, Washington to retrieve his daughter against the wishes of Catherine. According to newspaper coverage, Catherine followed Frank and Josephine to Seattle immediately, cross country, and initiated legal proceedings for custody of Josephine. While coverage indicated another hearing on May 24, 1893, the outcome of the petition is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Edda L. A. Evenson filed for a writ of habeas corpus. The petition and motion to dismiss for want of jurisdiction was scheduled to be heard by Judge Eleazer Wakeley at a later date. Newspaper coverage indicates Edda was the daughter of Henrekka and Andrew Evenson, who separated. Henrekka took Edda to a convent school in Minneapolis, but Andrew kidnapped her and retuned with Edda to Omaha. Henrekka filed a habeas writ as part of a divorce proceeding. The resulting custody settlement is not known.

Summary of Proceedings: Samuel Jackson, a Chilkat Alaskan Native, was arrested after he "struck one M. A. Reason with his hands and fists" at the Chemawa Indian School. He was charged with assault and battery in the Justice's Court of Salem, Oregon and jailed when he refused to pay the $20 fine. Jackson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the Marion County Circuit Court, which was granted. Jackson argued that the Justice's Court did not have the jurisdiction to try him, since he committed the offense on federal land. After hearing the evidence, Jackson was released. (A second petition was found in this file. There is no obvious relationship between the two petitions.)

Summary of Proceedings:
Peter Clifford filed two petitions for habeas corpus, eventually combined into one in June 1904. Clifford was the ex-husband of Grace Williams and lived in San Francisco. Divorced the prior year, Williams was awarded custody of their daughter Alice, and Clifford was awarded visitation rights every week. 

In his petition, Peter claimed that Grace had "surreptitiously and secretly" left Seattle for San Franciso and that he had received a ruling in his favor from a San Francisco court that reversed the custody arrangement and placed Alice in his custody. Between their divorce and Peter's claim in California, Grace married Herbert Williams and the couple formally adopted Alice and renamed her Alice Williams in a Seattle court in December 1903. 

The primary arguments in this case revolved around jurisdictions. Initially, Judge Tallman ruled for the Williams's and seemed to have been swayed by Grace's testimony about Peter's abusive alcoholism. Clifford claimed that the U. S. Constitution's clauses forced the state of Washington to accept and respect a California court's ruling in his favor. The case then moved to Federal Court (it is not entirely clear how it got from State court to the Ninth Circuit) and Judge Hanford upheld Grace's custody and dismissed the habeas petitions.

Summary of Proceedings: John Barton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his nephew and ward, Horatio Marsden, from Stephen Denny, who was Marsden's brother-in-law. (The documentation vacillates on whether Barton or Marsden was the legal petitioner.) Barton accused Denny of illegally detaining Marsden. Denny countered that he did not detain Marsden, but rather that Marsden chose to live with him; that Barton was abusive; and that, in any case, Marsden had departed from his home. The court granted Barton's petition, but Marsden's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Carl O. Nelson is the father of Georgia Catherine Nelson, a three-year-old girl in the custody of her grandmother, Pearl Nelson. Pearl was Carl's mother, but Carl filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus against Pearl, claiming she is holding his daughter illegally. Pearl stated that young Georgia has been under her care since Georgia's mother passed away because Carl had consented for Pearl to adopt Georgia; however, the adoption was never done. Carl recently remarried after the passing of Georgia's mother and argued that he and his new wife would provide a stable and loving household for Georgia. The courtroom debate got heated: Carl's sister, in the audience, stood up and said "He is not entitled to this child. Look at what he did to his first wife," after which Pearl burst into tears.The judge agreed and granted Carl a writ of habeas corpus, ordering Pearl to release the child from her custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Mori Tsuchine, a Japanese immigrant, was arrested and charged with being an "alien prostitute" on August 22nd, 1910, along with four other immigrants. She filed for a writ of habeas corpus on November 4th, 1910. Judge Donworth initially denied the writ, but allowed the writ after Tsuchine appealed it on November 21st, 1910. The fate of the bound party is unknown, but records suggest that Tsuchine and the four other immigrants that were arrested with her left the immigration detention station on February 14th, 1911.

Summary of Proceedings: James Hallahan filed this petition stating that he was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by John Briggs, the Chief of Police for South Omaha, and Michael Corcoran, one of the jailors. He was taken into custody on 16 May 1913. The petition stated that no complaint or indictment was filed against him in the state of Colorado. Despite this, he was taken into custody. Section 330, Page 2481 of the Compiled Statutes of Nebraska required that a complaint, charge, or affidavit must be filed against someone in order for them to be taken into custody. Moreover, the petition stated that Hallahan was only 17 and, thus, was a minor. So, even if he had been charged with a crime he would have been treated as a delinquent, not as a criminal in the city jail. On 19 May 1913, Judge A. C. Troup allowed the writ. The Appearance Docket stated that Hallahan’s release was ordered on 21 May 1913.

Summary of Proceedings: Irene Pearson filed a writ of habeas corpus for her husband Gilbert R. Pearson. In the petition, Irene argues that Gilbert has been arrested at the request of a firm from Los Angeles, California. She notes that Gilbert is in debt to this firm and this arrest is purely an attempt by them to have him repay the money he owes them. The petition argues that no charge or complaint has been levied against Gilbert and this arrest is illegal and without authority in law. The petition is missing several pages and does not include the outcome of the petition.

Summary of Proceedings: In December 1916, upon entry into the United States, Kunijiro Toguchi, a native of Japan, was denied entry and detained under an order from the Secretary of Labor. Toguchi petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus alleging that the Secretary of Labor wrongfully adjudged the petitioner to be a contract laborer seeking entry into the U.S., which was in violation of the current immigration law. Judge Neterer authorized the writ and in his ruling stated that the petitioner came to the United States at the request of his uncle to take a position as a salesman. Judge Neterer stated that the only question before the court was whether Toguchi's work status fell under the contract labor provision of the Immigration Act. In his final ruling, Judge Neterer ruled that Toguchi did not fall within the list of exemptions to the contract labor provision and there was nothing to indicate the petitioner was not accorded a fair trial, therefore the writ was discharged and Toguchi was remanded to the custody of the Immigration Commissioner. The final record in the file is a motion by the U.S. attorney ordering the government may permanently with draw their files from the record.

Summary of Proceedings: Frankie Sutsinger was arrested on a warrant issued by J. J. L. Peel. Peel issued the warrant based on a complaint by R. J. Rusk which said that she was keeping a house in Spokane Falls for the purpose of inhaling opium. This was in violation of a local ordinance and Sutsinger was forced to pay a fee. Sutsinger was held by James Glisten and petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. She argued that there was improper jurisdiction and a complaint without offense. She also argued that the ordinance itself made the warrant void. Judge Turner granted the writ and Frankie was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: C. H. Kelley brought forth a petition for a writ of Habeas on behalf of Mary M. Claybourn. Kelley alleged that he and his wife, Mary Kelley, had been entrusted with the care of Mary Claybourn since Mary was only 3 years old and cared for her as their own child. Kelley further claimed that William Claybourn had forcibly kidnapped Mary Claybourn on February 9, 1888. The judge, J. H. Broady agreed to hear the case, setting the date for February 27, 1888, and summons were issued by the sheriff for various witnesses to appear for the intended proceedings. The events and outcome of that proceeding is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Aspasia was born in Kaskaskia, Illinois around 1806 to an enslaved mother who allegedly had been brought to the region before the passing of the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Aspasia was treated as enslaved herself and sold to multiple parties. In 1821, Pierre Menard purchased the girl from Baptiste Gindreau. Shortly after that, Menard gave Aspasia to his daughter and son-in-law, Bernice and Francois Chouteau, who brought her to St. Louis. Late in 1827, Aspasia petitioned for the right to sue as a poor person and to have her freedom determined by the court. She charged Francois Chouteau and Pierre Menard with assault, battery, and false imprisonment and asked for $1,000 in damages. In response to the charge, Menard had Aspasia jailed, at which point she petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. Her fate is unknown, although the defendants in her freedom suit claimed that she was legally enslaved because her mother had been brought to Northwest Territory before the passage of the 1787 Ordinance, which broadly prohibited the introduction of enslaved people into the region.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 23, 1923, Anna and Vince Wardyn entered an agreement with Margie and Fred O. Mueller concerning their two-year-old daughter Margie Wardyn. The Muellers were the girl's aunt and uncle. According to the petition filed on August 24, 1923, the Wardyns believed they were signing documents agreeing to compensate and temporarily allow the Muellers to take care of Margie. However, they were actually signing adoption papers. Anna Wardyn specified that she was born in Poland and is not familiar with the English language. Vince said that he was intoxicated while signing the papers and didn't even remember the event. The adoption proceedings took place on July 24 and Judge Bryce Crawford entered the adoption decree on August 8. The respondents replied to the writ and argued that they received the consent of the Wardyns to adopt Margie. They also argued that Anna attended night school for several years and knew how to read, write, and speak in English. The Muellers filed a motion to dismiss the writ. On August 29, 1923, the hearing for the writ was denied. Judge Day didn't believe that Anna and Vince hadn't understood the writ, and to give them their child back would be to "reward perjury." Sometimes, he said, the court had to consider the legal aspects of the case before a child's welfare.

Summary of Proceedings: Taik (Emma Hamilton) was a 13 year old Tlingit girl who was taken to the Sheldon Jackson Institute (aka Indian Training School at Sitka) in January of 1885 by Sheldon Jackson and Alonzo E. Austin. Taik's mother was said to have died around March 1885, and one Anna Vine became the parent- appointed guardian of the child. The story was that after the death of Hitch- sah- See, Taik's mother, Vine came in March 1885 to take Taik from the school to her home in Victoria, British Columbia, the school administrators, including Jackson and Austin refused to grant the release. When her complaints for release went unanswered, Hitch- sah- See filed for a writ of habeas corpus with her husband, Don- ah- Clah, against Jackson, Austin, and a woman referred to as "Mrs. McFarland." After the case was filed it was discovered that Taik's mother had not actually died, but was still alive, as was her father, Don-ah-clah. The case was transferred to them, and they became the new petitioners. The defendants argued that they had made a verbal agreement to enroll Taik for a period of 5 years in the school with her parents. With this alleged verbal agreement, the defendants claimed to be the legal guardians of Taik.  Judge Ward McAllister ruled against the defendant, in favor of Hitch- sah- see and Don-ah-clah. He wrote that the school officials had no authority to make "contracts with Indians" under the provisions of the federal government. Additionally, administrators could not take Native children from their parents, and were required to return them if that's what parents wished.

Summary of Proceedings: Lee Mee Gin returned to China in 1880 after living in Portland, Oregon for 20 years in order to get married. Then he returned to the United States as a Merchant and continued to work in Portland while his wife remained in China. Later, his wife, Mrs. Lee Mee Gin, and 9 year old daughter traveled to join him in the United States on the Steamship Danume. Master William Meyers denied their entry to port as he believed they were violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Lee Mee Gin petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of his wife and daughter, which the judge granted and discharged them from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 9, 1893, Lee One filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he claimed that he was being illegally detained by Steamship Danube Captain William Myer. Myer claimed that the Collector of the Port of Portland T.J. Black refused to allow Lee One to land at the port because of the Chinese Exclusion Act. Judge Charles Bellinger disagreed with Black and granted the writ of habeas and ordered Lee One released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Frances Anzalone, the bound party, is the wife of Sebastino Anzalone and the daughter of Joe Valendi. However, her status as a minor and first cousin to Sebastino Anzalone led to her forceful removal from her home to the Riverview Detention Home for Juveniles. This arrest was made under the claim that she was bound to an illegal marriage for her age and consanguinity with Anzalone. The petitioners argued that in Italian culture, it is normal for young girls to be married at her age and that the couple is only related as half-blood first cousins. Additionally, the marriage was consensual and had the approval of Valendi, the wife's father. According to the appearance docket, the case was dismissed for want of prosecution.

Summary of Proceedings: Al Horn petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Commissioner of Immigration Luther Weedin and Immigration Inspector Thomas M. Fisher. Horn alleged he was born in Russia, but was a resident alien of the United States and had lived in Seattle, WA for nearly 10 years. Horn claimed Fisher arrested him at the Canadian border as he attempted to re-enter the United States after a recreational trip. Weedin and Fisher replied that they held Horn in the Immigration Station to await deportation by the authority of a warrant. The warrant for arrest claimed Horn’s arrest was justified as he was “a person likely to become a public charge.” The outcome of the case and the fate of Horn are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 31, 1920, Mabel Brooks, with the assistance of her attorney, Daniel Horrigan, filed a writ of habeas corpus claiming that she was unlawfully detained by Alvin Patton, superintendent of the Douglas County hospital. She claimed that she was committed to the hospital without a complaint, hearing, or official finding from the Insanity Commission, but rather, an "arbitrary and unauthorized action of one of the members of the said Insanity Commission." William A. Redick oversaw a hearing on February 2, 1920, in which it was found that Mabel had been regularly committed, but ordered that she be discharged. A writ and return was filed to this effect on February 6, 1920.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 8, 1894, Wong King filed for a writ of habeas corpus for Law Look, Fon Chong, Loey Hin Kee, Back Yuen, and Young Chong Tai. Wong King claimed that they were being illegally detained on the steamship Signal by Captain George Beudegard. Wong King further claimed that Law Look, Fon Chong, Loey Hin Kee, Back Yuen, and Young Chong Tai were Chinese Merchants who were exempt from the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Charles Bellinger agreed, and released Law Look, Loey Hin Kee, Back Yuen, and Young Chong Tai from Custody. Bellinger denied the writ for Fon Chong and remanded him back to the custody of the respondent. Included in the case file are signed affidavits from Portland merchants.

Summary of Proceedings: Joseph L. Williams petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to establish custody of his son, Joseph T. Williams, which was granted. The younger Williams was being held by a man named Elmer Harris, whose wife appeared in court to surrender the boy to his father. Elmer Harris was the boy's grandfather, and his daughter, the boy's mother, had died shortly after the child's birth. Since the respondents attempted no defense, the younger Williams was released into the custody of his father.

Summary of Proceedings: Frederick C. Test claimed that his 6 month old son, Jo Janelene Test, was unlawfully detained by F.A Birby and Lou Birby. He claimed to have been the natural guardian and only gave temporary custody to Jo’s maternal grandmother, F.A Birby, preceding his wife’s death in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He was a lieutenant in the U.S Army and desired to take his son back to New Mexico, as Mrs. and Mr Birby were refusing to give him back his custody. Ultimately, Test was granted back full custody of his child.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 28, 1914, Hazel May Mangen was committed to the Nebraska Institution for the Feeble Minded. Six years later, on November 1, 1920, Peter Mangen, possibly her father, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against Douglas County's juvenile officer, A.H. Vosburg. A writ and return was filed on November 3, and Mangen also subpoenaed a Dr. Young and Miss Anthony to testify in the case. On November 4, 1920, judge A.C. Troup denied the application and remanded custody of Hazel May to the institution.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 6, 1922, Joseph Buckley filed for habeas against Chief of Police, Michael Dempsey, and Chief of Detectives, Charles H. Van Dusen. In the petition, Buckley argued that he was, since January 3, being held without any charges, complaint or commitment. On the return of the issued writ, the respondents explained that a warrant was issued by Police Magistrate W. F. Wappich on January 6, 1922, for the charge of fugitive from justice. The case was later dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924; the fate of Buckley is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 22nd, 1912, Theodore Mazzine petitioned for the freedom of his 12 year old daughter, Martha Mazzine. Martha was taken a decade prior after the death of her mother by the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart, a convent and orphanage specifically serving Italians. According to witness testimonies, Theodore Mazzine and the convent came to the deal that Martha would be returned after a year. According to Theodore, he has since consistently asked for the return of Martha, culminating finally in this Habeas Corpus suit. The petition was granted on March 4th, 1912, and a date in court was set for March 18th, 1912. The next documentation is from April 9th, which includes 9 witnesses testifying on behalf of Theodore’s character as a man and father. The outcome of the case is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 16, 1890, Thomas Rice was charged with the crime of habitual drunkenness. Judge John F. Miller sentenced him to 25 days in the city jail. On April 18, 1890, Rice petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus stating that Judge Miller had denied his attempt to pay his bond of $50. Rice also stated that keeping him in the city jail constituted an unlawful and illegal restraint of his liberty. In the petition, Rice stated that he was arraigned without knowing the crime he was being held for. Rice also disputed his guilty plea, stating that he only plead guilty to having been drunk, not to being a habitual drunkard. On April 19, 1890, Judge J. A. Stratton allowed the writ and found that Thomas Rice was illegally restrained of his liberty.

Summary of Proceedings:
Petitioner George Nelson was arrested by Edward Cudihee for the charge of burglary on July 26, 1902. He was confined in jail until his hearing on August 12, 1902, when he was judged by T. H. Cann, Justice of the Peace. On November 11, 1902, Nelson filed a writ of habeas corpus with his counsel, attorney Frank B. Wiestling. Nelson contends that he is being restrained illegally as Cann had not filed any of the transcripts or records of the case proceedings. This includes the charge and indictment of Nelson. 

Nelson had his writ approved by Judge George E. Morris on November 12, 1902.

Summary of Proceedings: In 1820, James Watt petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. The exact date of his petition is unknown. Watt had been charged with larceny and receiving stolen goods for receiving stolen beaver pelts from George Late, a slave of recently deceased Manuel Lisa, an Indian Agent and the founder of Fort Lisa in what would become the city of Omaha, Nebraska, and the Missouri Fur Trading Company. The outcome of the case and the fate of Watt are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Lee Loon Toy and Lee Gee Ting traveled on the Steamship Danube and arrived in Portland, Oregon, on July 15th, 1893. They were stopped by customs, who suspected they were Chinese laborers and thus arriving in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. The Collector of Customs T. J. Black refused to see their witnesses H.W. Williams and W. H Wallace, and did not consider their certificates of merchant status. Thus, the two individuals were detained for lack of identification and not allowed to leave the Steamship. The case includes the trial transcript but does not present the case outcome.

Primary field: Habeas Corpus of Schoenbeck against A. E. Griffiths, Chief of Police et al
Repository: ["[Washington State Archives, Puget Sound Regional Branch (Bellevue, Washington)](hc.loc.000032)"]
Summary of Proceedings: On May 18, 1914, George W. Schoenbeck and his lawyer William Wray filed a petition of habeas corpus. They claimed that Austin E. Griffiths and Charles Tennant were illegally holding Schoenbeck in jail, as they didn’t believe there was any official judgment ordering his detainment. Tennant produced evidence that Schoenbeck had, in fact, been charged with grand larceny in Ramsey County, Minnesota, and was a fugitive from justice. Based on this evidence, John F. Murphy, the prosecuting attorney, asked Judge Archibald W. Frater to dismiss the writ. Frater and Wray agreed, and the writ was dismissed. Schoenbeck was placed in the custody of an unnamed Minnesotan agent to be taken back to Minnesota.

Summary of Proceedings: Egnats Weiss petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff Robert T. Hodge. Weiss claimed he was being held illegally under a warrant from the state of New York claiming he had abandoned his children. He alleged that he supported his children to the best of his ability and, in fact, left New York to find work that would allow him to further support his family. Neither the outcome of the case nor the fate of Weiss is known. Weiss would file another petition for a writ of habeas corpus a few days later.

Summary of Proceedings: During May of 1902, Frances Garrison got into a fight with Jane Hall in Franklin county, Washington. Garrison was arrested by police officer J. P. Morris, but Hall did not want to press charges claiming that she had instigated the fight against Garrison. George M. Johnson, a witness to these events, claimed the same. Garrison was judged guilty by Fred Tucker, Justice of the Peace of Franklin county, and sent to the King County jail by Sheriff Cudihee. On June 3, 1902, Garrison filed for a writ of habeas corpus to Judge Griffin, claiming she had been jailed and convicted without right.

Writ was granted and Judge Greene said he should be discharged from custody and recover his costs against the sheriff (McGraw).

Summary of Proceedings: On February 2nd, 1887, Nancy O'Brien took her son, Harry O'Brien, away from their home in Fremont, Nebraska, without the knowledge of Samuel O'Brien, Nancy's husband and Harry's father. Nancy and Harry O'Brien travelled to the Dakota territory and then to the territory of Washington. On July 9th, 1887, Samuel O'Brien filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of Harry. On July 12th, 1887, Sheriff James Glispin brought Harry O'Brien to court on orders from Judge George Turner. Judge Turner then ruled in favor of Samuel O'Brien and gave custody of Harry to Samuel.

Summary of Proceedings: In October 1924, Harry Reed petitioned for a writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds he was being unlawfully restrained of his liberty. Seven years prior, in 1917, a divorce was entered against the petitioner in favor of his former spouse, Chloe Reedy, in Atchison, Kansas. The court found Harry guilty of gross neglect and awarded Chloe custody of their two minor children and an alimony of $5 per week. In Douglas County, October 1924, Harry was arrested for non-support of his minor children and being a fugitive of justice from Kansas. The petition alleges Harry was not a fugitive of justice from Kansas and by decree of the divorce he was not guilty of any felonies. Judge Stauffer allowed the writ, and Harry Reedy was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Walter Roseker was arrested in Omaha, Nebraska on December 28,1923 along with Robert Thomas. On December 29, 1923, Thomas was charged with the unlawful sale of intoxicating liquor while Roseker was held as a witness, he then testified that he did not purchase any liquor from Thomas, the Municipal Court for the city of Omaha then sentenced Roseker to 30 days in jail for perjury. Roseker, with the help of his attorney, C. E. Walsh, filed a writ of Habeas Corpus on January 25, 1924, claiming that Roseker was being unlawfully detained after he was not given a fair trial and that the court did not have jurisdiction in pronouncing his sentence, based on the perjury provisions set in the Statutes of Nebraska for 1922. On that same day, Judge Charles A. Goss ruled in favor of Roseker and ordered his release.

Summary of Proceedings:
Albert and Nora Hanna lived in Washington with their two children, Zetta and Ruth. However, the married couple separated in the beginning of February 1903. As a result, a child custody agreement was made that granted Nora sole custody of the two young children. While the children were in her custody, Nora permitted Albert to take the children to see his mother, their grandmother. Albert, however, did not return the children. Because of this, Nora filed a writ of habeas corpus on January 8, 1903. Albert would counter Nora's attempts to regain custody of their children by calling her immoral and claiming she had beaten Zetta. Judge Boyd Tallman ultimately granted the petition the same day, but the fate of the children is unknown. 

During the trial, Nora was represented by the Shepard and Lyter Law firm. However, the names of the attorneys and their individual roles were never mentioned in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 19, 1876, P. Bently accused William McCon of assaulting him with intent to kill. The next day, McCon was brought in front of a grand jury and justice and found guilty. Justice of the peace O.P. Lacy set bail at $1000. As McCon was unable to pay bail, he was confined to the Walla Walla County Jail to await his next hearing in May. On January 31, 1877, McConn filed a writ of habeas corpus against Walla Walla County Sheriff George F. Thomas, stating that his bond was unfairly high and he was unable to pay it. MCon said that if his bail was reduced, he would happily pay it. Judge Samuel C. Wingard allowed the writ, but the outcome of the petition and McCon's fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Wang Cheug petitioned for Habeas Corpus on behalf of Yip Fou, Chin Fouk, and Chung Mau, who were detained on the Steamship Haytian Republic. The Master of the Steamship John Ross suspected they were arriving in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act, so he did not allow them to enter the port. Judge Deady decided they were laborers and not merchants, so their writ was denied and they were remanded to the Master of the Haytian Republic to be returned to China.

Summary of Proceedings: Adolph Guldahl, a Norwegian immigrant, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson. Guldahl alleged that he was being held illegally at Spokane County Jail under the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. He admitted he was a member of the I.W.W., but claimed he never read or distributed the organization’s literature and didn’t truly believe in most of their messaging. Judge Frank H. Rudkin ruled that Guldahl had already been discharged from custody, and thus the writ was dismissed. This was Guldahl's second petition for habeas corpus.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 10, 1899, Annie Downie petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus after Sheriff A. T. Van de Vanter removed her children, Adelaide and Hazel Shawl, from her custody.  In her petition, she alleged that this removal was at the insistence of Aaron Shawl, her former husband.  However, the Seattle Post Intelligencer reported that Annie Downie had actually kidnapped the children. She stated in the petition that while the family was living in California, Shawl brought other women into the house, abused her and her children, and was idle.  She continued that she left Shawl and, with his consent, took the children from California to Washington. She added that she married John Downie and stated that they had the means to care for the children.   She concluded the petition by expressing concern that the children would be removed from Washington jurisdiction and taken to California, where Shawl resided. The petition itself was directed to A.T. Van de Vanter rather than Shawl. Judge Jacobs issued the writ, but the June 11, 1899 issue of the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reported that the children had been released from custody and returned to Downie.  It notes that Downie must still appear before the court with her children on June 12, 1899.  The definitive outcome of this specific case is unclear.  However, the October 20, 1900 issue of the Seattle Post-Intelligencer indicates that Downie and Shawl continued to fight over custody.  It states that Shawl applied for a writ of habeas corpus to remove the children from their mother’s custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 21, 1919, Wade Gregory and Clarence J. Burress, two brothers-in-law, allegedly stole a car in Omaha, Nebraska. At some point, they left for St. Joseph, Missouri, where Burress had family, and it was there that they were arrested without a warrant on August 26 by Charles Van Deusen, an Omaha policeman. A warrant for their arrest wasn't issued until September 9. They were taken through Iowa to Omaha, and incarcerated in Douglas County Jail, and Douglas County sheriff wrote to the governor on August 30 for extradition. At some point, they tried to pay a bail of $2,500, but defaulted. On September 13, 1919, while still being held in Douglas County, they filed a writ of habeas corpus. This writ was accepted by judge William A. Redick, and he asked Clark to justify why the men were being held in a hearing on September 19, 1919. On September 22, 1919, their application was denied, and the men were remanded to the custody of the Douglas County sheriff.

Summary of Proceedings: Petitioner, Rosie Wise, was arrested by the Omaha Police Department on 25 July 1912. Immediately thereafter, the Douglas County Attorney filed a complaint against Wise alleging that she had committed assault with intent to commit great bodily harm on Mary Mott. The petition stated that she was refused a preliminary hearing. Wise was granted a thirty day continuance to secure a bail bond, she was unable to secure bail in that time. During that period, she was continuously denied a preliminary hearing. She was granted a second thirdy day continuance where she still failed to secure bail and was again refused a preliminary hearing. Wise submitted this petition stating that she was being kept against her will, “with complete want of authority and without process of law.” On 24 September 1912, Judge A. L. Sutton ordered that the writ be allowed, returnable on 26 September 1912. On 28 September 1912, Judge Sutton ordered that the writ be denied and the petition dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings: Francis Williams filed for a writ of habeas corpus at the same time as Sue Bellmont and Edward Twitty. In his petition, Williams argued that he was illegally being restrained of his liberty by Joel Warren, the Chief of Police, and J. S. McBride, the City Health Commissioner. Warren and McBride had detained Williams stating that he had a dangerous, contagious, and infectious disease. The case file never states which disease that Williams was claimed to have and Williams denied that he had any disease. Instead, he alleged that he was “the victim of malice and caprice of the Health and Police Departments.” In his return to the writ, J. S. McBride stated that Williams was taken into custody on a warrant issued by John B. Gordon which charged Williams with violating City Ordinance No. 16046 on the preservation of public morality, peace, safety, and good order in the City of Seattle. This case file does not include the outcome of this case, however, newspaper coverage highlights that these petitions were denied.

Summary of Proceedings: Lee Lock petitioned for habeas corpus on behalf of Lee Bing and Lee Yoo Doon who were held on the Steamship Signal by Captain Bendergard. The Collector of Customs T. J. Black refused to allow them entry to the port believing they were chinese laborers arriving in violation of the Chinese Exclusion Act. The Judge decided they were both genuine merchants and thus granted the writ and discharged them from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Oliver M. Wilson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve Addaline A. and Oliver P. Wilson, presumably his children, from their mother, Florence Morgan, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, the writ was denied and the children remanded to the custody of their mother. However, all of the Wilsons are shown living together in Lincoln in the 1920 census, so apparently Addaline and Oliver managed to work out their differences.

Summary of Proceedings: Young Wong, Lim Mon, Young Hing and Fong Cow were confined by T. J. Black in the Steamship Haytian Republic for allegedly violating the Chinese Exclusion Act. Cross examinations are in the casefile.

Summary of Proceedings: This case involves 69 longshoremen that were arrested during a worker’s strike. They were arrested while protesting near the Seattle General Hospital during the night and early morning of September 14th and 15th. The police officers that arrested the strikers called the striking workers "The I.W.W. element of longshoremen.” The strikers were charged with unlawful assembly and their bail was set at $500 each. Newspaper coverage of the arrests note that the longshoremen’s bail was eventually reduced to $50, however, despite the reduction only one of the longshoremen was able to raise bail. Immediately following their arrests, longshoremen with their attorney Thomas Byron MacMahon filed for a writ of habeas corpus, however, newspaper coverage notes that Judge King Dykeman denied their writ of habeas corpus. The strikers still received public support while in prison. The Seattle Star noted that after their habeas petition was denied several people came by the King County Jail to give the strikers watermelons, cantaloupes, fruits, and berries.

Summary of Proceedings: Lee Barrington was detained in Seattle city jail on January 24, 1903, and transferred to King County jail on January 27, where he remained until January 28. During his detention at the county jail, Justice of the Peace T.H. Cann requested him to provide evidence in a case against his wife, Elisa Barrington, who according to local newspaper coverage, had a pending case for shooting him while he was at work about one week prior. The petitioner refused, causing Cann to impose a $250 bond on him. Unable to pay the bond, Lee continued to be held in jail as a witness. On February 3, 1903, Lee Barrington petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County sheriff Ed Cudihee. The petition argued that his detention was unlawful since no subpoena had ever been served to him, and he requested to be released from custody. The petitioner further argued that he could not be legally forced to testify against his wife. On February 4, Judge William R. Bell allowed the writ. However, it was ruled that since the crime was committed against Barrington, he could indeed be compelled to testify. The petitioner thus remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings:
On November 15, 1912, Louisa Tubbs and her attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, in which she claimed that her husband Samuel Tubbs was being illegally imprisoned by his mother and step-father, Caroline and Charles Spink. Louisa claimed that Samuel, who had partial paralysis from a spine related condition, was not of sound mind and therefore could not make a decision in his best interest. She claimed that her in-laws were attempting to poison his mind against her and the two daughters she and Samuel had, Nellie (17) and Beatrice (15), with the hope of getting put into Samuel’s will. Louisa also claimed she and her daughters were not allowed to visit Samuel. 
Caroline and Charles, along with Samuel’s doctor and in-home nurse, argued that he was of sound mind and wished to stay with his mother and step-father, a sentiment which Samuel echoed. Caroline and Charles also alleged that Louisa, Nellie, and Beatrice were allowed to visit but did not visit often. They felt that Louisa would be unable to properly care for Samuel because she was also running the businesses that he used to run. Additionally, they stated that Samuel had made efforts to ensure that his property went to Louisa, and that they had no intention of being added to his will. 
Judge Ronald dismissed the case, and both parties agreed to discontinue the case without cost to either party. Samuel remained with his mother and step-father.

Summary of Proceedings: William Mullins resided in Kansas City, Missouri and said he provided his children a good home after the children’s mother had died. On October 7th, 1908, the children ran away from said home and came to South Omaha in Douglas County where they were kept by Ella T. Mullins who was the mother of the step children and the wife of William. William argued that Ella was not entitled to the children and that she took them into her possession and unlawfully restrained them from their liberty. Ella returned them to William wherein he placed them in the custody of Mrs. Cramer who owned a boarding house. When one of the children objected, he struck Charles with his umbrella and knocked him down. The children, William and Charles, were required to sleep in the same room with a son of the boarding house keeper by the name of Elmer Cramer, who was between the ages of 17 and 18. Elmer took Charles to a house of prostitution and then also took off his clothes and exposed himself to the Mullins children. Elmer also “practiced a vicious and loathsome vice in their presence and on several occasions attempted to instruct Charles in said practice.” William E. Mullins also refused to send Charles to school and advised said son that he would rather have him grow up big, strong, and healthy than to be an educated fool.” The father also called the son a "green eyed liar" and "little bastard." Ella alleged that when she married William E. Mullins took the children, Florence, William, and Charles, into her home and loved them. She owned a hotel in South Omaha called the Delmonico Hotel and she said that William and their children resided there until he left them and took Florence to live with a family member and left the two boys. Four years later, William requested the children and they were returned to him and then three months later they left to their own volition back to Omaha. The last documented happening of the case was the response from Ella to William and the fate of the children is unknown. However, 1910 census records indicate that an 11-year-old named Willie Mullins was living with Ella in South Omaha.

Summary of Proceedings:
Andrew Knelp was a waiter at the California Restaurant. While working on March 15, 1902, he stopped by a neighboring house, referred to as the “Welcome House”, in order to collect a small sum of money he was owed. When he was inside the house, the inmates inside attacked him– pushing him down the stairs and scratching his face. When Knelp was pushed down the stairs, he was met with a police officer ready to arrest him. 

Knelp was charged with assault and battery, to which his attorney, Henry S. Noon, claims was a false and pretended charge. Knelp filed a petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus on March 16, 1902. His case was heard by Judge Arthur E. Griffin on March 18, and Knelp’s writ was granted.

Summary of Proceedings: Natalie Chandler petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of Frederick Chandler against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham. Natalie Chandler alleged that Frederick Chandler was being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail without cause. The case outcome and the fate of Frederick Chandler are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
On September 20, 1918, Jesse Mackey was arrested and imprisoned in the Seattle City Jail. On October 11, Mackey filed a writ of habeas corpus against the Chief of Police, Joel F. Warren, stating that his imprisonment is illegal since he has not been charged with any crime. In his return to the writ, Warren states that Mackey was no longer in his custody but instead was in the custody of the Seattle Commissioner of Health, John S. McBride. Warren states that Mackey was found to have an ““dangerous, infectious, and contagious disease” although he admits that the investigation to see if he had any diseases may have been hampered by “the obstinate attitude of the petitioner.” Warren also states that a warrant for Mackey’s arrest was issued on October 8 charging him with being a disorderly person on May 1, 1918 for “willfully and unlawfully being idle and having no lawful means of support, and wandering about with no visible calling or business to maintain himself.” 

Mackey submits a response to Warren’s return stating that he is not and has not been placed in quarantine noting that he has been continuously held in the Seattle City Jail in a cell with dozens of other inmates. Furthermore, he mentions that his interactions with other inmates and police officers has not been restricted since his arrest. Mackey also claims that the arrest warrant made against him is illegal and void since it came eighteen days after his initial arrest. 

Before the hearing for Mackey's petition for a writ of habeas corpus, Joel F. Warren submitted a supplemental return stating that a blood test taken on October 14 showed that Mackey was not infected with any disease and as of October 16, he has been returned to the custody of the Chief of Police and is being held on being in default of his fine for his charge of “being a disorderly person.” Judge A. W. Frater held the hearing for Mackey writ of habeas corpus. Following the hearing, Frater ruled that Jesse Mackey was wrongfully and unlawfully imprisoned and ordered that the petitioner be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On March 17th, 1919, William Wernsen was arrested in Omaha and sentenced to pay a fine of $100 for being convicted of vagrancy. Wernsen filed a petition for a writ of Habeas Corpus, arguing that because the State of Nebraska has set the limit for vagrancy fines at $50, his imprisonment is unlawful. His petition was allowed and Juedge Redick ordered the Douglas County Sheriff to produce Wernsen in court on March 25th, 1919. The outcome of the suit was not filed with the rest of the case documents, however, the appearance docket reveals that Wernsen's writ was dismissed for want of prosecution and he remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Abraham Verber petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles M. Beckingham. Verber claimed he was being held illegally in the Seattle City Jail as he was not arrested under order of a warrant, he was not granted due legal process, and no criminal accusation had been made against him. The case file does not reveal the outcome of the case, nor the fate of Verber.

However, the sheriff could not locate DeFord in Lancaster County, prompting his counsel to withdraw the petition. Later articles suggest he was wanted on a paternity charge.

Summary of Proceedings: Henry McCullough petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of his two-and-a-half year old son, John. McCullough claimed that John’s mother placed him in the custody of the Washington Children’s Home Society under duress and without permission. McCullough filed the writ against the superintendent of the Washington Children’s Home Society, Harrison D. Brown. Brown responded that John had been freely given up to the Washington Children’s Home Society and adopted by K.H. and Ella K. Opdal. McCullough included the Opdals as respondents in a supplemental petition, claiming they had no legal right to adopt John. Brown returned that the Washington Children’s Home Society found neither McCullough nor John’s mother to be suitable guardians, which McCullough denied. The outcome of the case and John’s fate are unknown. McCullough filed a separate petition for writ of habeas corpus to regain custody of his other child, Gladys.

Summary of Proceedings: A. L. Hanot filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus for William Hanot after he was arrested on March 25, 1919, by the Chief of Police, Joel F. Warren. William Hanot was arrested because the Justice of the Peace, John B. Gordon issued a warrant that charged Hanot with being a fugitive from justice. The warrant alleged that Hanot was wanted for the crime of abandoning his wife in the State of California. The outcome of the petition and the fate of the bound party are not included in the case file.

Summary of Proceedings: J. J. Blevins petitioned for writs of habeas corpus in the county and circuit courts to retrieve his three young sons, Henry, John, and Thomas, from his father-in-law, Thomas Small, both of which were granted. Smalls claimed that his grandchildren refused to return to their father, saying that they "cried Piteously" at the thought of leaving. Smalls added that Blevins was an unfit parent, and that for the past three years Smalls and his wife, Elizabeth, had been supporting Blevins and the children. After hearing the evidence, the district court judge remanded the three boys to the custody of their father. Blevins and Smalls spent the next two years litigating a property dispute in civil court.

Summary of Proceedings:
On April 1, 1891, Kate Burns placed her daughter, Maggie McGee, aged eight years old, in the House of the Good Shepherd with the expectation of a one-month stay. Kate failed to recover her daughter despite multiple attempts. Sister Superior Mary repeatedly refused to release Maggie back into Kate’s custody. 

In October 1891, Kate filed a second writ of habeas corpus for the release of her daughter. Sister Superior Mary continued to detain Maggie and asserted that Kate was unfit.

John H. Morgan filed for a writ of habeas corpus on March 3, 1897. After being convicted of petit larceny, Morgan was sentenced to thirty days in jail and a fifty-dollar fine. He chose to pay his fine by serving additional days, at the rate of two dollars per day. After seventy-two days in jail, he filed a writ of habeas for his release. Morgan’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
George Webster was charged with first degree murder in May, 1897 and was subsequently found guilty and sentenced with the death penalty. The petitioner and his attorneys filed a motion to quash on grounds the court had no jurisdiction, and probable cause was not established. When that was unsuccessful, the petitioner and his attorneys filed a Writ of Error Coram Nobis, alleging that one of the jurors, Isador Lipschuetz, was not a resident of Washington, and therefore ineligible to be a juror. The writ of error contained multiple affidavits from Idaho and Washington election officials establishing Lipshchuetz's voting records and an affidavit from another juror alleging that Lipshuetz was bitter and malicious towards the petitioner and had his mind made up before the trial. 
The Supreme Court of Washington affirmed the sentence and set the execution date. Subsequently, the petitioner and his attorneys filed a writ of habeas corpus alleging the petitioner was imprisoned without having first been indicted by a grand jury and was not accorded a speedy and impartial trial. The U.S. Circuit Court refused to grant said writ, and upon appeal to the Supreme Court, the judgment was affirmed. The petitioner was likely executed.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 17, 1918, Clara May Pearce filed for Habeas against mother-in-law, Julia Pearce, for keeping her 17-month-old, George Taylor Pearce, from her. A writ was ordered and on May 18, Judge Redick ruled that the infant be placed in custody of the father and mother. Newspapers give details of personal relationships and speak of ongoing public divorce between Clara and Harry Pearce. Clara accused Harry of threatening her with a revolver and beating her, as well as forcing her to ride while she was pregnant. The couple made up in November 1918 after Harry literally went down on his knees and begged her to take him back.

Summary of Proceedings: Dick Pfeffer caught Hebert N. Humphrey violating Nebraska Game law by having a Black Bass less than 8 inches in his possession. This violation resulted in a complaint against Humphrey, where a justice of the peace sentenced him to 5 days in county jail. A relative of his, Roy M. Summary of Proceedings:
Samuel Carr petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to retrieve his two young sons, Harry and Herbert Carr, from William and Nina Helms, which was granted. A few years earlier, Samuel had placed the boys in the Home for the Friendless in Lincoln, Nebraska, from which institution the Helmses obtained custody of the two. The Helmses did not formally adopt Harry and Herbert, whom they put to work in their traveling minstrel show. After hearing the evidence, Harry and Herbert were released back into the custody of the Home for the Friendless. The judge ordered that Samuel could retrieve his children once he demonstrated that he could properly care for them and after he paid off his debt to the state. 

For background on this case, see the 15 and 16 November 1906 issues of the Hastings Daily Republican.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 31, 1906, John S. Burnell petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus to gain custody of his eight-year old daughter, Lotta Burnell, from her maternal grandmother, Elizabeth L. Crossman.  Burnell’s petition stated that Crossman claimed the right to custody over Lotta and denied Burnell custody.   Burnell argued that Crossman was aged and lacked the means to support the child.  He also explained that he was divorcing Susie C. Burnell, Lotta’s mother.  He expressed concern that Charles Fentz, who he claimed had “broken up” his family through “undue attentions” toward Susie, was influencing Lotta.  This was because Lotta, Susie, and Fentz were all living with Crossman.  Burnell believed that Susie and Crossman were planning to take Lotta beyond the court’s jurisdiction.  Judge Griffin issued the writ, and then the case was transferred to Judge Morris.  Judge Morris temporarily gave custody of Lotta to K.M. Donnelly, Lotta’s aunt, until the divorce proceedings ended.

The city recorder ordered the arrest of Zaueker and set bail at $240. After hearing the evidence, Zaueker was released and Rosseter ordered to pay his fees.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 8, 1903, W. H. Upplinger and his attorney petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus. Upplinger had been tried and convicted of “conducting an employment agency without a license”, which a recent city ordinance had criminalized. Upplinger believed that the ordinance was unconstitutional as it deprived people of their property without due process, and that the framing of the ordinance made compliance with its terms impossible, thus essentially prohibiting employment agencies. Judge Rudkin ruled in Upplinger’s favor, finding the ordinance unconstitutional and releasing Upplinger from imprisonment.

Summary of Proceedings: On February 4, 1920, Pottawattamie County, Iowa justice of the peace J.K. Cooper issued a warrant for the arrest of Tom Kelly, Wiley Compton, Frank A. Caine, also known as "Ping-Pong" Bill Myers, and Joe Pearson. They were accused of breaking into the Council Bluffs home of Norton C. Arbuckle and stealing $1,030 worth in jewelry. On February 8, Tom Kelley, Wiley Compton and Frank A. Caine were taken into custody in Omaha, Nebraska. Five days later, the men, with the assistance of their attorneys from the firm of Jameson and O'Sullivan, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus against captain of police John J. Dunn. They argued that no official complaint had been filed against them in Nebraska and that they were not held based on the findings of a judicial tribunal. In return, Dunn produced the Pottawattamie County arrest warrant and stated that not only were the men robbers, but fugitives from justice. At a hearing in front of judge A.C. Troup on Valentine's Day 1920, the men's application was denied and custody was remanded to Dunn. The petitioners filed a motion for a new trial and to quash the respondents' answer and return, but this motion was also overruled. Wiley Compton and Joe Pearson were also involved in a liquor-running scheme involving the forging of bank documents in Canada, and they, along with other men, were extradited there on July 7, 1921.

Summary of Proceedings: On August 12th, 1889, the District Court for the 2nd Judicial District of Washington ordered Albert Tait to provide testimony in the case against C E. Case. The relationship between the two men is unknown; however, Tait refused to provide his testimony and eluded the court's commands. Sheriff James H. Price of Pierce County, Washington, promptly arrested Tait for refusing to comply with the court's orders. Tait responded by filing a habeas corpus petition on August 14th, 1889. Upon hearing the arguments of the bound and holding parties, Judge Frank Allyn denied Tati's writ and ordered him to appear in Case's trial to provide testimony.

Summary of Proceedings: On April 27th, 1888, H. J. Mann filed a writ of habeas corpus on behalf of his daughter, Bessie Mann, who was living with her mother, Cynthia Mann. H. J. claimed that Cynthia had left him for G. A. Rhea, was financially dependent on him, and that she was unfit to care for Bessie as she was "a lewd, unchaste, unvirtuous, immoral and immodest woman." Cynthia claimed that she was never unfaithful, and that H. J. had abandoned her and taken their other two children without her consent. Cynthia also claimed that H. J. had attempted to coerce her into having "criminal intercourse" with Rhea, so that H. J. could blackmail him for money, which Cynthia said she refused to do. Cynthia also stated that H. J. would frequently threaten to take her children away from her if she did not go along with his blackmail plan. Cynthia and her lawyers asked that the case be dismissed, which was not granted. Judge Langford granted H. J. full custody, claiming that he was the proper person to have custody of Bessie, but stated that Cynthia should be allowed to see Bessie at proper times under proper circumstances.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 31, 1906, Cassie Hartman was arrested for a “breach of the peace,” specifically for provoking an assault.   William G. Richards, Justice of the Peace of Ravensdale, issued the warrant for her arrest.   She stated that she was taken from her home in Franklin and brought to Ravensdale, where Judge Richards sentenced her to 27 days in jail, 15 days imprisonment, and a $36 fine. On February 5, 1906, Hartman petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus.  She argued that she did not have a fair and impartial trial.  She stated that she was denied counsel, lacked the opportunity to gather evidence, and was sentenced to an indefinite term in the King County Jail.  Additionally, she argued that Judge Richards acted beyond his authority. He did so by bringing Hartman to Ravensdale for her trial and sentencing when there was a qualified justice of the peace in Franklin, where the crime was committed.  She also stated that she was without funds in her petition, and she asked that the writ be issued without cost.  Judge Griffin obliged and issued the writ without cost. However, the outcomes of Hartman’s petition and case are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 19th, 1913, Albert H. Young and Kamasaburo Sugiuro petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, having been in a county jail awaiting trial under the custody of Joseph R. H. Jacoby. In 1921, a grand jury indicted Young and Sugiuro for violation of the White Slave Traffic Act, commonly known as the Mann Act, both for the violation itself and conspiring to commit the offense. The two men, along with several others, were accused of transporting a woman for the purpose of prostitution. They were placed on trial in February of 1913 and charged in May of the same year. They were committed to jail and had been held there since, while awaiting their indictment trial. In their petition they asserted that the upcoming indictment trial was a violation of the double jeopardy clause of the fifth amendment. In his response, Jacoby presented that the petition did not state facts to cause action against him. In July 1913, the court sustained Jacoby's response and ruled the petition be dismissed. The fate of the two petitioners is unknown, although it seems likely that they remained in custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On November 20, 1906 J. W. Goldstein acting as next friend of Al Krugman, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on Kingman’s behalf. Goldstein claimed that Krugman was being held illegally due to having been purposefully arrested late at night in order to force him to stay in jail overnight and thus be denied bail.  Newspaper coverage indicated that Krugman was an auctioneer for Goldstein, and had been arrested before. Newspapers stated that he was arrested for misrepresenting the quality of goods at auction, and the case file indicated it was for violating city ordinances. The outcome of this case and the fate of Kingman are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Otto F. Schmidt, a German immigrant, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against immigration inspector A. F. Richardson and Spokane County Sheriff George L. Reid. Schmidt alleged that he was being held illegally at Spokane County Jail under the charge of advocating or teaching the unlawful destruction of property. He claimed he was denied a hearing for six months, denied his right to counsel, and compelled to give evidence against himself under intimidation. The court’s judgement stated that it appeared Schmidt had been discharged for unknown reasons, and thus his writ was dismissed.

Summary of Proceedings:
On March 29, 1905, Norborne T. B. Pentreath, a citizen of the United States, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Thomas Delaney, stating that he was being detained illegally due to a request by officials in British Columbia. Judge Cornelius H. Hanford ordered that Delaney show cause in court for Pentreath's detention. 
The acting Seattle Chief of Police, D. F. Willard, filed a return stating that Delaney had detained Pentreath lawfully because he had received messages from Canadian peace officers that Pentreath had committed a crime. A complaint had been filed in the Seattle Justice Court and Pentreath was charged with the extraditable offense of "unlawfully and fraudulently uttering a forged document, as if it were genuine, knowing it was forged and with intent to defraud." 
On April 4, 1905, Judge Hanford ruled that Pentreath had been detained unconstitutionally and ordered that he be released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 18, 1869, William W. Armstrong filed for divorce against his wife of one year, Lydia Armstrong. He alleged that she had treated him with extreme cruelty over the past summer, beating him with a stick and threatening to kill him so many times that he fled his house in fear. Lydia contested these charges, saying that she was served her divorce summons under duress and that they weren't properly authenticated or endorsed. They had a baby daughter named Mary Jane Armstrong who William wanted custody of. William also accused Lydia of "breaching the peace" by threatening to kill himself and John A. Dunn, and she was committed to the county jail, but later released on October 18, 1869. While these divorce proceedings were going on, Willam Armstrong brought Mary Jane to the house of a friend, John A. Dunn. Because of this, on October 21, 1869, Lydia filed a writ of habeas corpus against her ex-husband and Dunn, saying that her daughter was being unlawfully detained. Dunn said that he had taken in the child as an "act of humanity," and that if he hadn't, Mary Jane would have been in the custody of the courts. The outcome of this case is unknown, but Lydia and William had reconciled by 1880, and were living together in Beatrice with Mary Jane and three other siblings born after the divorce suit.

Summary of Proceedings: In August 1902, Joseph Janda, a minor, enlisted in the U.S. Navy in Omaha, Nebraska, but took no further action. In November, he was arrested for desertion after having failed to show up at the Navy Yard in Norfolk, Virginia. In December, his parents, Thomas and Frances Janda, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, which was granted. After hearing the evidence, Joseph was released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: Frank Kadlec’s roommate, James Kasper, picked up a pair of glasses belonging to Kadlec. In retaliation, Kadlec took Kasper's watch and told him that he would not return it until he got his glasses back. Kasper then filed a complaint claiming Kadlec had committed grand larceny for taking the watch. Kadlec was described as being a “foreigner, unable to read or write the English language readily” and therefore did not have a good understanding of the law. He was the sole provider for his wife and five kids and during his incarceration one his sons died because his family endured starvation and poverty. For these reasons, he wanted to be released from jail. The judge approved the writ and Kadlec was released from jail.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 9, 1924, Herbert G. Flood applied for a writ of habeas corpus against Peter Dillon (Omaha Chief of Police) and Charles H. Van Deusen (Omaha Chief of Detectives). Flood alleged that he had been arrested by Omaha police on May 6 and charged with being a fugitive from justice. He asserted that no complaint had been filed against him, which made his detention illegal. Judge James M. Fitzgerald commanded that Van Deusen and Dillon come to the Court and show cause for Flood's detention. Van Deusen and Dillon returned the writ with a document from John W. Yeager (the Chief Deputy County Attorney) stating that they were holding Flood on behalf of B. S. Grannis, the Commonwealth Attorney for the 19th Judicial District of the State of Kentucky. Grannis had telegraphed them with a bench warrant from Bracken County, Kentucky, alleging that Flood committed the crime of bigamy. After a hearing, Flood's application was granted, and the court docket states that he was discharged.
