Summary of Proceedings: William C. MacFarland filed a writ of habeas corpus on April 26, 1918. In his petition, MacFarland argues he was being illegally restrained by Tim Long. Long was holding MacFarland on a warrant issued by the Governor of Ohio. MacFarland denied that he was a fugitive from justice in his writ and argued that the warrant did not have sufficient evidence to justify his arrest. The outcome of the writ and the fate of the bound party were not stated in this case file.

Summary of Proceedings: Ruth Dolan and Mannie Wrightson petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against King County Sheriff A. T. Vandevanter. The two petitioners were arrested for vagrancy, and when they failed to pay the $250 bond set for them, they were both sentenced to three months in King County Jail. The petitioners claimed that the three months had passed, and thus they were now being held illegally. They filed an affidavit presenting that they had no means to pay the court costs for their writ, and the judge ordered that the writ be allowed to proceed without cost. The case file does not reveal the outcome or fate of the petitioners, but newspaper records indicate that both were released from jail.

Summary of Proceedings: Washington Johnson was arrested in Mandan, North Dakota on March 29, 1894, for charges of grand larceny by means of defrauding his business partner Edward O’Melia of $160. Johnson was supposed to pay O’Melia $160 of the $360 check that he received subsequent to the completion of a manufacturing job. Washington failed to show up to an appointment where this payment was supposed to take place and instead took a train out of the state ending up in North Dakota. After being arrested there for charges of grand larceny and being extradited back to Washington. Johnson, with the assistance of his attorney Frank R. Sims filed a writ of Habeas Corpus against Sheriff James H. Woolery who was holding him in jail in Seattle, Washington. Judge Thomas J. Humes initiated the writ and began proceedings but ultimately did not allow the writ to stand. Johnson would eventually be released on bail. According to a newspaper on June 15, 1894, Johnson and his attorney would swear out a warrant of their own in Hume’s court against O’Melia for assaulting Johnson in North Bend, Washington.

Summary of Proceedings: Joe Fong and Coon Lee (also written as Lee Coon) were arrested around midnight on March 22, 1916. The following day, Fong and Lee filed a writ of habeas corpus stating that they were arrested and being detained without warrant or legal process. They also state that there has been no charge filed against them and that the Chief of Police, Louis M. Lang, denied them permission to see legal counsel.  Judge J. T. Ronald accepted their writ of habeas corpus and ordered that Fong and Lee be discharged and released from custody. He also ordered that their legal costs be paid for by the City of Seattle. Newspaper coverage features Joe Fong as an informant on the nature of Chinese Tongs and identifies him as the secretary of Bow Leongs at 666 King St. Coverage of the arrest indicates the men were arrested along with others on a warrantless raid targeting Chinese opium traffic and that the investigation also implicated Barney Sloman/Slomen.

Summary of Proceedings: In September 1919, according to some surviving court records, the Umatilla County Circuit Court sentenced W. Burlingame to serve at least ten but not more than twenty years in the Oregon State Penitentiary for "obtaining money by false pretenses." In November 1920, his next friend, Nettie Patterson, petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on his behalf, which was granted. Patterson maintained that the maximum sentence for "obtaining money by false pretenses" was five years under Oregon law, meaning Burlingame's commitment was illegal. During the proceedings, the Umatilla County district attorney submitted an affidavit that Burlingame had not, in fact, been convicted of "obtaining money by false pretenses," but rather "knowingly uttering and publishing a forged customer's draft," which did carry a sentence of at least ten but not more than twenty years. After hearing the evidence, Burlingame was remanded back into the custody of the penitentiary warden.

The outcome of this case and the fate of William Setter are unknown

Summary of Proceedings: Chew Lun, Fun Way, Chew Bun Gen, Chew Pun, King Yen, Chew Sam, Sit King, and Lum Foot were arrested and confined in the Steamship Danube by William Myers because it was alleged they were Chinese laborers instead of merchants. Sid Que petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus for all of them. The case file includes affidavits claiming that the bound parties are Chinese merchants and it also includes photo identification. The writ of habeas corpus was granted by Judge Charles B. Bellinger, and they were ordered to be released.

Summary of Proceedings: This petition is the second writ of habeas corpus filed by George Roberts. Roberts in the petition argued that he is being restrained of his liberty by Thomas L. Ryan. Ryan is holding Roberts to return him to San Francisco to face trial for grand larceny for stealing $80 from W. L. Perry. In this second petition for writ of habeas corpus, Roberts and his lawyers are asking for his custody be transferred away from Ryan before the hearing for habeas corpus because they believed there was a risk that Ryan would remove Roberts from the jurisdiction of King County and return him to San Francisco. Judge W. R. Bell agreed to hear the writ of habeas corpus. However, in his response to Judge Bell’s order to Thomas L. Ryan commanding him to bring the body of George Roberts before him to hear his petition for habeas corpus, Ryan asked the judge to dismiss the petition because he did not have custody of George Roberts. The outcome of this petition is not included in the court document files.

Summary of Proceedings: On 23 September 1914, a complaint was filed against Madge and Frank Howard by Fred W. Anheuser which stated that they were keeping an ill-governed house. In a petition filed on 10 October 1914, Madge Howard states to the court that she was tried and convicted of keeping an ill governed house, in violation of the Nebraska statutes. She was sentenced to pay a fine of $100 and costs. She filed this petition to show to the court that the charge does not constitute an offense under the Statutes of Nebraska and , thus, that all of the following proceedings were unlawful and that she was being unjustly and unlawfully deprived of her liberty. Her petition asks the court to issue a writ of Habeas Corpus and discharge her from said unlawful imprisonment. The Court’s Appearance Docket notes that the writ was accepted and Madge was discharged from custody on 21 October 1914.

Summary of Proceedings: Edward J. Margett petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Seattle Chief of Police Charles Beckingham and Captain of Detectives Charles Tennant. Margett alleged he was arrested without a warrant and with no criminal complaint lodged against him and, thus, was being imprisoned illegally in the Seattle City Jail. He also claimed his attorney, John J. Sullivan, was denied access to him by Beckingham and Tennant. The outcome of the case and the fate of Margett are not revealed in the case file. Newspaper coverage indicates Margett was a former police officer involved with bootlegging.

Summary of Proceedings: Foster Crays petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus on the behalf of his infant daughter, Dorothy Irene Crays, against James E. and Rose O’Connell. Foster Crays alleged that the O’Connells adopted Dorothy Crays in legal proceedings wherein Foster Crays was accused of abandoning his wife and children. He claimed that these allegations were false and that he was not made aware of the adoption proceedings when they occurred, as he was working in California. The O’Connells claimed that they had adopted Dorothy Crays, now Dorothy O’Connell, through the proper legal channels and provided the order of adoption, which stated that Foster Crays had abandoned the child and her mother gave her up willingly. The court determined that Foster Crays had not abandoned Dorothy Crays and that he was a fit and proper guardian. The writ was allowed, and Dorothy Crays was released from the custody of the O’Connells.

Summary of Proceedings: Fred S. Walton petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against City Marshal John G. Boyle on September 7, 1901, stating that he was arrested, charged, fined, and detained under a North Yakima licensing ordinance for peddling "Quaker medicine" without paying a licensing fee. Walton's petition argued that the ordinance was unconstitutional for two reasons. First, it contained an unreasonable licensing fee that infringed upon his right to engage in business on equal terms with residents of Yakima (the right for people to have "like privileges, rights and immunities in every other state"), which likely referred to the Comity Clause of the Constitution and possibly referred to the 14th Amendment. Second, it violated the right of commerce and the right of citizens of different states to engage in commerce, which was likely referring to the Commerce Clause. Judge Cornelius H. Hanford commanded that Boyle show cause for Walton's detention to the Court; Boyle returned the writ and stated that Walton had violated the peddling statute and was convicted through proper legal processes. Boyle also responded that he had already released Walton on September 7, six hours before he received the writ of habeas corpus. He denied Walton's constitutional challenges and charged that Walton had sufficient money to pay for a license and that he had burdened police by hosting open air concerts as a marketing strategy. Supplemental research reveals that this case was a test case organized by Quakers to test the constitutionality of the peddling ordinance.

Summary of Proceedings: On July 16, 1924, Mike Jaska was arrested for the unlawful possession of still, mash, and intoxicating liquor. On August 2, he was found guilty and Judge Frank M. Dineen sentenced him to 30 days in the Douglas County Jail along with a $500 fine. On December 22, Mike petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus and cited the 1913 Nebraska statutes 9138, 9144, and 9199. According to the appearance docket, the hearing was continued and then his writ was denied. He was then remanded to the custody of the respondents.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 16, 1918, Marie Wells filed for habeas alongside attorney, John M. Macfarland, against the city Health Commissioner, Ernest T. Manning. A writ was issued, and on return, Manning explained that Wells had been found to have a venereal infection and required, under his authority, isolation and quarantine. The writ was denied, and Wells motioned for a new trial, arguing that such evidence was contrary to facts. The motion was overruled on October 19 and Wells remained in custody of the detention home.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 11, 1920, Stella Taylor purchased and drank beer in the company of Robert Johnson. She was arrested by a police officer and charged with vagrancy and prostitution. On October 14, 1920, she filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus with her attorney Noah W. Ware. In the petition, Stella Taylor provided the address of her home and stated that she had been married to W. M. Taylor, with whom she had a four-year-old child, for 12 years. She also mentioned her husband’s employer, Armour’s & Co. The writ was allowed and delivered to the respondents. On October 19, 1920, the respondent, Marshall Eberstein, replied to the writ stating that Stella Taylor was ordered to pay a fine of $50 by Oct. 13, 1920, and was arrested and jailed under Charles E. Foster after not paying the fine. She was then transferred to the Omaha City Detention Home by order of the police court judge and the Omaha Health Commissioner where she was subjected to forced physical examinations to ascertain if she had contracted a venereal disease. They determined she was afflicted with a venereal disease and the judge denied the hearing for the writ based on those results. The court then remanded her to the custody of the respondents.

Summary of Proceedings:
On September 2, 1905, Turner Jackson petitioned for habeas corpus against U. S. Marshal C. B. Hopkins. Jackson argued that Hopkins refused to discharge him despite his sentence being complete due to United States laws that entitled him to a deduction from his sentence for time in which he was a good prisoner. 
On September 4, Judge Cornelius H. Hanford commanded that Hopkins show cause for Jackson's detention. Hopkins responded that Jackson was not entitled to release because, under the United States laws in force at the time of his imprisonment, his term still had more than a year left. In an opinion, Hanford determined that, although a "good conduct" statute passed in 1902 was contradictory, it was intended to apply retroactively. On September 9, 1905, Hanford ordered that Jackson be discharged.
United States attorney Jesse Frye and Marshal Stringer appealed to the Circuit Court of Appeals, and Hanford fixed Jackson's bail at $10,000. Jackson eventually secured recognizance and Hanford ordered that he be at large pending the appeal. Newspaper coverage indicated Jackson has been arrested for aiding in the escape of a prisoner, when in fact he had disrupted a lynch mob in Skagway, Alaska, and was then arrested and convicted after the lynching target escaped. Jackson received a pardon. One of the newspapers covering his habeas hearings described him as "negro," but there are no additional records to confirm he was Black.

Summary of Proceedings: Philip Chiantis, the petitioner, was drafted into the military on the basis that he was of draft age and selected under the selective draft laws and regulations of the US. The petition argued that despite this Chiantis was illegally confined because he was a subject of Greece, had never declared intention to be a citizen of the nation, and therefore could not be forced to serve. Judge Edward E. Cushman did find this petition to be valid and Chiantis was ordered to be released from service.

Summary of Proceedings: Blanche Powers was the wife of Walter Powers, a man who had been arrested on April 20th, 1920, for allegedly committing grand larceny in Kansas and being a fugitive from justice. Mrs. Powers filed a petition for Habeas Corpus, claiming that her husband had been arrested without any pretense as no affidavit had been filed against him, and he was charged with no evidence for his crime. She also cited her inability to provide for herself and that her husband's restraint placed her in dire need. Her petition was granted, and the judge was set to hear her case on April 27th, 1920. Unfortunately, no documents were filed that reveal the petition's final outcome.

Summary of Proceedings: On September 16, 1891, Ah Lin filed for a writ of habeas corpus because she claimed that she was unlawfully detained by the Steamship Grandholm Captain John Mason. Mason claimed that he was ordered to detain Ah Lin by the Collector of the Port of Portland E.P. Earhart. Collector Earhart claimed that Ah Lin was not allowed to land because of the Chinese Exclusion Acts. Judge Matthew P. Deady disagreed with Earhart and granted the writ and ordered Ah Lin released from custody.

Summary of Proceedings: On October 1st, 1894, Seattle’s Chief of Police Bolton Rogers stated that on September 28th, 1894 he received a telegram from Portland, Oregon’s Chief of Police Charles H. Hunt which instructed him to arrest J. P. Black on the charge of forgery. Black is described as a twenty-four year old with light complexion, who worked at some point for the Schwabacher Brothers in Washington. Either the 28th or the 29th(the second number is unclear) of September, J. Lesser petitioned on Black’s behalf for a writ of habeas corpus. Lesser's relationship to Black is unknown. Lesser said there was no valid warrant or authority of law, that Rogers was refusing to let Black talk to a lawyer or any of his family or friends, and that the cause of Black’s arrest was unknown to him. Judge Richard Osborn allowed the petition, and said the case was to be heard in the court of Thomas J. Humes. Rogers stated that on the day the writ was served to him, he received instructions from Hunt to release Black.  Due to Black being released prior to the hearing, the petition outcome is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On May 25, 1916, Dicey Hays, a resident of Sarpy County, Nebraska asked a justice of the peace to swear a warrant against the father of "her bastard son." The accusation and statement made by Dicey Hays is not included in the case file. There are details to the charges other than that she claimed Fred Jolly was the father of her child. The justice of the peace issued a bond for Jolly's appearance in court. Jolly's application claimed that this justice of the peace in Sarpy county issued the bond for Jolly to appear in Douglas County court, outside of his jurisdiction. Jolly was arrested on June 1, 1916 and placed in jail "in default of bail." Jolly's application for a writ claimed that the justice in Sarpy County "wholly neglected his duties" and "having no jurisdiction... made a pretended finding" and was detaining Jolly "wholly illegally and unlawfully." The petition was granted and request was copied to Sheriff McShane, but further details are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Jarvis F. Riley (occasionally spelled Reiley) sought a writ of habeas corpus to challenge his detainment at the King County Jail by Sheriff John H. McGraw. He was detained there on August 9, 1890 by order of Judge Claudius M. Rivers for allegedly committing robbery with Joseph Oakley on August 8 of the same year. Bail was set at $500. On August 18, Riley and his lawyer, T. M. McNamara, filed the writ, citing several reasons that they believed his detainment was illegal. They included that Judge Rivers did not have proper jurisdiction, there was no probable cause for either his supposed guilt or detainment, that he did not stand proper trial, and, vitally, that there was not a proper warrant issued at the time of his detainment. The next day, August 19th, a warrant was issued for his arrest, despite him already being detained. It is important to note that there was, seemingly, a two page response from Sheriff McGraw, but the transferring of these documents to microfilm has rendered the vast majority of it unreadable. The writ of habeas corpus was sent to Judge J.A. Stratton who allowed the petition and summoned Riley to appear in court on the 20th. Riley’s fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 13, 1922 Lila Murry was charged with prostitution and sentenced to be committed to the State Reformatory for Women at York, Nebraska. In her petition Murry stated that she lived in the Salvation Army Rescue Home in Omaha after becoming pregnant around January 5, 1922, and that she gave birth here and remained there until around June 13, when she was taken to the police station where she was charged with prostitution and committed to the Detention Hospital for Women in Omaha. She alleged that at the hearing no one came forth to testify against her, but that she was falsely charged with vagrancy, and that the attending physician at the Detention Hospital declared her cured from all ailments and she was pronounced released. However, she alleged that it was after this that she was ordered to be committed to State Reformatory in York, three weeks after her conviction and only after she filed for a writ of Habeas Corpus. The petition was dismissed for want of prosecution on January 21, 1924. Lila Murry's fate is unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Violet Larcher petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus against Immigration Inspector Thomas M. Fisher. Larcher claimed she was being held in Spokane County Jail to await illegal deportation. She alleged that she was a prostitute who married one of her clients, a naturalized citizen, and though they lived together for only three days, they had never legally divorced. Thus, Larcher claimed she was a citizen. A. F. Richardson appeared in court in the stead of Fisher, and he claimed that Larcher’s initial trial nullified her marriage, stating it was not solemnized. Judge Rudkin ruled that the initial ruling denied Larcher citizenship on a moral basis, which would be in constant uncertainty. Rudkin agreed that Larcher was a citizen, that the writ should be allowed, and Larcher should be released.

Summary of Proceedings: On June 1, 1899, John C. Verbiest was arrested on charges of grand larceny while in town with his daughter, Susie Verbiest. John alleged that he was held in jail without trial for seventeen weeks before being released. On June 7, while John was imprisoned, Sheriff Lind Nelson, while claiming to be the legal guardian of Susie, entrusted her into the case of the Nebraska Children's Home Society of Omaha Nebraska without John’s knowledge or consent. Susie was then adopted from the Home Society by Michael and Alice Finkenbinder on December 13. John Verbiest then filed for a writ of habeas on Susie’s behalf in order to regain custody of her where he claimed he was the legal guardian of Susie, that Sheriff Nelson had no right to give Susie to the Home Society, and that the Finkenbinders are incapable of properly caring for Susie, and physically abuse and beat her. Judge Letton granted the writ and agreed to hear the petition, though the final outcome of the proceedings are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings: Thomas Phillips and Stephen Lyts were both charged with grand larceny after stealing from F. W. Miller.  Lyts had bought “knock-out drops'' and given them to Phillips to place in Miller’s beer.   Phillips then took $380.00 from Miller when he was unconscious.  After being charged, Lyts paid a bond of $250 and was released. Deputy Prosecuting Attorney John R. Hart ordered that Lyts be detained and required to pay another bond in an effort to force him to testify as a witness against Phillips.  Lyts filed a writ of habeas corpus on July 19, 1899.  The writ was heard, but the outcome of the petition and Lyts’ fate are unknown.

Summary of Proceedings:
In 1907, Gwoo Shee Ah Look came to the United States from China via the Steamer "Siberia." Gwoo and her husband on November 1st, 1913, rented a room at the place of arrest. On November 4th, 1913, police raided the residence on suspicion it was a place of prostitution and arrested multiple women, Gwoo being one of them. The two arresting officers testified that they had seen Gwoo in the room since early October and had been investigating the place weeks prior to the raid, and on the day of the arrest found a Chinese man in bed with Gwoo. Wong Sing Lung, Gwoo's husband, filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus alleging that the day after Gwoo's arrest, immigration officials conducted an investigation and examination secretly without the presence of any person and took testimony from the two arresting officers secretly in violation of department rules. The petition further alleged that Immigrant Inspector Barbour refused to let counsel see bound party and failed to notify counsel when further hearings were to be conducted. Gwoo's attorney, A.L. Clark, stated she did not speak English and "did not understand her rights or understand the dangers which she was encountering without having counsel present." Gwoo's attorney was told by Immigration Inspector Barbour that examinations were conducted in secret until a certain point when it was deemed proper to advise Gwoo she was entitled to an attorney. Clark was only given a transcript of the proceedings after the Secretary of Commerce ordered Gwoo to be deported. The petition further alleged that the acting Inspector of Immigration secretly and without authority, removed the petitioner from the Oregon County Jail to Seattle and refused to let her husband know where she was being detained. In May 1914, Judge Jeremiah Neterer ruled that the petitioner was not accorded with a proper hearing in accordance with the Immigration Act of 1907 and was denied the assistance of counsel and therefore entitled to a discharge. In June 1914, the US attorney motioned for the government to permanently withdraw the Bureau of Immigration Transcript from the case file. 
For related case of another woman arrested during the same police raid, see related petition of Yut Yow.

Summary of Proceedings: Daniel Doodey petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus claiming that he was being unlawfully deprived of his liberty by Sheriff Trompen after he was judged insane by a commission the day previous. Judge Tuttle granted the petition. After hearing evidence, Tuttle allowed the writ and ordered that Doodey be released from custody. The next day, Doodey filed for divorce from his wife, Mary Ann Doodey, claiming that she gave false testimony that resulted in him being institutionalized in an insane asylum. The Judge granted the divorce, but sided with Mary Ann and granted her custody of their children.

Summary of Proceedings:
George Francis Rowe filed for a writ of habeas corpus on January 29, 1920. A New York Grand Jury had indicted Rowe on grand larceny in relation to a far-ranging fraud scheme involving mining investments. Accomplices to the scheme operated in Alaska, Oregon, Washington, and New York. 

Rowe’s writ of habeas corpus was denied because he had been released on bond. Rowe returned to custody and his legal representation continued the petition for habeas corpus through a bill of exceptions. The fate of Rowe is unknown.

This case file contains extensive interview transcripts.

Summary of Proceedings: On January 8, 1891, William McDonald filed for a writ of habeas corpus because he claimed that he was being illegally detained by US Marshal L.T. Barin. Marshal Barin claimed that William McDonald was actually William Crook, and that Crook was a fugitive on the run from the United Kingdom. British Consul James Laidlaw filed for an arrest warrant for William Crook because he was wanted in the United Kingdom for the crime of forgery. Eventually, Judge Deady denied the writ of habeas corpus and Crook remained in custody.
